title: I audited draw.io Desktop 32.4.1. No exploitable vulnerability — and that is the interesting part.
description:
I spent a full analysis pass on draw.io Desktop 32.4.1, a 116 MB Electron app, using
static analysis only: JavaScript/AST parsing plus an Electron-specific pass, and Ghidra
for the native module.

The headline result is "no exploitable vulnerability". I'm writing this up anyway,
because the second result is the one I think security-minded developers should care
about: the report ended with 92,468 explicitly registered unknowns and 10 declared
limitations — instead of pretending it covered everything.

Most audit reports I've read hide that part. This one makes it the product.

How the artifact was handled

Nothing runs on an unverified artifact.

  1. Downloaded drawio-amd64-32.4.1.deb from the official release and verified its SHA-256 against the publisher's own Files-SHA256-Hashes.txt. It matched.
  2. Extracted app.asar and analysed the JavaScript as inert text — no execution, no dynamic analysis, no network.
  3. Ran an Electron-specific pass over the main process: BrowserWindow configuration, the IPC surface, and the preload / contextBridge bridge.
  4. Ran a native overview of chrome_crashpad_handler (ELF x86-64) through Ghidra.

Both analysis runs were public GitHub Actions runs, linked below. Every number in this
article can be recomputed by a third party.

What the inventory actually covered

Relevant files inventoried 1,292
Text read (inert) 34 MB
AST nodes visited 3,267,398
Findings emitted 3,246
Parse failures 0
Application graph 4,804 nodes / 7,121 edges
Semantic graph 33,455 nodes / 19,074 relations

Zero parse failures on 34 MB of minified production JavaScript is the part I'd call
impressive. Most of it is a graph, not a grep.

The dependency tree

82 packages with exact versions, 9 of them direct. Nothing alarming, but three
duplicated families showed up: debug (2.6.9 and 4.4.3), ms (2.0.0 and 2.1.3),
semver (7.7.4 and 7.8.5). The debug@2.6.9 line dates from 2017 and arrives
transitively — not a CVE, but a maintenance signal: two lines of the same library are
alive in the same tree.

The CVE cross-check covered 5 candidate packages against public databases (NVD, GitHub
Advisory, GitLab GLAD, Snyk). 0 active. One nuance is worth more than the zero:
builder-util-runtime sits on 9.7.0, which is exactly the first version that fixes
CVE-2026-54673. Zero margin. Any stale lockfile resolution below it makes the
updater chain vulnerable.

The Electron posture

Five BrowserWindow instances.

Four of them are built with literal options, and all four are correctly locked:
contextIsolation: true, nodeIntegration: false, webSecurity: true,
webviewTag: false.

The fifth (electron.js:565) builds its options dynamically. Statically, that is a
black box. I flagged it for manual review instead of guessing what the values were.

Two smaller findings: sandbox is declared explicitly in only 1 of 5 windows (the
others don't declare it, and a static analyser shouldn't assume defaults), and the
preload is referenced through a template literal, so it never resolves as an entrypoint.
Reading the bridge from the other side gave the actual surface: contextBridge exposes
exactly 2 APIs / 6 members (electron.listenOnce, registerMsgListener, request,
sendMessage, process.type, process.versions). No require, no ipcRenderer, no
fs. That's a deliberately small surface, and it's the right shape.

The IPC surface

35 operations, 28 literal channels, 29 handlers in the main process, 0 unpaired
literals, 3 dynamically-computed operations.

Of the 29 handlers, 2 show sender-validation candidates (a != comparison whose
expected value is null, with enforcement unknown). For the other 27, enforcement is
UNKNOWN — and I want to be precise about what that means: I could not observe
validation in static syntax. It does not mean those handlers are unsafe. A
missing observation is not an observation of absence, and a report that conflates the
two is lying by omission.

Secrets: 0 hits across 5 pattern families (Bearer tokens, key formats, credentials in
URLs, api_key/secret/token assignments, JWTs) in the audited scope.

The part most reports skip

This is the section I would point a reviewer at.

10 declared limitations. Some examples, all of them real:

  • The run over the whole bundle was interrupted: the giant minified app.min.js exhausted the 1 GB heap and the 300 s budget. The report says so, names the file, and lists what that means.
  • CSP was not evidenced. It lives in the renderer HTML, outside the scope of these runs. "Not evidenced" is not "absent" — the report says it was out of scope.
  • Only the .deb was audited. AppImage, Windows and macOS builds of the same release can differ.
  • The CVE cross-check was 5 candidates, not the full catalogue.

92,468 unknowns were registered, each with its own ID and re-queryable by that ID.
Uncertainty is counted, indexed and shipped — not dropped.

What this means if you ship an Electron app

The cheapest, most useful question you can ask about your own app is not "am I
vulnerable". It's:

  1. What's actually in the bundle? (SBOM with exact versions, from the shipped artefact, not from a lockfile)
  2. Which of my BrowserWindows can't be verified statically?
  3. Which of my IPC handlers don't expose any sender validation at all?
  4. What did the analysis not reach? — and can you say so precisely?

The last one is the one that distinguishes a report from a checklist.

If you ship an Electron or JS app and you genuinely don't know what your installer
carries, that's a fixed-scope engagement: dependency + risk report, 48 hours, delivered
with the evidence bundle, the graph IDs and the declared limitations — so a third party
can recompute it.

The full report (EN + ES), the report template, the engagement authorisation, the
proforma and the complete evidence bundle are public here:
https://github.com/albrth647-png/electron-security-audit

The two analysis runs are public too:
https://github.com/albrth647-png/Ghidra/actions/runs/38856900076
https://github.com/albrth647-png/Ghidra/actions/runs/38858685634

Reproduce it yourself 

# 1. download and verify the artifact
curl -LO https://github.com/jgraph/drawio-desktop/releases/download/v32.4.1/drawio-amd64-32.4.1.deb
sha256sum drawio-amd64-32.4.1.deb   # → f4455b3b…  (matches the publisher's hash file)

# 2. run the same analysis (static, no execution)
rea analyze-javascript-application <asar-or-src/main> --json

If your team ships an Electron app and wants the same report for it, the sample above
is exactly the deliverable — the offer and terms are in the repo.

Static analysis only. Nothing was executed. §6 of the report lists every limitation,
and the evidence bundle carries the recomputable IDs.

title: The storm is only the beginning: how design shapes system failures
description:
Every morning, the coffee brews, the phone charges and the lights come on. None of it feels like infrastructure. Each one sits at the end of a long chain of power, water, shipping and people, and we only notice the chain when it breaks.

When it does break, we go looking for a cause: a storm, a strike, a bad deploy. That instinct is natural, but stopping at the trigger leaves much of the failure unexplained.

I recently worked through the Foundations of Disruptive Systems module from WorldQuant University, and one idea stayed with me. A trigger starts the disruption. The system's design helps determine how far it spreads and how hard recovery becomes.

Developers already half-know this. A useful postmortem traces how a config change exposed a missing safeguard and how that allowed an outage to spread. This post takes that habit outside software, to power grids, supply chains and coffee farms. The lessons travel straight back to the systems we build.

The shape of it

```plain text
trigger (the storm, the fire, the bad config file)

  • enabling conditions (tight coupling, no buffers, no redundancy)
  • feedback loops (failures that feed further failures)
  • missing safeguards (what could have stopped the cascade) = a cascade, and someone downstream who pays for it ```

A system is a set of connected parts working towards a purpose. A part can fail without much happening. Whether a failure stays local or spreads depends on the design around it: how tightly the parts are connected, whether buffers absorb the shock, and whether another path exists when one route fails.

1. Single points of failure are design outcomes

A single point of failure is a component whose breakdown can stop the whole system. The component isn't necessarily fragile. The system simply has no alternative to it.

In March 2021, the Ever Given ran aground in the Suez Canal and blocked it for six days. The blockage disrupted trade and delayed shipments. The grounding was the trigger. Dependence on one narrow route helped spread the disruption through supply chains.

This is familiar territory for developers. One region, one database primary, one DNS provider, one maintainer of a tiny package that half the internet installs. Each choice made sense when things were normal. Each one turns into the whole system's problem on a bad day.

2. Efficiency and resilience pull against each other

Just-in-time supply chains keep inventory low and schedule deliveries to match demand. The savings are real, but reducing reserve stock can leave less room to absorb a disruption.

Resilience comes from three design mechanisms:

Mechanism Physical world Software
Buffers Reserve stock of medicine or fuel Queues, caches, rate-limit headroom
Redundancy Three suppliers for a critical part Replicas, multi-region, fallback providers
Slack Empty surge beds in a hospital Spare capacity, on-call time that isn't already booked

Each one costs money: storage, duplicate contracts, capacity that sits idle most of the time. That makes the trade-off a decision about who carries the risk. Removing a buffer doesn't remove the risk. It moves it downstream, to customers, communities and workers who have less room to absorb it. COVID-19 made that visible when lean supply chains left hospitals short of protective equipment.

Resilience also tends to be cheaper than recovery. A 2019 study by the US National Institute of Building Sciences estimated that federal hazard-mitigation grants save about $6 for every $1 spent (Natural Hazard Mitigation Saves). The useful question isn't "does resilience cost money?" It does. The question is whether it costs less than the cascade it prevents.

3. Texas, 2021: how the cold became a wider crisis

In February 2021, extreme cold hit Texas, and millions of people lost power for days. The headline was simple: cold weather caused a blackout. The FERC and NERC review tells a more useful story.

Freezing gas wells and equipment cut fuel to power plants, so generation fell. The grid shed load to stay up, and some of those rolling outages cut power to gas facilities. That reduced the gas supply further, so generation fell further. That is a reinforcing feedback loop: each failure made the next one worse.

The cold exposed weaknesses in how the gas and power systems were prepared and connected:

  1. Much of the gas infrastructure wasn't weatherised for extreme cold.
  2. Disruptions to gas production and processing left some power plants short of fuel.
  3. Gas facilities needed electricity, while gas-fired power plants needed a steady fuel supply. That dependence made recovery harder.

These weaknesses gave the disruption several ways to spread. Addressing them could have reduced the scale and duration of the outages. The final report made 28 recommendations, including changes to winterisation standards and coordination between gas and electricity systems.

4. Map the cause as a chain, not a culprit

A headline like "Cold weather caused the Texas blackout" leaves out the conditions that made the blackout so severe. A causal chain map helps identify where people could have reduced the damage. It separates four elements:

Element What it is In Texas
Trigger The proximate shock. Visible, easy to blame, rarely enough on its own. Extreme cold
Enabling conditions The design choices that let the trigger spread. No weatherisation, thin buffers, two-way coupling
Feedback loops How the first failures amplify or dampen. Less gas → less power → less gas
Missing safeguards What could have interrupted the cascade. Winterisation standards, backup fuel, protecting gas sites from load shedding

The software version is easy to find. In July 2024, a faulty CrowdStrike content update crashed Windows machines around the world (root cause analysis). The bad file was the trigger. The enabling conditions were the ones worth reading about: a failure in content validation, an error the sensor could not safely handle, and a content update distributed broadly without an initial canary rollout to a small group.

A useful trick: rewrite any failure headline as a condition. Under what conditions does [trigger] cause [outcome]? Then ask which conditions people could have changed and which safeguards could have limited the damage.

5. Watch the margins before they run out

Lagging indicators tell you something failed: outages, incidents, losses. Leading indicators tell you the margins are shrinking: falling reserve margins, a growing maintenance backlog, near misses that luck absorbed.

Texas had leading indicators for years, including deferred winterisation and earlier cold snaps that came close. Systems near a nonlinear threshold look fine right up to the point where a small push produces an outsized result. The point of watching leading indicators is to notice you're near the edge before you find it.

If you run production systems, you already have useful signals. Rising saturation and queue depth can warn that capacity is running short. Error-budget burn measures how quickly you are using your allowance for unreliability. It records problems already happening and can warn that you are on course to miss a reliability target. Near misses also deserve attention before a safeguard fails.

6. Draw the stakeholder boundary wider

Cascades reach people who never signed the contract. A flood at one supplier's factory directly hits that supplier and its buyer. Indirectly, it reaches consumers who never knew the supplier existed, retailers relying on just-in-time restocking, and workers whose shifts disappear.

A power–interest matrix sorts stakeholders by how much influence they have and how much they have at stake. Two zones matter most:

  • High stakes, low power: workers, nearby residents and small retailers. They feel the consequences and rarely get a say in the design.
  • High stakes, high power: buyers, regulators and platform owners. They are the ones who can add buffers, redundancy and slack.

The first group often only becomes visible in a crisis. During COVID-19, warehouse staff, delivery drivers and carers moved from "background" to "critical" almost overnight. A system that designs out slack also designs out the people who would have absorbed the surge.

A simple way to start: draw one ring for the people directly affected, then a second ring for the people affected by their response. Ask "who depends on this actor?" and "who supplies this actor?" at each step.

7. Test accountability with leverage, foreseeability and capacity

Direct contracts are one way to draw an accountability boundary. They do not settle every question about who bears the consequences. Three questions help test that boundary:

  1. Leverage: can we shape upstream conditions through price, contract terms or volume?
  2. Foreseeability: is the risk documented, or has it happened before somewhere similar?
  3. Capacity: do we have the money, knowledge and access to act?

The course uses coffee as its example. Climate shocks have hit smallholder coffee farmers hard, while the brands buying the beans hold contracts with exporters, not farmers. When all three answers are "yes", "our contracts end at the exporter" isn't a neutral description of the system. It's a design choice about who carries the risk. Price premiums, long-term contracts and investment in drought-resistant varieties aren't charity. They protect the brand's own supply.

The same questions apply to software. If your platform makes a decision that breaks your users' users, ask the three questions before you decide whose problem it is.

Watching a cascade happen

Tables explain the parts. It helps to watch them interact, so here's a small generative sketch called Load Bearing. You can run it in your browser. About 1,100 points link to their nearest neighbours. Each carries one unit of load, and most have only a little spare capacity, while a few have a lot. One point near the centre fails. Each failed point hands its load to its neighbours, slightly amplified, and any neighbour pushed past capacity fails next. This is an illustrative model, not a forecast of a real grid or supply chain. Its results follow the load-sharing rules and capacity limits chosen for the sketch.

Three settings shape the result, and each one maps to an idea from this post:

  • Coupling is how many neighbours each point links to. In this model, those links give a failure paths along which to spread. The effect of adding links depends on the load-sharing rules and available capacity.
  • Slack is the average spare capacity. Less slack means a smaller push tips a point over.
  • Feedback is how much the load grows each time it's passed on. Above 1, the loop reinforces itself.

The defaults sit just below a tipping point, so the outcome is nonlinear in the sense of section 5. On seed 12345, halving the coupling from 4 to 2 links cuts the failures from 508 to 22. Trimming slack from 0.6 to 0.4 takes them to 1,061 of 1,100. The trigger is identical every time. Only the architecture changes.

The sage rings are worth a second look. They mark points that took extra load and held: the buffers that worked, which never make the headline.

In the interactive version, try this:

  1. Watch the baseline play out. A readout counts failures round by round. Pause and Step let you follow the front one round at a time, and you can see it feed itself.
  2. Pick a "What if…" scenario. Each one keeps the same seed and the same shock, and changes one design choice: cut the buffers, add slack, tighten or loosen coupling, or amplify or damp feedback.
  3. Click anywhere on the artwork to move the shock. The same network fails very differently depending on where it's hit, which is the single-point-of-failure question from section 1.
  4. Try other seeds to see how often a system that looks fine is one push from the edge.

On seed 12345, the scenarios go from 16 failures (add slack) to 1,061 (cut the buffers), all from the same trigger.

Using this on your own systems

Next time something breaks, or before it does:

  1. Name the trigger, then trace what let the disruption spread.
  2. List the enabling conditions: coupling, missing buffers, missing redundancy, no slack.
  3. Look for feedback loops where a failure feeds itself, such as retries that pile onto an overloaded service.
  4. Name the missing safeguards and who could add them.
  5. Track leading indicators, not just incidents.
  6. Draw two rings of stakeholders, and check who's in the high-stakes, low-power corner.
  7. Run the three accountability questions before deciding something is "not our problem".

The next time you read "X caused Y", what was designed in a way that made Y possible, and who could have designed it differently?

title: I Built an AI Coding Agent That Researches the Web Before It Writes Code
description:
What if an AI coding agent could research documentation before generating code instead of relying entirely on what an LLM already knows?

That question led me to build a research-first AI coding agent using Context.dev, TypeScript, OpenCode, and OpenRouter on my Mac mini.

Most coding workflows begin with a prompt: describe a feature, ask an AI model to implement it, and then review the output. But for real-world development, having a plausible answer isn't enough. APIs change, libraries introduce breaking changes, and implementation details can vary between versions. Without relevant documentation, an AI-generated solution can look correct while missing important details.

I wanted to experiment with a different approach: research first, plan second, generate code third.

The idea was to build an agent that searches the web for relevant technical sources, retrieves useful documentation, creates a research brief, and passes that context to an LLM before generating an implementation plan and proposed code.

For the research layer, I used Context.dev. OpenCode helped me integrate the workflow into a TypeScript project, while OpenRouter provided access to an LLM through an OpenAI-compatible API.

To test the workflow, I gave the agent a practical task:

Build a TypeScript HTTP client with retry handling and timeouts.

Rather than immediately generating code, the agent researched HTTP client implementations, retry strategies, and timeout handling. It then produced a structured implementation plan and proposed TypeScript source files.

In this article, I'll walk through how I set up the project, integrated Context.dev, connected the LLM, tested the workflow, and handled some of the issues I encountered along the way.

This is an experiment in making AI coding workflows more research-driven—not a claim that generated code is automatically correct. I'll also explain what worked, what still needs validation, and what I would build next.

Step 1: Initialize the Project

I started by setting up a standalone TypeScript project on my Mac mini for building an AI coding agent powered by Context.dev. The goal is to create an agent that researches official documentation before writing code.

mkdir -p ~/projects/context-coding-agent
cd ~/projects/context-coding-agent

npm init -y
npm install context.dev dotenv
npm install -D typescript tsx @types/node

npx tsc --init

The project initialized successfully, and all dependencies were installed without reported vulnerabilities. npm did flag an approval warning for the esbuild install script, which I will resolve before running the application.

I chose TypeScript for the implementation, tsx for running code during development, and dotenv for loading environment variables locally.

Step 2: Configure the Project

After initializing the project, I configured the npm scripts, created the source directory, and added a .gitignore file to keep dependencies, environment secrets, and generated files out of version control.

Run the following commands in the terminal:

npm pkg set type="module"
npm pkg set scripts.dev="tsx src/index.ts"
npm pkg set scripts.check="tsc --noEmit"

mkdir -p src
touch .env .env.example .gitignore

Then add the following entries to .gitignore:

node_modules/
.env
dist/
coverage/

Verified the file using cat .gitignore. The output confirmed that all four entries were present.

Step 3: Get a Context.dev API Key

To let the coding agent access live web data, you need a Context.dev API key.

  • Visit the Context.dev website.
  • Sign up for an account or sign in if you already have one.

  • Open your dashboard and find the API keys section.
  • Create a new API key and copy it securely.

Context.dev offers a free sign-up tier advertised as including 1,000 credits per month, so check your account's current plan and usage limits before running requests.

Next, open the project directory in your terminal and add the API key to your .env file:

nano .env

Add the following line, replacing the placeholder with your actual key:

CONTEXT_DEV_API_KEY=your_actual_api_key_here

Save the file and exit the editor. In Nano, press Ctrl + O, then Enter, and finally Ctrl + X.

Step 4: Integrate Context.dev into the Coding Agent

I used OpenCode, an AI coding agent, to integrate Context.dev into the project. After configuring the API key in .env, I opened OpenCode in my project directory and pasted the setup prompt generated by Context.dev.

The prompt instructed OpenCode to inspect the codebase, configure the SDK, implement the web research workflow, and verify the integration with one real API request.

The implementation includes a centralized wrapper in src/context/client.ts for API requests, authentication, retries, and credit tracking. The research module in src/research/researcher.ts searches the web, ranks relevant URLs, retrieves page content, and prepares a research brief before the agent begins planning.

OpenCode also created automated tests and a dry-run mode to validate the workflow without consuming API credits.

Step 5: Test the Integration

Before testing the agent with a live API request, I ran the type checker, automated tests, and dry-run workflow to validate the implementation.

Run the following commands from the project directory:

npm run check
npm test
npm run dry-run

The type check completed without errors, and all 34 automated tests passed.

The dry run exercised the research and planning pipeline using fixture data, without making live Context.dev requests. It demonstrated how the agent derives search queries from a coding task, ranks relevant URLs, collects page content, and generates a research-backed implementation plan.

The sample task was to build a TypeScript HTTP client with retry handling and timeouts. The resulting plan included documentation references, implementation steps, failure-handling considerations, and code examples.

Because this run used fixture data, the displayed sources and credit figures are simulated rather than results from a live API request. This makes the dry run useful for testing the workflow without spending API credits.

With the local checks passing, the next step is to verify the research workflow against the live Context.dev API.

Step 6: Run the Agent on a Real Coding Task

With the CLI argument issue fixed, I ran the agent on a practical coding task:

npm run dev -- "Build a TypeScript HTTP client with retry handling and timeouts"

The agent started by researching the web instead of immediately generating code. Context.dev returned eight relevant sources, including the Ky HTTP client repository and documentation covering retries and timeouts.

The research module ranked the results, retrieved two pages in full, and passed the gathered information into the planning stage. The agent then produced a five-step implementation plan covering documentation review, API design, core logic, error handling, and tests.

This run used eight Context.dev credits, leaving 966 credits available. Because no LLM API key was configured, the planner ran in offline mode and returned a research-backed plan with reference implementations rather than creating finished source files.

This confirmed that the main research-and-planning workflow was running end to end. The next step is to connect an LLM so the agent can use its research to plan and generate code, then verify that code with tests.

Step 7: Connect an LLM and Generate Code from Research

The research workflow was working, but the planner was still running in offline mode. To take the project further, I connected an LLM through OpenRouter so the agent could use its research findings to generate a structured implementation plan and source code.

I configured the OpenAI-compatible API settings in my local .env file:

OPENAI_API_KEY=your_openrouter_api_key
OPENAI_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1
OPENAI_MODEL=minimax/minimax-m3.1-flash:free

I kept the API key in .env rather than hardcoding it into the source code. The project already supported OpenAI-compatible chat completions, so I could connect OpenRouter without introducing another SDK.

Next, I tested the API connection directly. After resolving an empty-response issue caused by the model's reasoning and output limits, I adjusted the request to use low reasoning effort and a deterministic temperature.

I then ran the project checks:

npm run check
npm test

The TypeScript check passed, and all 45 automated tests passed.

With the LLM connection working, I ran the same coding task again:

npm run dev -- --mode llm "Build a TypeScript HTTP client with retry handling and timeouts"

This time, the agent completed the research phase and passed the collected documentation into the LLM planner. Context.dev returned 10 sources, and the agent read two pages in full. The research included the Ky HTTP client repository, documentation on retries and timeouts, and guidance on handling transient HTTP failures.

The LLM generated a four-step implementation plan covering:

  • Defining the HTTP client and request types.
  • Implementing timeout and cancellation handling.
  • Adding retries with exponential backoff.
  • Exporting the client and its types.

It also produced proposed source files: src/http-client.ts and src/index.ts. The generated HTTP client included configurable timeouts, retry limits, exponential backoff, and support for caller-provided cancellation signals.

The final output confirmed that the planner was running in LLM mode rather than falling back to the offline planner.

This was an important milestone: the agent could now research relevant documentation first, use that research to generate an implementation plan, and produce code artifacts for review.

The generated code still needs its own validation before being integrated into a real project. In particular, retry behavior, non-JSON responses, timeout handling, cancellation, and compatibility with the existing project structure should be tested.

With both research and LLM-based planning connected, the next step is to validate the generated code and improve the agent's ability to test its own implementations.

Conclusion

Building this research-first AI coding agent gave me a practical way to explore how web research and LLM-based code generation can work together.

The key idea is simple: instead of asking an LLM to generate code immediately, I built a workflow that researches relevant documentation first, retrieves useful source material, and passes a research brief to the planner before generating an implementation plan and proposed code.

Using Context.dev, TypeScript, OpenCode, and OpenRouter, I was able to take the project from initial setup to a working research-and-planning workflow with LLM-based code generation.

The experiment also exposed some of the challenges involved in building coding agents. Model responses need to be handled carefully, generated code needs independent validation, and a successful plan does not automatically mean the implementation is correct.

At this stage, the agent can research technical topics, generate a structured implementation plan, and produce code artifacts for review. I have not yet integrated the generated HTTP client into the project or verified it with dedicated implementation tests.

What's Next?

There are several improvements I would explore next:

  • Controlled file writing: Let the agent write approved code into a dedicated workspace without overwriting existing project files.
  • Automated validation: Run TypeScript checks and tests against generated code.
  • Iterative debugging: Feed test failures back to the LLM so it can propose fixes.
  • Better source selection: Prioritize official documentation and version-specific references.
  • Safer execution: Run generated code and tests in an isolated environment.

The long-term goal is to move beyond an agent that researches and proposes code toward one that can implement a task, validate its work, and explain the decisions behind its changes.

For now, this project is a useful starting point for experimenting with research-backed coding workflows—and a reminder that generated code still needs engineering judgment.

If you're building AI coding agents, I'd be interested to hear how you're handling documentation retrieval, code validation, and the gap between generating a plausible solution and verifying that it actually works.

Thank you so much for reading
