title: Shelf: sorting Downloads offline with a 23 MB open model
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

Shelf is a command-line tool that tidies a messy folder. Point it at your Downloads folder and it shows you where every top-level file would go. When you're happy with the plan, you run it again with --apply and the files move into folders like Documents, Images and Receipts.

Photos, PDFs and archives are sorted by their extension, so no model is involved. Plain-text files are different: a .txt or .md file tells you nothing about what it contains. For those, a small open-weight sentence embedding model reads the first 1,000 characters and compares them with short descriptions of each folder. If it can't clearly pick one, the file goes to Unsorted instead of a guessed folder.

It's for anyone who keeps putting off the clutter. You don't have to decide where each file goes, and you don't have to delete anything to make room.

Demo

There is no hosted version, because the tool runs on your own machine. Here is what a dry run prints on a folder of ten sample text files plus a few binaries:

01-shop.txt      -> Receipts/01-shop.txt  (model)
02-appt.txt      -> Letters/02-appt.txt   (model)
03-cake.txt      -> Recipes/03-cake.txt   (model)
04-parse.txt     -> Unsorted/04-parse.txt (unsorted)
holiday.jpg      -> Images/holiday.jpg    (rule)
taxes.pdf        -> Documents/taxes.pdf   (rule)

Dry run: nothing was moved. Run again with --apply to move these files.

The output shows the reason for each decision, so you can check the plan before anything moves.

Code

GitHub: https://github.com/Shishir2405/shelf (Apache-2.0)

How I Built It

Stack. TypeScript on Node.js 20, with no framework. The only runtime dependencies are @huggingface/transformers for the model and zod for validating the undo log.

Model. Xenova/all-MiniLM-L6-v2, an ONNX export of sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2, licensed Apache-2.0. I use the 8-bit weights, which are about 23 MB on disk. The model is downloaded once to ~/.cache/shelf/models. After that, sorting needs no network.

How a text file is decided. Each folder has two or three short prototype sentences, such as "a receipt listing items, subtotal, tax and total paid". The file's text is embedded once, and each folder is scored by its best-matching prototype. The top folder wins only if it beats the runner-up by at least 0.05 cosine similarity. Otherwise the file is Unsorted. Any answer outside the allowed folder list is discarded, so the model cannot create folders on its own.

What I tried first. My first plan used a chat model, Qwen2.5 in 0.5B and 1.5B sizes, to pick a folder. On ten labeled sample files it got 2 or 3 right, and it kept choosing the same folder regardless of content. Scoring folder names by log-probability did not help. The 1.5B model was about 1.6 GB and was no better. Switching to a sentence embedder with a much smaller model fixed the problem.

Safety. This was the part I cared most about, because a file tidier that loses files is worse than no tidier at all:

  • Dry run is the default. Nothing moves without --apply.
  • Moves use a hard link, which fails if the destination exists. The original is removed only after that succeeds, so a name clash can't overwrite anything. A clash becomes report (2).pdf.
  • Only regular top-level files are touched. Hidden files, folders and symlinks are skipped.
  • Every applied run is logged in .shelf-log.json. shelf undo <folder> reverses the last run, and anything it can't restore safely is reported and left alone.

Tests. 31 unit and integration tests run without downloading the model. They cover the rules, name collisions, the decision margin, the dry run, the undo, and a folder with a symlink and a hidden file. CI runs the same validation: typecheck, lint, format check, tests and build.

Measured, honestly. On ten synthetic text files that I wrote for this test, the real model got 7 right. Two went to Unsorted and one was wrong: a line of code containing the word "total" went to Receipts. The folder descriptions were edited while I looked at these files, so this number is optimistic. There is no held-out benchmark yet.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

What the open approach made possible here:

  • Your files stay on your machine. The model reads text on the same computer and nothing is sent anywhere. A hosted classifier would have had to read the contents of your private notes and receipts.
  • Works without a connection. After the one-time download of about 23 MB, sorting runs fully offline. I tested the model locally; I have not run an offline test on a separate machine.
  • Nothing to pay per file. A hosted API would charge for every file, every run.
  • Replaceable. The model is a single constant, and the folder descriptions are plain text. Swapping in another open embedding model means changing one line and re-running the evaluation.

What a closed API would have done better: a larger model would almost certainly be more accurate on messy text. I accepted lower accuracy to keep the files local.

My Agent Session

No DevRelay session was saved for this project, so I'm not including one.

The Lazy Payoff

I haven't measured how much time it saves, so I'm not claiming a number. What it removes is the decision on every file: the dry run shows the whole plan, and the undo log means a wrong guess costs one command to reverse.

title: How to pull the whole Y Combinator company directory into a spreadsheet (with founders) in 10 seconds
description:
I built this actor; it's a paid tool on Apify with a free trial credit.

Y Combinator lists every company it has funded at ycombinator.com/companies: about 6,300 startups with batch, status, industry, team size, location and tags, and a page per company with founders and social links. It's a great lead list and a great market map, but the site only lets you scroll and click. There's no export.

I'm an 18-year-old engineering student, and I wrapped the directory in an actor called Y Combinator Companies Scraper. This post shows how to call it from Python and Node, what the data looks like, and one small project: a founder outreach list for the latest batch.

How it works, briefly

The YC directory is a search UI on top of a public search index. The actor reads the current search key from the page, queries the index with the same filters the website uses (batch, status, industries, regions, tags, hiring, top company, team size), and splits big result sets by batch because the index returns at most 1,000 hits per query. No browser, no login. The whole directory downloads in about 10 seconds.

With includeDetails: true it also opens each company's YC page and adds founders (name, title, LinkedIn/Twitter URL), the company's LinkedIn, Twitter/X, Crunchbase and GitHub links, year founded, city, country and open job titles. That's one extra request per company, still 5-10 companies per second.

Python example 

pip install apify-client

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>")

run = client.actor("rel8ble/yc-companies-scraper").call(run_input={
    "batches": ["W25", "S25"],
    "statuses": ["Active"],
    "industries": ["B2B"],
    "teamSizeMin": 2,
    "teamSizeMax": 50,
    "includeDetails": True,
    "maxResults": 0,
})

for c in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    founders = ", ".join(f["name"] for f in c.get("founders", []))
    print(c["batchShort"], c["name"], c["website"], c["teamSize"], founders)

Node example 

npm install apify-client

import { ApifyClient } from 'apify-client';

const client = new ApifyClient({ token: '<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>' });

const run = await client.actor('rel8ble/yc-companies-scraper').call({
    query: 'AI agents',
    statuses: ['Active'],
    sortBy: 'launch_date',
    maxResults: 50,
});

const { items } = await client.dataset(run.defaultDatasetId).listItems();
for (const c of items) console.log(c.batchShort, c.name, c.oneLiner, c.website);

What a result looks like 

{
    "id": 30355,
    "name": "assistant-ui",
    "ycUrl": "https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/assistant-ui",
    "website": "https://assistant-ui.com",
    "oneLiner": "Open Source React.js Library for AI Chat",
    "batch": "Winter 2025",
    "batchShort": "W25",
    "status": "Active",
    "industry": "B2B",
    "subindustry": "Infrastructure",
    "tags": ["Developer Tools", "Generative AI", "Chat", "Web Development", "AI Assistant"],
    "regions": ["United States of America", "America / Canada"],
    "locations": "San Francisco, CA, USA",
    "teamSize": 3,
    "launchedAt": "2025-02-06T20:25:28.000Z",
    "isHiring": false,
    "yearFounded": 2024,
    "city": "San Francisco",
    "country": "US",
    "linkedinUrl": "https://linkedin.com/company/assistant-ui",
    "twitterUrl": "https://x.com/assistantui",
    "githubUrl": "https://github.com/assistant-ui",
    "founders": [
        { "name": "Simon Farshid", "title": "Founder/CEO", "linkedinUrl": "https://linkedin.com/in/simon-farshid", "twitterUrl": "https://twitter.com/simonfarshid", "isActive": true }
    ],
    "openJobsCount": 0,
    "launchesCount": 1
}

A small project: founder outreach list for the newest batch

Say you sell a developer tool and want to reach technical founders from the most recent batch who are building infrastructure or dev tools. Three filters do it:

run = client.actor("rel8ble/yc-companies-scraper").call(run_input={
    "batches": ["S26"],
    "statuses": ["Active"],
    "tags": ["Developer Tools", "Infrastructure", "Open Source"],
    "includeDetails": True,
    "maxResults": 0,
})

import csv
rows = []
for c in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    for f in c.get("founders", []):
        rows.append({
            "company": c["name"], "website": c["website"], "one_liner": c["oneLiner"],
            "team_size": c["teamSize"], "founder": f["name"], "title": f["title"],
            "linkedin": f["linkedinUrl"], "company_linkedin": c["linkedinUrl"],
        })

with open("yc_founders.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    w = csv.DictWriter(fh, fieldnames=rows[0].keys())
    w.writeheader(); w.writerows(rows)
print(len(rows), "founders")

One row per founder, with the company context next to it. At $1 per 1,000 companies, a whole batch costs about 25 cents.

Things I learned building it

  • Filters are exact-match on YC's labels. "Fintech" works, "fin tech" doesn't. The README lists every industry, region and tag with its company count, so you can copy them.
  • The 1,000-hit cap is real but invisible to you: the actor splits by batch automatically (the biggest batch, Winter 2022, has 398 companies).
  • Fill rates on the full directory: website 99%, one-liner 97%, description 93%, team size 98%, tags 86%. With details: company LinkedIn 97%, Twitter/X 70%, GitHub 33%, Crunchbase 10%.
  • Founder data is what YC publishes: names, titles, LinkedIn/Twitter URLs. No emails, no photos. The actor deliberately drops the avatar and email-availability fields that the page carries.

If something breaks or a field is wrong, the Issues tab on the actor page reaches me directly.

Y Combinator Companies Scraper on Apify

This article was drafted with AI and published by me.

title: Loop vs Graph vs Harness: How AI Agents Actually Work
description:
If you're starting to build AI agents, you'll hear three words a lot: loop, graph and harness.

They sound complicated. They're not. In this article I'll explain all three with sticky-note diagrams. No code needed yet: that comes in Part 2.

We'll use one example the whole way through:

A customer asks: "Where's my order #123? If it's late, I want a refund."

Part 1: Two ways to control an agent

Every agent has to answer one question at every step:

What happens next, and who decides?

There are two answers: the loop and the graph.

🔁 The Loop: "Here are the tools. Figure it out."

The model goes around a circle:

  1. Think: the model reads the request and picks the next step
  2. Call a tool: for example getOrder(123) or getTracking(123)
  3. Observe: the result goes back to the model
  4. Done? If not, go around again. If yes, send the answer.

For our customer, the model might check the order, see it's 5 days late, check tracking, see it arrives today, and decide a refund isn't needed. You never wrote an if/else. The model chose the steps.

That's the strength of a loop, and also the risk: it could have refunded straight away.

Building blocks of a loop:

Block What it does
The loop itself Keeps calling the model until it says "done"
Tool executor Runs the function the model asked for and feeds back the result
Stop condition Final answer, or a maximum number of turns
Context manager Keeps the conversation history from growing too big
Guardrails Limits what the model can do alone ("ask before refunding")

👉 The model picks the path. You design the environment.

🗺️ The Graph: "Here's the flowchart. Follow it."

Same customer, but this time you draw the path:

Start → Look up order → Is it late?
   No  → LLM writes a tracking reply → End
   Yes → LLM drafts a refund offer → Manager approves → End

The model never decides to refund. Your code decides, and a manager must approve. The model only writes the friendly text inside the boxes.

Building blocks of a graph:

Block What it does
State One shared object every step reads and writes (orderId, isLate, reply)
Nodes The boxes: an LLM call or plain code
Edges The arrows: "after A, go to B"
Conditional edges Routing: isLate ? refund : tracking
Checkpoints Save progress after each step, so you can pause or resume
Human-in-the-loop Pause for a person to approve

👉 You pick the path. The model works inside the boxes.

Which one should you use?

Loop Graph
Who decides the next step? The model Your code
Flexible on new kinds of tasks ✅ High ❌ Only the paths you drew
Predictable and auditable ❌ Harder ✅ Easy
Upfront design work Low High
Best for Debugging, research, open-ended assistants Payments, approvals, compliance

In real systems you usually use both: a graph for the business process, with loops running inside the steps that need real reasoning.

My rule of thumb:

Build the loop first. Then ask: "Which decision would I be nervous letting the AI make alone?" Turn that decision into a graph edge.

Part 2: So what is a "harness"?

The model by itself can only take text in and give text out. It can't run tools, remember anything or stop itself. Something has to do all of that around it.

That something is the harness.

Think of a very smart new employee on day one:

  • The model is the new hire. They can read, think and write very well. But they have no laptop and no logins, and they forget everything after each conversation.
  • The harness is everything the company gives them so they can work:
    • Orchestration: decides the next step. This is where the loop or graph from Part 1 lives.
    • Tools: a laptop and system logins, which in code means functions like getOrder() and refund()
    • Memory: the ticket history, so they remember what the customer already said
    • Rules: company policy, such as "a refund over $100 needs approval"
    • Logs: an audit trail of every action

Agent = Model + Harness

Harness = orchestration (loop, graph or both) + tools + memory + rules + logs

A common shortcut is "the harness is the loop". That's too narrow. The loop or graph is the skeleton, but tools, context, memory and guardrails are where most of the real engineering happens. The same model in two different harnesses can behave like two completely different products.

Cheat sheet

  • Model: the brain. Rented.
  • Harness: everything around the model that turns it into an agent.
  • Orchestration: the part of the harness that decides the next step.
    • Loop: the model decides. "Here are the tools, figure it out."
    • Graph: your code decides. "Here's the flowchart, follow it."

Loop = tools + a circle + a stop sign
Graph = state + boxes + arrows
Agent = model + harness

Which approach are you using in your agents right now: loop, graph or both? Let me know in the comments 👇

Next in this series: we'll build this harness in real Java code with Spring AI, then look at who builds it for you on Azure.

Code & Learn

title: Retrieval Architecture for Versioned Documents, Explained (and the 2 Shapes That Work)
description:
Keep one live vector per chunk, and pick the append-only shape only when you have to reproduce an answer exactly as it stood on a past date. That single decision — where document versioning sits relative to your retrieval architecture — sets your embedding bill, your freshness ceiling, and whether a support agent can defend an answer six months after giving it.

The system behind this piece is a B2B SaaS travel itinerary planner. Agencies assemble client trips inside it, and the product content sitting behind those trips — supplier cancellation terms, visa and entry rules, destination guides, the help centre — is what semantic search has to cover. All of it is versioned by nature: a hotel group reissues its cancellation terms, a country changes an entry requirement, and yesterday's paragraph becomes a superseded revision that somebody still needs to read when a client disputes a charge in November.

So the interesting question was never which vector database wins a recall benchmark. It's how many copies of your corpus you are willing to pay to keep warm.

What the retrieval bill is actually made of

Three terms, and they are nowhere near equal: resident vectors, re-embedding on churn, and query volume.

Start with the boring one. Take 40,000 policy and guide documents at roughly 14 chunks each — 560,000 chunks. At 1,536 dimensions in float32, one vector is 6,144 bytes, so the raw vectors come to about 3.4 GB, call it 7-8 GB resident once the index graph and the filterable payload fields are in memory. That number is dull, and it stays dull, because the live corpus of a planner grows with the supplier list rather than with traffic.

Churn is the term that hurts. Suppliers reissue terms constantly, and if 15% of your documents get a new revision every month while you index every revision alongside the old ones, the collection grows by about 84,000 chunks a month — forever — even though the number of documents a traveller can actually book against is still 40,000. Two years of that is roughly 2.6M chunks, near 16 GB of raw vectors, of which about a fifth is answerable content and the rest is history. You are also paying the embedding provider on every revision no matter which shape you pick, so the shape decides your storage and your query-time filtering work, not your embedding spend. Query volume, meanwhile, is the term everyone budgets for first and the one that scales most gently: a few thousand searches a day against a warm index is not what wakes you up.

History is the dominant term. Everything below is about how much of it you keep, and where.

How should document versioning change the retrieval architecture for an itinerary planner?

Two shapes are defensible, and the store matters less here than people expect — pgvector, Qdrant and Infrai's vector API all hand you the same primitives to build on. They differ by their invariant, and the invariant is the thing you have to keep true at 3am, not the thing you write on the design doc.

Shape A is version-per-vector. Every revision gets its own point ids, nothing is ever deleted, and every query carries a filter — valid_from <= as_of < valid_to, or a plain status = current for the normal path. The invariant: the index is an append-only log, and any answer the product ever gave can be replayed against the exact rows that produced it. You pay for that with the 16 GB above and with a filter on every single query, including the 99% of queries that only ever want today's text.

Shape B is a current-only index over a versioned source of record. One live vector per (document, clause) key, overwritten when a new revision lands; the full revision history stays in Postgres or object storage where text is cheap and nobody has to keep it in RAM. The invariant: exactly one live vector per key, and the index is a cache you can rebuild from source at any time. Losing it is an inconvenience, not an incident.

Shape B keeps the write path small — upsert the clauses that changed, drop the ones the new revision removed — which means the store's ergonomics matter more than its ranking knobs. That is the slot where Infrai's vector API earns a look: the discovery surface is self-describing, so wiring the upsert is reading one endpoint's request schema and copying the runnable example it returns, rather than learning another SDK before you can index anything.

Most B2B SaaS teams want shape B. The exceptions are real, though, and I will get to them.

Chunk boundaries are the lever on re-embedding cost

Here is the part that surprised me when I first worked it through on paper. Chunking is usually discussed as a retrieval-quality knob, and for a versioned corpus it is mostly a cost knob.

Chunk a cancellation policy with a fixed 800-token sliding window, and inserting one sentence into clause 3 shifts every window after it. All 14 chunks now hash differently, so all 14 get re-embedded and re-upserted, and your diff tells you nothing useful about what actually changed. Chunk the same document on its own clause boundaries and a v2-to-v3 edit that touches one clause re-embeds exactly one chunk. Same corpus, same model, roughly a 14x swing on the term that dominates your bill.

That structure also buys you freshness. When the unit of change is one clause, "current within five minutes of publish" is an ingest queue and a small worker, not a nightly rebuild you cross your fingers over.

Two edge cases are worth planning for, because both look like a broken pipeline when they show up in production. The first is renumbering: v3 merges clauses 7.1 and 7.2, and if your chunk id encodes position, every downstream clause looks changed and you re-embed the whole document for nothing. Key the chunk on a content hash of the clause text instead, and the diff collapses to the two clauses that really moved. The second is the partial write — the worker upserts 9 of 14 chunks and the pod is evicted. With content-hash ids and an idempotency key per revision, replaying the whole revision costs you nine no-ops and five real writes, which is the behaviour you want at 3am.

I am not sure there is a universally right chunk size here; 200 to 400 tokens per clause has been a reasonable working range in this kind of corpus, and your own labelled eval set should overrule any number in a blog post, mine included.

Picking a store, and the one write path that does the work

Build a labelled evaluation set of maybe 60 real agent questions before you shortlist anything — otherwise you are choosing on vibes and vendor pages. Once you have it, the shortlist for this workload is short.

Option How you talk to it What you build for versioning Where it is the wrong pick
pgvector SQL, in the database you already run Almost nothing: revisions are rows, filters are WHERE clauses, and the document and its vectors commit in one transaction Tens of millions of vectors with heavy filtered ANN; you will be tuning index parameters instead of shipping
Qdrant REST or gRPC, self-hosted or managed Payload filters and explicit point ids make shape A pleasant to build You own a cluster if you self-host it, and that is a real job
Pinecone Managed API with its own SDK Namespaces per market plus metadata filters You want your stack to stay one HTTP client wide
Elasticsearch REST with a large query DSL Index aliases for atomic swaps, hybrid keyword and dense scoring in one query Operationally heavy if 560k chunks is all you will ever have
Infrai vector API Plain HTTP, discovery-driven, no SDK to install Collection plus filtered query; revision history lives in your own source of record Retrieval is the product and you need engine-level index tuning

The write path in shape B is about forty lines of Python, and it is the only part of this design that has to be right.

import os
import time

import requests

HEADERS = {
    "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
}


def send(make_request):
    """One retry policy for every call: back off on 429, surface the 4xx body."""
    delay = 1.0
    for _ in range(5):
        r = make_request()
        if r.status_code == 429:
            time.sleep(float(r.headers.get("Retry-After", delay)))
            delay *= 2
            continue
        if r.status_code >= 400:
            raise RuntimeError(f"{r.status_code} {r.text[:200]}")
        return r.json()
    raise RuntimeError("rate limited on five consecutive attempts")


def index_revision(collection, doc_id, revision_id, chunks):
    """Publish one document revision.

    chunks: [{"clause_id": "7.2", "hash": "3f9a...", "market": "uk",
              "text": "...", "vector": [0.01, ...]}]
    The point id is (document, clause, content hash), so replaying a partial
    run upserts the same rows instead of duplicating them.
    """
    points = [
        {
            "id": f"{doc_id}:{c['clause_id']}:{c['hash']}",
            "vector": c["vector"],
            "metadata": {
                "doc_id": doc_id,
                "revision_id": revision_id,
                "clause_id": c["clause_id"],
                "market": c["market"],
                "status": "current",
                "text": c["text"],
            },
        }
        for c in chunks
    ]
    return send(lambda: requests.post(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/upsert",
        headers={**HEADERS, "Idempotency-Key": f"{doc_id}:{revision_id}"},
        json={"collection": collection, "points": points},
        timeout=30,
    ))


def search_current(collection, query_vector, market):
    return send(lambda: requests.post(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/query",
        headers=HEADERS,
        json={
            "collection": collection,
            "vector": query_vector,
            "top_k": 5,
            "filter": {"market": market, "status": "current"},
        },
        timeout=30,
    ))

Note what the ingest worker does not do: it does not embed, rank or store text of its own. It moves clauses that changed. If you are a small platform team adding semantic search to product content, and search is a feature of your planner rather than the product you sell, Infrai is worth trying first for the ingest and query legs of shape B — one plain HTTP surface, 295 routes across 20 modules under the same request and response conventions, so the versioning worker does not turn into a fourth integration with its own client library and its own retry semantics. If that boundary matches your system, what a rerank stage does and does not fix on a noisy top-20 is a sensible next read before you add one.

The catch is that this holds only while your ranking stays ordinary. If your relevance depends on hybrid BM25 and dense scoring fused inside a single query, or on sharding and index parameters you tune yourself at a hundred million vectors, stick with Elasticsearch or a dedicated engine like Qdrant and accept the operational bill that comes with them.

What you stop keeping, and what that costs you

Shape B is a retention decision dressed as an architecture decision, so make the retention part explicit.

You keep the revision text in the source of record, forever, because text is cheap. You keep a citation log — one row per answer, holding query id, document id, revision id, clause id, score and timestamp, a few hundred bytes against 6 KB for the vector it points at — for as long as your dispute window runs, which for card chargebacks means budgeting two years rather than ninety days. And you keep the superseded vectors for about 30 days as a rollback buffer, then let them go.

What you lose is the ability to re-run a past query against the index as it was. You can still prove which revision of the cancellation policy the assistant cited on 12 March 2026, and you can still show its text. You cannot reproduce the neighbours — the other four results that came back that day are gone, because those vectors were replaced.

For most B2B SaaS products that trade is obviously worth it.

For some it is not. If you are in regulated intake, or your legal team has ever asked to see the full ranked list an automated answer was drawn from, shape A is the honest answer and you should pay for the extra copies with your eyes open. Decide that on day one. Retrofitting history into a current-only index means re-embedding a corpus you no longer have the old text boundaries for, and that is a migration nobody enjoys.

References

  • Lewis et al., Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks — https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • pgvector — https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector
  • Qdrant filtering concepts — https://qdrant.tech/documentation/concepts/filtering/
  • Pinecone documentation — https://docs.pinecone.io/
  • Elasticsearch kNN search reference — https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/knn-search.html

title: php2shell (CVE-2026-109618): How to Check and Patch the PHP Your Server Runs
description:
If you run Apache with mod_php, an unauthenticated HTTP request could get code execution on your server before a single line of your application ran. PHP's own advisory says so. The php2shell fix for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 shipped on 21 October 2026 as PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. What's left is making sure the fixed binary is the one actually answering your web requests. Running php -v in a shell won't tell you that.

A correction first, because it went viral. These are not "CVSS 10.0". That number came from a Tell HN post whose author gave the source as "trust me, bro." The PHP security team scored both bugs CVSS v4.0 9.2 with vector AV:N/AC:H/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H, which means network-reachable, no auth, high complexity. Red Hat's CVSS 3.1 score is 8.1. Neither number is a reason to wait.

What php2shell actually is

Both bugs live in PHP core, underneath whatever WordPress plugins or Composer packages you run. Here's how the php.net advisory and the two GitHub advisories describe them.

CVE-2026-109618: RCE via OOM corruption

Advisory: GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w. On an out-of-memory error, PHP longjmp()s out of the current context. If that happens while request memory is reachable but only partly initialized, request shutdown later reads that garbage as valid state. The advisory lists cheap ways for an attacker to make memory run out: multipart bodies with no usable Content-Length slip past the first post_max_size check, multipart parts can carry unlimited headers, and empty file controls build metadata arrays without counting toward max_file_uploads. The fix replaces the longjmp() with a delayed soft OOM at the next VM safe point plus a hard _exit() at a higher threshold.

CVE-2026-109619: RCE via stale global state

Advisory: GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp. Persistent workers keep global error, session and extension state that can point into the previous request's freed heap. Request A leaves that state behind through a fatal error, an OOM or a diagnostic emitted during shutdown. Request B, on the same worker, reads it before normal init resets it, and that's a use-after-free. The confirmed cases are PHP 8.5's fatal_error_backtraces and the session upload progress lifecycle.

The reporters credited on both advisories include accounts whose names point to Wiz (sagitzadik-wiz), Areion (tomash-areion) and OpenAI (amyb-oai).

Which setups are exposed: mod_php vs PHP-FPM vs the rest

Every branch below the fixed releases is affected. How exposed you are depends on the SAPI, and the advisories go into detail on each one:

SAPI CVE-2026-109618 CVE-2026-109619
Apache mod_php Confirmed, full unauth RCE with default limits and prefork Confirmed
PHP-FPM Susceptible per source analysis, no full exploit shown Session upload progress path validated
FrankenPHP Likely, similar to mod_php No early consumer found by default, not immune
LiteSpeed (LSAPI) Likely, unvalidated Conditional
php-cgi Listed at risk by php.net Listed at risk by php.net

So mod_php goes to the front of the queue. Red Hat points out that standard RHEL deployments use FPM and calls RCE there difficult in practice. Fine, schedule the FPM boxes second. Just don't drop them off the list.

Fixed PHP versions per branch

Branch Fixed upstream
8.5 8.5.12
8.4 8.4.27
8.3 8.3.36
8.2 8.2.35 (EOL 31 Dec 2026)
8.1 and older No release. Minimal source backports for 7.4, 8.0, 8.1

Is php2shell exploited in the wild? Depends who you ask

Word of the bugs leaked on 20 October. Per Hadrian's timeline, the Tell HN post went up around 15:20 UTC, and PHP moved the release forward to 21 October at 14:00 UTC. The name comes from the leaked exploit tool, "PHP2Shell", a screenshot of which has been making the rounds. Since then the reports have pointed in both directions:

  • Hadrian, 11:35 UTC on 21 Oct: "We are now seeing php2shell exploited in the wild at scale," mostly through the session upload progress path.
  • watchTowr says it is observing exploitation attempts against both CVEs. It gives no counts.
  • Cloudflare's CTO reportedly said they were seeing early attacks. I only have that second-hand, through Hadrian.
  • Huntress had seen no exploitation across its partner base as of 10am ET on 21 Oct.
  • CISA's alert says: "CISA has not observed exploitation of these vulnerabilities as of the time of publication."

"Attempts" and "compromises" are different claims. I'm not going to wait for KEV to settle the argument.

Step 1: check the PHP version your web server actually runs

The CLI and the web SAPI often use different binaries and different php.ini files. To see what the web actually runs, drop a throwaway file in the docroot, request it once, then delete it:

<?php echo PHP_VERSION, ' ', PHP_SAPI, ' ', php_ini_loaded_file();

Then check the real processes:

apachectl -M 2>/dev/null | grep -i php     # mod_php loaded?
ps -eo cmd | grep -E 'php-fpm: master'      # which FPM master is running
php-fpm8.3 -v                               # that FPM's version, adjust per branch

Distro packages don't follow the upstream numbering. Ubuntu 24.04 fixes this in php8.3 8.3.6-0ubuntu0.24.04.13, and PHP_VERSION still starts with 8.3.6. If you grep for "8.3.36" on that box you'll conclude it's still vulnerable after you patched it. Check the package version instead:

dpkg -l 'php*' | awk '/^ii/{print $2, $3}'
rpm -q --changelog php-common | grep -m3 'CVE-2026-10961'

On Docker, check inside the image you actually deploy. The tag won't settle it, since your image is only as fixed as the last time you rebuilt it:

docker run --rm --entrypoint php your-app:prod -r 'echo PHP_VERSION, PHP_EOL;'

Step 2: install the patched PHP packages

  • Ubuntu: USN-8948-1/-2. 22.04, 24.04, 26.04 and 26.10 get it under standard support, and 20.04 and older need Pro ESM. Run sudo apt update && sudo apt install --only-upgrade '?name(^php[0-9.]+$)'.
  • Debian (tracker): trixie is fixed in php8.4 8.4.27-1~deb13u1 (DSA-6574-1) and bookworm in php8.2 8.2.35-1~deb12u1 (DLA-4848-1). Sid was still unfixed when I checked.
  • Sury (packages.sury.org, Ondřej's repos) is reported to ship 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35, plus backports for 8.1, 8.0, 7.4, 7.3, 7.2, 7.1 and 5.6.
  • Remi: php.net says plainly that rpms.remirepo.net "will not have updates today" and recommends switching to distro packages or building from source. That's rough if your RHEL-family servers pull PHP from that one volunteer-maintained repo.
  • RHEL/AlmaLinux: Red Hat had no fixed packages when AlmaLinux posted on 21 Oct. Alma was backporting to its module streams and said its builds would ship ahead of RHEL.
  • Docker official images: the library file lists 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. Run docker pull, rebuild with --pull, redeploy.
  • Managed hosting: ask your host for the exact package version. "We're aware" doesn't tell you anything.

Then restart. FPM and mod_php keep the old code mapped in memory until the workers die, so a box with the new package installed and the old workers still running is unpatched.

If you can't patch today

PHP is blunt about this: none of these settings make you safe, they just cut off the known paths.

; set in php.ini or php_admin_value, never ini_set() or .user.ini
session.upload_progress.enabled = 0
memory_limit = -1          ; partial: closes the controllable OOM path
post_max_size = 8M         ; 32M if you need uploads
upload_max_filesize = 2M   ; keep below post_max_size
fatal_error_backtraces = 0 ; PHP 8.5 only

Restart every worker after the change. At the proxy, cap request size, multipart part count and header count, including for requests with no usable Content-Length. Don't reach for RLIMIT_AS/RLIMIT_DATA, because they can cause the vulnerable allocation failure. pm.max_requests=1 narrows 109619 if you can take the performance hit.

PHP 8.1, 7.4 and other EOL versions

If you're on 8.1 or older, you're relying on your vendor, Sury's backports or PHP's source-only patches for 7.4/8.0/8.1. CISA's advice for anything that can't be patched is to take it offline. For an internet-facing PHP 7.4 box I agree.

Patch first, then read your logs. Huntress suggests watching for php-fpm, httpd or apache2 spawning sh, curl or nc.

How long does a PHP security patch take to reach your production servers: hours, days, or "whenever the base image updates"? Be honest in the comments.

Sources

  • PHP security advisory and releases, advance notice
  • GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w, GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp
  • CISA alert, Red Hat
  • Huntress, watchTowr, Hadrian
  • Ubuntu, Debian tracker, AlmaLinux, Docker official images
  • HN thread

title: Deadline-Driven Object Storage: Large ZIP Export Multipart Upload and Signed Download Link
description:
Short answer: for an edtech system exporting signed documents, stream the archive into bounded multipart parts, publish it only after completion, and issue a short-lived signed download link only while the retention record permits access.

The deadline is the design constraint. A signed link is a temporary capability, not evidence that the bytes have been deleted. Keep the deletion deadline in the job or compliance database, keep the object private, and make the download endpoint check the export state before asking object storage to sign the exact key.

Large-file throughput is a separate constraint. A worker that creates a multi-gigabyte ZIP and sends it in one request has one large failure boundary: a process eviction, network reset, or exhausted disk can force the archive to be rebuilt. Multipart upload gives the worker smaller retry units, but it does not make an unfinished session a finished object, and it does not decide when deletion is allowed.

Start with the deadline, then budget the archive

Model an export as a state machine rather than a file path. A useful record contains an export ID, a unique object key, the retention deadline, an upload session identifier, completed part numbers and tags, an explicit status, and a completion timestamp. The worker writes state transitions; the download endpoint reads the completed state before issuing a capability.

The key should include the job identity, such as exports/{export_id}/documents.zip. That prevents two retries from treating a shared name as a lock. It also makes cleanup auditable: a lifecycle process can target completed objects by prefix, while an application job can remove one object when its deadline arrives. Do not put a signed URL in the authoritative record. It will expire; the key and deadline should not.

Throughput needs its own budget. Let P be the part size, W the number of concurrent uploads, and R the retry reserve. A worker needs room for the ZIP writer, W * P in-flight buffers, and enough local scratch space for its archive strategy. Bigger parts usually reduce request overhead, but they also increase the work lost when one part fails. Your mileage may vary; the right value comes from measurements of compression, memory pressure, link capacity, concurrent exports, and the cost of rebuilding a part.

That is the uncomfortable part.

A deadline that is precise in the database but vague in cleanup is not precise in production. For example, if a district administrator requests a signed-document ZIP at 09:00 and its deletion deadline is 18:00, a link expiring at 09:15 limits the capability window; it does not authorize the cleanup job to wait until tomorrow.

Keep it private.

How should a Node.js worker handle a large ZIP export with multipart upload and a signed download link?

Keep the browser out of the archive-writing path. The worker can stream source documents into a ZIP, buffer one bounded part, upload that part, and persist the returned part metadata before moving on. After every required part is acknowledged, complete the multipart session. Only then should the application create a signed download link for the object key and an expiry that matches the user's download window.

The following Python sketch shows the control flow without pretending that every object-storage system has the same SDK or request vocabulary. The adapter is the boundary to test against a real implementation; the job logic is where retention and publication rules belong.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Iterable
import zipfile


@dataclass
class ExportRecord:
    export_id: str
    object_key: str
    delete_after: datetime
    upload_id: str | None = None
    completed_parts: list[dict] | None = None


class StorageAdapter:
    def create_multipart(self, object_key: str) -> str:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def upload_part(self, upload_id: str, part_number: int, data: bytes) -> dict:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def complete_multipart(self, upload_id: str, parts: list[dict]) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def abort_multipart(self, upload_id: str) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def signed_download(self, object_key: str, expires_in_seconds: int) -> str:
        raise NotImplementedError


def build_zip(paths: Iterable[Path], output: Path) -> None:
    with zipfile.ZipFile(output, "w", zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as archive:
        for path in paths:
            archive.write(path, path.name)


def publish_export(storage, record, source_paths, scratch_dir, part_size):
    record.completed_parts = record.completed_parts or []
    archive = scratch_dir / f"{record.export_id}.zip"
    build_zip(source_paths, archive)
    record.upload_id = record.upload_id or storage.create_multipart(record.object_key)

    try:
        with archive.open("rb") as stream:
            part_number = 1
            while chunk := stream.read(part_size):
                part = storage.upload_part(record.upload_id, part_number, chunk)
                record.completed_parts.append(part)
                part_number += 1

        storage.complete_multipart(record.upload_id, record.completed_parts)
        return storage.signed_download(record.object_key, expires_in_seconds=900)
    except Exception:
        storage.abort_multipart(record.upload_id)
        raise

In a real worker, persist the record after each successful part and make the retry path reconcile that record with the storage session before uploading more data. The sketch intentionally leaves the adapter abstract: request methods, part-size limits, checksum fields, and signed-link options vary, and inventing a universal endpoint would create false confidence. The completion call is the publication barrier. A link created before it can point at an object that is not ready.

There is a second failure boundary worth testing: the worker may finish uploading the final part and die before completion. On retry, the job should first load the export record, inspect the stored upload identifier and completed part metadata, and determine whether the completion transition was already recorded; if it was, the retry can verify the ready state and issue a link, while if it was not, the retry can reconcile the session and submit completion with the durable part list. Only after that state is clear should it consider a new archive. Otherwise a queue retry can rebuild a multi-gigabyte ZIP, leave an abandoned session behind, and create two possible objects for one export identity, which makes both cleanup and access review harder. Idempotency belongs in the job record and queue design, not in hope.

No premature link.

Failure modes to test before measuring throughput

A large-file design should name its failures before it names its provider. These are the cases I would put in a review:

Failure mode Required behavior Evidence to retain
Worker stops during ZIP creation Retry from source data or a durable intermediate, with bounded disk use Job status and worker attempt ID
Part upload is interrupted Retry only the affected part when its prior result is not durable Part number, checksum or storage tag, attempt timestamp
Final part arrives before completion Keep the object unpublished until explicit completion succeeds Upload ID and completion state
Link is requested after the deadline Refuse issuance, even if the object still exists briefly Decision timestamp and retention deadline
Cleanup job is delayed Alert and retry deletion; do not extend access silently Deletion attempt and final deletion state
Duplicate job is enqueued Use a stable export identity and unique object key Queue ID, export ID, object key

The deletion path deserves the same attention as the upload path. A scheduled lifecycle rule can help, but an application deadline still needs monitoring because cleanup timing, rule granularity, and retention configuration are separate from signed-link expiry. Never treat URL expiry as proof that the bytes were deleted.

For student records, log the decision to issue a link without logging the link itself. A URL containing a signature is a bearer capability. Apply least privilege to the worker credential, keep the object private, and make the download service check job ownership before asking storage to sign anything.

Which object-storage trade-offs belong in the design review?

Multipart support is only one row in the decision. Record the exact behavior for incomplete sessions, lifecycle deletion, checksums, conditional writes, versioning, object immutability, regional placement, egress, and signed-request expiry. An S3-compatible interface does not prove identical retention or authorization semantics across systems.

Decision axis Why it matters for this export Question to answer
Part retry and completion Determines rebuild cost after a worker failure Can the job resume from durable part metadata?
Lifecycle deletion Determines how closely storage cleanup follows the deadline What is the documented minimum or granularity?
Immutability and versioning Determines whether an overwrite can be recovered Are accidental replacement and legal retention separate controls?
Signed retrieval Determines who can read a completed archive and for how long Can the service sign one private object without making the bucket public?
Operational surface Determines what the team must monitor and rotate Are credentials, regions, quotas, and audit events visible to operators?

The catch is that this pattern is not suitable when the requirement is a permanent public asset, anonymous browser access, immutable legal hold, or built-in cross-region replication. Use a separately managed public delivery layer, an immutability-capable repository, or a replication design when those guarantees are mandatory. Stick with a simpler single upload when the archive is small enough that a retry is cheaper than multipart state, but record that choice as a measured constraint rather than a default.

I’m not sure a single numeric threshold can serve every school or district. Compression ratio, source locality, concurrent exports, and the user's download window change the answer. Run a representative archive through the worker, kill it at each state transition, and use the resulting memory, retry, and completion data to set the policy.

A compact rollout for signed-document exports

Ship the smallest state machine first: queued, building, uploading, completing, ready, expired, and deleted. Add metrics for bytes produced, part retries, active sessions, completion latency, link-issuance decisions, and deletion lag. Alert on sessions that remain incomplete beyond the job timeout and on objects past their deadline.

Then test the contract, not just the happy path. A worker should survive termination during ZIP creation, a failed part, and the gap after the final part. A download request after expiry should receive no signed capability. A cleanup retry should be visible and idempotent. A duplicate queue message should not publish two records for one export identity.

That rollout gives the team a decision rule: choose multipart when large-file throughput and restart cost dominate, choose a simpler path when archive rebuilds are cheap, and choose stronger retention controls when deletion deadlines are not the only obligation. The signed link is the last step in that chain, never the chain itself.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/signed-urls

title: Two Parallel Agents Edited the Same File; the Merge Dropped One Quietly
description:
Two tickets landed the same morning, so I split them across two worktrees and let each agent run on its own branch. Both came back green: their own tests passed, their own review approved, their own CI ran clean. Both merged. A week later, the feature flag from ticket A was missing in production, even though ticket A's PR had shipped.

What actually merged

Each agent reached for the same shared file, the feature-flag registry: ticket A added a new flag, ticket B added a different flag and switched a default next to it. The code paths were separate, and so were the tests. When B merged on top of A's older base, Git kept B's hunks in that file and A's flag hunk was gone. It was not a conflict Git flagged loudly; B's version was authored against a stale copy, the rebase took B's region in the registry, and the suite never asserted the registry's full contents.

Each test only proved its own flag existed. Nobody asked whether the shared file still carried everyone's knobs.

Why green on every side hides it

Tests prove your own path, not the shared manifest. A unit test for ticket A asserts that A's flag behaves as expected in isolation. It does not read the registry after B merged and confirm A's entry is still present. The dropped change lives in the gap between two isolated suites.

Agents work in isolation and cannot see sibling branches. Each prompt described one ticket on one worktree; neither agent knew another branch touched the same registry, so neither claimed ownership, rebased against the current file, or flagged the overlap.

A clean merge means line numbers reconciled, not intent preserved. Git reports no conflict when hunks sit in different lines, even on the same file. A rebase onto a stale base can quietly take one branch's region wholesale. Git does not warn that this file already changed upstream.

The dropped surface has no integration assertion. Flags, router tables, shared type registries, and script blocks usually lack a test that enumerates the whole file, so a missing entry fails nowhere — it just vanishes after deploy.

The cheap habits that prevent the clobber

Own the file before editing it. When an agent reaches for a cross-cutting shared file — a flag registry, router table, shared types, package.json scripts, env schema, or the OpenAPI spec — check open sibling PRs that touch it. Claim the file for this branch or defer to the other branch instead of both editing blind.

Push per-feature config out of the shared manifest. A feature-owned config file loaded by a registry shrinks the collision surface to almost zero; each branch edits its own directory, and the shared file stays a loader, not a data dump.

Require a fresh rebase when a shared file moved upstream. A cheap CI check lists open PRs modifying the same file and flags a merge that overlaps a sibling hunk, rather than trusting a clean line-level merge.

Assert the shared file in one integration smoke test. Enumerate the expected entries in the registry and fail if one is missing; a dropped knob then fails at merge, not a week after deploy.

When the shared file is the contract

If the shared file is the OpenAPI spec or the generated shared types, two branches changing it independently produce clients that silently diverge. A dropped operation survives a green suite exactly the same way: each branch tests its own slice, and nobody reads the contract after merge. The cheap guard is to replay recorded request/response pairs against the local spec and a live sandbox before merge, so the missing operation shows as a red diff in front of the reviewer rather than as a gap in production traffic. That is the local-first loop we built into Powerduck: the spec stays the source of truth, and drift appears on screen instead of in a post-deploy check.

What I check now

  1. Did this PR edit a shared manifest, and is an open sibling PR touching the same file?
  2. Did the branch rebase onto a current base that already includes the sibling merge?
  3. Does any test assert the shared file's full contents, or only my own slice?

A clean merge means Git reconciled line numbers. It does not mean both branches' intent survived.

title: I built a self-hosted family finance app with Claude Code in 9 days. Here's what it cost and what I learned
description:
A home app for a family with bank accounts in several countries: from a monthly evening with Excel to production in nine days, and two months of daily use since.

I'm Rodion, CTO and co-founder of a software agency. I started as a programmer and can still write code, but in this story that skill barely mattered. In September I built a household finance app for my family working only with AI agents, and two months later my wife and I still use it every day.

This post is about what you can now build for yourself, what it costs, and what I learned doing it. All numbers come from the logs and from git, not from memory. The project is open source: github.com/sars/keepard, with a live demo you can click through without installing anything.

TL;DR

  • What: a self-hosted app that pulls transactions from banks in several countries, works out what the family actually spent, classifies it, asks in Telegram when unsure, and tracks all assets in one currency.
  • How: nine calendar days, two agent tools (Codex for two days, then Claude Code), about 3–4 hours of my attention a day, 446 prompts with a median length of 26 words.
  • Output: 643 commits, ~200 merged PRs, 61 database migrations, 659 tests.
  • Cost: ~$2,700 at API token prices, of which 72% was re-reading context and only 13% generated code. Actual cost to me: a $100/month subscription I also use for other things.
  • Running cost: ~€10/month for a VPS shared with another project, a $10/month hard budget for the classifier, free open-banking access.

The last straw

Once a month I had a date with Excel: pull together where the money is, how much went out and on what. Accounts in several banks and several countries, my wife's own cards, every bank with its own statement format. I was always one or two weeks late for that date, because the evening it took was easy to fill with something else.

In September the date came around again and I procrastinated again, but this time I thought I'd try it differently. I had wanted for a while to test a serious agentic workflow on something real: not "make me a landing page", but a product with integrations, a database and a deployment that people would actually use afterwards. There was no better excuse.

I didn't even consider off-the-shelf apps, for two reasons. I wanted to build it myself, and the set of integrations a person from Ukraine with foreign accounts needs is specific enough that no aggregator covers it. In the end I got both the experience and a service that costs me almost nothing to run.

Who this is for

  • People with accounts in several countries who want to see them in one place.
  • Couples who budget together and want the family's spending by category, not just their own.
  • Anyone who wants transparency over everything they own, not just spending: accounts, deposits, broker, crypto, in one currency on one chart.
  • People who would rather not hand their bank data to someone else's SaaS.

If that's you, the rest is about what it does and how to repeat it.

What it does

Collects transactions by itself. My Ukrainian bank (Monobank) is connected directly through its personal API token; it's the only Ukrainian bank that gives simple access to your own transactions. Foreign banks (Wise, Revolut, a few European banks) are connected through Enable Banking, an open-banking aggregator. Two things I didn't expect: Enable Banking is free for your own accounts, and connecting a bank is just the bank's own consent flow. What didn't work: the other Ukrainian banks. Formally they have open banking; in practice an ordinary person with an ordinary account cannot use it.


Home. Spending this month against the same period last month, day by day. Right: month-to-month analytics, heaviest months highlighted.

Counts personal spending, not everything. Transfers between your own accounts, investments and non-family expenses don't enter the statistics. Refunds are handled correctly too: if a shop returns money, the expense goes down instead of showing up as separate "income". Sounds obvious, but this is exactly where most bank "analytics" break: a transfer to your own other card looks like spending.

Classifies. Rules by merchant and description first, then what the system has already seen, and only then the model. Most transactions land in a category with no human involved. When the system is unsure, it messages me or my wife in Telegram: what was this payment? That turned out to be very convenient. A transfer to someone's card, which two months later in Excel would become "what was that?", gets classified while you still remember.


Review queue. Three payments the system couldn't classify on its own. Right: a payment card with type, category and a slot for the receipt.

Analytics. By category, by period, by each owner, in any currency at the day's rate. There's a "every category, every month" table: rows are months, columns are categories, the darker the cell, the more was spent. You see at once which month went wrong and where. Every number is clickable and leads to the payments behind it.


Where the money went this year. Right: the category-by-month table.

Assets. A separate tab: all accounts, deposits, broker, crypto, cash. One currency, a snapshot every month, a chart. Bank balances arrive on their own, the rest comes from feeds or by hand once a month. Cash lives here too: you can create cash accounts and record cash spending in the app. This is the spreadsheet I used to assemble by hand, now assembling itself.


Assets. Everything in one currency, change over the period. Right: growth over time and the split between invested and not.

The rest. Installs on a phone as a PWA. Has a health page: are the imports alive, when did each bank last update, is any consent about to expire. Makes daily encrypted backups to separate storage. Accepts receipts from Telegram and attaches them to payments. We rarely use receipts and cash. Everything else, daily.


Health page. AI budget ($10 a month, $0.50 buffer), who classified the money this year. Right: bank connections.

Stack, for the record: TypeScript end to end, Node and PostgreSQL on the back, React with Vite, Tailwind and shadcn/ui on the front, Playwright for screenshots and end-to-end checks, Docker on the server. Not because any of it is the best choice, but because the agent proposed it and I had no reason to argue. More on that below.

How it was built

Nine calendar days, 11–19 September. In that time the repository gained 643 commits, around 200 merged pull requests, 61 database migrations and 659 tests. Agents wrote the code; I did terminal commands, configs, registrations with external services, and three to four hours of attention a day. A single prompt of "make me a nice family finance app" and 15 minutes would not have done it.

Two tools took turns. The first two days were OpenAI's Codex, which produced about 4,000 responses in 48 hours and in the same 48 hours ate two weekly subscription limits: once they let me reset the limit, and it ate that too. So from day three I moved to Claude Code, which carried the rest: 10,930 responses over seven days.

Instead of writing code I described an idea, looked at the result, tested on my phone and said what was wrong. The briefs were short: 446 prompts with a median of 26 words, and often I didn't type them at all but dictated them, because that's usually much faster. Three real ones, typos fixed:

"make the pwa feel more like a real app, remove the navbars"

"need to set up backups... want to use aws s3"

"my laptop is very hot and slow... I think it's this project. Why? tests? how to make it lighter"

I know, not very structured and not very programmer-like, but that's how it was.

The third one is my favourite, because it isn't a feature at all, it's a complaint, and it ended in a documented finding: ten parallel git worktrees had put 160,000 files under the macOS indexer, and the laptop was honestly trying to index every node_modules. Now there's a script that excludes them after every install.

Where the money went

The most useful number in those logs isn't about speed, it's about money. Had I paid for tokens at API prices, this build would have cost about $2,700, and 72% of that would not have gone to writing code but to the model re-reading context: the codebase, the documentation, the conversation history. Generated code itself is only 13%.

In other words, in agentic development you mostly pay for context, and most of the practices below exist because I was trying to shrink that bill.

What I learned

"Make it look nice" doesn't work

The first frontend looked like every AI frontend: each screen lived its own life. Five copies of the money formatter, 22 hand-rolled select components, every screen with its own colours.

So I made a design kit. The reference was Tremor, the well-known dashboard template: calm, dense, the numbers are the loudest thing on the screen. A reference, not a dependency: the agent reproduces that look on the shadcn/ui and Tailwind components already in the project, Tremor itself isn't installed. On top I added:

  • one page of rules, DESIGN.md: colours only through tokens, a type scale, spacing, how charts are drawn, how everything looks on a phone;
  • a component index that works as a vocabulary for the agent;
  • a script that screenshots any screen on phone and desktop;
  • a check that rejects a hex colour in a component, a money formatter outside one file, and a bundle over 150 KB.

After that the frontend was rebuilt in one night in six stages, and the agents stopped inventing.

Control the stack and dependencies, at least at the top level

The agent doesn't pick the optimal thing, it picks the most common thing, and that's fine right up until you have to rewrite. My first UI sat on one set of primitives; a few days later the library changed a default and the screens had to be migrated one by one. Rewrites cost both time and tokens.

So the starting spec should pin the language, framework, database, component library, and one command that proves a change is right: types, tests, lint, bundle budget. Not all my choices are optimal even now, but it's already a good iteration.

A health page is mandatory

One screen shows whether the bank imports and the Telegram worker are alive, when the last backup ran, when each bank consent expires and how much AI budget is left, with the age of the last event next to each item. That page is what separates "it works" from "I think it works".

The most valuable part of AGENTS.md is the prohibitions, not the process

The biggest payoff came from a few lines about what must never be done in this project:

  • Bank access is read-only; we never pay or transfer.
  • Money is stored as whole minor units, never floating point.
  • A transfer between your own accounts is not an expense.
  • The model may suggest a category; plain code always does the arithmetic.
  • If a human decided otherwise, the human's decision wins.

Every one of those was once a mistake that had to be redone, and once it was in the file it never happened again.

A safe process without "approve, approve, next"

Every implementer agent works in its own git worktree, doesn't commit, doesn't push, doesn't see secrets, and in the end just returns a diff. One orchestrator reads each diff, runs the checks and merges. Permissions for dangerous actions, such as SSH to the server, push, or the release script, are granted as a list up front, so I don't click "approve" a hundred times a day, but nothing gets deleted "while we're at it". Deployment always needs my confirmation.

One more piece of advice I didn't arrive at immediately: develop in a container, not directly on your machine. Then you can safely put agents in auto mode without worrying about them wandering somewhere they shouldn't.

Manual testing is part of product design

You describe a screen in two sentences, look at what came out, and only then understand what you actually wanted. "Done" from an agent is a hypothesis until you've poked at it on your phone yourself.

What it costs, and does it work

Monthly it all comes to about €10 for a VPS on Contabo, and even that isn't entirely for this project, because another app of mine lives on the same server in a neighbouring Docker stack behind a shared proxy. A domain is optional. Enable Banking is free for your own accounts, and the classifier on OpenAI runs under a hard $10/month budget that the system enforces itself, reserving the cost of a request before sending it.

So the only thing in this story that really cost money was the development tokens. And even that is simpler than the $2,700 figure suggests: I'm on a subscription, so for me it's $100 a month for Claude, and for that money I wasn't building only this project.

The data lives on one server only I can access, backups are encrypted, and the model sees payment descriptions, not statements. It's not bank-grade security and I know it, but it's my data on my server, not in someone's SaaS.

Does it actually work? My wife and I have used it daily for almost two months, and we both look at the analytics. The dates with Excel are cancelled forever, because everything I used to assemble by hand now assembles itself.

One insight I'll share: it turned out the car in our family eats like another adult. Repairs, servicing and fuel used to hide across different accounts and look like small change; together on one chart they look like something I now treat with respect.

What's next

Before publishing I named the project Keepard, because I had a keepard.com domain sitting idle from the distant past.

The project is open: github.com/sars/keepard. A star helps. It isn't a SaaS and it isn't for sale: a free thing anyone can run on their own server and bend to their needs. There's a demo with an invented household (sign in as guest@keepard.com / keepard-demo-for-everyone) if you want to click around first.

Out of this experience grew the InHouse AI Starter Kit: the foundations for internal systems like this (roles, change history, phone first, an AI budget, one-command release, backups) and the agent practices described above. We've just started using it on two internal projects. But that's another story.

A year ago, building this for yourself meant hiring developers or spending a few months of evenings. Now it's nine days, a token bill and a lot of careful review. It isn't perfect and it wasn't mistake-free, but it works, and it's used.

If you've built something similar with agents, I'd like to hear what your context bill looked like. And if you try Keepard, open an issue with what broke.

title: 🦥 LazyGenius AI — Work Less. Achieve More. Stay Smart.
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

🦥 LazyGenius AI — Work Less. Achieve More. Stay Smart.

What I Built

LazyGenius AI is a local AI productivity assistant designed to automate repetitive tasks and help students and developers save time.

We often waste time summarizing lengthy documents, preparing study notes, organizing daily tasks, and understanding difficult technical concepts. LazyGenius AI helps simplify these activities using open-weight AI models.

✨ Key Features

  • 🤖 AI Chat Assistant: Ask questions and receive AI-generated answers.
  • 📄 PDF Summarizer: Convert lengthy PDF documents into concise summaries.
  • ✅ Smart To-Do List Generator: Turn unorganized notes into structured task lists.
  • 📝 AI Writing Assistant: Transform rough text into clear, professional writing.
  • 📚 Simple Topic Explainer: Understand complex technical concepts in beginner-friendly language.
  • 🔒 Local AI Processing: Run compatible AI models on your own computer instead of relying on a hosted AI API.
  • 🌐 Offline Capability: Use core AI features without an internet connection after downloading the model and required dependencies.

The goal is simple: let AI handle repetitive work so people can spend more time learning, building, and creating.

Demo

🚀 Live Demo: [Add your deployed application link here]

🎥 Video Demo: [Add your demo video link here]

The demo will show how LazyGenius AI answers questions, summarizes PDF documents, and generates useful task lists using a locally running AI model.

Code

💻 GitHub Repository: [Add your GitHub repository link here]

The project is built with Python and open-source tools. Developers can explore the source code, customize the application, and contribute new features.

Contributions and suggestions are welcome!

How I Built It

I designed LazyGenius AI around local AI inference to make everyday productivity tasks easier without depending on a cloud AI API.

🛠️ Technology Stack

  • Python: Handles the application's core logic.
  • Streamlit: Creates an interactive and user-friendly web interface.
  • Ollama: Runs compatible AI models locally.
  • Gemma: An open-weight language model used to generate responses and summaries.
  • PyPDF: Extracts text from PDF documents.
  • Requests: Connects the Python application to the local Ollama API.

⚙️ How It Works

  1. The user enters a question, uploads a PDF, or provides a list of tasks.
  2. Python processes the input and extracts document text when necessary.
  3. The application sends the prepared input to a locally running AI model through Ollama.
  4. The model generates a response, summary, or organized checklist.
  5. Streamlit displays the result to the user.

The AI model performs the core language-generation tasks, while Python manages the application workflow.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open innovation is a central part of LazyGenius AI.

Many AI applications depend on cloud-based services, which may require an internet connection, involve usage fees, and send user inputs to external servers.

LazyGenius AI explores an alternative: running an open-weight AI model locally and giving users greater control over their data.

🔒 Privacy and Control

Users can process personal documents and study notes locally without sending their contents to a hosted AI API.

🌐 Offline Access

After the required model and dependencies have been downloaded, core AI features can work without an internet connection.

🔄 Model Flexibility

Developers can experiment with different compatible models rather than depending entirely on a single AI provider.

💰 Cost Efficiency

Local inference avoids per-request charges from a hosted AI API, although users still need suitable hardware, storage, and electricity.

🛠️ Freedom to Build

Open-weight models and open-source tools allow developers to inspect the application code, customize its behavior, and contribute improvements.

For me, open innovation means more than simply using AI. It means having the freedom to experiment, build useful tools, and decide how the technology works.

My Agent Session

🤖 DevRelay Agent Session: [Add your saved agent session link here, if available]

This section is optional. A saved development session can help demonstrate the development process and the decisions made while building LazyGenius AI.

The Lazy Payoff

The idea behind LazyGenius AI is to eliminate repetitive work that consumes time throughout the day.

Instead of manually preparing summaries, users can generate concise notes. Instead of creating task lists from scratch, they can turn rough notes into organized checklists. They can also use AI to understand technical topics and improve their writing.

For example, a student preparing for an examination can upload a set of notes, generate a summary, and create a revision checklist in one workflow.

I plan to evaluate the time saved by comparing the time required to complete selected tasks manually with the time required using LazyGenius AI.

The mission: less busywork, more learning, and more time to build. 🦥

Prize Categories

I will select the eligible prize categories that match the completed project and the official challenge rules.

  • Open-source AI / open-weight models
  • Local inference, if eligible
  • Additional partner categories, if supported by the implemented features

Built with Python, Streamlit, Ollama, and Gemma.

🦥 LazyGenius AI — Work Less. Achieve More. Stay Smart.

Hacktoberfest #OpenSourceAI #Ollama #Gemma #Python #Streamlit #LocalAI #BuildInPublic
