title: Your captcha token was solved but the site still rejected it: 7 causes and fixes
description:
You automated the boring part. The solver returned a token, you dropped it into the form, you hit submit, and the site came back with "verification failed". No stack trace, no useful error, just a page that looks exactly like the one you started on.

This happens to everyone who automates anything behind a captcha, whether it's an end-to-end test suite for your own signup flow, a monitoring job, or an agent that fills in forms. The token itself is rarely "wrong". Almost always, it's valid but used in a way the site's backend refuses.

Here are the seven causes I see most often, roughly in order of how often they bite, and what to do about each one.

1. The token expired before you submitted it

Captcha tokens are short-lived on purpose.

  • reCAPTCHA: Google's docs say each response token "is valid for two minutes, and can only be verified once."
  • Cloudflare Turnstile: tokens are valid for 300 seconds (five minutes) after they're generated.

Two minutes sounds like plenty until you look at what a real script does between "token received" and "form submitted": it waits for a page to settle, fills ten other fields, uploads a file, retries a flaky selector. If your flow takes 90 seconds before it even asks for the token, you're cutting it close.

Fix: request the token as late as possible, right before submit. Don't fetch it at the start of the test "to have it ready". If your form has a long multi-step flow, fill everything else first and solve the captcha last.

2. You used the same token twice

Both Google and Cloudflare reject a token the second time it's verified. On the server side this shows up as timeout-or-duplicate, and both vendors use that same code for "too old" and "already used", which is why it's so confusing.

The classic way to hit this: a retry loop. The submit fails for an unrelated reason (a validation error on another field, a 502 from the backend), your code retries the submit, and the retry carries the token that the first attempt already burned.

Fix: treat a token as single-use in your code too. If you retry a submit, get a fresh token for the retry.

3. The sitekey or page URL doesn't match the page you're on

A token is tied to the sitekey it was issued for and to the site it was solved on. Google returns a hostname field in the verification response so the site can check where the challenge was solved.

Two ways this goes wrong:

  • Wrong sitekey. Many sites have more than one: a staging key and a production key, or a separate key for the login page and the checkout page. Scrape the data-sitekey from the exact page you're submitting, not from a config file you copied last month.
  • Wrong URL. Send the full URL of the page where the captcha actually appears, not the site's homepage. For an SPA, that's the route the widget renders on.

4. reCAPTCHA v3: wrong action, or a score below the site's threshold

v3 doesn't show a challenge. It returns a score between 0.0 and 1.0, and Google's own guidance is that "by default, you can use a threshold of 0.5". Each site picks its own threshold, and it can be stricter on sensitive pages.

v3 also has actions. Google tells site owners to "verify that the action name is the name you expect". If the page calls grecaptcha.execute(key, { action: 'login' }) and your token was generated for submit or no action at all, a careful backend will reject it even with a decent score.

Fix: read the action name from the page's own JavaScript (search the bundle for execute() and pass it through when you request the token. Only ask for a minimum score as high as the site actually needs.

5. The token was earned by a different browser than the one submitting it

This is the one that catches people with Turnstile and with anti-bot vendors like DataDome. The token or cookie is minted in one browser context (one IP address, one user agent) and then submitted from another.

  • If you solve through a remote service, pass your own proxy so the solve happens from the same IP your script uses.
  • Pass the same user agent your browser uses, or, if the solver hands back the user agent it used, set your browser to that one before submitting.

Fix: keep the IP and user agent consistent between "earn the token" and "use the token". For DataDome you'll get a cookie rather than a token; set it on the same session and keep using the same proxy.

6. You put the token in the wrong place

Each widget expects the token in a specific spot:

  • reCAPTCHA v2 and v3: a hidden textarea named g-recaptcha-response.
  • Turnstile: a hidden input named cf-turnstile-response.

Many modern sites don't read that field at all. They register a JavaScript callback (data-callback="onSolved") and only enable the submit button, or only attach the token to their fetch request, when that callback fires. Setting the field's value does nothing if the callback never runs.

Fix: check the widget's data-callback attribute. If there is one, call that function with the token after you set the field:

await page.evaluate((token) => {
  document.querySelector('[name="g-recaptcha-response"]').value = token;
  const cb = document.querySelector('[data-sitekey]')?.getAttribute('data-callback');
  if (cb && typeof window[cb] === 'function') window[cb](token);
}, token);

7. It's reCAPTCHA Enterprise, not classic reCAPTCHA

Enterprise keys look the same but load from recaptcha/enterprise.js and are verified through a different API. A token solved as classic v2 or v3 won't pass an Enterprise check.

Fix: look at the script tag. If you see enterprise.js, or calls to grecaptcha.enterprise.execute, tell your solver it's Enterprise.

A quick checklist before you blame the solver

  1. Am I requesting the token right before submit?
  2. Does every retry get a fresh token?
  3. Is the sitekey from this exact page, and am I sending this exact URL?
  4. For v3: the right action, and a score the site will accept?
  5. Same IP and user agent for solving and submitting?
  6. Is the token in the right field, and did the callback fire?
  7. Is it actually Enterprise?

How we handle this at CaptchaNo

Full disclosure: I work on CaptchaNo, a captcha solving API, and several of these causes shaped how the API works. One request covers reCAPTCHA v2, v3 and Enterprise, Turnstile, DataDome and image captchas. The call waits for the token instead of making you poll, which helps with cause #1. You can pass proxy, userAgent, action and minScore for causes #4 and #5, and failed solves aren't billed. Even if you use something else, the checklist above applies to every solver.

Whatever you're automating, keep it to things you're allowed to automate: your own sites, systems you have permission to test, and data collection the site's terms permit.

title: Python Automation, Machine Learning, or AI? A Practical Guide
description:
Python gives you several ways to solve a problem: a deterministic script, a machine-learning model, or an AI feature that works with unstructured input. The right choice is usually the least complex approach that meets the requirement and can be checked.

Start with the shape of the problem

Ask what the software must do, what information it can use, and what happens when it is wrong. A stable rule and a fuzzy prediction are different engineering problems, even if both can be described as “using AI.”

Need A sensible starting point Why
Move, rename, validate, or transform known data Python automation The rules are explicit and results are repeatable.
Apply a stable business rule Ordinary Python logic A test can describe the expected result directly.
Predict a category or value from examples Machine learning A model may help when patterns are difficult to encode as fixed rules.
Summarize or extract meaning from varied text A language model with review The input is unstructured, and outputs need evaluation and guardrails.

The table is a starting point, not a substitute for requirements. A Python application can combine these approaches: validate inputs with ordinary code, call a model for one uncertain step, and keep a person in the loop when the result matters.

When rules are enough

Use a regular Python function when the rule is known and should behave the same way every time. Rules are easier to test, explain, and maintain. They are often the right answer for file processing, format checks, calculations, integrations, and workflow automation.

If the rule list keeps growing because inputs vary in subtle ways, that is a signal to review the problem. More exceptions do not automatically mean machine learning is needed; the process or data may simply need clarification.

When machine learning may help

Machine learning is worth evaluating when there are representative examples, a pattern to learn, and a measurable definition of success. Before training or selecting a model, check that the examples reflect real use, labels are consistent, and the evaluation data is kept separate from training data.

Choose a metric that matches the cost of mistakes. In a screening workflow, for example, a false negative may matter more than a false positive. Accuracy alone can hide that difference. Review errors by category and test on new examples before relying on predictions.

When generative AI fits

A language model can be useful for varied text tasks such as drafting, summarizing, or extracting candidate fields. Its output is probabilistic: the same prompt can produce different wording, and a confident answer can still be wrong.

Treat generated output as a suggestion unless the task is low risk and quality has been carefully tested. Validate structure, protect sensitive data, set clear limits, and provide a review path for uncertain or consequential results. A model should not quietly make a decision that the process owner expects a person to make.

A practical evaluation sequence

  1. Define the outcome and what counts as an acceptable result.
  2. Build the smallest deterministic baseline you can measure.
  3. Collect representative examples and identify likely failure cases.
  4. Compare alternatives using the same evaluation set and cost assumptions.
  5. Decide how to handle low-confidence, invalid, or high-impact cases.
  6. Monitor behavior after release; input patterns and model performance can change.

Python is useful across this process: it can prepare data, run checks, connect services, expose a web API, and automate repeatable work. The model is only one component. Good system design also accounts for privacy, latency, cost, maintenance, and a way to recover when something fails.

The short version

Choose Python rules when the rules are known. Evaluate machine learning when examples reveal a pattern that is difficult to express directly. Consider generative AI for genuinely unstructured tasks, with testing and human oversight appropriate to the risk. If a simple baseline solves the problem, keep the solution simple.

I'm Kyle Keon, a Python developer in Pembroke, Ontario, focused on practical work across AI, workflow automation, machine learning, and web development. Portfolio and contact.

title: A Practical Python Checklist for Automating Repetitive Work
description:
Python automation works best when it removes a repeatable step without making the process harder to trust. Before writing a script, define the input, output, rules, and what should happen when something is missing.

Start with a one-sentence specification

Write down the job in this form: “Given this input, produce this output, using these rules, and stop or report when this condition occurs.” If those details are still changing, clarify the process before automating it.

For example, a monthly contact export might need consistent names and email addresses. That is a good candidate for a small Python script if the file format and rules are stable. A workflow that includes judgment, approvals, or exceptions may need a human review step instead of full automation.

Separate reading, validation, and writing

A reliable workflow has a few visible stages:

  1. Read the source without changing it.
  2. Check that required fields and assumptions are present.
  3. Transform the data in memory.
  4. Write a new output only after validation succeeds.
  5. Report what happened so the result can be checked.

Here is a small standard-library example for cleaning a CSV. Test it on a copy of the input first. It refuses to overwrite an existing output file, so a previous report is not silently replaced.

import csv
from pathlib import Path

source = Path("inbox/contacts.csv")
destination = Path("reports/contacts_clean.csv")
required_columns = {"name", "email"}

with source.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8-sig") as file:
    reader = csv.DictReader(file)
    missing = required_columns - set(reader.fieldnames or [])
    if missing:
        raise ValueError(f"Missing columns: {', '.join(sorted(missing))}")

    cleaned_rows = []
    for line_number, row in enumerate(reader, start=2):
        name = (row.get("name") or "").strip()
        email = (row.get("email") or "").strip().lower()
        if not email:
            raise ValueError(f"Missing email on row {line_number}")
        cleaned_rows.append({"name": name, "email": email})

destination.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
with destination.open("x", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    writer = csv.DictWriter(file, fieldnames=["name", "email"])
    writer.writeheader()
    writer.writerows(cleaned_rows)

print(f"Wrote {len(cleaned_rows)} rows to {destination}")

The example makes the rules explicit: trim whitespace, normalize email casing, and stop if a required value is missing. It does not send messages, delete source data, or make decisions about whether a contact is valid. Those boundaries are part of a safe automation design.

Make reruns predictable

A script should be safe to run again. Prefer a clearly named output, avoid accidental appends, and decide what to do if that output already exists. For tasks that update an external system, add a way to identify work already completed so a retry does not create duplicates.

Also plan for failure. A useful run should make it clear which input was processed, how many records succeeded, and where an error occurred. For sensitive or business-critical tasks, add logging, alerts, access controls, and a human review before the automation performs an irreversible action.

Start manually, schedule later

Run the script by hand on representative sample files. Compare its output with a known-good result and test missing columns, blank values, empty files, and existing output paths. Only after those checks should you consider a scheduler such as cron or Windows Task Scheduler.

Where AI fits

Python automation is a strong fit when rules are known and repeatable. AI or machine learning may help when the input is unstructured or patterns are difficult to express as fixed rules, but it adds uncertainty. Keep a measurable baseline, test representative examples, and route uncertain or high-impact decisions to a person.

A short checklist

  • Is the task repeated often enough to justify automation?
  • Are the inputs, rules, and expected outputs clearly defined?
  • Can the script validate data before changing anything?
  • Is rerunning safe, and are failures visible?
  • Has the result been tested on copies before scheduling?

A small, well-scoped Python tool can be more valuable than a large system. Start with one stable task, make its behavior observable, and expand only when the first version is dependable.

I'm Kyle Keon, a Python developer in Pembroke, Ontario, focused on practical work across Python, workflow automation, AI, machine learning, and web development. Portfolio and contact.

Understanding of component-based architecture, state management, and reusable UI components.

Who We're Looking For

We value developers who take ownership of their work, care about the details of user experience, and can turn product requirements into practical, high-quality interfaces.

How to Apply

  3. Your current location and availability.
  4. Your expected salary or hourly rate.

title: Cap the Fan-Out: Building a UAE Mover-Quote Flow That Does Not Sell Your Phone Number to Ten Companies
description:
TL;DR

  • Most "free moving quotes" products are lead-resale funnels. The customer's number becomes inventory.
  • A useful comparison marketplace needs structured intake, a small matched set of suppliers, and replies people can compare in writing.
  • In Dubai, the quote sits inside a larger dependency chain (building NOC, tenancy registration). Ignoring that produces quotes that cannot be used on the date the customer asked for.
  • We ship a short form, match up to three vetted movers, and keep replies on email or WhatsApp text — no calls required.

Moving flats in Dubai has a familiar failure mode. You fill in a form. Your phone rings. Then it rings again. By evening you have numbers in WhatsApp threads, PDFs, and voice notes. One includes packing. One does not say. One is a single figure with "+ VAT" at the end. Nobody asked which floor you live on.

I am building a small quote-comparison service for movers in the UAE. This post is for people who build two-sided products, not for people looking for a truck. It is about the product decisions that matter before the matching algorithm gets interesting.

The quote is the product — and free text destroys it

A moving price depends on variables customers do not always know they need to share:

  • Home size as a proxy for volume (even "2BR" varies a lot)
  • Floor and lift access, including whether a service lift must be booked
  • Packing scope
  • Distance and route (JVC to Marina is not the same job as Marina to Abu Dhabi)
  • Move date, including weekend and month-end lease turnover
  • Building rules: most towers want a move-in or move-out permit (NOC) with time windows and often a deposit

A free-text "tell us about your move" box captures maybe two of these. The mover then either calls (your phone rings) or quotes high to cover unknowns. Either way, the customer cannot compare like with like.

So the first engineering job is intake design: turn a fuzzy request into a record a mover can price without a call.

What we ask today

We keep the form short. Every field costs completions. The live flow asks for:

  • Name, origin area, destination area
  • Home size from a fixed list (Studio, 1BR, 2BR, 3BR, Villa, Office) — not free text
  • Move date
  • A WhatsApp number and an email
  • Optional notes

The fixed list for home size does more work than it looks like. It turns the biggest pricing variable into an enum, which means routing can prefer movers who actually handle that size of job.

The next product step — and the one I would push anyone in this space to take — is collecting access details as structured fields too: floor, service lift yes/no, NOC already booked yes/no. Each tap removes a reason for a call.

The W3C forms tutorial is still a good reminder that labels, grouping, and clear instructions matter as much as field count.

Lead resale is the default model — and the incentives show

Charging movers instead of customers keeps the service free for the person moving. That part is fine. We do the same: movers pay, customers do not.

The broken part is fan-out. If you earn per lead and the customer does not pay, every extra company that receives the lead is extra revenue. Leads get blasted wide. Customers get ten calls. Movers compete on who dials first, not who quotes best.

Moving is a rare, high-stakes transaction. People move infrequently. The job involves everything they own. There is little repeat purchase to win back if it goes wrong. Volume-first lead models fit poorly.

So we made two decisions that cost short-term revenue:

  1. Each request goes to up to three movers, chosen for fit. Three is enough to compare and few enough that each mover treats the job as winnable.
  2. Replies come by email or WhatsApp text. No calls needed. Written quotes leave a record, sit side by side, and can be forwarded to a partner. Many people moving in the UAE are juggling a job start, a lease, and a school search. A text they can answer at midnight is worth more than a call they missed.

Normalise the output or you are just forwarding messages

Even with good intake, quotes arrive in different shapes. Comparison needs a shared schema. The fields I think belong on a comparable quote:

Field Why it matters
Total price, VAT included or excluded Most common "that's not what you quoted" fight
Packing scope (none / fragile / full) Biggest hidden difference between "similar" quotes
Materials included Often charged separately
Dismantling / reassembly Commonly excluded by default
Crew size and vehicle Proxy for duration
Insurance / liability terms What happens if something breaks
Payment terms Deposit vs balance on completion
Validity date Quotes expire around month-end

You do not need machine learning for this. You need a template movers can fill, plus patience to map free-text replies. Once quotes share a schema, "compare" stops meaning "read three WhatsApp threads."

Honest limitation: you can normalise what is written, not what is left out. If dismantling is not mentioned, the UI should say not stated — not invent "included" or "excluded."

Trust signals customers can check

"Vetted movers" is empty on its own. Trust only works if the customer can verify something, or if the platform states exactly what it checked.

What belongs on a mover profile, in my view:

  • Licensing stated precisely (what was checked, when)
  • Scope of work: residential vs office, local vs inter-emirate, packing in-house vs subcontracted
  • Reviews tied to real jobs where possible, and labelled clearly where not

For search engines, the same honesty applies to structured data. schema.org has a MovingCompany type. Fill only what the page shows. Google's spam policies call out region/city doorway pages that funnel users to one URL. Area pages should exist where there is real coverage and something specific to say — for example, towers in an area known for tight lift booking windows.

The move is not only the truck

In Dubai, the quote sits inside a sequence. The new tenancy often needs registration through Ejari with the Dubai Land Department. Utilities need connecting. The building wants its NOC. If the NOC is not booked, the best quote in the world still cannot happen on the requested date.

A useful quote product nudges these dependencies at the right moment without trying to own every step. A short checklist beside the quote ("Have you booked your building's move permit?") prevents more failed moves than a slightly cheaper price.

Official Ejari fee figures are published by Dubai Land Department on that service page (registration plus knowledge, innovation, and partner fees depending on channel). We do not invent market averages; we point people at the authority and at the operational checklist.

What I'd tell anyone building a lead-gen marketplace

  • Design intake for the supplier's pricing model, not for your CRM's vanity fields.
  • Cap the fan-out. Fewer, better-matched leads produce better quotes and a customer who does not regret giving you a number.
  • Normalise the output. Without a common schema you are a forwarding service.
  • Make trust checkable. Say exactly what you verified.
  • Respect the channel. Let people reply by text.

That is the thinking behind the flow at MoveWise UAE: one short form, up to three matched movers, replies by email or WhatsApp text. There is still more to build on the normalised comparison table. The hard part was never the code. It was deciding what not to do with the customer's phone number.

If you've shipped a marketplace with a "who pays" tension like this, how did you balance supplier revenue against customer experience?

About the author: Waqas Jawed builds MoveWise UAE, which helps people moving in Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Sharjah and Ajman compare quotes from vetted movers. Contact: cs@movewiseuae.com.

title: MCP Transports Explained: stdio vs Streamable HTTP
description:
MCP Transports Explained: stdio vs Streamable HTTP

An MCP client and server need a path to talk. That path is called a transport. Two common choices are stdio and Streamable HTTP. They carry the same MCP messages, but they fit different jobs.

The short rule is simple. Use stdio when one local app starts one local server. Use Streamable HTTP when many users or services need a server over a network.

## What stdio does

Stdio means standard input and standard output. The client starts the MCP server as a child process. It sends JSON-RPC messages into the process and reads replies from it.

This works well for a desktop tool, command-line app, or local coding helper. Setup is small. There is no web endpoint to run. The process also gives each client a natural session.

The tradeoff is reach. A local process is hard to share with a team. Each user may need the same package, runtime, settings, and secrets. Logs can also sit on many laptops.

Use stdio when:

  • The client and server run on the same machine.
  • One client owns one server process.
  • You want a fast local setup.
  • You do not need a shared network service.

## What Streamable HTTP does

Streamable HTTP puts the MCP server behind an HTTP endpoint. A client sends MCP messages with HTTP POST. The server can also stream messages back when the session needs it.

This fits remote and shared servers. A platform team can run one service for many users. Normal web controls can sit in front of it, such as TLS, access tokens, rate limits, logs, and a load balancer.

HTTP also adds work. Teams must set timeouts, handle retries, protect the endpoint, and watch network errors. If the server keeps session state, the client may receive an Mcp-Session-Id. Later calls send that ID back. A load balancer must then route the session with care, or the state must live in a shared store.

Use Streamable HTTP when:

  • The server is remote or shared.
  • Many clients need the same tools.
  • Central access rules and audit logs matter.
  • The team can run and secure a web service.

The official MCP transport specification gives the wire rules for both choices.

## Side-by-side choice

Question stdio Streamable HTTP
Where does the server run? On the client machine On a remote or shared host
Who starts it? The client starts a process A service platform runs it
Session shape One process is one natural session Stateless or tracked with a session ID
Main strength Small local setup Shared access and central control
Main risk Setup and secrets spread to laptops Auth, retries, scaling, and network failures

## Two setup examples

For stdio, the client config points to a command and its arguments:

{
  "transport": "stdio",
  "command": "python",
  "args": ["server.py"]
}

For Streamable HTTP, the client points to one MCP URL and sends its access token through a safe secret store:

{
  "transport": "streamable-http",
  "url": "https://tools.example.com/mcp"
}

Exact fields differ by SDK. Keep the design choice the same: a local child process or a managed network service.

## Test before you launch

Start with five checks.

  1. Identity: Can the server tell which user or agent made the call?
  2. Secrets: Are tokens outside source files, logs, and client config shared in chat?
  3. Failure: What happens when a process exits or a network call times out?
  4. Session: Can a client reconnect, and does state go to the right place?
  5. Audit: Can the team see which tool ran, when it ran, and whether it failed?

Add cost to the test. A remote service has hosting and network cost. A local setup has support time and repeated setup work. Count retries and human review too. The cheapest request is not always the cheapest safe result.

Where a gateway fits

As the server list grows, teams need one place to find tools, apply access rules, and read audit events. The Axiom Studio platform describes a governed path for model and tool calls. The Axiom documentation covers the wider product set. Teams that also send model requests can use the LLM Gateway guide and its product page to plan routing, credentials, fallbacks, and usage tracking.

A gateway does not remove transport choices. It makes remote access easier to govern. Keep local stdio for small tools. Move shared tools to Streamable HTTP when the team is ready to own the web service and its controls.

A practical decision

Pick stdio for one user, one machine, and one short path. Pick Streamable HTTP for shared tools, remote access, and central rules. Then test identity, failure, sessions, and audit records before more agents depend on the server.

title: Travel Itinerary Retrieval Chunk Boundaries: A Freshness-First Architecture
description:
Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that survives all the way into the itinerary answer. Chunk by a traveler-meaningful unit (usually one day, policy, or place), attach dates and region metadata, and measure the result on a small labeled set before calling the system production-ready.

I learned to treat chunk boundaries as an operational contract, not an embedding tweak. In an itinerary planner, a user may ask for “a rainy-day option on day three” while an airline changes a timetable and a museum edits its opening hours. If the retriever returns a paragraph that mixes day two transport, day three lunch, and an old closure notice, the language model can produce a fluent answer with the wrong premise. The incident is quiet: no 500, no obvious exception, just a plan that no longer matches the source.

The invariant is simple: every answer claim needs a bounded retrieval unit, a freshness signal, and a citation path. That contract drives the architecture below. For this workflow, Infrai is a plausible collection and query layer when the team wants one REST credential across backend capabilities; it does not decide your chunk boundaries for you.

How should a travel itinerary planner set chunk boundaries for retrieval?

Start from the answer a traveler can see, then work backward to the retrieval unit. A day-by-day recommendation should retrieve a day block; “is this pass valid on Sunday?” should retrieve the pass policy as one unit; a venue recommendation should retrieve the venue facts without adjacent booking boilerplate. Splitting every PDF at an arbitrary token count is fast, but it hides these boundaries from both filters and reviewers. In one rollout review, a 900-token split looked tidy in the index, yet it crossed a train reservation cutoff and a restaurant's cancellation policy; the top result scored well, the generated answer sounded certain, and the support engineer had to trace the citation line by line to find that the two facts came from different dates. The fix was not a new embedding model. We made the itinerary day and policy paragraph the atomic units, then rejected chunks whose valid_until preceded the requested travel date. That extra metadata made the error visible in traces and made the retrieval contract testable before any prompt change.

For each chunk, keep a stable identifier and metadata such as trip_id, day, city, source_url, valid_from, valid_until, and updated_at. The date fields are not decoration. They let a query bound its search to the itinerary version the user is viewing and let a freshness check reject a stale timetable before generation.

Ingestion, querying, and citation are separate observable stages. Log the collection name, filter set, result identifiers, score distribution, and source timestamps; then record which identifiers were actually cited. This makes an SLO meaningful: for example, a retrieval-quality SLO can require that at least 9 of 10 labeled questions return a relevant chunk in the top five, while a freshness SLO can require that no answer cites a chunk past its validity window. I am not claiming those thresholds fit every product; your mileage may vary, but writing them down exposes the trade.

Build a tiny evaluation set first. Twenty to fifty real questions, labeled for the right day, place, and policy, will reveal boundary mistakes earlier than a dashboard full of aggregate similarity scores. Keep one adversarial question in the set: ask about a changed opening hour and verify that the old PDF is filtered out.

The staged design and its failure boundaries

The first stage discovers the explicit collections that represent your corpus partitions. The second issues a bounded vector query against the collection for the current itinerary and metadata window. The final stage packages the retrieved text with source identifiers so the answer writer cannot silently lose provenance.

A collection might hold “Tokyo trip, 2026-04” while another holds evergreen visa policy. That separation costs a little ingestion bookkeeping, yet it prevents a broad query from blending volatile itinerary facts with durable guidance. Keep top_k small enough to review; a top-20 dump is not a strategy.

Here is the smallest Go probe I use to verify credentials and collection discovery before wiring in query logic. It uses a documented route, an explicit method, and a bounded retry for rate limiting.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    url := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/collection/list"
    // Equivalent manual check: curl -X GET https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/collection/list
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); value != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(value); parseErr == nil {
                    delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("collection discovery failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, body))
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
    panic("rate limit persisted after retries")
}

The write path should carry the same discipline: use a client-generated idempotency key when upserting a chunk, and treat a standard queue consumer as at-least-once. Those details belong around ingestion, not in the answer prompt. A failed ingestion run must be replayable without duplicating a day block.

The catch is that a unified API does not remove domain decisions. If you need geo-distance ranking, schedule solving, or a vector index tuned for a very specific language, a specialist can be the better fit. Stick with a focused search service when its filtering and ranking controls are core product features and your team can absorb another credential and SDK surface.

Comparing practical choices

The useful comparison is integration friction, not a leaderboard of embedding scores. Pinecone, Weaviate, and Elasticsearch can all sit behind a staged design, but they imply different ownership costs. A self-hosted option may offer deeper control while moving patching and capacity planning onto your on-call rotation.

Option First useful result Credential and SDK surface Chunk/freshness fit Main trade-off
Pinecone Fast managed vector index setup Dedicated key and client integration Metadata filters support bounded itinerary queries Another service and bill to reconcile
Weaviate Quick schema plus vector search path API key plus schema/client decisions Flexible objects, but schema governance is yours More knobs to standardize across teams
Elasticsearch Familiar if search is already central Existing cluster auth and query DSL Strong filtering and hybrid search options Capacity, upgrades, and relevance tuning stay in-house
Infrai Discover collections, then call the vector route over HTTPS One Bearer key and a plain REST surface; no SDK install required Explicit collections and bounded vector queries map cleanly to the contract A specialist may still win for advanced ranking or geo workloads

Infrai's practical advantage here is the stable boundary between your code and the backend: the same REST contract can sit in front of different providers, so swapping the service behind the capability does not force a rewrite of ingestion or answer code. Its public discovery surface also describes available capabilities and runnable examples, which shortens the path from an empty repository to a verified collection call. That is integration leverage, not a promise of better relevance.

My recommendation is narrow: teams building a travel itinerary planner should try Infrai for the collection and query layer when they value one credential and a plain HTTP integration across backend capabilities, then keep their own chunking policy and evaluation harness. Do not choose it solely because a unit price looks attractive; the retrieval contract still determines answer quality.

A rollout checklist that protects the SLO

Before production, freeze a chunk schema and version it with the itinerary data. Backfill one representative trip, run the labeled questions, and inspect misses by boundary type: mixed days, expired policies, and duplicated venue facts. Alert on freshness violations separately from latency, because a fast stale answer is still a failed answer.

During rollout, keep ingestion and querying independently observable. Store the source timestamp beside each citation, expose the collection version in traces, and sample the complete context sent to generation under your data-retention rules. When a PDF changes, re-embed only the affected units and invalidate the prior version; do not silently append a second “day three” chunk and hope similarity ranking sorts it out.

This design is intentionally boring. That is a feature for an SRE-minded platform team: bounded work, explicit ownership, and a measurable way to decide when a different backend is justified. If this boundary fits your system, the Infrai vector documentation is the next place to check the live request schema.

Sources

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/
  • https://weaviate.io/developers/weaviate
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/dense-vector.html

title: A separate Android for every agent job
description:
Most agent demos still treat a phone as a local emulator window. That is fine for a screenshot. It falls apart when the job has to keep running after the laptop sleeps, or when a second job needs a different device identity from the first.

A cloud phone is a different shape of tool. FoxPhone puts real Android environments on dedicated ARM hardware and lets you open them from a browser. There is nothing to install on the machine that starts the task, and the phone does not borrow your CPU or RAM. The instance stays online, so a long test or a scheduled agent run does not depend on one workstation staying awake.

Isolation is the part that matters once you have more than one job. Every cloud phone has its own device fingerprint: its own IMEI, MAC address, serial number and the other hardware identifiers a mobile app expects to see. Each one also has its own network path and a dedicated IP. You can place that IP in regions such as the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Japan or India. One job does not inherit the identity of another job, and neither one inherits the identity of the computer that clicked start.

That is the setup AI agents actually need. An agent can install an app, launch it, tap through a flow and repeat the same steps across many devices at once. A person can still step in. One-click sync lets a master window drive the other selected phones, which is useful when you want to check that an agent is about to do something sensible. Bulk app management, one-click device switching and team sharing mean one operator can cover work that used to need a row of handsets on a desk.

The same fleet is a practical Android lab. QA can keep Android 10 through Android 15 available without a hardware cabinet. Developers can park a long-running script on what is effectively an Android VPS instead of leaving a laptop open overnight. Teams that already think in terms of a device farm can treat the farm as something you provision in seconds and shut down when the campaign ends. The device farm page is the longer description of that model if you want the product view rather than this essay.

The work we see is ordinary, which is the point. Content teams publish through mobile apps. Commerce teams check storefronts from a specific region. Ad and affiliate teams want to see what a person in that region would see. Game sessions and app tests need a real Android, not a stretched desktop emulator. Agent builders need a place where the agent can tap, type and install, then leave the device running while the next step is planned.

Pricing is usage-based. You pay for the devices and the time you use, and a free trial is there so you can try a single phone before you talk about a fleet. In directory terms it is freemium: start small, then scale the number of phones rather than buying hardware. There is no rack to ship back when a project ends.

If you are comparing this with a local emulator, the tradeoff is simple. An emulator is a good UI check on your own machine. A cloud phone is what you want when the device must stay up, stay isolated, and be one of many. The interesting part of mobile agents is not the prompt. It is whether the phone on the other side of the prompt is real, separate, and still there an hour later.

A quiet checklist before you rent one: can you open it without an install, can two phones refuse to share a fingerprint, can an agent install an app without you watching, and can you turn the phone off when the job is done? If those four answers are yes, you have infrastructure. If they are no, you have a demo.

title: Spring Boot Integration Tests Are Slow and Messy: Here's How to Fix Them
description:
Integration test suites can get slow without anyone deciding they should. Another @SpringBootTest here, some in-memory H2 wiring there, a flaky test "fixed" with a stray @DirtiesContext – and eventually the suite is the thing everyone quietly dreads before merging a PR, flaky on every other CI run, with nobody able to point to the one change that caused it.

Spring Boot integration tests do real work, validating behavior across controllers, services, repositories, databases, and messaging systems. That breadth is what makes them valuable, and it's also what makes them expensive. When you wire together a real application context, connect to databases, and exercise multiple layers in a single test run, costs add up fast. The question is whether those costs are unavoidable or whether your test suite pays for things it doesn't need.

This article walks through the specific mechanisms that make Spring Boot integration suites slow and brittle, and the practical strategies that address them. You'll also see how Kotlin's extension functions, DSLs, data classes, named arguments, and scope functions reduce the boilerplate that accumulates in integration test code over time, making the resulting suite easier to maintain regardless of the language you're already using.

Why Spring Boot integration tests slow down over time

Most suites start with a single @SpringBootTest class and a handful of tests. That first test class is harmless. The problems compound when a second developer adds another @SpringBootTest with a slightly different configuration, a third adds @ActiveProfiles("integration") to one class and @ActiveProfiles("test") to another, and a fourth drops a @DirtiesContext on a test that was flaky. Six months later, the suite boots five or six separate application contexts across a single run, and nobody realizes it.

Before you optimize anything, profile the actual bottleneck. Spring Boot's context initialization is usually the dominant cost, but database container startup and heavyweight test setup can be significant too. Run your tests with -Dspring.test.context.cache.maxSize=10 alongside JUnit's --report-dir output to see how many contexts are being created. If you see more than two or three distinct contexts in a moderate-sized suite, context proliferation is your problem.

Nearly every fix in this article reduces to a single idea: repeated initialization is the thing you're paying for, not the tests themselves. Whether that initialization is a Spring application context, a database container, or heavyweight test data, the fastest fix is almost always to do it once and reuse it rather than make each instance cheaper.

Keep the number of Spring application contexts small

@SpringBootTest loads your full application context, all beans, all configuration, all auto-configuration. For a non-trivial Spring Boot application, that initialization can take several seconds. The Spring TestContext Framework caches loaded contexts and reuses them across compatible tests, so the first test in a group pays the startup cost and subsequent tests don't.

The cache key is a composite of everything that affects the context, including configuration classes, active profiles, property sources, and context customizers. Change any of these between two test classes and Spring boots a second context. Common cache-busting patterns include using different @ActiveProfiles values across test classes, importing different @TestConfiguration classes with incompatible beans, and overusing @DirtiesContext.

@DirtiesContext signals that a test has modified the application context and that Spring should discard it. Using it broadly because a single test is flaky trades a flakiness problem for a performance problem. The test that genuinely modifies shared mutable state may warrant it, but the test that just needs a clean database table doesn't.

The practical target is a single shared context for your full integration tests, achieved by keeping configuration consistent. A shared base class or a single shared @TestConfiguration import applied consistently across test classes is the most reliable way to ensure the cache key matches. In Kotlin, the recommended approach combines constructor injection with @TestConstructor(autowireMode = TestConstructor.AutowireMode.ALL), which avoids lateinit vars and keeps test fields immutable:

@SpringBootTest
@TestConstructor(autowireMode = TestConstructor.AutowireMode.ALL)
class OrderServiceIntegrationTest(
    private val orderService: OrderService,
    private val orderRepository: OrderRepository
) {

    @Test
    fun `placing an order persists it to the database`() {
        val order = orderService.place(OrderRequest(productId = "p-42", quantity = 3))
        val saved = orderRepository.findById(order.id)
        assert(saved.isPresent)
    }
}

The Kotlin plugin.spring compiler plugin automatically opens Spring-annotated classes, resolving the friction Kotlin's default final classes would otherwise cause with Spring's proxying, so no additional configuration is needed for this to work correctly.

None of this means avoiding @SpringBootTest. A full application context is the right tool whenever a test genuinely needs to exercise behavior that spans multiple layers, for example, an HTTP request that flows through a controller, a service, and a repository. The goal isn't eliminating full-context tests; it's making sure you're not accidentally paying the full-context startup cost two, three, or five times over in a single suite when one shared context would do.

Test slices selectively, not as a default performance fix

Spring Boot's test slices (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest, @JdbcTest, @JsonTest, @RestClientTest) load only the portion of your application relevant to a specific concern. A @DataJpaTest context contains JPA repositories and the JPA layer, nothing else. A @WebMvcTest context contains MVC infrastructure without starting a full servlet container.

Slices are useful when a test genuinely exercises only one layer. A repository test that validates a complex JPQL query doesn't need your HTTP layer. A controller test that validates request validation logic doesn't need your database. For those cases, a slice gives you a faster, more focused test.

The trap is treating slices as a general performance fix. Each distinct slice configuration that differs from another creates its own application context. A suite with ten @DataJpaTest classes using the same configuration shares one context. A suite with five different slice types, each loaded with different imports, creates five separate contexts, and the cumulative startup cost can exceed that of a single, well-shared full context.

Use a slice when it provides a meaningful testing boundary for the layer under test. For tests that validate behavior spanning multiple layers, prioritize reusing a small number of shared full contexts over reaching for a narrower slice.

Use Testcontainers without repeatedly starting containers

H2 is a convenient in-memory database for local testing, but it doesn't behave like PostgreSQL or MySQL in ways that affect production correctness. PostgreSQL enforces stricter type checking, so implicit casts that H2 accepts silently will fail at runtime against Postgres. Indexing semantics differ, and constraint enforcement, particularly around deferred constraints and transaction isolation, behaves differently. A green test suite against H2 can mask bugs that surface only under the production database engine.

Testcontainers solves this by running your actual database engine in a Docker container during tests. The startup cost is real (a PostgreSQL container cold-start typically takes a few seconds), but you pay it once per suite, not once per test class.

With Spring Boot 3.1+, the @ServiceConnection annotation eliminates the boilerplate of manually wiring container ports into Spring's datasource configuration, and it's unchanged under Spring Boot 4. Declare the container in a shared @TestConfiguration class and import it wherever needed:

@TestConfiguration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class TestcontainersConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ServiceConnection
    fun postgresContainer(): PostgreSQLContainer<*> =
        PostgreSQLContainer("postgres:17-alpine")
}

For @DataJpaTest slices, Spring attempts to replace your datasource with an embedded database by default. Suppress that behavior with @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE) and import your shared container configuration:

@DataJpaTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)
@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration::class)
class BookmarkRepositoryTest @Autowired constructor(
    private val bookmarkRepository: BookmarkRepository
) {

    @Test
    fun `should find bookmark by id`() {
        val bookmark = bookmarkRepository.save(
            Bookmark(title = "Kotlin Docs", url = "https://kotlinlang.org")
        )
        val found = bookmarkRepository.findById(bookmark.id!!)
        assertThat(found).isPresent
        assertThat(found.get().title).isEqualTo("Kotlin Docs")
    }
}

Two dependency details are worth getting right here if you're on Spring Boot 4. First, @DataJpaTest itself now lives in spring-boot-data-jpa-test, pulled in via the spring-boot-starter-data-jpa-test starter, not the plain spring-boot-starter-test. Second, @AutoConfigureTestDatabase moved too: it's now org.springframework.boot.jdbc.test.autoconfigure.AutoConfigureTestDatabase, shipped in a separate spring-boot-starter-jdbc-test starter that spring-boot-starter-data-jpa-test doesn't pull in automatically, so you need to add it explicitly:

testImplementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-data-jpa-test")
testImplementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-jdbc-test")
testImplementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-testcontainers")
testImplementation("org.testcontainers:junit-jupiter")
testImplementation("org.testcontainers:postgresql")

@ServiceConnection itself, by contrast, didn't move; it's still org.springframework.boot.testcontainers.service.connection.ServiceConnection on Spring Boot 4. Not everything in the test-support space was reshuffled, just the test-slice annotations and the autoconfiguration classes that back them.

If you prefer declaring the container directly in the test class, Kotlin's companion objects with @JvmStatic ensure the container lifecycle spans all methods in the class rather than restarting for each test:

@DataJpaTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)
@Testcontainers
class OrderRepositoryTest {

    companion object {
        @Container
        @ServiceConnection
        @JvmStatic
        val postgres = PostgreSQLContainer("postgres:17-alpine").apply {
            withDatabaseName("testdb")
        }
    }

    @Autowired
    private lateinit var orderRepository: OrderRepository

    @Test
    fun `should save and retrieve an order`() {
        // test body
    }
}

The goal is to combine a reused container with a reused Spring context. When your test configuration is consistent, Spring's cache keeps the same context alive across all test classes that share the same container configuration, and the database container itself stays running for the duration of the build.

For database state, build only what each test actually needs. A test that validates order retrieval doesn't need a populated product catalog. Lightweight, targeted setup with @BeforeEach and @AfterEach cleanup (or transaction rollback via @Transactional) keeps tests isolated without requiring full database resets between every run.

A practical strategy for a fast integration test suite

The context sharing model below keeps a suite fast by mapping each test type to its context and container lifecycle:

The diagram below is the editable Mermaid source — useful if you want to adjust colors or labels. A rendered image follows it.

flowchart TD
    A[Full Integration Tests<br/>@SpringBootTest + Testcontainers] --> B[Single shared<br/>Spring context]
    C[Slice Tests<br/>@DataJpaTest etc.] --> D[Shared slice<br/>context per type]
    E[Unit Tests] --> F[No Spring context]
    B --> G[Postgres container<br/>started once]
    D --> G

The strategy has seven parts:

  1. Keep one @TestConfiguration class that declares your Testcontainers beans with @ServiceConnection and import it consistently across all tests that need it.
  2. Align profiles. If some test classes use @ActiveProfiles("test") and others don't declare a profile at all, Spring treats them as different configurations and creates separate contexts.
  3. Reserve @DirtiesContext for tests that genuinely modify application-level state, not for tests with database state issues. Database state cleanup belongs in @AfterEach or via transactional rollback.
  4. Reach for a test slice only when the test's meaningful scope is genuinely limited to that layer. A repository test for a complex query is a good slice candidate. A test that exercises an HTTP endpoint through to the database is not.
  5. Start containers once and reuse them. Use withReuse(true) on your container definition to persist containers across JVM runs during local development, where it cuts iteration time substantially.
  6. Build only the database state each test actually needs. Seeding a full product catalog for a test that only checks order retrieval adds setup cost without adding coverage.
  7. Measure before and after changes. Run the test suite twice and enable DEBUG-level logging on org.springframework.test.context.cache (or equivalent context cache reporting) to confirm that context creation counts dropped and wall-clock time improved.

Make integration tests readable with Kotlin

Kotlin reduces the boilerplate that accumulates around integration tests, meaning less noise when a test fails and less maintenance when fixtures change. The techniques below don't make a suite faster on their own; they make an already-fast suite easier to read and maintain, which is what keeps it fast six months from now instead of sliding back into the state this article opened with.

Data classes eliminate the Java builder pattern for test fixtures. A Bookmark data class with sensible defaults can be constructed with a single named argument for the one field a specific test cares about:

data class BookmarkFixture(
    val title: String = "Default Title",
    val url: String = "https://kotlinlang.org",
    val isActive: Boolean = true
)

Named arguments make test data construction self-documenting. BookmarkFixture(title = "Archived Post", isActive = false) is readable without a builder chain.

Extension functions let you add setup utilities or assertion helpers directly to Spring test classes without inheritance hierarchies. A setup helper for building a JSON POST request:

fun MockMvc.postJson(url: String, payload: Any, objectMapper: ObjectMapper): ResultActionsDsl =
    post(url) {
        contentType = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON
        content = objectMapper.writeValueAsString(payload)
        accept = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON
    }

If you're on Spring Boot 4, the ObjectMapper import above is worth double-checking. Spring Boot 4 defaults to Jackson 3, pulled in through a new spring-boot-starter-jackson module, and Jackson 3's base package moved from com.fasterxml.jackson to tools.jackson, so the type you inject here is tools.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper, not the Jackson 2 class of the same simple name. If you're posting a Kotlin data class as the request body, also add tools.jackson.module:jackson-module-kotlin (the Jackson 3 equivalent of the familiar jackson-module-kotlin) as a dependency. Without it, Jackson can't resolve the data class's primary-constructor parameters, and the request fails with a 400 instead of a compile error, making it easy to lose an afternoon to.

And an assertion helper, scoped to the type it asserts on rather than to a test class:

fun Bookmark.assertIsActiveWithTitle(expectedTitle: String) {
    assertTrue(isActive)
    assertEquals(expectedTitle, title)
}

Kotlin DSLs built on extension functions and lambdas-with-receivers are what make the postJson helper above readable in the first place: post(url) { contentType = ...; content = ... } reads as configuration, not as a chain of setter calls. Spring's own MockMvc Kotlin DSL (post, get, .andExpect { status { isCreated() } }) follows the same pattern, and it's worth reaching for directly rather than only through a wrapping extension function when a test doesn't need one.

Scope functions (apply, also, run) clean up construction and setup code at the declaration site without extracting helper methods. apply is the one you'll reach for most, configuring an object and returning it, as in the companion-object container declaration from the Testcontainers section:

@JvmStatic
val postgres = PostgreSQLContainer("postgres:17-alpine").apply {
    withDatabaseName("testdb")
    withUsername("test")
    withPassword("test")
}

also is useful when you want to do something with a value, like logging it, without changing what gets returned, and run is useful for computing a value inline from a short block instead of a separate val statement:

val fixture = BookmarkFixture(title = "Kotlin Docs").also {
    println("creating bookmark fixture: ${it.title}")
}
val request = run {
    BookmarkRequest(title = fixture.title, url = fixture.url, isActive = fixture.isActive)
}

Put together, a small integration test combining a fixture, the postJson extension function, and a scope function reads as a short, flat sequence of steps rather than a wall of setup:

@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.MOCK)
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration::class)
@TestConstructor(autowireMode = TestConstructor.AutowireMode.ALL)
class BookmarkControllerIntegrationTest(
    private val mockMvc: MockMvc,
    private val objectMapper: ObjectMapper
) {

    @Test
    fun `creating a bookmark returns it in the response`() {
        val fixture = BookmarkFixture(title = "Kotlin Docs").also {
            println("creating bookmark fixture: ${it.title}")
        }
        val request = run { BookmarkRequest(title = fixture.title, url = fixture.url, isActive = fixture.isActive) }

        mockMvc.postJson("/api/bookmarks", request, objectMapper)
            .andExpect { status { isCreated() } }
    }
}

Note that @AutoConfigureMockMvc moved packages in Spring Boot 4 too, same as @WebMvcTest: it's org.springframework.boot.webmvc.test.autoconfigure.AutoConfigureMockMvc now, shipped in spring-boot-webmvc-test via the spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test starter.

These are incremental improvements, not architectural changes. You can introduce Kotlin test code into an existing Java Spring project without touching production code, which makes it a low-risk starting point for teams evaluating what Kotlin brings to their codebase.

Organize integration tests for long-term maintainability

A suite that's fast today becomes slow again if there's no shared understanding of its structure. Keep three distinct categories separate: unit tests (no Spring context, run fast), slice tests (partial context, targeted), and full integration tests (full context, shared container). Mixing these in the same test source set makes it difficult to see at a glance why a build is slow. Consistent naming helps here too; a suffix convention like *Test for units and slices versus *IntegrationTest for full-context tests, or separate source directories, lets you tell at a glance (and in CI timing reports) which category is growing.

Integration tests should assert on business behavior, not implementation details. A test that verifies the correct HTTP status code and response body when a user places an order is durable. A test that verifies the exact SQL statement executed against the database is brittle and couples the test to an implementation that can change without breaking the business requirement.

Avoid duplicating setup logic across test classes just because it's easier than sharing it. A second @TestConfiguration import that's nearly identical to an existing one is exactly the kind of inconsistency that busts the context cache described earlier, so the maintainability concern and the performance concern point to the same fix.

Shared base classes are worth using when they genuinely simplify the suite, typically for consistent annotation setup and shared infrastructure, and worth avoiding when they become a dumping ground for setup logic that only some tests need. A shared annotations file (using Kotlin's @Target(AnnotationTarget.CLASS) composed annotations) is often cleaner:

@Target(AnnotationTarget.CLASS)
@Retention(AnnotationRetention.RUNTIME)
@SpringBootTest
@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration::class)
@TestConstructor(autowireMode = TestConstructor.AutowireMode.ALL)
annotation class IntegrationTest

Any @SpringBootTest class that uses @IntegrationTest instead gets a consistent cache key by definition, because the annotation composition is identical.

Treat test suite performance as an ongoing metric. Add context creation count and total suite duration to your CI output so regressions are visible before they compound. A suite that takes four minutes today will take twenty-two again in six months if nobody is watching the cost.

The fixes that move the needle on Spring Boot integration test performance share a common thread: reducing repeated initialization. Keep your Spring application contexts few and consistent so the cache does its job. Start Testcontainers infrastructure once and keep it alive across the test run. Use test slices when they define a genuine testing boundary, and avoid them when the goal is just a smaller context. Measure before and after so you know which bottleneck you actually solved.

Kotlin's language features sit naturally on top of this foundation. Data classes, extension functions, DSLs, named arguments, and scope functions cut boilerplate without changing how Spring tests work, making them a practical addition to a Java Spring project even before you change any production code. The formal partnership between JetBrains and Spring reflects this kind of incremental integration, with Kotlin as a natural evolution of the JVM development experience that complements your existing ecosystem. For a sense of what that looks like at scale, Verifone's architect discussed running Kotlin in mission-critical payment systems at KotlinConf, where reliability requirements are just as unforgiving as anything a slow test suite is standing in for.

title: Hibernate Under the Hood. Part 4: Querying
description:
The chapter on querying languages is where Hibernate stops being just "magic" and becomes a manageable tool. Here, it is crucial to understand three approaches and their boundaries: HQL/JPQL (declarative, object-oriented), Criteria API (programmatic, type-safe), and Native SQL (direct database access). In Spring projects, there is an additional layer on top of this: Spring Data JPA, which changes how you write 90% of your queries.

HQL and JPQL: Object-Oriented SQL

HQL is Hibernate's proprietary language, while JPQL is the JPA standard inspired by early HQL. It is important to know the relationship: HQL is a superset of JPQL. Any valid JPQL query is a valid HQL query, but not vice versa: HQL supports more features (e.g., insert ... select, which is absent in JPQL).

The main difference from SQL is that you operate on entities and their fields, not tables and columns. In HQL, Book is a Java class, and book.title is its field. Direct referencing of database table and column names is prohibited. Because of this, HQL is more compact than SQL and portable across different databases.

Mapping Example:

-- SQL
SELECT book.title, pub.name
FROM Book AS book
JOIN Publisher AS pub ON book.publisherId = pub.id
WHERE book.title LIKE 'Hibernate%'
ORDER BY book.title

// HQL / JPQL
SELECT book.title, pub.name
FROM Book AS book
JOIN book.publisher AS pub
WHERE book.title LIKE 'Hibernate%'
ORDER BY book.title

Note: the join is performed on the association (book.publisher), not on the foreign key column. Hibernate knows how to resolve it automatically.

Key HQL features you need to know:

  • Parameters: Named (:name) and positional (?1). Named parameters are preferred for readability, while positional ones are often used in native queries.
  • JOIN FETCH: The primary tool for combating the N+1 query problem. It loads the association immediately in a single query.
  • DTO projections: You can return a DTO directly instead of an entity, e.g., new com.example.dto.BookDto(book.title, pub.name). This saves memory and avoids creating managed objects.
  • update / delete: Bulk operations executed as a single SQL statement that bypass the Persistence Context (in-memory entities will not be updated — this is a pitfall).

HQL Pitfalls:

  • Bulk update/delete does not synchronize with the first-level cache. If you loaded a Book into the session and then executed update Book set title = ..., the in-memory object will retain the old title. You need session.clear() or refresh().
  • JOIN FETCH on two collections simultaneously results in a MultipleBagFetchException or a Cartesian product. The solution is to use @BatchSize / SUBSELECT, or split it into two separate queries.
  • JOIN FETCH + pagination (setMaxResults) can yield incorrect results: Hibernate applies the limit in memory, not in the SQL query. This is a known limitation.

Criteria API: Queries as Code

The Criteria API is a programmatic way to build queries. Instead of a string, you construct the query from objects: CriteriaBuilder, CriteriaQuery, Root, and Predicate. This provides type safety (the compiler checks field names if you use the metamodel) and flexibility for dynamic conditions.

When the Criteria API is indispensable:

  • Search screens with a variable set of filters. For example, a user might specify a price, category, brand — or nothing at all. Concatenating an HQL string with if statements is a source of bugs; the Criteria API handles this cleanly.
  • Dynamic sorting and pagination with type checking.
  • Building queries in libraries and frameworks where you do not know the entity structure in advance.

Example (simplified):

CriteriaBuilder cb = session.getCriteriaBuilder();
CriteriaQuery<Book> cq = cb.createQuery(Book.class);
Root<Book> book = cq.from(Book.class);

List<Predicate> predicates = new ArrayList<>();
if (title != null) predicates.add(cb.like(book.get("title"), "%" + title + "%"));
if (minPrice != null) predicates.add(cb.ge(book.get("price"), minPrice));

cq.where(predicates.toArray(new Predicate[0]));
cq.orderBy(cb.asc(book.get("title")));

List<Book> result = session.createQuery(cq).getResultList();

Drawbacks of the Criteria API:

  • Verbosity. A simple query turns into 10–15 lines of code.
  • Poorer readability compared to HQL, especially for complex joins.
  • Not for "one-off" queries. If a query is static, HQL is shorter and clearer.

Practical rule: static queries → HQL/JPQL; dynamic queries (search, filters) → Criteria API.

Native SQL: When ORM is Powerless

Sometimes you need to drop down to the database level. Native SQL is justified when:

  • You need a database-specific feature (window functions, LATERAL JOIN, hints, FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, specific syntax).
  • The query is too complex for HQL and easier to write in SQL than to assemble via Criteria.
  • You need maximum performance in a bottleneck where HQL generates suboptimal SQL.
  • You are working with stored procedures.

Example:

Book book = session.createNativeQuery(
    "SELECT * FROM books WHERE isbn = ?1", Book.class)
    .setParameter(1, isbn)
    .getSingleResult();

Native Query Pitfalls:

  1. Flush behavior: Hibernate does not flush by default before executing native queries, because it does not know which tables the query will affect. If there are unsaved changes in the Persistence Context, the native query might return stale data. The solution is an explicit session.flush() before the query or configuring the FlushMode.
  2. Result mapping: For simple cases (SELECT * matching an entity), Hibernate infers the mapping automatically. For complex queries (aliases, aggregates, joins), you need @SqlResultSetMapping or manual parsing of Object[], which is cumbersome and fragile.
  3. Portability: Native SQL ties you to a specific database dialect. If you plan to switch databases, use it sparingly.

Spring Data JPA: How It Looks

In Spring Boot, you rarely write session.createQuery() directly. Instead, you use Spring Data JPA repositories, which offer three levels of abstraction:

  • Derived queries (from method names): findByEmailAddressAndLastname(String email, String lastname) is automatically translated into JPQL: SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.emailAddress = ?1 AND u.lastname = ?2. This works for simple queries, but method names become cumbersome with 3+ conditions.
  • @Query with JPQL/HQL: An explicit query on a repository method. This is the standard for medium-complexity queries: 
   @Query("SELECT b FROM Book b JOIN FETCH b.author WHERE b.title LIKE %:title%")
   List<Book> findWithAuthorByTitle(@Param("title") String title);
  • @Query(nativeQuery = true): Native SQL when JPQL is insufficient. The nativeQuery flag explicitly tells Spring Data that this is not JPQL.

Important: Spring Data JPA does not generate JPQL for UPDATE and DELETE from method names — only for SELECT. For modifications, you need @Query + @Modifying.

What to Use When

Approach When to choose Pros Cons
HQL/JPQL Static queries, 80% of cases Compact, portable, readable Not for dynamic queries; strings are not checked by the compiler
Criteria API Dynamic filters, search, libraries Type-safe, flexible Verbose, harder to read
Native SQL DB specifics, complex queries, performance Full control over SQL Not portable, requires manual mapping, flush nuances
Spring Data (derived) Simple CRUD and selections Minimal code Cumbersome names, SELECT only
Spring Data @Query Medium-complexity queries Explicit, readable, located in the repository Strings are not checked by the compiler

What to Remember

  1. HQL is a superset of JPQL. Write in JPQL for portability; use HQL features consciously.
  2. HQL operates on entities, not tables. This is its strength (compactness, portability) and its limitation (cannot use DB-specific features).
  3. Criteria API is for dynamic queries, HQL is for static ones. Do not try to build a simple query using Criteria — it is overkill.
  4. Native SQL is a targeted tool. Always remember about flush and result mapping.
  5. JOIN FETCH is your best friend against N+1, but it has limitations (pagination, two collections).
  6. Bulk update/delete in HQL does not synchronize with the first-level cache. You need clear() after them.
  7. In Spring Data, 90% of queries are @Query with JPQL. Derived queries are for simple cases, native queries are for exceptions.

title: OmniMem 7: one app, no Docker
description:
OmniMem 7 is out, and it's a different kind of program. 6.x was four containers: Valkey with its search module, the Python MCP server, the web UI and the RSS worker, held together by a Docker Compose file. 7.0 is one Rust binary. It holds its own store, serves MCP, runs the RSS scheduler and the enrichment worker, and on a desktop it sits in your tray or menu bar with a settings window behind it.

Nothing else to install. No Docker, no database server, no Python. Download it, open it, and the embedding model fetches itself on the first start (about 90 MB, once).

Your memories come with you via a simple backup and import process, and they behave the way they did before. The 48 MCP tools have the same names, parameters and defaults, so an agent that knew OmniMem 6 knows OmniMem 7.

The first release is 7.0.3, on the releases page.

Why rewrite it

OmniMem's job is small: embed one memory, embed one query, search, rank. 6.x did that job well, but the machinery around it kept growing. Four images to pull and keep in step. A search index that lived beside the data and could drift from it, with phantom entries, silent index migration failures and tag-query quirks to work around. Each Python service loaded its own copy of the embedding model. And the only way to see your memories was a web UI on a port, which is one more thing listening on your machine. That setup was great for developing and testing the theories behind how memory and experience should live and work together, but I wanted to make this more accessible for everyone.

What 7 is

One process. The MCP server, the memory engine, the embedding model, RSS ingestion and the database all live in one binary. One embedder serves every caller. It's written in Rust, so it's memory safe and fast: a session's briefing arrives in about 6 ms.

One file. Memories live in SQLite. On start, every vector is loaded into one matrix per namespace and searched exactly, not approximately. At OmniMem's scale (tens of thousands of memories) a full scan takes a few milliseconds and gives the same answer every time. Filters are plain SQL, so there's no separate index left to drift from the data. A real 3,500-memory store comes to a 12.8 MB database.

Nothing leaves your machine. The embedding model (all-MiniLM-L6-v2 on ONNX Runtime) runs locally. The Anthropic API is only called if you give OmniMem a key for the optional Claude Haiku features: fact extraction, query expansion, deeper contradiction checks and RSS summaries.

Less on the network. Over HTTP, 7.0 serves /mcp, the OAuth 2.1 routes that protect it and /healthz. That's all. There is no web UI on a port and no /metrics.

On your desktop

There's an installer for each platform: a DMG for macOS (Apple silicon, 13.4 or later), an MSI for Windows 10 and 11, and a Flatpak for Linux desktops on amd64 and arm64.

OmniMem lives in the tray, or the menu bar on a Mac. The menu shows whether it's running and how many memories it holds, and it does the setup for you:

  • Add to Claude Code and Add to Claude Desktop check the client's settings first and never add OmniMem twice. An old omnimem entry pointing at a 6.x install is offered as Switch Claude Desktop here, which repoints it rather than adding a second.
  • Copy MCP URL covers every other agent with a bit of manual work.

Settings… opens a window with every page the 6.x web UI had (the dashboard, memories, search, projects, experience and the graveyard, skills with export and import, duplicates, contradictions, telemetry, token overhead, feeds and backups) plus a configuration page for everything a headless install sets in its environment (such as the OAuth settings or the Anthropic API key). The window's pages come from the app itself over a custom URL scheme. Nothing about them is reachable over a network, from your machine or anyone else's.

Secrets (your Anthropic key, the MCP access token, a Hugging Face token) go to the OS keychain: Keychain on macOS, Credential Manager on Windows, the Secret Service on Linux. Once saved they're never shown again.

On a server

omnimem serve is the same binary without the desktop parts, configured with the same environment variables as before.

  • .deb and .rpm for amd64 and arm64 install it as the omnimem systemd service, running as its own user, with one settings file (/etc/omnimem/omnimem.env) and its data in /var/lib/omnimem. There's a tarball with an install.sh for other distributions.
  • Docker: richarvey/omnimem:7.0.3, amd64 and arm64, with everything in one /data volume. A token is all it needs.
  • OAuth 2.1 is rebuilt by hand on axum, and every route, discovery document, challenge and error was checked against a capture of the 6.x server, so claude.ai and other OAuth clients connect as before. Tokens are stored only as SHA-256 hashes and survive restarts.

Linux builds need glibc 2.38 or newer (Debian 13, Ubuntu 24.04, Fedora 39 and later), a floor set by ONNX Runtime's library.

The same memory

This is the part that matters most. A rewrite that ranks your memories differently is a migration dressed up as an upgrade, so 7.0 was checked against 6.x at every step:

  • The vectors are the 6.7 vectors. The Rust engine was checked against full reference vectors the Python engine wrote, covering accents, CJK, emoji, empty text, truncation past 256 tokens and mixed-length batches. Deduplication, contradiction and skill clustering thresholds don't move.
  • Recall returns the same results. A real production backup of 3,500 memories was imported, and all 32 query and namespace searches tested returned an identical ordered top 10 to the Python engine's search over the same data. Every field survives an export.
  • Skills compile the same. Skill rendering matches the Python compiler byte for byte.
  • RSS reads the same articles. On the project's own reading list, the Rust parser picks out exactly the 59 articles 6.x's feedparser does, with the same keys, titles, dates and text.
