Recall scoring has three deliberate changes, all in the changelog:

  1. Recency declines from the day a memory is written, reaching 0.9 at 90 days and then falling 5% every 30 days to a 0.3 floor. 6.x held it flat at 1.0 for 90 days, so yesterday's memory and one from three months ago scored alike. The relevance floor reads raw similarity, so nothing extra is dropped.
  2. An abandoned outcome scores 1.0, not 0.1. The old weight buried the write-up of a failure along with the approach, so the one memory explaining why something didn't work ranked below almost everything else.
  3. Recording an abandonment no longer suppresses anything. Suppression hid the memory that explained the failure, and it was store-wide, so a dead end on one project silenced unrelated memories on another.

Memory your agent doesn't have to ask for

One finding shaped this release more than any other. Across twenty runs with OmniMem attached and the answer already in the store, the agent made zero memory calls of its own. The memory was there. Nothing asked it.

So 7.0 ships Claude Code hooks. omnimem hook puts the project's briefing into every session's opening context, read-only, in about 6 ms. Before a tool call that changes something, it checks the graveyard, and if the call proposes an approach this project already abandoned, it stops it and hands back what was abandoned, why, and what worked instead. It never guards a read, and it fails open on any error. At the end of a session it records what the session did, skips sessions that changed nothing and redacts credentials before writing.

Measured over ten pairs of runs on one task: every attempt at the abandoned approach was stopped before it ran, no run with the hooks reached a failing test suite (against 8 of 10 without them), and the runs cost 27% less.

Hardened before release

The whole Rust workspace was security reviewed before 7.0.0, with fixes in every crate. The headlines: the OAuth routes are size-capped, rate limited and strict about PKCE and redirect URIs; the settings panel carries no inline JavaScript and sends a Content Security Policy; skill bundles are read against their declared sizes, so a zip bomb is refused rather than inflated; RSS fetches refuse private and loopback addresses and re-check every redirect; and the model download verifies a sha256 from the hub. CI now runs cargo audit and gitleaks on every push. The full list is in the changelog.

Coming from 6.x

Your 6.x install keeps working, and nothing upgrades itself. When you're ready:

  1. On 6.x, take a backup: ask your agent to call dump_to_file(), or use the old web UI's Backups page.
  2. Stop 6.x, or at least make sure it isn't on port 8765.
  3. Install 7, then restore the backup on the settings window's Backups page, or run omnimem import omnimem_backup.json.

Backups don't carry vectors, so every memory is embedded again from its text. That's about 8 ms a memory, so a few thousand take well under a minute and 25,000 take roughly three and a half minutes. It also has a side benefit: any memory 6.x had stopped finding, because its stored vector had gone missing or stale, is found again.

If you aren't ready, the 6.x Docker stack carries on from the v6.7.x branch, and the old one-line installer still sets up 6.7.

A few things are gone on purpose: Valkey and every VALKEY_* setting, the Compose stack, the web UI on port 8080, /metrics and the SSE transport. If an agent's config still says "type": "sse" or ends in /sse, point it at http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp instead. The configuration reference lists every setting that went.

Rough edges

  • No Intel Mac build. ONNX Runtime ships no prebuilt library for Intel macOS, so the DMG is Apple silicon only.
  • The Windows installer isn't signed yet, so SmartScreen asks first: More info, then Run anyway.
  • In the Flatpak, Add to Claude Code can't work, because the sandbox can't see a claude installed outside it. The menu says so, and claude mcp add does the job.
  • Stock GNOME doesn't show tray icons without the AppIndicator extension. Where there's no tray, OmniMem opens its settings window instead and says which extension to install.

Get it now

  • OmniMem 7.0.3 on the releases page, with a .sha256 beside every file
  • Quick start
  • omnimem.org

OmniMem is open source, MIT licensed, and free. Issues and ideas are welcome on GitHub.

title: What max.poll.interval.ms bounds in Kafka Streams, measured
description:
Kafka Streams scales by dividing the work. Each partition of the input becomes a task. The tasks are spread over the stream threads of all the instances that share an application.id. Add an instance, or raise num.stream.threads, and the group hands the new threads some of the tasks.

The threads share no state, so they need no coordination among themselves. The consumer group coordinates them instead. It distinguishes a working thread from a stuck one by the poll: a thread has to call poll() at least every max.poll.interval.ms. If it does not, the group rebalances. It takes the thread's tasks away and hands them to the others.

A rebalance has a cost. Whatever a thread had done since its last commit is done again by the next owner of its tasks. A stateful task that moves to another instance cannot resume until its state stores are restored from their changelog topics. Kafka's docs name that restoration as the main cost of moving a task (Fault Tolerance). A standby replica shortens it. Another instance keeps a copy of the state up to date, and the task moves there. Standbys are off by default.

When you add an instance, the rebalance that follows is worth its cost. When a slow thread causes one, it is best avoided. This post is about the second kind.

Polling in time is easy while each record takes microseconds or milliseconds. A remote call changes that. Each record takes as long as the service takes to answer, or until a timeout cuts the call off. The thread waits either way. This is not yet the common case for Kafka Streams, and the standard advice is not to block a stream thread at all. On the other hand, we expect such calls to become more common. More teams now call external services on events as they arrive: an AI model's API above all, but also a scoring service, or anything else that answers in seconds.

A service's answer time also changes over the day. It answers quickly when it is quiet and slowly when it is busy. It is often busiest just when your stream has the most to send it. A slow service is a known hazard. A service that becomes slow is a different one. It hurts the threads that had been keeping up, not the ones that were already behind. We come to why later in the post.

The usual reading is that max.poll.interval.ms bounds one call. Keep each call under it, and the thread keeps its tasks. It bounds something larger. On Kafka Streams 4.2.0, we saw threads evicted from the group even though every call took well under the poll interval. Here is what we found, with the section that shows each:

  • The poll interval bounds more than one call. A thread with several tasks makes a call for each of them between two polls (the round).
  • A thread that had been fast was evicted again and again once its service slowed, at the default settings (a fast thread's service slows down).

Two things depend on the group, not the thread. A rebalance opened by another member can evict a thread whose settings are safe. And under Kafka's newer streams protocol, what an eviction costs depends on who else is in the group. Both are measured in a coming post.

We measured each case in a run, and predicted each run before it ran. Every run used a single machine with one broker and a stub HTTP service whose latency we set. Every run used the classic group protocol, Kafka Streams' default group.protocol. A mapValues called it and blocked until it answered. The use case is illustrative: a stream that sends each new security advisory, a CVE, to a service that scores it. The records were real, newly published CVEs, replayed from one captured window. The numbers describe the shape of the problem, not your cluster. The method, and the predictions that were wrong, are in How the numbers were made.

The stream thread's loop

Matthias J. Sax explains the stream thread's loop in his talk The Nuts and Bolts of Kafka Streams. From about nine minutes in, he covers the buffers, the bursts of records per task and why their size is adjusted. We build on his picture and follow one case: what that adjustment does to a thread whose every record waits on a slow call.

Between two polls, the thread has work that comes due. A commit is due once the commit interval has passed, and a poll before the poll interval runs out. A punctuation is due when it is scheduled. Checking for due work after every record would cost time. Checking too rarely would make that work late. So the thread works in passes of up to N records per task and checks after each pass. While nothing is due, it adds one to N, and the passes grow. When something comes due, it halves N, so the next check comes sooner. It is the rule TCP uses for its congestion window: grow slowly, back off fast. The rule assumes a record is cheap, microseconds or milliseconds. A remote call breaks that assumption. The rest of this post follows what happens then, and which settings keep a thread in its group.

A poll hands its records to queues, one for each task and input partition. When a queue holds more than buffered.records.per.partition records, 1,000 by default, its partition is paused (StreamTask). The thread stops fetching from it until the queue is back within the limit. It still has to poll in time. In a pass, the tasks take turns. Each runs up to N records from its queue, one after another, before the next task starts (TaskExecutor). With three tasks, A, B and C, and N at 2, a pass runs two records from each in turn: A, A, B, B, C, C. After each pass, the thread decides what comes next (StreamThread, lines 1298 to 1320).

The loop: what a stream thread does after each pass, in Kafka Streams 4.2.0.

after each pass:
  run any punctuation that is due
  commit, if commit.interval.ms has passed on the commit clock
  if the pass processed nothing:
      go back and poll
  else if the time since the last poll is past half of max.poll.interval.ms:
      halve N, and go back and poll
  else if the pass committed or punctuated:
      halve N, and run another pass
  else:
      add one to N, and run another pass

The figure below follows the loop for three tasks at the default settings. Each call takes 40 seconds, longer than most, so that every pass is wide enough to see. Every pass takes longer than the 30-second commit interval, so every pass ends in a commit. Each commit halves N, and N never drops below 1, so each pass runs one record per task. The first pass ends at 120 seconds, short of the half-way mark, and the thread runs another. The second ends at 240 seconds, past the mark, and the thread polls with 60 seconds to spare.

Almog Gavra's Kafka Streams 101 on configs names the half-interval check. Two facts the rest of this post leans on are less known. N starts at 1 when the thread starts (line 877) and is never reset. It is carried from one poll to the next and, as we will see, across a rebalance. And a pass processes nothing only when none of its tasks has a record it can process. With a slow call and a backlog there always is one, so only the half-interval check sends the thread back to poll.

This is the default loop of 4.2.0. A second one, with processing threads, sits behind an internal flag that defaults to false. The code itself describes it as incomplete, and nothing here applies to it.

The unit is the round

A thread polls only after a whole pass, so what has to fit inside max.poll.interval.ms is not one call. It is at least one record of each of the thread's tasks, one after another. We call that a round: with T tasks on a thread and a call of L seconds, about T x L. A. Sophie Blee-Goldman put it in one sentence in Kafka Streams 101: Optimizing your apps: a thread makes progress as long as it processes one record per task within the poll interval.

The round grows with the tasks on a thread, as the figure below shows. An input topic of 32 partitions gave a single thread 32 tasks, and a round of 32 calls. With 32 threads, each had one task, and a round of one call.

In the figure above, every round fits the poll interval with room to spare, so a slow call costs only throughput. A round longer than the poll interval costs more. To show it, we set up a case on purpose: three tasks on one thread, a 12-second call, and a 30-second poll interval, so a round takes 36 seconds. The figure below draws its first pass. Every call fits well inside the poll interval, even inside half of it. The round does not, and at 30 seconds the client leaves the group.

We stopped the run after 210 seconds. In that time the thread was evicted four times and never committed. Each CVE should give one output record, but the thread had written 17 records for only 7 CVEs, the first few of each partition, again and again. Left running, it would have written more records for the same 7, and never reached the rest of the backlog.

The 30-second poll interval is the default of 300 scaled down tenfold, only to keep the run short. Later sections call these runs the scaled runs. At the default, the same case is thirty tasks and a 12-second call. Thirty tasks is what the default of one thread gets from a topic with thirty partitions, and an AI model writing a long answer can take 12 seconds. Or it is three tasks and a 120-second call. A call can take that long when the service is overloaded, or when the client retries with backoff. Several later runs use a 120-second call on a single task. What counts is the round, and ten tasks at 12 seconds make the same 120-second round. One task is simply easier to follow.

The commit interval is the other clock

With slow calls, leave commit.interval.ms at its default. Raising it saves little, and it opens a way to be evicted. The mechanism still matters, because a pass without a commit is also how a later case ends in an eviction: a thread whose service slows.

The round is not the whole story. How many rounds a thread runs before it polls depends on commits, as the loop shows. A commit is due when commit.interval.ms has passed on the thread's commit clock, which starts at the last commit (maybeCommit). A pass that commits halves N, the number of records each task runs in a pass. A pass without a commit grows it.

The defaults are a 30-second commit interval against a 300-second poll interval. Every pass longer than 30 seconds then commits, so N stays at 1, and a thread whose round fits the poll interval polls in time. That holds for a latency that has been steady since the thread started, and in a group with no rebalance under way. The first condition comes back below, and the second in a coming post. We checked it without scaling: one task, a 120-second call, 15 minutes. The thread committed after every record and never rebalanced, and the output held 7 records of 7 CVEs.

Each commit costs work: the thread flushes its state stores and writes its offsets, and processes nothing meanwhile. Raising commit.interval.ms saves some of that, which can buy throughput. With calls that take seconds, the saving is small, and the cost is what follows.

Raise commit.interval.ms above the length of a round, and a pass can end with no commit due. We ran the same one-task, 120-second call with both intervals at 300 seconds. The first pass after the poll ended at 120 seconds. That was not past the half-way mark of 150, and no commit was due. So N went to 2, and the next pass took two records, another 240 seconds. The thread could poll again only at 360 seconds, past the poll interval. A rebalance followed at 363.8 seconds, and the output held 7 records for 4 CVEs.

We call the range this round falls in the band: longer than a third of the poll interval, shorter than half. A round in the band ends its first pass before the half-way mark, so the thread does not poll. With no commit due, N goes to 2, and the second pass takes two rounds. The thread can poll only after three rounds, and three rounds run past the interval. A round under a third survives, because three rounds still fit. A round over half survives too, because its first pass crosses the half-way mark and the thread polls.

It is the client that leaves. When the poll timer expires, its own heartbeat thread sends the leave, and the processing thread learns of it at its next commit.

Runs on both sides of the band agree. In the scaled runs, the commit interval was left at 30 seconds against a 30-second poll interval, so commits were rare by accident. A round of 12 seconds (0.4 of the poll interval) was evicted and wrote 96 duplicates in 256 records. Rounds of 9 seconds (0.3) and 17 seconds (0.57) were not. One case needs care even at the defaults. A round just under half polls only after two rounds, seconds before the poll interval runs out. We measured the band with the commit interval equal to the poll interval. Other settings above the round follow from the loop, not from a run.

The same clock explains a smaller oddity. Commits land later than the commit interval says: about 35 seconds apart with a 300 ms call, and 35 to 40 with a 3-second one in a scaled run. A commit waits for the pass in progress, and between commits the passes grow by a round each. Apurva Mehta and A. Sophie Blee-Goldman's exactly-once guide calls the commit interval a lower bound, and this is why.

After an eviction

Go back to the band run of the last section: one task, a 120-second call, and both intervals at 300 seconds. It was evicted, and rebalanced at 363.8 seconds. Our first reading of the loop said it would then be evicted every time it rejoined, since it would start the same way again. It was not. After rejoining, it kept its place, because a rebalance is not a fresh start. One thing survives it that a restart would reset, and one thing restarts.

N survives. The failed commit that reveals the eviction throws from the commit check, before N is adjusted, and N is reset only when the thread starts. So the first pass after rejoining took two records, 240 seconds, crossed the half-way mark and polled in time.

The commit clock restarts. The clock counts the time since the last commit. Once it passes the commit interval, the next commit check commits, and restarts the clock even when there is nothing to commit (line 1881). After the rejoin, the task needs a moment to start, and the thread runs a few passes that process nothing. The first of them finds a commit overdue, commits nothing and restarts the clock. So the next real commit falls due 300 seconds after the rejoin. The log does not show those empty passes. We inferred them because nothing else fits the timings, and we predicted the next eviction from them.

We ran the same settings again for 1,500 seconds, and they did what that predicted. The thread rebalanced at 363.4 and 1,203.9 seconds, committed once between them at about 725, and wrote 12 records for 7 CVEs. A thread in the band is evicted again, but not every time it rejoins. When depends on where N and the commit clock stand. Each eviction costs the calls made since the last commit, made and written again.

When a fast thread's service slows down

That N survives a rebalance has a consequence that matters more than the band, and it needs no setting raised. N has no upper limit in the code. It grows by one after every pass that neither committed nor punctuated, however few records the pass held. A stream that keeps up therefore carries a large N. Ours, at 25 records a second with the service answering at once, reached 221 in two minutes. A pass runs at most N records per task, but only the records waiting in the queues. So a large N means a pass takes everything waiting.

A commit halves N only when the check falls on a pass that held records. On an idle pass it leaves N alone, and most passes of a stream that keeps up are idle. In another run of the same two minutes, one check did land on a pass with records, and N ended at 124. Kafka logs N at DEBUG in every pass, as "iterations", which is where these numbers come from (line 1283).

Then we slowed the service to 10 seconds a call, a thirtieth of the poll interval, with 40 records waiting and every setting at its default. The thread took the 40 as one pass of 400 seconds, with no look at the clock inside it. The poll timer expired at 300. The pass's commit, the first attempt in 415 seconds, failed. N was 222 after the rebalance as before it, so the next pass was the same records again. It was evicted every time it rejoined: 401, 811 and 1,222 seconds after the slow-down, and a fourth was under way when the run ended. In all, 155 records were written for 41 CVEs, 154 of them from calls of 10 seconds, and not one was committed.

The same 40 records at the same 10 seconds were no trouble for a thread that starts on them. N went 1, 2, 1, 2, with a commit after every second pass. There was no rebalance, and all 40 were done in about 400 seconds. The two threads differ only in their history. No setting states it, and nothing about the slow call shows it.

Ten seconds after an instant answer is an extreme slow-down. We chose it so that one run would be short and leave no doubt. The arithmetic of the loop puts the line much lower. With N at 222 and that many records waiting, a pass is 222 calls back to back. It has to end within the 300-second poll interval, so each call can take at most 300 ÷ 222, about 1.35 seconds. Any slower, and one pass outlasts the poll interval. The 222 is measured. The 1.35 seconds is only that division: we did not run a slow-down to it.

One more condition belongs here. We placed the backlog whole: the thread was held in one call while the 40 arrived, so that its next poll returned all of them. A backlog that builds by itself reaches the thread one poll at a time. Each pass then takes what arrived during the one before. When records arrive faster than the service answers, each pass is longer than the last. Arriving more slowly is not enough on its own: a backlog already waiting is taken in one pass, up to max.poll.records of it, and that pass still has to fit the poll interval. This follows from the loop, and we did not run it either.

The thread does not get out by itself. Each time it rejoins, N is still 222, the pass is the same 40 records, and the commit that would halve N is the one that fails. Only a new thread starts N at 1 again. Restarting the instance gives one, and so does replacing the thread at runtime with removeStreamThread() and addStreamThread(). The thread that started on the backlog shows what follows. A restart redoes the uncommitted records once. It is a cure, not a prevention: once the service is fast again, N grows back, and the next slow-down sets the same trap. To stay out, cap max.poll.records, so that a poll's worth of slow calls fits inside the poll interval. It saved this thread with nothing else changed, as the levers below show.

The levers, and what each costs

max.poll.interval.ms. Raising it lets a longer round fit, so a thread that was being evicted keeps its place and its calls are not made again. It adds no throughput: a stream that was being evicted falls behind quietly instead. And it has two costs.

The first: a thread that is alive but stuck, on a call with no timeout, keeps its partitions until the poll interval runs out. A process that dies is still noticed sooner, by the session timeout, because heartbeats come from a thread of their own.

The second: with the classic protocol, the default, a rebalance waits for every member to rejoin, up to the poll interval, as Blee-Goldman's guide to rebalancing describes. A busy thread rejoins only after the pass that takes it past half the poll interval. So with a 30-minute poll interval, a new instance can wait 15 minutes for its tasks, and longer by however long that pass takes. That follows from the loop, and we did not measure it. Until Kafka 2.3, Streams set this interval to effectively infinite. KIP-442 returned it to the consumer's default.

commit.interval.ms. Lowering it means more commits, and each one is a flush and an offset write during which the thread processes nothing. Raising it above the length of a round opens the band from a third to a half of the poll interval. Keep a round under a third then.

max.poll.records. Streams sets it to 1,000, and every run but one left it there. It caps what one poll hands the thread. For a thread whose N is larger than that, it caps the pass. We ran the fast stream that slows once more, with nothing changed but this setting, at 20. The poll returned 20 of the 40 waiting records, and the pass was 200 seconds. Its commit went through with 100 seconds to spare and halved N, and the other 20 went the same way. There was no eviction, and each record was done once, where at the default it had been evicted every time it rejoined.

KAFKA-14382 names lowering it as a workaround that shortens the processing loop. This is that, measured for one value. By the loop, the rule is that a poll's worth of calls has to fit the poll interval: max.poll.records times the call. What it costs a stream while it is fast, more polls for the same records, we did not measure.

More instances. They add threads, and threads add throughput when a round fits. They do not rescue a round in the band. A coming post shows that a second instance made the repeated work worse.

For a long call, then, these settings keep a thread in its group. Start with a timeout on every call, retries included. The other settings rest on it: without a timeout, no record has an upper limit, and no setting is safe. Keep commit.interval.ms at its default, below a round, so every pass commits and N stays at 1. Give each thread few enough tasks that a round fits well inside the poll interval. Cap max.poll.records so that a poll's worth of calls at the timeout fits too. That cap is what kept the thread whose service slowed. Raise max.poll.interval.ms last, for the costs above.

What we did not measure

A single machine with one broker, and a stub whose latency has no tail. A round just under half the poll interval has no margin for one.

A latency that changes, beyond one case. Every run but two held the call's latency steady from the start. The fast stream that slows was run twice, at 10 seconds, on one task, with its backlog placed whole: once at the default max.poll.records, and once at 20. A slow-down that comes gradually, a backlog that builds by itself, a service that recovers while a pass is under way, and other latencies are readings of the loop.

Exactly-once. Every run was at-least-once. A transactional commit takes another path through the broker, and the commit interval's default is different.

Kafka Streams 4.2.0 only. In that version, restoration runs on a separate state-updater thread by default, which is one way the loop can differ from older versions. We make no claim about any version whose source we have not read. Nor do we claim anything about the loop with processing threads, which 4.2.0 keeps switched off.

And one thing we saw and have not explained. In the run of The unit is the round, three tasks at 12 seconds against a 30-second poll interval, the rebalances came 36 seconds apart. Once, the gap was 72. If you know why, or have seen the same on your own cluster, tell us in Discussions. We will add what we learn to this post.

How the numbers were made

Every run was written down as a prediction before it ran. Its result was added after, without editing the prediction. The early runs were predicted from a model of the loop, the later ones from its source.

Several predictions were wrong, two of them about the mechanism. The first model, one round per poll, predicted that one task per thread would make a 12-second call safe against a 30-second poll interval. It was evicted. Reading StreamThread is how we found the adaptive pass. Sax's talk, which we found afterwards, explains it too. The prediction for the 120-second call with rare commits rested on a false detail, that the first pass would commit, so its eviction came earlier than predicted. Two more missed a number: commits predicted 30 seconds apart came 35 apart, and one end count was an arithmetic slip.

A note on names, for readers who open the source. The field that holds N is called numIterations. Kafka's thread metrics count an iteration as one poll and all the processing after it, which can hold several passes. We say pass to keep the two apart.

The stub, the replay script and the application are not published. If you want to run them against your own numbers, write to info@alginte.com and we will send them.

This post is one of a few on calling a service from Kafka Streams. A coming one starts from the timeout on every call: how to make sure a call is really cut off, and the arithmetic that then says which settings are safe. To get it, follow the blog's RSS feed or @alginte_sw on X, where we post each one.

Related reading

  • Matthias J. Sax, The Nuts and Bolts of Kafka Streams (Current 2023): the architecture this post rests on, from the threading model to restoration.
  • A. Sophie Blee-Goldman, Kafka Streams 101: Optimizing your apps (2025): the round, in one sentence.
  • KAFKA-14382: stream threads that process too long miss rebalances, and what shortens it.

title: 15 of 16 Mac UI tests failed: what SwiftUI on macOS taught us
description:
Our notes app, MindPage, is one SwiftUI codebase for iPad, iPhone and Mac. The iPhone and iPad UI tests were green. Then we ran the Mac suite, which drives the real app with mouse and keyboard through XCUITest. 15 of 16 tests failed. By the end of the day it was 16 of 16, alongside 43 iPhone and 44 iPad tests.

Roughly half the failures were real Mac bugs, and half were the tests. Here is each one, with the cause, because most of them are SwiftUI-on-macOS behaviours that aren't obvious if you build iPad first.

The scoreboard

Run Passing What changed
1 1 / 16 first Mac run
2 6 / 16 sidebar width, a button label, a missing test ID
3 9 / 17 choose() skips disabled items, text queries narrowed, ⌘V fixed (+1 temporary probe test)
4 15 / 16 undo version, pen bar hit area, photo accessibility, Search/Summarize/Word lookups
5 16 / 16 last query narrowed

Real bug 1: toolbar items silently moved to the overflow menu

On macOS, .toolbar items attached to a NavigationSplitView sidebar render in the toolbar above the sidebar. Our sidebar was 148 pt wide. Three buttons plus the system "Hide Sidebar" button didn't fit next to the traffic lights, so macOS moved New folder, sync status and Settings into "more toolbar items". No warning, no layout error.

#if os(macOS)
.navigationSplitViewColumnWidth(min: 300, ideal: 300)
#endif

230 pt was not enough; the window controls take about 100 pt.

Real bug 2: a split button announced as "add"

A Menu with a primaryAction becomes a pop-up button on macOS. Its inner button took its accessibility label from the SF Symbol (plus), so VoiceOver said "add". .accessibilityLabel("New notebook") on the menu fixes VoiceOver; in XCUITest you then find it as app.popUpButtons["New notebook"], not app.buttons.

Real bug 3: undo history wiped after every stroke

Our canvas sends each edit to the model as a small value: the page, the strokes before and after, and the version of the page it was drawn on. That version field had a default of 0.

If an edit's version is older than the model's, the page was reloaded by sync in between, so the model redraws from the merged page and bumps its version. The canvas reacts to a version bump by clearing undo history, because older steps may not fit the merged page.

The iPad canvas passed version. The Mac canvas didn't, so every edit had the default 0. Every stroke looked like it came from before a reload, and the history was wiped after each one. ⌘Z never had anything to undo.

The fix stamps the version on edits, and on undo/redo steps as they are replayed. The lesson is about defaults: a field with a harmless-looking default of 0 compiled fine and failed silently.

Real bug 4: .buttonStyle(.plain) only hits the glyph

The pen bar uses .plain so icons keep their own colours. On macOS a plain button's hit area is the drawn content. The accessibility frame of our Undo button was 12×12 pt inside a 30×30 frame, and the centre of arrow.uturn.backward is empty space. XCUITest clicks the centre, so nothing happened. A human hits it some of the time.

Button(action: undo) {
    Image(systemName: "arrow.uturn.backward")
        .frame(width: 30, height: 30)
        .contentShape(.rect)   // the whole square is the target
}
.buttonStyle(.plain)

In the same change we also took the bar's decorative capsule border out of hit testing (.allowsHitTesting(false)), so we can't say which of the two mattered more. Both are cheap; do both.

Real bug 5: ⌘V never reached the notebook

We had a Paste button in an Insert menu with .keyboardShortcut("v"). On macOS the main menu gets key equivalents first, and Edit ▸ Paste found no responder that could paste, so our shortcut never fired. The Mac way is to answer the standard command:

.onPasteCommand(of: [.image, .pdf, .fileURL, .plainText]) { _ in pasteFromClipboard() }

That only works when something in the view has focus, so the canvas also takes focus when the page opens (.focusable(interactions: .edit) plus @FocusState).

Real bug 6: the sign-in sheet had nowhere to appear

Not found by the suite. Google sign-in on Mac showed nothing. ASWebAuthenticationSession asks its context provider for a presentation anchor, and ours returned ASPresentationAnchor(). On iOS that's a fresh UIWindow, which happened to work. On macOS it's a fresh NSWindow that is never on screen. Return the app's key window instead. (The fix is in TestFlight; we're waiting on the first real sign-in to confirm.)

The test bugs

Failure Actual cause
Deleted notebook "still in the library" app.menuItems["Delete"] matched the menu bar's disabled Edit ▸ Delete first. Filter with isEnabled == true.
Can't click "Create" in a dialog The Touch Bar exposes a "Create" button too, and it can't be clicked. Query app.sheets.buttons or app.dialogs.buttons.
"Timed out while evaluating UI query" descendants(matching: .any).matching(predicate) over a page canvas and menu bar. Query typed elements (staticTexts, textViews, buttons) instead.
Word import "didn't open" It did. The page counter's text is in value, not label.
Stroke count unreadable macOS doesn't expose .accessibilityValue on a generic element. We moved the count into the label: "Page, 2 strokes".

What helped most

  1. Screen recordings. XCUITest attached an .mp4 per test to the .xcresult. One frame with ffmpeg -sseof -3 usually showed the answer. Search, Summarize and Word import were all visibly working while their tests failed.
  2. A probe test. A throwaway test that logs app.debugDescription and the state before/after one action found the undo and pen bar bugs in two runs.
  3. A separate bundle id for tests. The Mac suite launches com.mindscend.mindpage.uitest, ad-hoc signed with its own sandbox, so -resetLibrary never touches a real library.

About MindPage

MindPage is a local-first notes app for handwriting and PDFs: sync through your own Google Drive or iCloud Drive, AI on the device. Search runs on our own model, MindPage Search v2, fine-tuned from EmbeddingGemma 2 on what Apple Vision really reads from handwriting (R@1 85.9 vs 80.3 for v1 on 234 Vision-read handwritten pages). iPhone/iPad 1.1 is submitted to App Review, Mac is in TestFlight, and the web app is at mindscend.academy.

More: mindscendinc.com/mindpage

title: JUnit 6 Parameterized Tests: The Complete Guide to Data-Driven Testing on the JVM
description:
Writing the same test five times with different inputs is copying, not testing. Parameterized testing breaks that habit by letting you write a single assertion once and run it against as many datasets as the problem demands. JUnit 6 (the Jupiter framework) gives you a rich set of argument sources, clean display names, and enough flexibility to handle everything from a handful of strings to deeply nested domain objects.

For developers building Spring Boot services, getting good at parameterized testing pays compound interest. Service layer logic, validation rules, pricing calculations, and repository queries all share the same structure: given some input, expect some output. Parameterized tests make that pattern explicit and give you a test suite that grows with your domain model.

Most developers run into friction with complex inputs: DTOs, entity objects, configuration records, and the boilerplate required to construct them in Java.

This guide walks through every major parameter source in JUnit 6, shows when and why to reach for each one, covers the specific patterns that surface in Spring Boot test suites across every layer (service, controller, repository, and configuration), and then demonstrates how Kotlin's data classes and named arguments cut test setup code without touching a single line of production Java.

What parameterized tests are

A parameterized test is a test method that JUnit runs multiple times, injecting a different set of arguments on each invocation. You write the assertion logic once, and the framework handles the loop. Each invocation is tracked, named, and reported independently in the test runner, so a failure on input three doesn't mask a pass on input five.

The key annotation is @ParameterizedTest, which replaces @Test. You pair it with a source annotation that tells JUnit where to pull argument values from. JUnit 6 ships with sources for inline values, CSV rows, CSV files, factory methods, and pluggable providers, each suited to a different complexity tier.

Setup for parameterized tests

Required dependencies

If you're starting from a Spring Boot project, spring-boot-starter-test already pulls in the JUnit Jupiter engine. You need to add junit-jupiter-params explicitly if it's not coming in transitively from your BOM.

JUnit 6 raises the minimum Java version to 17 (JUnit 5 only required 8), and if you're writing tests in Kotlin, you'll need Kotlin 2.2 or newer. Spring Boot 4.x already baselines on Java 17 and manages compatible JUnit and Kotlin versions for you, so the simplest path is to build on Spring Boot 4.

Gradle (Kotlin DSL):

plugins {
    id("org.springframework.boot") version "4.1.1"
    id("io.spring.dependency-management") version "1.1.7"
    kotlin("jvm") version "2.3.21"
    kotlin("plugin.spring") version "2.3.21"
}

dependencies {
    implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-web")
    implementation("org.jetbrains.kotlin:kotlin-reflect")
    testImplementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-test")
    testImplementation("org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter-params")
}

tasks.withType<Test> {
    useJUnitPlatform()
}

For Maven, add junit-jupiter-params with test scope alongside spring-boot-starter-test.

IDE support

IntelliJ IDEA renders each parameterized invocation as a child node in the Run tool window, using whatever display name you configure. It warns you at edit time if you declare @ParameterizedTest without a source, highlights type mismatches between the source and the method signature, and excludes @MethodSource provider methods from "unused declaration" warnings. The gutter run icon lets you execute the entire parameterized suite or rerun only the specific invocations that failed.

Running tests in Maven and Gradle

Both build tools need useJUnitPlatform() (Gradle) or the maven-surefire-plugin configured for JUnit Platform to pick up Jupiter tests. Without this, parameterized tests either skip silently or report as errors rather than test failures.

One JUnit 6 constraint worth knowing up front: Maven Surefire and Failsafe versions older than 3.0.0 are no longer supported. If your pom.xml pins an older plugin version, bump it, or parameterized tests may not execute under the JUnit Platform at all.

Display names

@ParameterizedTest accepts a name attribute. The placeholders {index}, {0}, {1}, and {arguments} let you build readable names from the supplied values:

@ParameterizedTest(name = "[{index}] discount for {0} loyalty years = {1}%")

The test runner displays something like [3] discount for 5 loyalty years = 10%, which makes failures self-explanatory without opening the test body.

Using @ValueSource

@ValueSource supplies a single array of literals (strings, ints, longs, doubles, or class references) and is the right choice when your test needs one argument per invocation and the values are small enough to inline.

@ParameterizedTest
@ValueSource(strings = {"radar", "level", "kayak"})
void isPalindrome(String word) {
    assertTrue(IsPalindromeChecker.check(word));
}

When your data grows beyond three or four values, or when you need more than one argument per invocation, move to @CsvSource or @MethodSource.

Using @NullSource, @EmptySource, and @NullAndEmptySource

These three annotations inject edge-case inputs for null and empty states. They're most useful on service methods and validators that need to handle blank input gracefully.

@ParameterizedTest
@NullAndEmptySource
@ValueSource(strings = {" ", "\t", "\n"})
void rejectsBlankUsername(String username) {
    assertThrows(InvalidInputException.class,
        () -> userService.register(username, "valid@example.com"));
}

Combining @NullAndEmptySource with @ValueSource on the same method covers null, empty string, and whitespace-only inputs in one test method. JUnit 6 supports stacking these annotations.

One interop detail matters if the method under test is written in Kotlin: a Kotlin function with a non-nullable parameter (fun register(username: String, ...)) compiles a null-check at the start of the method body. Feed it a literal null from @NullSource, and you get a bare NullPointerException before your own validation logic ever runs — not the InvalidInputException the test expects. Declare the parameter as nullable (username: String?) and check it with username.isNullOrBlank() if you want @NullAndEmptySource to exercise your validation path rather than Kotlin's own null-check.

Using @CsvSource

@CsvSource supplies multiple arguments per invocation as comma-separated rows defined inline. Use it when you need two or three related values, and you want to keep the data close to the test:

@ParameterizedTest(name = "{0} + {1} = {2}")
@CsvSource({
    "1, 2, 3",
    "5, 5, 10",
    "-1, 1, 0",
    "100, -100, 0"
})
void addsCorrectly(int a, int b, int expected) {
    assertEquals(expected, calculator.add(a, b));
}

JUnit handles type conversion automatically, so the string "3" becomes the int 3 without any adapter code. For values that contain commas, wrap the field in single quotes, as in "'Smith, John', john@example.com, 30".

Under the hood, JUnit 6 replaced the CSV parser (it now uses FastCSV instead of univocity-parsers), and a few edge cases around quoting changed as a result — extra characters after a closing quote now throw instead of being silently ignored, for example. The common case above, including quoted fields containing commas, parses exactly the same as it did under JUnit 5.

@CsvSource starts to strain when you have more than six or seven rows, when values are long, or when you're reusing the same dataset across multiple test classes. At that point, use @CsvFileSource.

Loading test data with @CsvFileSource

@CsvFileSource reads rows from a file on the classpath:

@ParameterizedTest
@CsvFileSource(resources = "/test-data/pricing-scenarios.csv", numLinesToSkip = 1)
void calculatesPriceCorrectly(String tier, int loyaltyYears, boolean isVip, String expectedPrice) {
    // assertions
}

The numLinesToSkip = 1 skips the header row. The file sits under src/test/resources. Reach for this approach when your test dataset is large enough to be maintained separately, when it's shared with non-Java stakeholders (QA, product), or when it's generated by another tool.

Creating dynamic test data with @MethodSource

@MethodSource delegates to a factory method that returns a Stream<Arguments>, a List, or an Iterable. It's the right choice for complex objects, computed values, and any scenario where inline CSV can't express your data structure.

@ParameterizedTest(name = "{index}: {0}")
@MethodSource("pricingScenarios")
void calculatesPriceForAllTiers(PricingScenario scenario) {
    DiscountResult result = pricingService.calculate(scenario.input());
    assertEquals(scenario.expected(), result);
}

static Stream<Arguments> pricingScenarios() {
    return Stream.of(
        Arguments.of(new PricingScenario(
            "VIP with 5 loyalty years",
            new DiscountInput(new BigDecimal("200.00"), 5, true),
            new DiscountResult(new BigDecimal("150.00"), 25)
        )),
        Arguments.of(new PricingScenario(
            "Standard user, no discount",
            new DiscountInput(new BigDecimal("100.00"), 0, false),
            new DiscountResult(new BigDecimal("100.00"), 0)
        ))
    );
}

The factory method must be static by default because JUnit instantiates a new test class per invocation under the default PER_METHOD lifecycle. You can lift that restriction with @TestInstance(TestInstance.Lifecycle.PER_CLASS), which becomes particularly useful in Kotlin (covered in a later section).

Supplying data with a custom ArgumentsProvider

When you want to share a dataset across multiple test classes, or load data from an external source at runtime, implement ArgumentsProvider:

public class DiscountScenariosProvider implements ArgumentsProvider {
    @Override
    public Stream<? extends Arguments> provideArguments(ParameterDeclarations parameters, ExtensionContext context) {
        return Stream.of(
            Arguments.of(new DiscountInput(new BigDecimal("100.00"), 5, false),
                new DiscountResult(new BigDecimal("90.00"), 10)),
            Arguments.of(new DiscountInput(new BigDecimal("200.00"), 0, true),
                new DiscountResult(new BigDecimal("170.00"), 15))
        );
    }
}

Then reference it with @ArgumentsSource(DiscountScenariosProvider.class). The provider has access to the ExtensionContext, which means it can read annotations on the test class, inspect the test method name, or pull configuration from the JUnit store. That access is useful when you want a single provider to behave differently across different test contexts.

Note the two-argument provideArguments(ParameterDeclarations, ExtensionContext) signature above. The older single-argument provideArguments(ExtensionContext) still compiles and runs under JUnit 6, but it's deprecated — the compiler will flag it, and new providers should use the two-argument form.

Testing complex objects

Passing plain primitives through @CsvSource works until you need to test against DTOs, entity objects, or configuration objects. At that point, use @MethodSource or a custom ArgumentsProvider and construct your objects directly in the factory method.

DTOs. For a Spring Boot user registration endpoint, a validation test might look like this:

@ParameterizedTest(name = "{index}: {0}")
@MethodSource("invalidRegistrationRequests")
void rejectsInvalidRequests(String scenario, UserRegistrationRequest request, int expectedViolations) {
    Set<ConstraintViolation<UserRegistrationRequest>> violations = validator.validate(request);
    assertEquals(expectedViolations, violations.size(), scenario);
}

static Stream<Arguments> invalidRegistrationRequests() {
    return Stream.of(
        Arguments.of("blank username",
            new UserRegistrationRequest("", "valid@example.com", 25), 1),
        Arguments.of("invalid email",
            new UserRegistrationRequest("alice", "not-an-email", 25), 1),
        Arguments.of("negative age",
            new UserRegistrationRequest("bob", "bob@example.com", -1), 1),
        Arguments.of("blank username and invalid email",
            new UserRegistrationRequest("", "not-an-email", 25), 2)
    );
}

The scenario string argument doubles as a display name fragment and as an assertion message, so a failure tells you exactly which case broke without making you decode an index number.

Entity objects. The same pattern applies directly to JPA entities — construct them in the factory method and assert against their behavior:

@ParameterizedTest(name = "{index}: {0} matches category {1}? {2}")
@MethodSource("productsByCategory")
void filtersProductsByCategory(Product product, String category, boolean expectedMatch) {
    assertEquals(expectedMatch, product.getCategory().equals(category));
}

static Stream<Arguments> productsByCategory() {
    return Stream.of(
        Arguments.of(new Product("Laptop", "ELECTRONICS", new BigDecimal("999.00")), "ELECTRONICS", true),
        Arguments.of(new Product("Laptop", "ELECTRONICS", new BigDecimal("999.00")), "BOOKS", false)
    );
}

Configuration objects. Configuration-bound objects can be constructed directly too, which is useful for testing the logic that consumes them without spinning up a Spring context:

@ParameterizedTest(name = "{index}: enabled={0}, cap={1} -> bonus={2}")
@MethodSource("pricingConfigurations")
void loyaltyBonusRespectsConfiguration(boolean enabled, int cap, int expectedBonus) {
    PricingProperties properties = new PricingProperties(enabled, cap);
    int bonus = properties.isLoyaltyBonusEnabled() ? properties.getLoyaltyBonusCap() : 0;
    assertEquals(expectedBonus, bonus);
}

static Stream<Arguments> pricingConfigurations() {
    return Stream.of(
        Arguments.of(true, 10, 10),
        Arguments.of(true, 5, 5),
        Arguments.of(false, 10, 0)
    );
}

This verifies the logic that reads a configuration object in isolation. When you need to verify that Spring actually binds your application.properties values into that object correctly, that's a job for @SpringBootTest or ApplicationContextRunner, covered next.

Parameterized testing in Spring Boot

Combining @ParameterizedTest with Spring test slice annotations gives you data-driven coverage across every layer of a Spring Boot application.

Service layer tests run with plain constructor instantiation or with @SpringBootTest and @Autowired constructor injection:

@SpringBootTest
@TestInstance(TestInstance.Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)
class PricingServiceTest {

    @Autowired
    private PricingService pricingService;

    @ParameterizedTest
    @MethodSource("pricingCases")
    void calculatesPriceCorrectly(DiscountInput input, DiscountResult expected) {
        assertEquals(expected, pricingService.calculate(input));
    }

    Stream<Arguments> pricingCases() {
        return Stream.of(
            Arguments.of(new DiscountInput(BigDecimal.valueOf(100), 5, false),
                new DiscountResult(BigDecimal.valueOf(90).setScale(2), 10))
        );
    }
}

Validation tests follow the pattern shown earlier, building a jakarta.validation.Validator directly (no Spring context required) and running each invalid payload through it.

Before wiring up controller or repository tests, there's a dependency change worth knowing about: Spring Boot 4 split its test-support autoconfiguration into per-feature modules. spring-boot-starter-test alone no longer pulls in @WebMvcTest or @DataJpaTest — each needs its own starter:

testImplementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test")
testImplementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-data-jpa-test")

The annotations also moved packages. @WebMvcTest is now org.springframework.boot.webmvc.test.autoconfigure.WebMvcTest, and @DataJpaTest is org.springframework.boot.data.jpa.test.autoconfigure.DataJpaTest. Spring Boot's own @MockBean was removed in the same release — use Spring Framework's @MockitoBean (org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito.MockitoBean) in its place.

Controller tests with @WebMvcTest and MockMvc work naturally with @CsvSource or @MethodSource. You build the request body, fire it through mockMvc.perform(), and assert the response status per invocation:

@WebMvcTest(UserController.class)
class UserControllerParameterizedTest {

    @Autowired
    private MockMvc mockMvc;

    @MockitoBean
    private UserService userService;

    @ParameterizedTest(name = "{index}: {0}/{1} -> {2}")
    @CsvSource({
        "alice, valid@example.com, 201",
        "'', valid@example.com, 400",
        "bob, not-an-email, 400"
    })
    void registersUser(String username, String email, int expectedStatus) throws Exception {
        mockMvc.perform(post("/api/users")
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .content("""
                    {"username": "%s", "email": "%s", "age": 30}
                    """.formatted(username, email)))
            .andExpect(status().is(expectedStatus));
    }
}

Repository tests with @DataJpaTest can drive @ParameterizedTest to verify query correctness across different filter combinations (entity status enums, date ranges, or tier codes) without repeating setup for each case:

@DataJpaTest
class ProductRepositoryTest {

    @Autowired
    private ProductRepository productRepository;

    @ParameterizedTest(name = "{index}: {0} has {1} product(s)")
    @MethodSource("categoryExpectations")
    void countsProductsByCategory(String category, long expectedCount) {
        productRepository.save(new Product("Laptop", "ELECTRONICS", new BigDecimal("999.00")));
        productRepository.save(new Product("Monitor", "ELECTRONICS", new BigDecimal("199.00")));
        productRepository.save(new Product("Novel", "BOOKS", new BigDecimal("15.00")));

        long count = productRepository.findByCategory(category).size();
        assertEquals(expectedCount, count);
    }

    static Stream<Arguments> categoryExpectations() {
        return Stream.of(
            Arguments.of("ELECTRONICS", 2L),
            Arguments.of("BOOKS", 1L)
        );
    }
}

Configuration property testing with Spring's ApplicationContextRunner lets you verify that each possible value for a feature flag or config property produces the expected binding, with every scenario named and independently reportable — without the overhead of a full @SpringBootTest:

@ParameterizedTest(name = "{index}: enabled={0}, cap={1} -> bonus={2}")
@CsvSource({
    "true, 10, 10",
    "true, 5, 5",
    "false, 10, 0"
})
void loyaltyBonusRespectsConfiguration(boolean enabled, int cap, int expectedBonus) {
    new ApplicationContextRunner()
        .withUserConfiguration(PricingPropertiesConfig.class)
        .withPropertyValues(
            "pricing.loyalty-bonus-enabled=" + enabled,
            "pricing.loyalty-bonus-cap=" + cap)
        .run(context -> {
            PricingProperties properties = context.getBean(PricingProperties.class);
            int bonus = properties.isLoyaltyBonusEnabled() ? properties.getLoyaltyBonusCap() : 0;
            assertEquals(expectedBonus, bonus);
        });
}

This combines Spring's test infrastructure with parameterized execution in both directions: the ApplicationContextRunner builds a minimal context per invocation, and @CsvSource drives the property values through it.

@TestInstance(TestInstance.Lifecycle.PER_CLASS) is worth applying to Spring integration tests by default, because it allows @MethodSource factory methods to live as instance methods rather than static methods. This is particularly useful in Kotlin, where a companion object with @JvmStatic is the alternative and instance methods are the cleaner option.

Cleaner parameterized tests with Kotlin

Kotlin's interoperability with the JVM means you can call JUnit 6 from Kotlin without any adapters. The annotations work identically. The gain comes from what Kotlin removes from the picture: builder classes, new, verbose static-factory-method requirements, and the noise that accumulates when you construct several complex objects inline.

How to call JUnit 6 from Kotlin

By default, JUnit's @MethodSource requires a static factory method. Kotlin uses a companion object with @JvmStatic for this purpose. You can avoid that boilerplate entirely by annotating the test class with @TestInstance(TestInstance.Lifecycle.PER_CLASS), which lets the factory method be a regular Kotlin instance function:

@SpringBootTest
@TestInstance(TestInstance.Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)
class PricingServiceTest @Autowired constructor(
    private val pricingService: PricingService
) {
    fun pricingCases() = listOf(
        Arguments.of(DiscountInput(BigDecimal("100.00"), 5, false),
            DiscountResult(BigDecimal("90.00"), 10)),
        Arguments.of(DiscountInput(BigDecimal("200.00"), 0, true),
            DiscountResult(BigDecimal("170.00"), 15))
    )

    @ParameterizedTest
    @MethodSource("pricingCases")
    fun `calculates price correctly`(input: DiscountInput, expected: DiscountResult) {
        assertEquals(expected, pricingService.calculate(input))
    }
}

Data classes for concise test cases

A common pattern in Kotlin test suites is defining a small data class that bundles the inputs and the expected output for a single scenario. Because data class auto-generates a readable toString(), the test runner displays each invocation with a meaningful description rather than an index number.

@TestInstance(TestInstance.Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)
class PricingServiceParameterizedTest {

    private val pricingService = PricingService()

    data class PricingTestCase(
        val description: String,
        val input: DiscountInput,
        val expected: DiscountResult
    )

    private fun pricingScenarios() = listOf(
        PricingTestCase(
            description = "Standard user with no loyalty gets no discount",
            input = DiscountInput(BigDecimal("100.00"), loyaltyYears = 0, isVip = false),
            expected = DiscountResult(BigDecimal("100.00"), 0)
        ),
        PricingTestCase(
            description = "VIP with high loyalty (>=5 yrs) gets 25%",
            input = DiscountInput(BigDecimal("200.00"), loyaltyYears = 6, isVip = true),
            expected = DiscountResult(BigDecimal("150.00"), 25)
        )
    )

    @ParameterizedTest(name = "{index} => {0}")
    @MethodSource("pricingScenarios")
    fun `should calculate discounted price accurately`(testCase: PricingTestCase) {
        val result = pricingService.calculate(testCase.input)
        assertEquals(testCase.expected, result)
    }
}

(The data class above is declared without private — a public @ParameterizedTest method can't expose a parameter type that's private to the class, so if you factor your test case class out, keep its visibility at least as public as the test method that consumes it.)

Named arguments for improved readability

Kotlin named arguments make each test case self-documenting. Compare the Java version of a complex object construction:

// Java
new DiscountInput(new BigDecimal("200.00"), 6, true)

With the Kotlin version:

// Kotlin
DiscountInput(basePrice = BigDecimal("200.00"), loyaltyYears = 6, isVip = true)

At a glance, the Kotlin version tells you what each argument means. Scale this across fifteen test cases and the readability difference compounds.

Cleaner object construction than Java builders

When a Java constructor has more than a couple of same-typed parameters sitting next to each other (two ints, two booleans), teams often reach for a builder to make call sites self-describing:

DiscountInput input = new DiscountInputBuilder()
    .basePrice(new BigDecimal("200.00"))
    .loyaltyYears(6)
    .isVip(true)
    .build();

That builder exists purely to work around Java's lack of named arguments — it's an entire extra class (fields, a fluent setter per field, a build() method) whose only job is call-site clarity. Kotlin's named arguments give you the same clarity directly at the call site, with no builder class to write or maintain:

val input = DiscountInput(basePrice = BigDecimal("200.00"), loyaltyYears = 6, isVip = true)

For test suites specifically, this matters more than it might in production code: a parameterized test's factory method constructs the same object repeatedly with different values, so every parameter it's missing a name for is a small tax paid on every single test case.

Destructuring declarations and extension functions

Destructuring declarations let you unpack a data class in the test method signature when you prefer to work with its fields directly:

data class ValidationCase(
    val description: String,
    val request: UserRegistrationRequest,
    val expectedViolations: Int
)

private fun validationCases() = listOf(
    ValidationCase("valid payload", UserRegistrationRequest("alice", "alice@example.com", 30), 0),
    ValidationCase("blank username", UserRegistrationRequest("", "alice@example.com", 30), 1)
)

@ParameterizedTest(name = "{index}: {0}")
@MethodSource("validationCases")
fun `validates registration requests`(testCase: ValidationCase) {
    val (_, request, expectedViolations) = testCase
    assertEquals(expectedViolations, validator.validate(request).size)
}

Extension functions on the test class give you reusable assertion helpers scoped to the test context, which is a clean way to extract repeated assertion logic without moving it to a utility class:

private fun DiscountResult.assertMatchesExpected(expected: DiscountResult) {
    assertEquals(expected.discountedPrice, this.discountedPrice)
    assertEquals(expected.discountPercent, this.discountPercent)
}

Java vs Kotlin side by side

The same @MethodSource test in Java and Kotlin illustrates where Kotlin cuts boilerplate:

// Java
static Stream<Arguments> pricingCases() {
    return Stream.of(
        Arguments.of(
            new DiscountInput(new BigDecimal("100.00"), 0, false),
            new DiscountResult(new BigDecimal("100.00"), 0)
        ),
        Arguments.of(
            new DiscountInput(new BigDecimal("200.00"), 6, true),
            new DiscountResult(new BigDecimal("150.00"), 25)
        )
    );
}

// Kotlin
fun pricingCases() = listOf(
    Arguments.of(
        DiscountInput(basePrice = BigDecimal("100.00"), loyaltyYears = 0, isVip = false),
        DiscountResult(discountedPrice = BigDecimal("100.00"), discountPercent = 0)
    ),
    Arguments.of(
        DiscountInput(basePrice = BigDecimal("200.00"), loyaltyYears = 6, isVip = true),
        DiscountResult(discountedPrice = BigDecimal("150.00"), discountPercent = 25)
    )
)

The Kotlin version is shorter, each argument is named, and there's no static, new, or explicit Stream.of(). The test assertions stay identical because you're calling the same JUnit 6 API against the same JVM bytecode.

For teams with existing Java Spring Boot services, Kotlin test code compiles to the same bytecode and runs on the same JVM, so you can introduce Kotlin in the test source set (src/test/kotlin) without touching a single production class. The two coexist without conflict, which reflects the strategic partnership between JetBrains and the Spring team, a collaboration aimed at improving the experience for backend developers on both sides of the language boundary. For a real-world account of Kotlin running mission-critical backend systems at scale, see this KotlinConf recap of Verifone's work on Kotlin in payments infrastructure.

Best practices for maintainable parameterized tests

  • Keep datasets focused. A factory method that returns forty rows is probably testing more than one logical concept. Split by concern: one method for valid inputs, one for invalid inputs, and one for edge cases.
  • Prefer descriptive argument names. When your test case object has a description or scenario field, surface it in the display name with {0}. A failure that reads [3] VIP with 5 loyalty years gets 25% discount is actionable; [3] is not.
  • Separate data generation from assertions. The factory method should only construct data, and the assertion logic lives in the test method. This separation makes both easier to read and refactor independently.
  • Use reusable providers. When the same dataset validates both a service and a controller, extract an ArgumentsProvider implementation and reference it from both test classes with @ArgumentsSource. Copying and pasting the factory method creates a maintenance problem.
  • Balance flexibility with readability. A generic @MethodSource that builds objects from a dozen intermediate variables is harder to follow than an explicit list of typed data class instances. Optimize for the next developer reading the failure report, not for line count.
  • Organize shared datasets across modules. In multi-module Gradle or Maven builds, a shared test-fixtures source set (Gradle's java-test-fixtures plugin) lets you publish ArgumentsProvider implementations that multiple modules can depend on.
  • Avoid over-parameterization. If every test in a class is parameterized, the class is probably doing too much. Use parameterized tests for cases where variation in data genuinely changes the outcome. A test that always expects the same result with cosmetically varied inputs isn't verifying anything new.
  • Choose the simplest source that fits the problem — whether @ValueSource for a handful of scalars, @CsvSource for related tuples that fit on one line each, @MethodSource for complex objects, or a custom ArgumentsProvider for shared or dynamically loaded datasets. Reaching for the most powerful option by default makes tests harder to scan than necessary.

JUnit 6's parameterized testing API covers how each source annotation works, why you'd choose one over another, and how the patterns map to real Spring Boot test suites across service, validation, controller, repository, and configuration layers.

The Kotlin patterns covered here (data classes, named arguments, @TestInstance(PER_CLASS), extension functions) reduce test setup code without any production-side changes. For teams already on Spring Boot with Java production code, writing Kotlin in the test source set is a low-risk, incremental adoption path. The two languages share the same classpath, the same JUnit 6 runner, and the same Spring test infrastructure. Your production code stays exactly as it is while your test tables get measurably cleaner, which is the right way to evaluate any addition to a working stack: ask whether it solves a real friction point without demanding a wholesale commitment.
