title: AssertJ vs Kotest Assertions: picking the right assertion library for JVM tests
description:
JUnit 6 ships with assertEquals, assertTrue, and a handful of other primitives. They work, but they leave a lot to be desired the moment a test fails. You get a message like expected: <true> but was: <false>, with no context about what was actually wrong. In a large Spring Boot project with dozens of test classes, that kind of noise slows everyone down.

AssertJ and Kotest Assertions both give you fluent, human-readable assertions with failure messages that tell the full story. They come from different design philosophies, and the one that fits your team depends on whether you're working in a pure Kotlin codebase, a mixed Java/Kotlin project, or something in between.

This article compares AssertJ and Kotest Assertions on syntax and readability, IntelliJ IDEA support, custom assertion strategies, soft assertions, Spring Boot integration, and adoption. The goal is a practical answer, not a feature matrix.

How this comparison works

Each section covers one dimension of the decision, starting with language design and syntax, then IDE support, custom assertions and soft assertions, Spring Boot integration, and a final recommendation. Code examples use real domain objects you'd find in a Spring Boot service, including a User entity, a REST response DTO, and a repository query result.

Both libraries are treated with equal seriousness. AssertJ has a decade-long track record as the default assertion library in the Spring Boot starter. Kotest Assertions brings a Kotlin-native DSL that aligns with how idiomatic Kotlin reads and works. Each fits a specific context, and that's what this article maps out.

Language design, syntax, and readability

AssertJ was designed for Java. Its API is a fluent chain of method calls, so assertThat(user.getName()).isEqualTo("Alice").startsWith("A") translates cleanly to Kotlin with no changes required. Kotlin adds things Java can't express, though, and AssertJ's API doesn't take advantage of them.

Kotest Assertions was built specifically for Kotlin. It uses infix functions and extension functions to produce assertions that read like natural language:

// AssertJ
assertThat(user.name).isEqualTo("Alice")
assertThat(user.email).isNotNull().endsWith("@example.com")

// Kotest
user.name shouldBe "Alice"
user.email.shouldNotBeNull() shouldEndWith "@example.com"

The difference becomes more pronounced when null safety comes into play. AssertJ runs on top of the JVM and doesn't know whether your value is nullable. To assert on a nullable field, you call .isNotNull() first, then continue chaining. Kotest's shouldNotBeNull() asserts the value is non-null and returns it as a non-null-typed result, so you can keep chaining matchers directly off the return value, without an extra null check of your own.

Exception assertions follow the same pattern. AssertJ uses assertThatThrownBy, which wraps the code under test in a lambda. For Kotest, shouldThrow does the job:

// AssertJ
assertThatThrownBy { userService.findById(-1L) }
    .isInstanceOf(NotFoundException::class.java)
    .hasMessageContaining("User not found")

// Kotest
val exception = shouldThrow<NotFoundException> {
    userService.findById(-1L)
}
exception.message shouldContain "User not found"

Kotest returns the thrown exception as a typed value, which means you can assert on its specific fields with full type information. AssertJ gives you an AbstractThrowableAssert, and while you can chain off it, you lose the concrete type unless you cast (or reach for assertThatExceptionOfType/catchThrowableOfType, which do return the concrete type if you need it).

For collection assertions, both libraries are capable, but their ergonomics differ. AssertJ uses extracting and containsExactly to navigate through collections, while Kotest delegates to standard Kotlin operations and then applies matchers:

val users = listOf(
    User(id = 1L, role = "ADMIN"),
    User(id = 2L, role = "USER")
)

// AssertJ
assertThat(users)
    .hasSize(2)
    .extracting("role")
    .containsExactly("ADMIN", "USER")

// Kotest
users shouldHaveSize 2
users.map { it.role } shouldContainExactly listOf("ADMIN", "USER")

The Kotest version reads like code you'd write anyway. The AssertJ version is clear, but extracting("role") uses a string property name, which loses type safety and won't be caught by the compiler if you rename the field. (AssertJ also has a type-safe overload, extracting(User::getRole), that avoids this specific problem if you prefer a method reference over a string.)

Use AssertJ when you need a single assertion style that works uniformly across Java and Kotlin sources. Kotest Assertions earns its place when your codebase is Kotlin-first and you want assertions that feel native to the language.

IDE support and developer experience

Both libraries work well inside IntelliJ IDEA, but their discoverability stories differ.

AssertJ's API is a method chain off assertThat(...). Once you type that call, IntelliJ's autocomplete presents the full list of available matchers for the specific type you passed in. Type a dot and browse the options. Static imports for Assertions.assertThat are handled by IntelliJ's import completion. IntelliJ's "Click to see difference" diff viewer opens side-by-side on assertion failure, and the IDE's general type-mismatch inspections apply to AssertJ calls the same way they apply to any other Java/Kotlin method chain — if you're not sure how far IntelliJ's AssertJ-specific inspections go in your version, it's worth checking the current release notes rather than assuming a specific check exists.

Kotest's extension functions change the discovery model. Because Kotest matchers are Kotlin extension functions defined on specific types, IntelliJ surfaces them through the same mechanism that surfaces any extension function, giving you autocomplete on the object itself. Type user.name and then a space, and IntelliJ will suggest shouldBe, shouldNotBe, and every other matcher that applies to String. The matchers are tied to the type system, so you won't see a string matcher when you're asserting on a number.

For teams new to Kotest, this has a practical effect: developers discover matchers organically by typing on their object and reading what appears. There's less need to memorize the API surface or rely on static import completion, because the type system does some of the teaching. That said, Kotest's API surface is still large, and a team new to the library will spend real time learning which matcher names exist in the first place, especially for the less common ones (shouldBeEqualIgnoringScale, shouldContainExactlyInAnyOrder, and similar) — autocomplete narrows the list, but it doesn't substitute for reading the matcher catalog once.

The Kotest project also publishes an IntelliJ IDEA plugin, distributed through the JetBrains Marketplace. Install it, and you get gutter icons next to individual test blocks, a dedicated Kotest tool window for browsing test hierarchies, and IntelliJ's diff viewer wired directly to Kotest assertion failures. For BehaviorSpec and DescribeSpec styles, the plugin renders the nested Given/When/Then or Describe/It hierarchy in the Structure tool window, which makes navigating a large test class much faster.

Navigation and refactoring behave the same way they do for any other Kotlin or Java code: go-to-declaration on a Kotest matcher takes you to its extension-function source, and renaming a property is a standard Kotlin rename-refactor regardless of which assertion library references it afterward. AssertJ's assert classes are ordinary Java types, so navigation into them (and documentation popups showing their Javadoc) works the same way it does for any other library on your classpath. Kotest's matchers carry KDoc, so hovering a matcher name shows the same kind of documentation popup you'd get from any Kotlin extension function.

AssertJ's experience is more static-import-dependent. On a new machine or a fresh project, getting assertThat to resolve without a red squiggly requires the import to be present. Teams used to this workflow find it natural, but teams migrating from JUnit's built-in assertions sometimes find the static import pattern mildly tedious until they configure IntelliJ's "add unambiguous imports on the fly" setting. That's the main developer frustration on the AssertJ side; on the Kotest side, the more common frustration is the opposite problem — so many matchers exist across so many modules that it can take a project or two before a team has internalized the vocabulary.

For daily use in a Kotlin project, Kotest's extension function-based discovery and the dedicated plugin make it the more ergonomic option inside IntelliJ IDEA. For mixed Java/Kotlin codebases where both languages write tests, AssertJ's consistent method-chain API across both languages is a real advantage.

Custom assertions and soft assertions

Custom assertions

Every meaningful Spring Boot project reaches the point where you're writing the same group of assertions in multiple test classes. A User entity has a handful of fields you always check together. A REST response DTO carries a status, a message, and a payload that need coordinated verification. A validation result needs its error list checked as a group. The right answer is a reusable custom assertion.

With AssertJ, you have two patterns. The first uses Kotlin extension functions on ObjectAssert<T>, which keeps your custom matchers chainable without subclassing:

fun ObjectAssert<User>.isActiveAdmin(): ObjectAssert<User> = satisfies(Consumer { user: User ->
    assertThat(user.status).isEqualTo(Status.ACTIVE)
    assertThat(user.role).isEqualTo("ADMIN")
})

// In tests
assertThat(user).isNotNull.isActiveAdmin()

Note the explicit Consumer { ... } wrapper around the lambda. AssertJ's satisfies method has three overloads — one taking a Condition, and two taking varargs of Consumer or ThrowingConsumer — and Kotlin can't infer which functional interface a bare trailing lambda should become when two of those overloads have an identical shape. Wrapping the lambda in Consumer { ... } resolves the ambiguity.

The second pattern extends AbstractAssert directly for complex domain objects where you want a dedicated assertion class with its own failure messages:

class UserAssert(actual: User?) : AbstractAssert<UserAssert, User>(actual, UserAssert::class.java) {
    fun hasValidEmail(): UserAssert {
        isNotNull()
        if (actual.email?.contains("@") != true) {
            failWithMessage("Expected valid email but was <%s>", actual.email)
        }
        return this
    }
}

fun assertThatUser(actual: User): UserAssert = UserAssert(actual)

// In tests
assertThatUser(user).hasValidEmail()

Two details matter here. First, actual.email is nullable, so the check needs a safe call (actual.email?.contains("@") != true) rather than a direct .contains(...) call. Second, name your factory function something other than assertThat. If you call it assertThat(actual: User): UserAssert — which is the more common way this pattern is written — it will silently lose to org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat the moment both are in scope in the same file, which is any file that also uses plain AssertJ assertions elsewhere. Kotlin's import-scope rules rank an explicitly imported name above a same-named function declared in your own package, so assertThat(user) resolves to the generic AssertJ overload every time, and your custom method never gets called — it just fails with "unresolved reference" at the call site, with nothing wrong-looking in the custom class itself. Naming the factory assertThatUser (or putting it behind an aliased import) avoids the collision entirely.

Kotest handles custom assertions through extension functions on the subject itself, which fits naturally with how Kotlin is written:

fun User.shouldBeActiveAdmin() {
    this.status shouldBe Status.ACTIVE
    this.role shouldBe "ADMIN"
}

// In tests
user.shouldBeActiveAdmin()

Kotest also supports Matcher<T>, a composable interface that lets you build matchers from other matchers and give them reusable names. This scales well for assertion libraries shared across multiple modules in a large project.

The Kotest approach produces less boilerplate and doesn't require you to understand the AbstractAssert class hierarchy or its overload quirks. For a team writing Kotlin, extension functions on the subject type are the pattern they already know, and reusing them in tests feels consistent with the rest of the codebase.

A validation result is a good example of a domain object that benefits from this treatment, since you're usually checking a boolean flag and a list of messages together:

data class ValidationResult(val valid: Boolean, val errors: List<String>)

// AssertJ
assertThat(result.valid).isFalse()
assertThat(result.errors)
    .hasSize(2)
    .contains("email must not be blank", "age must be positive")

// Kotest
result.valid shouldBe false
result.errors shouldContainExactlyInAnyOrder listOf(
    "email must not be blank",
    "age must be positive"
)

Wrapping either version in a hasValidationErrors(vararg messages: String)-style custom assertion (an AbstractAssert subclass for AssertJ, an extension function for Kotest) removes the repetition once this check shows up in more than one test class — the same tradeoff as the User examples above.

Soft assertions

Both libraries support soft assertions (Kotest's assertSoftly included), which collect all failures in a block instead of stopping at the first one. When you're asserting ten fields on a response object, reporting all failures at once saves debugging cycles.

// AssertJ
SoftAssertions.assertSoftly { softly ->
    softly.assertThat(order.status).isEqualTo(OrderStatus.CONFIRMED)
    softly.assertThat(order.totalPrice).isEqualByComparingTo(BigDecimal("99.99"))
    softly.assertThat(order.items).hasSize(3)
}

// Kotest
assertSoftly(order) {
    status shouldBe OrderStatus.CONFIRMED
    totalPrice.shouldBeEqualIgnoringScale(BigDecimal("99.99"))
    items shouldHaveSize 3
}

Kotest's assertSoftly block scopes the receiver, so you reference status, items, and totalPrice directly without repeating softly.assertThat(order.x) on every line. The reduction in noise is real in test classes that verify complex aggregates like an Order with nested line items or a validation result with multiple error messages. shouldBeEqualIgnoringScale is the Kotest equivalent of AssertJ's isEqualByComparingTo here — it compares the numeric value and ignores trailing-zero scale differences, so BigDecimal("99.99") and BigDecimal("99.990") are treated as equal. AssertJ's assertSoftly requires the softly prefix on every assertion line, which is more verbose but also more explicit about which assertion library you're calling.

Spring Boot integration

AssertJ ships inside spring-boot-starter-test. Add the Spring Boot test starter and AssertJ is available with no additional configuration:

dependencies {
    testImplementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-test")
}

Kotest Assertions requires an additional dependency. If you want Kotest's full test framework (its FunSpec, BehaviorSpec, and other styles), you also add the JUnit Platform runner. For teams that want only Kotest's assertion DSL inside JUnit 6 tests, kotest-assertions-core is enough. If you're also mocking with MockK inside Spring test slices (as in the controller example below), add springmockk for its @MockkBean annotation:

dependencies {
    testImplementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-test")
    testImplementation("io.kotest:kotest-assertions-core:5.9.1")
    // Optional: full Kotest framework
    testImplementation("io.kotest:kotest-runner-junit5:5.9.1")
    testImplementation("io.kotest.extensions:kotest-extensions-spring:1.3.0")
    // Needed for @MockkBean in Spring test slices
    testImplementation("com.ninja-squad:springmockk:4.0.2")
}

Both libraries integrate with the full Spring Boot test stack. A @WebMvcTest controller test using MockK for mocking and Kotest for assertions looks like this:

@WebMvcTest(UserController::class)
class UserControllerTest(@Autowired private val mockMvc: MockMvc) {

    @MockkBean
    private lateinit var userService: UserService

    @Test
    fun `should return user by id`() {
        val user = User(id = 42L, email = "alex@example.com", status = Status.ACTIVE)
        every { userService.findById(42L) } returns user

        val response = mockMvc.get("/api/users/42") {
            accept = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON
        }.andExpect {
            status { isOk() }
        }.andReturn().response.contentAsString

        val dto = jacksonObjectMapper().readValue<UserResponseDto>(response)
        dto.email shouldBe "alex@example.com"
        dto.status shouldBe "ACTIVE"
    }
}

For a thinner service-layer test — no Spring context, no web layer, just the business logic — the same syntax from the opening sections applies directly, with no annotations at all:

class UserServiceTest {
    private val userService: UserService = InMemoryUserService()

    // AssertJ
    @Test
    fun `assertj service test`() {
        assertThat(userService.findById(1L).status).isEqualTo(Status.ACTIVE)
    }

    // Kotest
    @Test
    fun `kotest service test`() {
        userService.findById(1L).status shouldBe Status.ACTIVE
    }
}

For repository tests with @DataJpaTest, the AssertJ version uses satisfies to group assertions on a single result.

The following is an example of a Java test next to its Kotlin counterpart — in a mixed codebase, AssertJ's API doesn't change shape between the two:

// Java
@DataJpaTest
class UserRepositoryJavaTest {

    @Autowired
    private UserRepository repo;

    @Autowired
    private TestEntityManager em;

    @Test
    void shouldFindActiveUsersByDomain() {
        repo.save(new User(0L, "Alice", "alice@company.com", "USER", Status.ACTIVE));
        repo.save(new User(0L, "Bob", "bob@company.com", "USER", Status.INACTIVE));
        em.flush();

        List<User> results = repo.findActiveByDomain("company.com");

        assertThat(results).hasSize(1);
        assertThat(results.get(0).getEmail()).isEqualTo("alice@company.com");
        assertThat(results.get(0).getStatus()).isEqualTo(Status.ACTIVE);
    }
}

// Kotlin
@DataJpaTest
class UserRepositoryTest(
    @Autowired private val repo: UserRepository,
    @Autowired private val em: TestEntityManager
) {
    @Test
    fun `should find active users by domain`() {
        repo.save(User(email = "alice@company.com", status = Status.ACTIVE))
        repo.save(User(email = "bob@company.com", status = Status.INACTIVE))
        em.flush()

        val results = repo.findActiveByDomain("company.com")

        // AssertJ
        assertThat(results).hasSize(1).first().satisfies(Consumer { u ->
            assertThat(u.email).isEqualTo("alice@company.com")
            assertThat(u.status).isEqualTo(Status.ACTIVE)
        })

        // Kotest equivalent
        results shouldHaveSize 1
        with(results.single()) {
            email shouldBe "alice@company.com"
            status shouldBe Status.ACTIVE
        }
    }
}

As with the custom-assertion example earlier, .satisfies(...) needs an explicit Consumer { ... } wrapper in Kotlin — a bare trailing lambda doesn't compile against AssertJ's vararg overloads.

If your repository tests run against a real database via Testcontainers instead of an embedded one, none of the assertion syntax above changes — assertThat(...) and shouldBe/shouldHaveSize work the same way against a Testcontainers-backed PostgreSQLContainer as they do against H2, since they're asserting on the List<User> the repository returns, not on anything container-specific. The assertion library and the integration-test infrastructure are orthogonal choices.

When using the full Kotest test framework alongside Spring Boot, you register SpringExtension to enable context loading and constructor-based dependency injection inside Kotest specs:

@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
class UserServiceIntegrationTest(
    private val restTemplate: TestRestTemplate
) : FunSpec({
    extension(SpringExtension)

    test("should fetch user profile") {
        val response = restTemplate.getForEntity("/api/users/1", String::class.java)
        response.statusCode shouldBe HttpStatus.OK
        response.body.shouldNotBeNull()
    }
})

Notice the constructor parameter has no @Autowired annotation. Kotest's SpringExtension resolves constructor dependencies itself, independently of Spring's own TestConstructor autowire mode (which, under plain JUnit, defaults to requiring @Autowired per parameter or a global property, as covered in our companion piece on JUnit, Testcontainers, MockK, Kotest, and Spring Boot Test). Inside a Kotest spec specifically, it just works.

For teams already using Mockito in Java test sources, AssertJ slots in without friction. For teams that have adopted MockK (the idiomatic Kotlin mocking library), pairing it with Kotest Assertions produces a consistent, Kotlin-native test stack.

One real-world consideration worth noting: Kotest's native coroutine support applies to the full Kotest test framework, not to Kotest Assertions by itself. Inside a Kotest spec (FunSpec, BehaviorSpec, and the rest), test bodies are themselves suspend lambdas run by the Kotest engine, so you can call suspend functions directly with no wrapper. If you're using only kotest-assertions-core inside an ordinary JUnit @Test method, that method is not a suspend function, and calling a suspend function from it fails to compile — you still need runBlocking or runTest around the call, exactly as you would with any other assertion library.

Which assertion library to choose

There's no universally correct answer, but the decision tree is short.

Choose AssertJ when your team maintains both Java and Kotlin test sources and wants a single assertion style across both. AssertJ is already in spring-boot-starter-test, so the cost of adoption is zero. Its method-chain API is widely understood by Java developers and requires no onboarding. Teams that value a minimal dependency footprint and standard tooling will find AssertJ the path of least resistance.

Choose Kotest Assertions when your project is Kotlin-first and you want assertions that align with idiomatic Kotlin. The infix DSL reduces noise in test output and in code review. The assertSoftly scoping removes softly.assertThat(...) repetition. Null safety is handled through return-type narrowing rather than manual checks. If you're already using the Kotest test framework for its spec styles, this is the obvious choice. You can also adopt Kotest Assertions inside JUnit 6 tests without migrating to the full framework, which makes it a low-risk addition to an existing Spring Boot project.

On performance and adoption: neither library adds meaningful runtime overhead to a test suite. Both are thin DSL layers over ordinary JVM assertion failures — the cost is a method call or two per check, not a separate execution engine (the one exception is adopting the full Kotest test framework as your test runner, which does replace JUnit's default test discovery and execution, though not in a way that changes wall-clock test time in any way that matters day to day). On adoption, AssertJ has the longer track record simply by virtue of having shipped as the Spring Boot default for about a decade; Kotest's adoption has grown alongside Kotlin's own growth on the backend, particularly among teams already using Kotest's spec styles or MockK. Neither is a niche choice at this point — the decision is about fit with your codebase's language, not about betting on an unproven library.

Mixing assertion libraries is viable within limits. Using Kotest Assertions inside JUnit 6 tests alongside AssertJ for specific cases (such as Condition-based matchers already established in the codebase) works without conflict. Mixing the full Kotest test framework with JUnit 6 test classes in the same module requires more care in configuration but is supported. Mixing becomes a liability when new team members can't tell which style to follow when writing a new test; in that case, the team is better served by picking one library and standardizing.

Migrating from AssertJ to Kotest Assertions in a Kotlin codebase follows an incremental path: start with new test classes, use shouldBe and assertSoftly there, and leave existing AssertJ tests in place. The two styles don't interfere, and the migration pressure comes naturally as old tests get refactored.

Choosing based on language gravity

AssertJ and Kotest Assertions both make test failures informative and test code readable, but they reflect different assumptions about who's writing the tests and what the language can do. AssertJ's Java-first fluent API surprises no JVM developer and integrates at zero cost via the Spring Boot starter. Kotest's Kotlin-native DSL aligns with how Kotlin code reads and works, particularly around null safety and extension function discoverability in IntelliJ IDEA — though its native coroutine-testing story is a feature of the full Kotest spec framework, not of Kotest Assertions on its own.

For Java developers working in mixed codebases and evaluating whether to bring Kotest into their Kotlin test sources, you can adopt Kotest Assertions incrementally, one test class at a time, without disturbing what's already there. The kotest-assertions-core dependency is the only addition required, and it coexists cleanly with AssertJ and JUnit 6. The official JetBrains–Spring partnership continues to improve Kotlin's position as a first-class language for Spring development, and Kotest is part of a mature Kotlin testing ecosystem that includes MockK, kotlin.test, and full Spring Boot test integration. For a concrete account of Kotlin running mission-critical backend systems in production, see this KotlinConf recap of Verifone's work on Kotlin in payments infrastructure.

Pick the library that matches your codebase's language gravity. If your tests are trending Kotlin, Kotest Assertions will feel like a natural fit.

title: Transactional Email API: The Complete Cresca Guide
description:
Cresca's transactional email API is a REST API at https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1 that sends one-to-one email, such as password resets, receipts and verification codes, from your own verified domain. You authenticate with an API key in an Authorization: Bearer header, POST JSON to /emails, and get back an id you can use to check delivery. This guide covers every v1 endpoint, with a full worked example and code you can copy.

In this guide

  • Every endpoint at a glance
  • Authentication: API keys and the Bearer header
  • Worked example: your first email, end to end
  • Emails API: send, batch, list, reschedule, cancel
  • Templates API: create, publish and send by alias
  • Contacts API
  • Idempotency, lifecycle, suppression, limits and errors
  • Frequently asked questions

All requests go to https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1 over HTTPS, and requests and responses are JSON. There is no SDK package to install: any HTTP client works, so the examples below use cURL, Node.js 18+ (built-in fetch) and Python (requests). Field names follow the conventions of popular email APIs, so an existing integration is mostly a change of base URL and key.

The API is for transactional email: messages a person expects because of something they did. Newsletters and promotions belong in Cresca campaigns. If the line is unclear, read transactional vs marketing email.

Every endpoint at a glance

Paths are relative to the base URL. "Sending" means a sending-access key works; "Full" needs a full-access key.

Method Path Purpose Key Docs
POST /emails Send one email (up to 50 recipients) Sending Send email
POST /emails/batch Send up to 100 emails in one request Sending Send batch
GET /emails/:id Retrieve one email and its last_event Full Retrieve email
GET /emails List emails, newest first Full List emails
PATCH /emails/:id Reschedule a scheduled email Full Update email
POST /emails/:id/cancel Cancel a scheduled or queued email Full Cancel email
POST /templates Create a template draft Full Create template
GET /templates/:id Retrieve a template by id or alias Full Retrieve template
GET /templates List templates Full List templates
PATCH /templates/:id Update the draft Full Update template
POST /templates/:id/publish Publish the draft as the next version Full Publish template
DELETE /templates/:id Delete a template Full Delete template
POST /contacts Add up to 1,000 contacts to a list Full Add contacts

Authentication: API keys and the Bearer header

Create keys on the API keys page of the Cresca app. Keys start with cr_live_ and are shown once; Cresca stores only a hash. Send the key as a bearer token:

Authorization: Bearer cr_live_xxxxxxxxx

The X-API-Key header also works. Keep keys on your server, never in browser code, URLs or public repositories.

Permission Can do Use it for
Sending access Send emails and batches. Can be limited to one verified domain. Production servers
Full access Everything: send, read and cancel emails, manage templates, add contacts Scripts and internal tools

Authentication errors: 401 missing_api_key (no key), 403 invalid_api_key (unknown or revoked key, or suspended account) and 401 restricted_api_key (a sending-access key called a full-access endpoint). Details are on the Authentication docs page.

Worked example: send your first transactional email

This is the whole path from a fresh account to a delivered email. It mirrors the quickstart.

Step 1: Verify a sending domain

In the app, open Sending Domains, add your domain and publish the DNS records Cresca shows you: DKIM, a custom MAIL FROM domain and an ownership record. If your DNS is on Cloudflare, Cresca can publish them for you. The domain becomes active once the records verify. A subdomain such as mail.acme.com keeps the reputation of app email separate from campaigns. See sending domains and SPF, DKIM and DMARC done right.

Step 2: Add a sender

On the same page, create a sender such as hello@acme.com with a display name and an optional Reply-To. Every API from address must be an active sender on a verified domain.

Step 3: Create an API key

Create a Sending access key for your server and store it as CRESCA_API_KEY. Create a separate full-access key for the status check in step 5.

Step 4: Send the email

The Idempotency-Key header makes the request safe to retry.

curl -X POST 'https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/emails' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer cr_live_xxxxxxxxx' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Idempotency-Key: password-reset/reset-request-9f2c' \
  -d '{
    "from": "Acme <hello@acme.com>",
    "to": "user@example.com",
    "subject": "Reset your password",
    "html": "<p>Click <a href=\"https://acme.com/reset?token=abc\">here</a> to reset your password.</p>"
  }'

// Node.js 18+, run as an ES module for top-level await
const response = await fetch('https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/emails', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.CRESCA_API_KEY}`,
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',
    'Idempotency-Key': 'password-reset/reset-request-9f2c',
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    from: 'Acme <hello@acme.com>',
    to: 'user@example.com',
    subject: 'Reset your password',
    html: '<p>Click <a href="https://acme.com/reset?token=abc">here</a> to reset your password.</p>',
  }),
});

const data = await response.json();
if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`${data.name}: ${data.message}`);
console.log(data.id);

import os
import requests

response = requests.post(
    "https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/emails",
    headers={
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['CRESCA_API_KEY']}",
        "Idempotency-Key": "password-reset/reset-request-9f2c",
    },
    json={
        "from": "Acme <hello@acme.com>",
        "to": "user@example.com",
        "subject": "Reset your password",
        "html": '<p>Click <a href="https://acme.com/reset?token=abc">here</a> to reset your password.</p>',
    },
    timeout=30,
)
response.raise_for_status()
print(response.json()["id"])

A 200 response returns the id as soon as the email is accepted; sending happens in the background within seconds.

{ "id": "4ef9a417-02e9-4d39-ad75-9611e0fcc33c" }

Step 5: Check the status

Retrieve the email with your full-access key, or open Transactional in the app for the full timeline.

curl 'https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/emails/4ef9a417-02e9-4d39-ad75-9611e0fcc33c' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer cr_live_xxxxxxxxx'

{
  "object": "email",
  "id": "4ef9a417-02e9-4d39-ad75-9611e0fcc33c",
  "from": "Acme <hello@acme.com>",
  "to": ["user@example.com"],
  "cc": null,
  "bcc": null,
  "reply_to": null,
  "subject": "Reset your password",
  "html": "<p>Click <a href=\"https://acme.com/reset?token=abc\">here</a> to reset your password.</p>",
  "text": "Click here (https://acme.com/reset?token=abc) to reset your password.",
  "created_at": "2026-10-19T09:14:03.120Z",
  "scheduled_at": null,
  "last_event": "delivered",
  "tags": []
}

last_event moves from queued through sending and sent to delivered (or bounced). Emails are kept for 30 days; another account's id returns 404 not_found.

Emails API

The email sending API has six endpoints. POST /emails takes these fields; the deep dive is in the send email API guide.

Field Type Required Notes
from string Yes* hello@acme.com or Acme <hello@acme.com>; an active sender
to string or string[] Yes Up to 50 recipients across to, cc and bcc
subject string Yes* Single line, up to 998 characters
html / text string One of html, text, template Text is generated from HTML if omitted; "" leaves it out
cc, bcc, reply_to string or string[] No reply_to defaults to the sender's Reply-To
template object No { "id", "variables" }; cannot be combined with html or text
scheduled_at string No ISO 8601, up to 30 days ahead; a past time sends now
tags object[] No Up to 10 { "name", "value" } pairs
headers object No Up to 50 custom headers; Cresca-controlled ones are refused
attachments object[] No Up to 20, 7 MB total, base64 content and filename

*Optional when a template supplies a default. Unknown fields are ignored. Attaching by URL (path) is not supported.

The shorter Node.js examples below use this helper:

const cresca = (method, path, body) =>
  fetch(`https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1${path}`, {
    method,
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.CRESCA_API_KEY}`,
      'Content-Type': 'application/json',
    },
    body: body ? JSON.stringify(body) : undefined,
  }).then((res) => res.json());

Send a batch

POST /emails/batch takes a JSON array of up to 100 emails with the same fields, except attachments and scheduled_at. A batch is all or nothing: if one email is invalid, nothing is sent and the message names it, for example Email 3: ... (zero-based).

curl -X POST 'https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/emails/batch' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer cr_live_xxxxxxxxx' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Idempotency-Key: weekly-digest/2026-10-19' \
  -d '[
    { "from": "Acme <hello@acme.com>", "to": "ana@example.com",
      "subject": "Your weekly summary", "html": "<p>Hi Ana, here is your summary.</p>" },
    { "from": "Acme <hello@acme.com>", "to": "ben@example.com",
      "subject": "Your weekly summary", "html": "<p>Hi Ben, here is your summary.</p>" }
  ]'

const { data } = await cresca('POST', '/emails/batch', emails); // array of up to 100 emails

{
  "data": [
    { "id": "b6d1f2a0-5e2f-4c8e-9a51-0c8b5f1d2e33" },
    { "id": "0f7e3c11-9b2a-4f6d-8e44-7a1c2d3e4f55" }
  ]
}

List emails

GET /emails accepts limit (1 to 100, default 20) and either after or before (an email id). Items leave out html and text.

import os
import requests

response = requests.get(
    "https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/emails",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['CRESCA_API_KEY']}"},
    params={"limit": 1},
    timeout=30,
)
print(response.json())

{
  "object": "list",
  "has_more": true,
  "data": [
    {
      "object": "email",
      "id": "4ef9a417-02e9-4d39-ad75-9611e0fcc33c",
      "from": "Acme <hello@acme.com>",
      "to": ["user@example.com"],
      "cc": null,
      "bcc": null,
      "reply_to": null,
      "subject": "Reset your password",
      "created_at": "2026-10-19T09:14:03.120Z",
      "scheduled_at": null,
      "last_event": "delivered",
      "tags": []
    }
  ]
}

For the next page, pass the last item's id as after while has_more is true.

Reschedule and cancel

PATCH /emails/:id takes one required field, scheduled_at, and only works while the status is scheduled. POST /emails/:id/cancel works while the email is scheduled or queued; a canceled email does not count toward your allowance.

curl -X PATCH 'https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/emails/4ef9a417-02e9-4d39-ad75-9611e0fcc33c' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer cr_live_xxxxxxxxx' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{ "scheduled_at": "2026-10-21T09:00:00Z" }'

curl -X POST 'https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/emails/4ef9a417-02e9-4d39-ad75-9611e0fcc33c/cancel' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer cr_live_xxxxxxxxx'

await cresca('PATCH', `/emails/${id}`, { scheduled_at: '2026-10-21T09:00:00Z' });
await cresca('POST', `/emails/${id}/cancel`);

Both return { "object": "email", "id": "4ef9a417-..." }. Rescheduling an email that is not scheduled, or canceling one that is already sending, returns 422 validation_error.

Common Emails API errors: 403 invalid_from_address (not an active sender, or the key is limited to another domain), 422 missing_required_field (no to, from or subject), 422 validation_error (bad address, more than 50 recipients, template combined with html), 422 invalid_attachment, 429 monthly_quota_exceeded and 404 not_found.

Templates API

Templates let you design an email once, publish it, and send it by alias with variables written as {{{NAME}}}. Edits change the draft; sends always use the published version. All six endpoints need a full-access key, and :id accepts the id or the alias. More depth: the email templates API guide and Templates and variables.

Field Required Notes
name Yes Up to 120 characters, unique in your account
html Yes Body with {{{VARIABLE}}} placeholders
alias No Lowercase letters, numbers, dashes, underscores; up to 64
subject, text, from, reply_to, preview_text No Defaults used at send time
variables No Up to 50 { "key", "type", "fallback_value" }; type is string or number

Create and publish 

curl -X POST 'https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/templates' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer cr_live_xxxxxxxxx' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "name": "Password reset",
    "alias": "password-reset",
    "subject": "Reset your password",
    "from": "Acme <hello@acme.com>",
    "html": "<p>Hi {{{NAME}}},</p><p><a href=\"{{{RESET_LINK}}}\">Reset your password</a>.</p>",
    "variables": [
      { "key": "NAME", "type": "string", "fallback_value": "there" },
      { "key": "RESET_LINK", "type": "string" }
    ]
  }'

curl -X POST 'https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/templates/password-reset/publish' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer cr_live_xxxxxxxxx'

const { id } = await cresca('POST', '/templates', { name: 'Welcome', alias: 'welcome', html: '<p>Hi {{{NAME}}}</p>' });
await cresca('POST', `/templates/${id}/publish`);

Create returns 201 with { "object": "template", "id": "6713b1f4c2a94e0012ab34cd" }. Publish returns the new version number:

{ "object": "template", "id": "6713b1f4c2a94e0012ab34cd", "version": 1 }

Send by alias with variables 

const response = await fetch('https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/emails', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.CRESCA_API_KEY}`,
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    to: 'user@example.com',
    template: {
      id: 'password-reset',
      variables: { NAME: 'Ana', RESET_LINK: 'https://acme.com/reset?token=abc' },
    },
  }),
});
console.log(await response.json()); // { id: '...' }

Subject and sender come from the template unless your request sets them. Values are HTML-escaped in the HTML body. A variable with no value and no fallback stops the send with 422 validation_error naming it; an unpublished template also returns 422.

Retrieve, list, update and delete 

curl 'https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/templates/password-reset' -H 'Authorization: Bearer cr_live_xxxxxxxxx'
curl 'https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/templates?limit=10' -H 'Authorization: Bearer cr_live_xxxxxxxxx'
curl -X PATCH 'https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/templates/password-reset' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer cr_live_xxxxxxxxx' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{ "subject": "Reset your Acme password" }'
curl -X DELETE 'https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/templates/password-reset' -H 'Authorization: Bearer cr_live_xxxxxxxxx'

await cresca('GET', '/templates/password-reset');
await cresca('GET', '/templates?limit=10');
await cresca('PATCH', '/templates/password-reset', { subject: 'Reset your Acme password' });
await cresca('DELETE', '/templates/password-reset');

Retrieve returns the template object (list wraps the same objects in { "object": "list", "has_more", "data" }):

{
  "object": "template",
  "id": "6713b1f4c2a94e0012ab34cd",
  "name": "Password reset",
  "alias": "password-reset",
  "subject": "Reset your password",
  "from": "Acme <hello@acme.com>",
  "reply_to": null,
  "preview_text": null,
  "html": "<p>Hi {{{NAME}}},</p><p><a href=\"{{{RESET_LINK}}}\">Reset your password</a>.</p>",
  "text": null,
  "variables": [
    { "key": "NAME", "type": "string", "fallback_value": "there" },
    { "key": "RESET_LINK", "type": "string", "fallback_value": null }
  ],
  "status": "published",
  "version": 1,
  "published_at": "2026-10-19T08:30:00.000Z",
  "created_at": "2026-10-18T16:02:11.000Z",
  "updated_at": "2026-10-19T08:30:00.000Z"
}

Update returns { "object": "template", "id" } and changes only the draft; send null for alias to remove it. Delete returns "deleted": true, and later sends that reference the template fail with 404 not_found. Typical errors: 422 missing_required_field (no name or html) and 422 validation_error (duplicate name or alias, bad variable).

Contacts API

POST /contacts adds up to 1,000 contacts per request to a list for your marketing campaigns, creating the list if needed. It needs a full-access key and is limited to 120 requests per 15 minutes. Full walkthrough: the contacts API guide.

Field Type Required Notes
list_name string Yes Created if it does not exist
contacts (string \ object)[] Yes 
import os
import requests

response = requests.post(
    "https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1/contacts",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['CRESCA_API_KEY']}"},
    json={
        "list_name": "Newsletter signups",
        "contacts": [{"email": "ana@example.com", "first_name": "Ana"}, "ben@example.com"],
    },
    timeout=30,
)
print(response.json())

{
  "object": "contact_import",
  "list": { "id": "6713b2a8c2a94e0012ab3511", "name": "Newsletter signups", "created": false },
  "summary": {
    "received": 2, "created": 1, "updated": 0, "already_present": 1,
    "rejected": 0, "added_to_list": 1, "limit_reached": false
  },
  "errors": []
}

Invalid, disposable, role, suppressed and duplicate addresses are listed in errors with their index; the rest are still added. An inactive plan returns 403 plan_inactive; a missing list_name returns 422 missing_required_field.

Idempotency, lifecycle, suppression, limits and errors

Idempotency

Send an Idempotency-Key (1 to 256 characters) on POST /emails or /emails/batch. The same key and body within 24 hours return the original response with idempotent-replayed: true and nothing is sent again. The same key with a different body returns 409 invalid_idempotent_request; a key still in flight returns 409 concurrent_idempotent_requests. A failed request releases its key. Derive keys from the event, such as invoice/inv-2026-0042. See Idempotency.

Email lifecycle: statuses and events

last_event Meaning
queued / scheduled Accepted, waiting to send (or to its scheduled_at)
sending / sent Being handed to, then accepted by, the mail infrastructure
delivered The recipient's server accepted it
delivery_delayed Delivery is being retried
bounced / complained Rejected, or marked as spam
failed / suppressed / canceled Not sent, every recipient suppressed, or canceled

Status only moves forward, while last_event is the latest event. delivered means the receiving server accepted it, not that it reached the inbox. Full table: Email lifecycle.

Suppression

Hard bounces, repeated soft bounces (3 in 30 days), spam complaints and manual suppressions block API email; suppressed recipients are skipped and the others still receive it. A marketing unsubscribe does not block a password reset. If every recipient is suppressed you still get 200, and the status is suppressed. See Suppression.

Rate limits and quotas

Plan Requests per second Emails per second with batches
Free 2 up to 200
Professional 10 up to 1,000
Premium 20 up to 2,000
Ultra 50 up to 5,000
Enterprise 100 up to 10,000

The limit is per account, shared by all keys, and an inactive plan gets the Free limit. Authenticated responses carry ratelimit-limit, ratelimit-remaining and ratelimit-reset; a 429 rate_limit_exceeded adds retry-after. API email shares your plan's monthly email allowance with campaigns, one unit per recipient; when it runs out you get 429 monthly_quota_exceeded. Request bodies are capped at 10 MB. See Rate limits and quotas and pricing.

Errors

Every error has the same shape. Branch on name, not message:

{
  "statusCode": 422,
  "name": "validation_error",
  "message": "Invalid `to` field. The email address needs to follow the `email@example.com` or `Name <email@example.com>` format."
}

Retry 429 rate_limit_exceeded, 409 concurrent_idempotent_requests, 500 application_error, 503 service_unavailable, timeouts and network errors with exponential backoff and jitter, using an Idempotency-Key. Do not retry other 4xx responses; fix the request. The full list is on Errors.

Frequently asked questions

Is there an official SDK for the Cresca email API?

No. Cresca does not publish an SDK package; the API is plain HTTPS and JSON, so cURL, Node.js fetch, Python requests or any HTTP client works. Field names and responses follow the conventions of popular email APIs, so moving an existing integration is mostly a change of base URL and API key. The docs show every request in cURL, Node.js and Python.

Can I send marketing email through the transactional email API?

No. The API is for messages a person expects because of something they did, such as receipts, password resets and alerts. Newsletters and promotions belong in Cresca campaigns, which add the unsubscribe link and sender address marketing email legally requires. Keeping them apart also protects deliverability, as explained in transactional vs marketing email.

How do I know an email was delivered?

Call GET /emails/:id with a full-access key and read last_event, or open Transactional in the Cresca app for the per-recipient timeline of sent, delivered, bounced and complained events. delivered means the receiving server accepted the email. Webhooks are on the roadmap; today you read status from the API or the dashboard.

Does API email count toward my plan?

Yes. API email uses the same monthly email allowance as your campaigns, and each recipient in to, cc and bcc counts as one email. Suppressed recipients, canceled emails and emails that fail before sending are given back. When the allowance is used up, sends return 429 monthly_quota_exceeded until the next billing period or an upgrade. See pricing.

What happens if my server retries after a timeout?

If the request carried an Idempotency-Key, the retry returns the original response with the header idempotent-replayed: true, and no second email is sent. Without a key, a retry can send a duplicate. Derive the key from the event that caused the email, such as welcome/user-123, so every retry produces the same key.

Do I need SPF, DKIM and DMARC to send transactional email?

Your from address must be on a domain verified in Cresca, which means publishing the DKIM, custom MAIL FROM and ownership records Cresca shows you. Gmail and Yahoo also expect a DMARC record from bulk senders. The Gmail and Yahoo sender requirements post lists every rule.

Start sending

A transactional email service should take minutes to set up: verify a domain, create a key, send one request. Try Cresca free for 30 days, then follow the quickstart to send your first email.

title: Rust vs C++: Who Checks the Lifetime, and When
description:
Short version for the impatient: the real difference between Rust and C++ is not speed. Both compile to native code and both can hit the same hardware limits. The difference is who checks your lifetimes, and when. C++ lets you check them yourself, with discipline and tooling. Rust makes the compiler check them before the program exists.

I want to show that with a small program rather than a slogan, because I've read a lot of "Rust vs C++" posts that are just two benchmark charts and a fan club. I write mostly PHP, Go and TypeScript for clients, so I'm not a systems programmer, and I won't pretend to have shipped a game engine in either language. What I can do is take a mistake that every C++ beginner makes, run it on a real machine, and compare it to what Rust does with the same idea.

The bug that compiles

Here is a C++ program that moves a string out of a smart pointer and then reads from the pointer anyway.

#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <string>

int main() {
    auto name = std::make_unique<std::string>("report.pdf");
    auto other = std::move(name);
    std::cout << *name << "\n";
}

I built this with g++ -Wall -Wextra on a Linux box. No warnings. No errors. It ran and died with a segmentation fault (exit code 139). The move constructor did exactly what it promises: name is now an empty pointer, and dereferencing an empty pointer is undefined behaviour. The compiler knew that std::move had just been called on name. It let me carry on anyway, because the language says a moved-from object is valid but unspecified, and the language leaves it to me to remember.

That's not a knock on C++. A segfault in a toy program is the good outcome. The bad outcome is the same mistake inside a request handler where the pointer isn't null but points at memory something else now owns. Nothing crashes. Something gets quietly overwritten.

Now the same idea in Rust:

fn main() {
    let name = String::from("report.pdf");
    let other = name;
    println!("{name} {other}");
}

This does not build. The compiler stops with error E0382, "borrow of moved value", and points at the line where name was moved and the line where I used it afterwards. There is no runtime to crash, because there is no executable. The Rust Book chapter on ownership states the rules in three lines: each value has an owner, there is one owner at a time, and when the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped. The move bug above is simply the second rule being enforced.

Ownership is a rule, not a convention

C++ has all the same ideas. Smart pointers, RAII and move semantics are the C++ answer to manual memory management, and modern C++ written with them is far safer than the C-with-classes code that gave the language its reputation. The C++ Core Guidelines are full of advice in exactly this direction: prefer unique_ptr, avoid raw owning pointers, don't hold references past the lifetime of the thing they point at.

So if both languages have the idea, what's the difference? Enforcement. In C++ the guidelines are guidelines. A tool such as clang-tidy or a static analyser can flag many violations, and a code reviewer can catch more, but the language itself accepts the program. In Rust the same rules are part of the type system, and a program that breaks them is not a valid Rust program.

I find it useful to think of it as the difference between a speed limit sign and a speed bump. Most drivers slow down for both. Only one of them works at 3am when you're tired.

There's a cost, and I'll get to it. First, the second kind of bug, because it is the one that actually worries me.

Dangling references and the lifetime annotation

Returning a reference to something that no longer exists is the classic. In C++ it looks harmless:

const std::string& longer(const std::string& a, const std::string& b) {
    return a.size() >= b.size() ? a : b;
}

int main() {
    const std::string& r = longer("a long literal", std::string("hi"));
    std::cout << r << "\n";
}

The temporary std::string("hi") is destroyed at the end of the full expression. If it happened to be the longer one, r would now refer to a dead object. Here the literal wins, so this particular run probably prints correctly, which is the whole problem: it works until the inputs change. I'm describing that behaviour from the language rules, I didn't run this one to see what my compiler does with it.

Rust forces you to say how long each reference lives:

fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if a.len() >= b.len() { a } else { b }
}

fn main() {
    let result;
    {
        let short = String::from("hi");
        result = longest("longer text", &short);
    }
    println!("{result}");
}

The 'a says that the result lives no longer than the shorter of the two inputs. Because short is dropped at the closing brace and result is used after it, the compiler rejects the program with E0597, "short does not live long enough". The function is correct. The caller is wrong, and Rust tells the caller.

Those annotations are the most disliked part of the language, and I get why. They look like noise until you've been bitten by the thing they prevent. The Rustonomicon is blunt about where the boundary sits: in safe Rust the compiler guarantees the absence of this class of bug, and in unsafe blocks the guarantee becomes your job again. That is a much smaller area to audit than "the whole codebase".

What Rust costs you

I'd be doing the thing I complained about at the top if I stopped here. Rust costs real time.

The borrow checker will reject programs that are fine. Graph structures, doubly linked lists and anything with cyclic references fight the ownership model, and the usual escape hatches (Rc<RefCell<T>>, indices into a Vec, unsafe) each give up something. When I read Rust written by people who are new to it, the pattern I see most is .clone() sprinkled on until the errors go away. That works, and it quietly spends the performance you chose Rust to keep.

Compile times are slower than I'd like. The ecosystem is younger, so a library you take for granted in C++ for audio, CAD or an old hardware vendor's SDK may not exist, or may be a thin wrapper over the C++ one anyway. And if you have a decade of C++ in production, rewriting it is a business decision, not a technical one. I covered a smaller version of that trade in my post on Rust 1.99 and the box leak habit I had to drop, where even a language that polices ownership still lets you leak memory on purpose if you ask.

C++ has costs too, and they're mostly invisible until they aren't. The language is huge, with decades of overlapping ways to do one thing. Two engineers on the same team can write "modern C++" that looks like two different languages. Undefined behaviour doesn't announce itself.

How I'd choose

I'd pick C++ when the code has to live next to an existing C++ codebase, when a library only exists there, or when the team already has people who know where the bodies are buried. Rewriting a working system to get memory safety is rarely worth it by itself, and incremental approaches that put new code in Rust next to the old code are usually kinder to the schedule.

I'd pick Rust for new code that handles untrusted input, runs for a long time, or gets maintained by people who weren't in the room when it was written. Parsers, network services, command-line tools and anything that sits between the internet and a database are good fits. The ownership rules double as documentation. When a function takes String instead of &str, that signature tells the next developer who is responsible for the memory.

For the kind of work I do for clients, neither is the default. A Laravel app or a Go service covers most of what people hire me for, and I reach for a systems language only when a hot path justifies it. You can see what that mix looks like on my portfolio.

Try it yourself this week

Don't take my word, or any benchmark's word, for any of this. Spend an hour on it:

  1. Write the unique_ptr move bug above in C++ and compile it with -Wall -Wextra. Then compile the same file with -fsanitize=address,undefined and run it. See what each tool tells you.
  2. Install Rust with rustup and write the longest function with the nested block. Read the full E0597 message, not just the first line. Then delete the 'a annotations and read the different error you get.
  3. Pick one small function from your own C++ code that returns a reference or a pointer. Write down, in a comment, who owns the thing it points at. If you can't answer in one sentence, you've found the kind of bug Rust is built to catch.

If step three turns up a real question, that is a better reason to learn Rust than anything I've written here.

Originally published at abrarqasim.com. I write there about React, PHP, Rust, Go and the AI tooling around them.

title: Companies that sponsored green cards for frontend developers in 2026 (free list from DOL PERM data)
description:
If you're a frontend developer on a work visa, "does this company sponsor green cards?" is one of the hardest questions to answer from a job post. Most listings say nothing, and a recruiter's "we support visas" can mean H-1B only.

There's a better signal: the US Department of Labor publishes every PERM labor certification decision. PERM is the step most employer-sponsored green cards go through, so if a company filed PERM for a frontend role this year, it has actually done the paperwork before.

I went through the latest DOL PERM disclosure file (FY2026 Q3, decisions from Oct 1, 2025 to Jun 30, 2026) and pulled every case with a frontend-style job title (front end, frontend, front-end, UI developer, UI engineer, React developer). That's 151 cases at 103 employers. Here are the top 15.

Free sample: top 15 frontend green card sponsors (FY2026)

Employer PERM cases Certified Median offered wage Top worksite
ByteDance Inc. 17 16 $177,440 San Jose, CA
TikTok Inc. 5 5 $184,662 San Jose, CA
FMR LLC (Fidelity) 4 4 $161,363 Westlake, TX
U.S. Bank National Association 4 4 $142,522 Irving, TX
IBM Corporation 3 3 $153,807 San Jose, CA
Interglobe IT LLC 3 3 $105,997 Irving, TX
Milwaukee Electric Tool Corporation 3 3 $100,500 Brookfield, WI
Snap Finance, LLC. 3 3 $120,000 West Valley City, UT
TruStartIT LLC 3 3 $87,610 Richardson, TX
Advantis Global, LLC 2 2 $164,320 Mill Valley, CA
Apptegy, Inc. 2 2 $62,920 Little Rock, AR
AvidXchange, Inc. 2 2 $144,900 Charlotte, NC
Barclays Services Corp. 2 2 $175,000 Whippany, NJ
LOGIWARE, INC. 2 2 $83,325 Alpharetta, GA
Purchasing Power LLC 2 2 $142,002 Atlanta, GA

Source: DOL OFLC PERM disclosure data, FY2026 Q3. Ties at 2 cases are shown in file order; more employers have 2 cases than fit here.

👉 Get the full list free: Frontend & Software Green Card Sponsors FY2026 (pay what you want, $0 is fine). It has all 103 frontend employers plus a software developer tab with the top 1,150 sponsors, as a Google Sheet and CSV files.

How to read the columns

  • PERM cases: how many PERM applications DOL decided for that employer with a frontend-style title in this window. It counts applications, not people hired.
  • Certified: how many DOL approved (this includes "certified-expired", meaning it was approved but the next step wasn't filed in time). Across all 151 frontend cases, 146 were certified, 3 denied and 2 withdrawn.
  • Median offered wage: the middle of the yearly wages the employer wrote on those applications. It's what they offered for that specific role and location, not a company-wide salary band.
  • Top worksite: where the job actually is. This often differs from headquarters (Fidelity is based in Boston, but most of its cases here are in Westlake, TX).

The full list also has the top job titles per employer and the date of the latest decision, which tells you how recently they filed.

How to use the list in a job search

  1. Start with your location or the places you'd move to. Filter the sheet by worksite. A company with three cases in your city is a better lead than a famous name that only sponsored in another state.
  2. Look at the job titles. Many cases are senior, lead or principal roles. If an employer only filed for "Principal Front End Engineer", that tells you the level they're willing to sponsor.
  3. Check their careers page. Search for frontend, UI or React openings. Past filings don't mean they're hiring now.
  4. Ask early, and ask the right question. "Do you sponsor H-1B?" and "Do you sponsor green cards (PERM)?" are different questions. Ask both in your first recruiter call so neither of you wastes time.
  5. Track who said what. Once you're talking to 20+ companies, it's easy to forget which one said "case by case". I keep mine in a simple sheet (Job Application Tracker), but any spreadsheet works.

If frontend roles are too narrow for you, the software developer tab is much bigger: DOL decided 25,078 PERM cases for software developers and web developers (SOC codes 15-1252 and 15-1254) at 5,188 employers in the same window. The list covers the top 1,150 of them by case count (each with 4 or more cases, 19,254 cases in total). That's not every sponsor: the other 4,038 employers, the smaller filers, aren't in it.

Limits (please read before you rely on this)

  • This is PERM, not H-1B. A company can file lots of H-1Bs and few or no PERM applications, or the other way around.
  • Small numbers. Most frontend employers here (82 of 103) had a single case. A "100% approval rate" on 1–3 cases means very little.
  • Title matching isn't perfect. I matched job titles, not job descriptions. Some titles are senior or managerial, and a few aren't web work at all (Milwaukee Tool's cases are for a "Senior Concept Design Engineer – Front End Innovation", which reads like a product design role). Check the titles in the full list.
  • Staffing and IT consulting firms appear. Some employers place workers at client sites. That's a legitimate route for some people, but it's a different job than working in-house, so look them up.
  • Past filings don't promise future sponsorship. Budgets, policies and headcount change.
  • The data lags. DOL publishes disclosure files quarterly, and this one ends on Jun 30, 2026. Cases decided since then aren't in it yet. The raw files are public on the DOL FLAG site.
  • Not legal advice. For your own case, talk to an immigration attorney.

I left employer tax IDs out of the list on purpose. Everything else comes straight from the public DOL file.

For developers: pull your own fresh list

If you'd rather query the data yourself, by job title, city or salary, I published the tool I used to build this list: PERM Green Card Sponsors on Apify. It reads the DOL disclosure files directly and groups cases by employer. Most job seekers won't need it; the sheet is easier.

Get the full list

The free sample above is 15 of 103 frontend sponsors. Download the full Frontend & Software Green Card Sponsors FY2026 list: pay what you want, including $0.

If you spot an employer that's mislabeled or a mistake in the numbers, tell me in the comments and I'll fix it.
