title: The Agent Bumped a Major Version and CI Stayed Green
description:
The PR looked like housekeeping. The agent bumped one dependency across a major version, updated the lockfile, described it as "chore: upgrade queue-client to v4," ran the suite, and merged. CI was green.

Three days later, the nightly sync job started returning only the first page of records. The queue library kept responding, the job kept logging success, and nobody had touched pagination logic. The bump had.

Why a green suite missed the break

Unit tests rarely call the real dependency. They build a fake that matches the surface the wrapper remembers from the previous version. That fake still answers when the code calls the old method with the old arguments, so the test passes whether or not the installed package still behaves that way.

A major version exists because something on the outside changed. The suite proves your wrapper compiles against your mock. It does not prove the installed package still returns what the wrapper expects. Agents usually resolve "upgrade" to "latest" and never open the upstream removed list; the context window fills with the diff it generated, not the document that explains what changed.

The three breaks tests cannot see

A renamed response field. The client used to return { "records": [...] }. v4 renamed the key to { "items": [...] }. The wrapper reads records, gets undefined, iterates an empty list, and logs a clean run. The hand-written fixture in the test still builds records, so the test never meets v4's real shape.

A dropped config option, silently ignored. v4 removed the maxPerPage setting and capped page size at the SDK default. Old code passes the key; the new client ignores it. No exception, no deprecation warning, just shorter pages.

A changed callback contract. A hook that used to receive a second argument (the raw page token) drops it in v4. The handler reads the argument, gets undefined, computes "no more pages," and stops after the first response.

Each of these fails quietly: the program keeps running, the log line looks normal, the test stays green. The failure lives in the gap between the mock and the real backend, which CI never bridges.

The habit that costs one extra pass

Keep one direct dependency per PR. Never let the agent fold a major bump into a feature diff. A reviewer reading both cannot tell which change altered runtime behavior, and the agent cannot reason about the upgrade when the feature context dominates the prompt.

Read the breaking-changelog section for the target range, not the marketing "what's new" line. The breaking list for a major bump is usually short — renamed exports, removed options, response-field changes. The "new features" section tells you what you gained; the removed list tells you what you lost.

Run the built app against a sandbox, not just the suite. Execute the real job path against a test backend and compare the record count, page length, and response shape before merge. A mocked suite cannot reveal a renamed field; one real call does.

Review the lockfile diff by hand. Major bumps ride transitive dependencies along for free. Pin those separately so the reviewer sees what moved and can skip the ride-along upgrades on the first pass.

When the dependency wraps your own backend

If the upgraded package is an API client generated for your own service, the cheapest check is to replay recorded request/response pairs against the local OpenAPI spec and a live sandbox endpoint before merge. A renamed response field or a dropped option shows up as a red diff against the contract instead of as a partial nightly job three days later. That is the local-first loop we built into Powerduck: the spec stays the source of truth, and drift appears in front of the reviewer rather than in the logs.

What I check now

Before approving an agent-authored major bump, I ask three things:

  1. Is this PR a single direct dependency, or did the upgrade ride along with feature work?
  2. Did anyone open the breaking-changelog section for the target range, or only the release-notes headline?
  3. Did the agent run the real path against a sandbox, or did it stop at the mocked suite?

A green CI on a major bump means your mocks still compile. It does not mean the new version behaves.

title: MongoDB vs PostgreSQL in 2026: Why Postgres Is the Safer Default
description:
"SQL or NoSQL?" used to start long arguments. In 2026 the data points to a clear default, with a few real exceptions.

The 30-second version:

Adoption

In the 2025 Stack Overflow survey, roughly 45% of developers used PostgreSQL against about 25% for MongoDB. Adoption isn't everything, but it means more hiring options, more tooling and more answers when something breaks at 2 AM. Current versions are PostgreSQL 17 and MongoDB 8.

Transactions and correctness

Full ACID compliance is a core design principle of PostgreSQL. MongoDB has supported multi-document ACID transactions since version 4.0, so "Mongo can't do transactions" is outdated. It's still not the shape the database was built around.

Scaling

MongoDB's native sharding is a genuine strength when you need horizontal scale with heavy write throughput. PostgreSQL scales out with read replicas, partitioning, or extensions like Citus. It works, but you assemble more of it yourself.

So which one?

PostgreSQL is the stronger default for most applications. Choose MongoDB when your data is genuinely schema-less and document-shaped, and you need high write throughput with horizontal scale from day one.

The full comparison, scores and FAQ: MongoDB vs PostgreSQL — full breakdown.

title: Free SQL practice: why SUM(DISTINCT) doesn't fix inflated payment totals
description:
Free SQL practice, with the full data and solution below. No account, paid course, cloud service, or API key is needed. This is a SQLite exercise using synthetic payment data, with a Python standard-library runner if you do not have the SQLite CLI.

Two distinct capture events are each worth 1000 USD cents. A report should show 2000 cents. After a join, one query reports 4000; adding DISTINCT reports 1000. Both are wrong.

I maintain a free, MIT-licensed fintech data engineering roadmap. This article works through the class of bug explored in its C07 scenario: independent detail tables multiply one another before aggregation.

First, define the report's grain

We want one row for each payment and currency with at least one capture:

  • gross_minor: sum of capture amounts.
  • net_minor: captures minus fees in the same currency.
  • attempt_count: attempts at the payment grain, shared across that payment's currencies.

For this synthetic exercise, a missing fee match means zero fees, and a missing attempt match means zero attempts. That is an explicit fixture contract, not a general rule that unknown monetary data should become zero. Fee-only payments are outside the report's population.

Set up the data

Save this block as setup.sql. Run it once in a fresh database.

CREATE TABLE captures (
  id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, payment TEXT, currency TEXT, amount INTEGER
);
CREATE TABLE fees (
  id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, payment TEXT, currency TEXT, amount INTEGER
);
CREATE TABLE attempts (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, payment TEXT);

INSERT INTO captures VALUES
  ('c1', 'p1', 'USD', 1000),
  ('c2', 'p1', 'USD', 1000),
  ('c3', 'p1', 'EUR', 500),
  ('c4', 'p2', 'USD', 700);
INSERT INTO fees VALUES
  ('f1', 'p1', 'USD', 50),
  ('f2', 'p1', 'EUR', 20);
INSERT INTO attempts VALUES ('a1', 'p1'), ('a2', 'p1');

c1 and c2 have different event IDs and the same amount. Neither is a duplicate event. p1 has both USD and EUR captures. p2 has a capture but no matching fee or attempt.

Before running anything, calculate p1 / USD by hand: 1000 + 1000 = 2000 gross; subtract the 50-cent fee to get 1950 net; there are two attempts.

The query that looks plausible 

SELECT c.payment, c.currency,
       SUM(c.amount) AS gross_minor,
       SUM(c.amount) - COALESCE(SUM(f.amount), 0) AS net_minor,
       SUM(DISTINCT c.amount) AS distinct_amount_shortcut,
       COUNT(a.id) AS attempt_count
FROM captures AS c
LEFT JOIN fees AS f
  ON c.payment = f.payment AND c.currency = f.currency
LEFT JOIN attempts AS a ON c.payment = a.payment
GROUP BY c.payment, c.currency
ORDER BY c.payment, c.currency;

For p1 / USD, its output is:

Field Wrong output Expected
gross_minor 4000 2000
net_minor 3800 1950
distinct_amount_shortcut 1000 2000
attempt_count 4 2

There are two captures, one USD fee, and two attempts. Their joins create four rows. Each capture appears twice; the same fee appears four times. Summing those joined rows inflates gross and fee totals independently.

SUM(DISTINCT c.amount) removes repeated values. The two valid 1000-cent captures collapse into a single value, so it returns 1000. It does not deduplicate by event ID. This follows SQLite's aggregate DISTINCT behavior.

COUNT(DISTINCT a.id) could repair this particular attempt count, but it would not repair the monetary sums. The report needs a consistent grain for each independent measure.

Aggregate each input before joining

Save this corrected query as report.sql.

WITH capture_totals AS (
  SELECT payment, currency, SUM(amount) AS gross_minor
  FROM captures
  GROUP BY payment, currency
), fee_totals AS (
  SELECT payment, currency, SUM(amount) AS fee_minor
  FROM fees
  GROUP BY payment, currency
), attempt_totals AS (
  SELECT payment, COUNT(*) AS attempt_count
  FROM attempts
  GROUP BY payment
)
SELECT c.payment, c.currency, c.gross_minor,
       c.gross_minor - COALESCE(f.fee_minor, 0) AS net_minor,
       COALESCE(a.attempt_count, 0) AS attempt_count
FROM capture_totals AS c
LEFT JOIN fee_totals AS f
  ON c.payment = f.payment AND c.currency = f.currency
LEFT JOIN attempt_totals AS a ON c.payment = a.payment
ORDER BY c.payment, c.currency;

The independently specified expected output, also checked by executing the query in SQLite, is:

payment currency gross_minor net_minor attempt_count
p1 EUR 500 480 2
p1 USD 2000 1950 2
p2 USD 700 700 0

Each capture and fee CTE has one row per payment/currency. The attempts CTE has one row per payment. The final joins therefore do not multiply these input aggregates.

LEFT JOIN retains p2. Joining fees on both payment and currency prevents an EUR fee from reducing a USD total. SQLite documents the relevant FROM and JOIN processing.

The two attempts appear on both p1 currency rows because the contract measures attempts per payment. Do not sum that column across currencies and report four attempts. Measures with different grains need different aggregation rules.

Run it with Python, without extra packages

If Python includes sqlite3, save the setup and corrected query under the filenames above, then save this as run_report.py in the same directory:

import sqlite3
from pathlib import Path

with sqlite3.connect(":memory:") as db:
    db.executescript(Path("setup.sql").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    query = Path("report.sql").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    for row in db.execute(query):
        print(row)

Run python run_report.py, or py -3 run_report.py on Windows if needed. The in-memory database starts clean each time.

Try breaking your fix

Add a second USD fee with a different ID but the same 50-cent amount. The correct p1 / USD result should become 2000 gross and 1900 net, with two attempts. A DISTINCT-on-fee-amount shortcut would fail that check too.

Then add a third attempt. Gross and net should remain 2000 and 1900; only attempt_count should become three. These changes test that unrelated detail rows cannot change the monetary total.

Pre-aggregation fixes fan-out; it does not establish that the source events are correct or that settlement agrees. Duplicate delivery and conflicting event identities need separate ingestion checks.

Continue with the free practice repository

The C07 task, hints, cases, and reference extend this into a runnable repair exercise. After cloning the repository:

python challenges/run.py init C07
python challenges/run.py grade C07

The starter intentionally contains a defective query. Edit work/challenges/C07.py, then grade it again. The full repository has 100 English lessons, 40 foundation exercises, and 8 scenario labs, freely available on GitHub. Core practice uses Python 3.12+ and SQLite without paid infrastructure.

Disclosure: I maintain the linked repository. Its first edition and this article were prepared with AI assistance using Codex. All data here is synthetic, and these are teaching examples.

Which extra case would you use to catch a report that accidentally multiplies financial amounts?

title: Node.js Healthcare Appointment Retrieval: Latency-Bounded Reranking and Failure Recovery
description:
Short answer: a healthcare appointment assistant retrieval architecture should bound retrieval and reranking with one response deadline, return evidence with a source URL or document ID, and use failure recovery only when the resulting answer remains truthful.

For a healthcare appointment assistant, failure recovery is not "try every retriever until one answers." The deciding constraint is the patient's wait time. A fresh clinic notice that arrives after the response deadline has zero practical value, while a fast old policy can be actively misleading. The architecture needs to optimize retrieval quality inside a latency budget, then make the evidence loss visible.

This is the useful before/after. Before: collect candidates, rerank everything, and discover the timeout at the UI. After: reserve time for each stage, cancel late work, and label the evidence class that survived. Tiny change. Big operational difference.

Put the latency budget ahead of the fallback order

Start at the user-visible deadline and work backward. Suppose the product owns a 2,000 ms response budget. That number is an example configuration, not a benchmark. Reserve part of it for answer generation and transport; retrieval and reranking get what remains. A timeout must be explicit at every boundary, because one slow source cannot be allowed to consume the complete interaction.

The order should follow the question. A request such as "What documents should I bring?" can use deliberately indexed clinic guidance. "Is the 3:30 appointment still available?" needs live, authoritative context. Vector search is the durable path; live retrieval is the freshness path. Combining them is useful when a reply needs both policy and a changing fact, but the combination is valid only if each claim keeps its own citation.

Do not hide this behind a single search_failed counter. Record the stage, elapsed budget, attempt, candidate count, accepted evidence count, and terminal decision. The diagram in words is short: intent -> parallel retrieval -> deadline gate -> rerank -> citation gate -> answer or handoff.

The deadline gate matters more than an optimistic retry count.

How should Node.js healthcare appointment retrieval balance quality, latency, and failure recovery?

Use a small state machine. Run only the retrieval paths required by the intent, cap their candidate counts, and rerank the evidence that arrives before the deadline. A retry is allowed only when enough budget remains for both the retry and the downstream reranker. On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when it is present and apply exponential backoff. Don't tight-loop.

Here is a copyable orchestration core using Infrai's verified vector-query and web-search routes. Export request JSON that conforms to each route's public discovery schema into INFRAI_VECTOR_QUERY_JSON and INFRAI_WEB_SEARCH_JSON; this keeps the sample runnable without guessing fields that can be checked mechanically. The code does not interpret either response shape. It sends both typed-at-the-boundary payloads, retains successful raw evidence, and makes the deadline decision explicit.

const baseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;

if (!baseUrl || !apiKey) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_BASE_URL and INFRAI_API_KEY are required");
}

function readJson(name: string): unknown {
  const value = process.env[name];
  if (!value) throw new Error(`${name} is required`);
  return JSON.parse(value) as unknown;
}

async function postWithRetry(
  path: "/v1/vector/query" | "/v1/web/search",
  body: unknown,
  signal: AbortSignal,
): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 3; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(new URL(path, baseUrl), {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(body),
      signal,
    });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 2) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "0");
      const delayMs = Math.max(retryAfter * 1_000, 500 * 2 ** attempt);
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
      continue;
    }

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`retrieval rejected (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }
    return response.json() as Promise<unknown>;
  }
  throw new Error("retry budget exhausted");
}

async function retrieveWithinDeadline(timeoutMs = 1_200) {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  const timer = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), timeoutMs);

  try {
    const [durable, live] = await Promise.allSettled([
      postWithRetry(
        "/v1/vector/query",
        readJson("INFRAI_VECTOR_QUERY_JSON"),
        controller.signal,
      ),
      postWithRetry(
        "/v1/web/search",
        readJson("INFRAI_WEB_SEARCH_JSON"),
        controller.signal,
      ),
    ]);

    const evidence = [durable, live].flatMap((result) =>
      result.status === "fulfilled" ? [result.value] : [],
    );
    return { evidence, decision: evidence.length > 0 ? "review" : "handoff" };
  } finally {
    clearTimeout(timer);
  }
}

const result = await retrieveWithinDeadline();
process.stdout.write(`${JSON.stringify(result)}\n`);

There is a deliberate hard edge here: raw responses go to a schema-aware citation and reranking step before any generated appointment claim. No citable evidence means a staff handoff or a request to confirm. That is a successful recovery outcome. It preserves trust and gives operations a clean signal instead of burying uncertainty inside fluent text.

One implementation detail deserves scrutiny. Promise.allSettled retains results from a failed sibling, which is useful for partial recovery, but the example's timer cancels only adapters that respect AbortSignal. Test that behavior. I'm not sure what timeout fits your scheduling system; your mileage may vary with geography, upstream rate limits, and the reranker. A trace-derived percentile, measured per intent, resolves that uncertainty better than a universal constant.

Make reranking loss observable

Reranking improves ordering only over the candidates it receives. Under pressure, candidate loss can happen before ranking: a live source times out, a durable query returns no match, or a citation gate removes a result. If the dashboard reports only reranker duration, a quality regression looks mysterious.

Emit one structured event per request with retrieval_deadline_ms, path_completed, path_timeout, candidates_before_gate, candidates_after_gate, rerank_input_count, rerank_output_count, and decision. Do not log raw patient questions or retrieved page bodies by default. Apply the organization's health-data handling rules to identifiers and free text.

Then alert on outcomes, not vibes. A rising handoff rate with stable reranker latency points upstream. A stable candidate count with fewer accepted citations points at metadata or source lifecycle. A growing timeout share after increasing top-k suggests that the quality knob consumed the latency budget.

That last case is easy to miss — and wonderfully testable. Replay fixed, non-sensitive queries against several candidate limits, then compare accepted evidence and deadline misses. The best top-k is the smallest value that delivers enough relevant, citable context within the budget; more candidates are not automatically better.

Recovery also starts during indexing

Runtime fallbacks cannot repair a collection that still serves deleted appointment guidance. Re-index changed content deliberately, preserve stable document identifiers, and remove records that disappeared from the source. Publish a new revision only after its current chunks are present and its deleted chunks are gone.

Consider a clinic page split into six records. Staff change Friday hours and delete the walk-in paragraph. An upsert of only the edited hours leaves the obsolete walk-in claim searchable. The correct unit of completion is the source revision, not the last successful chunk write: stage the current six-or-fewer records, delete records absent from that revision, mark the revision complete, and only then make it eligible. If ingestion stops early, keep the last complete revision available or require live evidence for affected intents. Every returned chunk must carry its source URL or document ID so a reviewer can trace the answer without recreating the retrieval run.

Keep it boring.

This lifecycle creates three metrics that runtime traces can actually use: active revision age, deletion lag, and rejected stale candidates. Together they distinguish "the reranker chose badly" from "the reranker never received current evidence."

Compare the operating model, not a feature checklist

The main choice is who owns the index, how live context enters the request, and how much latency control the team needs. These are different operating models, even when each product can return vectors.

Option Best fit in this assistant Latency and recovery trade-off Evidence handling
PostgreSQL + pgvector Appointment records already governed beside relational data Retrieval load can compete with transactional work; the team controls fallback logic Stable row IDs can anchor review and deletion
Elasticsearch Teams needing lexical and vector retrieval with detailed index control More tuning and cluster operations, with explicit control over query behavior Source metadata remains under team control
Pinecone Teams preferring a managed vector service A network dependency remains part of the request path Citation fields must be modeled as metadata
Live web retrieval Public clinic notices that change quickly Page availability and extraction add variable latency URLs are visible, but source trust still needs a policy

Infrai can fit a polyglot team that wants verified vector and web capabilities through a plain REST API: no SDK is required, so any service that sends HTTP can use the same integration style. Infrai uses one key for both sides of this fallback and puts the calls on one bill, removing a credential and reconciliation boundary from the recovery path. Its 295 routes across 20 modules use consistent interface conventions, so vendor routing does not require application code changes. The API is genuinely self-describing: its public discovery surface needs no key and returns the request and response schemas, billing details, and runnable examples for each capability. That gives CI a concrete contract to validate before a retrieval change ships. The platform does not choose freshness rules, citation policy, or the deadline budget for you.

The catch is real. Stick with PostgreSQL plus pgvector when data locality and relational transactions dominate. Choose Elasticsearch when custom index control and an existing operations model matter more than a smaller integration surface. Use Pinecone when managed vector search is the central requirement. Call an authoritative scheduling system directly when it is the only valid source for live availability; a general retrieval layer should not sit between a patient and the system of record without a concrete reason.

Test the degraded answer, not merely the happy path

Build deterministic fixtures for an empty durable result, a delayed live response, HTTP 429, a deleted document, and evidence without a citation. Assert the terminal decision and the evidence IDs, not model prose. For the 429 case, assert bounded exponential backoff and Retry-After handling; for the delayed source, assert that cancellation leaves enough time for reranking and response delivery.

The release decision is equally crisp. Ship a recovery change only when citation retention and accepted relevance improve without pushing deadline misses beyond the product's chosen threshold. If quality rises but latency breaches the patient-facing budget, narrow the candidate set, move volatile facts to the authoritative live source, or keep the existing path. Failure recovery is working when the assistant can say less, promptly, rather than invent more after waiting.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/dense-vector.html
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/get-started/overview
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/429

title: The Multi-Cloud Drawdown
description:
The exclusive frontier partnership died the moment enterprise procurement stepped in.

OpenAI announced that its frontier models and Codex workflows are coming to Google Cloud's Model Garden, letting corporate customers draw down their existing Google Cloud spend commitments to run GPT workloads. Six months ago, the exclusive intellectual property license with Microsoft quietly ended, followed twenty-four hours later by an agreement with Amazon Web Services. OpenAI's models now sit natively inside all three hyperscalers.

Industry coverage frames this as a distribution race, but the underlying accounting tells a more constrained story. Enterprise buyers rarely pay for AI API calls out of fresh discretionary cash. They pay out of multi-year, nine-figure minimum spend commitments negotiated with their primary cloud infrastructure provider. If a Fortune 500 bank or insurer has committed three hundred million dollars over five years to Google Cloud or AWS, every dollar routed to Azure to query an OpenAI endpoint counts as an unbudgeted cash leak. The CFO asks why the lab cannot simply burn down the committed balance sheet credits sitting on GCP.

For two years, Microsoft used exclusivity to force those buyers onto Azure, treating OpenAI's frontier weights as the sole anchor tenant capable of moving legacy workloads. That works when frontier models hold a wide, unquestioned performance lead. It breaks down once Anthropic and open-weights models close the capability gap, while enterprise CIOs refuse to take on multi-cloud egress penalties or duplicate security audits just to run inference. The cost of friction began to exceed the value of the exclusivity payout.

On the lab side, OpenAI is raising capital at a 1.4 trillion dollar valuation while managing staggering compute bills and an impending public offering. At that scale, you cannot leave two-thirds of the addressable enterprise balance sheet untouched. Frontier labs have transitioned from proprietary research institutions into software wholesalers. They need every sovereign balance sheet and corporate committed-spend bucket open for depletion.

The hyperscalers accept the arrangement because they have already won the base layer. Hosting competing frontier models keeps enterprise data pipelines, vector indexes, and compute instances inside their own data centers. When model margins inevitably compress under cross-cloud price matching, the underlying kilowatt-hours and networking egress remain high-margin annuities for the landlord.

title: My Agent Swore It Fixed the UI. The Button Disagreed. 🫠
description:
Hey tech adventurers! 👋

My coding agent told me it fixed the UI. Tests green. Lint green. A very confident little summary with a ✅ at the end.

The button was off-screen. 🫠

So I built Pawprint. Agents now have to bring pics.

Green checks can't see 👀

Here's the thing nobody puts on the slide. Your CI is blind. It knows the function returns true. It has no idea the modal now covers the whole checkout page, or that "dark mode fix" means white text on a white background.

For backend work, tests get you most of the way. For anything a human actually looks at, the only real proof is... looking at it.

And I'm not pulling every branch, running the app, and clicking around to check an agent's homework. That was supposed to be the agent's job. That's the whole deal. 🤝

So the agent shows its work 📸

With Pawprint, the agent publishes evidence for the change and links it in the PR. Each publish has:

  • a description of what changed 📝
  • the list of changes 📋
  • before and after comparisons, side by side 🔀
  • screenshots and video when a still frame isn't enough 🎬

You open the PR, click the pawprint, and know in about ten seconds whether "fixed" means fixed. No checkout. No npm run dev. No vibes.

Your staging app is not public content 🔐

Here's the part I cared about most. Agents screenshot everything, and everything includes your unreleased app.

So the evidence sits behind GitHub sign-in. Share it with your org and the people in it can see it. Leave the org out and only you can. GitHub itself just shows a generic Pawprint card, so the internet sees a dog and nothing else. 🐕

You can make a page public when you actually want to show it off. You can't do it by accident.

"Done" should look like something 🧾

I keep saying it, and I'll keep saying it: agents love the word "done." Done is cheap. Done is a token.

Evidence is expensive in the right way. It's the agent proving it actually opened the thing it changed. And it's the only kind of review that still scales when agents are opening more PRs than you have hours.

Pawprint doesn't replace reviewers. It just means that when someone does look, there's something to look at.

Here's an example evidence page if you want to see what a receipt looks like.

P.S. Yes, everything I build is named after my dog. No, I will not be taking questions. 🐾

title: One zone lost power in London, and the banks went dark with it
description:
Tuesday, just after 7am

Tuesday morning in London. People tapped their bank cards at the till and the payment was declined. Revolut transfers froze mid-send. Lloyds and HSBC customers could not get into their apps. In courts across England and Wales, video hearings stalled because the courts' video platform was down. Royal Mail tracking went quiet, and delivery networks wobbled.

None of these companies had a power cut. A Google Cloud data center zone did.

Just after 7am London time on Tuesday, October 20, a power event knocked out europe-west2-b, one of three availability zones inside Google Cloud's London region. Google's own status text put it plainly: "A power event caused an outage within europe-west2-b zone. The power event is mitigated."

What followed is the part worth studying. One zone, one of three, lost power. And banks, courts, and couriers across the country felt it.

Google has said it will publish a full analysis once its internal investigation is finished. Until then, nobody outside Google knows the complete chain of events. What follows is what the status page and the press record show, plus the mechanics of what a zone failure actually breaks. If you run anything in the cloud, this is your blast radius lesson for the week.

What Google said

The timeline, from Google's status page and press reports:

  • Just after 7am London time (06:08 UTC), Tuesday Oct 20. The power event hits zone europe-west2-b. Google: "Multiple services are experiencing issues in the europe-west2 region."
  • Through the morning. "Google Cloud services are unavailable in europe-west2-b zone; some services in europe-west2 region may experience elevated errors and intermittent network issues." The incident page listed dozens of affected products: Compute Engine, Google Kubernetes Engine, Cloud Run, Cloud SQL, Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Pub/Sub, Memorystore, Persistent Disk, Cloud Load Balancing, Virtual Private Cloud, and more.
  • Around midday. Most services were back to normal by about 12:10pm London time, roughly six hours in. Full recovery of existing workloads was tentatively expected by early afternoon.
  • Late afternoon. The Ministry of Justice confirmed the courts' Cloud Video Platform had still not fully recovered. Some wounds take longer to close.

The customer list reads like a tour of British daily life: Revolut, Lloyds, HSBC, Halifax, Barclays, Bank of Scotland, NatWest, Nationwide, credit-reference firm Equifax, Royal Mail, DPD, property site Rightmove. The Telegraph reported cards declined at tills. The Guardian reported courts disrupted and millions unable to move money.

What a zone is, and what dies with it

A quick glossary, because the rest of this piece depends on it.

A region is a geographic area where a cloud provider operates, like London. Inside each region are availability zones: separate buildings, or clusters of buildings, each with its own power feed, its own cooling, and its own network connections. The London region, europe-west2, has three: a, b, and c. The idea is simple. If one building has a bad day, the other two keep going.

Your virtual machine lives in exactly one zone. Your disk lives in one zone too, with copies kept elsewhere for safety, but those copies are managed by the platform, not by you.

So when the power goes in zone b, everything physically in zone b stops at once. Virtual machines halt instantly, with no graceful shutdown. Disks stop being reachable. Anything that had its database primary in zone b stops answering. There is no orderly wind-down. The lights go out and the machines stop.

This is the part people nod along to and then get wrong in practice, because "we run in multiple zones" feels like a shield. It is a shield with holes. Here are the holes.

Why the surviving zones did not just absorb it

Failover takes time. Nothing in a distributed system switches over instantly. A database has to notice its primary is gone, hold an election, and promote a replica. A load balancer has to fail several health checks before it stops sending traffic to dead backends. DNS answers are cached, and each cached answer has a TTL, a countdown timer after which it expires. During every one of those windows, requests fail. Multi-zone does not mean zero-downtime. It means downtime measured in minutes instead of hours, if everything works as designed.

Your dependencies have zones too. Your app can run happily in zone a and still die, because it calls something that lived in zone b. A database primary. A NAT gateway. A load balancer component. A queue. Google's own status text admitted the mechanism: services across the region saw "elevated errors and intermittent network issues" because of shared infrastructure dependencies. A zone is not a sealed box. The region shares plumbing, and the plumbing runs through every zone.

You could not build replacements during the fire. Read this line from the status page again: "Customers may not be able to yet create new workloads." The system that creates virtual machines and clusters, the control plane, was itself degraded. Your running apps are the data plane. The API that manages them is the control plane. They are different systems, and this event hurt both. The usual escape plan, spin up fresh capacity in the surviving zones, was partially locked during the exact hours people needed it. The fire escape was bolted during the fire.

Two zones doing the work of three is not the same as three zones. Failover plans quietly assume spare capacity. When a third of a region's machines vanish, the survivors absorb their load on top of their own. Everything gets slower, queues grow, and some things fail that would have survived a smaller shock. One engineer's account in the press said the peer zones did not fully absorb the load. Capacity is the quiet part of every failover plan, and it is the part nobody load-tests.

The single-region trap

Here is the structural fact that made this outage national news instead of a footnote: europe-west2 is Google's only UK region. Customers who had built everything in London, sensibly, to keep data close to users, had no second UK location to fail over to.

Multi-zone protects you against one zone failing. Nothing inside a single region protects you against the region's shared systems failing, or against a zone failure cascading the way this one did through shared dependencies. Real protection is multi-region: running in London and somewhere else, with a tested plan to shift traffic. That roughly doubles your bill and your complexity, which is why most teams do not have it. The banks that went dark on Tuesday are a reminder of what that savings costs.

This happened before

The London region has been here before. On July 19, 2022, during the hottest day ever recorded in the UK, cooling failed in a building hosting europe-west2-a. Google's engineers could not get temperatures down, so they deliberately powered down part of the zone to save the hardware. That decision terminated about 35 percent of the virtual machines in that zone.

Different zone, different cause, same lesson. A zone is a unit of failure. It can go dark from heat, from power, from a bad config push, from a backhoe through a fiber bundle. The cause changes. The shape of the failure does not.

Audit your own blast radius

"We run multi-AZ" is a claim. Here is how to check whether it is true.

# Where do your VMs actually live? Not where you think. Where they are.
gcloud compute instances list --format="table(name,zone.basename())"

# Are your Kubernetes nodes spread across zones, or quietly all in one?
kubectl get nodes -L topology.kubernetes.io/zone

Then ask the questions no dashboard answers for you:

  • Which zone holds your database primary right now? Your managed database console will tell you. Write it down.
  • If that zone went dark, how long until a replica gets promoted, and have you ever watched it happen? If the answer is "the docs say it is automatic," you have not tested it.
  • Which zone do your NAT gateways, load balancers, and file stores live in? These are the shared plumbing. They have zones too.
  • During the last incident, could you have created new capacity? If your control plane calls were failing, your runbook's step one was fiction.

The cheapest version of this audit is a game day: pick a zone, pretend it is gone, and walk through what breaks. The 2022 incident's official workaround was "relaunch your workloads in another region." That advice only helps if you know, before the bad day, that you can.

The question

Draw your blast radius on paper. Pick the single thing, a zone, a database primary, a region, whose failure at 7am would ruin your day. If you cannot name it, that is the audit, and it is overdue.

Do you know, right now, which zone your database primary lives in? When did you last check?

title: Try tsrs without replacing your TypeScript build
description:
The new Rust port of TypeScript caught my deliberate type error. The setup surprise was more ordinary: tsrs --init doesn't work. 😅

I installed the published package, checked an imported function, broke its caller, then repaired it. Here's the small, disposable project I used. You can try the checker without changing your app's build.

Recorded command output, typeset for readability. This checks a tiny fixture; it isn't a speed comparison.

Cloudflare and VoidZero announced their collaboration on tsrs on 20 October. It's a Rust port intended to follow TypeScript's language behavior, incubated in Oxc. The announcement calls the npm release experimental. [1]

Give it a disposable project 🧪

You'll need Node.js and npm, plus a platform supported by the package's native binary. My run used Node 22.22.1 and npm 10.9.4. No Rust toolchain was needed for this npm installation.

In a new working directory:

mkdir tsrs-smoke
cd tsrs-smoke
npm init -y
npm install --save-dev --save-exact tsrs@0.18.0-ts7.1.0-dev.20260929
mkdir src

That long version is intentional. A moving latest tag makes tomorrow's bug report harder to reproduce. Keep the generated lockfile too.

Create tsconfig.json:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "strict": true,
    "noEmit": true,
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "NodeNext",
    "moduleResolution": "NodeNext"
  },
  "include": ["src/**/*.ts"]
}

Now src/price.ts:

export function label(price: number): string {
  return `Total: ${price.toFixed(2)}`;
}

And src/main.ts:

import { label } from "./price.js";
console.log(label(12.5));

The .js import is deliberate: this fixture uses NodeNext module resolution. Leave it as shown for this check. [3]

Run:

npx --no-install tsrs --version
npx --no-install tsrs --project tsconfig.json --pretty false

The version command identified the installed tsrs package and its TypeScript revision. The project check printed nothing and exited successfully. ✅

--no-install matters here: I want the package already pinned in the project, rather than asking npx to fetch an absent command. [4]

Make sure the checker can say no

Change the call in src/main.ts to:

console.log(label("12.50"));

Keep the import. Run the same project check again. My output was:

src/main.ts(2,19): error TS2345: Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'number'.

The process exited with code 2. Restore label(12.5), rerun it, and the exit code returns to 0.

That's more useful than checking an empty project. The fixture exercises an import and an exported function signature, then gives the checker something it should reject. 💡

The familiar setup command that fails

I also ran:

npx --no-install tsrs --init

It exited with code 5:

error: --init is not supported by tsrs.

The upstream README also lists --showConfig as unsupported. For this pinned package, write the small config explicitly or use an existing checked config. [2]

Original meme over my typeset command output.

Where I would put the first real-project check

Keep the current compiler as the build gate. Run tsrs separately against the same config, then inspect any diagnostic differences before changing CI. For a useful bug report, preserve the package version, config, smallest failing source, and exact output.

The project targets TypeScript's development branch and describes full conformance as a goal. It also documents diagnostic ordering differences. A matching tiny fixture is a starting point, not proof that a large app behaves identically. [2]

I haven't measured compile time or memory here. This article answers a narrower question: can I install the published package, check actual source, and catch an intentional mistake? For this fixture, yes.

References

  1. Cloudflare: Introducing tsrs, 20 October 2026.
  2. tsrs README at the inspected revision.
  3. TypeScript: NodeNext module resolution.
  4. npm exec and npx behavior.

Asset credits: original output panel and meme by Shivam Pandit, made from the recorded tsrs commands. The panel is typeset output, not a terminal screenshot.

AI disclosure

AI was used to draft the article.

title: The Interop 2027 CSS shortlist reads like a list of hacks you get to delete
description:
You want hairlines between the cells of a 3×3 grid. Two cells have content. Seven are empty. And an empty grid cell has no element, so there is nothing to put border: 1px solid on.

So you fake it. Paint the grid container red, set gap: 1px, give every child a white background, and pad the markup with seven empty divs so the background only shows through the gaps. It works. It's also seven DOM nodes that exist purely to hide paint.

Josh W. Comeau shows that exact workaround in his new post on Interop 2027, and then shows the property that makes it unnecessary. That's the useful way to read his whole list. Most of the ten features he voted for replace something we currently fake.

How the list gets made

Interop is the yearly project where the browser vendors (Comeau names Google, Apple, Microsoft and Mozilla, along with Igalia and Bocoup) agree on a set of focus areas and work on them together. He writes that a focus area added to Interop often reaches near-100% support across the major browsers within a year.

His example is subgrid. Firefox implemented it in 2019, other browsers barely moved for years, then it went into Interop 2023 and was widely available across modern browsers by the end of that year.

For 2027, the team at Mozilla built a ranking system where developers upvote the features they want, and Comeau writes that they plan to use that ranking data to decide what goes into next year's Interop.

Lines that belong to the grid

Gap decorations add a border-like syntax to the grid itself:

.grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
  grid-template-rows: repeat(3, 1fr);
  gap: 1px;
  border: 1px solid red;
  rule: 1px solid red;
}

rule is a shorthand, like border. Width, style, color. Use row-rule or column-rule when you only want lines in one direction.

Comeau lists three problems with the background trick: the empty nodes, the fact that it only works on a solid page background, and the lost flexibility. For example, you can't leave space between the grid's outer border and its inner lines. The mechanism explains all three. The lines come from paint showing through a gap, so the gap is all you get to style. rule makes the line its own thing.

Corners the border box follows

border-radius puts a quarter-circle on each corner. corner-shape swaps that curve for something else: squircle, bevel, notch, scoop.

.box {
  border-radius: 16px;
  corner-shape: bevel;
}

You could already cut shapes like these with clip-path or masks. The difference is where the change happens. According to Comeau, corner-shape changes the shape of the border box itself, so borders, outlines and box-shadows follow the new corner. A clip only hides pixels, so the border and shadow get cut off with everything else instead of tracing the new edge.

border-shape goes a level lower. You draw the border yourself out of straight lines, arcs and Bézier curves, and the same thing holds: the real border box changes, so outlines and shadows trace it. Comeau calls corner-shape a perfect progressive enhancement. Unsupported browsers fall back to the plain rounded corner, which is fine.

auto gets a transition

You can't animate to height: auto. You've hit this. interpolate-size fixes it, alongside the related calc-size() function. Comeau's accordion demo opts in at the root and animates the ::details-content pseudo-element:

html {
  interpolate-size: allow-keywords;
}

@supports (interpolate-size: allow-keywords) {
  details {
    overflow: hidden;

    &::details-content {
      height: 0;
      transition:
        height 300ms,
        content-visibility 300ms;
      transition-behavior: allow-discrete;
    }
    &:open::details-content {
      height: auto;
    }
  }
}

Keep that @supports gate. Comeau warns that without it, unsupported browsers get a brief delay added. He also notes this has been in Chrome since 2024, which is a long time to wait for an accordion.

State you used to read from JavaScript

Several picks are queries for state that CSS couldn't see before.

  • Scroll-state container queries. Put container-type: scroll-state on a sticky header and @container scroll-state(stuck: top) matches once it sticks. The same API answers scrollable: top and scrollable: bottom, which is all you need to fade those scroll-hint gradients in and out.
  • Anchored container queries, from Level 2 of Anchor Positioning. They let you check whether a positioned element is using a fallback position, so a tooltip's pointer can flip when the tooltip does.
  • Scroll-triggered animations. These are a separate proposal from scroll-driven ones: the animation starts when the user scrolls to a point and then runs over a specified duration. Today that means IntersectionObserver.
  • reading-flow and reading-order. Tab order follows the DOM, not the layout, so a grid that rearranges on mobile focuses things in the wrong order. reading-flow: grid-rows on the grid makes focus follow the visual rows.

Functions, and one that exists nowhere

@function lets you define a custom function, such as --gradient-to-transparent(--color, --direction: bottom), and return its value with result. Call it like any other value: background: --gradient-to-transparent(red). Comeau writes that it is already implemented in Chromium browsers.

Then there's inherit(). Comeau says he couldn't find it implemented in any browser. It takes the inherited value and lets you do math on it, which is exactly what nested radii need:

p {
  border-radius: calc(inherit() - 4px);
}

He'd be a bit surprised if it makes the 2027 cut. I'd vote for it anyway.

Where support stands

The support tables in Comeau's post, marked current as of October 2026, list Chrome 155 and Edge 154 as supporting each feature that has a table, and Firefox 157 and Safari 27 as not supporting it. inherit() has no table because it isn't listed on caniuse. That's one engine family carrying every tabled feature today, which is the gap Interop exists to close.

For your next layout, sort by fallback. corner-shape and the gated interpolate-size accordion degrade to something perfectly usable, so ship them now. Gap decorations are harder. The fallback is no lines at all, so the background trick stays until rule ships in more than one engine. Whether that happens in 2027 depends partly on how the Mozilla ranking comes out.

title: Free fintech data engineering lab: find a missing dollar with Python + SQLite
description:
Free and open source: 100 English lessons, 40 foundation exercises, and 8 scenario labs for fintech data engineering. The repository's lessons and core practice are available without payment or a signup wall. Clone it and start locally with Python 3.12+ and SQLite: no paid cloud account or API key is needed.

I maintain this learning project. This walkthrough uses six synthetic payment events to show why a balanced journal can still disagree with an external settlement.

Three checks that answer different questions

Idempotency: if a delivery is repeated, do we count the same business event twice?

Journal balance: do the signed entries for each event and currency add up to zero?

Reconciliation: does our internal expected amount agree with an independently supplied settlement record?

None of these checks replaces the other two. A balanced pair of entries can faithfully record an incorrect amount. A replay-safe pipeline can faithfully reproduce that incorrect amount every time.

Run the experiment

Use Python 3.12 or later with SQLite support. From a terminal:

git clone https://github.com/antony502189-max/fintech-data-engineering-roadmap.git
cd fintech-data-engineering-roadmap
python -m fintech_lab.quickstart

On Windows, use py -3 instead of python if necessary.

Every run starts with a fresh in-memory SQLite database and writes no files. The first delivery inserts six events; repeating the delivery inserts zero and recognizes six duplicates. The journal check passes.

Reconciliation still produces two exceptions:

Payment Currency Expected minor units External minor units External minus expected Result
p1 USD 7700 7700 0 matched
p2 EUR 4900 4900 0 matched
p3 USD 2500 2400 -100 amount mismatch
p9 USD unknown 500 unknown unexpected external payment

Explain the dollar before fixing the code

For p1, capture minus fee minus refund is:

10000 - 300 - 2000 = 7700 USD minor units

For p3, the internal record expects $25.00, but the external settlement reports $24.00. The difference is negative 100 USD minor units: a $1.00 shortfall.

For p9, there is no corresponding internal payment. Its expected amount is unknown, so the difference is unknown too. Treating that missing value as zero would hide the distinction between a known zero balance and a payment we cannot explain.

USD and EUR are kept separate throughout. Adding them together would not produce a meaningful monetary total.

Change one input and predict the result

In the repository's fintech_lab/synthetic.py, find p3 inside settlement() and change its net_minor from 2400 to 2500.

Run the quickstart again. p3 should now match. p9 should still be unexpected. Repairing one amount does not explain an unrelated external payment.

Restore 2400 afterward: the repository's tests expect the original deliberate defect.

You can also keep the full database and report for inspection:

python -m fintech_lab --out work/article-demo

That command writes warehouse.db and report.json and includes historical customer tiers and late-event feature examples. Use a new output directory for a clean run: unlike the in-memory quickstart, this version retains its database.

Where to go next

If the example is useful, the repository includes 100 English lessons, 40 foundation exercises, and 8 scenario labs. C07 is a SQL bug hunt about join fan-out; C06 covers backup recovery; C08 covers feature availability and delayed labels.

Start with the first-win walkthrough, or browse the repository.

The goal is to produce an explanation backed by code and checks, rather than only read a roadmap. If this helps you learn or teach, a voluntary GitHub star is appreciated. A reproducible edge case is even more useful feedback.

Scope and disclosure: I maintain the linked project. Its first edition and this article were prepared with AI assistance using Codex. The data is synthetic, and the signed journal is a simplified teaching model, not a production banking system. The repository documents its provenance and limitations.

Which reconciliation edge case would you add next: a partial refund, an unmatched fee, or a late settlement adjustment?
