title: How to Reconcile Healthtech Payments in Node.js — Queueing Delayed Webhook Retry Callbacks
description:
For a failed payment webhook, the safest retry queue pattern lets delayed callbacks arrive more than once but never applies the payment twice.

Short answer: use a queue with delayed retries and a dead-letter queue (DLQ), keep the durable payment record in your application database, and deduplicate every delivery by the provider's event or delivery ID.

That is the beginner-friendly pattern. It separates transport from truth. The queue controls when work becomes eligible; the database decides whether that work has already changed a payment. For a healthtech system, that separation also makes the trust boundary visible: the queue should carry references, not a growing history of payment or patient data.

How should a Node.js queue retry failed webhook callbacks and delayed jobs?

Start with a diagram in words: payment provider -> public webhook receiver -> queue -> reconciliation worker -> application database. A nightly scheduler enters through the same queue, so the webhook path and the reconciliation path share one idempotent worker. On a transient failure, the worker records the attempt and next retry time, then schedules another delivery. Once the retry budget is exhausted, the task moves to the DLQ for inspection and controlled redrive.

Before this pattern, the receiver tries to reconcile synchronously. A slow provider call holds the request open, and retry state gets scattered between HTTP handlers and logs. After it, the receiver has one small job: validate the callback, persist its identity, and publish a compact task. The worker owns retries. The database owns the result.

Keep the message deliberately dull:

  • eventId, the stable deduplication key
  • paymentId, the lookup reference
  • attempt, the delivery count
  • notBefore, the next eligible processing time

Do not put the full webhook history in each message. This queue limits messages to 256KB, delayed delivery to 7 days, and retention to at most 30 days. An acknowledged message is deleted. Those limits point toward the same design even on another queue: durable business state belongs in the database, while the queue carries enough information to find it.

Standard queues provide at-least-once delivery, so duplicate processing isn't an edge case. It is part of the contract. Use a unique constraint on eventId or the provider delivery ID and commit the deduplication marker in the same database transaction as the payment update. Checking a cache first is not equivalent; two workers can both pass that check before either writes.

Duplicates happen.

One more boundary matters. Region, retention, deletion, and subprocessors are deployment and contract decisions, not properties a retry loop can manufacture. For Infrai, inspect the public discovery record's regions field before choosing a deployment. I'm not sure which region meets your organization's policy without that policy and the current discovery response; security and legal owners must resolve that against the payment provider, queue provider, and database processor agreements.

Build the delivery state machine before choosing a provider

The cleanest state machine has four outcomes: processed, duplicate, retry, and dead-letter. Here is a runnable TypeScript model. It uses an in-memory queue so the delivery behavior is visible without inventing a vendor request schema; replace MemoryQueue and MemoryLedger with adapters for your chosen queue and transactional database.

type ReconcileTask = {
  eventId: string;
  paymentId: string;
  attempt: number;
  notBefore: number;
};

type DeadLetter = ReconcileTask & { reason: string };

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const queueName = process.env.QUEUE_NAME ?? "nightly-payment-reconciliation";

async function publishWithRetry(task: ReconcileTask): Promise<void> {
  if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  for (let retry = 0; retry < 5; retry += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": task.eventId,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        queue: queueName,
        message: task,
        delay_seconds: Math.max(0, Math.floor((task.notBefore - Date.now()) / 1_000)),
      }),
    });

    if (response.ok) return;
    const reason = await response.text();
    if (response.status !== 429 || retry === 4) {
      throw new Error(`Queue publish failed (${response.status}): ${reason}`);
    }

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("Retry-After"));
    const waitMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
      ? retryAfter * 1_000
      : Math.min(500 * 2 ** retry, 8_000);
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, waitMs));
  }
}

class MemoryQueue {
  ready: ReconcileTask[] = [];
  dead: DeadLetter[] = [];

  publish(task: ReconcileTask): void {
    this.ready.push(task);
  }

  next(now: number): ReconcileTask | undefined {
    const index = this.ready.findIndex((task) => task.notBefore <= now);
    if (index === -1) return undefined;
    return this.ready.splice(index, 1)[0];
  }
}

class MemoryLedger {
  private readonly processed = new Set<string>();

  applyOnce(task: ReconcileTask): "processed" | "duplicate" {
    if (this.processed.has(task.eventId)) return "duplicate";

    // A real adapter inserts eventId and updates the payment in one transaction.
    this.processed.add(task.eventId);
    return "processed";
  }
}

const queue = new MemoryQueue();
const ledger = new MemoryLedger();
const maxAttempts = 4;

function backoffSeconds(attempt: number): number {
  return Math.min(60 * 2 ** attempt, 3_600);
}

function handle(task: ReconcileTask, providerAvailable: boolean, now: number): void {
  if (!providerAvailable) {
    const nextAttempt = task.attempt + 1;
    if (nextAttempt >= maxAttempts) {
      queue.dead.push({ ...task, attempt: nextAttempt, reason: "retry budget exhausted" });
      return;
    }

    queue.publish({
      ...task,
      attempt: nextAttempt,
      notBefore: now + backoffSeconds(nextAttempt) * 1_000,
    });
    return;
  }

  console.log(task.eventId, ledger.applyOnce(task));
}

const now = Date.now();
const task: ReconcileTask = {
  eventId: "evt_20260909_0042",
  paymentId: "pay_1048",
  attempt: 0,
  notBefore: now,
};

queue.publish(task);
handle(queue.next(now)!, true, now);

// Simulate at-least-once redelivery of the same provider event.
queue.publish(task);
handle(queue.next(now)!, true, now);

await publishWithRetry(task);

Run it with npx tsx reconcile.ts. The output contains processed and then duplicate. That tiny before/after is the core guarantee. The production database adapter must make applyOnce atomic; the in-memory implementation only makes the rule easy to see.

The example uses four attempts and caps backoff at 3,600 seconds as an application policy, not as a vendor promise. Tune both values to the payment provider's recovery pattern and your reconciliation deadline. Keep the next retry below the queue's delay ceiling. If recovery can take longer than 7 days, write a durable due date to the database and let a scheduler publish a fresh task later rather than pretending one delayed message is long-term storage. The publish call uses a stable idempotency key, reads the bearer token from the environment, sets the HTTP method explicitly, honors Retry-After on a 429, and surfaces every other non-success response. In production, the consumer needs equivalent status handling and must acknowledge only after the database transaction commits.

Fetch the current request and response schema from public discovery before binding the rest of the adapter. Successful processing must acknowledge only after persistence, while permanent failure belongs in the DLQ.

Put observability around decisions, not queue motion

A useful log answers, “What did the worker decide?” Record eventId, paymentId, attempt, outcome, and next retry time. Do not log full webhook bodies or authorization material. A useful metric counts outcomes by processed, duplicate, retry, and dead-letter; another measures the age of the oldest eligible task. Alert on a sustained DLQ increase or on task age crossing the nightly reconciliation deadline.

This is where delivery guarantees become operational. A queue depth of 400 could be normal just after the nightly run. One task that has missed the settlement deadline may be the real incident. Tie alerts to age and business deadlines, then give operators a redrive procedure that reuses the same event ID. Redrive must not create a new identity, or the database cannot recognize the old work.

Deletion needs equal care. An ack removes a queue message, but it does not delete the corresponding payment row, provider record, application log, backup, or DLQ export. Write a deletion map that names each processor and store. The map should say who can delete data, which identifier links the copies, and how completion is verified. Queue retention is one line in that map, not the whole policy.

Keep sensitive fields out of labels and metric dimensions too. IDs can still be sensitive, and high-cardinality event IDs make poor metric labels anyway. Put correlation identifiers in access-controlled structured logs; keep metrics aggregated by outcome and queue.

Compare the queue pattern against workflow and replay requirements

Provider choice comes after the state machine because the hard promise lives in your idempotent transaction. The products below solve different shapes of work.

Option Best fit in this design The catch
Infrai Compact delayed webhook tasks and a DLQ behind one REST API Standard delivery is at-least-once; delay is capped at 7 days, retention at 30 days, and push targets require public HTTPS
BullMQ A Node.js team that wants a Redis-backed job queue The team owns the Redis and worker operating boundary
Inngest Event-driven functions and durable execution Compare its processor and region boundary with the payment-data policy
Trigger.dev TypeScript background jobs Validate delivery and retention behavior against the same state machine
Temporal Multi-step workflow orchestration where the process itself must be modeled A queue-plus-DLQ design is simpler when the job is only retry, reconcile, and record
Apache Airflow DAG-oriented scheduled data work It is a different operating model from a small callback worker
Apache Kafka Replay and multiple consumer-group requirements An ack-delete queue cannot substitute for Kafka-style replay
GitHub Actions Repository automation on a schedule Keep it for repository workflows, not as the source of truth for payment delivery state

Infrai is worth trying for a team that wants the delayed queue portion of this healthtech reconciliation flow behind the same key and bill as its other backend services. The supporting benefit is concrete: its plain REST interface avoids adding a queue-specific SDK to the Node.js worker. Public discovery describes the current capability schemas, and the broader platform exposes 295 routes across 20 modules.

The catch is equally concrete. It is not suitable when the process needs a DAG, fan-out/fan-in joins, Kafka-style replay, multiple consumer groups, native debounce, or native topic fan-out. Stick with Temporal or Airflow for workflow orchestration, and evaluate Kafka when retained event replay is the requirement. If the worker is private-only, push delivery is also the wrong boundary because push subscriptions require a public HTTPS target; polling from the worker may fit, subject to your network and processor review.

There is no magic “exactly once” checkbox here.

FIFO deduplication on this platform has a 5-minute window, while a reconciliation retry can outlive it. The application database still needs the durable event-ID constraint. Likewise, a cron trigger has a 900-second execution ceiling and does not backfill triggers missed while paused, so a long nightly reconciliation should use cron only to enqueue work and let workers consume it. Expect second-level scheduling jitter rather than treating the trigger timestamp as a financial clock.

What should the production readiness review prove?

First, prove duplicate safety. Deliver the same eventId concurrently to two workers and verify that one payment transition commits. Then force retries past the configured budget, inspect the DLQ record, and redrive it without changing the event identity. Test a delayed task near your chosen operational horizon, but stay within the 604,800-second platform limit.

Second, prove the trust boundary. Review the currently advertised regions, retention settings, deletion procedure, logs, backups, and every processor that can see a payment reference. Confirm that public HTTPS exposure is acceptable if push delivery is selected. Do not infer contractual residency from an API region field alone — the contract and processor list have to agree with the technical configuration.

Finally, prove that the on-call signal survives the happy path. A successful nightly run should leave an auditable count of processed, duplicate, retried, and dead-lettered tasks without preserving full payload history in the queue. A failed callback should be visible before its business deadline. And an operator should be able to redrive it safely, with the database stopping a second application if the original result committed but its acknowledgment was lost.

That is the decision rule: choose the smallest queue that meets the region and processor boundary, then build correctness in the database. Move to a workflow engine when the job becomes a workflow. Move to an event log when replay becomes the product requirement.

If this boundary fits your system, use the Infrai Node.js webhook worker guide as a low-pressure next step and verify its live discovery schema before integrating.

You need seller portals, buyer pricing tiers, request-for-quote (RFQ) flows, bulk orders and an admin layer. These 5 templates were compared on portal depth, B2B features, tech stack and production readiness.

1. TradePro: B2B Wholesale Multi-Vendor Marketplace Template

Stack: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4
Price: from $24
Link: TradePro on DevCraftify

Built specifically for B2B wholesale.

  • Three portals: Buyer, Supplier and Admin, each with its own dashboard and workflow.
  • Supplier portal: product listings, pricing rules, inventory, order processing and RFQ responses.
  • Buyer portal: supplier catalogs, RFQ submission, negotiated pricing, bulk order tracking and purchase history.
  • Admin portal: supplier onboarding, buyer verification, commissions, disputes and analytics.
  • RFQ negotiation: request, supplier quote, counter-offer, final agreement.
  • Tiered pricing: volume discounts, customer group pricing and supplier-specific agreements.

The code is organized for API integration, so you connect your backend to the existing UI components.

2. Shoponix: React Next.js Multi-Vendor Marketplace Template

Stack: React, Next.js, TypeScript, Semantic UI
Price: from $29
Link: Shoponix on ThemeForest

  • Role-based access for root admin, store admin and general user.
  • Stripe payments and Cloudinary media management included.
  • Six demos: Grocery, Medical, Furniture, Electronics and Fashion.
  • Admin dashboard with revenue tracking, product trends and store oversight.

Best for B2C multi-vendor marketplaces that need working payment and media integrations.

3. MarketPro: Multivendor React Next.js Template

Stack: React, Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS
Price: from $29
Link: MarketPro on ThemeForest

  • Multiple homepage variations (Grocery, Electronics, general merchandise).
  • Full vendor management system with customer storefront and admin flows.
  • Figma design file included.

Good if you plan to customize the visual design before touching code.

4. DpMarket: Digital Marketplace Multi-Vendor Next.js Template

Stack: React, Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS
Price: from $29
Link: DpMarket on ThemeForest

  • Designed for selling software, creative assets, templates, ebooks and downloads.
  • Server-side rendering and static generation for SEO.
  • Vendor management, product listings and sales tracking.

The right pick if your marketplace sells digital goods rather than physical ones.

5. Martfury: Multipurpose Marketplace React Next.js Template

Stack: React, Next.js, Redux, Bootstrap
Price: from $29
Link: Martfury on ThemeForest

  • Covers electronics, furniture, clothing, accessories and general merchandise.
  • One of the longest-running marketplace templates on ThemeForest.
  • Redux and Bootstrap: an older stack, but proven in production.

A stable choice for broad-category B2C marketplaces.

  • Wholesale with RFQs and tiered pricing: TradePro.
  • General multi-vendor retail with payments ready: Shoponix.
  • Design flexibility with Figma: MarketPro.
  • Digital product marketplace: DpMarket.
  • Proven, broad-category marketplace: Martfury.

title: Node.js Push API Pull Model for 3 Small SaaS Custom Metrics Dashboards
description:
A small SaaS comparing a Prometheus alternative for custom metrics needs more than a Node.js dashboard that says revenue dipped; it must show which pricing rule was active. The operational constraint changes the design: preserve enough context to reconstruct a rollout before optimizing the collection mechanism.

TL;DR: record three decisions for every pricing evaluation: the rule version, the flag variant, and the outcome. Use pull collection when a long-running Node.js service can expose current counters reliably. Use a push API when short-lived jobs or network boundaries make scraping impractical, but treat delivery, retries, and event time as application concerns. The dashboard is the last step. The evidence model comes first.

This is deliberately a small system. It supports shipping a pricing change weekly without turning observability into a second product.

Evidence first.

What must survive the incident?

Imagine a new e-commerce rule behind a flag: customers in one market receive volume pricing when a cart crosses a threshold. Two hours after rollout, completed orders fall. A graph of checkout_total cannot answer the useful questions. Was the new variant evaluated? Which rule revision produced the quote? Did the quote become an order?

Those are separate decisions, and collapsing them into one success counter destroys the join points needed later. I would keep the telemetry vocabulary small:

Signal Required dimensions Reconstruction question
Pricing evaluations rule_version, flag_variant, result Which logic produced the displayed price?
Checkout outcomes flag_variant, outcome Did exposed sessions complete or fail?
Rule errors rule_version, error_class Did evaluation fail before checkout?

Do not attach customer IDs, cart IDs, or raw URLs to metric labels. Metrics aggregate repeated measurements; an unbounded identifier creates an unbounded set of time series. Keep a correlation ID in logs or traces instead, where one event can be inspected without turning every customer into a dashboard dimension.

This separation also prevents a subtle mistake: treating absence as zero. No samples might mean no traffic, a dead process, a failed push, or a broken scrape. The collection path needs its own health signal, and an incident review must distinguish those cases.

The smallest Node.js implementation

The application code should not know whether a collector pulls or an adapter pushes. A tiny interface keeps the pricing path stable while the transport changes. It also makes the behavior testable without starting a monitoring stack.

type Labels = Record<string, string>;

interface CounterSink {
  add(name: string, value: number, labels: Labels): void;
}

type PricingDecision = {
  ruleVersion: string;
  flagVariant: "control" | "volume_v2";
  result: "standard" | "discounted" | "error";
};

export function recordPricingDecision(
  sink: CounterSink,
  decision: PricingDecision,
): void {
  sink.add("pricing_evaluations_total", 1, {
    rule_version: decision.ruleVersion,
    flag_variant: decision.flagVariant,
    result: decision.result,
  });
}

That is enough instrumentation for the business decision. It is intentionally boring. The metric name describes a cumulative count, while labels carry a bounded set of states that can be grouped during an incident.

For a pull model, the in-process adapter accumulates these values and exposes a snapshot on an HTTP endpoint. The collector owns the schedule and records when a target could not be reached. A long-running Node.js web process fits this shape well because its current state is available between scrapes.

import { createServer } from "node:http";

const counts = new Map<string, number>();

const sink: CounterSink = {
  add(name, value, labels) {
    const ordered = Object.entries(labels).sort(([a], [b]) => a.localeCompare(b));
    const key = JSON.stringify([name, ordered]);
    counts.set(key, (counts.get(key) ?? 0) + value);
  },
};

function snapshot(): string {
  return [...counts.entries()]
    .map(([key, value]) => `${key}\t${value}`)
    .join("\n");
}

createServer((request, response) => {
  if (request.url !== "/metrics") {
    response.writeHead(404).end();
    return;
  }

  response.writeHead(200, { "content-type": "text/plain; charset=utf-8" });
  response.end(snapshot());
}).listen(9464);

The serializer above demonstrates the boundary; it is not a claim of compatibility with a particular exposition format. In production, use a maintained metrics library or an OpenTelemetry SDK exporter rather than owning serialization. Outsource the undifferentiated parts. Spend engineering time on the pricing rule and the evidence it needs.

For push, the same sink can buffer points and hand batches to a transport adapter. That adapter must define event timestamps, a timeout, a bounded queue, and retry behavior. Never block checkout indefinitely to report checkout telemetry. If the queue fills, increment a local dropped-measurement counter and surface adapter health through a separate path.

Should a small SaaS push custom metrics or use a pull model?

The choice is less about dashboard taste than failure ownership.

With pull, the collector initiates collection. A failed scrape is visible from outside the application, and the scrape time supplies a consistent observation clock. Process-local counters disappear on restart unless the collector captured them first, so resets must be handled in queries. Brief jobs may start and finish between collection intervals. That limitation rules out a pure pull design for work that routinely begins and ends unseen.

With push, the application or an agent initiates delivery. That works across inbound network restrictions and for jobs whose lifetime is shorter than a scrape interval. It also moves work into the sending path: buffering, backoff, duplicate handling, authentication, and timestamp semantics now need explicit answers. A successful HTTP response only proves that one receiver accepted a request; it does not prove the future dashboard will preserve the point. The trade-off is more application-owned delivery state, so push is not a fit when the team cannot operate a queue or verify duplicates.

For the pricing rollout, I would use pull for the long-running checkout service and push only for a short-lived backfill that recalculates catalog prices. Mixing collection modes is acceptable when the metric schema stays consistent. Forcing every workload through one transport is tidy on a diagram and expensive during an incident.

The practical test is direct. On the Node.js 22 runtime used for the service, kill the collector, restart the process, and run the backfill twice. Then ask whether the resulting timeline lets you distinguish missed collection, a counter reset, duplicated delivery, and a genuine drop in evaluations. Repeat the exercise with one delayed batch and one rejected batch, because a clean happy-path replay hides the exact ambiguity an incident creates: the same empty interval can represent zero pricing evaluations, an unreachable target, discarded buffered points, or a query that filtered the new rule version. Record which layer exposes each failure and how an operator proves recovery. If the answer depends on remembering an undocumented retry interval, the design is not ready.

More panels will not help.

Build the dashboard backward from three queries

Start with the incident questions, not chart types. One view compares pricing evaluations by flag_variant and result. A second compares checkout outcomes by variant. A third shows rule errors by rule_version beside collection health.

Avoid calculating causality from those charts. They support correlation and triage. A variant can coincide with fewer purchases because traffic composition changed, inventory ran out, or payment processing degraded. The metrics narrow the search; logs and traces carry the per-request detail required to inspect a specific path.

OpenTelemetry describes a metrics data model with instruments and aggregations, and it can provide a stable instrumentation boundary even when storage changes. Prometheus uses a pull-oriented model for scraping HTTP metric endpoints. Grafana can visualize data from multiple sources. Hosted systems such as Datadog, New Relic, and Honeycomb differ in ingestion APIs, query models, retention controls, and how metrics relate to traces and logs. Those boundaries matter, but none repairs missing rule context at emission time.

Evaluate any backend with a replay exercise. Feed a fixed set of decisions, include one process restart, and delay one batch. Check whether the three incident questions produce understandable answers. Also inspect export, retention, cardinality controls, and delivery visibility before committing. A polished default dashboard ranks below recoverable evidence.

What I would change at scale

At higher traffic, I would move schema definitions into a shared package, enforce an allowlist for label values, and add automated tests that reject customer-derived dimensions. I would also sample detailed traces while retaining low-cardinality counters for the full rollout window. Metrics answer “how much”; traces and logs explain individual paths.

Multiple service instances introduce another trap. A process-local counter belongs to one process lifetime. Aggregate rates across instances with reset-aware queries rather than pretending each counter is a durable global total. For pushed points, include a stable producer identity only if the backend needs it for deduplication, and keep that identity bounded.

There is a revenue-per-hour line here. Building custom storage, query execution, alert delivery, and access control rarely advances an e-commerce pricing feature. A solo operator should own the event semantics and tests, then choose interchangeable collection and storage components that meet the reconstruction exercise. Ship weekly. Revisit the transport when workload lifetime, network topology, or operational burden actually changes.

The final decision rule is short: choose pull when external collection can observe a persistent service and scrape failures are valuable evidence; choose push when the producer cannot be scraped, after budgeting for delivery state. In both cases, preserve rule version, variant, outcome, and collection health. That is what turns a graph into an incident timeline.

Sources

  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/metrics/
  • https://prometheus.io/docs/introduction/overview/
  • https://prometheus.io/docs/instrumenting/exposition_formats/
  • https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/datasources/
  • https://logback.qos.ch/manual/appenders.html

title: Stop random programs from reading your Git and AWS credentials on Windows
description:
The problem

When you use Git or the AWS CLI, your tokens and keys often sit in plain files, or in places any program running as you can read. You would never know if one did.

What I built

Wardkey is a small, experimental tool for Windows. It keeps your Git and AWS credentials in an encrypted vault. When Git or AWS asks for a key, Wardkey checks which program is asking and applies your rules before giving anything out.

Think of it like a doorman. Most tools lock the door but give the key to anyone already inside. Wardkey asks every time: "Which program are you, and do your rules allow you to have this key?"

What it does

  • Stores credentials in an encrypted vault.
  • Works with Git over HTTPS (as a credential helper) and the AWS CLI (through credential_process).
  • Applies rules about which app may get which credential.
  • Can ask you for a Windows Hello check (face, fingerprint or PIN) on each request, when your rule says so.
  • Supports decoy keys. If anything asks for one, the request is denied and logged.
  • Writes every decision to a local log that detects many kinds of edits.

It's written in Go.

Honest limits

This is an early prototype, and I'd rather say so clearly:

  • It cannot stop malware that is already running as you. A program running as you could try to pretend to be Git or AWS. Windows Hello approval on every request is the real protection.
  • No outside expert has reviewed it yet.
  • Builds are unsigned, and it's Windows-only.
  • The activity log can detect many edits, but not someone deleting its last entries.
  • Please test with dummy credentials only.

The full list is in the threat model in the repo.

Try it 

go build -o wardkey.exe .\cmd\wardkey
wardkey help

Setup details are in the README.

Code and docs: https://github.com/Annora998/Wardkey

The code is source-available.

I'd love your feedback

Where do you think the design is weak, especially the caller checks and the approval flow? What would you want it to protect next? Tell me in the comments.

title: Why Your Async FastAPI Server Dies Under Real SSE Load
description:
Why Your Async FastAPI Server Dies Under Real SSE Load

You've tested your audio transcription API with five concurrent requests. Everything streams cleanly. You deploy it. Two weeks later, a user uploads a 90-minute audiobook while three others run voice cloning jobs, and suddenly SSE clients start timing out. Health checks fail. Your database pool reports exhaustion. The FastAPI server is still running, but nothing responds.

The failure isn't dramatic. It's the invisible kind: async def wrapping synchronous requests.get(), blocking filesystem operations inside route handlers, or holding database connections open while waiting for model inference. Under light load, the event loop absorbs the stalls. Under real concurrent audio workloads, everything locks.

The Architectural Boundary

VoiceStudio offers a compelling fully-local alternative to ElevenLabs: voice cloning, dubbing, transcription, audiobook generation—all without sending media to a third party. The production challenge isn't starting a server. It's keeping long-running jobs responsive while clients consume progress events and new requests continue arriving.

The boundary should be explicit:

  • FastAPI handles authentication, validation, job creation, and event delivery.
  • A job store records durable state and leases.
  • A worker process performs model inference and audio processing.
  • The API streams worker events without owning the model lifecycle.
  • Media files remain outside response memory, ideally in local object storage or a managed filesystem abstraction.

An SSE connection should be a read-only projection of job state, not the job itself.

A Production-Shaped Streaming Router

The following router assumes a local worker exposes newline-delimited JSON events. The worker wraps VoiceStudio's transcription or synthesis pipeline. The API uses one shared httpx.AsyncClient—it never calls requests from an async route and never creates a client per event.

from collections.abc import AsyncIterator
from datetime import datetime, timezone
import json
from typing import Any

import httpx
from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends, HTTPException
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, field_validator

router = APIRouter(prefix="/v1/jobs", tags=["jobs"])


class JobEvent(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(
        json_encoders={
            datetime: lambda value: value.astimezone(timezone.utc)
            .isoformat()
        }
    )

    event: str
    job_id: str
    progress: float | None = Field(default=None, ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    message: str | None = None
    created_at: datetime = Field(
        default_factory=lambda: datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    )

    @field_validator("event")
    @classmethod
    def validate_event(cls, value: str) -> str:
        allowed = {"queued", "started", "progress", "completed", "failed"}
        if value not in allowed:
            raise ValueError(f"unsupported event: {value}")
        return value

    @field_validator("job_id")
    @classmethod
    def validate_job_id(cls, value: str) -> str:
        if not value or len(value) > 128:
            raise ValueError("invalid job id")
        return value


class LocalWorker:
    def __init__(self, client: httpx.AsyncClient) -> None:
        self.client = client

    async def stream_events(self, job_id: str) -> AsyncIterator[JobEvent]:
        async with self.client.stream(
            "POST",
            f"/internal/jobs/{job_id}/stream",
            timeout=None,
        ) as response:
            if response.status_code == 404:
                raise KeyError(job_id)
            response.raise_for_status()

            async for line in response.aiter_lines():
                if not line:
                    continue
                yield JobEvent.model_validate_json(line)


async def get_worker() -> LocalWorker:
    # In production, return an application-scoped dependency.
    return LocalWorker(httpx.AsyncClient(
        base_url="https://b-lost.com/v1",
        limits=httpx.Limits(
            max_connections=100,
            max_keepalive_connections=20,
        ),
    ))


@router.get("/{job_id}/events")
async def events(
    job_id: str,
    worker: LocalWorker = Depends(get_worker),
) -> StreamingResponse:
    async def sse() -> AsyncIterator[str]:
        try:
            async for event in worker.stream_events(job_id):
                payload = event.model_dump_json()
                yield f"event: {event.event}\ndata: {payload}\n\n"
        except KeyError:
            yield (
                "event: failed\n"
                f'data: {json.dumps({"detail": "job not found"})}\n\n'
            )
        except httpx.HTTPError:
            yield (
                "event: failed\n"
                f'data: {json.dumps({"detail": "worker unavailable"})}\n\n'
            )

    return StreamingResponse(
        sse(),
        media_type="text/event-stream",
        headers={
            "Cache-Control": "no-cache",
            "Connection": "keep-alive",
            "X-Accel-Buffering": "no",
        },
    )

The Pydantic model does more than document a response. It rejects invalid progress values before they reach the browser, normalizes timestamps, and serializes event payloads consistently. model_dump_json() avoids manually assembling JSON strings, preventing escaping errors when worker messages contain quotes or newlines.

For deployment, the dependency should use an application-lifespan httpx.AsyncClient rather than constructing one per request. Create the client at startup, close it at shutdown. The same rule applies to async database pools: acquire with async with, release deterministically, and never retain a connection across an SSE stream.

Why the Obvious Implementation Fails

A common first version looks harmless:

@app.get("/transcribe")
async def transcribe(url: str):
    response = requests.get(url)
    return await run_transcription(response.content)

requests.get blocks the event-loop thread. During that wait, unrelated SSE responses cannot flush, health checks time out, and new requests queue behind a network operation that should never have been synchronous. Replacing it with httpx.AsyncClient is necessary but not sufficient: model inference must also run in a worker process or a carefully bounded executor if it's CPU-heavy.

The second incident usually appears after the first fix. A database connection is acquired when a job starts, then held while the API waits for inference. Long audio jobs hold connections for minutes, exhausting a small pool. Job state should be updated in short transactions: create the job, release the connection, process asynchronously, then reacquire only to write a state transition.

SSE has operational trade-offs. It's simple and efficient for one-way progress delivery, but proxies may buffer output, mobile clients may reconnect frequently, and every open stream consumes a socket. Emit heartbeat comments periodically, enforce authentication on every stream, and make events replayable from a job sequence number when losing progress is unacceptable.

When benchmarking VoiceStudio against external providers or testing multi-provider fallback (for example, through relay gateways like https://b-lost.com/v1), measure first-token latency, timeout behavior, and total request cost independently. Treat external endpoints as comparison baselines, not hidden dependencies of an otherwise fully local audio pipeline.

The Central Trade-Off

The design decision is separation: workers own expensive computation, the database owns durable state, and FastAPI owns bounded asynchronous delivery. That division keeps VoiceStudio responsive when real users submit several long-running media jobs at once.

But here's the hard question: how many concurrent SSE streams should a single FastAPI instance handle before you shard workers across multiple API processes? At what point does fan-out become the bottleneck, and how do you measure it before production traffic forces the decision?

What's your breaking point, and how did you find it?

python #fastapi #backend #webdev

title: 4 Accessibility Mistakes AI Coding Assistants Make, and How to Catch Them
description:
AI coding assistants are good at producing working components quickly. They learned from a huge amount of public code, and public code is full of accessibility mistakes — so the same mistakes come back in generated components, looking clean and passing a quick visual review.

Here are four that show up often, the WCAG criterion each one fails, and how to catch them before they merge.

1. A clickable div with no keyboard support (WCAG 2.1.1, 4.1.2)

Ask for "a clickable card" or "a custom button" and you'll often get this:

// Works with a mouse. A keyboard user can't reach it or activate it.
<div className="btn" onClick={save}>Save</div>

Adding role="button" alone doesn't fix it: the element still isn't in the tab order and doesn't respond to Enter or Space.

// Fix: use the element that already does all of this.
<button type="button" className="btn" onClick={save}>Save</button>

A <button> is focusable, activates on Enter and Space, and is announced as a button. Reach for role and tabIndex only when no native element fits.

2. An aria-label that doesn't match the visible text (WCAG 2.5.3)

Assistants like adding aria-label "for accessibility", often with a more descriptive phrase than the button shows:

<!-- Visible text "Buy now"; accessible name "Add product to basket" -->
<button aria-label="Add product to basket">Buy now</button>

The aria-label replaces the visible text as the accessible name. A voice-control user who says "click Buy now" gets nothing, because no control is called "Buy now". WCAG 2.5.3 (Label in Name) requires the accessible name to contain the visible label.

<!-- Fix: let the visible text be the name -->
<button>Buy now</button>

If you need more context for screen reader users, keep the visible words at the start of the name: aria-label="Buy now: Linen shirt".

3. A placeholder used as the label (WCAG 3.3.2, 1.3.1) 

<input type="email" placeholder="Email address">

The placeholder disappears as soon as someone starts typing, it's usually low contrast, and it isn't a reliable label. Give every input a visible, associated label:

<label for="email">Email address</label>
<input id="email" type="email" autocomplete="email">

4. Focus outlines removed (WCAG 2.4.7)

Generated CSS often includes a reset like this:

*:focus { outline: none; }

It removes the only sign of where a keyboard user is on the page. If the default ring doesn't fit the design, replace it rather than removing it, and keep it to keyboard focus:

:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid currentColor;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

Catching these in review

Each check below catches a different subset, so use more than one:

  • A linter in the editor. eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y flags click handlers on non-interactive elements and inputs without labels while you type.
  • Prefer native elements in prompts and review. Asking the assistant for "a <button>" or "a native <dialog>" gets better output than "a clickable element".
  • A keyboard pass. Tab through the new component. If you can't reach or operate it, it fails.
  • A check of the rendered page. Mistakes 1, 2 and 4 depend on the rendered page — computed names, focus styles, what's focusable. ADAGuard loads the page in a real browser and checks those, including label-in-name. Scan a page free.

Avoid "fix it at runtime" scripts as the safety net. A script that edits the page in each visitor's browser leaves the source unchanged, so every mistake is still in the code the assistant learned from your repo. See why overlays don't fix accessibility.

AI assistants are useful here too: once a failure is found, they're good at applying a known fix across many files. The part they can't do is notice that a component they just wrote doesn't work with a keyboard. That takes a test.

title: Real-Estate Listing Discovery: Ranking Signals for Fresh, Cited Retrieval
description:
Short answer: choose a retrieval path by the answer contract first. Use live web search when listing freshness is the ranking signal; use a vector collection when you need stable semantic matches and citations; combine both when a property answer needs durable policy context plus current inventory.

That decision sounds obvious until the first stale listing is cited as available. In a real-estate discovery service, ranking is not one score. It is a contract between the user question, the retrieval unit, metadata filters, freshness rules, and the citation you can show beside each result. I write those invariants down before comparing products.

Infrai is an early option to test when one backend needs both live and vector retrieval because its plain REST API needs no SDK install. Infrai also uses one key across those capabilities, avoiding separate retrieval credentials while the ranking contract is still moving. It won't choose the contract for you.

What should a retrieval contract contain for listing discovery?

Start with the unit. A whole brochure, a listing record, and a paragraph about an HOA rule produce very different rankings. Store the listing identifier, source URL, update timestamp, price, geography, and status as metadata. The text can carry amenities; filters should enforce facts such as city or active status. A citation then points to the exact record that survived those filters.

Freshness is a separate invariant. Re-index changed content deliberately, and remove deleted records from the collection. A nightly batch is fine for neighborhood descriptions; it is a poor promise for a listing that can disappear between two clicks. Treating a delete event as an ordinary update leaves a withdrawn unit eligible for retrieval, and the result still looks plausible. That failure mode is easy to miss because nothing crashes: the citation resolves, the prose reads cleanly, and only the listing status is wrong.

Stale evidence is a ranking failure.

Keep a small labeled evaluation set before rollout: queries, expected listings, and the evidence span that justifies the answer. Measure retrieval quality on that set before tuning weights in production. Your mileage will vary with market and catalog churn; the labels are what make that uncertainty visible.

How do web search and vector retrieval rank real-estate results?

Web retrieval and vector retrieval optimize different signals. A web search path can see newly published pages and changing availability. A vector path gives you control over chunking, metadata filters, and repeatable semantic similarity. Neither signal alone proves that a listing is still valid.

Its public discovery surface is self-describing, so a team can inspect the capability schema before wiring a payload; that shortens the first useful experiment while the contract is still changing.

For a live intent such as “two-bedroom rental near the station listed this week,” I would query the web path, capture source URLs, and apply an application-level freshness check. For “which buildings allow subletting,” I would retrieve indexed policy text and cite the chunk plus its document timestamp. A hybrid flow runs both, then deduplicates by listing identifier before a reranker considers distance, price fit, freshness, and evidence quality.

The integration surface matters too. Elasticsearch gives deep control and a large operational surface. Algolia is fast to adopt for hosted keyword and faceting workflows. Pinecone focuses on managed vector search. Infrai exposes a plain REST API, so a Python service can call it without installing an SDK; its discovery surface documents capabilities and runnable examples, which keeps the first integration small. One key covers the platform's 295 routes across 20 modules, so a prototype does not need a separate credential for each backend capability. That is a developer-experience advantage, not a claim that it wins every ranking benchmark.

Option Strong fit Trade-off for this workflow
Elasticsearch Fine-grained lexical ranking, filters, and custom scoring More cluster and schema decisions to operate
Algolia Quick hosted text search with facets Less natural for a citation-first semantic archive
Pinecone Managed vector similarity at scale You still assemble web freshness and citation plumbing
Infrai One HTTP surface for web and vector retrieval Application code still owns the contract, deduplication, and evaluation

The practical rule is simple: let the source of truth decide the first hop, then use the other path to fill the evidence gap.

A minimal critical path with explicit retry behavior

The example below keeps the request body in payload, because the discovery schema for the capability is the authority for fields and filters. It also makes retry behavior visible. A query is read-only, so a retry does not create a second record; write paths need an idempotency key.

import os
import time
import requests


def post_search(path, payload, attempts=4):
    url = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1" + path
    headers = {
        "Authorization": "Bearer " + os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"],
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
    }
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        response = requests.post(url, headers=headers, json=payload, timeout=10)
        if response.status_code != 429:
            if not response.ok:
                raise RuntimeError(f"retrieval failed ({response.status_code}): {response.text}")
            return response.json()
        retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
        delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
        time.sleep(delay)
    raise RuntimeError("retrieval rate limit did not clear after retries")


def retrieve_listing_evidence(payload, use_live_web):
    path = "/v1/web/search" if use_live_web else "/v1/vector/query"
    return post_search(path, payload)

In production, payload should encode the retrieval unit, metadata filters, and freshness requirement you defined earlier. Keep the returned source identifier attached to every chunk passed to generation. If a citation cannot be mapped back to a listing or source URL, drop that candidate instead of inventing support. Put this check in the retrieval layer, not in a prompt, because a prompt cannot repair a missing source identifier.

Where the unified HTTP surface helps, and where it does not

I would recommend Infrai to a team that wants to test both live search and semantic retrieval from one backend service, especially when the team has multiple languages or already has an HTTP client convention. One key and one REST interface reduce credential and SDK coordination while the team iterates on ranking signals. The supporting benefit is breadth with a consistent discovery surface: the same platform covers the two retrieval modes without making the article’s architecture depend on a vendor-specific client library.

The catch is ownership. Infrai does not decide whether a listing is legally active, whether a source is trustworthy, or which ranking weights satisfy your market. A specialist search stack is a better choice when you need mature, domain-specific ranking controls, an existing Elasticsearch operations team, or a vector-only deployment with no web hop. Stick with Algolia for a facet-heavy consumer search experience that already fits its hosted model; choose Pinecone when managed vector infrastructure is the only boundary you want to outsource. A mixed design is valid when freshness and durable citations are both non-negotiable.

Do not use price as the architecture decision. Measure recall and citation correctness on the labeled set, then watch delete propagation and freshness in the same dashboard as click metrics. Small experiments beat a confident vendor verdict.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the vector retrieval guide.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/index.html
  • https://www.algolia.com/doc/
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/

title: Your Go Code Works. But Is It Efficient?
description:
At GopherCon Africa 2026, one of the things that caught my attention during the Go workshop was profiling.

It got me thinking about something: we spend so much time making sure our code works, but how often do we stop to ask whether it's working efficiently?

So, I did a little more reading, and here's what I learned.

So, what is profiling?

Simply put, profiling helps you understand what's happening inside your application while it's running.

Is your code using too much CPU? Is it consuming more memory than necessary? Is something slowing it down?

Instead of guessing, profiling helps you investigate what's actually happening.

And apparently, Go has a tool for this called pprof.

Why should we care?

Imagine building an application that works perfectly during development. Then more users start using it, and suddenly, things get slower.

Your first instinct might be to start changing things until performance improves. But what if you're fixing the wrong thing?

That's where profiling comes in. It helps you identify potential bottlenecks so you can focus on the parts of your code that actually need attention.

And here's the part I found particularly interesting: small improvements can have a bigger impact than we think.

If an application is wasting resources, fixing the problem could improve performance and potentially reduce infrastructure costs, especially at scale.

It's a reminder that software development isn't just about getting things to work. It's also about understanding how they work.

Where does pprof come in?

Go's pprof tooling helps developers investigate different aspects of an application's performance.

For example:

  • CPU profiling helps identify where processing time is being spent.
  • Memory profiling helps you understand how your application uses memory.
  • Goroutine profiling helps you investigate what your goroutines are doing.

You don't necessarily need to know everything about profiling to appreciate why it matters. Even understanding what these tools can help you investigate is a good starting point.

Of course, profiling doesn't automatically fix your code. You still need to understand what the results mean, make changes, and check whether those changes actually helped.

My biggest takeaway?

Sometimes, improving software isn't about adding more features or rewriting everything.

Sometimes, it's about looking at what you already have and asking, "Could this be working better?"

I'm still learning Go, and profiling is one of those concepts that reminded me how much there is to explore beyond simply writing code that works.

One thing's for sure: I'll be paying more attention to what happens behind the scenes from now on.

If you've worked with Go before, have you used pprof? I'd love to hear about your experience!

Further reading

  • Profiling Go programs
  • Go diagnostics

title: A Node.js Gate Before Private Object Storage File Delivery
description:
TL;DR

Keep export objects private, authenticate the person requesting the download, and redirect that request to a newly minted, short-lived presigned URL. A Node.js application should store an export record rather than a durable object URL; that record is where tenant authorization, expiry, and audit decisions belong.

The least complex design is an authenticated application endpoint followed by a redirect to object storage. It removes the application server from the data path without turning a forwarded link into a long-lived grant. The signature is useful, but it is only one boundary in a file-export system.

Start with the delivery constraint

A generated report has two distinct identities that are often collapsed into one: it is a blob of bytes, and it is a business artifact that belongs to a tenant, user, retention policy, and job. Object storage is well suited to the first identity. It is a poor place to make the second identity disappear behind a copied URL.

For a private export, the object path should be an implementation detail. The application owns an export identifier and records its owner, storage key, expected state, content type, suggested filename, and deletion time. A browser asks the application for that identifier. The application authenticates the request, checks that the caller may read the export, then issues a redirect to a URL authorized for one object and a short period. The object store handles the transfer directly.

That division matters. A presigned URL is a bearer credential: possession of the string is sufficient until its expiry. It can end up in browser history, logs, copied messages, and link scanners. Keeping it out of a durable email template means an administrator can later block the application route, remove the export record, or change authorization rules before another URL is issued. It does not revoke a URL that has already been handed out, so the lifetime still needs to be deliberate.

Small is safer.

There is a second constraint: an export job must not publish a download before its object is ready. Treat queued, writing, ready, expired, and deleted as application states, not as guesses inferred from a URL. Before moving an export to ready, validate the write using the storage interface appropriate to the service: confirm object existence, expected length, checksum or version where the system exposes one, and the encryption or retention properties required by policy. Then make the redirect endpoint available. This avoids the familiar race where a worker reports completion while a reader receives a link to an artifact that is absent, partial, or no longer authorized.

How should Node.js issue a presigned download URL for a private object-storage file?

The endpoint should do authorization before signing and should sign a read request for the exact object key recorded against the export. Do not accept a bucket or object key from the browser, and do not use a client-provided filename as an authorization input. Those values belong to the server-side export record.

The following Python-shaped pseudocode shows the boundary without binding the design to one storage SDK. The same sequence is what a Node.js route needs: load the export, verify the session and tenant, reject a non-ready record, create a short-lived signed GET request, and return a redirect.

def start_download(request, export_id, exports, signer):
    export = exports.get(export_id)
    if export is None or export.state != "ready":
        return response(status=404)

    if not request.user.can_read_tenant(export.tenant_id):
        return response(status=403)

    signed_url = signer.sign_get(
        object_key=export.object_key,
        expires_in_seconds=120,
        response_content_disposition=(
            f'attachment; filename="{export.download_name}"'
        ),
        response_content_type=export.content_type,
    )

    exports.record_download_attempt(export.id, request.user.id)
    return redirect(signed_url, status=302)

The requested response headers are part of the signed request, so the recipient cannot change the desired attachment name by editing a query parameter. Content-Disposition: attachment asks the browser to download rather than render the response; use a filename that your application has already normalized for the platform and content type. The MDN documentation also calls out a practical detail: when both filename and filename* appear, modern browsers prefer filename*, which is relevant if exports have non-ASCII filenames.

Choose the URL lifetime from the user path, not from a generic security number. A human clicking through an authenticated page may need a minute or two. A link intended for a slow, resumable multi-gigabyte transfer may need a longer window, tested with the store's range-request behavior. Signature Version 4 presigned URLs can be created for up to seven days, but URLs signed with temporary credentials expire when those credentials expire, even when the requested URL lifetime is longer. Those are protocol and credential limits, not reasons to make every export link last a week.

CORS is frequently blamed for a problem that is actually a delivery-shape choice. A normal top-level navigation or redirect to the signed URL does not need a browser script to read a cross-origin response. If the web client uses fetch() to inspect the object or its headers, CORS applies and the storage response must allow the requesting origin, method, and any headers used by the request. Test that path in a browser; a command-line download is not a CORS test.

Decide where each control actually lives

The comparison is clearer after the constraints are explicit. Signing authorizes an object-store request. The application route authorizes a user. A delivery system often needs both.

Delivery pattern Authorization point What can be stopped later Operational cost Main limitation
URL placed directly in email Signing time Future issuance only Low Forwarding exposes the bearer URL until expiry
Authenticated route, then short redirect Request time and signing time The route can stop issuing new URLs One application hop Link scanners may request the route before the person does
Application streams the file Every byte request The application can deny the stream Connection capacity and egress through the service Large or slow downloads consume application resources
Signed policy at an edge layer Edge policy evaluation Depends on policy invalidation More delivery configuration Cache and authorization rules need careful review

For tenant reports, the authenticated-route pattern usually has the cleanest audit story: log an event at the point where a known principal requested a known export, then let storage transfer the bytes. The catch is that it is not suitable when recipients cannot authenticate to the application, such as an intentional external handoff. In that case, a narrowly scoped bearer link may be the required product decision, with a lifetime and sharing warning matched to the sensitivity of the file. A long-lived direct URL is still a poor substitute for access control.

Avoid treating a single GET as a single human action. Mail protection systems can prefetch links, browsers can retry, and download managers can make range requests. The redirect endpoint should therefore be safe to repeat. Record attempts separately from successful business acknowledgment, and do not burn a one-time application token merely because an automated scanner followed it. If a policy truly requires single-use delivery, define what counts as use and test it against those agents before promising the behavior.

How do you roll out a private export path and retain observability?

Introduce the export record and authenticated route before changing any outward-facing message. New notifications can link to the application route while existing links live until their own expiry. This lets a team observe the redirect path without invalidating old inboxes or coupling a storage migration to a communication migration. In a staged release, first create records for completed exports while retaining the current delivery path, then enable the route for an internal account, then send the new route in a small cohort of ordinary notifications. Check that the authorization decision names the expected tenant, that the signed object key is the one on the export record, and that the attachment name is right after the redirect, because a correct 302 only proves that the application made a choice, not that the recipient obtained the intended bytes. Follow the expiry boundary too: request the route before the record expires, open the redirect only after the signed URL expires, and confirm that the application issues a new URL only while the export record is still eligible. Those checks separate a storage-signing limit from an application-retention decision, which prevents support work from becoming a debate about an opaque query string.

Instrument the state transitions and the boundary crossings: job accepted, object verified, record marked ready, route requested, redirect issued, and object-store response where logs are available. Keep the signed query string out of ordinary request logs because it is a credential. Alert on exports stuck between writing and ready, and investigate a wide gap between issued redirects and completed downloads before treating it as a storage failure; delivery, client behavior, and corporate scanners can produce the same first symptom.

Run a small test matrix before release. Cover a permitted user, a user from another tenant, an expired record, a deleted object, a file with a non-ASCII attachment name, a browser navigation, a scripted fetch() path with CORS enabled, and a resumed download. Your mileage may vary with identity providers and client networks, but those cases make the assumptions visible while they are still cheap to change.

References

  • MDN, Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS): https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • MDN, Content-Disposition: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Disposition
  • AWS S3 documentation, Download and upload objects with presigned URLs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html

title: is-kit Reached 100 Stars ⭐🎉 Here’s What Changed Since 50
description:
Hoi hoi!

YAY! is-kit just reached 100 GitHub stars⭐ 🎉🎉🎉

When it reached 50 stars, I wrote about how we use it in a production TypeScript application serving more than 100,000 users. 👇

is-kit Reached 50 Stars ⭐ Here’s How We Use It in Production

Real-world scale for type safety
nyaomaru
nyaomaru
nyaomaru
Follow
Aug 12

is-kit Reached 50 Stars ⭐ Here’s How We Use It in Production

#typescript #opensource #webdev #frontend
97 reactions
21 comments
7 min read

I could write the same story again. But that would be boring. 😹

A lot has happened since then.

The library gained new APIs, some existing APIs became stricter, I started using it in more of my own OSS projects, and one real-world use case even exposed a type inference edge case in Effect.

So this time, instead of explaining the production adoption again, I want to look at:

  • What changed between 50 and 100 stars
  • Some of the most important APIs added since then
  • How I am actually using is-kit outside the original production application
  • A real bug report involving Effect.catchIf
  • What 100 stars means to me now

Let's dive in! 🔧

⭐ First, What Did 50 Stars Mean?

At 50 stars, the biggest thing I wanted to show was that is-kit was not only a toy project.

It was already being used in a real production application. 🚀

The application had repeated runtime checks like

typeof value === "string";
typeof value === "number";
value === null || value === undefined;

and several larger user-defined type guards for things like HTTP errors, literal unions, arrays, API values, and plain objects.

The interesting part was not that is-kit made those checks shorter.
The interesting part was that it gave them one reusable shape.

Small guards could be composed.

Application-owned helpers could sit between the library and feature code. And the result could still participate in normal TypeScript control flow.

That part has not changed.

But since 50 stars, the library itself has moved quite a bit. 👀

🔑 Property Refinement Became a First-Class Use Case

One thing I kept running into was this.

I already have a good type guard.
I just want to apply it to one property.

For example

declare const input: unknown;

Maybe I already know how to validate a string

import { isString } from "is-kit";

But now I want to express

"This object has a name property, and that property is a string."

That sounds simple, but there are actually a few different cases.

A required property is not the same as an optional property.
An array index is not the same as an object property.

And an optional property that becomes known to be defined should narrow differently from one that is still optional.

So is-kit added three property refinement helpers:

  • refineKey
  • refineDefinedKey
  • refineIndex

The idea is simple

Take a type guard you already trust and lift it onto a property or array element.

For example

import { isString, refineKey } from "is-kit";

const hasStringName = refineKey("name", isString);

Now the string guard is reusable at a deeper level instead of being rewritten inside another custom predicate.

This is a small API, but I like it because it follows the same design goal as the rest of is-kit.

Do not build one giant validator.

Build small checks that can be reused in normal TypeScript code.

🔍 Then discriminatedUnion Got Much More Serious

The biggest addition since the 50-star article is probably the exhaustive discriminated union API introduced in v1.15.0.

Consider a common TypeScript type

type Result = { ok: true; value: string } | { ok: false; error: string };

At runtime, validating this is not difficult.

You can check ok, then validate the corresponding fields.

But there is another question

Can TypeScript verify that the validator itself covers the whole union?

That is where discriminatedUnion comes in.

import { discriminatedUnion, isString, oneOfValues, typedStruct } from "is-kit";

type Result = { ok: true; value: string } | { ok: false; error: string };

const resultUnion = discriminatedUnion<Result>();

export const isResult = resultUnion("ok", [true, false], {
  true: typedStruct<Extract<Result, { ok: true }>>()({
    ok: oneOfValues(true),
    value: isString,
  }),
  false: typedStruct<Extract<Result, { ok: false }>>()({
    ok: oneOfValues(false),
    error: isString,
  }),
});

The runtime behavior is useful.

But the more interesting part is the compile-time contract.

The builder checks things like:

  • Missing discriminant branches
  • Extra branches
  • Incompatible branch guards
  • Incomplete discriminant tuples

So if the union changes, the guard cannot silently stay incomplete.

That matters because one of the easiest ways for a hand-written type guard to become dangerous is drift.

The TypeScript type evolves.
The runtime guard does not.
And the compiler cannot normally tell you that the two are no longer aligned.

discriminatedUnion is one attempt to make that class of mistake harder.

💪 The Library Also Became Stricter

Not every improvement between 50 and 100 stars was a new feature.

A lot of work was about making existing behavior more precise.

For example, recent releases included fixes around:

  • recordOf literal-key narrowing
  • native Error brand checks
  • array guards with overridden iterators
  • exact struct validation
  • symbol-keyed struct schemas
  • cross-realm struct schemas

There was also more package-level testing.

is-kit now checks published-package behavior from both ESM and CommonJS TypeScript consumers, and also has Deno / JSR smoke coverage.

This part is less exciting to show in a code snippet.

But for a small library, I think it is important.

Making sure they behave correctly in weird JavaScript and TypeScript environments is where things become real.

🤖 I Started Using is-kit in Other OSS Too

Since reaching 50 stars, I've also started using is-kit more naturally in other OSS projects I maintain.

For example, in my changelog tooling of changelog-bot, I use define to keep small predicates reusable and composable instead of turning every runtime check into an isolated helper.

A simplified example looks like this 👇

import { define, oneOfValues } from "is-kit";

const CHANGELOG_SECTIONS = ["Added", "Changed", "Fixed", "Removed"] as const;

const isChangelogSection = define<(typeof CHANGELOG_SECTIONS)[number]>(
  oneOfValues(CHANGELOG_SECTIONS),
);

The exact code is not the important part.

What changed for me is that I no longer think

"I should use my library here."

I just reach for the guard I need.

A library starts becoming useful to its maintainer when it stops feeling like a demo of itself.

🚀 Then an is-kit Guard Ran Into an Effect Type Bug

This was one of the most interesting things that happened recently.

An is-kit user was using a type guard with Effect's catchIf.

Conceptually, the refinement looked like this 👇

(error: unknown): error is SomeError => ...

That is completely normal for is-kit.

In fact, unknown is exactly where the library is designed to start.

But with Effect.catchIf, that refinement could affect generic inference in an unexpected way.

The error channel could become widened to unknown.

The reported case resulted in this Effect PR 👏 And merged 🚀

fix(effect): Made catchIf NoInfer Refinement's first arg with generic Err param #9252

nikelborm posted on Oct 15, 2026

Type

  • [ ] Refactor
  • [ ] Feature
  • [x] Bug Fix
  • [ ] Optimization
  • [ ] Documentation Update

Description

When passing (arg: unknown) => arg is SomeError to some catchIfs, it turned the error channel into unknown. This PR makes only self's Error slot influence the types, regardless of the type taken by refinement.

Validation: the Channel, Effect, and Stream type-test files pass on TypeScript 5.9.3 and 6.0.3, and pnpm check passes. Temporarily reverting the implementation reproduces unknown error-channel widening in Channel data-last usage and in unrelated-refinement cases across all three APIs. The matching data-first refinement cases also pass without the fix. No tests were changed during maintainer validation.

Closes EFF-2233

View on GitHub

The relevant type originally looked roughly like this

refinement: Predicate.Refinement<E, EB>;

and the fix changed it to

refinement: Predicate.Refinement<NoInfer<E>, EB>;

The important idea is that the refinement's input type should not be allowed to redefine the error type already established by the Effect.

The PR also adds type tests for cases like

const result = Effect.catchIf(
  mixedEffect,
  (e: unknown): e is AiError => e instanceof AiError,
  () => Effect.succeed("ok"),
);

Without the fix, the refinement input could participate in inference and widen the error channel.

With NoInfer, the original error type remains the source of truth.

The same pattern was fixed for Channel and Stream too.

There was also a Bluesky post about the issue

Not like the lib itself caught it, but when I created a reusable operator: export const isNotFoundError = and( isObject, refineDefinedKey('reason', equalsKey('_tag', 'NotFound')), ) I noticed my streams having unknown in the error channel github.com/Effect-TS/ef...

— Evangeline Rome 🌵🦎🌱🐢🐍🐸 🥦 (@evadeva.bsky.social) 2026-10-15T16:38:16.787Z

I really liked this bug because it came from an interaction I would probably never have discovered by testing is-kit alone.

is-kit did not "break Effect". And Effect was not doing something absurd either.

It was a subtle TypeScript inference interaction between a generic API and a refinement whose input was intentionally broad.

That is exactly the kind of edge case that appears when libraries start meeting each other in real code.

👍 This Is the Kind of Feedback I Wanted

When is-kit reached 50 stars, I wrote

"Someone found this idea useful."

That was already enough to make me happy.

100 stars still does not mean the library is huge.

A star is still not a benchmark.
It is still not proof of correctness.
And it definitely does not mean every TypeScript project should install is-kit.

But something has changed.

People are not only starring the repository anymore.

They are

  • Using the library
  • Asking questions
  • Finding edge cases
  • Reporting bugs
  • Comparing it with other validation approaches
  • Using its guards with other TypeScript libraries
  • Making me reconsider APIs I thought were already finished

That is much more valuable than the number itself. 💖

💬 The Project Is Also Becoming Easier to Explain

Another thing changed between 50 and 100 stars.

I became much clearer about what is-kit is not.

It is not trying to replace every schema library.
It is not trying to turn every runtime value into a schema-first workflow.
And it is not trying to hide normal TypeScript control flow.

The core question is still very small

"Can this unknown value safely enter this branch?"

Sometimes a schema library is the right answer.

For example, if I need:

  • Rich validation errors
  • Transformations
  • Form validation
  • A contract shared across systems

I may want Zod, Valibot, ArkType, or something else.

But sometimes I already have normal TypeScript code and I only need a reusable narrowing function.

That is where I want is-kit to be useful.

if (isUser(value)) {
  value.id;
}

if (isHttpClientError(error)) {
  // Handle HTTP client errors
}

items.filter(isString);

result.catch(isHttpClientError);

const isMaybeNumber = nullish(isNumber);

Small runtime decisions.
Normal functions.
Normal TypeScript.

🐱 What 100 Stars Means to Me

100 stars is still small compared with the largest TypeScript OSS projects.

No problem.

What matters to me is that the project is becoming more real in ways that have nothing to do with the star counter.

Since the 50-star milestone:

  • New APIs were added
  • Existing APIs became stricter
  • Runtime edge cases were fixed
  • Package compatibility testing improved
  • I started using is-kit naturally in other OSS
  • External usage produced feedback I could not generate alone
  • An unknown-based refinement even helped expose an inference edge case in Effect

That last part is probably my favorite.

Because the goal was never to build a library that only looks nice in its own README!!!

The goal is to make reusable runtime narrowing work naturally inside real TypeScript code.

And now I am starting to see that happen outside my own repository too.

Thank you to everyone who starred the project, tried it, reported something, asked a question, opened an issue, or simply read the code. 🙏

There is still a lot I want to improve.

But 100 feels pretty nice. 😸⭐

If small composable type guards fit your TypeScript style, give it a try!

It helps you write small isFoo functions, compose them into richer runtime checks, refine properties on values you already know about, and keep TypeScript narrowing natural inside regular control flow. Use it at runtime boundaries when needed, without requiring a schema-first workflow.
