title: Build vs Managed Vector Database: A Total-Cost Framework
description:
For most teams under roughly 200 million vectors, a managed vector database costs less in total than self-hosting, because people cost more than servers. In our model, a 20M-vector production workload runs about $21K–$27K a year on Weaviate Cloud or Pinecone, including staff time to manage the vendor. Self-hosting the same workload costs $58K–$114K in year one, depending on whether the operators are offshore, nearshore or US-based. The cloud bill for self-hosting is only about $13.7K of that.

Self-hosting starts to win at large scale when your query pattern is expensive on usage-based pricing, when data residency rules out SaaS, or when a platform team already runs stateful clusters and can absorb the work. The single biggest swing factor is not build vs buy. It is how your data is partitioned, which can move a managed bill by more than 100x.

Year-one total cost at a glance

P*ilot (1M vectors, 0.5M queries a month)*. Managed costs about $10.2K on Weaviate Cloud and $10.3K on Pinecone. Self-hosting costs $26.8K with offshore operators, $36.9K nearshore and $52.0K with a US in-house team.

Growth (20M vectors, 10M queries a month). Managed costs about $21.4K on Weaviate Cloud and $26.9K on Pinecone with partitioned data, but $300.9K on Pinecone if every query scans one namespace. Self-hosting costs $58.3K offshore, $80.7K nearshore and $114.1K in-house.

Scale (200M vectors, 100M queries a month). Managed costs from about $55.1K on Weaviate Cloud (lowest published rates; a quote is needed) and $90.3K–$152.1K on Pinecone with partitioned data. Self-hosting costs $168.1K offshore, $214.9K nearshore and $284.9K in-house.

All figures are modeled estimates built from sourced unit prices and the documented assumptions in Part 1. Managed totals include vendor-management staff time; self-host totals include cloud infrastructure, initial build and ongoing operations. Embedding, LLM and application costs are excluded because they are the same either way.

What "total cost" means for a vector database

A vector database bill has five lines, and only two of them show up on an invoice.

  1. Platform or infrastructure: the managed subscription, or EC2/VM compute, block storage and snapshots.
  2. Usage: read units, write units, stored dimensions or egress on managed plans; cross-AZ traffic when self-hosting.
  3. Initial build: cluster design, infrastructure-as-code, backups, monitoring, load testing and recall evaluation.
  4. Ongoing operations: upgrades, re-indexing, capacity planning, incident response, security patching.
  5. Vendor management: cost monitoring, quota tuning, support tickets and contract reviews on managed plans.

Self-hosting shrinks lines 1–2 and grows lines 3–4. Managed services do the opposite. The decision comes down to which side grows faster for your workload.

Managed vector database pricing (October 2026)

• Pinecone Standard: usage-based on reads, writes and storage. $16–18 per 1M read units, $4–4.50 per 1M write units and $0.33/GB-month, with a $50/month minimum. No uptime SLA is listed.

• Pinecone Enterprise: the same model at $24–27 per 1M read units and $6–6.75 per 1M write units, with a $500/month minimum and a 99.95% SLA.

• Weaviate Cloud Flex: priced on stored dimensions and storage, from $0.00465 per 1M dimensions, $0.12/GiB storage and $0.03036/GiB backup. The minimum is $45/month and the SLA is 99.5%.

• Weaviate Cloud Premium: a prepaid contract from $400/month. Shared clusters start at $0.003875 per 1M dimensions and dedicated at $0.002718, with SLAs up to 99.95%.

• Qdrant Cloud: billed on provisioned CPU, RAM and disk after a free tier. Rates appear only in its pricing calculator; Standard carries a 99.5% SLA and Premium higher.

• Zilliz Cloud: compute units on dedicated plans or vCUs on serverless, after a free tier. Storage is $0.040/GB-month from January 2026 and internet egress starts at $0.09/GB.

Two details matter more than headline rates. First, Pinecone charges reads by namespace size: each query costs 1 read unit per GB of the namespace searched, with a 0.25 RU minimum. Second, Weaviate prices on stored dimensions with no per-query fee in its published table, and its rates vary with index type, compression and region. Zilliz's own engineering blog shows the same workload pricing at about $7,000/month on dedicated and about $10,800 on serverless. The pricing model you pick can matter as much as the vendor.

Self-hosted infrastructure cost

Self-hosting Qdrant, Weaviate or Milvus is mostly a memory problem. Qdrant's capacity-planning guide gives a rough formula for keeping float32 vectors in RAM:

\text{RAM} = \text{vectors} \times \text{dimensions} \times 4\ \text{bytes} \times 1.5

Quantizing to int8 replaces the 4 bytes with 1 and keeps full-precision originals on disk for rescoring. That is the design we assume from 20M vectors up.

AWS us-east-1 rates used in the model:

• r7g.xlarge (4 vCPU, 32 GiB): $0.2142/hour on demand, about $156/month, or $0.1552/hour on a 1-year Compute Savings Plan.

• r7g.2xlarge (8 vCPU, 64 GiB): $0.4284/hour, about $313/month, or $0.3104/hour on the Savings Plan.

• r7g.4xlarge (16 vCPU, 128 GiB): $0.8568/hour, about $625/month, or $0.6208/hour on the Savings Plan.

• EBS gp3 block storage: $0.08/GB-month. EBS snapshots: $0.05/GB-month.

The people line: in-house vs nearshore vs offshore

Engineering time is the largest cost of self-hosting at every scale we modeled. We price it three ways.

• US in-house hire: $101.18/hour, or $194,257 a year per FTE. This is the BLS median software developer wage of $135,980 (May 2025, reported here) divided by 0.70, because wages are 70.0% of private-industry compensation per BLS.

• Nearshore senior engineer (Latin America): $67.50/hour, or $129,600 a year per FTE. This is the midpoint of the $60–75/hour senior range in FullStack's 2026 report.

• Offshore senior engineer (South Asia): $45/hour, or $86,400 a year per FTE. This is the midpoint of the $40–50/hour India senior range in Full Scale's 2026 guide.

The US figure is conservative for this work. SRE total compensation has a reported Levels.fyi median of about $200,200 before benefits, per KORE1's 2026 guide. Vendor rates for nearshore and offshore teams already include the vendor's overhead, so no benefits multiplier is applied to them.

Scenario 1 — Pilot: 1M vectors, 500K queries/month, 1M upserts/month

• Pinecone: reads in one namespace are 500K queries × 7.15 RU × $16/M = $57.20. Writes are 1M upserts × 7 WU × $4/M = $28.00, and storage is 7.15 GB × $0.33 = $2.36. That totals $87.56 a month, which falls under the $50 minimum once the data is split into 10 or more namespaces.

• Weaviate Flex: 1,536M dimensions × $0.00465 = $7.14 plus under $1 of storage, so the $45 minimum applies.

• Self-host infrastructure: three r7g.xlarge nodes at $156.37 each cost $469; the 8.6 GiB of vectors fits easily. Adding 150 GB of gp3 ($12) and snapshots ($0.36), then the 15% allowance, gives about $554 a month.

• Self-host operations: 0.15 FTE costs $2,428 a month in-house, $1,620 nearshore or $1,080 offshore.

• Initial build: 4 engineer-weeks cost $16,188 in-house, $10,800 nearshore or $7,200 offshore, once.

At pilot scale the managed bill is close to its minimum. The self-hosted three-node cluster alone costs more than ten times the managed subscription before anyone touches it. Verdict: managed, without much debate.

Scenario 2 — Growth: 20M vectors, 10M queries/month, 10M upserts/month

• Pinecone reads: one 143 GB namespace costs 10M queries × 143 RU × $16/M = $22,880 a month. Split into 500 tenant namespaces, it costs 10M × 0.286 RU × $16/M = $45.76.

• Pinecone writes, storage and support: 70M WU × $4/M = $280, 143 GB × $0.33 = $47.19, plus the $250 Pro support add-on. The total is $623 partitioned or $23,457 in a single namespace.

• Weaviate Flex: 30,720M dimensions × $0.00465 = $142.85, plus 133.2 GiB × $0.12 = $15.98 storage and $4.04 backup, for about $163 a month.

• Self-host infrastructure: three r7g.2xlarge nodes cost $938 ($680 on a 1-year Savings Plan). Int8 vectors take 42.9 GiB, or 85.8 GiB with two replicas, out of 192 GiB. Adding $48 of EBS and $7 of snapshots, then 15%, gives about $1,142 a month.

• Self-host operations: 0.35 FTE costs $5,666 a month in-house, $3,780 nearshore or $2,520 offshore.

• Initial build: 8 engineer-weeks cost $32,376 in-house, $21,600 nearshore or $14,400 offshore, once.

Weaviate Flex is a shared cluster with a 99.5% SLA. A team that needs SSO, private networking or a higher SLA moves to Premium at $400/month or more. Even then, managed stays well under the self-host total. Verdict: managed, provided your data partitions cleanly.

Scenario 3 — Scale: 200M vectors, 100M queries/month, 50M upserts/month

• Pinecone Enterprise reads: with 2,000 namespaces, 100M × 0.715 RU × $24/M = $1,716 a month. With 500 namespaces, 100M × 2.86 RU × $24/M = $6,864.

• Pinecone writes and storage: 350M WU × $6/M = $2,100 and 1,430 GB × $0.33 = $471.90. The total is $4,288–$9,436 a month for partitioned data; a single 1.4 TB namespace is not viable on usage pricing.

• Weaviate Premium (shared, lowest published rates): 307,200M dimensions × $0.003875 = $1,190, plus $133 storage and $28 backup, for about $1,352 a month. A quote is required.

• Self-host infrastructure: eight r7g.4xlarge nodes cost $5,004 ($3,625 on a 1-year Savings Plan). Int8 vectors take 429 GiB, or 858 GiB with two replicas, out of 1,024 GiB. Adding $320 of EBS and $72 of snapshots, then 15%, gives about $6,204 a month.

• Self-host operations: 0.75 FTE costs $12,141 a month in-house, $8,100 nearshore or $5,400 offshore.

• Initial build: 16 engineer-weeks cost $64,752 in-house, $43,200 nearshore or $28,800 offshore, once.

At this scale the answer depends on query shape. With fine-grained tenant partitions, managed stays cheaper. If queries must search large shared namespaces, an offshore-operated cluster ($139K/year steady state) undercuts Pinecone's 500-namespace case ($152K/year with vendor management).

Weaviate's figure uses the lowest published rate and will rise with HNSW indexes, dedicated tenancy or specific regions. Verdict: get vendor quotes and run the break-even test below.

The read-unit trap: partitioning changes the bill 100x

On Pinecone serverless, cost per query scales with the size of the namespace searched. The same 20M-vector, 10M-query workload costs:

• One namespace of 143 GB: 143 read units per query, about $23,457 a month.

• Ten namespaces of 14.3 GB: 14.3 read units per query, about $2,865 a month.

• 500 namespaces of 0.29 GB: 0.286 read units per query, about $623 a month.

Multi-tenant SaaS products fit this model well, since each customer's queries hit only their own namespace. A global semantic search across one large corpus does not. Check your query pattern before you compare vendors; it is the most consequential input in this framework.

Break-even: when self-hosting wins

Self-hosting pays off when the managed bill exceeds the infrastructure cost plus the extra engineering time it takes to run the cluster:

\text{Break-even managed bill per month} = \text{self-host infra per month} + \Delta\text{FTE} \times \text{monthly cost of 1 FTE}

ΔFTE is self-host operations effort minus managed vendor-management effort. One FTE costs $16,188/month in-house in the US, $10,800 nearshore and $7,200 offshore at the rates above.

• Growth (20M vectors): infrastructure of $1,142 plus 0.25 extra FTE puts the break-even at about $5,189 a month with a US team, or $2,942 with an offshore team.

• Scale (200M vectors): infrastructure of $6,204 plus 0.55 extra FTE puts the break-even at about $15,107 a month with a US team, or $10,164 with an offshore team.

If your managed quote sits above these lines for a steady workload, self-hosting deserves a serious look. A 1-year Savings Plan lowers both break-even points by roughly a quarter of the compute line.

Non-cost reasons that override the math

• Data residency or air-gapped requirements: self-host, or use bring-your-own-cloud options from Pinecone, Qdrant Hybrid Cloud or Zilliz BYOC.

• Predictable spend: provisioned models (Qdrant Cloud, Zilliz dedicated, self-hosted) do not spike with query volume.

• Latency control: self-hosting lets you co-locate the index with the application and tune HNSW and quantization directly.

• Team focus: every hour spent on re-indexing is an hour not spent on retrieval quality, which usually matters more to the product.

Team composition and timelines for a self-hosted build

• Pilot (1M vectors): a part-time senior platform or SRE engineer leads, with part-time ML help for recall testing and a security checklist. Modeled effort is 4 engineer-weeks.

• Growth (20M vectors): a senior platform engineer leads, one backend engineer handles ingestion and migration, ML help is part-time, and security gets a review. Modeled effort is 8 engineer-weeks.

• Scale (200M vectors): a senior platform lead plus an on-call rotation, one or two backend engineers, a dedicated ML or data engineer for quantization tuning, and a formal security review. Modeled effort is 16 engineer-weeks.

The build effort figures are illustrative estimates, not benchmarks. A 16-week Scale build spread across two or three engineers typically fits a quarter, and the on-call rotation needs at least two trained people to be sustainable.

Engagement models compared

• In-house hire: best for long-lived platform teams already running stateful systems. The risk is hiring time and dependence on one person.

• Dedicated nearshore team: best for real-time collaboration with US teams, with 4–6 hours of overlap per Full Scale. The trade-off is a higher rate than offshore.

• Dedicated offshore team: best for well-specified builds and follow-the-sun operations. The risk is handoff discipline across time zones.

• Fixed-price migration project: best for one-off moves between vendors or to self-hosting. The risk is scope creep once production traffic is live.

• Managed service plus an advisory retainer: best for teams that want managed infrastructure but need help with schema, partitioning and cost tuning. Its value depends on clear goals.

A five-step decision framework

  1. Model your query shape first. Write down vectors, dimensions, queries per month, upserts per month and the size of the partition each query searches. On usage-priced plans the last number can swing the bill by two orders of magnitude.

  2. Get three real quotes. Price one usage-based service (Pinecone), one dimension-based service (Weaviate Cloud) and one provisioned service (Qdrant Cloud or Zilliz dedicated) for your exact workload.

  3. Price self-hosting with people in it. Use the RAM formula to size the cluster, then add build effort and an honest ops fraction. If nobody on the team has run a stateful cluster through an upgrade, use the high end.

  4. Run the break-even test. If the best managed quote sits below infrastructure plus the extra engineering cost, stay managed and revisit at the next scale step.

  5. Apply the non-cost filters. Residency, compliance, latency and lock-in can justify self-hosting or a bring-your-own-cloud option even when the math says otherwise.

Pilot-to-production budgeting

Most AI teams move through three budget stages. A pilot fits inside managed minimums of $45–$50 a month, so the real cost is engineering time on ingestion and retrieval quality. A first production launch typically adds a support plan and a higher-SLA tier, which in our Growth scenario still lands under $1,000 a month on managed plans. Enterprise scale is where contracts, committed-use discounts and dedicated capacity enter, and where a self-hosted or bring-your-own-cloud option is worth pricing properly.

Budget the vector database as one line in a larger retrieval stack.
Embedding generation, reranking, LLM inference and evaluation tooling are excluded from this model and often cost more than the database itself.

Frequently asked questions

How much does a managed vector database cost per month?

At pilot scale, roughly $45–$90 a month on Weaviate Cloud Flex or Pinecone Standard as of October 2026. At 20M vectors and 10M queries a month, our modeled range is about $160–$620 when data is partitioned well, and over $23,000 on Pinecone if every query scans one large namespace.

Is self-hosting a vector database cheaper than Pinecone?

The cloud bill usually is; the total cost usually is not. In our 20M-vector scenario, self-hosted infrastructure costs about $1,142 a month, but operations and build effort bring year one to $58K–$114K depending on where the team sits.

How much RAM does a vector database need?

A common estimate is vectors × dimensions × 4 bytes × 1.5 for float32 vectors held in memory. One million 1,536-dimension vectors need about 8.6 GiB before replication. Int8 quantization cuts that by roughly four times.
When does self-hosting a vector database make sense? When managed quotes exceed the break-even line (about $3K–$5K a month at 20M vectors and $10K–$15K at 200M in our model), when data must stay in your own environment, or when an existing platform team can absorb the operations work.

Does an offshore or nearshore team change the decision?

It lowers the break-even point. At the rates used here, an offshore-operated cluster costs about 41–49% less in year one than the same cluster run by a US in-house team. It does not remove the need for at least two people who can handle an incident.

How often should these numbers be re-checked?

Quarterly. Weaviate changed its price book in September 2026, and Qdrant restructured its tiers in 2026, so cost guides in this category go stale quickly.

title: Hibernate Under the Hood. Part 3: Entity Mapping
description:
Entity mapping is the foundation of working with Hibernate/JPA. It defines how Java objects are mapped to database tables.

Basic Annotations: Where an Entity Begins

Any mapping starts with declaring a class as an entity and defining its primary key.

  • @Entity: Marks the class as an entity that will be mapped to a database table. This is a mandatory annotation.
  • @Table: Allows you to explicitly specify the table name. If omitted, Hibernate will default to the class name (e.g., for User, the table will be User).
  • @Id: Defines the field that serves as the primary key.
  • @GeneratedValue: Specifies that the primary key value will be generated automatically. The GenerationType.IDENTITY strategy (database auto-increment) is one of the most common and straightforward.
  • @Column: Used for fine-tuning the column: you can specify its name, length, precision, forbid null values, etc.

Example of a simple entity:

@Entity
@Table(name = "users")
public class User {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @Column(name = "full_name", nullable = false)
    private String name;

    // ... getters and setters
}

Relationship Types: From One-to-One to Many-to-Many

In JPA, there are four main types of relationships. The key concept to understand is the owning side. It is on the owning side that the relationship is defined in the database (e.g., which table will hold the foreign key or the join table).

  • @ManyToOne (Many-to-One): The most common and basic relationship. It maps directly to a foreign key in the table. Important: By default, JPA uses FetchType.EAGER for this, which is almost always undesirable. 
@Entity
public class Book {
    // ...
    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY) // Explicitly specify lazy loading!
    @JoinColumn(name = "publisher_id") // Name of the foreign key column
    private Publisher publisher;
}
  • @OneToMany (One-to-Many): The inverse side of @ManyToOne. In JPA, this relationship is almost always bidirectional and must be the non-owning (inverse) side. For this, the mappedBy attribute is used, pointing to the field in the child entity that owns the relationship. 
@Entity
public class Publisher {
    // ...
    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "publisher", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true)
    private List<Book> books = new ArrayList<>();
}

  • @OneToOne (One-to-One): A relationship where one record in table A corresponds to exactly one record in table B. Like @ManyToOne, it defaults to EAGER fetching. To enable lazy loading on the child side (where the foreign key resides), you must explicitly use @JoinColumn.

  • @ManyToMany (Many-to-Many): Requires an intermediate join table. The owning side defines this table using the @JoinTable annotation.

// Owning side
@Entity
public class Student {
    @ManyToMany
    @JoinTable(
        name = "student_course",
        joinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "student_id"),
        inverseJoinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "course_id")
    )
    private Set<Course> courses = new HashSet<>();
}

// Inverse (non-owning) side
@Entity
public class Course {
    @ManyToMany(mappedBy = "courses")
    private Set<Student> students = new HashSet<>();
}

Cascades (CascadeType) and orphanRemoval

These mechanisms determine how operations performed on one entity affect its related entities.

  • CascadeType: Defines which operations (persist, remove, update) should be cascaded to related entities.

    • CascadeType.PERSIST: When the parent is saved, new child entities are automatically saved as well.
    • CascadeType.REMOVE: When the parent is deleted, all related child entities are also deleted.
    • CascadeType.ALL: Applies all operations. Use with caution, only if the child entity cannot exist without the parent.

  • orphanRemoval = true: A more specific and powerful tool. It deletes a child entity if it is "unlinked" from the parent (e.g., removed from the List<Book> collection in Publisher), even if the parent entity itself is not deleted. This is ideal for modeling strict "composition" relationships.

Fetch Strategies (FetchType): LAZY vs EAGER

This is one of the most critical topics for application performance.

  • FetchType.LAZY (Lazy): Hibernate loads the related entity only upon the first access to it. This is the recommended default approach for all relationships, especially for collections (@OneToMany, @ManyToMany), as it prevents the N+1 query problem and excessive data loading.
  • FetchType.EAGER (Eager): Hibernate loads the related entity immediately, along with the parent. While this might seem convenient, in practice, it often leads to loading massive amounts of unnecessary data and severe performance issues.

The golden rule: Always explicitly specify fetch = FetchType.LAZY for all @ManyToOne and @OneToOne relationships, as EAGER is their default value.

Best Practices and Common Pitfalls

  1. Always use FetchType.LAZY for @ManyToOne and @OneToOne. This is the single most important rule for avoiding performance bottlenecks.
  2. Define the owning side correctly. For @OneToMany, use mappedBy on the "one" side, and @JoinColumn on the "many" (owning) side.
  3. Be cautious with CascadeType.ALL. Apply it only for true compositions, where the child object has no business meaning without the parent.
  4. Use orphanRemoval = true for clean deletion of child entities when they are removed from a collection.
  5. Don't forget @JsonIgnoreProperties (or @JsonManagedReference/@JsonBackReference) when serializing bidirectional relationships to JSON to avoid infinite recursion.
  6. To load lazy relationships, use JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph, rather than relying on OpenSessionInView, which is widely considered an anti-pattern.

title: Beam model by Reflection is now available on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart and AWS Trainium
description:
Beam, the first open weight model offered by US-based Reflection, is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, the model hub in Amazon SageMaker AI. According to Beam, they operate at the frontier of open weight models in its class, with strong performance across reasoning, coding, and agentic benchmarks. Beam is for teams who build on and with an open weight model, not just call one. Customers who want to adapt a frontier model to their own domain can fine-tune it, inspect and modify its weights, and embed it deep in their agents and workflows, all while keeping full control of their data and infrastructure. Beam runs alongside other models that customers already use in SageMaker AI and scales to meet production demand with the same controls, audit trails, and monitoring built into every SageMaker AI deployment. Additionally, Beam was ported and optimized for AWS Trainium3, giving customers a high-performance, cost-efficient option for deploying and scaling the model from day one. “Reflection is delivering frontier AI that developers can actually control, not just rent through an API. Bringing Beam to SageMaker AI puts that capability in front of millions of developers on infrastructure they already trust, running in their own AWS account, on their own data, fully in their control," said Misha Laskin, co-founder and CEO, Reflection.

Teams building on Beam can take it well beyond calling an API: fine-tune it on proprietary code and data, specialize it for their own domains, and wire it into multi-step agentic workflows across their tools. In practice that means resolving real software issues, generating and reviewing code, automating operations work, and tackling advanced math and science reasoning on a model they can shape rather than one they simply consume. Because Beam is released under the Apache 2.0 license, customers can inspect and customize the model, while also running it in their own AWS accounts, so data stays private and under their control, protected by the same AWS security and compliance capabilities they already rely on. “Advanced AI models like Beam, now available on Amazon SageMaker, let us run open weight frontier AI entirely inside our own secure environments, with full visibility into the weights, the data, and the pipeline. In the age of multi-model AI, the pairing of openness and managed infrastructure is an essential addition to the AI ecosystem. The freedom to deploy and adapt advanced AI, tailored to mission problems with client-specific security and controls, gives more agencies greater flexibility to deploy advanced AI across their enterprise,” said Garrett Berntsen, Chief AI Officer, Accenture Federal Services.

Beam is initially available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart in US East (N. Virginia) and US East (Ohio). The model is available in BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 checkpoint variants, and can be deployed through a fully managed SageMaker JumpStart endpoint. To start, search for "Beam" in SageMaker JumpStart within Amazon SageMaker Studio, or deploy it directly on Sagemaker AI.  To learn more, read the AWS Machine Learning blog: Introducing Reflection Beam, SageMaker AI documentation and SageMaker JumpStart documentation for deployment guidance.

title: Tailwind v4 Design Tokens: Colors, Dark Mode and Contrast
description:
TL;DR

Tailwind v4 design tokens are CSS variables: keep the values that change between light and dark in :root and .dark, then map them to utilities with @theme inline, so bg-surface or text-muted-foreground follow the theme with no dark: prefix. A complete set names roles instead of colors: surfaces in the order they stack, text levels, tones split into a solid fill and a readable text color, plus radius, elevation, z-index and motion scales. Check every text and surface pair for 4.5:1 contrast in both themes with a script, because a color that passes on white often fails on a dark popover.

Tailwind CSS v4 moved configuration out of tailwind.config.js and into CSS, and many guides stop at the first step: put a few brand colors in @theme and call them tokens. A component library needs more than a palette. It needs Tailwind v4 design tokens for every decision a component makes: which surface sits in front of which, how muted secondary text can get, what a warning uses as a fill and as text, how round a 32px button is next to a 48px one, how a popover casts a shadow on a black page, and which layer a select opens on inside a dialog. This guide is the token system we use in Wingo UI, a React 19 and Tailwind CSS v4 component library, with the real CSS and the contrast numbers behind each choice. We build Wingo UI, so we are not neutral; outside facts link to their sources and are dated.

What are design tokens in Tailwind v4?

Design tokens in Tailwind v4 are CSS custom properties. Tailwind v4 theme variables, the ones you declare inside an @theme block, do two jobs at once: they are CSS variables you can read with var(), and their namespace decides which utilities Tailwind generates. --color-surface creates bg-surface, text-surface and border-surface; --shadow-raised creates shadow-raised. Tailwind CSS v4.0 shipped this CSS-first configuration on January 22, 2025 (release post), and the theme variables docs list the namespaces. We run Tailwind 4.3.3 as of October 2026.

The namespaces a component library uses most:

Namespace Utilities it creates What we keep there
--color-* bg-*, text-*, border-*, ring-*, fill-* surfaces, text levels, tones, borders, the focus ring
--shadow-* shadow-* three elevation levels
--radius-* rounded-* a legacy scale that new code avoids (see the radius section)
--z-index-* z-* seven stacking layers
--ease-*, --transition-duration-* ease-*, duration-* motion curves and durations
--font-* font-* font families
--spacing p-*, m-*, gap-*, w-*, h-* the 4px grid (0.25rem)

--z-index-* and --transition-duration-* are not in the docs table as of October 2026, but Tailwind 4.3 compiles them: our CSS has .z-modal { z-index: var(--z-modal) }.

How should you layer Tailwind v4 design tokens?

Use three layers. Raw values that change between themes go in :root and .dark. A mapping in @theme inline turns them into utilities. Components then paint through a few runtime variables that a prop sets, so a tone or a custom color never needs its own class.

Here is a trimmed but working excerpt of our app/globals.css, with the real values:

@import "tailwindcss";

@custom-variant dark (&:is(.dark *));

:root {
  --background: oklch(1 0 0);
  --foreground: oklch(0.3211 0 0);
  --surface: #ffffff;
  --popover: oklch(1 0 0);
  --muted-foreground: oklch(0.52 0.0234 264.3637);
  --success: #15803d;
  --success-foreground: #ffffff;
  --success-soft: #e7f6ec;
  --success-soft-foreground: #166534;
  --elevation-raised: 0 0 0 1px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.07), 0 1px 2px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.05), 0 2px 8px -2px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.06);
}

.dark {
  --background: oklch(0 0 0);
  --foreground: oklch(0.9219 0 0);
  --surface: #1a1a1a;
  --popover: #262626;
  --muted-foreground: oklch(0.7155 0 0);
  --success-soft: #0d2315;
  --success-soft-foreground: #4ade80;
  --elevation-raised: inset 0 1px 0 0 rgb(255 255 255 / 0.06), 0 0 0 1px rgb(255 255 255 / 0.08), 0 1px 2px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.5);
}

@theme inline {
  --color-background: var(--background);
  --color-foreground: var(--foreground);
  --color-surface: var(--surface);
  --color-popover: var(--popover);
  --color-muted-foreground: var(--muted-foreground);
  --color-success: var(--success);
  --color-success-foreground: var(--success-foreground);
  --color-success-soft: var(--success-soft);
  --color-success-soft-foreground: var(--success-soft-foreground);
  --shadow-raised: var(--elevation-raised);
}

The success fill and its white text are the same in both themes (5.02:1), so this excerpt declares them only in :root and .dark inherits them. Everything that changes is redeclared under .dark, and a component uses the same classes everywhere:

export function InvoiceRow() {
  return (
    <div className="flex items-center justify-between rounded-2xl bg-surface p-4 text-foreground shadow-raised">
      <div>
        <p className="text-[15px] font-medium">Invoice 1042</p>
        <p className="text-sm text-muted-foreground">Emma Carter, New York</p>
      </div>
      <span className="rounded-full bg-success-soft px-2 py-0.5 text-xs font-medium text-success-soft-foreground">Paid</span>
    </div>
  );
}

The raw names follow shadcn/ui's convention on purpose: --background, --card, --popover and --muted-foreground are shadcn names, and the ones shadcn does not have (--surface, --canvas, the --success-* family) use the same name and name-foreground pattern. A project that already has shadcn tokens can take ours without renaming anything.

When do you need Tailwind v4 @theme inline?

Use @theme inline whenever a theme variable points at another variable, which is every token that changes with the theme. The Tailwind docs say it directly: with inline, "the utility class will use the theme variable value instead of referencing the actual theme variable". Here is what that means in compiled CSS:

/* @theme inline { --color-surface: var(--surface); } */
.bg-surface {
  background-color: var(--surface);
}

/* @theme { --color-surface: var(--surface); } */
:root, :host {
  --color-surface: var(--surface);
}
.bg-surface {
  background-color: var(--color-surface);
}

The difference shows up below the root. A custom property inherits its computed value, and var() is substituted where the property is declared. In the second version --color-surface is resolved once, on :root, and every element inherits that result. A .dark class on <html> still works, because <html> is the root. A dark section inside a light page (<section className="dark">), a dark preview pane or a data-theme attribute on a container does not: the section inherits the light value that :root already resolved. With inline, bg-surface reads var(--surface) on the element itself, so it picks up the nearest override. The Tailwind docs explain the option with the same kind of parent and child example.

One catch remains with inline: if you write var(--color-surface) yourself, in an arbitrary value like bg-[var(--color-surface)] or in plain CSS, Tailwind 4.3 emits --color-surface: var(--surface) on :root to satisfy it, and that reference is resolved on the root again. Inside components, read the raw variable instead: bg-(--surface) or var(--surface).

Two more rules from the docs: theme variables must sit at the top level, never under a selector or a media query, so per-theme values live outside @theme anyway; and Tailwind only emits the theme variables your code uses, unless you write @theme static. The raw variables in :root always ship, which helps when a chart library reads a token with getComputedStyle.

Which semantic color tokens does a component library need?

Name colors by role, never by hue. A component library needs surfaces in the order they stack, text levels with a contrast floor, translucent tints for hover and fills, a border and a focus ring, and status tones. With semantic color tokens, components never contain bg-gray-100 or text-blue-600, so a theme can change every value without touching a component.

Surfaces, back to front

Token Light Dark Use
background #FFFFFF #000000 the page
canvas #F6F7F9 #0E0E10 the page of an app (dashboards, admin), under white panels
card #EBEBEB #121212 flat gray tiles with no shadow
surface #FFFFFF with shadow-raised #1A1A1A raised panels: list groups, stat cards, forms
popover #FFFFFF with shadow-floating #262626 everything that floats: menus, selects, dialogs, sheets, toasts
primary #000000 #FAFAFA the neutral solid fill and tooltips

In dark mode the surfaces get lighter as they come forward: #000, #121212, #1A1A1A, #262626. In light mode most of them are white, so the shadow does the separating. canvas exists because a dashboard on a white page has nothing to set white cards against; a cool gray page makes every bg-surface panel read as a card.

Text levels

Level Class Use Lowest ratio in our token pairs
Primary text-foreground titles, values, labels 10.60:1 (light card)
Secondary text-muted-foreground descriptions, helper text, timestamps 4.62:1 (light card)
Disabled text-foreground/45 disabled labels only none required
Tone text text-success-soft-foreground and its siblings errors, deltas, links 5.28:1 (brand on the light card)

text-muted-foreground is the floor for anything people must read. The disabled level has no contrast target because WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.3 exempts text in inactive controls, which is why it is never used for anything else.

Tints instead of gray fills

Hover states, field fills, chips, tracks and skeletons use translucent foreground: bg-foreground/5, /7, /10 and /15, plus border-foreground/10 for hairlines. Tailwind 4.3 compiles the opacity modifier to color-mix(), with the plain color as a fallback:

.bg-foreground\/5 {
  background-color: var(--foreground);
  @supports (color: color-mix(in lab, red, red)) {
    background-color: color-mix(in oklab, var(--foreground) 5%, transparent);
  }
}

A tint is relative to whatever sits behind it, so it moves one step toward the text color on every surface, in both themes. A fixed fill cannot do that. Our dark --muted is #171717: lighter than the black page and darker than the #1A1A1A surface, so the same field would look raised on one and sunken on the other. The full-strength fallback only shows in browsers without color-mix(), which are all below Tailwind's browser baseline of Chrome 111, Safari 16.4 and Firefox 128.

shadcn/ui's secondary and accent stay in our file so ported components keep working, but our --accent is an orange tint, and new components never use either.

How do status colors work without a class per color?

Give each status tone four tokens: a solid fill, the text on that fill, a soft tinted surface, and tone text that reads on the soft surface and on every neutral surface. Then let components paint through five generic variables that one class sets. That is the whole idea behind the free Tones utility.

The four tokens per tone, for brand, success, warning, destructive and info:

--success: #15803d;                 /* bg-success: buttons, solid badges, progress */
--success-foreground: #ffffff;      /* text on the fill */
--success-soft: #e7f6ec;            /* bg-success-soft: soft badges, alerts, selected rows */
--success-soft-foreground: #166534; /* colored text on the tint and on any neutral surface */

The split between fill and tone text is the easiest rule to skip, and it is where dark mode breaks. Fills are tuned to carry white text, and they make poor text. text-destructive (#DC2626) on our dark popover is 3.13:1; text-destructive-soft-foreground (#FF8A80) on the same surface is 6.63:1. The warning fill is amber (#F5A524) at 2.04:1 against white, so it carries dark text (#2B1700, 8.40:1) and is never used as text on a neutral surface.

Component variables

A component with a tone prop does not map tokens itself. toneClasses[tone] sets five variables, and every variant paints with them:

// lib/tones.ts (excerpt)
success:
  "[--tone:var(--success)] [--tone-foreground:var(--success-foreground)] [--tone-soft:var(--success-soft)] [--tone-soft-foreground:var(--success-soft-foreground)] [--tone-border:color-mix(in_oklab,var(--success)_45%,transparent)]",

The neutral tone maps --tone to --primary (black in light, near-white in dark) and builds its soft surface from color-mix(in oklab, var(--foreground) 7%, transparent), which is why a neutral soft button works on any surface. A badge built this way:

import type { ComponentProps } from "react";
import { colorVars, toneClasses, type Tone } from "@/lib/tones";
import { cn } from "@/lib/utils";

type StatusBadgeProps = ComponentProps<"span"> & { tone?: Tone; color?: string };

export function StatusBadge({ tone = "neutral", color, className, style, ...props }: StatusBadgeProps) {
  return (
    <span
      data-slot="status-badge"
      className={cn(
        toneClasses[tone],
        "inline-flex rounded-full bg-(--tone-soft) px-2 py-0.5 text-xs font-medium text-(--tone-soft-foreground)",
        className,
      )}
      style={{ ...colorVars(color), ...style }}
      {...props}
    />
  );
}

bg-(--tone-soft) is Tailwind v4's shorthand for bg-[var(--tone-soft)]. The free Badge is the full version of this pattern, with solid, soft and outline variants. colorVars(color) builds the same five variables from any CSS color as an inline style. Its text-on-fill value uses relative color syntax, oklch(from <color> clamp(0, (0.7 - l) * 1000, 1) 0 0): white when the color's OKLCH lightness is below 0.7, black above. As of October 2026, caniuse lists full support for relative color syntax from Chrome 131, Safari 18 and Firefox 133, and partial support before that, so full support arrived later than Tailwind's own baseline. Where a browser cannot compute the value, the declaration is invalid at computed-value time and the text inherits its parent's color. If you support those browsers, force the text color with className="[--tone-foreground:white]".

Live demo: Tones. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Each row paints one tone three ways from the same five variables, and the last row is built by colorVars from one hex value, #0EA5E9. Switch the site theme: the solid fills stay, while the soft tints and the tone text take their dark values). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Tones docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add tones

The free Button is the reference consumer. Its variant map contains no color at all:

const VARIANTS: Record<ButtonVariant, string> = {
  solid: "bg-(--tone) text-(--tone-foreground) shadow-raised",
  soft: "bg-(--tone-soft) text-(--tone-soft-foreground)",
  outline: "border border-(--tone-border) text-(--tone-soft-foreground)",
  ghost: "text-(--tone-soft-foreground)",
  link: "rounded-[4px] text-(--tone-soft-foreground) underline decoration-current/35 decoration-1 underline-offset-4 transition-[color,text-decoration-color] hover:decoration-current",
};

Six tones times five variants, plus any custom color, from five lines. Hover and press are a layer of currentColor at 8% and 12% opacity, so they also work for every tone without extra classes.

How do you design dark mode with tokens?

Treat dark as a second set of values for the same roles, picked by hand, and switch it with a class. Components keep the same classes in both themes, so almost nothing in a component needs a dark: prefix.

The variant: our tokens, like shadcn/ui's, use @custom-variant dark (&:is(.dark *));. The Tailwind dark mode docs show &:where(.dark, .dark *), which also matches the element that carries the class and adds no specificity. With the class on <html>, both behave the same for normal use. The class itself comes from next-themes, which writes it before the first paint: wrap the app in its ThemeProvider with attribute="class" (the full provider file is in the props section below), and render <html lang="en" suppressHydrationWarning> in the root layout, because next-themes changes the class before React hydrates:

// app/layout.tsx
import type { ReactNode } from "react";
import { Providers } from "./providers";
import "./globals.css";

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en" suppressHydrationWarning>
      <body className="bg-background text-foreground">
        <Providers>{children}</Providers>
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}

What a designed dark theme looks like in practice, from our token file:

  • Surfaces lighten as they come forward. #000 page, #121212 card, #1A1A1A surface, #262626 popover.
  • Fills stay, soft surfaces flip. The brand fill is #D63F00 in both themes, so white text keeps 4.59:1. Its soft surface goes from #FFEFE6 to #2A1509, and its text from #B03400 to #FF8A4C.
  • The neutral fill inverts. primary is black with white text in light mode and #FAFAFA with #171717 in dark, so the neutral solid button keeps 21:1 in light and 17.16:1 in dark.
  • Elevation changes technique. A drop shadow barely shows on black, so dark shadows lean on a lit top edge and a white hairline (see the elevation levels below).
  • The focus ring shifts. --ring is oklch(0.60 0.20 36.93) in light and oklch(0.6617 0.2215 36.93) in dark, deeper on white so a 2px outline keeps 3:1 on white and on the gray card.
  • Some components need an exception. Our soft Card uses bg-card in light but bg-foreground/7 in dark, because the dark --card is the same gray as a dark sidebar or stage and the card would vanish there. An inversion script never makes that call.

How do you check contrast for every token pair?

List the pairs that are meant to be used together, convert both colors to sRGB, compute the WCAG ratio in both themes, and fail the build below 4.5:1. WCAG asks for 4.5:1 for body text and 3:1 for large text (1.4.3), and 3:1 for UI components and focus indicators against what is next to them (1.4.11).

Our check covers 54 pairs per theme, 108 in total, and reports 0 below 4.5:1 as of release 1.7.0. The tightest pairs are brand-foreground on brand at 4.59:1 and muted-foreground on the light card at 4.62:1. Here is a self-contained version you can drop into scripts/ and run with npx tsx scripts/check-contrast.ts. It reads hex and oklch() values (decimal or percent lightness), follows var() references and exits with code 1 on a failure. It expects the token names used in this guide; if yours differ, edit SURFACES, TONES and PAIRS:

// scripts/check-contrast.ts
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";

type Rgb = [number, number, number];
const css = readFileSync("app/globals.css", "utf8").replace(/\/\*[\s\S]*?\*\//g, "");

// every --name: value inside the blocks that start with this selector
function vars(selector: string) {
  const map = new Map<string, string>();
  const block = new RegExp(`(?:^|\\n)${selector.replace(".", "\\.")}\\s*\\{([^}]*)\\}`, "g");
  for (const m of css.matchAll(block))
    for (const d of m[1].matchAll(/(--[\w-]+)\s*:\s*([^;]+);/g)) map.set(d[1], d[2].trim());
  return map;
}

export function oklchToRgb(l: number, c: number, h: number): Rgb {
  const a = c * Math.cos((h * Math.PI) / 180);
  const b = c * Math.sin((h * Math.PI) / 180);
  const l3 = (l + 0.3963377774 * a + 0.2158037573 * b) ** 3;
  const m3 = (l - 0.1055613458 * a - 0.0638541728 * b) ** 3;
  const s3 = (l - 0.0894841775 * a - 1.291485548 * b) ** 3;
  const linear = [
    4.0767416621 * l3 - 3.3077115913 * m3 + 0.2309699292 * s3,
    -1.2684380046 * l3 + 2.6097574011 * m3 - 0.3413193965 * s3,
    -0.0041960863 * l3 - 0.7034186147 * m3 + 1.707614701 * s3,
  ];
  // clamp into srgb, then gamma-encode
  return linear.map((v) => {
    const x = Math.min(1, Math.max(0, v));
    return x <= 0.0031308 ? 12.92 * x : 1.055 * x ** (1 / 2.4) - 0.055;
  }) as Rgb;
}

function parse(value: string, map: Map<string, string>): Rgb {
  const ref = value.match(/^var\((--[\w-]+)\)$/);
  if (ref) return parse(map.get(ref[1]) ?? "", map);
  if (value.startsWith("#")) {
    const hex = value.length === 4 ? [...value.slice(1)].map((ch) => ch + ch).join("") : value.slice(1);
    return [0, 2, 4].map((i) => parseInt(hex.slice(i, i + 2), 16) / 255) as Rgb;
  }
  const ok = value.match(/^oklch\(\s*([\d.]+)(%?)\s+([\d.]+)\s+([\d.]+)\s*\)$/);
  if (ok) return oklchToRgb(ok[2] ? +ok[1] / 100 : +ok[1], +ok[3], +ok[4]);
  throw new Error(`cannot parse "${value}"`);
}

const channel = (c: number) => (c <= 0.04045 ? c / 12.92 : ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4);
const luminance = ([r, g, b]: Rgb) => 0.2126 * channel(r) + 0.7152 * channel(g) + 0.0722 * channel(b);

export function contrast(fg: Rgb, bg: Rgb) {
  const [hi, lo] = [luminance(fg), luminance(bg)].sort((x, y) => y - x);
  return (hi + 0.05) / (lo + 0.05);
}

const SURFACES = ["background", "card", "popover", "surface", "canvas"];
const TONES = ["brand", "success", "warning", "info", "destructive"];
const PAIRS = [
  ["foreground", "background"],
  ...SURFACES.map((s) => ["muted-foreground", s]),
  ...TONES.flatMap((t) => [
    [`${t}-foreground`, t],
    [`${t}-soft-foreground`, `${t}-soft`],
    ...SURFACES.map((s) => [`${t}-soft-foreground`, s]),
  ]),
];

const light = vars(":root");
const themes = { light, dark: new Map([...light, ...vars(".dark")]) };
let failures = 0;
for (const [theme, map] of Object.entries(themes)) {
  for (const [fg, bg] of PAIRS) {
    const ratio = contrast(parse(map.get(`--${fg}`) ?? "", map), parse(map.get(`--${bg}`) ?? "", map));
    if (ratio < 4.5) {
      failures++;
      console.log(`FAIL ${theme}: ${fg} on ${bg} is ${ratio.toFixed(2)}:1`);
    }
  }
}
console.log(`${PAIRS.length * 2} pairs checked, ${failures} below 4.5:1`);
process.exitCode = failures ? 1 : 0;

This trimmed version checks 82 pairs. Our full script adds the remaining surface, primary and legacy pairs and composites translucent values over the page first. The pair list is the valuable part: it encodes which text may sit on which surface, so a new token is checked the day it is added. Run it in CI next to the type check.

Should you write Tailwind v4 OKLCH values or hex?

Use whichever format you can reason about; the format does not change contrast. Tailwind's own palette moved "from rgb to oklch, taking advantage of the wider gamut" in v4.0 (release post), and its colors reference lists every Tailwind v4 OKLCH value, such as --color-red-500: oklch(63.7% 0.237 25.331). OKLCH earns its place when you derive colors in code, because lightness is its own channel: you can move it while hue and chroma stay put, and the result still looks like the same color.

In our file, neutrals are oklch() with zero chroma (oklch(0.3211 0 0) is the light foreground), and the tone values are hex, tuned by hand against the contrast check. The theme generator goes the other way: you pick a base color for each tone (brand, success, warning, danger, info), and it derives that tone's fill, soft surface and text in OKLCH. For light mode it puts the soft surface at lightness 0.965 with chroma capped at 0.035, then walks the tone text's lightness down from 0.6 in 0.005 steps until it reaches 4.6:1 on the soft surface and on every neutral surface. Move oklchToRgb and contrast from the contrast script into their own module, scripts/color.ts, so importing them does not run the check, and the same search is a few lines:

import { contrast, oklchToRgb } from "./color";

type Rgb = [number, number, number];

// keep hue and chroma, walk lightness until the color reads on every surface it can sit on
export function findReadable(c: number, h: number, surfaces: Rgb[], from: number, to: number, target = 4.6): Rgb {
  const step = from < to ? 0.005 : -0.005;
  for (let l = from; step > 0 ? l <= to : l >= to; l += step) {
    const rgb = oklchToRgb(l, c, h);
    if (Math.min(...surfaces.map((bg) => contrast(rgb, bg))) >= target) return rgb;
  }
  return oklchToRgb(to, c, h);
}

The target is 4.6 rather than 4.5 so rounding to hex cannot push a color under the line. One caution: a high-chroma OKLCH value can fall outside sRGB, and what a screen then shows depends on the display and the browser. Keep token values inside sRGB, or at least measure the clamped sRGB value, as oklchToRgb does.

How do radius, elevation, z-index and motion become tokens?

They become scales with a fixed set of steps, each with one job, so a component picks a step instead of a number. A Tailwind v4 design system that only tokenizes color still ends up with one-off shadows and a z-[9999] somewhere.

Radius follows size

Tie radius to the control's size. A 32px and a 48px button only read as the same shape when the larger one has the larger radius. Our controls copy this map from the Button:

type Scale = "sm" | "md" | "lg";
type ButtonRadius = "none" | "sm" | "md" | "lg" | "full";

const RADII: Record<ButtonRadius, Record<Scale, string>> = {
  none: { sm: "rounded-none", md: "rounded-none", lg: "rounded-none" },
  sm: { sm: "rounded-[6px]", md: "rounded-[8px]", lg: "rounded-[10px]" },
  md: { sm: "rounded-[8px]", md: "rounded-[10px]", lg: "rounded-[12px]" },
  lg: { sm: "rounded-[10px]", md: "rounded-[14px]", lg: "rounded-[16px]" },
  full: { sm: "rounded-full", md: "rounded-full", lg: "rounded-full" },
};

Surfaces use rounded-2xl (16px) for cards, menus and popovers, rounded-3xl (24px) for dialogs, and rounded-t-[28px] for bottom sheets. Anything inside a padded surface takes the outer radius minus the padding: a rounded-2xl p-1.5 menu has rounded-[10px] items. Sizes follow the same thinking: 32, 40 and 48px, with the 40px size growing to 44px on touch screens, the rule from our mobile-first React components guide.

The trap is a global radius token. Our file still carries shadcn/ui's older scale for ported components: --radius: 0.375rem, --radius-lg: var(--radius) and --radius-sm: calc(var(--radius) - 4px). That remaps Tailwind's rounded-sm, rounded-md, rounded-lg and rounded-xl to 2, 4, 6 and 10px everywhere, including markup pasted from Tailwind's docs (the compiled .rounded-lg is border-radius: var(--radius)), so new components never use those four classes. As of October 2026, shadcn/ui's theming docs derive the scale by multiplication instead (--radius-sm: calc(var(--radius) * 0.6) up to --radius-4xl), which has the same project-wide reach. If you theme radius globally, own every component that uses it.

Three elevation levels

Three levels cover a library: shadow-raised for buttons, cards and thumbs, shadow-floating for popovers, menus and toasts, shadow-modal for dialogs and sheets. Each level carries its own 1px hairline, so an elevated surface needs no border:

:root {
  --elevation-floating: 0 0 0 1px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.06), 0 4px 12px -2px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.08), 0 16px 36px -10px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.16);
}
.dark {
  /* on a black page a drop shadow barely shows: a lit top edge and a hairline do the work */
  --elevation-floating: inset 0 1px 0 0 rgb(255 255 255 / 0.07), 0 0 0 1px rgb(255 255 255 / 0.09), 0 8px 24px -4px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.6), 0 20px 48px -12px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.7);
}
@theme inline {
  --shadow-floating: var(--elevation-floating);
}

An interactive Card moves between two of these levels on hover, and the lift runs as a CSS transition on a spring curve (below), so a grid of fifty cards animates without JavaScript.

Live demo: Card. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Hover the card to see it lift from shadow-raised to shadow-floating, then press it to see the dip to 98% (phones get only the press). Switch the site theme to see the dark elevation draw a lit top edge instead). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Card docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add card

Stacking layers

Class Value Use
z-dropdown 1000 in-flow panels that are not portaled
z-sticky 1100 sticky headers, tab bars, CTA bars
z-overlay 1200 the dimmed backdrop
z-modal 1300 dialogs, sheets, drawers
z-popover 1400 portaled menus, selects, popovers
z-toast 1500 toasts
z-tooltip 1600 tooltips, always on top

Popovers sit above modals on purpose: a select inside a dialog has to open over it. No overlay in the library uses a raw number like z-50; small values such as z-10 only order parts inside one component.

Motion

CSS transitions use three durations (duration-fast 150ms, duration-normal 240ms, duration-slow 400ms) and named curves (ease-smooth is cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1), ease-sheet is cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1)). Our JavaScript springs are also sampled into CSS linear() easings: ease-spring with duration-spring (500ms) matches a spring with stiffness 300 and damping 30.

Can component props work like design tokens?

Yes, for the decisions that are props: the radius of every button, the default size of fields, the variant of every card. CSS variables cannot set a prop, so Wingo UI reads those from a React provider, and UIProvider defaults works as a token layer for props. The free UIProvider merges app-wide defaults under the props each component receives, keyed by its data-slot name:

// app/providers.tsx
"use client";

import type { ReactNode } from "react";
import { ThemeProvider } from "next-themes";
import { UIProvider } from "@/lib/ui-config";

export function Providers({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <ThemeProvider attribute="class" defaultTheme="system" enableSystem disableTransitionOnChange>
      <UIProvider locale="en-US" defaults={{ button: { radius: "full" }, card: { variant: "outline" } }}>
        {children}
      </UIProvider>
    </ThemeProvider>
  );
}

Inside a component, the first line reads the defaults, and the signature defaults stay the last fallback:

export function Button(buttonProps: ButtonProps) {
  const { variant = "solid", tone = "neutral", size = "md", radius = "md", ...rest } = useDefaults("button", buttonProps);
  // ...
}

Explicit props win, then the provider, then the component's own defaults. An undefined prop does not override a provider value, so wrappers can pass props through without erasing the theme. The same signature takes ref as a regular prop, with no forwardRef wrapper; our React 19 forwardRef migration guide moves older components to that pattern, TypeScript types included.

Live demo: UIProvider. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (The first button uses its built-in defaults; the two below get radius full, size lg and tone brand from a UIProvider, and the outline one keeps the variant it passes itself). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the UIProvider docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add ui-config

How do you add these tokens to an existing Next.js project?

Run npx wingo-ui@latest init in a project that has Tailwind CSS v4. It writes wingo-ui.json and lib/utils.ts (the cn helper), installs clsx and tailwind-merge, and merges the tokens into the stylesheet that contains @import "tailwindcss". It only adds missing names and keeps your values; add later brings any tokens a new component needs. The full block, 74 variables in :root plus their dark values and Tailwind mappings, is served at /r/tokens.css, and coding agents get the same CSS from the MCP tool get_theme_tokens (see our component library MCP guide). The theming docs show the main tokens with their light and dark values, and the two dark mode setups the CLI supports: a .dark class, or prefers-color-scheme when your stylesheet already uses it.

To restyle, open the theme generator, pick a brand color, neutrals, radius, font and component defaults, check its contrast report, and apply the export:

npx wingo-ui@latest theme apply ./theme.json

It replaces the values of the tokens the theme sets, in light and dark, adds Tailwind mappings for new ones and prints the UIProvider defaults and locale to paste into your provider.

Coming from shadcn/ui: the shared names line up, but two keep different meanings. Our --card is a flat gray tile where shadcn's is the card background, and our --accent is an orange tint. Because init keeps your existing values, a shadcn project keeps its own --card and --accent, so check the soft Card variant after the merge. Our shadcn alternatives comparison covers the wider differences between the two libraries.

Which mistakes break a Tailwind v4 design system?

The same few mistakes show up in most token files:

  • dark: classes in components. A component that needs dark:bg-zinc-900 is missing a token.
  • Palette names in components. bg-blue-600 cannot follow a theme; use a role or a tone.
  • Fill colors as text. text-destructive on a dark surface fails AA; use the soft foreground.
  • Per-theme values in plain @theme. Keep them in :root and .dark, mapped with inline.
  • A global radius that rewrites Tailwind's scale. Every pasted rounded-lg changes with it.
  • Raw z-index numbers. Two z-50 overlays from two authors will collide.
  • No contrast check. Tokens drift with every tweak; a check in CI catches it the same day.

Where should you start?

Run npx wingo-ui@latest init in your Next.js project, then npx wingo-ui@latest add button, which brings the Tones and UIProvider items with it. Replace one hard-coded color in a real screen with a role token, open it in both themes, and add the contrast script to CI. Two more guides in Next.js and Tailwind CSS cover the component code around the tokens: the React 19 forwardRef migration and an SSR-safe React use mobile hook that hydrates without a mismatch.

Components in this post

  • Button (Free): The button every screen starts with: five variants, six tones, three sizes plus icon sizes, and a loading state that never jumps. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add button
  • Tones (Free): One way to color a component: a tone or any CSS color becomes five CSS variables every variant paints with. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add tones
  • UIProvider (Free): App-wide configuration for Wingo UI: default props for every component, the Intl locale and the reduced-motion policy. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add ui-config
  • Card (Free): The surface listings, stats, settings and plans sit on: media, header, body and footer parts, four variants and a lift-and-press mode. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add card
  • Badge (Free): Status chips, removable filters and animated counts in three variants and six tones, plus an anchor that pins a count or dot to any corner. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add badge

FAQ

Where do design tokens go in Tailwind v4?

In the global CSS file, after @import "tailwindcss". Variables in an @theme block become utilities (--color-surface gives bg-surface), and values that change per theme live in :root and .dark and are mapped with @theme inline. A tailwind.config.js file is no longer required.

What is the difference between @theme and @theme inline in Tailwind v4?

With @theme, the utility references the theme variable, so bg-surface compiles to var(--color-surface), which is resolved once on :root. With @theme inline, the utility gets the referenced value written in, so bg-surface compiles to var(--surface) and resolves on the element that uses it. Use inline whenever a theme variable points at another variable.

Should Tailwind v4 colors be OKLCH or hex?

Either works, because tokens are plain CSS colors and the format does not change contrast. Tailwind's own palette moved to oklch in v4.0. OKLCH helps most when you derive colors in code, since you can keep hue and chroma and move lightness until a contrast target passes.

How do I add dark mode to Tailwind v4 design tokens?

Redefine the same variables in a .dark block and add @custom-variant dark (&:is(.dark *)); so dark: utilities follow the class too. next-themes with attribute="class" sets the class before the first paint. Components that use semantic tokens then need no dark: classes.

How do I check color contrast for design tokens?

List every text token with each surface it can sit on, convert the values to sRGB, and compute the WCAG ratio for light and dark. Fail the build below 4.5:1 for body text; focus rings and other UI shapes need 3:1.

Are the Wingo UI design tokens free?

Yes. npx wingo-ui@latest init merges the tokens into your stylesheet without an account, and the Button, Card, Tones and UIProvider items in this guide are free. As of release 1.7.0, 75 of the 326 registry items are free and the rest need Pro.

This article was originally published on the Wingo UI blog: Tailwind v4 Design Tokens: Colors, Dark Mode and Contrast. The original has the live, interactive demos and is kept up to date.

title: Google Cloud's Backup Generators Failed to Engage, and a Single London Zone Took Down UK Banks
description:
Google Cloud's backup generators failed to engage when mains power cut out at a London data center on October 20, 2026, and the resulting outage in a single availability zone reached far beyond that zone's own customers. Revolut, Lloyds, HSBC, Royal Mail, and England and Wales's court video system all went down for hours, and the UK's financial regulators are now being asked in Parliament how much of the country's banking infrastructure sits behind one cloud region.

Jump to what we checked in our own redundancy claims if your own architecture assumes a zone failure stays contained to that zone.

What Happened in Google's London Region

The outage began at 06:08 UTC when the europe-west2-b zone, one of three availability zones in Google's only UK region, lost power at what Google later described as a third-party facility. According to an internal engineering update reported by Computer Weekly, mains power returned relatively quickly, but the site's backup generators failed to engage. That forced Google's engineers to keep a frontend and backend traffic drain on the zone while onsite technicians manually verified backup power was actually working.

Google's status page listed 38 distinct products affected, including Compute Engine, Google Kubernetes Engine, Cloud SQL, BigQuery, and Cloud Run. The company's own incident record shows the first public acknowledgment at 08:35 UTC with no workaround offered, a workaround added at 10:24 UTC advising customers to migrate workloads to another zone or region if they could, and the cause named around 12:12 UTC. Most customers were back by roughly 14:00 UTC, nearly eight hours after the power event began.

Why a Single Zone Outage Reached a Whole Region

Google's own architecture promises that regional services run across all three zones in a region specifically so that losing one zone costs capacity, not availability. That promise is why Compute Engine VMs and zonal disks pinned to europe-west2-b went down with no workaround, while regional services were supposed to keep running on the two healthy zones.

They mostly didn't. Google's status updates describe services across the broader europe-west2 region, not just the b zone, experiencing elevated errors and intermittent failures throughout the morning. Google has not yet explained why its two unaffected zones didn't fully absorb the load that the failed zone would normally have carried, and that gap is the detail its promised incident analysis will need to answer.

What We Checked in Our Own Redundancy Claims

We reviewed every place at Krova Cloud where we tell customers a service is "regionally redundant" and checked whether we had actually tested a full zone failure against it, rather than just designing for one. We found one internal monitoring service that was architecturally spread across zones but had never been through a real failover drill. We scheduled one for the following week, since a redundancy design nobody has tested is a hypothesis, not a guarantee.

What to Check in Your Own Cloud Architecture

  • If a vendor tells you a service is "regional" or "multi-zone," ask whether that claim has been tested against an actual single-zone failure, not just designed for one, since Google's own regional services didn't fully absorb this zone's load.
  • Identify every workload you run pinned to a single zone, since Google's own workaround for this incident, migrate to another zone or region, only works for architectures built to support it in advance.
  • Check whether your incident communications depend on the same cloud region you're reporting an outage about, a common and easy-to-miss single point of failure.
  • Ask your downstream vendors, banking apps, courts systems, and logistics platforms among them this time, which cloud region and zone each of their critical paths actually runs in, since the blast radius of this outage reached well past Google's own customer list.

The limitation worth stating plainly is that Google has not yet published the technical analysis it promised, so the exact reason regional services degraded alongside the failed zone is still unconfirmed.

The verdict doesn't need that analysis to land, though: a backup generator failing to engage at one facility was enough to disrupt banking, courts, and parcel delivery across an entire country, and the zone-isolation guarantee did not hold as cleanly as the architecture promises it should.

The Rule

A multi-zone design only protects you from a single-zone failure if the other zones can actually absorb that zone's load when it happens, not just in the architecture diagram. If you've never tested your own "regional" service against a real zone outage, you don't know whether you have that protection, you're just hoping the backup generator engages when the lights go out.

Frequently Asked Questions

What caused the Google Cloud outage on October 20, 2026?

A power event at a third-party facility hosting Google's europe-west2-b availability zone in London. Mains power returned, but backup generators failed to engage, requiring manual verification by onsite technicians before services could be restored.

Which services and companies were affected?

Google listed 38 affected products including Compute Engine, GKE, Cloud SQL, BigQuery, and Cloud Run. Downstream, Revolut, Lloyds, HSBC, Royal Mail, DPD, Rightmove, and England and Wales's court video hearing system all reported disruption.

How long did the outage last?

The incident began at 06:08 UTC and Google reported most services mitigated by roughly 14:00 UTC the same day, nearly eight hours later, though some customers reported longer recovery times.

Why did a single zone failure affect the whole region?

Google's regional services are designed to run across all three zones in europe-west2 so a single zone's loss doesn't cause a regional outage. Google has not yet explained why the two unaffected zones didn't fully absorb the failed zone's load during this incident.

I'm Rohit, founder of Krova Cloud: disposable VMs with redundancy claims we've actually drilled, not just diagrammed. More debugging stories at debugly.dev.
