title: Secure Multi-Tenant SaaS: Node.js, PostgreSQL & Row-Level Security for Scale
description:
Introduction & The Problem

When building Software as a Service (SaaS) products, one of the most significant architectural decisions is how to manage data for multiple customers, or 'tenants'. The goal is simple: each tenant should have a logically isolated view of their data, completely unaware of other tenants' information. The challenge, however, is complex. Common approaches range from entirely separate database instances per tenant (high cost, complex operations) to a single shared database where tenant identification is handled solely at the application layer (high risk of data leaks, complex queries).

Leaving this problem unresolved leads to several severe consequences: spiraling infrastructure costs as your tenant count grows, increased operational overhead for managing numerous database instances, and, most critically, a heightened risk of data breaches where one tenant's data could inadvertently become accessible to another. This not only erodes trust but can incur severe financial and legal penalties, impacting your SaaS's reputation and long-term viability.

This article addresses this fundamental challenge by presenting a robust, production-ready solution: leveraging Node.js with PostgreSQL's powerful Row-Level Security (RLS) feature. This approach offers a secure, scalable, and cost-efficient way to build multi-tenant SaaS applications, ensuring strict data isolation without the overhead of separate database instances.

The Solution Concept & Architecture

Our solution hinges on the 'shared database, shared schema' multi-tenancy model, augmented by PostgreSQL's Row-Level Security. Instead of creating a separate database or schema for each tenant, all tenant data resides within the same tables, but each row is explicitly tagged with a tenant_id. PostgreSQL's RLS policies then enforce that a database session can only see and manipulate rows belonging to its designated tenant_id.

The architectural flow is as follows:

1. Client Request: A client application (web, mobile, or API consumer) initiates a request to the Node.js backend. This request implicitly or explicitly includes the tenant context (e.g., via an API key, JWT token, or a dedicated X-Tenant-Id header).

2. Node.js API Service: The Node.js application, typically an Express.js server, receives the request. It performs authentication and authorization checks. Crucially, it extracts the authenticated tenant's ID.

3. Database Connection with Tenant Context: Before executing any database queries, the Node.js application sets a session-local variable (e.g., app.tenant_id) in PostgreSQL to the extracted tenant ID. This is achieved using SET LOCAL.

4. PostgreSQL RLS Enforcement: With RLS enabled on relevant tables and policies defined, PostgreSQL automatically filters all subsequent queries within that session. Any SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE operation will only affect rows where the tenant_id matches the session's app.tenant_id.

This architecture elegantly centralizes data isolation logic at the database level, preventing application-level mistakes from compromising tenant data. It reduces the complexity of application code and strengthens your security posture significantly.

Step-by-Step Implementation

Let's walk through building this solution.

Prerequisites:

  • Node.js (LTS version) installed.
  • PostgreSQL database (version 9.5+ for RLS) running.
  • Basic knowledge of SQL and Node.js/Express.

1. Database Setup (PostgreSQL)

First, connect to your PostgreSQL instance and set up the database, a dedicated user, and our tables. Note the tenant_id column in users and products.

-- Connect as a superuser or admin
CREATE DATABASE saas_multitenant;
CREATE USER saas_user WITH PASSWORD 'strong_password';
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE saas_multitenant TO saas_user;

-- Connect to the new database
\c saas_multitenant

-- Create the Tenants table
CREATE TABLE tenants (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    created_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

-- Create the Users table with tenant_id
CREATE TABLE users (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    tenant_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES tenants(id),
    email VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    password_hash VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    UNIQUE (tenant_id, email) -- Ensure email is unique per tenant
);

-- Create the Products table with tenant_id
CREATE TABLE products (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    tenant_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES tenants(id),
    name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    description TEXT,
    price NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

-- Insert some sample data
INSERT INTO tenants (name) VALUES ('Acme Corp'), ('Globex Inc.');

INSERT INTO users (tenant_id, email, password_hash) VALUES
    ((SELECT id FROM tenants WHERE name = 'Acme Corp'), 'john@acme.com', 'hashed_password_acme'),
    ((SELECT id FROM tenants WHERE name = 'Globex Inc.'), 'jane@globex.com', 'hashed_password_globex');

INSERT INTO products (tenant_id, name, description, price) VALUES
    ((SELECT id FROM tenants WHERE name = 'Acme Corp'), 'Acme Product A', 'Description for Acme Product A', 10.50),
    ((SELECT id FROM tenants WHERE name = 'Acme Corp'), 'Acme Product B', 'Description for Acme Product B', 25.00),
    ((SELECT id FROM tenants WHERE name = 'Globex Inc.'), 'Globex Product X', 'Description for Globex Product X', 150.00);

2. Implementing Row-Level Security (RLS)

Now, enable RLS on the tables containing tenant-specific data and define policies. These policies refer to a custom session variable app.tenant_id which we will set from our Node.js application.

-- Enable RLS for users and products tables
ALTER TABLE users ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE products ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

-- Create a policy for users table
CREATE POLICY user_isolation_policy ON users
    USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::UUID);

-- Create a policy for products table
CREATE POLICY product_isolation_policy ON products
    USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::UUID);

-- Optionally, create policies to allow tenants to view their own tenant record (if needed)
-- CREATE POLICY tenant_view_policy ON tenants
--     USING (id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::UUID);

-- Grant specific permissions to our saas_user
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON users TO saas_user;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON products TO saas_user;
GRANT SELECT ON tenants TO saas_user;

3. Node.js Application Setup

Initialize a new Node.js project and install necessary packages.

npm init -y
npm install express pg dotenv

Create a .env file for database credentials:

DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432
DB_USER=saas_user
DB_PASSWORD=strong_password
DB_DATABASE=saas_multitenant

Next, create src/db.js to handle database connections. We'll use the pg client directly for more control over session variables.

// src/db.js
const { Pool } = require('pg');
require('dotenv').config();

const pool = new Pool({
    user: process.env.DB_USER,
    host: process.env.DB_HOST,
    database: process.env.DB_DATABASE,
    password: process.env.DB_PASSWORD,
    port: process.env.DB_PORT,
});

// Middleware to get a client, set tenant_id, and release
async function withTenantDbClient(req, res, next) {
    const client = await pool.connect();
    try {
        const tenantId = req.tenantId; // tenantId set by previous middleware
        if (!tenantId) {
            return res.status(401).json({ message: 'Tenant ID is missing' });
        }

        // Set the session-local app.tenant_id variable
        await client.query("SET LOCAL app.tenant_id = $1", [tenantId]);
        req.dbClient = client; // Attach client to request object
        next();
    } catch (error) {
        console.error('Error setting tenant_id or getting DB client:', error);
        res.status(500).json({ message: 'Database error' });
    } finally {
        // The client must be released after the request is complete
        // This will be handled in a final middleware or route handler
    }
}

module.exports = { pool, withTenantDbClient };

Now, create src/index.js for our Express application. We'll implement a simple middleware to extract the tenant ID (from a header for this example, but could be from a JWT) and then use withTenantDbClient.

// src/index.js
const express = require('express');
const { pool, withTenantDbClient } = require('./db');

const app = express();
const PORT = process.env.PORT || 3000;

app.use(express.json());

// Middleware to extract tenant ID (e.g., from X-Tenant-Id header or JWT)
app.use((req, res, next) => {
    // In a real application, this would come from an authenticated JWT token
    // For demonstration, we'll use a custom header.
    // Make sure the tenantId provided corresponds to an actual tenant in your 'tenants' table.
    const tenantId = req.headers['x-tenant-id'];
    if (!tenantId) {
        return res.status(400).json({ message: 'X-Tenant-Id header is required.' });
    }
    req.tenantId = tenantId;
    next();
});

// Apply the tenant database client middleware to routes that require RLS
app.use('/api', withTenantDbClient);

// Release the database client after each request
app.use((req, res, next) => {
    res.on('finish', () => {
        if (req.dbClient) {
            req.dbClient.release();
            // console.log('DB client released.'); // For debugging
        }
    });
    next();
});

// --- API Routes ---

// Get all products for the current tenant
app.get('/api/products', async (req, res) => {
    try {
        const { rows } = await req.dbClient.query('SELECT id, name, description, price FROM products');
        res.json(rows);
    } catch (error) {
        console.error('Error fetching products:', error);
        res.status(500).json({ message: 'Failed to fetch products' });
    }
});

// Create a new product for the current tenant
app.post('/api/products', async (req, res) => {
    try {
        const { name, description, price } = req.body;
        if (!name || !price) {
            return res.status(400).json({ message: 'Name and price are required.' });
        }
        // tenant_id is automatically added by RLS policy if not explicitly provided and policy allows
        // However, it's good practice to explicitly include it or rely on the RLS INSERT policy
        // For simplicity, here we let RLS handle it from current_setting('app.tenant_id') for INSERT
        const { rows } = await req.dbClient.query(
            'INSERT INTO products (tenant_id, name, description, price) VALUES (current_setting(\'app.tenant_id\')::UUID, $1, $2, $3) RETURNING id, name, description, price',
            [name, description, price]
        );
        res.status(201).json(rows[0]);
    } catch (error) {
        console.error('Error creating product:', error);
        res.status(500).json({ message: 'Failed to create product' });
    }
});

// Get a specific product by ID for the current tenant
app.get('/api/products/:id', async (req, res) => {
    try {
        const { id } = req.params;
        const { rows } = await req.dbClient.query(
            'SELECT id, name, description, price FROM products WHERE id = $1',
            [id]
        );
        if (rows.length === 0) {
            return res.status(404).json({ message: 'Product not found or not accessible.' });
        }
        res.json(rows[0]);
    } catch (error) {
        console.error('Error fetching product by ID:', error);
        res.status(500).json({ message: 'Failed to fetch product' });
    }
});

// Get all users for the current tenant
app.get('/api/users', async (req, res) => {
    try {
        const { rows } = await req.dbClient.query('SELECT id, email FROM users');
        res.json(rows);
    } catch (error) {
        console.error('Error fetching users:', error);
        res.status(500).json({ message: 'Failed to fetch users' });
    }
});

// Start the server
app.listen(PORT, () => {
    console.log(`Server running on port ${PORT}`);
    console.log('Test with curl, e.g.:');
    console.log('curl -H "X-Tenant-Id: " http://localhost:3000/api/products');
});

process.on('SIGINT', async () => {
    console.log('Shutting down...');
    await pool.end();
    console.log('Database pool closed.');
    process.exit(0);
});

To test, first get the UUIDs for your tenants from the tenants table:

SELECT id, name FROM tenants;

Then, you can use curl:

# For Acme Corp
curl -H "X-Tenant-Id: YOUR_ACME_CORP_UUID" http://localhost:3000/api/products

# For Globex Inc.
curl -H "X-Tenant-Id: YOUR_GLOBEX_INC_UUID" http://localhost:3000/api/products

# Attempt to access without tenant ID (should fail)
curl http://localhost:3000/api/products

You will observe that queries for products or users will only return data belonging to the tenant_id specified in the X-Tenant-Id header, thanks to PostgreSQL's RLS. If you try to create a product, it will automatically be associated with the tenant ID from the session variable.

Optimization & Best Practices

Implementing RLS effectively requires attention to several details:

Performance Considerations

  • Indexing: Ensure that the tenant_id column in all RLS-enabled tables is indexed. This is crucial for query performance, as every query will implicitly filter by tenant_id.
  • RLS Policy Complexity: Keep RLS policies as simple as possible. Complex policies can add overhead. If a table has very specific, varying access rules, consider if a different architectural pattern might be more suitable or if you can simplify the RLS conditions.
  • Query Plan Analysis: Regularly use EXPLAIN ANALYZE on your queries to understand how RLS policies affect their execution plans. Identify and optimize any bottlenecks.

Security Best Practices

  • Tenant ID Validation: Always validate the incoming tenant_id against your actual list of active tenants in the tenants table. While RLS prevents cross-tenant data access, ensuring a valid tenant ID prevents unnecessary database lookups or potential attacks where a malicious actor tries to guess valid UUIDs.
  • Authentication & Authorization: The tenant ID should always be derived from a secure, authenticated source (e.g., a signed JWT token after a user logs in). Never trust a raw header from an unauthenticated request.
  • Principle of Least Privilege: Grant your application's database user (saas_user in our example) only the necessary permissions. Avoid giving it superuser or administrative roles. RLS operates regardless of the user's role, but overall security relies on this principle.
  • Secure Coding Practices: Always use parameterized queries to prevent SQL injection, even when setting session variables like app.tenant_id.

Schema Design

  • Shared vs. Tenant-Specific Data: Not all data needs to be RLS-protected. Global data (e.g., system configurations, public listings) can exist in tables without RLS, while sensitive tenant-specific data requires it. Clearly define which tables fall into which category.
  • Foreign Keys: When establishing foreign key relationships between RLS-protected tables, ensure that the tenant_id is part of the foreign key constraint if it's a composite key, or that the foreign key column itself is also filtered by RLS policies if it references an RLS-protected primary key.

Operational Considerations

  • Tenant Provisioning: Automate the creation of new tenants in the tenants table. This should be part of your SaaS onboarding workflow.
  • Monitoring: Monitor PostgreSQL logs for RLS-related warnings or errors to quickly identify any misconfigurations or potential breaches.

Business Impact & ROI

Implementing multi-tenancy with Node.js and PostgreSQL RLS delivers substantial business value and a strong return on investment (ROI):

  • Significant Cost Reduction: By sharing a single database instance across multiple tenants, you drastically reduce infrastructure costs compared to provisioning a separate database for each customer. This translates directly to higher profit margins or more competitive pricing for your SaaS.
  • Enhanced Security & Compliance: RLS provides a robust, database-enforced layer of data isolation. This significantly mitigates the risk of data leaks and simplifies compliance with regulations like GDPR, HIPAA, or SOC 2, which demand strict separation of customer data. This builds trust with your enterprise clients.
  • Faster Time-to-Market: A standardized and secure multi-tenant architecture allows you to onboard new customers more rapidly. You don't need to spin up new database instances or adjust complex schemas for each client, accelerating your sales cycle and growth.
  • Simplified Operations & Maintenance: Managing a single, well-optimized PostgreSQL instance is far simpler than juggling dozens or hundreds of disparate databases. This reduces the burden on your DevOps team, freeing them to focus on innovation rather than maintenance.
  • Improved Scalability: Your Node.js application can scale horizontally by adding more instances, while PostgreSQL can be scaled vertically or through advanced techniques like read replicas. The RLS approach does not impede database scaling and supports a growing number of tenants efficiently.
  • Reduced Developer Overhead: Developers can write cleaner, more focused queries without needing to manually add WHERE tenant_id = '...' clauses everywhere, reducing the chances of human error and improving code maintainability. The database handles the critical security aspect.

In essence, this architectural pattern not only solves a complex technical challenge but directly contributes to the financial health, security posture, and competitive advantage of your SaaS product.

Conclusion

The journey of building a scalable and secure SaaS application inevitably leads to the critical decision of how to manage multi-tenancy. Relying solely on application-level logic for data isolation is a precarious path fraught with security risks and operational complexity. By harnessing the power of Node.js in conjunction with PostgreSQL's Row-Level Security, we've demonstrated a robust, efficient, and highly secure architectural pattern.

This approach centralizes data isolation directly within the database, providing an impenetrable barrier between tenants' data. It offers significant advantages: substantial cost savings through shared infrastructure, a drastically improved security posture that simplifies compliance efforts, and streamlined operational workflows that allow your team to focus on feature development rather than database management. For any SaaS architect or developer seeking to build a resilient, scalable, and secure platform, adopting PostgreSQL RLS is not just an option, but a strategic imperative that delivers clear, tangible ROI. Embrace this pattern to empower your SaaS to grow securely and efficiently in today's demanding market. Your clients, and your bottom line, will thank you.

title: Schneider's modular AI design: what the 80% installation-time claim actually measures
description:
Schneider Electric announced RapidScale Modular Data Center Reference Design 115 on October 21, positioning it as a prefabricated blueprint supporting NVIDIA Vera Rubin infrastructure. The announcement also highlights an installation-time study with Compass Datacenters. For project teams, the study's boundaries matter as much as the percentage.

In its October 20 explanation of the work, Schneider reports a reduction from 75.5 to 15 hours per pod, approximately 80%, for the configuration analyzed. The comparison covers onsite activities preparing a pod for IT equipment installation.

The prefabricated durations were observed during a Compass deployment. The traditional comparison combines observed containment-installation durations with schedules developed by mechanical, electrical and plumbing specialists for equivalent additional infrastructure. Offsite manufacturing and activities after installation verification are excluded.

This is a supplier-and-customer study with a defined comparison, rather than an independently reproduced result or a measurement of total campus delivery time.

Operational analysis: put the saved activity on the project schedule

Before using the result in a business case, identify where the comparable work sits in your own programme. Does it delay the start of equipment installation, or can it already happen while another team completes a different dependency?

A shorter task affects the overall completion date when it removes time from the sequence that governs completion. If the project is waiting for another prerequisite, the benefit may instead be lower coordination pressure, additional schedule margin or earlier availability of one work area.

Those can be worthwhile outcomes. They should have their own evidence and cost assumptions.

I would ask the delivery team to show the baseline sequence and the prefabricated sequence side by side, with the same start and finish conditions. Then identify which dependencies changed and which remained. Keep the estimate of onsite installation savings separate from the forecast date for usable compute.

Include the work that moves upstream

Prefabrication creates a different allocation of work between factory and site. A complete procurement comparison should therefore track the manufacturing slot, design freeze, inspection records, transport and site receiving arrangements alongside field installation.

For each major interface, name the party responsible for confirming that the delivered assembly matches the receiving site. Record the approved dimensions, connection locations and configuration version. Changes made after those decisions need a visible route through manufacturing, logistics and site teams.

The purpose is to understand whether work has been removed, performed earlier or transferred to another organization. Each outcome has different implications for risk, staffing and cash flow.

Receiving a larger assembly also deserves a practical plan. Confirm access, staging space, lifting arrangements and the sequence in which work areas become available. These are proposed project checks, not allegations about the deployment studied.

Keep commissioning in the acceptance criteria

Schneider's technical explanation says the complete technology-cooling loop still requires final onsite flushing, pressure testing and commissioning, even where sections receive factory treatment and tests.

For a buyer, that is a useful prompt to define the handover boundary precisely. Request a list of factory checks, field checks and integrated acceptance tests, with an owner and retained record for each. Explain how shipping damage, field connections or a late configuration change affects the test plan.

The acceptance package should show what was verified and under which conditions. An assembly arriving with inspection records can reduce uncertainty, while the connected installation still needs evidence that its interfaces behave as intended.

Ask for a comparable result on your configuration

The reported comparison is a starting point for questions about a specific project. Ask which parts of your proposed configuration match the study and which require additional work. Require the estimate to name exclusions, site assumptions and the experience expected of the installation team.

Then agree how actual durations will be recorded. Distinguish elapsed time from labour effort, and record waiting time separately where it matters. That makes later comparisons more useful and helps the team locate the next constraint.

The new reference design and the study address related questions at different levels. One offers an infrastructure blueprint; the other quantifies a bounded installation comparison. Operators can use both most effectively when they connect them to a complete delivery schedule and explicit acceptance evidence.

title: Build a Highly Available App with ALB and Auto Scaling
description:
By Vishal Patil | #vishalcloudjourney

If your app runs on a single EC2 instance, you have a single point of failure. If that instance crashes, or its Availability Zone has a problem, your app goes down with it. In this hands-on guide, I'll show you how to fix that by combining an Application Load Balancer (ALB) with an Auto Scaling Group (ASG), so your app spreads across multiple Availability Zones, heals itself, and scales with demand.

What You Will Build

  • A VPC with two public subnets in two different Availability Zones
  • A Launch Template that boots a simple web server
  • An Application Load Balancer that distributes traffic
  • An Auto Scaling Group that keeps at least 2 healthy instances running
  • A scaling policy that adds instances when CPU gets high

Traffic flow:

User → ALB (spans AZ-a and AZ-b) → Target Group → EC2 instances managed by ASG (AZ-a, AZ-b)

Key Concepts in 60 Seconds

  • Application Load Balancer (ALB): Receives incoming HTTP/HTTPS traffic and routes it to healthy targets.
  • Target Group: The list of instances the ALB sends traffic to, plus the health check settings.
  • Launch Template: A blueprint for instances (AMI, instance type, security group, user data).
  • Auto Scaling Group (ASG): Launches, replaces, and removes instances to match your desired capacity.
  • High availability: Running across multiple AZs so one failure doesn't take you down.

Prerequisites

  • An AWS account with permissions to create EC2, ELB, and Auto Scaling resources
  • A VPC with at least two subnets in different AZs (the default VPC works for this lab)
  • Basic familiarity with the EC2 console

Cost note: The ALB and EC2 instances are billed while they run. Follow the cleanup section at the end so you don't leave resources running.

Step 1: Create the Security Groups

Use two security groups so only the load balancer can reach your instances.

ALB security group (alb-sg)

  • Inbound: HTTP (port 80) from 0.0.0.0/0

Instance security group (web-sg)

  • Inbound: HTTP (port 80) from alb-sg (select the security group as the source, not an IP range)

This is a good security habit: users can only reach your instances through the load balancer.

Step 2: Create a Launch Template

  1. Go to EC2 → Launch Templates → Create launch template.
  2. Name it web-lt.
  3. Choose Amazon Linux 2023 as the AMI.
  4. Choose a small instance type such as t3.micro (or t2.micro if that's what your Free Tier covers).
  5. Select web-sg as the security group.
  6. Under Advanced details → User data, paste this script: 
#!/bin/bash
dnf update -y
dnf install -y httpd
systemctl enable --now httpd

TOKEN=$(curl -s -X PUT "http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token" \
  -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 21600")
INSTANCE_ID=$(curl -s -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOKEN" \
  http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/instance-id)
AZ=$(curl -s -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOKEN" \
  http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/placement/availability-zone)

cat > /var/www/html/index.html <<EOF
<h1>Highly Available App</h1>
<p>Instance ID: $INSTANCE_ID</p>
<p>Availability Zone: $AZ</p>
EOF

This page shows which instance and AZ served your request, which makes load balancing easy to see later.

Step 3: Create the Target Group

  1. Go to EC2 → Target Groups → Create target group.
  2. Target type: Instances.
  3. Name: web-tg, Protocol: HTTP, Port: 80.
  4. Choose your VPC.
  5. Health check path: /.
  6. Create it without registering any targets. The ASG will register them automatically.

Step 4: Create the Application Load Balancer

  1. Go to EC2 → Load Balancers → Create load balancer → Application Load Balancer.
  2. Name: web-alb, Scheme: Internet-facing.
  3. Select your VPC and choose at least two subnets in different AZs.
  4. Security group: alb-sg.
  5. Listener: HTTP : 80, forward to web-tg.
  6. Create the load balancer and copy its DNS name for testing later.

Step 5: Create the Auto Scaling Group

  1. Go to EC2 → Auto Scaling Groups → Create Auto Scaling group.
  2. Name: web-asg, select the web-lt launch template.
  3. Choose your VPC and select the same two subnets across different AZs.
  4. Under load balancing, choose Attach to an existing load balancer and select the web-tg target group.
  5. Under health checks, turn on ELB health checks. This lets the ASG replace instances the ALB marks unhealthy, not only ones that fail EC2 status checks.
  6. Set group size:
    • Desired capacity: 2
    • Minimum capacity: 2
    • Maximum capacity: 4
  7. Under scaling policies, choose Target tracking scaling policy:
    • Metric type: Average CPU utilization
    • Target value: 50
  8. Create the Auto Scaling group.

Within a few minutes, two instances launch (one per AZ), register with the target group, and pass health checks.

Step 6: Test the Setup

Test load balancing

  1. Open the ALB DNS name in your browser.
  2. Refresh several times. You should see the Instance ID and AZ change, which proves traffic is being shared across instances and zones.

Test self-healing

  1. Go to EC2 → Instances and terminate one of the ASG instances.
  2. Keep refreshing the ALB URL. Your app keeps responding from the remaining instance.
  3. Watch the ASG launch a replacement automatically to get back to 2 instances.

Test scaling out

  1. Connect to one instance (EC2 Instance Connect or Session Manager).
  2. Install and run a CPU stress tool: 
   sudo dnf install -y stress-ng
   stress-ng --cpu 2 --timeout 300
  1. Watch CloudWatch or the ASG Activity tab. When average CPU stays above the target, the ASG adds instances up to the maximum of 4.
  2. After the load stops, it scales back in.

Common Issues and Fixes

Problem Likely cause Fix
Targets show unhealthy Instance SG doesn't allow traffic from the ALB SG Allow port 80 from alb-sg
ALB URL times out ALB SG blocks port 80 or ALB is in subnets without internet access Open port 80 on alb-sg and use public subnets
Page shows default or blank content User data didn't run Check /var/log/cloud-init-output.log on the instance
Instances keep getting replaced Health check path returns an error Make sure / returns HTTP 200
Scaling never triggers CPU not high enough or not long enough Increase the load or lower the target value

Production Tips

  • Put instances in private subnets and keep only the ALB public (use a NAT Gateway for outbound access).
  • Add an HTTPS listener with a certificate from AWS Certificate Manager.
  • Use a health check path like /health that verifies your app, not just the web server.
  • Set up CloudWatch alarms and SNS notifications for unhealthy host counts.
  • Define everything as code with CloudFormation or Terraform for repeatable deployments.

Clean Up

To avoid charges, delete in this order:

  1. Delete the Auto Scaling group (this terminates its instances)
  2. Delete the Application Load Balancer
  3. Delete the Target group
  4. Delete the Launch template
  5. Delete the Security groups (web-sg first, then alb-sg)

Conclusion

With an ALB and an Auto Scaling Group, you turned a fragile single server into an app that survives instance failures, spreads across Availability Zones, and scales with demand. This pattern is the foundation of most production web architectures on AWS, and a great skill to show in your cloud portfolio.

If you found this useful, let's connect and keep learning together.

Connect with me

  • LinkedIn: vishalpatil-devops-aws
  • dev.to: @vishal_patil_aws
  • GitHub: VishalPatil-DevOps-AWS

title: From Localhost to Production: Deploying Your Spring AI Agent
description:
Running an AI agent on your laptop is one thing. Putting it in front of real users is another. The agent itself doesn't change — but everything around it does.

API keys need to stay out of your code. Token costs add up fast if you're not watching. A slow model call that was fine during testing becomes a timeout in production. And when something goes wrong, you need logs that actually tell you what happened.

This article covers the practical side of shipping a Spring AI agent: secrets management, cost awareness, rate limiting, timeouts, and what to monitor once you're live.

The API key problem

During development, it's tempting to put your API key directly in application.properties:

spring.ai.openai.api-key=sk-proj-abc123...

Don't do this. That file gets committed to version control. The key leaks. You get a bill.

The right pattern: read the key from an environment variable.

spring.ai.openai.api-key=${OPENAI_API_KEY}

Now start the application with the key set in the environment:

export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-proj-abc123...
java -jar your-app.jar

On a cloud platform (Railway, Render, Fly.io, AWS), set this as a secret environment variable in the deployment settings — never in a config file that gets pushed.

What about local development? Use a .env file that is listed in .gitignore, and load it with a tool like direnv or just set the variable in your shell profile. Never commit .env.

Separating configuration by environment

Your app needs different settings in development vs production:

  • Dev: verbose logging, low timeouts, a small token limit so you don't burn through a quota while testing
  • Prod: tighter timeouts, higher token limits, structured logging

Spring Boot's profile system handles this cleanly.

src/main/resources/application.properties — shared defaults:

spring.ai.openai.api-key=${OPENAI_API_KEY}
app.agent.timeout-seconds=30
app.agent.max-tokens=2000

src/main/resources/application-dev.properties — development overrides:

logging.level.com.example=DEBUG
app.agent.timeout-seconds=60
app.agent.max-tokens=500

src/main/resources/application-prod.properties — production overrides:

logging.level.com.example=INFO
app.agent.timeout-seconds=20
app.agent.max-tokens=4000

Activate a profile at startup:

java -jar your-app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod

Your agent code reads these values without knowing which profile is active:

@Value("${app.agent.timeout-seconds}")
private int timeoutSeconds;

@Value("${app.agent.max-tokens}")
private int maxTokens;

Timeouts — set them everywhere

In development, a slow model call is annoying. In production, it blocks a thread, holds a connection, and can cascade into a full outage.

Set a timeout at every layer.

On the ChatClient call:

String response = CompletableFuture
    .supplyAsync(() -> chatClient.prompt()
        .user(request.message())
        .tools(travelTools)
        .call()
        .content())
    .get(timeoutSeconds, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

On the HTTP client Spring AI uses internally, you can configure it via properties:

spring.ai.openai.chat.options.timeout=20000

On your REST endpoint with Spring MVC:

@PostMapping("/chat")
@ResponseTimeout(20000)
public ResponseEntity<String> chat(@RequestBody ChatRequest request) {
    // ...
}

Pick one consistent timeout value and apply it everywhere. Thirty seconds is a reasonable ceiling for most agent calls. If your agent needs longer, it's probably doing too much in a single request — consider breaking it into smaller steps.

Token costs — what you're actually paying for

Every call to the model costs money based on tokens — roughly three-quarters of a word each. The bill comes from two places:

  • Input tokens: your system prompt + conversation history + the user's message + tool definitions
  • Output tokens: the model's response

Output tokens cost more than input tokens. A verbose system prompt that runs 500 tokens fires on every single request. Multiply by 10,000 users and it becomes significant.

Where token costs hide:

Source What it contains What to watch
System prompt Your instructions Keep it concise — every word fires on every call
Tool definitions @tool descriptions Long descriptions add up across many tools
Conversation history All prior messages Window size directly controls cost
Tool results What tools return Verbose JSON returns cost more than plain strings

How to track usage in Spring AI:

Every ChatResponse contains usage metadata:

ChatResponse chatResponse = chatClient.prompt()
    .user(request.message())
    .call()
    .chatResponse();

Usage usage = chatResponse.getMetadata().getUsage();
log.info("tokens — input: {}, output: {}, total: {}",
    usage.getPromptTokens(),
    usage.getGenerationTokens(),
    usage.getTotalTokens());

Log this on every production request. After a few days you'll see exactly where cost is coming from and whether it's growing as expected.

Rate limiting — protect yourself and the API

The model provider's API has rate limits — requests per minute and tokens per minute. Hit them and your app gets 429 errors.

Two problems to solve:

1. Protect against a single user hammering the API:

Use a simple in-memory rate limiter per user (or per IP if you don't have user identity):

@Component
public class RateLimiter {

    private final Map<String, AtomicInteger> callCount = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, Long> windowStart = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private static final int MAX_CALLS_PER_MINUTE = 10;

    public boolean allow(String userId) {
        long now = System.currentTimeMillis();
        long start = windowStart.computeIfAbsent(userId, k -> now);

        if (now - start > 60_000) {
            callCount.put(userId, new AtomicInteger(0));
            windowStart.put(userId, now);
        }

        return callCount.computeIfAbsent(userId, k -> new AtomicInteger(0))
                        .incrementAndGet() <= MAX_CALLS_PER_MINUTE;
    }
}

Check it in your controller:

if (!rateLimiter.allow(request.userId())) {
    return ResponseEntity.status(429)
        .body("Too many requests. Please wait a moment.");
}

2. Handle 429s from the provider gracefully:

try {
    return chatClient.prompt().user(message).call().content();
} catch (OpenAiHttpException e) {
    if (e.statusCode() == 429) {
        return "The service is busy right now. Please try again in a moment.";
    }
    throw e;
}

Never let a raw 429 surface to the user as a 500 error.

Retry with backoff — for transient failures

Model APIs have transient failures — brief network blips, occasional 500s. A single retry with a short wait handles most of them.

Spring Retry makes this straightforward:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.retry</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-retry</artifactId>
</dependency>

Enable it in your main class:

@EnableRetry
@SpringBootApplication
public class Application { ... }

Add retry to your agent call:

@Retryable(
    retryFor = { OpenAiHttpException.class },
    maxAttempts = 3,
    backoff = @Backoff(delay = 1000, multiplier = 2)
)
public String callAgent(String message) {
    return chatClient.prompt().user(message).call().content();
}

This retries up to 3 times, waiting 1s then 2s between attempts. It only retries OpenAiHttpException — not your own application errors.

Do not retry on 429 errors with short delays — you'll just accelerate into the rate limit. Retry on 500s and network errors only.

What to log in production

Good production logs answer: "What did the agent do, for whom, and how did it go?"

Minimum log fields on every agent request:

@PostMapping("/chat")
public ResponseEntity<String> chat(@RequestBody ChatRequest request) {
    String requestId = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
    long start = System.currentTimeMillis();

    log.info("[req:{}] agent call — userId={} conversationId={}",
        requestId, request.userId(), request.conversationId());

    try {
        String response = callAgent(request.message(), request.conversationId());
        long durationMs = System.currentTimeMillis() - start;

        log.info("[req:{}] agent complete — durationMs={} responseLength={}",
            requestId, durationMs, response.length());

        return ResponseEntity.ok(response);
    } catch (TimeoutException e) {
        log.warn("[req:{}] agent timeout after {}ms", requestId, timeoutSeconds * 1000);
        return ResponseEntity.status(504).body("Request timed out.");
    } catch (Exception e) {
        log.error("[req:{}] agent error — {}", requestId, e.getMessage(), e);
        return ResponseEntity.status(500).body("Something went wrong.");
    }
}

The requestId ties every log line for a single request together. The durationMs tells you if calls are getting slower over time. The error path always logs the full stack trace.

Health checks and readiness

Before a request reaches your agent, you want to know the application is healthy. Spring Boot Actuator gives you this for free:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>

management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info
management.endpoint.health.show-details=when-authorized

GET /actuator/health returns {"status":"UP"} when the app is running. Your deployment platform (Render, Railway, Kubernetes) pings this endpoint — if it returns anything other than UP, traffic stops going to that instance.

Add a custom health check that verifies your model API is reachable:

@Component
public class ModelApiHealthIndicator implements HealthIndicator {

    private final ChatModel chatModel;

    public ModelApiHealthIndicator(ChatModel chatModel) {
        this.chatModel = chatModel;
    }

    @Override
    public Health health() {
        try {
            chatModel.call(new Prompt("ping"));
            return Health.up().build();
        } catch (Exception e) {
            return Health.down()
                .withDetail("reason", e.getMessage())
                .build();
        }
    }
}

If the model API is down, your health check returns DOWN and the platform can route around the broken instance or alert you.

A deployment checklist

Before you ship:

Secrets

  • [ ] API key is in an environment variable, not in any committed file
  • [ ] .env is in .gitignore
  • [ ] No secrets appear in log output

Reliability

  • [ ] Every agent call has a timeout
  • [ ] 429 errors are caught and returned as readable messages
  • [ ] Transient errors have retry with backoff

Cost

  • [ ] Token usage is logged on every request
  • [ ] System prompt is as concise as possible
  • [ ] Conversation history window is bounded (chatHistoryWindowSize)

Observability

  • [ ] Every request gets a unique request ID
  • [ ] Duration is logged on every request
  • [ ] Errors log the full stack trace

Operations

  • [ ] Health check endpoint is configured
  • [ ] Logs go somewhere you can actually read them (not just stdout on a server you can't SSH into)

What's next

The agent is deployed and handling real traffic. The next question is scale — what happens when many users hit the agent at the same time, when conversation histories grow large, and when you need to update the model or tools without downtime.

Sham Prakash K — Backend Engineer, 4+ years in Java, Spring Boot, and distributed systems. Building AI backend infrastructure. Writing about what I actually learned, mistakes included.

title: API Calls: A Practical Guide
description:
TL;DR

  • An API call is a network transaction governed by standard HTTP specifications where a client exchanges structured messages with a remote server.
  • Robust client implementations require explicit timeout thresholds, idempotent retry policies, and truncated exponential backoff with jitter to survive network instability.
  • Generative AI workloads introduce distinct API call profiles characterized by persistent streaming connections, multi-second latencies, and token-based rate limits.
  • Bifrost, an open-source AI gateway written in Go by Maxim AI, standardizes API calls across multiple foundation model providers while adding automatic failover and sub-millisecond routing.

An API call is a structured network request sent from a client to a server over Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) to query, create, modify, or delete a remote resource. Modern software architectures rely on API calls to connect frontend interfaces to backends, decouple distributed microservices, and integrate third-party services such as payment processors and foundation model providers. Managing these network boundaries reliably requires an understanding of transport protocols, HTTP semantics, authentication standards, and error-recovery patterns. Infrastructure tools such as Bifrost help engineering teams orchestrate, govern, and observe high-volume API calls across complex multi-provider environments.

What Happens During an API Call: The Request-Response Lifecycle

An API call executes as a sequence of transport and application-layer operations that establish connectivity, authenticate identity, deliver structured data, and return a parsed response. The entire exchange follows standard client-server semantics defined by the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) in RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics.

Before any HTTP payload traverses the wire, the client resolves the domain name into an IP address using the Domain Name System (DNS). Once the IP address is known, the client establishes a Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) connection via a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK). If the connection uses Transport Layer Security (TLS), as is standard for HTTPS, client and server negotiate cryptographic parameters, verify server identity certificates, and exchange session keys.

Client                                                  Server
  |                                                       |
  |--- 1. DNS Resolution -------------------------------->|
  |--- 2. TCP Handshake (SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK) --------->|
  |--- 3. TLS Negotiation (Key Exchange, Certificate) --->|
  |--- 4. HTTP Request (Method, Headers, Body) ---------->|
  |                                                       | [Processing]
  |<-- 5. HTTP Response (Status Code, Headers, Body) -----|
  |                                                       |

After the encrypted transport tunnel is open, the client transmits an HTTP request message composed of a method, request target (URI), header fields, and an optional message body. The server processes the request, evaluates permissions, interacts with data stores or downstream services, and sends back an HTTP response message containing a status code, response headers, and response payload.

Anatomy of an HTTP API Request

Every HTTP API call consists of distinct structural components defined by standardized wire formats: the HTTP method, uniform resource identifier (URI), request headers, and request body.

HTTP Methods and Idempotency

HTTP methods indicate the desired action to be performed on the identified resource. RFC 9110 Section 9 categorizes methods by safety and idempotency:

  • Safe Methods: Methods that do not alter server state. GET and HEAD must only retrieve representations without modifying underlying data.
  • Idempotent Methods: Methods where multiple identical requests produce the same server-side outcome as a single request. GET, PUT, DELETE, and HEAD are idempotent. If a network timeout occurs during a PUT operation, the client can safely retransmit the request.
  • Non-Idempotent Methods: Methods where repeated requests create additional state transitions. POST and PATCH are typically non-idempotent. Retrying an unacknowledged POST request without an idempotency key can cause duplicate operations, such as double-charging a credit card.
Method Safe Idempotent Request Body Primary Use Case
GET Yes Yes Disallowed/No Semantics Retrieve a resource representation
POST No No Yes Create subordinate resources or run commands
PUT No Yes Yes Replace an entire resource or create if absent
PATCH No No Yes Apply partial modifications to a resource
DELETE No Yes Optional Remove the identified resource
HEAD Yes Yes No Retrieve headers identical to a GET

Headers and Content Negotiation

Headers are key-value pairs that convey operational metadata about the request context, client capabilities, authentication credentials, and body encoding. Key standardized headers include:

  • Host: Identifies the target domain and port number of the server.
  • Content-Type: Declares the MIME type of the accompanying request body (e.g., application/json).
  • Accept: Tells the server which media types the client can process in the response.
  • User-Agent: Identifies the client software originating the request. 
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/orders \
  -H "Host: api.example.com" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sec_tok_9942a" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: 7b9a5e82-411a-4dc2-b883-93d3b76a0841" \
  -d '{"item_id": "sku-2041", "quantity": 2}'

Authentication and Security Controls

Production API endpoints require verifiable authentication to establish client identity and enforce authorization boundaries. Applications employ three primary authentication mechanisms:

  1. API Keys: Unique alphanumeric strings transmitted via headers (e.g., X-API-Key: value) or query parameters. While simple to implement, static API keys lack granular scoping and cannot expire automatically without client rotation.
  2. Bearer Tokens (OAuth 2.0 and JWT): Short-lived cryptographic tokens transmitted in the Authorization header (Authorization: Bearer <token>). JSON Web Tokens (JWT) contain digitally signed claims that upstream servers can validate statelessly without querying a centralized database for every request.
  3. Mutual TLS (mTLS): A zero-trust security architecture where both client and server present and verify X.509 digital certificates during the initial TLS handshake, establishing bidirectional cryptographic identity verification.

Credentials must never be hardcoded in application repositories. Production codebases inject API secrets at runtime using environment variables, cloud secret managers, or credential injection systems.

Parsing Responses and Interpreting Status Codes

The server answers every API call with an HTTP status code grouped into five functional classes:

  • 1xx (Informational): Request received, continuing process (e.g., 101 Switching Protocols).
  • 2xx (Successful): The request was received, understood, and accepted.
    • 200 OK: Standard response for successful requests.
    • 201 Created: The request succeeded and a new resource was provisioned.
    • 204 No Content: The action succeeded, but no body payload is returned.
  • 3xx (Redirection): Further action needed to complete the request (e.g., 301 Moved Permanently, 304 Not Modified).
  • 4xx (Client Error): The request contains bad syntax or cannot be fulfilled.
    • 400 Bad Request: Malformed syntax or invalid parameters.
    • 401 Unauthorized: Missing or invalid authentication credentials.
    • 403 Forbidden: Authenticated identity lacks permission for the resource.
    • 404 Not Found: Target resource does not exist.
    • 422 Unprocessable Entity: Syntactically correct payload contains semantic validation errors.
    • 429 Too Many Requests: Client has exceeded rate limit thresholds.
  • 5xx (Server Error): The server failed to fulfill an apparently valid request.
    • 500 Internal Server Error: Generic unhandled failure on the server.
    • 502 Bad Gateway: Gateway or proxy received an invalid response from an upstream server.
    • 503 Service Unavailable: Server is temporarily overloaded or undergoing maintenance.
    • 504 Gateway Timeout: Gateway or proxy did not receive a timely response from upstream.

Client libraries such as JavaScript's native Fetch API resolve promises even on 4xx and 5xx errors; client applications must explicitly check the response.ok property before parsing JSON bodies:

async function executeApiCall(url, payload) {
  const response = await fetch(url, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      "Authorization": `Bearer ${process.env.API_SECRET_KEY}`
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(payload)
  });

  if (!response.ok) {
    const errorBody = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`HTTP Error ${response.status}: ${errorBody}`);
  }

  return await response.json();
}

Rate Limiting, Retries, and Backoff Strategies

Rate limiting protects servers from resource exhaustion and enforces tiered billing plans. When a client exceeds allowable volume, the server responds with status code 429 Too Many Requests, as specified in RFC 6585: Additional HTTP Status Codes.

Parsing Rate Limit Headers

Standards-compliant APIs communicate quota details in response headers:

  • Retry-After: Indicates how many seconds to wait (or provides a UTC date timestamp) before issuing the next attempt.
  • RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining, RateLimit-Reset: Standard draft headers detailing quota ceilings, remaining request allowances, and reset epochs.

Truncated Exponential Backoff with Jitter

Retrying failed requests instantly creates a thundering herd problem that overwhelms recovering services. Clients must apply exponential backoff combined with randomized jitter. Exponential backoff multiplies the wait duration exponentially across successive retry cycles, while jitter decorrelates concurrent retries across distributed clients:

$$t_{\text{wait}} = \min(t_{\text{max}}, t_{\text{base}} \times 2^{\text{attempt}}) \times \text{random}(0.5, 1.5)$$

import time
import random
import requests

def call_with_backoff(url, headers, payload, max_retries=5):
    base_delay = 1.0  # seconds
    max_delay = 32.0  # seconds

    for attempt in range(max_retries):
        response = requests.post(url, headers=headers, json=payload, timeout=10)

        if response.status_code == 200:
            return response.json()

        # Retry only on transient errors: 429 or 5xx
        if response.status_code in [429, 500, 502, 503, 504]:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            if retry_after and retry_after.isdigit():
                delay = float(retry_after)
            else:
                calculated = min(max_delay, base_delay * (2 ** attempt))
                delay = calculated * random.uniform(0.5, 1.5)

            time.sleep(delay)
            continue

        # Fail fast on non-retryable 4xx errors
        response.raise_for_status()

    raise RuntimeError("Exceeded maximum retry attempts.")

Managing Modern AI and LLM API Calls at Scale

Modern applications increasingly interact with generative AI APIs, such as those provided by OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Vertex AI, and AWS Bedrock. While these services expose HTTP interfaces, their operational profiles deviate significantly from standard CRUD REST APIs:

  1. Unpredictable Latencies: Traditional APIs respond within 50 to 200 milliseconds. Large language model (LLM) API calls frequently take 3 to 60 seconds depending on context lengths and reasoning parameters.
  2. Streaming Protocols: Rather than returning a single payload, LLM providers stream output incrementally using Server-Sent Events (SSE) over persistent HTTP connections.
  3. Compound Quotas: Providers throttle both requests per minute (RPM) and tokens per minute (TPM). An application can exhaust its token quota within three large prompt requests despite staying far below RPM thresholds.
  4. Provider-Specific Schemas: Disparate providers require different payload envelopes, authentication schemes, and parameter names. 
Client App ---> AI Gateway (Bifrost) ---> OpenAI (Primary)
                      |
                      +-- [If 429 / 5xx] -> Anthropic (Fallback)
                      |
                      +-- [If Cached] ----> Cache Store (Sub-millisecond)

To eliminate point-to-point coupling, platform teams route AI calls through dedicated infrastructure layers. Bifrost serves as a unified control plane for model traffic. Built in Go, Bifrost functions as a high-performance gateway that adds only 11 microseconds of overhead at 5,000 requests per second, as documented in published benchmarks.

Instead of embedding multi-SDK configurations inside client code, teams use Bifrost as a drop-in replacement for OpenAI-compatible endpoints. Bifrost handles:

  • Automatic Failovers and Model Routing: If an upstream provider returns a 429 or 503 status code, automatic fallbacks seamlessly reroute the API call to an alternate provider or secondary region without throwing an unhandled exception to the calling service.
  • Semantic Caching: Traditional HTTP caching relies on exact URL and header matches under RFC 9111: HTTP Caching. Bifrost implements semantic caching, evaluating embedding vector similarities to return cached completions for semantically identical prompts, cutting token expenditures and latency.
  • Virtual Key Governance: Centralized virtual keys enforce spending ceilings, rate limits, and access controls across internal teams without distributing master provider credentials.

Endpoint AI Governance and Developer Workstations

While backend services route API calls through centralized gateways, an increasing volume of API transactions originates on local employee hardware. Software engineers run terminal coding agents (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI), IDE integrations (Cursor), desktop applications, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool servers.

When local workstations send unmonitored API calls directly to external provider endpoints using personal or unmonitored credentials, security teams encounter shadow AI: sensitive source code, customer records, and internal credentials flow outside the perimeter without policy checks or audit logging.

Beyond routing, Bifrost applies governance and security controls (virtual keys, budgets, guardrails, audit logs) centrally, and Bifrost Edge extends that same governance and security to AI traffic on employee machines, with endpoint enforcement on each device.

Operating as an endpoint agent across macOS, Windows, and Linux, Bifrost Edge runs in alpha and deploys silently through standard Mobile Device Management (MDM) platforms such as Jamf and Microsoft Intune via MDM deployment profiles. The agent provides:

  • App Governance: Fleet administrators manage app governance policies, permitting approved developer tools while intercepting unauthorized AI applications before requests leave the local system.
  • MCP Tool Governance: Through MCP governance, the agent discovers local MCP servers configured across tools like Claude Desktop or Cursor, enabling security teams to audit and selectively block dangerous local system integrations.
  • Zero-Config Developer Experience: Developers authenticate once via enterprise Single Sign-On (SSO). The endpoint agent transparently maps local traffic to the organization's Bifrost deployment without requiring manual configuration of proxy URLs or base paths in individual tools.

Production Reliability Checklist for API Calls

To maintain high availability across distributed systems, verify that every client-side API implementation satisfies these operational requirements:

Dimension Risk Mitigated Implementation Standard
Explicit Timeouts Thread pool exhaustion Define separate connect (e.g., 2s) and read (e.g., 10s) timeout limits on all network requests.
Connection Pooling Socket exhaustion / TLS handshake latency Reuse persistent HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 keep-alive connections via pooled HTTP clients.
Idempotency Keys Duplicate writes during retries Send unique UUIDs in the Idempotency-Key header on mutating POST operations.
Circuit Breakers Cascading failure across dependencies Halt outbound calls after a defined failure rate threshold to allow upstream recovery.
Telemetry & Tracing Invisible failures and latency anomalies Propagate W3C Trace Context headers (traceparent) for end-to-end distributed observability.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between an API call and an HTTP request?

An HTTP request is the network-level message formatted according to HTTP protocol specifications. An API call is the broader architectural transaction where a client uses an HTTP request to invoke a specific programmatic interface, function, or service on a remote system and receive structured data in return.

Why should GET requests never include a request body?

Under RFC 9110 Section 9.3.1, GET requests have no defined semantics for payload bodies. Many caching proxies, gateways, and web servers either drop the body entirely or reject the request outright, making request bodies in GET calls unreliable across internet infrastructure.

What should an application do when receiving a 429 Too Many Requests response?

The application must halt outbound calls to that specific service, inspect the response for a Retry-After header, and wait for the specified period before retrying. If no header is present, the client should apply truncated exponential backoff with randomized jitter before attempting another request.

How does an AI gateway improve API call reliability?

An AI gateway decouples client applications from upstream provider instability. It unifies disparate provider schemas under a single interface, balances loads across multiple API keys, intercepts transient 429/5xx errors, and automatically routes failed requests to functional fallback models without interrupting user sessions.

How do token-based rate limits differ from standard request rate limits?

Standard rate limits measure the absolute count of HTTP requests over a fixed time window (e.g., 100 requests per minute). Token-based rate limits track the cumulative volume of text tokens processed across both prompt inputs and model completions, meaning a single large request can exhaust an organization's entire throughput allocation.

What security risks are associated with shadow AI API calls?

When employees use personal API keys or unmonitored desktop AI tools, proprietary codebases and sensitive enterprise data bypass corporate data loss prevention (DLP) systems, guardrails, and audit logs. This ungoverned traffic exposes organizations to data leakage, compliance violations, and unpredictable third-party data retention policies.

Getting Started

Building robust software requires rigorous handling of API calls across transport boundaries, error states, and rate limits. As software architectures integrate foundation models alongside traditional web services, centralized routing and endpoint governance become essential infrastructure requirements. Teams evaluating AI infrastructure can request a Bifrost demo or inspect the open-source repository to standardize model traffic across production systems and developer endpoints.

Sources

  • RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics (IETF Standard)
  • RFC 6585: Additional HTTP Status Codes (IETF Standard)
  • RFC 9111: HTTP Caching (IETF Standard)
  • MDN Web Docs: Using the Fetch API

title: Building a Backend for My Old Furniture Store
description:
A few years ago, I started a side project: a storefront that lists furniture for prospective customers. It was my first time understanding how a CMS works under the hood, so I decided to learn Sanity with it. I remember trying to understand GROQ queries and how all of it worked. I got there, and I built the storefront.

Then years went by.

Recently I decided to understand how the backend part of applications works. This was another friction moment. As a frontend engineer, I was used to consuming backend APIs, but I didn't really understand how they worked. So I went back to the furniture store and built a backend for it with NestJS and Postgres. Lo and behold, I found my way around.

This post walks through what I built, flow by flow: auth, cart, orders, and payments.

The mental model that helped

One mental model made everything click: build the logic from services up to controllers.

  • Services hold the core logic: creating a user, adding to a cart, placing an order.
  • Controllers set up the routes for those services. These are what I always saw as endpoints from the frontend side.

So when my frontend calls POST /auth/register, a controller receives the request and hands it to a service, which does the actual work. For years I only saw the endpoint. Now I know what sits behind it.

The new terms

Around services and controllers, NestJS has a few more pieces I had to learn.

  • Modules group everything for one feature: the auth module holds auth's controller, service, and guards.
  • Imports bring in other modules a module depends on. My auth module imports the users module and the JWT config module, because auth needs both.
  • Exports make parts of a module available to other modules. I export the auth guards so other modules, like cart and orders, can protect their routes.
  • Providers are the classes NestJS creates and manages for you, like services.
  • Constructors are where a class asks for the providers it needs. NestJS sees what a service asks for in its constructor and passes it in. This is called dependency injection.
  • Guards run before a request reaches the controller and decide whether it's allowed through. My auth guard blocks any request without a valid token.

Auth: creating an account and logging in

The core logic lives in the auth folder.

Registration. I collect basic information about the user. The password is never stored as the user typed it. It's hashed, which is one-way: there's no key that turns a hash back into the password. Even if someone got access to the database, they couldn't read the passwords.

The way it clicked for me: hashing is like a blender. You can't un-blend the result, but the same ingredients always produce the same mush.

Login. Nothing gets decrypted. The backend hashes the password the user just typed, the same way it was hashed at registration, and compares the result to the stored hash. If they match, the password is correct.

Tokens. After login, the user gets an access token. It contains the user's ID and is signed with the server's secret key, so the backend can tell that it issued the token and nobody changed it. Access tokens are short-lived, so I also use refresh tokens. These are long-lived and let users stay logged in without signing in again every time the access token expires.

Cart

The cart module is where a user goes through the store listing and saves items. Users can add available items to their cart, edit a cart item, and delete it.

There's no product table in my database. Products still live in Sanity, so the backend fetches them from Sanity before building a cart. Postgres holds the cart, orders, and inventory; Sanity holds the catalog.

When adding to the cart: if the item is already there, update it. If it isn't, create it.

Prices also come from Sanity on the backend. Before an order is created, the backend computes the cart items and their total. The frontend never sends a price, so nobody can change it before paying.

Orders and reservations

The goal here: no two customers can pay for the same item, even under high traffic.

When a customer places an order, the backend reserves the items in the database. The reservation is kept for 15 minutes. If the user doesn't complete payment in that time, the order expires, a background job releases the reservation, and the items become available again.

The tricky part is the reservation itself. If I checked stock first and reserved it after, there'd be a gap where two users both see "1 left" and both reserve it. So I do both in one statement:

const reservedRows = await tx.$executeRaw`
  UPDATE "Inventory"
  SET reserved = reserved + ${item.quantity}
  WHERE "productId" = ${item.productId}
  AND quantity - reserved - sold >= ${item.quantity}
`;

if (reservedRows === 0) {
  throw new BadRequestException(`${item.productName} is out of stock`);
}

The UPDATE only succeeds if enough stock remains. When two requests hit the same row at the same moment, Postgres makes the second one wait. It then re-checks the condition against the updated row. If the first request took the last item, zero rows are updated and the second user gets "out of stock."

Available stock is quantity - reserved - sold. Reserving doesn't reduce quantity; it increases reserved.

All of this runs inside a database transaction, along with creating the order and its order items. Either everything succeeds or nothing does. If a cart has three items and the third is out of stock, the reservations for the first two are rolled back too.

The order also stores its total and each item's price at the moment it's created. If a price changes in Sanity later, it doesn't affect an order that's already being paid.

Payments with Paystack

Once an order is created, the user pays through Paystack's widget. Paystack is in test mode for this project.

Starting a payment. The request first goes through my auth guard. The backend then calls Paystack with my Paystack secret key as a Bearer token in the authorization header. That key only ever lives on the backend. One gotcha: Paystack takes amounts in kobo, not naira, so the total has to be multiplied by 100.

The webhook. This was the flip for me as a frontend engineer. Normally I call the API. With a webhook, Paystack calls my backend to tell me the payment's status.

The webhook doesn't use my auth guard, because Paystack can't log in as a user. Instead, Paystack signs each webhook with my secret key and sends the signature in the x-paystack-signature header. My backend recomputes the signature and compares. If it doesn't match, the request is rejected, so nobody can fake a successful payment.

Paystack sends back the transaction reference, which is the order ID I sent when initializing the payment. What happens next depends on the order's status:

  • Pending: process the payment.
  • Already paid, processing, shipped, or delivered: treat it as a duplicate webhook and ignore it. Paystack can send the same webhook more than once, and this makes sure an order is never processed twice. This is called idempotency.
  • Cancelled, expired, failed, or refunded, or the amount doesn't match the order total: log the payment, but don't touch the inventory, because the customer hasn't received value for this transaction.

If a customer actually paid for an expired order, their money was taken, so the payment is flagged for a refund. For now, refunds are done manually.

Updating the order. For a valid payment, all the updates run in one database transaction, so either everything succeeds or nothing does. The order status changes to paid, the reservation is released, the sold count goes up, the cart items are deleted, and a successful payment row is created.

Where it stands

The backend runs locally, with Paystack in test mode. Next, I'm connecting the furniture storefront to these APIs, then deploying it. After that, I want to add AI features to the store.

title: Building a Multi-Role Platform in Spring Boot: What Five User Types Do to Your Design.
description:
Notes from building FarmNomad - an AgriTech platform where farmers, customers, drivers, food banks, and admins all share one system.

The interesting constraint in my dissertation project wasn't any single feature. It was that the platform had five different kinds of user, and each one effectively wanted the system to be a different product.

A farmer wants an inventory tool. A customer wants a shop. A driver wants a task list. A food bank (an "organisation" in the code) wants a feed of claimable surplus. An admin wants oversight of all of it. Five mental models, one backend.

This is a writeup of the design decisions that came out of that, with real code from the project.

The domain, briefly

FarmNomad connects rural UK farmers to buyers, delivery drivers, and food banks. A large share of farm-level surplus in the UK goes to waste not for lack of demand, but for lack of a system that coordinates the parties involved.

So the backend has to handle several flows over the same data:

  • Agricultural e-commerce (farmer lists produce, customer buys).
  • Surplus (products near expiry or overstocked, surfaced for redistribution).
  • Donations (a farmer flags surplus, an organisation claims it, a delivery order is generated).
  • Delivery coordination (a driver moves goods, whether a paid order or a donation).

Same actors, same inventory, different rules. The design job is keeping those rules from tangling.

Decision one: bounded contexts, not one big service package

The default instinct with an MVP is a single Spring Boot app with everything in one service package. The thing that pushed me away from it was noticing how little the flows actually share. A farmer's inventory workflow and an organisation's claim workflow have almost nothing in common except the Product entity - different lifecycles, different permissions, different reasons to change.

So the backend is organised into modules along domain boundaries: authentication, catalogue, orders, donations, surplus, and payments. The practical payoff showed up when I added the surplus-detection logic late in the build, it didn't require touching the ordering or donation code at all. The seams were already in the right places.

Decision two: enforce roles at the method, not the UI

With five roles, it's tempting to hide buttons on the frontend and call that access control. It isn't anyone with a token and curl can hit the endpoints directly. Role enforcement has to live on the server.

I use Spring Security's @PreAuthorize on the controller methods, so the rule sits right on the operation it governs:

@PostMapping
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('CUSTOMER')")
public ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> placeOrder(Principal principal,
                                                @RequestBody OrderRequest req) { ... }

@PostMapping
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('FARMER')")
public ResponseEntity<SurplusResponse> createListing(Principal principal,
                                                     @RequestBody SurplusRequest req) { ... }

@PostMapping("/claim/{productId}")
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ORGANISATION')")
public ResponseEntity<Void> claimSurplus(@PathVariable Long productId,
                                         Principal principal) { ... }

@PatchMapping("/{orderId}/status")
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('DRIVER') or hasRole('ADMIN')")
public ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> updateStatus(Principal principal,
                                                  @PathVariable Long orderId,
                                                  @RequestParam OrderStatus status) { ... }

A nice consequence is testability: you can assert that a CUSTOMER token gets a 403 on a farmer-only endpoint without standing up the whole application.

Where the rule is more than "which role," I push it into the service. For example, a single order should only be visible to the customer who placed it, the driver assigned to it, or an admin so the controller allows any authenticated user in, and the service decides. Crucially, an unauthorised requester is told the order doesn't exist rather than that they're forbidden, so order IDs can't be probed:

boolean isAdmin    = requester.getRole() == Role.ADMIN;
boolean isCustomer = order.getCustomer() != null
        && order.getCustomer().getId().equals(requesterId);
boolean isDriver   = order.getDriver() != null
        && order.getDriver().getId().equals(requesterId);

if (!isAdmin && !isCustomer && !isDriver) {
    throw new BadRequestException("Order not found");
}

Decision three: make the order lifecycle explicit, and guard the transitions

Orders move through states PENDING → ASSIGNED → IN_TRANSIT → DELIVERED and the transitions that should be impossible matter more than the ones that should be allowed.

The one I care about most: a driver should never be assigned to an order that hasn't been paid. Without that guard, a race between the payment webhook and an admin clicking "assign" could put a driver on the road for an order that never actually paid. So the assignment path checks both the state and the payment status before it does anything:

public OrderResponse assignDriver(Long orderId, Long driverId) {
    Order o = orderRepo.findById(orderId)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new BadRequestException("Order not found"));

    if (o.getStatus() != OrderStatus.PENDING ||
            o.getPaymentStatus() != PaymentStatus.PAID) {
        throw new BadRequestException("Only paid, pending orders can be assigned");
    }

    User driver = userRepo.findById(driverId)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new BadRequestException("Driver not found"));
    o.setDriver(driver);
    o.setStatus(OrderStatus.ASSIGNED);
    o.setUpdatedAt(LocalDateTime.now());
    return toDto(orderRepo.save(o));
}

Keeping that rule in the service not in a controller, and certainly not only on the frontend means every path that assigns a driver is protected by the same check.

Decision four: two kinds of surplus, deliberately kept distinct

This one is a modelling choice I think is worth calling out. FarmNomad has surplus from two different sources, and they are not the same thing:

  • Auto-detected surplus - products that are near their best-before date or overstocked. This is derived at read time from the product data, not stored as its own rows.
  • A donation - a farmer explicitly flags a quantity of a product as surplus to give away; an organisation claims it; a delivery order is generated.

Early on it's tempting to collapse these into one concept. Keeping them separate turned out to be the right call, because they answer different questions. Auto-detected surplus is "what's at risk of going to waste right now?" A donation is "what has a farmer committed to give, and who's claiming it?" The donation flow even has a claim-and-order endpoint that claims the donation and spins up the delivery order in one step, which only makes sense because a donation is a concrete, stateful thing, where auto-detected surplus is a live view.

Decision five: idempotent payment webhooks

Payments go through Stripe Checkout, and Stripe delivers webhook events at least once so the checkout.session.completed handler has to be safe to run more than once for the same session. I key idempotency on the Stripe session ID: each order records the session that created it, and the handler short-circuits if that session was already processed.

String sessionId = minimalSession.getId();

// Stripe delivers at-least-once; the same event can arrive twice.
if (orderRepo.existsByStripeSessionId(sessionId)) {
    return ResponseEntity.ok("");   // already handled - exit quietly
}

I wrote this one up in more detail as its own post, because webhook idempotency is one of those things that's invisible in development and bites under real traffic.

The stack

Layer Choice
Backend Java, Spring Boot, Spring Security
Frontend React, Next.js, Redux Toolkit Query, TailwindCSS
Database PostgreSQL
Payments Stripe Checkout + Webhooks
Infra Docker, Vercel

As a solo developer building to a deadline, I leaned on modern tooling throughout the architecture, the modelling decisions, and the trade-offs above are mine; the tooling helped me move faster on everything around them.

FarmNomad is live at farmnomad.vercel.app, and it was built as the practical component of my MSc dissertation at the University of Greater Manchester, which was awarded a Distinction.

If you're building multi-role systems in Spring Boot, or working anywhere near AgriTech, I'd like to compare notes - LinkedIn or GitHub.
