title: The Definitive Guide to the Service Integration Bus
description:
TL;DR

  • A Service Integration Bus (SIB or SIBus) is a managed messaging infrastructure that provides asynchronous transport, publish/subscribe routing, and mediation across distributed application servers.
  • Bus members host messaging engines that manage persistent storage through database-backed data stores or filesystem-backed file stores.
  • Enterprise applications interact with the bus through Java Message Service (JMS) resources and Java EE Connector Architecture (JCA) activation specifications.
  • High availability relies on cluster coordination and active/standby failover governed by database-level lock tables such as SIBOWNER.
  • As architectures shift toward event streaming and AI workloads, modern infrastructure pairs asynchronous messaging foundations with centralized gateways for governance and protocol translation.

A Service Integration Bus (often abbreviated as SIB or SIBus) is an interconnected messaging infrastructure that provides asynchronous communication, message routing, and service mediation across distributed application servers. Originally popularized within enterprise Java platforms such as IBM WebSphere Application Server, the architecture decouples message producers from consumers by hosting intermediate message destinations inside a managed environment.

Production systems rely on asynchronous messaging to prevent cascading failures when downstream services experience latency spikes or transient outages. Modern enterprises frequently operate heterogeneous environments that blend traditional service integration topologies with modern API and AI gateways. Bifrost, an open-source AI gateway written in Go, reflects similar decoupling principles at the intelligence layer by unifying downstream model routing, load balancing, and failover across disparate providers. Understanding the fundamentals of the Service Integration Bus provides platform engineers and system architects with the conceptual foundation required to manage reliable, transactionally sound message topologies.

Core Architecture and Components of a Service Integration Bus

At its foundation, a Service Integration Bus consists of cooperating nodes inside a common management cell. Rather than requiring applications to establish point-to-point network connections with every remote consumer, the bus serves as a logical virtualization layer.

The architecture comprises four primary building blocks:

  1. Bus Members: An application server, server cluster, or external IBM MQ queue manager that has been explicitly added to the bus definition. Adding a member grants it the ability to host messaging components and store messages.
  2. Messaging Engines (MEs): The core runtime execution units hosted inside bus members. A messaging engine receives incoming payloads, serializes them, routes them across bus boundaries, and delivers them to attached subscribers or consumers. In a clustered bus member, messaging engines can run in active/standby configurations or operate concurrently across multiple servers.
  3. Destinations: The logical addresses to which applications transmit messages. Destinations are decoupled from physical addresses and include:
    • Queue Destinations: Point-to-point endpoints where a message is delivered to exactly one consumer.
    • Topic Spaces: Publish/subscribe endpoints supporting multiple subscribers with optional durable subscriptions.
    • Mediation Destinations: Intermediary destinations that route messages through transformation logic before forwarding them to their final destination.
    • Alias Destinations: Logical pointers that map an abstract destination name to another concrete bus destination.
  4. Message Stores: The persistence subsystem utilized by a messaging engine to maintain transactional state and ensure delivery guarantees.

The following table summarizes the structural distinctions between these core components:

Component Scope Primary Responsibility Failure Recovery Mode
Bus Member Server or Cluster Provides the compute environment and network identity for the bus. Handled by application server node management.
Messaging Engine Subsystem within Bus Member Processes message delivery, client connections, and transactions. Managed by High Availability Manager (HAManager) failover policies.
Queue Destination Logical Bus Resource Holds messages intended for a single receiver using FIFO or prioritized order. Stored on disk or database until acknowledged.
Topic Space Logical Bus Resource Dispatches copies of published events to all matching active or durable subscribers. Durable subscriptions persist across engine restarts.
Message Store Storage Subsystem Stores unconsumed persistent messages, transaction state, and lock metadata. Relies on relational ACID guarantees or journal file replay.

Message Persistence: Data Store vs. File Store

A messaging engine requires persistent storage to support guaranteed message delivery across restarts. The two standard implementations are:

  • Data Store (Relational Database): The messaging engine connects via a JDBC data source to a relational database (such as DB2, Oracle, PostgreSQL, or Microsoft SQL Server). The database maintains a dedicated schema containing seven internal tables:
    • SIBOWNER: Establishes exclusive engine ownership of the database schema via row-level locks.
    • SIBOWNERO: Used in auxiliary locking routines.
    • SIBCLASSMAP: Maps Java class types for serialized message payloads.
    • SIBLISTING: Catalogs the dynamic storage tables allocated for queues.
    • SIBXACTS: Tracks active two-phase commit (XA) transactions.
    • SIBKEYS: Allocates monotonically increasing identifiers for message tracking.
    • SIBnnn (such as SIB000, SIB001): The actual storage tables holding persistent and non-persistent message bodies.
  • File Store (Operating System Filesystem): The messaging engine writes directly to three binary files on a local or networked filesystem: a log file, a data file, and a metadata file. File stores provide lower latency and higher sequential throughput by eliminating relational database overhead, but they require shared storage mechanisms (such as NFSv4 or SAN) when configuring high-availability failover across distinct physical hosts.

Message Exchange Patterns and Transport Semantics

The Service Integration Bus supports multiple communication patterns designed to accommodate varying reliability and latency requirements.

+------------------+         +----------------------------+         +------------------+
| Message Producer | ------> |  Service Integration Bus   | ------> | Message Consumer |
|  (JMS Client)    |         |                            |         |      (MDB)       |
+------------------+         | +------------------------+ |         +------------------+
                             | | Messaging Engine (ME)  | |
                             | |                        | |
                             | |   [ Queue Point ]      | |
                             | |          |             | |
                             | |   [ Message Store ]    | |
                             | +------------------------+ |
                             +----------------------------+

Point-to-Point Messaging

In a point-to-point exchange, an application sends a message to a queue destination. The message is deposited on a specific queue point located on a messaging engine. The bus ensures that even if multiple consumers are listening concurrently on the same queue, only one consumer receives and acknowledges each message. This pattern provides horizontal scaling for background worker pools processing compute-heavy jobs.

Publish/Subscribe Messaging

Publish/subscribe messaging distributes events to multiple independent subscribers through a topic space. When a producer publishes to a topic hierarchy (such as orders/na/processed), the bus evaluates subscription filters and delivers identical copies to every matched subscriber. Subscriptions can be configured as non-durable (messages are delivered only while the consumer is connected) or durable (the messaging engine retains messages on behalf of disconnected clients until they reconnect).

Reliability Qualities of Service

The SIBus specification defines distinct reliability levels that dictate how messages survive system crashes:

  1. Best Effort Non-Persistent: Messages are held exclusively in volatile memory. If the hosting messaging engine terminates abnormally, messages are permanently lost. This level offers minimal latency for telemetry or heartbeat metrics.
  2. Express Non-Persistent: Messages are held in memory and discarded upon server shutdown, but the engine employs internal buffer optimizations to prevent memory starvation under high load.
  3. Reliable Non-Persistent: The bus guarantees delivery unless a failure occurs while the message is in flight.
  4. Reliable Persistent: Messages are written to persistent storage (data store or file store). The message survives server restarts and engine crashes, ensuring at-least-once delivery semantics.
  5. Assured Persistent: Messages are committed to persistent storage under strict transaction boundaries. This mode provides exact-once semantics when paired with XA two-phase commit transactions.

Integrating Enterprise Applications via JMS and JCA

Enterprise applications interact with the Service Integration Bus using standard Java specifications: the Java Message Service (JMS) API and the Java EE Connector Architecture (JCA). In modern deployments running on Open Liberty or WebSphere Liberty, this extends to Jakarta Messaging 3.0.

Rather than exposing engine connection sockets directly to code, application servers use administered objects configured in JNDI:

  • Queue Connection Factory (QCF): Configures connection pooling, authentication credentials, and transport properties for establishing sessions with the bus.
  • JMS Destination Object: Maps an application-level JNDI lookup name (such as jms/OrderQueue) to the physical bus destination identifier.
  • JCA Activation Specification: Bridges asynchronous Message-Driven Beans (MDBs) to bus destinations. The activation specification defines concurrency limits, maximum batch sizes, and acknowledgment modes.

Configuration Code Example

The following standard Enterprise JavaBeans snippet demonstrates a Message-Driven Bean consuming incoming JSON order payloads from a Service Integration Bus queue using an activation specification:

package com.example.messaging;

import jakarta.ejb.ActivationConfigProperty;
import jakarta.ejb.MessageDriven;
import jakarta.jms.JMSException;
import jakarta.jms.Message;
import jakarta.jms.MessageListener;
import jakarta.jms.TextMessage;
import java.util.logging.Level;
import java.util.logging.Logger;

@MessageDriven(
    name = "OrderProcessingMDB",
    activationConfig = {
        @ActivationConfigProperty(
            propertyName = "destinationType", 
            propertyValue = "jakarta.jms.Queue"
        ),
        @ActivationConfigProperty(
            propertyName = "destinationLookup", 
            propertyValue = "jms/OrderQueue"
        ),
        @ActivationConfigProperty(
            propertyName = "maxEndpoints", 
            propertyValue = "10"
        ),
        @ActivationConfigProperty(
            propertyName = "acknowledgeMode", 
            propertyValue = "Auto-acknowledge"
        )
    }
)
public class OrderProcessingMDB implements MessageListener {

    private static final Logger LOGGER = Logger.getLogger(OrderProcessingMDB.class.getName());

    @Override
    public void onMessage(Message message) {
        try {
            if (message instanceof TextMessage) {
                String payload = ((TextMessage) message).getText();
                LOGGER.info("Processing order payload: " + payload);
                // Execute business logic, database transactions, or service calls
            } else {
                LOGGER.warning("Unrecognized message format received: " + message.getJMSMessageID());
            }
        } catch (JMSException e) {
            LOGGER.log(Level.SEVERE, "Failed to parse message from SIBus", e);
            // Throwing RuntimeException triggers container rollback for persistent messages
            throw new IllegalStateException("Message processing failure", e);
        }
    }
}

High Availability, Clustering, and Failover Mechanics

When high availability is required, adding an application server cluster as a bus member allows messaging engines to fail over between cluster nodes.

           +-----------------------------------------------+
           |               High Availability Cluster       |
           |                                               |
           |  +--------------------+  Heartbeat   +-----+  |
           |  | Node 1 (Active ME) | <----------> | Node|  |
           |  +--------------------+ (HAManager)  | 2   |  |
           |            |                         +-----+  |
           +------------|----------------------------|-----+
                        | Exclusive Lock             | Standby
                        v                            v
               +----------------------------------------+
               |          Shared Message Store          |
               | (Database SIBOWNER Table / Shared Disk)|
               +----------------------------------------+

The Role of the High Availability Manager (HAManager)

The application server cluster uses an internal cluster coordinator known as the High Availability Manager (HAManager). HAManager forms logical core groups that exchange heartbeats to detect JVM hangs, network partitions, or hardware failures.

When an active messaging engine terminates unexpectedly, HAManager initiates a failover sequence:

  1. HAManager marks the local engine instance as offline and isolates its network channels.
  2. A standby cluster member is selected according to core group policies.
  3. The standby node starts its messaging engine instance, which immediately attempts to acquire an exclusive lock on the underlying message store.
  4. Once the lock is verified, the standby engine reads the persistent log, re-instantiates active transactions, and opens the queue points for inbound consumer traffic.

Resolving the SIBOWNER Lock Contention Problem

A persistent challenge in clustered deployments involves orphaned locks on the SIBOWNER table. During startup, an active messaging engine writes a unique instance identifier into SIBOWNER and maintains an open database transaction or continuous row-level lock.

If a server crashes abruptly or loses its network connection to the database without executing a clean shutdown, the database engine may continue holding the TCP socket and associated row lock until a database timeout expires. When HAManager attempts to start the standby messaging engine on another server, the new engine outputs warnings such as:

CWSIS1538I: The messaging engine, ME_UUID=..., INC_UUID=..., is attempting to obtain an exclusive lock on the data store.
CWSIS1593I: The messaging engine has failed to gain an initial lock on the data store.

By default, the engine retries for up to 15 minutes before the HAManager disables the component. To eliminate prolonged failover intervals, modern versions introduce the Restrict Long Running Locks capability. Under this setting, the messaging engine does not hold an open database lock indefinitely. Instead, it uses short-duration locks combined with a periodic ownership revalidation timestamp, ensuring rapid release and handoff during ungraceful terminations.

Automating SIBus Provisioning via Jython Scripting

Configuring complex buses, queue destinations, and bus members through administrative graphical consoles is error-prone. Enterprise administrators automate these operations using wsadmin scripting in Jython.

The following script automates the creation of a bus, registers a cluster member with a JDBC data store, and defines a queue destination:

# SIBus Provisioning Automation via wsadmin / Jython
import sys

def configure_sibus():
    bus_name = "EnterpriseOrderBus"
    cluster_name = "MessagingCluster"
    data_source_jndi = "jdbc/SIBusDataSource"
    queue_name = "OrderQueue"

    print "Initializing Service Integration Bus creation: " + bus_name

    # 1. Create the Service Integration Bus
    existing_buses = AdminTask.listSIBuses().splitlines()
    if bus_name not in existing_buses:
        AdminTask.createSIBus(['-bus', bus_name, '-description', 'Primary transactional order bus'])
        print "Bus created successfully."
    else:
        print "Bus already exists. Skipping creation."

    # 2. Add Cluster Member with Data Store configuration
    print "Adding cluster member: " + cluster_name
    AdminTask.addSIBusMember([
        '-bus', bus_name,
        '-cluster', cluster_name,
        '-datasourceJndiName', data_source_jndi,
        '-createDataStore', 'true',
        '-authAlias', 'SIBusDBAlias'
    ])

    # 3. Create a Queue Destination on the Bus
    print "Configuring Queue Destination: " + queue_name
    AdminTask.createSIBJMSQueue([
        '-bus', bus_name,
        '-name', queue_name,
        '-queueName', queue_name,
        '-cluster', cluster_name,
        '-reliability', 'ReliablePersistent'
    ])

    # 4. Commit configuration changes
    print "Saving configuration changes to master repository..."
    AdminConfig.save()
    print "SIBus automation complete."

if __name__ == "__main__":
    configure_sibus()

Architectural Evolution: From SIBus to Event Streams and Modern Gateways

The Service Integration Bus model resolved core coupling issues for monolithic and service-oriented architectures (SOA) built in the 2000s and 2010s. However, changing operational requirements have shifted how organizations design integration backbones:

  • Log-Based Streaming vs. Stateful Queues: Technologies such as Apache Kafka and Apache Pulsar replaced message deletion semantics with immutable, append-only commit logs. While an SIBus deletes a message as soon as a consumer acknowledges it, stream platforms retain events, allowing disparate services to replay historical records at independent rates.
  • Microservices and Protocol Decentralization: Contemporary microservices favor lightweight protocols (gRPC, HTTP/REST) over enterprise Java Connector specifications. Rather than consolidating all inter-service traffic onto a heavyweight application bus, teams deploy lightweight message brokers alongside API gateways that govern request routing, rate limiting, and observability.
  • AI and Intelligence Integration: Modern systems increasingly integrate non-deterministic LLM endpoints alongside standard business logic. Unlike predictable database or queue transactions, AI model requests involve variable latencies, rate limits, and external vendor dependencies.

Modern infrastructure relies on unified edge and gateway components to govern traffic across distributed systems. Beyond internal routing, modern enterprise architectures require end-to-end policy management: Bifrost applies governance and security controls centrally, and Bifrost Edge extends that same governance and security to AI traffic on employee machines, with endpoint enforcement on each device. This pairing reflects the historical lesson of the Service Integration Bus: integration logic must be decoupled from application code to preserve organizational security, observability, and operational control.

Common Production Pitfalls and Troubleshooting

Operating an enterprise Service Integration Bus requires continuous monitoring of queue depths, database storage consumption, and engine availability. Production engineers regularly encounter three primary categories of operational failures:

1. Poison Messages and Exception Destinations

When a message contains corrupted data, an unparseable schema, or values that trigger application exceptions, a Message-Driven Bean may consistently fail and roll back the transaction. By default, the messaging engine re-delivers the message up to a configured threshold (typically five attempts).

Once exhausted, the message is routed to an Exception Destination (often formatted as _SYSTEM.Exception.Destination.ME_NAME) to prevent queue stalls. Monitoring teams must configure automated alerting on these exception queues to detect application-level contract breaks before upstream backpressure develops.

2. Message Engine Split-Brain and JVM Termination

When core group heartbeats fail across an unstable network, HAManager may conclude that an active node has failed while the node is still executing requests.

To preserve data integrity and prevent multiple engines from writing to the same data store simultaneously, the local member initiates a panic shutdown. In the server logs, this manifests as:

HMGR0130I: The local member of group WSAF_SIB_BUS=...,type=WSAF_SIB has indicated that it is not alive. The JVM will be terminated.
SystemOut O Panic:component requested panic from isAlive.

Mitigating these failures requires tuning HAManager heartbeat intervals, isolating cluster replication networks onto dedicated network interfaces, and guaranteeing low latency between the application server cluster and the backing database.

3. File Store and Database Storage Exhaustion

If consumer processing halts while producers continue publishing, messaging engines retain persistent payloads in storage. In a data store configuration, this leads to rapid table space expansion across the SIBnnn tables.

If table limits are reached, the messaging engine pauses all inbound producers by blocking socket connections. Operational teams must monitor database filesystem headroom and set maximum message depth quotas on queue destinations to shed load gracefully when consumers fall behind.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the primary difference between a Service Integration Bus and IBM MQ?

A Service Integration Bus is an application server component embedded directly within WebSphere Application Server, whereas IBM MQ is a standalone enterprise messaging middleware platform. IBM MQ offers broader multi-platform support across mainframes and external systems, while SIBus provides native integration for Java EE applications inside the application server runtime.

When should a data store be selected over a file store?

A data store should be chosen when an organization already maintains robust database replication, backup, and high-availability infrastructure. A file store is preferable when minimizing I/O latency is critical or when database licensing constraints prevent the provisioning of dedicated SIBus database schemas.

How does an activation specification differ from a listener port?

Listener ports rely on WebSphere-specific background threads to poll destinations and dispatch work to message beans. Activation specifications implement the standardized JCA 1.5/1.6 inbound resource adapter contract, offering superior thread pooling, standardized lifecycle management, and native workload distribution.

Can a Service Integration Bus communicate with external message brokers?

Yes. A Service Integration Bus can link to external systems through MQ Link connections, foreign bus definitions, or JMS bridges. This allows applications attached to an SIBus to route messages transparently to queues managed by external messaging platforms.

What occurs when an active messaging engine loses its database connection?

If the messaging engine loses connectivity to its data store, it cannot guarantee transactional consistency. The engine terminates its client connections and signals HAManager to halt the local instance, allowing an alternate standby node in the cluster to re-acquire the lock and resume message processing.

Sources

  • IBM Documentation: Service Integration Buses Overview
  • IBM Support: WebSphere Service Integration Bus 101 Architecture Guide
  • IBM Support: Troubleshooting SIBus Messaging Engine Failover Problems
  • Open Liberty Documentation: JMS Activation Specification Configuration

title: How to Design Recoverable Webhook Cleanup — Queue, Cron, Delayed Retries, and Dead Letters
description:
For an edtech platform cleaning up expired enrollment webhooks, the simplest architecture that still recovers cleanly is a durable queue plus a small HTTP worker; use cron to enqueue scans, delayed retries to pace failures, and a dead-letter queue (DLQ) for jobs that need a human decision. Keeping retry state in the request handler is the trap. It disappears when the process restarts.

The useful mental model is a conveyor belt: cron puts work on the belt, the queue remembers each package, the worker calls the HTTP endpoint, and the DLQ is the shelf for packages that never made it through. That separation makes an overnight incident a replay exercise instead of a spreadsheet exercise.

A field guide to the decision

Situation Queue Cron Practical choice
A student-status webhook fails and should retry in 30 seconds Durable attempt state and delayed delivery Too coarse unless it runs every minute Queue with a delayed job
Reconcile all records every night Holds individual work items Excellent trigger for a bounded scan Cron enqueues, queue executes
Provider returns 429 for an hour Backoff and visibility timeout Replays the whole batch unless you build more state Queue, with jittered delays
A payload is permanently rejected DLQ preserves payload and reason A cron log is easy to lose Queue plus DLQ

This is a decision table, not a product ranking. A managed queue, a Redis-backed worker, or a database table with leases can all implement the same contract. The contract matters more than the brand: durable state, an attempt counter, a next-run timestamp, and an idempotency key.

Pick cron alone when the job is a bounded report and a missed run can safely be rerun in full. Pick a queue when each webhook has its own retry timing or when one bad student record must not block the rest. Pick a database-backed worker when operating another service is not suitable for your team, and accept that you will own leasing, polling, and cleanup.

What should an HTTP worker record before retrying a webhook?

Record the decision before making the network call. In a Node.js service, a small job document is enough:

type WebhookJob = {
  id: string;
  enrollmentId: string;
  payloadHash: string;
  attempts: number;
  nextRunAt: string;
  status: "ready" | "processing" | "succeeded" | "dead";
  lastStatus?: number;
  lastError?: string;
};

function retryDelay(attempt: number): number {
  const base = Math.min(15 * 60_000, 2 ** attempt * 1_000);
  const jitter = Math.floor(Math.random() * 500);
  return base + jitter;
}

The worker claims one ready job with a lease, increments attempts, and sends the same idempotency key on every delivery. A successful 2xx response marks succeeded. A timeout, 408, 429, or 5xx response schedules nextRunAt; a 400 caused by a schema error goes to dead immediately. Your provider may define different transient codes, so keep that mapping in configuration and test it.

The order is deliberate. If the process dies after the HTTP call but before the success write, the queue will deliver again. The receiver must therefore treat (enrollmentId, payloadHash) as idempotent. HMAC signatures, calculated over the exact body bytes, protect authenticity; RFC 2104 describes the keyed-hash construction. Authentication does not prevent duplicates. Idempotency does.

I once started with a single setTimeout around fetch. It looked wonderfully small. A deploy erased the timer, and three hours of cleanup quietly vanished. That was the moment the retry record became part of the data model, not a detail of the worker process.

The following worker uses generic repository methods so you can back them with Redis, SQL, or another durable store. It keeps the HTTP request short: an API endpoint only inserts a job and returns 202 Accepted.

async function processOne(repo: {
  claimReady: (now: Date, leaseMs: number) => Promise<WebhookJob | null>;
  markSuccess: (id: string) => Promise<void>;
  reschedule: (id: string, at: Date, reason: string, status?: number) => Promise<void>;
  moveToDlq: (id: string, reason: string, status?: number) => Promise<void>;
}, send: (job: WebhookJob) => Promise<Response>): Promise<boolean> {
  const job = await repo.claimReady(new Date(), 60_000);
  if (!job) return false;

  try {
    const response = await send(job);
    if (response.ok) {
      await repo.markSuccess(job.id);
      return true;
    }
    const transient = response.status === 408 || response.status === 429 || response.status >= 500;
    if (!transient || job.attempts >= 8) {
      await repo.moveToDlq(job.id, `HTTP ${response.status}`, response.status);
      return true;
    }
    await repo.reschedule(job.id, new Date(Date.now() + retryDelay(job.attempts)), `HTTP ${response.status}`, response.status);
    return true;
  } catch (error) {
    if (job.attempts >= 8) await repo.moveToDlq(job.id, String(error));
    else await repo.reschedule(job.id, new Date(Date.now() + retryDelay(job.attempts)), String(error));
    return true;
  }
}

Run several workers, but cap concurrency per destination. A queue smooths bursts; it does not make a provider's rate limit disappear. Emit counters for claimed, succeeded, retried, dead, and latency_ms. Alert on age of the oldest ready job, DLQ growth, and the ratio of attempts to successes. Logs should include the job ID and attempt number, never the student's personal data.

Cron still has a job. Schedule a reconciliation every 15 minutes, query enrollments whose remote status is stale, and enqueue only missing idempotency keys. The schedule is a trigger, not the delivery mechanism. If the cron process runs twice, the unique key makes the second enqueue harmless.

Testing recovery instead of just the happy path

Test time as data. Freeze the clock, enqueue a job at 10:00:00Z, return a 429, and assert a later nextRunAt. Kill the worker after fetch resolves but before markSuccess; a second run should produce one receiver-side effect. Feed a malformed payload and assert a DLQ record with a human-readable reason.

For an edtech cleanup, the useful fixture is boring: 12 enrollments, two transient 503 responses, one permanent 400, and one duplicate cron tick. Start the fake provider at 10:00:00Z; return 503 for enrollment E-07, then let the second attempt succeed at the calculated nextRunAt. At 10:00:01Z, terminate the worker after fetch resolves but before the repository write, then restart it with the same queue row. The receiver should observe one state change because its idempotency key is stable, while the job record eventually becomes succeeded. The malformed payload for E-11 should skip retries and land in the DLQ with the response code and a redacted reason. The final assertion is 11 eventual successes, one DLQ item, and no duplicate state changes. Your mileage may vary with provider limits, so measure queue age and retry distribution in staging before choosing the eight-attempt ceiling.

Keep the test ugly.

Limits and when to choose differently

The catch is operational ownership. A queue adds a worker deployment, lease recovery, and retention policy. Cron-only is suitable when a complete rerun is cheap and a delay of several minutes is acceptable. A database poller is not suitable when you need sub-second scheduling or very high fan-out; use a queue designed for that load.

Do not retry authorization failures, invalid signatures, or deterministic schema errors. Do not put a student's full webhook body in an alert. Keep DLQ retention long enough to investigate, then delete according to your privacy policy. When the receiver cannot offer idempotency, slow down and add a deduplication table before increasing concurrency.

Three words: persist the decision.

Sources

  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/202
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/429
  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/http/

References are standards and public documentation; the architecture is vendor-independent.

title: Window Functions, Joins, CTEs and Subqueries in SQL: A Hospital Dataset Walkthrough.
description:
Every hospital runs on data: patients, bills, wards, diagnoses and doctors. Answering real questions from that data, like "Which doctor brings the most revenue?" or "Which patients came back for a second visit?", takes more than just the basic SELECT. In this article I use a small hospital database to explain four SQL topics

  1. Window Functions

  2. Joins

  3. Common Table Expressions (CTEs)

  4. Subqueries

The Dataset

The database lives in Postgres and has the following core tables:
doctors (doctor_id, doctor_name, doctor_gender, doctor_specialty, doctor_experience_years, email, city)
patients (patient_id, patient_name, patient_gender, patient_age, county, sub_county)
departments (department_id, department_name, manager_id)
wards (ward_id, ward_name)
diagnosis (diagnosis_id, diagnosis_name, diagnosis_category)
procedures (procedure_id, procedure_name, procedure_category)
fact_visits (visit_id, visit_date, patient_id, doctor_id, department_id, ward_id, diagnosis_id, procedure_id, admission_type, length_of_stay_days, triage_level, insurance_provider, total_bill_kes, payment_method, follow_up_required, patient_satisfaction_score)

fact_visits is the central table. It holds 30 visits from 1 to 15 June 2026, and the other tables describe who, where and why. The total billed across all visits is KES 488,000.

1. Window Functions

A window function performs a calculation across a set of rows related to the current row, without collapsing rows like GROUP BY does. Every window function needs a OVER() clause.

How OVER(), PARTITION BY, ORDER BY and Frames Work

  • OVER() defines the "window" the function operates on.
  • PARTITION BY splits rows into groups, like GROUP BY but each row keeps its identity.
  • ORDER BY inside OVER() defines the order used for ranking or running calculations.
  • A window frame (e.g., ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) limits which rows in the partition the function sees.

Ranking: ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), DENSE_RANK(), NTILE()

  • ROW_NUMBER() gives a unique number to every row, even when values tie.
  • RANK() gives ties the same rank and then skips numbers (1, 2, 2, 4).
  • DENSE_RANK() gives ties the same rank without skipping (1, 2, 2, 3).
  • NTILE(n) splits rows into n roughly equal groups. 
SELECT
    visit_id,
    total_bill_kes,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY total_bill_kes DESC) AS row_num,
    RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY total_bill_kes DESC) AS rnk,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total_bill_kes DESC) AS dense_rnk,
    NTILE(4)     OVER (ORDER BY total_bill_kes DESC) AS bill_quartile
FROM fact_visits;

This ranks every visit from the highest bill to the lowest. Visit 1017 (KES 82,000) comes first. Visits 1008 and 1020 both billed KES 6,500, so they show the difference between the functions: ROW_NUMBER gives them 15 and 16, RANK gives both 15, and the next bill (KES 5,500) gets 17, while DENSE_RANK gives both 15, and the next gets 16. NTILE(4) puts the 8 biggest bills in quartile 1, which helps identify the costliest visits.

WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT visit_id, department_id, total_bill_kes,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY total_bill_kes DESC) AS rn
    FROM fact_visits
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;

Use case: adding PARTITION BY department_id to ROW_NUMBER() and filtering for rn = 1 in a CTE gives the highest billed visit per department. This is a common interview question.

Value Functions: LAG, LEAD, FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE

LAG() reads a value from the previous row and LEAD() from the next row. FIRST_VALUE() and LAST_VALUE() return the first or last value in the frame.

SELECT
    patient_id,
    visit_date,
    LAG(visit_date)  OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY visit_date) AS previous_visit,
    LEAD(visit_date) OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY visit_date) AS next_visit,
    visit_date - LAG(visit_date)
        OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY visit_date) AS days_since_last_visit
FROM fact_visits
ORDER BY patient_id, visit_date;

For each patient, this shows the previous and next visit dates and the gap in days. A patient's first visit has NULL for previous_visit. This is useful for tracking follow-up compliance.

SELECT
    patient_id,
    visit_date,
    total_bill_kes,
    FIRST_VALUE(total_bill_kes) OVER (
        PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY visit_date
    ) AS first_bill,
    LAST_VALUE(total_bill_kes) OVER (
        PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY visit_date
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
    ) AS latest_bill
FROM fact_visits;

This compares each patient's first bill with their latest one. Common mistake: when a window has ORDER BY, the default frame ends at the current row, so LAST_VALUE() would just return the current row's value. Extending the frame to UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING fixes that.

Aggregate Window Functions: SUM(), AVG(), COUNT(), MIN(), MAX()

Used with OVER(), aggregates compute running totals and comparisons while keeping every row.

SELECT
    d.doctor_name,
    f.visit_id,
    f.total_bill_kes,
    SUM(f.total_bill_kes) OVER (PARTITION BY f.doctor_id) AS doctor_total,
    ROUND(AVG(f.total_bill_kes) OVER (PARTITION BY f.doctor_id), 2) AS doctor_avg,
    COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY f.doctor_id) AS doctor_visits,
    MIN(f.total_bill_kes) OVER (PARTITION BY f.doctor_id) AS doctor_min,
    MAX(f.total_bill_kes) OVER (PARTITION BY f.doctor_id) AS doctor_max,
    SUM(f.total_bill_kes) OVER (
        PARTITION BY f.doctor_id ORDER BY f.visit_date, f.visit_id
    ) AS running_total
FROM fact_visits f
JOIN doctors d ON d.doctor_id = f.doctor_id;

Every visit row keeps its own details and also shows its doctor's totals. The running_total column grows visit by visit because ORDER BY inside OVER() creates a cumulative window.

Window Frames

A frame decides exactly which rows are included. For example, a moving average of the current and two previous bills:

AVG(total_bill_kes) OVER (ORDER BY visit_date, visit_id ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)

Frame boundaries include UNBOUNDED PRECEDING, n PRECEDING, CURRENT ROW, n FOLLOWING and UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.

2. SQL Joins

Joins combine rows from two or more tables based on a related column, like fact_visits.doctor_id = doctors.doctor_id.

INNER JOIN

Returns only rows where the match exists in both tables.

SELECT f.visit_id, p.patient_name, d.doctor_name, f.total_bill_kes
FROM fact_visits f
INNER JOIN patients p ON p.patient_id = f.patient_id
INNER JOIN doctors  d ON d.doctor_id  = f.doctor_id;

This returns 30 rows, one per visit, with the patient and doctor names attached.

LEFT JOIN

Returns all rows from the left table plus matching rows from the right. Unmatched rows get NULL on the right side.

SELECT p.patient_name, COUNT(f.visit_id) AS visits
FROM patients p
LEFT JOIN fact_visits f ON f.patient_id = p.patient_id
GROUP BY p.patient_name
ORDER BY visits DESC;

This returns all 25 patients. Five patients have 2 visits and the rest have 1.

Use case: finding patients who registered but never visited. Adding WHERE f.visit_id IS NULL would check for patients without visits, which in my case returns no rows since every patient has a visit.

RIGHT JOIN

Keeps every row from the right table. It is a LEFT JOIN with the tables swapped.

SELECT d.doctor_name, f.visit_id
FROM fact_visits f
RIGHT JOIN doctors d ON d.doctor_id = f.doctor_id;

This lists every doctor with their visits, 30 rows here. A doctor with no visits would appear once with NULL in visit_id.

FULL OUTER JOIN

Keeps all rows from both tables, filling NULLs where no match exists; it is useful for data quality checks.

SELECT d.doctor_id, f.visit_id
FROM doctors d
FULL OUTER JOIN fact_visits f ON f.doctor_id = d.doctor_id
WHERE d.doctor_id IS NULL OR f.visit_id IS NULL;

This finds doctors with no visits and visits with no doctor. Here it returns no rows, which confirms the data is consistent.

CROSS JOIN

Produces the Cartesian product: every row from the first table paired with every row from the second. No ON clause.

SELECT d.doctor_name, dep.department_name
FROM doctors d
CROSS JOIN departments dep;

4 doctors x 4 departments = 16 rows. Use case: generating all possible combinations, like a roster of every doctor against every department to plan rotations.

SELF JOIN

A table joined to itself, useful when rows in one table reference other rows in the same table. Here it finds pairs of patients from the same county.

SELECT a.patient_name AS patient_1, b.patient_name AS patient_2, a.county
FROM patients a
JOIN patients b ON a.county = b.county AND a.patient_id < b.patient_id;

The a.patient_id < b.patient_id condition stops a patient from being paired with themselves and avoids duplicate pairs. This results in patients from the same county being listed together.

Quick Comparison

Join Rows kept Best for
INNER Matches in both tables Standard reports
LEFT All left table rows Finding missing matches
RIGHT All right table rows Same as LEFT, flipped
FULL OUTER All rows from both Reconciliation
CROSS All combinations Rosters, testing scenarios
SELF Table joined to itself Hierarchies and comparisons

3. Common Table Expressions (CTEs)

A CTE is a named temporary result set defined with WITH, readable only for that query. It makes complex logic clearer than nested subqueries.

Basic CTE 

WITH doctor_revenue AS (
    SELECT doctor_id, SUM(total_bill_kes) AS revenue
    FROM fact_visits
    GROUP BY doctor_id
)
SELECT d.doctor_name, dr.revenue
FROM doctor_revenue dr
JOIN doctors d ON d.doctor_id = dr.doctor_id
ORDER BY dr.revenue DESC;

The CTE totals revenue per doctor first, then the main query joins it to doctor names. This also shows a CTE working with a join and an aggregation.

WITH high_value_visits AS (
    SELECT *
    FROM fact_visits
    WHERE total_bill_kes > 20000
)
SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS expensive_visits
FROM high_value_visits
GROUP BY department_id;

The CTE filters bills above KES 20,000 first, then the main query counts them per department. The counts are department 10:3, 20:2, 30:3 and 40:1.

Multiple CTEs

Separate CTEs with commas. Later ones can use earlier ones.

WITH dept_revenue AS (
    SELECT department_id, SUM(total_bill_kes) AS revenue
    FROM fact_visits
    GROUP BY department_id
),
avg_revenue AS (
    SELECT AVG(revenue) AS avg_rev FROM dept_revenue
)
SELECT d.department_name, dr.revenue
FROM dept_revenue dr
JOIN departments d ON d.department_id = dr.department_id
CROSS JOIN avg_revenue a
WHERE dr.revenue > a.avg_rev;

The second CTE consumes the first, showing how CTEs chain. This query lists departments earning above the average departmental revenue. The average is KES 122,000, so only Cardiology is returned.

Recursive CTE

A recursive CTE references itself using UNION ALL to process hierarchical or sequential data. Here in this example it builds a calendar so days with no visits still appear.

WITH RECURSIVE calendar AS (
    SELECT DATE '2026-06-01' AS day
    UNION ALL
    SELECT day + 1 FROM calendar WHERE day < DATE '2026-06-17'
)
SELECT c.day, COUNT(f.visit_id) AS visits
FROM calendar c
LEFT JOIN fact_visits f ON f.visit_date = c.day
GROUP BY c.day
ORDER BY c.day;

Use case: recursive CTEs shine on organization charts (a doctor supervising other doctors but it does not apply on my dataset) or generating date series, like listing all days of June to find dates with zero visits.

CTEs vs Subqueries

  • Readability: CTEs name each step and read top to bottom. Deeply nested subqueries read inside out.

  • Reuse: a CTE defined once can be referenced multiple times in the main query. A subquery must be rewritten each time.

  • Recursion: only CTEs support WITH RECURSIVE.

  • Scope: both exist only for one query. Neither stores data permanently. For reusable storage, use a table or view

WITH avg_bill AS (
    SELECT AVG(total_bill_kes) AS avg_kes FROM fact_visits
)
SELECT f.visit_id, f.total_bill_kes
FROM fact_visits f
CROSS JOIN avg_bill a
WHERE f.total_bill_kes > a.avg_kes;

4. SQL Subqueries

A subquery is a query nested inside another query. It can appear in SELECT, FROM or WHERE.

Scalar and Non-Correlated Subqueries

A scalar subquery returns a single value. A non-correlated subquery runs once, independently of the outer query. This one is both:

SELECT visit_id, total_bill_kes
FROM fact_visits
WHERE total_bill_kes > (SELECT AVG(total_bill_kes) FROM fact_visits);

The average bill is about KES 16,267, so this returns 10 visits.

Correlated Subquery

A correlated subquery uses a value from the outer row, so it runs once per row. This finds visits where the bill is above that same doctor's average:

SELECT f.visit_id, f.doctor_id, f.total_bill_kes
FROM fact_visits f
WHERE f.total_bill_kes > (
    SELECT AVG(f2.total_bill_kes)
    FROM fact_visits f2
    WHERE f2.doctor_id = f.doctor_id
);

It compares each bill with the average for its own doctor, giving a fairer view than one hospital-wide average.

Nested Subqueries

A subquery inside a subquery. This finds patients treated in Cardiology:

SELECT patient_name
FROM patients
WHERE patient_id IN (
    SELECT patient_id
    FROM fact_visits
    WHERE department_id = (
        SELECT department_id
        FROM departments
        WHERE department_name = 'Cardiology'
    )
);

The innermost query finds the Cardiology ID, the middle one finds its visits, and the outer one returns the patients.

IN and EXISTS

IN checks whether a value is in a list. EXISTS checks whether the subquery returns any row and stops at the first match, so it can be faster on large tables.

-- IN
SELECT patient_name FROM patients
WHERE patient_id IN (SELECT patient_id FROM fact_visits WHERE admission_type = 'Inpatient');

-- EXISTS
SELECT p.patient_name FROM patients p
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM fact_visits f
    WHERE f.patient_id = p.patient_id AND f.admission_type = 'Inpatient'
);

Both return the same 9 inpatients. Prefer NOT EXISTS over NOT IN when the subquery could contain NULL, because NOT IN then returns no rows at all.

ANY and ALL

> ANY means greater than at least one value in the list. > ALL means greater than every value.

-- Bigger than at least one Mobile Money bill
SELECT visit_id, total_bill_kes FROM fact_visits
WHERE total_bill_kes > ANY (SELECT total_bill_kes FROM fact_visits WHERE payment_method = 'Mobile Money');

-- Bigger than every Mobile Money bill
SELECT visit_id, total_bill_kes FROM fact_visits
WHERE total_bill_kes > ALL (SELECT total_bill_kes FROM fact_visits WHERE payment_method = 'Mobile Money');

Mobile Money bills range from KES 1,900 to 24,000. ANY compares against the smallest, so it returns 28 visits. ALL compares against the largest, so it returns only the 7 visits above KES 24,000.

Subqueries in SELECT, FROM and WHERE 

-- In SELECT: a calculated value per row
SELECT p.patient_name,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM fact_visits f WHERE f.patient_id = p.patient_id) AS visit_count
FROM patients p;

-- In FROM: a derived table
SELECT department_id, avg_bill
FROM (
    SELECT department_id, AVG(total_bill_kes) AS avg_bill
    FROM fact_visits
    GROUP BY department_id
) dept_avg
WHERE avg_bill > 15000;
--for the WHERE subqueries check the examples above

The first returns 25 rows, one visit count per patient.The second returns departments 10 and 30, with averages af about KES 23,344 and 17,533.

Wrapping Up

  • Window functions add ranking, offsets and running aggregates without collapsing rows.

  • Joins combine tables; pick INNER for matches, LEFT or RIGHT to keep one side, FULL OUTER to keep both, CROSS for combinations and SELF for intra-table relationships.

  • CTEs break complex logic into named, reusable, even recursive steps.

  • Subqueries answer inner questions first; scalar for single values, correlated for row-by-row logic, and IN, EXISTS, ANY and ALL for set membership and comparison.

Mastering these four areas turns basic SELECT statements into the analytical queries interviewers and organizations actually need.

title: Debug HTTPS traffic with a free, open-source proxy (ProxyZip)
description:
Your app calls an API, something comes back wrong, and the only thing you can see is a spinner. The request is encrypted, the logs say nothing useful, and you end up guessing.

A debugging proxy fixes that: it sits between your app and the server, decrypts the HTTPS on your own machine and shows you every request and response. I built ProxyZip, a free, open-source HTTP and HTTPS debugging proxy, and this post walks through what it does using a small example.

TL;DR

  • Capture and inspect HTTPS traffic from any app on macOS, Windows and Linux
  • Pause a request, edit it and send it on
  • Mock an API that does not exist yet, or validate real traffic against an OpenAPI file
  • Turn captured requests into tests and run them in CI
  • MIT licensed, written in Rust, no account and no telemetry

What is ProxyZip?

ProxyZip is an HTTP and HTTPS debugging proxy with a desktop app and a command line. The engine is Rust (tokio, hyper, rustls); the app is Tauri and Svelte. The app and the proxyzip command run the same engine, so what you learn in one works in the other.

The example below uses a fictional shop API at api.shopwave.dev.

Install it 

# macOS
brew install --cask luispeixoto/proxyzip/proxyzip

# Windows
scoop bucket add proxyzip https://github.com/LuisPeixoto/scoop-proxyzip

Installers for macOS, Windows and Linux (.dmg, .msi, .exe, .AppImage, .deb, .rpm) are on the releases page. The command line alone installs with cargo install --git https://github.com/LuisPeixoto/ProxyZip proxyzip-cli.

Inspect HTTPS traffic

HTTPS needs one extra step. ProxyZip creates a local certificate authority on your machine; once you trust it, the proxy can show you what your apps send. The private key never leaves your disk, and you can exclude any host from decryption.

proxyzip ca install
eval "$(proxyzip env)"
proxyzip start --port 19191

proxyzip env points the current terminal at the proxy and makes curl, Node.js, Python, Go, Git, Cargo and others trust the certificate. Every finished request prints as it happens:

200 GET     https://api.shopwave.dev/v1/products 469B 1ms [mock]
200 GET     https://api.shopwave.dev/v1/products/sku_1042 142B 70ms [mock]

In the app you get the same requests as a list, with headers, cookies, timing, TLS details and the body as a JSON tree. Use jq filters on a body, or compare two requests side by side.

Binary protocols are covered too. gRPC, gRPC-Web and plain Protobuf messages are decoded even without the .proto files, which makes gRPC debugging a lot less painful.

Change traffic instead of only reading it

Right-click a request to set a breakpoint: the next matching request stops before it leaves, and you can edit the method, URL, headers or body. Map Local answers with a file from your disk, Map Remote sends the request to another host, and rewrite rules change headers, bodies and status codes. You can also throttle to a slow network or block a host to see how your app copes.

Mock an API that does not exist yet

When the backend is not ready, or has to fail in a specific way, a mock server answers for it: routes with status codes, headers, bodies and delays, plus a small template language. Right-click a captured response and choose Create a mock from this response, or import an OpenAPI 3 file.

proxyzip mock petstore.yaml --port 4010 --delay 200
proxyzip validate petstore.yaml capture.pzsession

proxyzip validate checks captured traffic against the specification and exits with 1 if anything does not conform, so it works as a CI step.

Turn requests into API tests

Select the requests of a flow, right-click and choose Add to a suite. A suite is a single .pzsuite file with checks on status and body, variables and environments, and values passed between steps with jq. It belongs in version control, and it runs headless:

proxyzip run checkout.pzsuite --env staging --junit report.xml

The command exits with 1 when a request fails and writes a JUnit report that CI systems can display. Postman collections run the same way.

Phones, emulators and AI assistants

To debug an iPhone or Android device, point its Wi-Fi proxy at your computer and open http://proxyzip.cert to install the certificate. The Devices window shows the address and a QR code, and has one-click setup for simulators and emulators. See the mobile debugging guide.

ProxyZip also has a built-in Model Context Protocol server, so assistants such as Claude Code, Cursor and VS Code can read your captured traffic. It is off by default, listens on localhost only, needs an access token and redacts secrets unless you ask otherwise. The MCP guide has the details.

Private and open

There is no account to create and nothing phones home; the only extra request is an optional, signed update check. The code is MIT licensed, so you can read it, fork it and ship it. Use it only on traffic you are allowed to inspect.

Try it

  • Website and docs: luispeixoto.github.io/ProxyZip
  • Source: github.com/LuisPeixoto/ProxyZip
  • Downloads: latest release

If it saves you an afternoon of guessing, a star on GitHub helps other developers find it, and issues and pull requests are welcome. What would you want from a debugging proxy that the tools you use today do not do?

title: Tailwind CSS Alternatives: Which One Fits the Problem You Actually Have
description:
"Tailwind alternatives" is one of those searches where the results are almost always useless, because every list gives you the same twelve tools ranked by GitHub stars and none of them ask why you're looking.

So let's start there. In my experience there are four reasons people go looking, and they lead to completely different answers. Three of them don't require leaving Tailwind at all.

First, work out what you're actually escaping

"My markup is unreadable." You open a component and there's a class attribute with forty utilities in it. This is by far the most common complaint, and it's the one where switching frameworks helps least. The problem isn't Tailwind, it's that nothing is giving names to your repeated patterns.

"I don't want a build step." You're working on a Django template, a Rails view, a static page, or something embedded, and running a watcher feels absurd for what you're doing.

"The engine is slow or awkward in my setup." Usually a large codebase, an unusual bundler, or a monorepo where the content scanning is painful.

"I don't want utility CSS at all." Fair enough. It's a style of working and it doesn't suit everyone.

Work out which one is yours before reading any further, because the right answer differs completely.

If your markup is unreadable: you don't need an alternative

This is worth saying plainly, because a lot of people switch frameworks to solve this and find the new one has the same problem.

Class soup happens when every button in your project spells out its own appearance. The fix is to name the pattern once. You can do that three ways, and only one of them involves leaving Tailwind.

Use @apply sparingly. It works, and it's built in. It's also widely discouraged because you end up with a second stylesheet that drifts from your markup, and the Tailwind maintainers themselves suggest reaching for components instead.

Extract components in your framework. A <Button> in React or a {% include %} in Django keeps the utilities in one file. This is the official answer and it's a good one, if you're in a framework that has components.

Use a component class library. Something that ships btn and card as real classes, built on top of Tailwind rather than instead of it. Frutjam is one, DaisyUI is the best known, and there are others. Your markup becomes <button class="btn btn-primary"> and the utilities are still there when you need to override something.

None of these are alternatives to Tailwind. They're ways to keep it and stop fighting it.

If you don't want a build step

Two real options here.

Tailwind's own browser build. A single script tag and you're writing utilities with no tooling. It's explicitly not for production, but for a prototype, an email template preview, or a page you edit by hand, it's exactly right.

A stylesheet you just link. Plenty of CSS frameworks are a single file, and so are the component libraries built on Tailwind if they publish a compiled bundle. Frutjam does, which means you can drop in a <link> tag and get every component without Node existing anywhere in the project:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/frutjam@2/dist/frutjam.components.css">

That ships everything rather than only what you use, so it's the wrong choice for an app and the right one for a prototype.

If you want a different utility engine

These are genuine Tailwind alternatives in the sense that they replace the engine while keeping the idea.

UnoCSS is the one most people land on. It's an atomic CSS engine with pluggable presets, and presetWind4 gives you Tailwind-compatible class names, so migration is mostly mechanical. It also does things Tailwind doesn't, like attribute mode, where <button btn="primary lg"> is valid input. It's fast and it's Vite-native.

Panda CSS takes a different angle: you write styles in TypeScript, it generates static CSS at build time, and you get type safety and design tokens as first-class things. Good fit if you're already deep in a typed React codebase. Heavier conceptually than Tailwind.

StyleX is Meta's take, also compile-time, also typed, built for very large codebases where style collisions are a real operational problem. Narrower audience.

Vanilla Extract is CSS-in-TypeScript with zero runtime, closer to CSS Modules than to Tailwind. Worth a look if the thing you miss is writing actual CSS.

A note on Windi CSS, which still appears on every list: it's no longer maintained, and its author went on to build UnoCSS. Don't start a project on it.

If you don't want utility CSS at all

Open Props is a set of CSS custom properties: colours, spacing, typography, easings, animations. No classes, no build, no opinions about your markup. You write normal CSS and use the variables. It's the gentlest step away from a framework.

Pico CSS is classless. You write semantic HTML and it looks good immediately. Brilliant for documentation, internal tools and prototypes; limiting the moment you need a specific design.

Bulma is a traditional CSS framework with component classes and no JavaScript. Mature, calm, nothing clever.

Bootstrap still exists and is still fine. You get components and a utility layer, and some interactive pieces want its JavaScript. If your team already knows it, that knowledge has real value.

Plain modern CSS deserves to be on this list. Nesting, custom properties, color-mix(), container queries, :has(), cascade layers. A lot of what frameworks were invented to paper over is now in the platform.

Quick comparison

Tool Replaces Tailwind? Build step Best for
Component class library No, sits on top Same as Tailwind Unreadable markup
Tailwind browser build No None Prototypes
UnoCSS Yes Yes Speed, attribute mode, Vite
Panda CSS Yes Yes Typed design tokens, React
StyleX Yes Yes Very large codebases
Vanilla Extract Yes Yes Writing real CSS with types
Open Props Yes None Tokens without opinions
Pico CSS Yes None Docs, internal tools
Bulma Yes None Classic components, no JS
Bootstrap Yes Optional Teams who already know it
Plain CSS Yes None Small projects, full control

Where Frutjam fits

Frutjam is a CSS-only component library. It gives you btn, card, modal, alert and sixty-odd others as real class names, so your markup reads like markup. Every colour pair is contrast-tested to WCAG AA, and interactive components use what the browser already has, so modals are <dialog> with the popover attribute, accordions are <details>, and tabs are radio inputs. There's no JavaScript bundle.

As of 2.3.0 it runs three ways, which is why it's in a post about alternatives at all:

With Tailwind, as a plugin. One line, and Tailwind ships only the components your markup uses.

@import "tailwindcss";
@plugin "frutjam";

With UnoCSS, as a preset generated from the same source files as the Tailwind plugin, so the two can't drift.

import { presetFrutjam } from 'frutjam/unocss';

export default defineConfig({ presets: [presetWind4(), presetFrutjam()] });

With neither. Import the stylesheet and you're done. No utility engine, no plugin, nothing to configure.

import 'frutjam/css';

So if what you want is to stop writing class soup, Frutjam solves that without you leaving Tailwind. And if you've decided to leave anyway, it follows you to UnoCSS or to plain CSS without changing a single class name in your templates.

Frequently asked questions

Is Tailwind actually a problem?

No. It's a good tool and the ecosystem around it is the best in the category. Most "Tailwind alternatives" searches are really "how do I stop my markup looking like this" searches, and that has a better answer than switching.

What's the closest drop-in replacement?

UnoCSS with presetWind4. Class names are largely compatible, so you're mostly changing config rather than templates.

Which alternative needs no build step at all?

Open Props, Pico, Bulma, Bootstrap and plain CSS. Frutjam also works this way through a single <link> tag or import 'frutjam/css'.

Can I use a component library and still write utilities?

Yes, and that's the normal way to use one. Components cover the repeated patterns, utilities handle the one-off spacing and layout. Frutjam emits its components into a cascade layer that sorts below utilities, so a utility always wins when you need to override something.

Is it worth migrating an existing Tailwind project?

Usually not for its own sake. Migrate when you have a concrete problem the new tool solves, not because something else is newer.

The bottom line

Pick by the problem, not the popularity.

Markup you can't read is a naming problem, and a component library fixes it without a migration. No build step points at a stylesheet or a CDN tag. A slow or awkward engine points at UnoCSS. Not wanting utilities at all points at Open Props, Pico, or writing the CSS yourself, which is more viable in 2026 than it has been in a decade.

If you want the component-library route, browse the Frutjam components or read the installation guide, which covers all three setups in about a page.
