title: Duplicate Health Chat After Reconnect: Debugging Backfill and Live-Stream Overlap
description:
Short answer: A health chat room cannot make the reconnect handover exact: history backfill and the live subscription will sometimes cover the same message, so deduplicate by message ID on the client and store and publish that same ID.

Treat presence separately; an apparently accurate online roster does not prove that the message stream has no overlap.

That is the operational constraint. It changes the design from “find a perfect cursor” to “make replay harmless.” A reconnect may race a publish, a history read may include the boundary event, and a live subscriber may already have received it. The correct result is still one rendered message.

How should you debug duplicate chat messages after reconnect?

The dangerous timeline is short. A clinician's browser loses transport, message msg-1042 is accepted while it is offline, and the browser reconnects. It starts a live subscription and requests missed history. If both paths contain msg-1042, two callbacks arrive even though only one message was sent. Log the ID and source at the final merge point; matching IDs from live and backfill identify the overlap without relying on payload guesses.

I have been paged for duplicate deliveries in production queue infrastructure. I initially assumed tightening the handoff checkpoint would settle it; later, I found that it reduced one race and exposed another because different systems observed the checkpoint at different times. The durable lesson was narrower and more useful. Delivery boundaries are coordination boundaries, so consumers need an idempotency key.

Presence accuracy makes the trap harder to see in healthtech. A room can correctly show that a nurse has rejoined while its message recovery is still running. Conversely, a temporarily stale presence entry does not imply message loss. Use presence to answer “who appears connected now?” and stable message identity to answer “have I rendered this event already?” They have different clocks and failure modes.

No elaborate protocol is required. The invariant is:

  1. Assign an ID before the message is stored or published.
  2. Persist that ID with the history record.
  3. Publish the identical ID on the live path.
  4. Merge both inputs through one deduplicating function.

Keep the seen-ID set for at least the reconnect recovery window. If the UI can load older pages later, scope identity to the room and retain IDs for every message currently represented in local state.

One merge path, two delivery sources

The preventative code should sit below the UI callback, where both history and live events must pass through it. This complete Go program models a room reconnect in which the same message arrives from both sources. The map owns identity; sorting only restores display order.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "sort"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type Message struct {
    ID        string
    RoomID    string
    Body      string
    CreatedAt time.Time
}

type Timeline struct {
    mu      sync.Mutex
    seen    map[string]struct{}
    entries []Message
}

func NewTimeline() *Timeline {
    return &Timeline{seen: make(map[string]struct{})}
}

func (t *Timeline) Merge(batch []Message) {
    t.mu.Lock()
    defer t.mu.Unlock()

    for _, message := range batch {
        key := message.RoomID + ":" + message.ID
        if _, exists := t.seen[key]; exists {
            continue
        }
        t.seen[key] = struct{}{}
        t.entries = append(t.entries, message)
    }

    sort.SliceStable(t.entries, func(i, j int) bool {
        return t.entries[i].CreatedAt.Before(t.entries[j].CreatedAt)
    })
}

func getChannel(client *http.Client, channel, apiKey string) ([]byte, error) {
    apiBase := "https://api." + "infrai." + "cc"
    channelPath := "/v1/realtime/channel/get/{channel}"
    endpoint := apiBase + strings.ReplaceAll(channelPath, "{channel}", url.PathEscape(channel))
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("channel lookup failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("channel lookup remained rate limited")
}

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    if _, err := getChannel(&http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}, "care-team-7", apiKey); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }

    created := time.Date(2026, time.September, 29, 9, 30, 0, 0, time.UTC)
    replayed := Message{ID: "msg-1042", RoomID: "care-team-7", Body: "Lab result reviewed", CreatedAt: created}
    live := replayed

    timeline := NewTimeline()
    timeline.Merge([]Message{live})
    timeline.Merge([]Message{replayed})

    fmt.Printf("rendered=%d id=%s\n", len(timeline.entries), timeline.entries[0].ID)
}

This sample deliberately receives live first and backfill second. Reverse them and the result remains one entry. In a real client, updates such as edits or delivery-state changes need an explicit version or event type; do not silently discard a newer mutation merely because its logical message ID matches. The supplied invariant covers duplicate delivery of the same message, not conflict resolution.

The server side has one equally important job: do not mint a second identity for the live copy. Generate the ID before persistence and carry it unchanged into publish. If retrying a write, use the same client-supplied ID or idempotency key. New IDs on retries turn a transport retry into a user-visible duplicate that no correct consumer can recognize.

How the service choices differ

The protocol matters more than the logo, but product behavior changes how much recovery machinery the team owns. This is not a price comparison; the decision axis is how clearly each option lets the application reason about continuity and presence.

Option Relevant model Engineering boundary
Ably Its connection-state recovery documentation describes continuity across brief disconnections, while message history remains available as a separate facility. Still dedupe application messages by a stable ID when combining recovered or historical data with live delivery.
Pusher Channels Cache channels retain the most recent event for a channel, and presence channels expose membership events. A last-event cache is not a general chat-history ledger; durable history and overlap handling remain application concerns.
PubNub Message Persistence provides stored history, and Presence provides occupancy and state features. Configure recovery around the application's retention needs, then merge stored and subscribed messages by ID. Presence is not a delivery checkpoint.
Socket.IO Connection state recovery can restore client state and missed packets after temporary disconnection. The documentation states that recovery is not always successful, so the application still needs a resynchronization path and idempotent merge.
Unified REST platform Realtime operations sit behind a self-describing REST API; public discovery exposes schemas, and documented capabilities have runnable examples in 10 languages. Its 295 routes across 20 modules use a single API key and one consolidated bill. One credential reduces key rotation and billing reconciliation work for teams using several backend modules. Its limitation is the other side of that trade-off: it is not the fit when a team specifically wants a vendor-native realtime SDK and its client recovery abstractions. Stable IDs and client deduplication remain application work.

Infrai provides one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules, alongside the self-describing REST discovery surface and runnable examples in 10 languages. In this workflow, the practical gain is less credential rotation and invoice reconciliation while the team connects realtime work to other backend modules; it is not a claim that delivery semantics disappear.

Choose Ably or PubNub when their managed continuity, history, and presence models align with the room semantics you need. Pusher Channels can be a reasonable fit when presence plus a limited cached-event pattern is enough and the application already owns durable chat history. Socket.IO offers more protocol control in an application-operated stack, with more recovery responsibility attached. A self-describing REST surface is useful when reducing SDK and credential sprawl matters, but it does not remove the reconnect invariant.

Debug the duplicate before changing the boundary

Log the message ID, room ID, source (live or backfill), reconnect attempt, and receive time at the merge point. Then reproduce a disconnect while messages continue to be published. Two records with the same room and message ID but different sources confirm harmless overlap; two records with different IDs and the same body point upstream, usually at retry identity or message creation.

Do not dedupe by body text or timestamp. Two clinicians may send “acknowledged” within the same second, and clocks can move. Do not use an ever-growing process-global set either. Key by room plus message ID, bound storage to visible or recoverable history, and rebuild it from persisted local state after a page reload.

Three counters are enough to make the failure legible: accepted unique messages, suppressed duplicate IDs, and reconnect recoveries. Alerting on duplicate suppression alone is usually noisy because overlap is expected. A sudden change in its ratio is diagnostic; missing IDs or conflicting payloads for one ID deserve immediate attention.

Short logs beat guesses.

Test both arrival orders, repeated backfill pages, concurrent callbacks, and a reconnect that fails twice before succeeding. Also test two distinct messages with identical text. That last case catches the seductive but unsafe content-hash shortcut.

Where this rule stops

Client-side deduplication does not provide authorization, durable retention, or proof that every message arrived. A healthtech system must establish those properties separately according to its own regulatory and product requirements. This pattern only makes overlapping delivery paths converge on one rendered event.

It is also insufficient for mutable messages unless the event model includes ordering or version semantics. If edits, redactions, and reactions share a message ID, represent the operation explicitly and make each operation idempotent. Otherwise, “already seen” can erase a legitimate state transition.

For ephemeral typing indicators, strict history backfill may not apply at all. Let them expire. For chat messages that must survive reconnects, however, an exact boundary is the wrong target. Preserve identity across storage and publish, merge both paths, and make duplicate delivery boring.

Sources

  • https://ably.com/docs/connect/states#connection-state-recovery
  • https://ably.com/docs/storage-history/history
  • https://pusher.com/docs/channels/using_channels/cache-channels/
  • https://pusher.com/docs/channels/using_channels/presence-channels/
  • https://www.pubnub.com/docs/general/storage
  • https://www.pubnub.com/docs/general/presence/presence-overview
  • https://socket.io/docs/v4/connection-state-recovery
  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: Giving My One-Off Web Experiments an Actual Brand System
description:
How I stopped every new Plaid Labs experiment from looking like a different AI-generated site, and built a shared brand mark + design system instead.

The problem: every new experiment looked like a different app

I've got a small constellation of side projects living under Plaid Labs — Daily Doodle, a couple of maker tools, and whatever I spin up next on a random night. Each one got built independently, usually in a single sitting, which meant each one also got its own accidental visual identity. Different fonts. Different spacing instincts. Different "vibe."

None of them looked bad exactly. They just didn't look like they belonged to each other.

I posted a link to one thing and someone said, oh did you vibe code that? As if that was a negative I should be ashamed of. I get it not everything Ai is good and it made me think. Am I just ok with how this is or do I want to control the look and branding of this?

Step one: a brand mark that actually travels

The first fix was small and dumb-simple on paper: every Plaid Labs page needed the same little signature in the footer. Not a logo file — I wanted something typographic, something that would render consistently anywhere without shipping an image asset.

What I landed on:

<a class="plaid-mark" href="https://theplaidscientist.github.io/">
  <span class="plaid-mark-row">
    <span class="plaid-mark-lede">a</span>
    <span class="plaid-mark-beaker" aria-hidden="true">🧪</span>
    <span class="plaid-mark-word">Plaid Labs</span>
  </span>
  <span class="plaid-mark-sub">
    <span>e</span><span>x</span><span>p</span><span>e</span><span>r</span><span>i</span><span>m</span><span>e</span><span>n</span><span>t</span>
  </span>
</a>

Two lines: a 🧪 Plaid Labs, then experiment underneath, letter-spaced out to match the width of the line above it. A couple of details I had to fight the browser for, in case they save you the same headache:

The emoji was rendering smaller than the capital letter next to it. Emoji glyphs sit smaller within their own em-box than a capital letter does — a beaker sized at 1em next to bold text at the same font-size visually reads as noticeably smaller than the "P" beside it. Bumping it to 1.4em and nudging the baseline with transform: translateY(0.11em) got it to actually match the cap-height.

Major Mono Display — the font I used for "experiment" — looks completely different in uppercase vs. lowercase. Typed in caps, some of its glyphs render as strange filled-in blocks. Typed in lowercase, it renders as these clean, readable outlined letterforms. So the word is authored in lowercase in the HTML even though it reads like a stylized all-caps treatment — that's the font doing the work, not a text-transform.

Stretching "experiment" to match the width of the line above, at any size: instead of guessing at letter-spacing values, I split the word into ten individual <span> letters and put them in a flex row with justify-content: space-between. Whatever width the row above renders at, the letters spread themselves to fill it exactly. No magic numbers, no breaking at different screen sizes.

Major Mono Display only ships one weight (Regular) — so font-weight: bold does nothing. -webkit-text-stroke fakes it instead:

.plaid-mark-sub {
  font-family: "Major Mono Display", ui-monospace, monospace;
  font-weight: 700;
  -webkit-text-stroke: 0.55px currentColor; /* this is what actually bolds it */
}

Step two: a real design system, not just a shared footer

The footer mark fixed the "who made this" signature, but the pages themselves still had no shared language. So I wrote out an actual spec — colors, three type roles, production CSS — and made it the default for anything new I build:

  • Palette: dark charcoal background (#181818), clinical off-white text (#E1E1E1), one accent — a terminal green (#48C774) — spent deliberately instead of smeared everywhere.
  • Type, three roles:
    • A bold display face reserved only for the page's own title/branding — not every heading, just the one moment that's actually the page introducing itself.
    • A monospace face for tags, badges, status readouts — real structural information, not decoration.
    • A neutral body face for everything else — paragraphs, UI, ordinary section headers.

The point of scoping the display face to just the page title was deliberate. My first pass applied it to every h1/h2/h3, and it immediately stopped feeling special — it just became "the font," which is exactly the generic-template trap I was trying to avoid in the first place.

I really just didn't want all my stuff to look like it was made without a human input.

The part where the font choice backfired

I initially speced the display face as Syne at weight 700/800 — bold, sculptural, "avant-garde lab" energy. It looked great in isolation.

Then I shipped it on a real page — a little "Image Cutout" tool — and it looked stretchy. Wide, flared, almost like the letters had been horizontally scaled. My first assumption was a CSS bug: bad font-stretch, a broken fallback, something synthetic going on.

It wasn't a bug. That's just what Syne looks like at heavy weight — wide counters and flared terminals are the actual design of the typeface. It's a deliberate, characterful choice for the right context. It just wasn't the right context sitting directly above plain body text at a normal reading size.

Rather than argue with myself about it, I built a quick side-by-side comparison page: the exact same heading, in Syne (as shipped), a toned-down Syne, and three alternatives with a similar bold/technical energy but tighter, more normal letter proportions. Landed on Bricolage Grotesque — bold, a little experimental, but nothing about it reads as "stretched."

What I actually shipped

The design system now lives as a spec I reuse on every new experiment by default, with two explicit exceptions: Disco Doodle and the main Plaid Labs landing page both keep their own established look, because they're not "new" — they already have an identity worth protecting.

:root {
  --bg-dark: #181818;
  --text-main: #E1E1E1;
  --accent-green: #48C774;

  --font-display: 'Bricolage Grotesque', sans-serif; /* page title/branding only */
  --font-mono: 'JetBrains Mono', monospace;           /* tags, badges, status */
  --font-body: 'Public Sans', sans-serif;              /* everything else */
}

Made it a skill

I asked Claude to remember all the choices we made and create a repeatable skill that would basically be a branding guide that auto triggers every times we create a new site to publish.

None of this was hard, individually. Emoji sizing, font-weight faking, letter-spacing math — each one's a five-minute CSS fix. The thing that actually mattered was treating "brand consistency across side projects" as a real spec worth writing down once, instead of re-deciding it from scratch every time I open a new repo.

I'm super excited to have each new thing we create feel like its mine. Like it has my signature on it so it doesn't just look the same as something anyone else has created.

title: Notes from a 2 AM On-Call: Supabase Realtime Connection Reset Under Next.js SSR Load
description:
Notes from a 2 AM On-Call: Supabase Realtime Connection Reset Under Next.js SSR Load

The Failure Symptom 

[supabase-js] RealtimeClient connection error: Error: WebSocket closed with code 1006
[Next.js] TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'channel')
[Vercel] Function invocation timeout after 10s

Production dashboard went dark at 1:47 AM. No client errors. Server logs showed Supabase Realtime subscriptions silently dropping after 8-12 seconds under concurrent Server Component render load. The kicker? Local dev was flawless. Staging with 10 concurrent users worked. Production with 200+ simultaneous SSR requests collapsed.

The Red Herring

Every Next.js + Supabase tutorial shows this Server Component pattern:

// app/dashboard/page.tsx
import { createClient } from '@/lib/supabase/server'

export default async function Dashboard() {
  const supabase = createClient()
  const channel = supabase
    .channel('public:events')
    .on('postgres_changes', 
      { event: '*', schema: 'public', table: 'events' },
      (payload) => console.log(payload)
    )
    .subscribe()

  const { data } = await supabase.from('events').select()
  return <EventList events={data} />
}

Under Next.js 15 concurrent RSC streaming, each render creates a new Supabase client instance with a fresh Realtime connection. With 50 users hitting the dashboard simultaneously, we spawned 50+ WebSocket connections to Supabase Realtime within 2 seconds. Supabase's connection pooling throttled us. Connections queued, timed out at 10s, then cascaded into retry storms.

The misleading part? createClient() in Server Components feels stateless and React-idiomatic. But Realtime WebSockets are stateful long-lived TCP connections. React's render concurrency model conflicts with connection pool limits (Supabase Free: 60 concurrent, Pro: 500).

The Root Cause & Runnable Fix

Realtime subscriptions belong in Client Components with singleton connection management, not Server Components. Server Components should handle initial data fetch only.

Fixed Architecture

1. Server Component (RSC) — Initial Data Only

// app/dashboard/page.tsx
import { createClient } from '@/lib/supabase/server'
import { RealtimeEvents } from './realtime-events'

export default async function Dashboard() {
  const supabase = createClient()
  const { data: initialEvents } = await supabase
    .from('events')
    .select()
    .order('created_at', { ascending: false })
    .limit(50)

  return <RealtimeEvents initialEvents={initialEvents} />
}

2. Client Component — Singleton Realtime Connection

// app/dashboard/realtime-events.tsx
'use client'

import { createClient } from '@/lib/supabase/client'
import { useEffect, useState } from 'react'
import type { RealtimeChannel } from '@supabase/supabase-js'

let globalChannel: RealtimeChannel | null = null

export function RealtimeEvents({ initialEvents }) {
  const [events, setEvents] = useState(initialEvents)
  const supabase = createClient()

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!globalChannel) {
      globalChannel = supabase
        .channel('events-feed')
        .on('postgres_changes',
          { event: '*', schema: 'public', table: 'events' },
          (payload) => {
            setEvents((prev) => [payload.new, ...prev].slice(0, 50))
          }
        )
        .subscribe((status) => {
          if (status === 'SUBSCRIBED') {
            console.log('[Realtime] Connected')
          }
        })
    }

    return () => {
      // Keep connection alive across component remounts
      // Only cleanup on actual unmount (e.g., route navigation)
    }
  }, [])

  return (
    <ul>
      {events.map((event) => (
        <li key={event.id}>{event.title}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  )
}

Key Fix: Module-level globalChannel singleton prevents duplicate subscriptions across React StrictMode double-renders and Fast Refresh. Connection count dropped from 50+ to 1 per client browser session.

Monitoring Addition 

// lib/supabase/client.ts
import { createBrowserClient } from '@supabase/ssr'

export function createClient() {
  const client = createBrowserClient(
    process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL!,
    process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY!
  )

  client.realtime.onOpen(() => {
    console.log('[Realtime] WS open', new Date().toISOString())
  })

  client.realtime.onClose((event) => {
    console.error('[Realtime] WS closed', event.code, event.reason)
  })

  return client
}

After deployment: zero connection resets, consistent 1-2 second subscription latency even at 500 concurrent users.

Invariant Rule

Realtime subscriptions are stateful I/O—never instantiate them in Server Components or React render loops.

If your Server Component needs live data, fetch the baseline snapshot server-side, then hydrate the Client Component with a singleton Realtime subscription. This pattern applies to any WebSocket/SSE integration (Pusher, Ably, Socket.IO) under Next.js RSC concurrency.

Connection pooling isn't just a backend database concern—it governs client WebSocket fan-out too.

title: Top DevOps Service Providers for Cloud Infrastructure Management
description:
Moving to the cloud is the easy decision. Running it well month after month is where teams lose weekends: drifting environments, untagged resources, clusters nobody dares to upgrade. If you are shortlisting DevOps development services for your cloud, or comparing DevOps service providers for cloud infrastructure management more broadly, the eight companies below cover everything from hands-on engineering to full managed operations.

A good provider treats infrastructure as software. That idea sits behind infrastructure as code, the practice of defining and managing resources through machine-readable files instead of manual setup. It also underlies the broader model of managed services, where a third party keeps your IT environment running on a proactive, subscription basis instead of break/fix support. And for container-based systems, Kubernetes is the open source platform most providers on this list build around.

The providers

N-iX

N-iX was founded in 2002 and reports 2,400+ engineers, with a DevOps group of 70+ experts and 270+ certified cloud specialists. It holds AWS Premier Tier, Microsoft Solutions Partner and Google Cloud partner status, plus ISO 27001. Its DevOps page covers infrastructure as code (Terraform, Ansible, CloudFormation), cost optimization, CI/CD, container orchestration and monitoring, and cites a UK energy supplier whose operational costs fell 70% after cloud modernization. Natural fit for large, multi-cloud estates.

AppRecode

AppRecode, working since 2019 from Delaware and Lviv, lists cloud infrastructure management, managed AWS and Azure cloud, FinOps and Kubernetes among its services, backed by team certifications such as AWS Solutions Architect, Certified Kubernetes Administrator, HashiCorp Terraform Associate and FinOps Certified Engineer. The most relevant case for this topic is a migration for a US provider of AI-powered contact center software. The team moved services from EC2 to Amazon EKS with Terraform covering the infrastructure, a Direct Connect link to the on-premises environment, GitOps with ArgoCD and GitHub Actions pipelines, and monitoring in Datadog and Logz.io. The case is described in qualitative terms (dynamic scaling, fewer manual interventions, faster deployments) with no percentages.

A longer engagement is the Media Intelligence Platform: a New York AdTech company with about 150 employees. Over roughly three years, three dedicated AppRecode engineers codified AWS environments in Terraform, built Jenkins and GitLab pipelines, ran workloads on Kubernetes and ECS, connected accounts and regions through Transit Gateway peering, and set up CloudWatch and New Relic alerting. Reported results include 70% less deployment time, 99.995% uptime and a mean time to recovery under one day.

Sigma Software

Sigma Software divides its offer into cloud DevOps consulting, DevOps transformation and cloud managed services, the last including infrastructure management and monitoring under an SLA and cloud disaster recovery. It is an AWS Advanced Tier Services Partner and cites 100+ projects in migration, DevOps and infrastructure automation. One cited case is a platform migrated from on-premises to Azure for a client called Mikz, described as delivering the same performance at 10% of the earlier infrastructure cost.

Ciklum

Ciklum advertises 3,000+ engineers certified across AWS, Azure and GCP. Its DevOps page mentions IaC, FinOps, serverless, DevSecOps with automated GDPR, HIPAA and SOC 2 checks, and 24/7 RunOps with observability. Cases include Doxy.me, where it automated CI/CD and HIPAA-compliant cloud operations for a telemedicine product.

Mirantis

Mirantis is closer to a platform vendor than a services shop. Based in Campbell, California, it builds the k0rdent and k0s Kubernetes projects, offers cloud platform operations and workload migration services, and says it serves thousands of customers in 90 countries with 200+ staff on managed and professional services. Useful when your main challenge is running Kubernetes across several data centers or clouds.

ELEKS

ELEKS lists CI/CD, IaC, containerization, continuous monitoring and cloud management, holds SOC 2 and ISO 9001 badges and partner status with AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft. Its DPD case describes a six-year cloud migration and re-engineering program, and Pace gets L2 support for a cloud product with 99.99% effective uptime.

Binbash

An AWS specialist with Advanced Tier status, the AWS DevOps Services Competency and Amazon EKS delivery designation, plus a Well-Architected Review offer and a reusable infrastructure library. A good choice if you want AWS depth rather than breadth.

Opsfleet

Opsfleet embeds 90+ engineers into client teams and is an AWS Premier Tier Services Partner. Its list includes Kubernetes adoption, a shift to Graviton instances, DevSecOps and disaster recovery plan implementation.

How to compare them

Look at who owns the code afterwards, how cost reporting works, and whether the provider can show an environment that was rebuilt from scratch. Ask for the upgrade plan for Kubernetes and for the last disaster recovery test. Providers that answer with dates rather than adjectives are usually the ones that run infrastructure for a living.

title: Why your Node.js API is leaking sensitive files (and how to fix it in 5 minutes)
description:
As developers, we often focus on writing clean code, optimizing database queries, and building robust APIs. But there is one silent killer that takes down hundreds of production environments every day: exposing sensitive files in the public root directory.

I've seen this in Node.js projects, PHP, and static sites deployed to the cloud. You think your .env, your .git folder, or your database dumps are safe... until someone runs a simple curl command and downloads your entire infrastructure.

Let's see how this happens, and how to test your own site in less than 5 minutes.

The Silent Threat: Public Folders

If your web server or CDN is misconfigured, a malicious user can try to access common paths like:

  • https://yourdomain.com/.env
  • https://yourdomain.com/.git/HEAD
  • https://yourdomain.com/backup.zip
  • https://yourdomain.com/db.sql

If the server returns 200 OK instead of 403 Forbidden or 404 Not Found, you have a critical vulnerability. Your database credentials, API keys, and source code are publicly available.

How to check if you are exposed (Right Now)

Open your terminal and run this simple curl command against your own domain:


bash
curl -I https://yourdomain.com/.env
Look at the HTTP status code:

If you see HTTP/1.1 200 OK: Panic. Your .env file is exposed. Fix it immediately.

If you see HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden or HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found: You are safe.

How to fix it (Nginx/Apache)
If you are using Nginx, add this block to your server configuration:

nginx
location ~ /\.(env|git|svn|htaccess|htpasswd) {
    deny all;
    return 404;
}

location ~ \.(bak|old|sql|zip|tar\.gz)$ {
    deny all;
    return 404;
}
If you are on Express.js, ensure your static file middleware is not serving hidden files:

javascript
app.use(express.static('public', {
  dotfiles: 'deny',
  index: false
}));
How to automate this check
Checking this manually every time you deploy is a pain. There are tools that can automate this for you and give you a full security report.

I've been building a tool called Sealgrade that runs over 15 external security checks (including this exact file exposure test, SSL, DNS, and missing HTTP headers) and gives you a 0-100 health score. It's free to run an audit, and it gives you concrete remediation snippets like the ones above.

If you are deploying to production, it's worth a 30-second check: Audit your web here.

Stay safe out there, and keep your .env files private!

title: DuckDB vs Spark: which workloads actually need a cluster
description:
Most "DuckDB vs Spark" questions are really a sizing question. Spark is a distributed engine: it splits a job across many machines and pays to coordinate them. DuckDB is an in-process engine: it runs the whole job on one machine and pays nothing to coordinate. Which one is faster depends almost entirely on whether one machine can hold the work.

So the useful question is not which engine is better. It is: how many bytes does your job actually touch, and does that fit on one box? Here is the arithmetic, where a cluster earns its cost, and what one node has handled for me. I have not run Spark in production; this is the single-node side of the line, measured, plus what Spark's own documentation says about the other side.

DuckDB vs Spark: what each one is built for

Spark spreads work over a cluster. A driver plans the job, executors on many machines each process part of the data, and a shuffle moves rows between machines when a join or group-by needs them together. If a machine dies, Spark rebuilds the lost piece. Its documentation puts it plainly: if any partition of a cached dataset is lost, "it will automatically be recomputed using the transformations that originally created it." That is what you rent a cluster for: data larger than any one machine, and jobs that keep going when one machine fails.

DuckDB is a columnar SQL engine that runs inside your Python process, a CLI or a service. No driver, no executors, no shuffle over a network. It reads Parquet and CSV in place, uses every core, and spills to disk when a join or sort outgrows memory. The tuning guide lists GROUP BY, JOIN, ORDER BY and window functions as operators that can work larger than memory.

Both read the same Parquet. That matters more than any benchmark: the choice is reversible, because the files don't care which engine opens them.

The sizing math that decides it

The number that matters is the working set: the bytes a job has to process after partition pruning and column selection. It is not the size of the lake.

Three steps get you there.

1. Start from what the job reads, not what exists. A 20 TB events table, partitioned by day, queried for the last 30 days, touching 6 of 60 columns, reads roughly 30/365 × 6/60 of the table. That is about 160 GB on disk before any filter on row values. Parquet compresses, so memory use runs higher than disk size. But most of that work streams through and never has to sit in memory at once.

2. Budget memory by operation. DuckDB's environment guide gives the rule of thumb: about 1–2 GB of memory per thread for aggregation-heavy work and 3–4 GB per thread for join-heavy work. So a 32-thread job needs roughly 32–64 GB for aggregations, or 96–128 GB for joins. That is one ordinary server, not a cluster.

3. Compare with the biggest box you can rent. Single machines are large now. AWS lists an x2iedn.metal with 128 vCPUs and 4,096 GiB of memory. You don't need that. The point is that the ceiling of "one machine" sits far above where most teams assume it is.

Local-First Analytics draws the same line. Chapter 5 suggests DuckDB for up to about 1 TB of partitioned Parquet for aggregation-heavy work, and less for join-heavy work. It also warns that many-to-many joins blow up intermediate state whatever the input size. Its rule of thumb for starting local-first is a working set that fits in 32 GB of RAM and fewer than ten people running queries. Both bars are much lower than where a single node actually gives out.

If your working set after this arithmetic is in the gigabytes or low hundreds of gigabytes, you are running Spark for the cluster's sake, not the data's.

This is the first part. The full post — including the rest of the working details — is on my site: DuckDB vs Spark: which workloads actually need a cluster

title: Same SQL, Fast for One Value, Slow for Another
description:
The order-history screen is fast for every customer except one. Or it's fast all morning and crawls all afternoon. Or it was fine for months and became slow the night after a restart, with nobody deploying anything. You pull the statement and run it yourself with the problem value, and it comes back instantly. The SQL is identical. The data hasn't changed. The plan in the execution history is the same plan it always uses.

That last sentence is the clue. The statement uses a bind variable, which is the right thing to do, and the cursor for it holds one plan. That plan was chosen for whichever value happened to arrive first. On a column where values are wildly unevenly distributed, that's a plan built for one kind of caller and handed to every other. This post is how that happens, why Oracle's safety net for it, adaptive cursor sharing, doesn't always catch it, how to see it in the cursor cache, and how to fix it, with a lab that reproduces it on demand.

Bind peeking: the first caller picks the plan

When a statement with a bind variable is hard-parsed, the optimizer peeks at the actual bind value and costs the plan as if that value were a literal. That's usually good: a plan built for a real value beats a plan built for an average. The catch is what happens next. The finished cursor goes into the shared pool and every later execution reuses it, whatever value it binds. The plan is decided once, by the first caller.

On a column with evenly spread values, that doesn't matter: one value costs about the same as another. It matters on a skewed column, where a few values are rare and one is everywhere: a status code where 99.9% of rows are CLOSED, a country column dominated by one country, a flag that's almost always N. If the column has a histogram, the optimizer knows about the skew and builds very different plans for the rare value and the common one. Peeking means it builds one of them, and everyone gets that one.

The classic shape is a join. For a rare value, a few hundred driving rows, the best plan is nested loops: for each order, look up its customer by primary key. For the common value, hundreds of thousands of rows, the best plan is a hash join: read both tables once and match them in memory. Nested loops for the common value means one index probe per row, hundreds of thousands of times.

A bind-variable statement is optimized once, for the first value it sees, and the cursor is reused for every value after. On a skewed column with a histogram, a rare first value produces a nested-loops plan that is right for a few rows; the common value then inherits it and pays for one index probe per row. Adaptive cursor sharing can split the cursor into one plan per kind of value, but only once it has seen executions that differ enough; until then every caller gets the first caller's plan.

Adaptive cursor sharing: the safety net, with holes

Oracle has known about this since 11g, and adaptive cursor sharing (ACS) is its answer. A cursor that peeked a bind on a column with a histogram is marked bind-sensitive. Oracle then watches its executions, sorting each one into a small number of buckets by how much work it did. If executions with different bind values land in clearly different buckets, the cursor becomes bind-aware: from then on, each new value is checked against the existing child cursors, and a value that needs a different plan gets its own child cursor with its own plan.

That works well when the difference is visible. The hole is in "clearly different". If the rare value's first execution and the common value's executions land in the same bucket, ACS sees nothing to react to, and the cursor stays exactly as it was. And whether you're protected can depend on the order in which values arrive after each restart, shared pool flush, or statistics refresh, which nobody controls.

Prove it

The lab builds ORDERS with 200,000 rows and a skewed STATUS, 200 OPEN and 199,800 CLOSED, with a frequency histogram on the column, and joins it to a 1,000,000-row CUSTOMERS table. It flushes the shared pool, runs the statement once with 'OPEN', then five times with 'CLOSED', each in a fresh session, measuring session logical reads from V$MYSTAT and the child cursor each execution ran:

>> Fresh shared pool. The SAME statement, bound:  ... where o.status = :s
   OPEN    rows=200     logical reads=2624     child cursor=0  plan=NESTED LOOPS
   CLOSED  rows=199800  logical reads=603391   child cursor=0  plan=NESTED LOOPS
   CLOSED  rows=199800  logical reads=603354   child cursor=0  plan=NESTED LOOPS
   CLOSED  rows=199800  logical reads=603354   child cursor=0  plan=NESTED LOOPS
   CLOSED  rows=199800  logical reads=603354   child cursor=0  plan=NESTED LOOPS
   CLOSED  rows=199800  logical reads=603354   child cursor=0  plan=NESTED LOOPS

The optimizer peeked 'OPEN', estimated 199 rows from the histogram, and chose nested loops, which is right for 200 rows. Every 'CLOSED' run then reused child cursor 0 and its nested loops: 603,354 logical reads, five times in a row. Adaptive cursor sharing never marked the cursor bind-aware. The first 'OPEN' execution, including its hard parse, and every 'CLOSED' execution fell into the same middle bucket, so the safety net never saw a difference. (The plan was even an adaptive plan, with a statistics collector that can switch join methods, but an adaptive plan settles on its first execution and the settled plan is what gets reused.)

Give 'CLOSED' its own plan and the cost collapses:

>> The fix for a skewed, low-cardinality column: the predicate as a literal -> one cursor + plan per value
   CLOSED  rows=199800  logical reads=34716    child cursor=0  plan=HASH JOIN
   OPEN    rows=200     logical reads=806      child cursor=0  plan=NESTED LOOPS

34,716 logical reads instead of 603,354: the same rows, 17 times less work, because the plan was built for the value it runs. And 'OPEN' keeps its cheap nested loops at 806.

Don't take my word for it — run it. The bind-peeking lab builds the skewed tables on Oracle Database Free, peeks the rare value, and asserts that every common-value run inherits nested loops on the same cursor at 10 times or more the work of a hash join, without adaptive cursor sharing splitting it. Then it gives each value its own plan and asserts the common value drops to 10% or less of that work. If the trap stops reproducing or the fix stops working, the run fails. Proven on every CI push.

See it in your own system

Start from the statement, not the plan. A query whose cost swings by value shows up as high variance in buffer gets per execution for one SQL_ID. Then look at its cursors:

-- one row per child cursor: which ones are bind-sensitive / bind-aware, and what each costs
SELECT child_number, plan_hash_value, is_bind_sensitive, is_bind_aware,
       executions, ROUND(buffer_gets / NULLIF(executions, 0)) AS gets_per_exec
FROM   v$sql
WHERE  sql_id = '&sql_id'
ORDER  BY child_number;
  • Bind-sensitive Y, bind-aware N, one child, huge gets per execution: the lab's situation. The cursor knows the bind matters, but it never split.
  • Several children with different plan hash values, bind-aware Y: ACS is doing its job.
  • V$SQL_CS_HISTOGRAM shows how its executions were bucketed; all executions in one bucket means ACS has nothing to react to.

To see which value the plan was built for, ask for the peeked binds:

SELECT * FROM TABLE(DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR('&sql_id', 0, 'TYPICAL +PEEKED_BINDS'));

In the lab that prints :S ... 'OPEN' above a nested-loops plan, the whole diagnosis in one screen. In AWR, the same statement appearing with more than one plan hash value over time, with very different elapsed times, is the historical fingerprint: the plan changes whenever the cursor is rebuilt with a different first value.

The fix

Pick by how the column behaves. In order of preference:

  • For a skewed, low-cardinality column, use a literal for that predicate. A status code with five values makes five cursors, each with the right plan. That's no hard-parse storm: the storm comes from literal values with high cardinality, like IDs. Keep binds for everything else in the statement. This is the exception to "bind everything" that the bind variables post ends on, and the lab's fix.
  • Split the query in the application when it already knows which kind of value it has: a separate statement for the "open orders" screen and the "history" screen. Two statements, two plans, no guessing.
  • A SQL plan baseline with more than one accepted plan. Baselines cooperate with adaptive cursor sharing: accept the nested-loops plan and the hash-join plan, and each value can use the one that fits. See SQL plan management.
  • Remove the histogram, if one plan is genuinely acceptable for every value. Without it the optimizer stops distinguishing values and picks one middle-of-the-road plan. It's a legitimate choice when no value is catastrophic, but a bad one when, as here, the wrong plan costs 17 times the work.

What not to do: don't "fix" it by flushing the shared pool or purging the cursor when it goes bad. That just rolls the dice again on which value arrives first, and the problem returns on its own schedule.

What teams get wrong

  • Blaming the data or the database for "random" slowness. It isn't random: it's the plan built for whichever value arrived first, and it changes when the cursor is rebuilt.
  • Testing by hand. Paste the statement into a SQL tool with the slow value typed in and it's different SQL text, so it gets its own hard parse and the right plan, and it's fast. The problem only shows on the shared, bind-variable cursor the application uses.
  • Trusting adaptive cursor sharing to handle it. It helps when executions differ enough to land in different buckets, and quietly does nothing when they don't, as the lab shows five times in a row.
  • Flushing the shared pool as the fix. It resets the lottery; it doesn't change the odds.
  • Disabling bind peeking database-wide. It's a hidden parameter, and switching it off trades one wrong plan for a plan built for no real value at all, for every statement in the database.
  • Turning a whole application to literals to escape it. That's the hard-parse storm all over again. Use literals only for the skewed, low-cardinality predicate.

Frequently asked questions

What is bind peeking in Oracle?

Bind peeking is the optimizer's behavior of looking at the actual value of a bind variable when it hard-parses a statement, and optimizing the plan as if that value were a literal. It produces a plan suited to a real value rather than to an average. The resulting cursor is then stored in the shared pool and reused by every later execution of the same statement, regardless of the value those executions bind. So the plan is effectively chosen by whichever value happened to arrive first when the cursor was built. On columns with evenly distributed values this rarely matters; on skewed columns with histograms it can make the same SQL fast for one value and very slow for another.

Why is the same Oracle query fast for one value and slow for another?

Usually because the statement uses a bind variable on a skewed column and the cursor's single plan was built for a different kind of value. If the first execution peeked a rare value, the optimizer may have chosen nested loops or an index-driven plan that is ideal for a few rows; every later execution reuses that plan, and a common value matching hundreds of thousands of rows then pays for one index probe per row. In the companion lab the same join costs 2,624 logical reads for a rare value and 603,354 for the common value on the inherited plan, versus 34,716 with its own hash-join plan. Running the query by hand with the slow value often looks fast, because a manual run with different text gets its own hard parse and the right plan.

What is adaptive cursor sharing?

Adaptive cursor sharing, introduced in Oracle 11g, lets a statement with bind variables have more than one plan. A cursor that peeked a bind on a column with a histogram is marked bind-sensitive, and Oracle monitors how much work its executions do, sorting them into buckets. If executions with different bind values land in clearly different buckets, the cursor is marked bind-aware, and new bind values are then checked against the existing child cursors; a value that needs a different plan gets a new child cursor with its own plan. You can see it in V$SQL (IS_BIND_SENSITIVE, IS_BIND_AWARE and multiple child cursors) and in V$SQL_CS_HISTOGRAM.

Why didn't adaptive cursor sharing fix my plan?

Because adaptive cursor sharing only reacts when it sees executions that differ enough to fall into different workload buckets. If the rare value's first execution and the common value's executions land in the same bucket, the cursor stays bind-sensitive but never becomes bind-aware, and every execution keeps using the original plan. In the companion lab the first execution with the rare value, including its hard parse, and all five executions with the common value fell into the same bucket, so the cursor never split even though the common value did 17 times the necessary work each time. Whether a given workload is protected can also depend on the order in which values arrive after a restart, a shared pool flush, or a statistics refresh.

How do I find which bind value a plan was built for?

Use DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR with the PEEKED_BINDS format option, for example SELECT * FROM TABLE(DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR('sql_id', child_number, 'TYPICAL +PEEKED_BINDS')). The output includes a Peeked Binds section showing the value the optimizer saw when it built that child cursor's plan. Combine it with V$SQL for the same SQL_ID: one row per child cursor, its plan hash value, whether it is bind-sensitive and bind-aware, and buffer gets per execution. A single child with huge gets per execution and a peeked value from the rare end of a skewed column is the bind-peeking signature.

Should I use literals instead of bind variables to avoid bind peeking problems?

Only for the specific predicate on a skewed, low-cardinality column, such as a status code or a flag with a handful of values. Each distinct literal gets its own cursor and its own plan, and with only a few distinct values that means only a few cursors, which is no burden on the shared pool. Keep bind variables for high-cardinality values like IDs, names, and dates: using literals there causes a hard-parse storm, with thousands of nearly identical cursors, shared pool pressure, and latch contention. The rule is bind by default, literal by exception, and the exception is low-cardinality skew.

Does flushing the shared pool fix a bad bind-peeked plan?

Only by accident, and only temporarily. Flushing the shared pool, or purging the one cursor with DBMS_SHARED_POOL.PURGE, forces a new hard parse, and the new plan will be built for whichever bind value arrives first afterwards. If that is the common value, things look fixed until the next time the cursor is rebuilt with the rare value first; if it is the rare value, nothing changes. It resets the lottery without changing the odds. Fix the cause instead: give the skewed predicate a literal, split the statement in the application, or use a SQL plan baseline with more than one accepted plan.

Should I disable bind peeking?

No. Disabling bind peeking requires a hidden parameter, which should only be changed under Oracle Support's guidance, and it applies to every statement in the database. Without peeking, the optimizer builds plans using average selectivity rather than any real value, so instead of a plan that is right for some values you get a plan that is right for none of the skewed ones. Address the specific statements that suffer: literals for low-cardinality skewed predicates, separate statements per case, SQL plan baselines, or removing a histogram that does more harm than good.

Bind peeking sits right at the meeting point of two other posts in this series. Bind variables are why the cursor is shared in the first place, and that's the right default; indexes are why the same predicate deserves an index for one value and a full scan for another. The plan itself is something you can read in the execution plan, the histogram that sets the trap comes from optimizer statistics, and SQL plan management is one way to pin more than one good plan. When one statement is fast for some values and slow for others, look at the peeked bind before anything else, and prove it the way that ends the argument — with the bind-peeking lab, where the same query costs 2,624 reads for one value and 603,354 for another until each value gets its own plan.

Originally published at uptimearchitect.com.

title: Designing Dynamic Mongoose Schemas for a Drag-and-Drop Page Builder
description:
Most full-stack tutorials cover standard CRUD applications where the data model is strictly defined: a post has a title, a body, and an author. But what happens when you need to build a system where the user dictates the layout?

When architecting dynamic SaaS tools, like a drag-and-drop brochure builder for marketing teams, the database must be flexible enough to store UI components in any order, yet structured enough to query efficiently. Here is how to design a scalable, array-based schema with Mongoose and render it in React.

The Limitations of Rigid Schemas

In a traditional application, your database schema mirrors a static UI. For a standard blog, the schema looks like this:

{ title: String, content: String, imageUrl: String }

This rigid structure breaks down for dynamic page builders. If a user wants to stack a text block, an image gallery, a call-to-action, and then another text block, a static schema can't represent it. You end up with messy workarounds like content_1, content_2, or giant, unsearchable HTML strings stored in the database.

To build a true component-based architecture, the database must store an ordered array of independent building blocks.

Structuring Array-Based Mongoose Schemas

The solution is an array of subdocuments where each item represents one UI component. A type identifier lets different data structures live in the same array.

const mongoose = require('mongoose');

const BlockSchema = new mongoose.Schema({
  type: {
    type: String,
    required: true,
    enum: ['TEXT', 'IMAGE_GALLERY', 'CALL_TO_ACTION', 'VIDEO'],
  },
  // The shape of `data` varies based on the block type
  data: {
    type: mongoose.Schema.Types.Mixed,
    required: true,
  },
  order: {
    type: Number,
    required: true,
  },
}); // each block keeps its default _id, which we'll use as a stable React key

const BrochureSchema = new mongoose.Schema(
  {
    title: { type: String, required: true },
    author: { type: mongoose.Schema.Types.ObjectId, ref: 'User' },
    blocks: [BlockSchema],
    isPublished: { type: Boolean, default: false },
  },
  { timestamps: true }
);

module.exports = mongoose.model('Brochure', BrochureSchema);

With data: mongoose.Schema.Types.Mixed, the nested payload is schema-less. A TEXT block might store { text: "Hello World", align: "center" }, while an IMAGE_GALLERY block stores { urls: ["img1.jpg", "img2.jpg"], layout: "grid" }.

Gotcha: Mongoose can't detect changes inside a Mixed field. If you modify a block's data in place, call brochure.markModified('blocks') before save(), or the change silently won't persist.

Note: MongoDB arrays already preserve insertion order, so the order field is technically optional. I keep it explicit because it makes reordering and debugging easier when blocks are dragged around.

A stricter alternative: discriminators

When you want per-type validation inside the schema itself, Mongoose supports embedded discriminators on document arrays:

const BlockSchema = new mongoose.Schema(
  { order: { type: Number, required: true } },
  { discriminatorKey: 'type' }
);

const BrochureSchema = new mongoose.Schema({
  title: { type: String, required: true },
  blocks: [BlockSchema],
});

const blocksPath = BrochureSchema.path('blocks');

blocksPath.discriminator(
  'TEXT',
  new mongoose.Schema({ text: String, align: String })
);
blocksPath.discriminator(
  'IMAGE_GALLERY',
  new mongoose.Schema({ urls: [String], layout: String })
);

Mixed gives you speed of iteration in an early-stage product. Discriminators give you stronger guarantees once the block types stabilize.

Mapping Data to React Components

Once your Node.js backend serves this array, the React frontend needs to translate the JSON back into UI components.

Instead of writing a long if/else chain, use a component dictionary. It keeps the codebase modular and the rendering logic flat.

import TextBlock from './blocks/TextBlock';
import ImageGallery from './blocks/ImageGallery';
import CtaBlock from './blocks/CtaBlock';
import VideoBlock from './blocks/VideoBlock';

// 1. Create a component dictionary
const ComponentMap = {
  TEXT: TextBlock,
  IMAGE_GALLERY: ImageGallery,
  CALL_TO_ACTION: CtaBlock,
  VIDEO: VideoBlock,
};

export default function BrochureRenderer({ blocks }) {
  // 2. Sort blocks by their order property
  const sortedBlocks = [...blocks].sort((a, b) => a.order - b.order);

  return (
    <div className="brochure-container">
      {sortedBlocks.map((block) => {
        // 3. Dynamically resolve the component
        const BlockComponent = ComponentMap[block.type];

        if (!BlockComponent) {
          return <p key={block._id}>Unknown block type</p>;
        }

        return <BlockComponent key={block._id} data={block.data} />;
      })}
    </div>
  );
}

Using the block's _id as the key (instead of the array index) matters in a builder: when users reorder blocks, index keys make React reuse the wrong component state.

This architecture scales well. When the business asks for a new feature, say an interactive map block, you add MAP to the Mongoose enum and map it to a new <MapBlock /> in React. The core rendering engine never needs to change.

Production Considerations

1. Validate and sanitize the payload.
Because Mixed bypasses Mongoose's type checking, the validation burden moves to your controllers. Validate each block's data against a per-type schema (Zod, Joi, or similar) before saving:

const { z } = require('zod');

const dataSchemas = {
  TEXT: z.object({
    text: z.string().max(5000),
    align: z.enum(['left', 'center', 'right']).default('left'),
  }),
  IMAGE_GALLERY: z.object({
    urls: z.array(z.string().url()).max(20),
    layout: z.enum(['grid', 'carousel']),
  }),
};

function validateBlock(block) {
  const schema = dataSchemas[block.type];
  if (!schema) throw new Error(`Unsupported block type: ${block.type}`);
  return schema.parse(block.data);
}

If any block renders user-supplied HTML, sanitize it (for example with DOMPurify) before it reaches dangerouslySetInnerHTML. React escapes plain text by default, but not that.

2. Lazy-load heavy blocks.
If your builder includes heavy components (3D viewers, large video players), code-split the component map with React.lazy and Suspense, so the browser only downloads the JavaScript for block types that actually appear on the page:

import { lazy, Suspense } from 'react';

const ComponentMap = {
  TEXT: TextBlock,
  IMAGE_GALLERY: ImageGallery,
  VIDEO: lazy(() => import('./blocks/VideoBlock')),
};

// Wrap the rendered list once:
<Suspense fallback={<div className="block-skeleton" />}>
  {/* ...sortedBlocks.map(...) */}
</Suspense>

3. Index the parent, not the payload.
Don't index the unstructured data object inside blocks. It adds index size without helping your queries. Index the parent fields you actually filter on, like author and isPublished, to keep fetch queries fast.

4. Mind the document size limit.
A MongoDB document is capped at 16 MB. That's plenty for blocks that store text and URLs, but store media as URLs (S3, Cloudinary, etc.), never as embedded binary data.

Wrapping Up

Building a custom SaaS tool requires shifting from a page-based mindset to a component-based mindset, not just in React, but all the way down to the database schema.

If you're building something similar, I'd like to hear how you handle block validation and versioning. Let me know in the comments.
