title: ER Diagram vs Database Schema: What’s the Difference?
description:
An ER diagram and a database schema can look like the same thing at first. They are related, but they are used at different moments: first, you plan how the data should connect; then you create the real tables, columns, keys, and rules in the database.

Think of a clinic named HyperClinic. This clinic needs to store patients, doctors, specializations, and appointments.

A quick way to do this is to store everything in one table, called appointments:
appointment_id patient_name patient_phone doctor_name specialization appointment_time
16 Marit Solheim 555-0147 Owen Wilson Cardiology 2026-10-20 10:00

This approach works for one row, but it causes problems when you add another appointment for Marit, change Dr. Wilson's specialization, or have two patients with the same name.

The patient information is repeated. The doctor information is repeated. A typo can lead to inconsistency. And nothing prevents creating an appointment for a doctor who does not exist.

To avoid these problems, the team needs to plan the database before creating tables.

ER Diagram vs Database Schema

The key point of differentiation is not the shape of the boxes and arrows. It is the stage of development.
Stage Key question Objects defined What the diagram shows
Conceptual ER diagram What does the company need to store? Entities and relationships Boxes and lines, no fields
Logical data model How should the data be structured? Attributes, keys, normalized relationships Fields with key icons and relationship lines, no data types
Physical database schema How will PostgreSQL implement it? Tables, columns, data types, constraints, indexes, and DDL statements Fields with data types

A *schema diagram* is a graphic representation of the database schema. Such diagrams are also referred to as physical ER diagrams.

A *database schema* is the actual structure stored in PostgreSQL and comprises objects such as tables, columns, primary and foreign keys, constraints, and indexes.

Thus, this is not a binary choice. A database design is typically developed from an ER diagram through the logical data model to the database schema.

In this article, we will build HyperClinic in the same order: Step 1 is the conceptual ER diagram, Steps 2 to 4 build the logical model, and Step 5 creates the physical PostgreSQL schema.

Start with the Requirements

Nobody will start writing CREATE TABLE before the team figures out the task.

In our case, HyperClinic must be able to:

  • save patient information
  • save doctors and their specializations
  • create appointments
  • show which patient sees which doctor
  • ensure appointments refer to existing patients and doctors

The job names depend on the company. Requirements may be gathered by a business analyst and designed by a database architect, data modeler, backend developer, or DBA. In a small company, one person may do several of these jobs.

What is important is the workflow, not the name.

The team should ask itself such questions as:

  • Is it possible for one patient to have several appointments?
  • Is it possible for one doctor to have many patients?
  • Do all doctors have only one specialization?
  • Is it possible to create an appointment without a doctor?
  • Is it possible to create two appointments with the same doctor for the same time?

These are the business rules that PostgreSQL won't be able to guess.

Step 1: Create the Conceptual ER Diagram

Before deciding on columns, data types, or SQL, first identify what HyperClinic needs to store:

  • Patient
  • Doctor
  • Appointment
  • Specialization

An *entity* is simply something the system needs to store.

This is a *conceptual ER diagram*. It helps the team see the big picture without getting into implementation details. The boxes show the entities. The lines show their relationships. There are no columns, primary keys, foreign keys, or PostgreSQL data types yet.

The relationships are:

  • A patient has many appointments.
  • A doctor has many appointments.
  • An appointment is made by one patient and one doctor.
  • A specialization has many doctors.
  • Each doctor has one specialization.

Step 2: Add Attributes and Primary Keys

This is the point where the model becomes *logical*.

The conceptual diagram tells us that HyperClinic has patients, doctors, appointments, and specializations. The logical model answers the next question: *what information belongs to each one?*

You now add attributes, choose identifiers, and organize the data so the same fact is not stored in several places. You are still designing the structure. You are not choosing PostgreSQL types such as VARCHAR(100) or TIMESTAMP yet.

Think of it like planning a house:

  • the conceptual diagram says the house needs a kitchen, bedrooms, and a bathroom;
  • the logical model decides what belongs in each room;
  • the physical schema gives the builder the exact materials and measurements.

The logical model takes three steps: attributes and primary keys (this step), normalization (Step 3), and foreign keys (Step 4).

Start with the attributes. For each entity, write down what the system needs to know about it:
Entity Attributes
Patient first name, last name, date of birth, phone
Doctor first name, last name, specialization
Specialization name
Appointment patient, doctor, date and time, reason, status

Then give every entity a *primary key*. A primary key is a column, or a set of columns, that uniquely identifies a row.

For instance, patient_id = 1 must identify only one patient. A name cannot be used as a primary key, as patients can have the same name and names change over time.

The same holds for doctors, specializations, and appointments: doctor_id, specialization_id, and appointment_id.

Step 3: Normalize the Logical Model

Normalization means organizing data so each fact is stored in the right place, instead of being repeated in several places.

You do not finish the ER diagram and normalize it later as a separate task. Usually, you draw the entities, test the structure, notice repeated data, and improve the model.

The examples below start from a flat table. The services are only for illustration: the final HyperClinic model does not include them.

First Normal Form: One Value per Field

First normal form, or *1NF*, means that one field should contain one value, not a list.

× Not in 1NF:
appointment_id patient_name doctor_name services appointment_at
16 Marit Solheim Owen Wilson Consultation, ECG 2026-10-20 10:00

The services field contains two values. This makes the data harder to filter, validate, or update.

✓ In 1NF:
appointment_id patient_name doctor_name service appointment_at
16 Marit Solheim Owen Wilson Consultation 2026-10-20 10:00
16 Marit Solheim Owen Wilson ECG 2026-10-20 10:00

Each row now contains one service. However, the appointment, patient, and doctor information is repeated. The next step fixes that.

Second Normal Form: Each Field Depends on the Whole Key

Second normal form, or 2NF, applies when a table uses a combined key.

Here, one appointment can have more than one service. The combination of appointment_id and service identifies one row.

× Not in 2NF:
appointment_id service patient_name doctor_name appointment_at
16 Consultation Marit Solheim Owen Wilson 2026-10-20 10:00
16 ECG Marit Solheim Owen Wilson 2026-10-20 10:00

The patient_name, doctor_name, and appointment_at values depend only on appointment_id. They do not depend on the full combination of appointment_id and service, so they are repeated.

✓ In 2NF:

appointments
appointment_id patient_name doctor_name appointment_at
16 Marit Solheim Owen Wilson 2026-10-20 10:00

appointment_services
appointment_id service
16 Consultation
16 ECG

Now the appointment information is stored once. The appointment_services table only stores the services linked to that appointment. The patient and doctor names are still text here. Step 4 replaces them with IDs.

Third Normal Form: Do Not Repeat Details That Belong Elsewhere

Third normal form, or 3NF, removes indirect repetition.

× Not in 3NF:
doctor_id first_name last_name specialization_id specialization_name
1 Owen Wilson 1 Cardiology
6 Odile Marchetti 1 Cardiology

The specialization name depends on specialization_id, not on the doctor. Storing it in doctors means it will be repeated for every cardiologist.

✓ In 3NF:

doctors
doctor_id first_name last_name specialization_id
1 Owen Wilson 1
6 Odile Marchetti 1

specializations
specialization_id specialization_name
1 Cardiology

Now Cardiology is stored once. If the clinic changes its name, the team updates one row in specializations, not every doctor.

After normalization, each table holds only its own facts:
Table Example Columns
patients patient_id, first_name, last_name, date_of_birth, phone
doctors doctor_id, first_name, last_name
specializations specialization_id, specialization_name
appointments appointment_id, appointment_at, reason, status

The lines show which tables are related, but the link columns, such as specialization_id in doctors, are not here yet. They come in the next step.

Step 4: Link Related Tables with Foreign Keys

To connect two tables, you add a column to one of them. That column is a foreign key: it stores the ID of a row in the other table. This is how a relationship is made.

An appointment should not store redundant information like a patient's name, phone, and date of birth.

Instead, it stores the ID of the linked patient:

appointment_id: 16
patient_id: 1
doctor_id: 1

The field appointments.patient_id is a foreign key that references patients.patient_id.

The field appointments.doctor_id links to doctors.doctor_id.

The field doctors.specialization_id links to specializations.specialization_id.

A foreign key performs two functions:

  1. It describes the relationship between tables.
  2. It prevents invalid references.

Without a foreign key, you can insert an appointment with patient_id = 9999, even if patient 9999 does not exist.

If there is a foreign key, PostgreSQL rejects this record.

A column named patient_id alone does not create a foreign key. The REFERENCES constraint creates it.

The diagram now shows the foreign key columns, marked with a link icon, and an arrow for each relationship. There are still no data types. Types depend on the database engine, so they come in the physical stage.

Step 5: Define the Physical PostgreSQL Model

The physical model describes the PostgreSQL tables, columns, data types, and rules that you want to create.

In this example, INT is used for IDs (the diagram shows it as INTEGER, which is the same type), VARCHAR for text, DATE for a date, and TIMESTAMP for a date and time.

Create the Database Schema

The physical model is ready. Now you need to create it on the PostgreSQL server.

You can do this in either of two ways:

  1. Run the CREATE SCHEMA and CREATE TABLE statements in the SQL Editor.

The following statements are DDL, short for Data Definition Language. DDL is the SQL used to create the database structure.

CREATE SCHEMA clinic;

CREATE TABLE clinic.specializations (
  specialization_id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  specialization_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE
);

CREATE TABLE clinic.doctors (
  doctor_id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  specialization_id INT NOT NULL
    REFERENCES clinic.specializations(specialization_id),
  first_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  last_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE clinic.patients (
  patient_id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  first_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  last_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  date_of_birth DATE NOT NULL,
  phone VARCHAR(30)
);

CREATE TABLE clinic.appointments (
  appointment_id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  patient_id INT NOT NULL
    REFERENCES clinic.patients(patient_id),
  doctor_id INT NOT NULL
    REFERENCES clinic.doctors(doctor_id),
  appointment_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  reason VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
  status VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'scheduled',
  CONSTRAINT appointments_status_check
    CHECK (status IN ('scheduled', 'completed', 'cancelled'))
);

This is how you can create it in VisuaLeaf's SQL Editor:

  1. You can also use Materialize instead of running the SQL yourself. Starting with an empty database, VisuaLeaf creates the clinic schema and its tables directly from the physical model.

Materialize can also apply later changes. In this example, the four original clinic tables already exist, so they are marked as up to date while the new lab_results table is created.

Use one method to create the original schema. If you run the same CREATE TABLE statements after the tables already exist, PostgreSQL returns an “already exists” error.

Step 6: View the Created Database Schema

After either option succeeds, open Schema Manager and select the clinic schema.

You can now see the patients, appointments, doctors, and specializations tables on the PostgreSQL server. This is the implemented database schema: it is no longer only a model or a plan.

This schema contains several constraints:

  • NOT NULL requires a value.
  • PRIMARY KEY makes each ID unique.
  • REFERENCES creates foreign-key relationships.
  • UNIQUE prevents duplicate specialization names.
  • DEFAULT 'scheduled' gives new appointments an initial status.
  • CHECK prevents unsupported status values.

For example, PostgreSQL will reject this appointment if patient 9999 does not exist:

INSERT INTO clinic.appointments (
  patient_id,
  doctor_id,
  appointment_at,
  reason
)
VALUES (
  9999,
  3,
  '2026-11-20 10:00',
  'Annual check-up'
);

PostgreSQL returns an error like this:

ERROR:  insert or update on table "appointments" violates foreign key constraint "appointments_patient_id_fkey"
DETAIL:  Key (patient_id)=(9999) is not present in table "patients".

This is the difference between drawing a relationship in a diagram and enforcing it in the database.

ER Diagram vs Database Schema: The Difference

The conceptual, logical, and physical models are the steps between the first idea and the finished database.

ER diagram Database schema
Main job Plans what data the system needs and how it connects Stores the real database structure
Includes Entities, attributes, and relationships Tables, columns, data types, keys, constraints, and indexes
In this example The HyperClinic models before the schema is created The clinic schema after the SQL is run or the model is materialized
Where you see it In the diagram designer In PostgreSQL and Schema Manager

An ER diagram helps the team decide what to build. The database schema is the structure PostgreSQL creates from that plan.

The tool used for this demonstration is VisuaLeaf. You can download it for free and follow the same steps: design the model, create the schema, and view the tables and relationships in one place.

title: What Is Ingress? Inbound Traffic, Kubernetes, and Modern Gateways Explained
description:
TL;DR

  • Ingress defines any network traffic entering a private boundary or cluster from an external client or network.
  • In traditional networking, ingress operates at Layers 3 and 4 to enforce firewall rules, mitigate spoofing via packet filtering, and manage network address translation.
  • In cloud-native systems, Kubernetes Ingress and the Kubernetes Gateway API act at Layer 7 to route HTTP, HTTPS, and gRPC traffic to backend microservices.
  • Application and AI infrastructure require protocol-aware ingress gateways to handle authentication, dynamic rate limiting, load balancing, and content filtering.
  • For teams running model inference workloads, Bifrost, an open-source AI gateway by Maxim AI, manages incoming Layer 7 traffic to deliver failover, caching, and enterprise governance across diverse providers.

In network engineering and distributed computing, ingress refers to any data traffic entering a network boundary from an external source. Whether managing physical edge routers, virtual private clouds (VPCs), or containerized clusters, ingress infrastructure governs authentication, security filtering, and protocol routing before packets reach application workloads. As production systems transitioned from monolithic servers to microservices and distributed artificial intelligence workloads, ingress expanded from simple IP packet inspection to sophisticated application-layer reverse proxies and gateways.

Managing ingress effectively ensures that internal microservices remain isolated from unauthorized internet access while legitimate client requests reach their targets with minimal latency. Beyond standard web APIs, modern infrastructure increasingly demands specialized ingress management to protect downstream compute resources and manage high-volume payloads.

The Fundamentals of Network Ingress

At its most fundamental level, network ingress describes the inbound direction of data transmission across a defined network boundary. In computer networking, every connection consists of two directions: ingress (traffic flowing into a network) and egress (traffic exiting toward external destinations).

[ External Client / Internet ]
              |
              | (Inbound: Ingress Traffic)
              v
+-------------------------------+
|     Perimeter Firewall        | <--- L3/L4 Filtering (RFC 2827 / BCP 38)
+-------------------------------+
              |
              v
+-------------------------------+
|      Ingress Gateway /        | <--- L7 Routing, TLS Termination, Auth
|       Reverse Proxy           |
+-------------------------------+
              |
      +-------+-------+
      |               |
      v               v
[ Service A ]   [ Service B ]   (Internal Private Network)

Ingress points serve as the perimeter checkpoint for internal systems. Without centralized ingress controls, individual application servers must manage their own public IP addresses, Transport Layer Security (TLS) certificates, DDoS defenses, and access control lists (ACLs). Exposing services directly increases the attack surface and introduces configuration sprawl across engineering teams.

By placing an ingress mechanism at the boundary, platform engineers consolidate traffic management into a hardened data plane. This architecture provides four core benefits:

  1. Attack Surface Reduction: Private IP subnets remain shielded from direct internet exposure. Only the ingress proxy maintains public-facing endpoints.
  2. Centralized TLS Termination: Encryption certificates are managed, renewed, and terminated at the ingress layer, eliminating the need to distribute private keys across application containers.
  3. Optimized Resource Utilization: Central ingress gateways reuse persistent TCP connections to backend services, reducing handshake overhead and conserving compute capacity.
  4. Unified Observability: Ingress points log request metadata, trace incoming headers, and collect telemetry for all inbound connections in a single location.

Ingress vs. Egress: Key Architectural Differences

Understanding ingress requires contrasting it with egress, as both define opposite directions of network communication with distinct operational and cost models.

Architectural Dimension Ingress Traffic Egress Traffic
Direction Inbound (External to Internal) Outbound (Internal to External)
Primary Security Concern Preventing unauthorized access, DDoS, and prompt/payload injection Preventing data exfiltration, secret leakage, and malware command-and-control
Inspection Focus IP validation, TLS termination, path routing, authentication, request validation Destination domain filtering, egress firewalls, response sanitation
Cloud Provider Cost Almost universally free across major cloud vendors (AWS, GCP, Azure) Metered per gigabyte; can represent a major infrastructure expense
Operational Component Reverse proxies, load balancers, Kubernetes Ingress controllers, API gateways NAT gateways, forward proxies, egress firewalls, DNS filters

Cloud providers generally do not charge for data ingress because receiving data encourages workload hosting. However, ingress traffic carries operational liabilities: it consumes bandwidth, triggers compute instances, and represents the primary vector for malicious intrusion. Conversely, egress traffic carries significant financial billing, making strict egress governance necessary to prevent unexpected cloud bills and data exfiltration.

Packet-Level Ingress: Layers 3 and 4

Before application payloads reach reverse proxies or container runtimes, network hardware must validate incoming packets at the Network (Layer 3) and Transport (Layer 4) layers of the OSI model.

Ingress Filtering and Anti-Spoofing (BCP 38)

A critical responsibility of edge routers during ingress is preventing IP address spoofing. In Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) reflection attacks, malicious actors generate packets with forged source IP addresses to weaponize third-party servers.

Under IETF RFC 2827 (BCP 38), network operators implement ingress filtering on border routers. Ingress filtering validates that incoming packets possess source IP addresses belonging to legitimate, reachable network ranges. If a packet arrives on an external interface claiming to originate from an internal private IP range (such as RFC 1918 blocks like 10.0.0.0/8 or 192.168.0.0/16), the router drops the packet immediately. Techniques such as Unicast Reverse Path Forwarding (uRPF) automate this verification by checking whether the router's routing table has a valid reverse path back to the source address.

Layer 4 Load Balancing

At Layer 4, ingress systems handle TCP SYN floods, manage stateful or stateless firewall rules, and distribute incoming connections across multiple proxy nodes using round-robin, least-connections, or hash-based algorithms. Technologies such as eBPF (Extended Berkeley Packet Filter) and IPVS (IP Virtual Server) inside Linux kernels allow edge nodes to direct inbound packets at line rate without incurring the context-switch penalties of user-space processing.

Layer 7 Ingress: Web Applications and Reverse Proxies

While Layer 3 and Layer 4 systems evaluate IP addresses and ports, modern application infrastructure relies predominantly on Layer 7 (Application Layer) ingress. Layer 7 proxies evaluate full HTTP, HTTPS, WebSocket, and gRPC requests.

A Layer 7 ingress gateway inspects:

  • Host Headers: Directing api.example.com to an API service and app.example.com to a web dashboard using a single public IP.
  • URI Paths: Directing /v1/checkout to an e-commerce microservice and /v1/search to an elastic cluster.
  • HTTP Methods and Headers: Routing requests based on authorization tokens, API versions, content types, or HTTP verbs.
  • Payload Inspection: Checking incoming JSON or form data for malformed structures, SQL injection patterns, or cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks.

Tools such as NGINX, HAProxy, and Envoy Proxy historically established this pattern by operating as reverse proxies that decouple public clients from internal network topographies.

Kubernetes Ingress: Managing Traffic in Container Clusters

In containerized environments orchestrated by Kubernetes, managing inbound traffic requires dynamic abstraction. Because Kubernetes pods are ephemeral—constantly being created, scaled, or destroyed with dynamically assigned private IP addresses—external clients cannot connect directly to pod endpoints.

Kubernetes addresses this challenge using two primary abstractions: the traditional Ingress API and the newer Gateway API.

How Kubernetes Ingress Works

The standard Kubernetes Ingress resource, documented in the Kubernetes Ingress concepts guide, is an API object that defines rules for external HTTP and HTTPS traffic reaching cluster services.

An Ingress setup requires two distinct components:

  1. The Ingress Resource: A declarative YAML manifest describing routing rules, hostnames, paths, and TLS secrets.
  2. The Ingress Controller: An active daemon (often running an Envoy or NGINX data plane) that watches the Kubernetes API server for Ingress resource changes and configures load balancers accordingly.

Here is an example of a declarative Kubernetes Ingress resource:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: production-ingress
  namespace: default
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - api.internal.enterprise
    secretName: enterprise-api-tls
  rules:
  - host: api.internal.enterprise
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /billing
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: billing-service
            port:
              number: 8080
      - path: /catalog
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: catalog-service
            port:
              number: 8081

In this configuration, external traffic targeted at api.internal.enterprise is intercepted by the controller. Requests targeting /billing route to the billing microservice, while /catalog routes to the catalog service.

Limitations of Kubernetes Ingress

While functional, the traditional Kubernetes Ingress API possesses architectural constraints that surfaced as clusters grew in complexity:

  • Single-Resource Contention: Infrastructure operators, security personnel, and application developers all modify the same Ingress object, creating configuration collisions in multi-tenant environments.
  • Annotation Overload: Advanced features like canary deployments, rate limiting, header manipulation, and path rewrites are not standardized in the API. Instead, they rely on non-portable, controller-specific annotations (such as nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/*).
  • Limited Protocol Support: The standard Ingress object natively accommodates only HTTP and HTTPS, lacking clean support for TCP, UDP, or advanced gRPC configurations.

The Next Evolution: Kubernetes Gateway API

To resolve the limitations of traditional Ingress, the Kubernetes project introduced the Kubernetes Gateway API as the official, extensible successor. The Gateway API establishes role-oriented resource definitions that split infrastructure provisioning from application routing.

               [ Infrastructure Provider / Cloud Admin ]
                                  |
                                  v
                         +-----------------+
                         |  GatewayClass   |
                         +-----------------+
                                  |
                   [ Cluster / Platform Operator ]
                                  |
                                  v
                         +-----------------+
                         |     Gateway     |  <-- Configures Ports, TLS, Public IP
                         +-----------------+
                                  |
                      [ Application Developer ]
                                  |
                                  v
                         +-----------------+
                         |    HTTPRoute    |  <-- Configures Paths, Filters, Rules
                         +-----------------+
                                  |
                         +--------+--------+
                         |                 |
                         v                 v
                  [ Service A ]     [ Service B ]

The Gateway API introduces a hierarchy of custom resources:

  • GatewayClass: Defined by cluster operators or cloud infrastructure providers to specify the underlying controller (for example, Cilium, Envoy, or cloud load balancers).
  • Gateway: Managed by platform engineers to configure external IP addresses, open ports, and TLS credentials at the cluster boundary.
  • HTTPRoute / GRPCRoute / TCPRoute: Managed by application developers to attach routing rules, path matches, and header mutations to an existing Gateway.

By separating responsibilities into distinct resources, platform teams can safely delegate route definitions to individual application teams without granting permissions to alter cluster-wide networking or TLS keys.

Ingress in the Era of AI and Large Language Models

As organizations adopt generative AI, ingress infrastructure faces demands that traditional web proxies were never built to handle. Standard REST services process sub-second requests with small JSON payloads. AI workloads, by contrast, introduce unique operational characteristics:

  • Long-Lived Streaming Connections: Server-Sent Events (SSE) and token streaming keep HTTP connections open for tens of seconds or minutes, stressing connection pooling.
  • High Payload Sizes: Document embeddings, multi-turn chat histories, and multimodal image uploads result in large request bodies that trigger traditional proxy timeouts or memory buffer bloat.
  • Downstream Provider Fragility: Upstream LLM providers experience frequent rate-limit errors (HTTP 429) and transient outages, requiring intelligent request redistribution at the ingress tier.
  • High Token Costs: Inbound requests directly generate significant billing on downstream model providers, demanding centralized budget caps, rate limiting, and caching at the perimeter.

To manage these challenges, engineering teams deploy specialized AI gateways as their Layer 7 ingress controller for all AI traffic.

How Bifrost Functions as an AI Ingress Gateway

Bifrost is a high-performance open-source AI gateway written in Go that unifies ingress traffic across more than 1,000 models and over 20 providers through an OpenAI-compatible API. Positioned at the network boundary, Bifrost adds only 11 microseconds of overhead per request at 5,000 requests per second according to published benchmarks.

As an ingress control plane, Bifrost decouples client applications from specific model providers:

[ Client Applications / CLI Agents ]
                 |
                 | (OpenAI-compatible Ingress Traffic)
                 v
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                     Bifrost Gateway                         |
|  - Semantic Caching                                         |
|  - Virtual Keys & Budget Enforcement                        |
|  - Automatic Fallback & Load Balancing                      |
|  - Guardrails & PII Inspection                              |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
         |                      |                      |
         v                      v                      v
[ OpenAI Endpoint ]   [ Anthropic Endpoint ]   [ AWS Bedrock / VPC ]

When client applications submit inference requests, Bifrost handles the ingress lifecycle through specialized middleware:

  1. Drop-In Interception: Client applications change only their target base URL to route traffic through Bifrost via drop-in replacement support for OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, and LangChain SDKs.
  2. Semantic Caching: Inbound prompts are evaluated for semantic equivalence using semantic caching. If a matching query was recently answered, Bifrost returns the cached vector response immediately, saving downstream API costs and lowering response latency.
  3. Resilient Provider Routing: If a downstream provider returns HTTP 5xx or 429 status codes, Bifrost initiates automatic fallbacks to redirect the request to alternative models or regions without client disruption.
  4. Hierarchical Governance: Incoming requests must present valid virtual keys. Bifrost evaluates per-key rate limits, user budgets, and team allocations at the ingress boundary before forwarding requests downstream.
  5. Observability and Tracing: Bifrost captures granular metrics, distributing spans via OpenTelemetry and exposing native Prometheus endpoints for real-time traffic analysis.

Beyond routing, Bifrost applies governance and security controls (virtual keys, budgets, guardrails, audit logs) centrally, and Bifrost Edge extends that same governance and security to AI traffic on employee machines, with endpoint enforcement on each device.

Security Best Practices for Ingress Management

Whether configuring an enterprise perimeter firewall, a Kubernetes Gateway, or an AI gateway, securing ingress traffic requires a defense-in-depth approach aligned with NIST SP 800-207 Zero Trust Architecture principles.

1. Implement Strict Boundary Filtering

Never assume traffic arriving from adjacent subnets is benign. Enforce perimeter IP allowlisting, validate DNS records, and employ ingress packet filtering to ensure that non-routable or spoofed packets are rejected before reaching application runtimes.

2. Enforce TLS 1.3 and Automated Certificate Management

Terminate public TLS at the ingress proxy using modern cipher suites (TLS 1.3 preferred, TLS 1.2 minimum). Automate certificate renewal through protocols like ACME (Automated Certificate Management Environment) to avoid unexpected service disruptions caused by expired certificates.

3. Deploy Rate Limiting and Circuit Breaking

Protect internal backends from traffic spikes, brute-force attacks, and rogue loops by enforcing token-bucket or leaky-bucket rate limits at the ingress layer. Implement circuit breakers that fail fast when downstream services become degraded, preventing cascading outages across internal services.

4. Validate and Sanitize Inbound Payloads

Perform deep packet inspection at Layer 7. Web applications must filter for SQL injection, cross-site scripting, and malformed JSON payloads. In AI workflows, ingress proxies should evaluate prompts for sensitive credentials using regex and secrets detection plugins, scrubbing API tokens and private information before data leaves the enterprise boundary.

5. Standardize on Declarative Configurations

Avoid manual proxy modifications. Use declarative configuration files tracked in version-controlled Git repositories (GitOps). In Kubernetes clusters, adopt the Gateway API to separate administrative infrastructure definitions from individual application routing rules.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between an API Gateway and an Ingress Controller?

An Ingress controller is a specialized Layer 7 reverse proxy tailored for Kubernetes that routes inbound HTTP/HTTPS traffic to internal cluster services based on host and path rules. An API gateway encompasses ingress routing but adds higher-level application features, such as API key authentication, OAuth token validation, request/response transformation, complex billing, and granular rate limiting.

What is ingress filtering in computer networking?

Ingress filtering is a packet-filtering technique defined in BCP 38 (RFC 2827) that checks incoming packets at a network interface to verify that their source IP addresses belong to legitimate, authorized networks. Its primary goal is preventing IP address spoofing, which is commonly used in Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks.

Why is the Kubernetes Gateway API replacing Ingress?

The Kubernetes Ingress API is frozen and will receive no new features. The Gateway API replaces it because Ingress relied heavily on non-portable custom annotations and forced cluster administrators and application developers to edit the same resource. The Gateway API provides native support for multiple protocols, role-oriented resource separation, and portable traffic splitting.

Does ingress traffic cost money in cloud platforms?

Across major cloud providers such as AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure, incoming data transfer (ingress) is generally free. However, public load balancers, NAT gateways, and specialized proxy instances that process that ingress traffic incur standard hourly compute and data processing fees.

What is ingress traffic in an AI gateway?

In an AI gateway, ingress traffic consists of incoming inference calls, prompt completions, and tool executions sent by client applications and coding agents. The AI gateway intercepts this traffic to enforce virtual key authentication, execute content guardrails, manage prompt caching, and route calls to appropriate downstream model providers.

Summary and Next Steps

Ingress infrastructure forms the primary gateway through which external requests transition into internal application services. From basic Layer 3 packet filtering under BCP 38 to advanced Layer 7 routing via the Kubernetes Gateway API, effective ingress management safeguards internal networks, optimizes performance, and establishes consistent observability across services.

As workloads evolve toward distributed AI architectures, ingress controllers must perform tasks beyond simple path routing. They must manage model availability, enforce token budgets, and inspect prompts at the perimeter. Platform teams evaluating infrastructure options can request a Bifrost demo or review the open-source repository to explore modern Layer 7 AI gateway architectures.

Sources

  • RFC 2827 (BCP 38): Network Ingress Filtering — IETF standard on mitigating denial-of-service attacks utilizing IP source address spoofing.
  • Kubernetes Ingress Documentation — Official Kubernetes concepts guide for configuring Layer 7 Ingress resources and controllers.
  • Kubernetes Gateway API Specification — Official documentation and architectural specifications for the next-generation Kubernetes Gateway API.
  • NIST Special Publication 800-207: Zero Trust Architecture — National Institute of Standards and Technology guidelines on perimeter security and continuous verification.

title: Building a Zero-Trust Two-Tier AWS Network
description:
When setting up cloud infrastructure in Amazon Web Services (AWS) as a beginner, the "VPC and more" console wizard gives a fast way to generate a complete networking setup including a VPC, subnets, route tables, NAT Gateway, Endpoints and Internet Gateway all in one go.

In this post, I will walk through how I used the "VPC and more" wizard to build a secure two-tier network, adjusted it to meet my project requirements (free-tier instances, single Availability Zone, and no NAT Gateway), created my SSH key pair, chained my Security Groups, and tested secure SSH access.

1. What a Bastion Host (Jump Box) Is and Why It Is Used

A bastion host (also called a jump box) is a hardened server placed in a public subnet that acts as the single entry point into an isolated private network.

In real-world environments, backend servers and databases should never be given public IP addresses or exposed directly to the internet. Doing so increases security risks and invites unauthorized traffic.

By putting our private servers behind a bastion host, we achieve better security:

  • Fewer Entry Points: Instead of exposing multiple servers to the public internet, we only allow access through one controlled bastion host.
  • Controlled Access: We configure our private servers to accept SSH connections only from the bastion host rather than from the open internet.

2. How I Built the Two-Tier Network Using "VPC and more"

Instead of building every network component manually from scratch, I used the automated "VPC and more" wizard in the AWS Console and customized it for my project.

Step 1: Automated Provisioning via "VPC and more"

  1. Open the VPC Dashboard in your AWS Console and click Create VPC.
  2. Select the VPC and more option.
  3. Fill in the settings:
    • Name tag prefix: two-tier
    • IPv4 CIDR block: 10.0.0.0/20
    • Number of Availability Zones (AZs): 1 AZ
    • Number of public subnets: 1
    • Number of private subnets: 1
    • NAT gateways: Select None (This ensures we do not create a NAT Gateway)
    • VPC endpoints: None
    • DNS options: Enable DNS hostnames Enable DNS resolution
  4. Click Create VPC. The wizard automatically generates your VPC, subnets, route tables, and Internet Gateway.

Step 2: Perimeter & Internal Security Group Chaining (Security Layer)

Next, I set up my firewall rules:

  1. Create the Bastion Security Group (bastion-sg):

    • Navigate to EC2 Dashboard -> Security Groups -> Create security group.
    • Security group name: bastion-sg
    • Description: Allow SSH only from my public IP
    • VPC: Select Hye-T-vpc.
    • Under Inbound rules, click Add rule:
      • Type: SSH (TCP, Port 22)
      • Source: Select My IP (verify it displays [INSERT_YOUR_PUBLIC_IP]/32).
    • Click Create security group.

  2. Create the Private Instance Security Group (private-instance-sg):

    • Click Create security group.
    • Security group name: private-instance-sg
    • Description: Allow SSH only from Bastion Security Group
    • VPC: Select Hye-T-vpc.
    • Under Inbound rules, click Add rule:
      • Type: SSH (TCP, Port 22)
      • Source: Select Custom -> Click the search field, type sg-, and select bastion-sg (sg-xxxxxxxx). Do not enter an IP or CIDR block.
    • Click Create security group.

  • "Why": AWS Security Groups operate as stateful virtual firewalls bound to an instance's Network Interface. Configuring bastion-sg to accept TCP port 22 only from your workstation's /32 public IP blocks all unauthorized internet scanners. Configuring private-instance-sg to accept TCP port 22 only from bastion-sg (selecting the Security Group ID as the source rather than an IP address) guarantees that only packets originating from an instance attached to bastion-sg are permitted to reach the private VM.

Step 3: Compute Tier Provisioning

A. Creating an AWS Key Pair

Before launching our virtual machines, we need an SSH key pair to authenticate securely:

  1. Navigate to the EC2 Dashboard in the AWS Console.
  2. In the left navigation menu, click on Key Pairs under Network & Security.
  3. Click the Create key pair button in the top right.
  4. Configure the settings:
    • Name: bastion-host-kp
    • Key pair type: RSA
    • Private key file format: .pem
  5. Click Create key pair. Your browser will automatically download the private key file (bastion-host-kp.pem). Move this file to your local ~/.ssh/ directory.

B. Launching the EC2 Instances

Using the key pair we just created, I launched two free-tier instances (t3.micro):

  1. Hye-Bastion: Placed in the public subnet with Auto-assign public IP enabled and attached to bastion-sg, selecting bastion-host-kp.

  2. Navigate to EC2 -> Instances -> Launch instances.

    • Name: Hye-Bastion
    • AMI: Amazon Linux 2023
    • Instance type: t2.micro or t3.micro
    • Key pair: bastion-host-kp.
    • Under Network settings -> Click Edit:
      • VPC: Hye-T-vpc
      • Subnet: Hye-T-subnet-public1-eu-south-1a
      • Auto-assign public IP: Enable
      • Firewall (security groups): Select existing security group -> bastion-sg
    • Click Launch instance.

  3. Hye-Private-Instance: Placed in the private subnet with Auto-assign public IP disabled and attached to private-instance-sg, selecting bastion-host-kp.

  • Navigate to EC2 -> Instances -> Launch instances.

    • Name: Hye-Private-Instance
    • AMI: Amazon Linux 2023
    • Instance type: t2.micro or t3.micro
    • Key pair: bastion-host-kp.
    • Under Network settings -> Click Edit:
      • VPC: Hye-T-vpc
      • Subnet: Hye-T-subnet-private1-eu-south-1a
      • Auto-assign public IP: Disable
      • Firewall (security groups): Select existing security group -> private-instance-sg
    • Click Launch instance.

  • "Why": The Bastion VM is placed in the public subnet with a Public IPv4 address so it can receive administrative SSH connections via the Internet Gateway. The Private VM is placed in the private subnet with Auto-assign public IP disabled, ensuring it possesses only a private IPv4 address (10.0.8.x/24) and cannot be reached directly from outside the VPC.

Step 4: Connect to the private VM through the bastion host using ProxyJump/Agent Forwarding

Connecting via ProxyJump

To avoid copying my private .pem key onto the bastion host, I connected from my local computer using SSH agent forwarding or ProxyJump:

# 1. Set key permissions and add to your local ssh-agent
chmod 400 ~/.ssh/two-tier-lab-key.pem

# 2. SSH ProxyJump from your Local PC into the Bastion Host with
ssh -i ~/.ssh/two-tier-lab-key.pem -J ec2-user@<INSERT_BASTION_PUBLIC_IP> ec2-user@<INSERT_PRIVATE_VM_PRIVATE_IP>

# If it says "permission denied"
#Try
ssh -o "ProxyCommand=ssh -i ~/.ssh/bastion-host-kp.pem -W %h:%p ec2-user@<BASTION_IP>" -i ~/.ssh/bastion-host-kp.pem ec2-user@<PRIVATE_IP>

  • "Why": I didn't copy my private SSH key (.pem) onto a Bastion host because that will violates cloud security best practices because any compromise of the perimeter Bastion host would expose the private key on disk or in memory, granting an attacker unrestricted access to all internal instances.
    • Using SSH Agent Forwarding (ssh -A) keeps the private key strictly inside your local PC's ssh-agent memory and forwards only cryptographic signature challenges over a secure Unix domain socket ($SSH_AUTH_SOCK).
    • Alternatively, ProxyJump establishes an end-to-end encrypted SSH session directly from your PC to the Private VM multiplexed over the Bastion connection.

3. Testing, Validation & Security Verification Matrix

Validation Test Verification Command / Action Expected Result Observed Status
Bastion SSH Access ssh -A ec2-user@<BASTION_PUBLIC_IP> Authenticates into 10.0.0.x public subnet shell [PASS]
No Private Key on Bastion ls -la ~/.ssh on Bastion Host Only authorized_keys present; no .pem key file on disk [PASS]
Private Instance SSH Hop ssh ec2-user@<PRIVATE_VM_IP> Authenticates into 10.0.8.x private subnet shell via agent socket [PASS]
Private Subnet Isolation ping -c 3 8.8.8.8 on Private Instance 100% packet loss (confirms complete absence of NAT Gateway / Internet route) [PASS]

4. Troubleshooting & Post-Assessment Teardown

Common Operational Failure Modes

  • Issue 1 — Permission denied (publickey) on First Hop (Bastion) with -J:

    • Cause: By default, the top-level -i <key> flag in OpenSSH is passed to the destination target, not the jump host. If the key is not loaded into your local session, the bastion hop rejects the connection.
    • Fix (One-Liner): Explicitly supply the key for both hops via ProxyCommand: 
    ssh -o "ProxyCommand=ssh -i ~/.ssh/bastion-host-kp.pem -W %h:%p ec2-user@<BASTION_IP>" -i ~/.ssh/bastion-host-kp.pem ec2-user@<PRIVATE_IP>
    • Fix (Persistent): Map the keys cleanly in ~/.ssh/config: 
    Host bastion
    HostName <BASTION_IP>
    User ec2-user
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/bastion-host-kp.pem

Host private-vm
    HostName <PRIVATE_IP>
    User ec2-user
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/bastion-host-kp.pem
    ProxyJump bastion

```bash
Then simply run `ssh private-instance`.
```

  • Issue 2 — Permission denied (publickey) on Second Hop (when using SSH Agent Forwarding):

    • Cause: The private key was not added to your local ssh-agent before initiating agent forwarding (ssh -A).
    • Fix: Run eval "$(ssh-agent -s)" and ssh-add ~/.ssh/bastion-host-kp.pem on your local machine before connecting.

  • Issue 3 — Connection timed out to Bastion Public IP: Confirm that the public subnet is explicitly associated with your public route table, that the 0.0.0.0/0 -> igw-xxxx route is active, and verify that your home ISP has not rotated your workstation's /32 public IPv4 address.

title: How I run my content pipeline with two AI bots, Cloudflare R2 and Postiz
description:
I'm a dev trying to grow on X, LinkedIn and dev.to without spending my whole day posting. so I set up a small pipeline where AI bots do the repetitive part and I only show up twice a day, around 8h and 19h (Brazil time), to do the stuff that needs a human, like replying to people.

this is a build log of how it works today. it's not finished and some parts broke along the way, so I'll show those too.

the setup in one paragraph

there are two bots. a creative bot makes the images (carousels) and the Instagram posts in Portuguese. a manager bot owns everything else: it uploads the files to a public Cloudflare R2 bucket, plans the day, writes the English posts for X, LinkedIn and dev.to, and schedules them through Postiz. I only talk to the manager. the manager talks to the creative bot.

why two bots and not one

at first each bot did a bit of everything. the creative bot was also uploading to storage, also scheduling stuff, and I had no idea who did what. when something broke I didn't know where to look.

so I split it by responsibility:

  • creative bot: makes the art, drops it in a handoff folder, tells the manager it's ready, and schedules Instagram once it gets the public URLs back
  • manager bot: storage, calendar, scheduling for every English channel, and my daily checklists

the creative bot doesn't have write access to the bucket anymore. one writer, one source of truth.

R2 as the archive

I didn't want my disk (or the bots' disk) filling up with PNGs. so the rule is: if it's published, it lives in R2, and the local copy gets deleted.

the layout is boring on purpose:


<insta|x>/YYYY/MM/<YYYY-MM-DD>_<HHhMM>_<slug>/

    <slug>_01.png

    <slug>_02.png

    notes.txt

    caption.txt

so a carousel scheduled for 12h today about a company called Conductor ends up in x/2026/10/2026-10-21_12h00_conductor/. there's also an x/latest.txt that just contains the prefix of the day's X carousel, so any routine can find today's files without listing the bucket.

notes.txt is the important one. it has the numbers for the case, where they came from, when they were checked, and which X handles were verified. the post writer is only allowed to use numbers that are in that file. that rule alone killed most of the "AI made up a stat" problems.

uploading with TypeScript

R2 speaks the S3 API, so the upload is just @aws-sdk/client-s3 pointed at the R2 endpoint:


// upload.ts

import { readdir, readFile } from "node:fs/promises";

import { join } from "node:path";

import { S3Client, PutObjectCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-s3";



const s3 = new S3Client({

  region: "auto",

  endpoint: process.env.R2_ENDPOINT!,

  credentials: {

    accessKeyId: process.env.R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID!,

    secretAccessKey: process.env.R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY!,

  },

});



const BUCKET = process.env.R2_BUCKET!;

const PUBLIC_BASE = process.env.R2_PUBLIC_BASE!; // your r2.dev or custom domain



const contentType = (name: string) =>

  name.endsWith(".png") ? "image/png" : "text/plain; charset=utf-8";



export async function uploadFolder(localDir: string, prefix: string) {

  const names = (await readdir(localDir)).sort();

  const urls: string[] = [];



  for (const name of names) {

    const Body = await readFile(join(localDir, name));

    await s3.send(

      new PutObjectCommand({

        Bucket: BUCKET,

        Key: `${prefix}${name}`,

        Body,

        ContentType: contentType(name),

      }),

    );

    urls.push(`${PUBLIC_BASE}/${prefix}${name}`);

  }

  return urls;

}



export async function setLatest(prefix: string) {

  await s3.send(

    new PutObjectCommand({

      Bucket: BUCKET,

      Key: "x/latest.txt",

      Body: prefix,

      ContentType: "text/plain; charset=utf-8",

    }),

  );

}

keys come from env vars, never from the code. and set the ContentType, or the public URL may download the PNG instead of showing it, which breaks things downstream.

checking before deleting anything

after upload the manager checks every public URL returns 200 before it deletes the local copy. Node 18+ has fetch built in, so no extra deps:


// verify.ts

import { rm } from "node:fs/promises";

import { uploadFolder, setLatest } from "./upload";



async function allOk(urls: string[]) {

  const res = await Promise.all(urls.map((u) => fetch(u, { method: "HEAD" })));

  const bad = urls.filter((_, i) => res[i].status !== 200);

  if (bad.length) console.error("not public yet:", bad);

  return bad.length === 0;

}



const local = "handoff/x/2026-10-21_12h00_conductor";

const prefix = "x/2026/10/2026-10-21_12h00_conductor/";



const urls = await uploadFolder(local, prefix);

if (await allOk(urls)) {

  await setLatest(prefix);

  await rm(local, { recursive: true });

}

if any URL fails, nothing gets deleted and latest.txt doesn't move. boring, but it means I never lose a file.

a tiny Go check

I also wanted a dumb health check I can run from anywhere, so here's one in Go. it reads latest.txt over plain HTTP and checks that the first slide is actually there:


package main



import (

    "fmt"

    "io"

    "net/http"

    "os"

    "path"

    "strings"

)



func main() {

    base := os.Getenv("R2_PUBLIC_BASE")



    res, err := http.Get(base + "/x/latest.txt")

    if err != nil || res.StatusCode != 200 {

        fmt.Println("latest.txt not reachable")

        os.Exit(1)

    }

    defer res.Body.Close()



    b, _ := io.ReadAll(res.Body)

    prefix := strings.TrimSpace(string(b))

    slug := strings.SplitN(path.Base(prefix), "_", 3)[2]



    slide := fmt.Sprintf("%s/%s%s_01.png", base, prefix, slug)

    head, err := http.Head(slide)

    if err != nil || head.StatusCode != 200 {

        fmt.Println("missing:", slide)

        os.Exit(1)

    }

    fmt.Println("ok:", prefix)

}

no SDK, no credentials. if the public side works, the bots can work.

Postiz for scheduling

Postiz is the piece that actually posts. it has an MCP server, so the manager bot can call it like a tool: upload media from a URL, get the schema for each platform, schedule a post with comments, list what's queued.

the nice part is that one call shape works for all channels. a post is a list where the first item is the post and the next items are comments. that's how sources end up in the first comment.

for media, I don't upload files from disk. the bot passes the public R2 URL to Postiz's upload-from-URL tool, gets back a hosted path, and attaches that. that's also why R2 has to be public.

the daily routines

everything runs on a schedule (Sao Paulo time):

  • 7h30: the morning plan. schedules the original X posts for the day, then sends me a checklist with replies to write and one quote tweet. I copy, paste, done
  • 10h: carousel day. reads x/latest.txt, reads notes.txt, uploads the PNGs to Postiz, writes the English text and schedules it on X for 12h
  • 18h30: the evening check. confirms the day's posts actually went out and sends me fresh replies plus a reminder to answer people who commented
  • Sunday 18h: drafts next week's posts so I can veto anything I don't like

the routines never ask me stuff during the day. if a step needs me, it goes into the 8h or 19h checklist. that was the only way this was going to survive my real life.

stuff that broke (lessons)

Postiz strips links on X. my first test post went out without the source link. now the source goes in the first comment as text, naming the creator and where to find it. no URL needed, and the person gets tagged, which is better anyway.

blank lines disappear. content goes in as HTML paragraphs, and two paragraphs in a row get glued together on X. to keep a visible blank line I need an empty

between them.

280 characters is real. I'm not on premium, so the writer counts characters before scheduling, and long ideas become a short post plus comments.

Postiz can't reply to other people. it can post and comment on my own posts, but not reply to someone else's tweet, and it can't delete something that already went live. so replies stay manual, which is why my checklists exist.

it wrote like a robot. the first posts were too clean. I had the bot read my real tweets and match them: lowercase, short blocks, no hashtags, no emojis.

no generic opinions. every original post needs a real number and a real source, usually a bigger account or founder.

what's next

LinkedIn and dev.to just joined the pipeline. LinkedIn gets the day's case rewritten in first person with the carousel images, dev.to gets one technical post a week like this one, in TypeScript or Go. all in English, only Instagram stays in Portuguese.

if you're running something similar, I'm curious what you automated and what you kept manual. drop it in the comments.

I post indie app breakdowns daily on X @felipe_rohde (https://x.com/felipe_rohde) and Instagram @feliperohde.dev (https://instagram.com/feliperohde.dev)

title: cornercase: a terminal multiplexer for running coding agents in parallel
description:
This post is written by the maintainers of cornercase. It's our own project, it's free and open source (MIT or Apache-2.0), and there's nothing paid behind it. We'd like to explain what it does, how it works, and where it still falls short.

The problem

Starting ten coding agents is easy. Keeping up with them is the hard part.

Once you have a few Claude Code or Codex sessions open at the same time, the questions pile up. Which one is waiting for an answer? Which one finished while you were looking at another? What did each one change? Did two of them edit the same file?

We kept answering those questions with tmux, git worktrees and a growing pile of scripts, and we kept re-wiring that setup. cornercase is the tool we built so we could stop.

What cornercase does

cornercase is a terminal multiplexer, in the same family as tmux or Zellij, built around running agents in parallel. It runs inside the terminal you already use.

From an issue to an agent at work. Open an issue from GitHub, GitLab, Linear, Jira, Plane, Asana or Shortcut and press start. cornercase creates a worktree on a branch named after the issue, opens a tab in it, and hands the issue to the agent as its first prompt. It works with Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Grok, Cursor, Copilot and nine more agents.

One worktree and one tab per agent, with status. Each agent gets its own branch, folder and tab, so two agents never touch the same file. Tabs show who is working (◐), who needs you (!) and who finished while you were away (✓), along with the model and how full its context is. ! and ✓ climb up to the workspace and project rows, and your terminal sends a notification, also over SSH.

The review next to the work. The changes panel shows the workspace's diff as the agent writes it: uncommitted changes, the agent's commits, or everything since a base branch. You can also see what is uncommitted across every project at once. Hover a hunk to open it in your editor, copy it, or hand it back to the agent. Recent releases added staging a file and discarding a file's changes from the same panel.

Close the window. Nothing stops. A background server owns the shells. Quit detaches and running cornercase again reattaches, from any terminal. Several windows can show the same session. cornercase remote <host> keeps the window on your laptop and the shells and agents on another machine, over your own ssh, and reconnects by itself when the connection drops. Below 90 columns the sidebar folds into a menu bar, so it also works from a phone over SSH.

Scripting, so one agent can run the others. Everything in the window is also a command:

pane=$(cornercase start claude --worktree fix-login --prompt 'Fix the login form, then commit')
cornercase wait --pane "$pane" --timeout 1800   # until the agent stops: idle, done, pending or waiting
cornercase read --pane "$pane" --last-message   # what it said, from its own transcript

cornercase --help lists the rest: open projects and worktrees, split panes, type into them, press keys, wait on one agent or several, and follow events as they happen. You can teach the commands to your agents as a skill:

npx skills add usecornercase/cornercase-terminal --skill cornercase -g

An account per pane. If you have separate accounts, for example one for work and one for personal projects, each pane shows its accounts in a row under it. Pick another account there and only that pane changes. Claude Code and Codex restart on the new account in the same conversation; Gemini CLI starts a new one.

One more design choice: everything is a click, and every key goes to the program in the active pane. There are no shortcuts to learn unless you choose a prefix key.

How it works, briefly

cornercase is written in Rust. Two decisions shape most of it.

Status comes from the agent's own files, not from hooks. For Claude Code, cornercase reads the session file Claude Code keeps for each running session in ~/.claude/sessions/. It reads that file and never writes it. We decided against hooks because they mean editing your ~/.claude/settings.json or shipping a plugin, and the Stop hook doesn't fire when you interrupt with Esc. We also decided against screen scraping, because Claude's screen changes too often to match reliably. The session file turns idle right after an interrupt and switches to waiting as soon as a prompt shows.

Panes run on libghostty-vt, Ghostty's terminal core. That is why nvim, fzf, htop and full-screen agents work as expected inside a pane, in your terminal's own colours.

Honest limits

  • It's early. The current release is v0.12.172, and the project changes daily. Expect rough edges, and expect things to move.
  • Linux and macOS only, on x86_64 and arm64. There is no Windows build.
  • It's a TUI. It lives in your terminal. If you want a desktop app with its own window, cornercase isn't that.
  • Building from source needs Zig 0.15.2 on your PATH, exactly that version, because it builds Ghostty's terminal core. The prebuilt binaries don't need it.

Install

With the install script:

curl -fsSL https://usecornercase.dev/install.sh | sh

Or with Homebrew:

brew install usecornercase/tap/cornercase

Then run it:

cornercase

That starts the server and opens the window. From there, + New → open project lets you pick a folder, and Issues → pick one → start gets an agent going. Quit closes the window and leaves everything running.

cornercase checks GitHub for a new release every hour and offers to install it. cornercase update does the same from a shell.

If you'd rather look before installing anything, there's an interactive simulation on usecornercase.dev. The full walkthrough is in First steps.

Feedback

We'd like to hear from people who run several agents at once. What's still painful in your setup? What breaks? What would make you switch from plain tmux?

  • GitHub: usecornercase/cornercase-terminal for issues and pull requests
  • Discord: discord.gg/aYqCa4xC4R for questions and ideas
  • Docs: usecornercase.dev/docs

Thanks for reading.

title: Breaking the Language Barrier: Our Journey to 10 Native Languages
description:
We have a simple mission at RahaLune: build professional-grade tools that are 100% free, private, and accessible to everyone.

But "accessible to everyone" is easier said than done.

Until recently, our QR Code Generator was English-only. We received feedback from users in the Middle East, South America, and Europe asking for native language support.

Today, I’m thrilled to announce that RahaLune QR Studio is now natively translated into 10 languages.

The 10 Languages

We now support:
🇺🇸 English, 🇫🇷 French, 🇪🇸 Spanish, 🇩🇪 German, 🇹🇷 Turkish, 🇨🇳 Chinese (Simplified), 🇮🇩 Indonesian, 🇲🇾 Malay, 🇸🇦 Arabic, and 🇵🇰 Urdu.

It’s Not Just Translation, It’s a Layout Shift

Translating the text was the easy part. The real challenge was supporting Arabic and Urdu.

These are Right-to-Left (RTL) languages, which means the entire user interface has to flip. We spent hours ensuring that the navigation bar, the QR input forms, and the design studio controls all look perfect when reading right-to-left.

We also made sure the fonts were correct (using Amiri or Noto Sans Arabic) so the text feels native, not machine-generated.

Still 100% Free & Private

Despite this massive update, our core promises haven't changed:

  1. No Logins: Just open the page and use it.
  2. No Ads: The tools are free, forever.
  3. 100% Client-Side: All translation files are loaded locally. Your QR code data never leaves your browser.

Try It Out

I'd love for you to test out the localization. Head over to the site, use the language dropdown in the top right corner, and let me know how it feels in your native language.

👉 Try RahaLune QR Studio

Happy building!
