title: Running OxiPNG, SVGO, rembg and FFmpeg in a browser tab: what actually worked
description:
A lot of the best file tools are command-line programs. OxiPNG shrinks PNGs losslessly, SVGO minifies SVGs, rembg removes image backgrounds, and FFmpeg does everything to video. They're excellent, but each one asks you to install Rust, Node, Python or a native binary first. That's fine on your own machine, and annoying on a locked-down work laptop, a Chromebook, or when you just need to do one file.

I build a small site of browser tools, and over the last few weeks I moved these engines into pages that run entirely in the tab. Here is what that involved, and where the browser version is honestly worse.

1. OxiPNG: the easy one

OxiPNG is written in Rust, and the jSquash project already publishes it compiled to WebAssembly (it's the same build Squoosh used). The .wasm file is only about 164 KB, so I self-host it instead of loading it from a CDN.

The whole pipeline is: read the file into an ArrayBuffer, call optimise(data, level), and compare sizes. Two things I learned:

  • Return the original when it doesn't get smaller. A lot of PNGs people upload were already optimised by some tool. Re-encoding them can produce a file that is the same size or larger, so the page keeps the input in that case.
  • Levels above 4 are not worth it in a tab. The CLI has -o 0 to -o 6 plus max. In single-threaded WASM even level 4 can take several seconds on a 5-megapixel image, and the higher levels only get slower, so I expose 1–4.

The rough CLI equivalent of what the page runs is oxipng -o 4 input.png --out output.png.

2. SVGO: use the browser build

SVGO 4 ships a svgo/browser entry point that avoids the Node-only config loader. I run it with preset-default and multipass: true, and let the user pick the number precision. That is close to npx svgo --multipass --precision 3 input.svg.

One SVGO 4 detail that bit me: removeViewBox is no longer in preset-default. Keeping the viewBox is usually what you want for responsive SVGs, so I made removing it an explicit opt-in with a warning.

Also worth saying: rendering the result as an <img> preview is not a sanitiser. The preview doesn't execute scripts, but the file you download is still the SVG you uploaded, minus whitespace.

3. rembg: same models, different runtime

rembg is a Python tool that runs the U²-Net family of segmentation models. You can't run rembg itself in a browser, but you can run the same ONNX models with ONNX Runtime Web. I use a small browser port of rembg's pre- and post-processing.

Practical choices:

  • Bundle the small model, fetch the big one on demand. U²-NetP is about 4.7 MB and ships with the site, so the first run works without a third-party request. The full U²-Net model is much larger, so it's only downloaded from Hugging Face if the user switches to it.
  • ONNX Runtime's WASM files are the real weight. They are around 13 MB, which is more than the model. I serve them from the site and load them only when someone opens the tool.
  • Not every model is available. rembg's newer models (isnet, BiRefNet, SAM) aren't on the page. The sensitivity slider is a cheap pixel pass on the mask, not rembg's alpha matting.

4. FFmpeg: it works, but it's slow

ffmpeg.wasm really does run FFmpeg commands in the tab. The trick that made the biggest difference was trying a stream copy first. To mute a video, the page runs:

ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -c:v copy -an -movflags +faststart output.mp4

That doesn't re-encode anything, so it finishes almost instantly even in WASM. Only if the copy fails does it fall back to re-encoding with x264.

Everything else is limited by one fact: it's single-threaded. The multi-threaded FFmpeg core needs SharedArrayBuffer, which needs the page to be cross-origin isolated (COOP/COEP headers). Turning that on breaks a lot of ordinary third-party embeds, so for a general tool site I kept the single-threaded core. It's fine for a 30-second screen recording, and painful for a 10-minute 4K file. For big batches, native FFmpeg is the right tool, and the page says so.

5. Show the command, not just the button

The most useful change wasn't technical. Each tool page now shows the engine name, the exact version shipped, the licence, the equivalent command or code, and a short list of how it differs from the original. Developers trust a tool more when they can see that "PNG optimizer" means "OxiPNG level 4". It also helps people who will eventually move the job into a script.

What I'd tell someone doing the same

  1. Check whether a WASM build already exists (jSquash, ffmpeg.wasm, Tesseract.js, ONNX Runtime Web) before compiling anything yourself.
  2. Self-host the WASM if it's small, and lazy-load it only on the page that needs it.
  3. Always compare output size against input and keep the original if you didn't win.
  4. Be upfront about threads. Single-threaded WASM is noticeably slower than a native multithreaded CLI on CPU-heavy jobs, so say so instead of hiding it behind a spinner.
  5. Credit the projects properly. They did the hard part.

The pages are on onemilliontools.com, and there's an index of the engines at onemilliontools.com/open-source. They're free, and the files stay in your browser.

Disclosure: I build this site. I used AI assistance while drafting this post. The numbers above are from the site's own build (file sizes and the commands it runs), not benchmarks against other tools.

title: reconD v0.5.0 - Linux Packaging
description:
In case you missed the dev.to's introduction post to reconD, here you go
https://dev.to/ercross/recond-pull-based-deployments-for-one-server-without-a-platform-1jjb

New in v0.5.0: install it like any other system service

Until now, using reconD meant cloning the repo, building it with Go, and writing your own systemd unit.
With the new [v0.5.0] release (https://github.com/ercross/reconD/releases/tag/v0.5.0), every release ships .deb and .rpm packages for amd64 and arm64.

On Debian or Ubuntu:

VERSION=0.5.0
ARCH=amd64   # or arm64
curl -fsSLO "https://github.com/ercross/reconD/releases/download/v${VERSION}/recond_${VERSION}_${ARCH}.deb"
curl -fsSLO "https://github.com/ercross/reconD/releases/download/v${VERSION}/checksums.txt"
sha256sum --ignore-missing -c checksums.txt
sudo apt install "./recond_${VERSION}_${ARCH}.deb"

On Fedora, RHEL-compatible, or openSUSE, it's the same with recond-${VERSION}-1.x86_64.rpm and dnf install or zypper install.

Then:

sudo cp /etc/recond/config.yaml.example /etc/recond/config.yaml
sudoedit /etc/recond/config.yaml
sudo systemctl enable --now recond
sudo journalctl -u recond -f

The packages behave the way you'd expect from a system service:

  • Install puts the binary at /usr/bin/recond, adds a systemd unit, an example config, and /var/lib/recond. It doesn't start anything until you've written a config, and it prints those setup steps if you haven't.
  • Upgrade restarts the service on the new binary if it was running, and leaves it stopped if it wasn't. Your config and state aren't touched.
  • Remove stops and disables the service and keeps your config and state. On Debian, apt purge removes those too.

CI tests all of this on every pull request, including upgrading a running service from the previous release, and a release can't be published unless those tests pass.

Heads-up if you already run reconD: this release is breaking. The default paths moved from /etc/reconD and /var/lib/reconD to lowercase /etc/recond and /var/lib/recond, and the binary is now recond. The changelog has the migration steps.

title: Four small problems from shipping a local-first task app
description:
OpenTodo is a self-hosted, local-first task manager: a Go server with SQLite, a React app embedded in the binary, and sync built on a field-level operation log. Every device applies changes locally first and converges with the others later. Version 0.9.0 came out today. The user-facing story is on the project blog. This post is about four problems from building it that turned out more interesting than they looked.

1. A title parser that only reads what you just typed

Quick add has always understood Call Anna tomorrow 3pm p1 #home. The obvious next step was to do the same when you edit an existing title: add tomorrow p1 at the end and the task gets a date and a priority.

The trap is the rest of the title. Parse the whole string again and "Review may report" suddenly gains a May date. That was there all along, but nobody asked for it.

The fix is to read only the edit. When editing starts, the current title becomes the base. On commit, the parser finds the common prefix and the common suffix of the base and the draft, treats those spans as if they were quoted, and reads only the text in between. Whatever it recognises becomes one patch: scalar fields overwrite, labels are added to the task's labels, and reminders become new records. The function is pure, with no reads and no writes, so it is easy to test with a table of before/after pairs. The whole change is undone by one Undo.

The parser has a Go twin (the CLI and the importers use it), and both are pinned to the same JSON test vectors, so #Home/Docs resolves to the same project in the browser and in ot add --natural.

2. One running timer, even when two devices started one offline

Time tracking has one rule that users care about: one timer runs at a time. On a single server that is a uniqueness check. In a local-first app it isn't. Your laptop and your phone can each start a timer while offline, and both writes are valid when they are made.

Refusing one of them at sync time would lose work. Instead, the rule is a deterministic repair that every device can compute on its own:

  • Among a user's running entries, the one to keep is the one with the greatest started_at, with ties broken by the greatest id.
  • Every other running entry is ended at the kept entry's started_at.

Because every device sees the same entries and applies the same ordering, every device writes the same ended_at values. The repairs converge like any other edit, and nobody's tracked time disappears; it just stops where the newer timer began. The rule lives in a small Go package with no dependencies besides ciphertext detection, and the TypeScript side is its twin, pinned by shared fixtures.

3. Importing issues without ever writing back

0.9.0 can turn the GitHub or GitLab issues assigned to you into tasks. The design decision that shaped everything else was that nothing is ever written back. The task follows the issue (completed when it closes, renamed when it's renamed), and that is all.

"Follows" needed a precise meaning, because the user can also edit the task. The rule: your own edits stand until the issue changes the same thing again. If you rename the task and the issue keeps its title, your name stays. If the issue is renamed later, the issue wins for that field.

Two more constraints come from running on someone else's server:

  • The server owner opts in. The feature is off by default, and the personal access tokens are kept outside the database and its backups.
  • Requests go only to the host you typed. Every request goes through one outbound policy: http(s) only, no private-network targets unless the owner allows them, the connection pinned to the address that was checked, and no redirects followed. The same policy covers webhooks and calendar subscriptions, so a typed URL can't be turned into a probe of the server's own network.

4. Encrypting a field as one value

Tasks now remember where they came from: a captured page, an email's Message-ID, an issue link. The field is a small object, {kind, provider?, id?, url?, title?}.

For accounts with end-to-end encryption, the server never sees task content. The question was which parts of the origin count as content. kind alone looks harmless, but url, title and id name the page, the mail or the issue, and even the combination leaks something. So the origin is encrypted as one whole value: the object is serialised, then encrypted into one ciphertext string. The server accepts that string wherever it would accept the object, stores it and serves it back unchanged. Another unlocked device decrypts it and shows the chip as usual.

It also fits the sync model. The origin is one last-writer-wins register, like the due date, so two concurrent origins never mix fields from both.

How it was built

Every change above started as a written spec, using the OpenSpec workflow: proposal, design, spec deltas, tasks, then code. That sounds heavy for a one-person project, but it is what made it possible to do most of this release in a few days with AI coding agents doing the typing. The specs are the contract the agents work against and that I review, and they are all in the repository.

OpenTodo is AGPL-3.0. You can try it without installing anything on the demo, read the 0.9.0 release notes, or run it with one container: ghcr.io/pixari/opentodo:stable.

title: From Zero to Production: How I Shipped Responsive UIs During My Frontend Internship
description:
Through my entire first semester of BTech, I didn't really know what I was doing.

I'm Sumit, a student at PW IOI, a new-generation college. Nobody around me had a clear picture of how the industry worked, and neither did I. It took me time to understand what companies expect from a developer and what I needed to learn to get there.

A few months later, I was working in an 11-person team, reading product requirement documents, reporting in daily scrum calls, and building responsive UIs in HTML, CSS and JavaScript on two-week deadlines.

This post is about how that happened, what the internship was like day to day, and what I learned that no tutorial taught me. If you're a student who feels behind or lost, I wrote it mainly for you.

Why the first semester felt so confusing

PW IOI Pune is a new-generation college, so there isn’t a long line of seniors to guide you on what to learn, what to focus on, or what to avoid. During my first semester, I often felt unsure about how the tech industry worked, which skills I needed to develop, and where to start.

I could follow lectures and finish assignments, but I couldn't answer basic questions: What does a developer actually do all day? How do teams build software together? What would a company expect me to know on day one? Without answers to those, it was hard to know what to practise.

If you're a first-year student feeling the same way, that's normal. For me, the confusion didn't go away because I studied harder. It went away when I met someone who could show me the path.

The turning point: finding PW LeapX

In February, I heard about PW LeapX.

PW LeapX is a program associated with PW IOI where students work on real-world projects in teams. For me, that meant building real projects with mentor guidance, working alongside other interns, and learning how a development team actually operates.

The hiring process hadn't started yet, so I used that gap to prepare properly instead of waiting. My interview was in mid-March, and I was selected as a frontend developer. I'm grateful to the two people who guided me through this stage.

Lesson: preparation before an opportunity opens counts. I wasn't ready in February, but I had a few weeks to get ready before the interviews started, and those weeks made the difference.

How the internship worked

The internship began in May 2026 and ran for about three months. We worked under mentors, who guided us through the projects and the daily scrum calls.

The structure looked like this:

  • Real-world projects. We weren't given toy exercises. Each project came as a real brief.
  • The PRD comes first. A product requirement document (PRD) was prepared for every project, and each intern (developer) had to read it before building.
  • Two weeks per project. Each project had a two-week window, and we had to deliver properly within it.
  • A team of 11. Eleven interns worked on one project together, so coordination mattered as much as code.
  • Daily scrum at 4 PM. Monday to Friday, we had a scrum call with our mentors.

Starting with the PRD

A PRD describes what a product should do and who it's for. Documents like this usually cover the goal of the project, the features required, and what counts as done.

Reading it properly before writing code sounds obvious, but it matters. When 11 people read the same document, everyone builds toward the same target. When someone skims it, you find out later, usually when two people's work doesn't fit together.

What happens in a scrum call

A scrum is a short, regular check-in. In ours, each of us explained what we had done the day before. If we were stuck, the mentors guided us right there.

This sounds simple, but it changed how I work:

  • You can't hide when you're stuck. You have to say it, and then you get unstuck faster.
  • You learn to summarize your work clearly and briefly, instead of rambling about everything you touched.
  • You learn how to report to seniors professionally, which isn't something you pick up from coding videos.
  • You see how other people are approaching their parts, which shows you problems before you hit them.

What we built

Our stack was HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Our team's GitHub organisation, LeapX-Pune, holds a set of public projects that gives a good picture of the kind of work we did:

  • A gym/club membership dashboard designed to work on desktop, tablet and mobile.
  • A product catalogue with search, filters, a cart and a validated checkout form.
  • Event listing and registration platforms with filtering, and an admin dashboard in one of them.
  • Kanban-style project management boards, including a Trello-style one with drag-and-drop.
  • A weather and news dashboard with separate JavaScript modules for weather, news and UI.
  • A student progress tracker.

Looking at that list, the pattern is clear. These projects aren't about fancy tools. They're about UI interactions, state handling, form validation, filtering logic and layouts that hold up on different screen sizes. These are the fundamentals that most frontend work is built on.

Working only in HTML, CSS and JavaScript also has a benefit. With no framework hiding the details, you see how the DOM, events and layout actually work, which makes frameworks easier to learn later.

Working in a team of 11

When 11 people build one project in two weeks, a few things become obvious very quickly:

  • Everyone depends on everyone else's work.
  • You need to communicate early, not when something is already broken.
  • Your code is not just yours. Others have to read it, build on it, and merge with it.

This is where Git and GitHub stopped being commands I had memorized and became a daily tool. I learned how teams actually use them, including raising pull requests (PRs) for our work.

What a pull request is for

A pull request is a request to merge your branch into the shared code. It gives teammates a chance to look at your changes first, and it leaves a record of what changed and why.

If you haven't used a team Git workflow yet, here is the generic shape of it. This is a common pattern, not a copy of our project's exact setup:

# Get the latest code
git checkout main
git pull origin main

# Work on your task in its own branch
git checkout -b feature/responsive-navbar

# Commit your changes
git add .
git commit -m "Make navbar responsive for mobile and tablet"

# Push the branch and open a pull request on GitHub
git push origin feature/responsive-navbar

A few habits make this work better in a big team:

  • Pull before you start. Working on stale code is how you create problems for everyone else.
  • Keep branches small and focused. One task per branch is easier to review and easier to undo.
  • Write clear commit messages. "Fix navbar overflow on mobile" tells your teammates something. "Update" doesn't.

With 11 people contributing to one codebase, merge conflicts are a normal part of the job, not a sign that someone did something wrong. Learning to read and resolve them calmly is a real skill.

Getting to responsive UIs

I started this internship without professional frontend experience, and by the end I could build properly responsive UIs. That didn't come from one big breakthrough. It came from repeating the same cycle: read the PRD, build, get stuck, explain it in scrum, get guided, fix, and repeat.

A responsive UI adapts to different screen sizes instead of breaking on them. Here are the building blocks, with generic examples to show each idea. None of this is code from our projects.

1. The viewport meta tag

Without this line in your HTML <head>, mobile browsers pretend the page is a desktop-sized screen and shrink it, so your media queries won't behave as you expect:

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

2. Media queries, mobile-first

Start with the layout for small screens, then add rules as the screen grows:

.card-grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 1fr;   /* single column on small screens */
  gap: 1rem;
}

@media (min-width: 768px) {
  .card-grid {
    grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr);  /* two columns on tablets */
  }
}

@media (min-width: 1024px) {
  .card-grid {
    grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);  /* three columns on desktops */
  }
}

3. Flexible layouts and units

Fixed pixel widths are a common reason layouts break. Flexible containers and relative units adapt on their own:

.container {
  width: 100%;
  max-width: 1100px;
  margin: 0 auto;
  padding: 0 1rem;
}

img {
  max-width: 100%;
  height: auto;
}

4. Test on real sizes

Browser DevTools has a responsive mode that lets you resize the page to common phone and tablet widths. It's the quickest way to catch overflowing elements, text that's too small, and buttons that are hard to tap. Testing on a real phone is better still.

The more important lesson is that responsiveness isn't something you add at the end. When you design for small screens first, you spend far less time fixing broken layouts later.

What I learned beyond code

Looking back, the technical skills were only part of it. This three-month internship was a life-turning point for me because of what else I picked up:

  • Team coordination: how to work with a large team on one deliverable.
  • Talking to mentors: how to ask for help clearly and at the right time.
  • Professional behaviour: how to carry yourself in a work environment.
  • Reporting in scrum: how to explain your progress to seniors.
  • Git and GitHub: how real teams use them, including raising PRs.

If I had to pick the most useful one, it would be asking for help early. In a team on a two-week deadline, a problem you raise on day two is a small problem. The same problem raised on day twelve is an emergency.

The people who made it possible

I didn't do this alone.

My fellow interns helped me go from zero to building properly responsive UIs. Working with ten other people on the same project taught me more than working alone ever could.

Thank you to all my mentors for the daily guidance, to the two people who pointed me in the right direction before the internship began, and to PW LeapX for the opportunity.

If you're where I was

If you're a student who feels lost about the industry, here is what worked for me:

  1. Find someone a few steps ahead of you. One conversation with the right person saved me months.
  2. Prepare before the opportunity opens. Use the waiting time.

title: ReconD: pull-based deployments for one server, without a platform
description:
The simple use case is this:

  • You have a machine
  • And a containerized app running on that machine.
  • Your CI pipeline already builds and publishes images.
  • You do not want a full container orchestrator for this workload, but you also do not want to SSH into the box and manually run deploy scripts every time a new image is ready.

That is the space reconD is designed for. reconD is a single-host deployment reconciliation agent. To put it simply, it watches your deployment metadata and deploys the latest version of your app.

A typical workflow for a sample app called my-app

Your CI publishes:

  • a container image to GHCR
  • a GitHub Release
  • a deployment-metadata.json file that specifies the image, its immutable manifest digest, and the git SHA.

On your virtual machine, reconD periodically asks: "What is the latest desired deployment for dev-my-app or staging-my-app?"

Then it checks: "Is this server already running that digest?" If not, it runs the command you configured:

sh make redeploy-app

That command can be a shell script, a Make target, a Docker command, or something that wraps Docker Compose.

reconD does not try to understand your whole app topology. It does not manage networking, volumes, secrets, scaling, scheduling, ingress, or clusters. That narrowness is intentional. It only owns the reconciliation loop:

  1. Fetch desired deployment metadata.
  2. Compare desired digest with local state.
  3. Inspect the runtime container.
  4. Apply an optional strategy, such as updating an env file with the new image tag.
  5. Run your deploy command.
  6. Wait for health.
  7. Commit deployment state.
  8. Roll back if the deployment fails.
  9. Notify you of deployment status

reconD just keeps asking: "Is this host running the latest version of your app yet?" And if the answer is no, it runs the one command you already trust. It is not Kubernetes. It is not trying to become Kubernetes. It is a small reconciliation loop for single-host deployments, built for the cases where that is exactly enough.
That's the whole model. The server pulls; nothing pushes into it. No inbound SSH from CI, no deploy keys in your pipeline, no open webhook port.

What reconD deliberately doesn't do

reconD doesn't know what Compose is. It runs your command. That command can be docker compose up -d, docker run ..., make redeploy, or a script that runs migrations first. All the knowledge about how to deploy on this particular machine stays in that command, where you can read and test it.

That keeps reconD small. It doesn't manage networks, volumes, secrets, ingress, scaling, or clusters. If a problem needs to understand your app's topology, it belongs in your deploy command, not in the agent.

Failure handling

The interesting part of deployment automation isn't the happy path. It's what happens with a bad release.

Bounded retries. Forward deployments and rollbacks retry with exponential backoff and jitter, up to limits you set:

deployment_retry:
  max_retry_forward_deployment: 3
  max_retry_rollback: 2

It remembers failures. Without this, a bad image gives you an endless loop: deploy, fail the health check, roll back, next poll, deploy the same bad image again. reconD records the failed digest in its state file and doesn't try it again automatically. If the rollback succeeds, your service is back up, but the failed version stays blocked. Pushing a newer release unblocks deployment.

It survives restarts. The current deployment, the previous one (the rollback target), and any terminal failure live in one JSON state file on disk. Restart the agent, or the host, and it picks up where it left off.

You can also point reconD at a Slack webhook to hear when a deployment starts, succeeds, or fails.

Try it

If you run apps on a single server and want deployments that are pulled, health-checked, and can roll back, without adopting a platform, give it a try:

github.com/ercross/reconD

Issues, ideas, and "this broke on my distro" reports are all welcome.

title: Blocking Temp-Mail Signups in a React Form with Real-Time Validation
description:
Throwaway addresses from services like Mailinator or 10 Minute Mail pass every basic regex check. They have a valid format, a real domain, and a working inbox, just one that disappears in an hour. If your signup form feeds a trial, a gated download, or a lead list, those signups add noise and sometimes abuse.

Here's a practical way to catch them in a React form: a debounced check while the user types, a small backend proxy so your API key never reaches the browser, and a server-side re-check on submit.

The architecture

Three pieces, and the order matters:

  1. React form that checks the email shortly after the user stops typing
  2. Your own backend route that calls the validation API, so the key stays secret
  3. A final check on submit on the server, because anything running in the browser can be bypassed

Skip piece 2 and you'll end up shipping an API key in your frontend bundle. Skip piece 3 and anyone can post straight to your signup endpoint and avoid the check entirely.

Step 1: A small debounce hook

Without debouncing, you'd fire a request on every keystroke.

import { useState, useEffect } from 'react';

function useDebounce(value, delay) {
  const [debounced, setDebounced] = useState(value);

  useEffect(() => {
    const timer = setTimeout(() => setDebounced(value), delay);
    return () => clearTimeout(timer);
  }, [value, delay]);

  return debounced;
}

Step 2: The form component 

export default function SignupForm() {
  const [email, setEmail] = useState('');
  const [status, setStatus] = useState('idle'); // idle | checking | ok | blocked
  const debouncedEmail = useDebounce(email, 600);

  useEffect(() => {
    // Skip empty or obviously malformed input
    if (!debouncedEmail || !/^\S+@\S+\.\S+$/.test(debouncedEmail)) {
      setStatus('idle');
      return;
    }

    const controller = new AbortController();
    setStatus('checking');

    fetch('/api/check-email', {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify({ email: debouncedEmail }),
      signal: controller.signal,
    })
      .then((res) => res.json())
      .then((data) => setStatus(data.allowed ? 'ok' : 'blocked'))
      .catch((err) => {
        // Ignore cancelled requests; fail open on real errors
        if (err.name !== 'AbortError') setStatus('ok');
      });

    // Cancel the in-flight request if the email changes again
    return () => controller.abort();
  }, [debouncedEmail]);

  return (
    <form>
      <input
        type="email"
        value={email}
        onChange={(e) => setEmail(e.target.value)}
        placeholder="you@company.com"
      />
      {status === 'checking' && <p>Checking...</p>}
      {status === 'blocked' && (
        <p>Please use a permanent email address, temporary inboxes aren't accepted.</p>
      )}
      <button type="submit" disabled={status === 'blocked' || status === 'checking'}>
        Sign up
      </button>
    </form>
  );
}

Two details worth noticing. The AbortController cancels stale requests so a slow response for an old value can't overwrite the result for the current one. And errors fail open: if the validation service has a hiccup, you let the signup through rather than blocking a real user.

Step 3: The backend proxy

A minimal Express route that keeps the key on the server:

const express = require('express');
const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

app.post('/api/check-email', async (req, res) => {
  const { email } = req.body;
  if (!email) return res.status(400).json({ allowed: false });

  try {
    const url =
      `https://api.gamalogic.com/v1/validate` +
      `?email=${encodeURIComponent(email)}` +
      `&api_key=${process.env.GAMALOGIC_API_KEY}`;

    const response = await fetch(url);
    const result = await response.json();

    res.json({ allowed: isAcceptable(result) });
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('Validation error:', err.message);
    res.json({ allowed: true }); // fail open
  }
});

// Placeholder logic: check the API docs for the actual response fields
// and map them here (disposable flag, validity, risk level, etc.)
function isAcceptable(result) {
  if (result.disposable) return false;
  if (result.valid === false) return false;
  return true;
}

app.listen(3000);

I'm calling Gamalogic's real-time validation API here, which runs syntax, domain, SMTP and risk checks in one request. The field names in isAcceptable are placeholders, so check the response schema in the API documentation and adjust the mapping to match.

Step 4: Re-check on submit, server-side

The client-side check is for user experience only. Your actual signup handler should validate again:

app.post('/api/signup', async (req, res) => {
  const { email } = req.body;

  const allowed = await checkEmailServerSide(email); // same logic as above
  if (!allowed) {
    return res.status(422).json({ error: 'Please use a permanent email address.' });
  }

  // ...create the account
  res.json({ ok: true });
});

Without this, a bot or a curious user can skip your React form and post directly to the endpoint.

Things to watch out for

  • False positives. No detection is perfect. Keep the error message polite and let users fix their input, rather than silently rejecting them.
  • Latency. Real-time checks add a delay. The debounce and the "Checking..." state keep the form feeling responsive, and you should test latency against your own traffic and region.
  • Rate limits and cost. Every keystroke pause is a billable call on most services. The debounce helps, and you can add a simple cache for addresses you've already checked.
  • Don't over-block. Some people use privacy aliases from legitimate services (like Apple's hide-my-email) that aren't throwaway inboxes. Decide what your policy is before you ship it.

Why use an API instead of a blocklist

A hand-maintained list of disposable domains goes stale quickly, since new services appear all the time, and it can't confirm whether a mailbox actually exists. A validation API handles the domain matching, the live SMTP check, and the risk scoring together. I work with Gamalogic on this side of things, and its fake and disposable email checker covers this use case. ZeroBounce and Kickbox have comparable APIs if you're already integrated with one of them.

title: After one React edit, what can your build skip?
description:
Compare an unchanged run with a run after a small source edit—and check the output before interpreting the timer.

An unchanged build and a build after an edit answer different questions. For this walkthrough, use a small React label change that you can actually see in the built app. Keep the command and project setup the same. That gives you a more useful comparison than a single “fast build” number: what happened with no edit, and what happened after the source changed?

Why should a frontend developer care?

You want to know whether the build loop improves when you are actually editing, not only when nothing changed. A visible mutation gives the comparison an output check that a timer cannot provide.

1. Keep one direct pilot command

Use one existing supported app. Keep the team’s existing scripts, linting and tests. Add a distinct script if you need one:

{
  "scripts": {
    "build:ionify": "ionify build"
  }
}

Merge this entry into the existing scripts object; do not replace other scripts. Record the installed package version and lockfile. From the app directory run:

pnpm run build:ionify

Let the process exit and run the same command again unchanged, retaining local state and output. Use fresh processes, the same configuration and the same command for the edited run too.

2. Change an imported React component

Replace the original rendered button with the edited version:

// Before
<button id="save-button">Save</button>
// After
<button id="save-button">Save draft</button>

These JSX fragments are illustrative, not observations. Build again. Serve the generated output with the app’s normal preview setup. For a root-page app using the default dist output, one local static preview is:

python3 -m http.server 4173 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory dist

Open http://127.0.0.1:4173/ and inspect #save-button. Expected after the edit: Save draft. Record what you actually see. Adapt the directory if you intentionally selected another output path; Python’s simple server does not supply SPA route fallback.

3. Name the state you compared

Case What it tells you Output check
Whole task restored, if applicable The task runner reused its recorded result; the engine may not have run Inspect the restored app
Task executed with retained engine state The command ran; unchanged and edited runs remain separate observations Inspect the exact label after each run
Fresh-state control in a separate disposable copy A different starting state, with the original fixture preserved Inspect that copy’s built app

The first row is conceptual. This walkthrough does not establish a named task-runner integration or provide invented runner commands. If your repository already has one, use its documentation to declare inputs and outputs, then verify restored versus executed status from its actual logs. If the label changed but the task remains a hit unexpectedly, preserve the evidence and investigate input declarations.

Running pnpm run build:ionify directly bypasses that orchestration. Do not compare its elapsed boundary with a whole-task restore as if they were identical work.

4. Separate output evidence from interpretation 

Installed version / checkout / exact command:
Mutation and retained local state:
Task outcome: restored / executed / unknown
Engine outcome: not invoked / completed / failed / unknown
Expected and observed label:
Served directory / URL / cache observations:
Elapsed boundary and observations, if measured:

A prior label experiment initially displayed an old label through same-origin HTTP 304 reuse; a fresh origin serving the retained-state output displayed the new one. Check the served directory, URL and browser reuse before concluding that generated output or engine reuse is correct or incorrect. Generated-string presence alone is not browser verification.

No timing, log or internal skip count is fabricated here. Use diagnostics supported by your installed release if you need to explain the work, and report an unexpected result as carefully as a favorable one. Which edit would you use as your smallest useful check?

Cover description: “One edit. Less repeat work”: an amber pencil touches one raised amber code tile among graphite tiles on an ivory background. Conceptual illustration.

title: The Clipped Dropdown in a Collapsed Sidebar — the Hidden Meaning of overflow-y: auto
description:
The QA report

"When the sidebar is collapsed, the '+ Create' menu gets cut off."

The screenshot showed exactly that: with the sidebar collapsed to 60px, the dropdown menu was sliced clean off at the sidebar's right border. Only the first character of "New folder" was visible.

The strange part: with the sidebar expanded (244px), the same menu rendered fine. Same code, same 190px menu width. It only broke when collapsed.

Where I got stuck

My first suspect was z-index — maybe the menu was hiding under something. But DevTools showed the menu was in the DOM with a plenty-high z-index. It wasn't hidden; it was being physically clipped at the sidebar's boundary.

Next suspect: overflow. But all the sidebar had was this:

.sidebar {
  width: 60px; /* collapsed; 244px when expanded */
  overflow-y: auto; /* vertical scroll for long item lists */
}

No overflow-x anywhere. "The horizontal axis is still visible, so anything sticking out should show" — or so I thought.

The cause: one non-visible axis drags the other along

The CSS spec has this rule:

When one of overflow-x / overflow-y is set to something other than visible, a visible value on the other axis computes to auto.

So the moment you write overflow-y: auto, the unspecified overflow-x silently becomes auto. Sure enough, the Computed tab in DevTools showed overflow-x: auto.

Now everything added up:

  • The menu was floated inside the sidebar with position: absolute
  • The sidebar was effectively an overflow: auto auto scroll container
  • A 190px menu inside a 60px container → the horizontal overflow gets clipped (or scrolled)

It had survived in the expanded state only because 244px happened to fit most of the menu, so the clipping wasn't noticeable. Structurally, it was doomed to clip from day one.

The fix: position: fixed only while collapsed

I couldn't drop overflow-y: auto — the scroll is needed. So instead, while collapsed, the menu escapes the scroll container's coordinate system. position: fixed positions against the viewport, so ancestor overflow can't clip it (caveat: an ancestor with transform etc. changes the containing block).

The position comes from the button's getBoundingClientRect(). In React, I store the coordinates in state on click and feed them into style:

const [menuPos, setMenuPos] = useState<{ top: number; left: number } | null>(null);

const handleOpen = (e: React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>) => {
  if (collapsed) {
    const rect = e.currentTarget.getBoundingClientRect();
    // float it just to the right of the button
    setMenuPos({ top: rect.top, left: rect.right + 8 });
  }
  setOpen(true);
};

<ul
  className={collapsed ? "menu menu--fixed" : "menu menu--absolute"}
  style={collapsed && menuPos ? { top: menuPos.top, left: menuPos.left } : undefined}
>

.menu--absolute {
  position: absolute; /* expanded: as before */
  top: 100%;
  left: 0;
}
.menu--fixed {
  position: fixed; /* collapsed: escape the sidebar */
}

I kept the expanded state on the old absolute path. Moving everything to fixed was tempting, but the expanded state has existing scroll-following behavior tangled in, so I limited the blast radius to the collapsed state.

To verify, I opened the menu in the collapsed state on a local build and compared rectangles in the console:

const menu = document.querySelector(".menu--fixed").getBoundingClientRect();
const sidebar = document.querySelector(".sidebar").getBoundingClientRect();
console.log(menu.left >= sidebar.right); // true → the menu is outside the sidebar
console.log(menu.right, document.documentElement.clientWidth); // still within the viewport?

menu.left sat to the right of the sidebar's edge and the whole menu fit in the viewport. Done.

Takeaways

Two lessons from this one.

1. A popover inside a scroll container will eventually get clipped.
The instant you write overflow-y: auto, that element becomes a container that clips horizontally too. Any dropdown or tooltip floated inside it with absolute gets cut the moment it outgrows the container. "It looks fine now" just means it happens to fit today. Put popovers on fixed or in a Portal — outside the scroll container — from the start.

2. Auxiliary states like "collapsed" deserve one pass per feature.
That same day we got three bug reports tied to the collapsed state: a drawer opening as a 60px sliver, the hamburger icon showing at desktop width, and this clipped menu. All of them worked perfectly when expanded and broke the moment you collapsed. We had only ever tested the default state. Of all the state combinations (expanded × collapsed, light × dark, desktop × mobile), the side you don't personally use is exactly the one worth a full lap.

Hope this saves someone the same detour.

title: Your Flex Child Won't Shrink, and overflow: hidden Isn't the Fix (It's min-width: 0)
description:
You build a dashboard. Sidebar on the left, content on the right, a table or a code block inside. It looks perfect with your sample data.

Then a user pastes a long URL into a field, and the whole page grows a horizontal scrollbar. The sidebar gets squeezed, the layout breaks, and you start adding overflow: hidden to everything until the symptoms go away.

There is a one-line fix, and it is not overflow: hidden.

The Layout That Breaks 

<div class="layout">
  <aside class="sidebar">Menu</aside>
  <main class="content">
    <pre>https://example.com/a-very-long-url-with-no-break-points-in-it-at-all-1234567890</pre>
  </main>
</div>

.layout {
  display: flex;
}
.sidebar {
  width: 240px;
  flex-shrink: 0;
}
.content {
  flex: 1;
}

.content is told to take the remaining space with flex: 1. Nobody told it to stay inside that space, and that is the entire problem.

Why It Happens

Flex items and grid items have a default of min-width: auto. For a flex item, auto means:

Do not shrink narrower than the smallest size your content can be.

For a paragraph of normal words, the smallest size is the longest single word, because the line can wrap between words. For a long URL, a <pre> block, a wide table or an image, there is nowhere to wrap, so the smallest size is the full width of the content.

So the browser is not ignoring your layout. It is obeying a rule you never knew existed: the item refuses to shrink below its content, and the overflow spills into the page.

Why overflow: hidden Looks Like a Fix (Sometimes)

Setting overflow to anything other than visible changes how min-width: auto is calculated. The automatic minimum becomes 0 for that item. That is why overflow: hidden on the right element makes the bug vanish.

It works by accident, and it has a cost: it clips content, can cut off focus outlines and dropdowns, and does nothing useful if you put it on the wrong element. Fixing the cause is cleaner.

Fix 1: min-width: 0 on the Flex Child 

.content {
  flex: 1;
  min-width: 0;
}

You are telling the item that it is allowed to shrink below its content. Now .content stays inside its space, and the long URL can be scrolled, wrapped or cut off by something you control:

.content pre {
  overflow-x: auto;
}

In Tailwind, the utility is min-w-0:

<main class="flex-1 min-w-0">
  <pre class="overflow-x-auto">...</pre>
</main>

Fix 2: Grid's 1fr Has the Same Trap 

.layout {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 240px 1fr;
}

1fr is not "one equal share, and no more". It is shorthand for minmax(auto, 1fr), so the column cannot get narrower than its content. The same long URL stretches the column and the page.

.layout {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 240px minmax(0, 1fr);
}

minmax(0, 1fr) allows the column to shrink to nothing if it has to. A useful side note for Tailwind users: grid-cols-2 and its siblings already compile to repeat(2, minmax(0, 1fr)), which is why many people never meet this bug in the grid, and then meet it as soon as they write a custom template column.

Fix 3: Truncating Text With an Ellipsis Inside Flex

This one catches almost everybody:

.row {
  display: flex;
  gap: 8px;
}
.title {
  white-space: nowrap;
  overflow: hidden;
  text-overflow: ellipsis;
}

It does not truncate, because the flex item sizes itself to the text. Add min-width: 0 to .title and the ellipsis appears. In Tailwind, truncate min-w-0 on the same element does it.

Fix 4: Long Words Need the Right overflow-wrap

For user-generated text such as comments, names and pasted links, allow breaking inside a word:

.comment {
  overflow-wrap: anywhere;
}

overflow-wrap: break-word looks equivalent, but it does not change the item's minimum size calculation, so inside a flex or grid item it can still leave the layout stretched. anywhere does take the break points into account, and the item can shrink.

Which One When

Symptom Fix
Flex child pushes the page wider min-width: 0 on that child
Grid column grows past its space minmax(0, 1fr) instead of 1fr
Ellipsis not appearing in a flex row min-width: 0 plus the truncation rules
Long pasted word or URL overflow-wrap: anywhere
Wide table or code block Own scroll container with overflow-x: auto

The Rule

Flex and grid items refuse to shrink below their content by default. If something inside a layout can be wider than the space it is given, tell the container it is allowed to shrink with min-width: 0 or minmax(0, 1fr), and decide where the overflow should scroll or wrap.

Quick audit: open your app and paste a 200-character string with no spaces into every input that is later displayed. Then widen a table to 40 columns. If the page grows a horizontal scrollbar, you have found a missing min-width: 0.

I test every layout in my Next.js and Tailwind templates against this kind of hostile content, because real users do paste long strings, and a dashboard has to survive it.

Get the templates: https://pixelanas.gumroad.com

What is the ugliest layout bug a single piece of user content has caused you? Drop it in the comments.

Anas, full-stack Next.js developer building SaaS products and premium templates. X: @ASheikh69751
