title: CrashLoopBackOff: how to find the real cause (and why deleting the pod won't help)
description:
A config change goes out. A couple of minutes later every request to the app fails, and kubectl get pods shows the status nobody wants to see:

NAME                      READY   STATUS             RESTARTS      AGE
go-api-7b45497dfd-qxqx2   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   4 (15s ago)   115s

I broke a small Go service on purpose to walk through this one properly, from the first symptom to a fix you can prove. The commands work on any cluster. The specific bug is just one example, and I'll come back at the end to the other things that cause the same status.

What CrashLoopBackOff actually tells you

It is easy to read CrashLoopBackOff as an error. It isn't one. It is Kubernetes describing what it is doing about an error.

The container starts and then exits. The kubelet on the node restarts it, because the pod's restartPolicy says so. If it exits again, the kubelet waits before the next try, and the wait grows each time: 10 seconds, 20, 40, and so on, capped at five minutes (Kubernetes docs: container restarts). While it is waiting, the pod shows CrashLoopBackOff.

So the status answers "what is happening?" (the container keeps dying) and says nothing about why. That second question is the whole job, and the pod has already written the answer down somewhere. You just have to know where to read it.

First, check whether anyone is still being served

Before digging into the crash, it's worth thirty seconds to find out how bad things are. A crash loop during a rollout is often harmless: with a rolling update and a readiness probe, the old pods keep serving until a new one becomes Ready. If the new pod never gets there, the rollout just stalls.

A Deployment keeps one ReplicaSet per version of its pod template, so listing them tells you whether an older version is still up:

$ kubectl get rs -n go-api
NAME                DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   AGE
go-api-5d8497557b   0         0         0       5m46s
go-api-7b45497dfd   1         1         0       2m9s

Not good. The old ReplicaSet is at zero, and the new one wants a pod and has none ready. Nothing is serving. In my drill I set it up that way on purpose, but you get the same picture in real life with a Recreate strategy, or when the crash only starts after the pod has already passed its readiness check. Either way, this isn't a stuck rollout any more. It's an outage.

The browser agreed:

That message comes from the ingress. It had a route for the app and no ready pod to send the request to.

A detour worth taking: the dashboard that says everything is fine

This was the part of the drill that surprised me most. Here is the Grafana dashboard during the outage. On the left is the app's own error rate (HTTP 5xx). On the right is the failure rate seen by k6, the load generator sending traffic from outside.

The app reports zero errors. The client sees 100% of requests fail. Both are telling the truth: a process that never finishes starting can't count the requests it never received, so its own metrics go quiet rather than red. If your alerting only looks at what the service says about itself, a total outage can look like a calm afternoon. Watch at least one signal from the client side too, whether that's an ingress or load balancer metric, a synthetic check, or a probe from outside the cluster.

Read the crash's last words: kubectl logs --previous

Plain kubectl logs shows the current container. In a crash loop the current container has often just started, or hasn't started yet, so you get nothing useful. The container that just died is still on the node, and --previous (or -p) asks for its logs:

$ kubectl logs -n go-api go-api-7b45497dfd-qxqx2 --previous
{"level":"INFO","msg":"server starting","port":"80800","service":"go-api"}
{"level":"ERROR","msg":"server error","error":"listen tcp: address 80800: invalid port"}

(I trimmed the timestamps.) Two lines, and the second one is the answer. The server tried to listen on port 80800. Port numbers stop at 65535, so the bind fails and the process exits.

Most of the time the logs get you this far. When they don't, the next command usually does.

Confirm it from Kubernetes' side: kubectl describe pod

describe is long, so I pipe it into less and search for Last State:

$ kubectl describe pod -n go-api go-api-7b45497dfd-qxqx2 | less
...
    Last State:     Terminated
      Reason:       Error
      Exit Code:    1
    Ready:          False
    Restart Count:  4
    ...
    Environment:
      PORT:                 80800
      READINESS_FAILURE:    false
      SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT:     10s

Three things to take from this block.

The exit code. 1 means the app chose to exit with an error. Nothing killed it. If you see 137 instead, the process got a SIGKILL (128 + 9), and a Reason of OOMKilled tells you it ran out of memory. Those two numbers send you down completely different paths, so it's worth reading this line before anything else.

The environment. The same 80800 again, now in the spec. So the bad value isn't something the app made up at runtime. Kubernetes handed it over.

The events at the bottom. In this case they only confirm the loop: Back-off restarting failed container. For other causes they carry the real clue, such as Liveness probe failed, a missing ConfigMap or Secret, or an image that can't be pulled.

The fix everyone tries first

With the pod clearly broken, deleting it is tempting. I tried:

$ kubectl delete pod -n go-api go-api-7b45497dfd-qxqx2
pod "go-api-7b45497dfd-qxqx2" deleted

$ kubectl get pods -n go-api
NAME                      READY   STATUS             RESTARTS      AGE
go-api-7b45497dfd-4c995   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   1 (21s ago)   22s

A new name, the same crash, within seconds. The pod was never the problem. A pod owned by a Deployment is a copy of the Deployment's pod template, and the ReplicaSet will keep making fresh copies of the same mistake for as long as you delete them. The only thing deleting achieved was resetting the restart counter, which made the situation look less serious than it was.

Fix it where it lives: the pod template

So the question becomes where the template gets PORT=80800 from. describe deploy shows the template:

$ kubectl describe deploy go-api -n go-api | less
...
  Containers:
   go-api:
    Image:      go-api:v1.2.0
    Port:       8080/TCP (http)
    Liveness:   http-get http://:http/health delay=15s timeout=5s period=10s
    Readiness:  http-get http://:http/ready delay=10s timeout=3s period=5s
    Environment:
      PORT:                 80800

The container declares port 8080, both probes use that named port, and the environment variable says 80800. One zero too many. The fix goes on the Deployment:

$ kubectl -n go-api set env deploy/go-api PORT=8080
deployment.apps/go-api env updated

Changing the template starts a new rollout. In a real team you'd make the same change in whatever produced the manifest (the Helm values, the Kustomize overlay, the GitOps repo) or the next sync will put the typo straight back. kubectl set env is fine for stopping the bleeding, as long as the real fix follows it.

kubectl rollout undo deploy/go-api -n go-api would have worked too. It returns the template to the previous revision, environment included. When you're paged and you know the last change caused it, rolling back first and investigating second is often the right call.

Prove the fix instead of assuming it

Don't eyeball get pods a few seconds after the change. rollout status waits until the new pods are actually Ready:

$ kubectl -n go-api rollout status deploy/go-api
Waiting for deployment "go-api" rollout to finish: 1 old replicas are pending termination...
deployment "go-api" successfully rolled out

$ kubectl get pods -n go-api
NAME                      READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
go-api-5d8497557b-r47rn   1/1     Running   0          26s

$ kubectl get rs -n go-api
NAME                DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   AGE
go-api-5d8497557b   1         1         1       9m8s
go-api-7b45497dfd   0         0         0       5m31s

Look at the ReplicaSet names. Kubernetes didn't create a third one. The fixed template is identical to the one from before the bad change, so the Deployment scaled the old ReplicaSet back up. It's a small detail, but it's a nice confirmation that the template now matches the last version that worked.

Then check from outside, the way users see it. The health URL answered again, and the request rate on the dashboard came back.

Try it on your own cluster

You don't need anything special to reproduce this. On a test cluster, take any Deployment whose app reads its port from an environment variable and give it an impossible one:

kubectl set env deploy/<your-test-app> PORT=80800
kubectl get pods -w

With the default rolling update you'll likely see the stalled-rollout version: the old pod stays Running while the new one crash-loops. That's a useful thing to see for yourself, because it's exactly why the ReplicaSet check at the start matters. Put it back with:

kubectl rollout undo deploy/<your-test-app>

If you'd rather practise the full outage version, with traffic, dashboards, alerts and a check that tells you when you've actually fixed it, this drill is one of the incidents in SnowOps Labs, a free, open-source Kubernetes lab that runs on a laptop. Disclosure: I build it. Every screenshot above is from it, and the code is on GitHub.

Other causes of the same status

The port typo is one cause among many. The Kubernetes docs group the usual suspects into application errors, configuration errors, resource limits, and failing health checks. In practice that looks like:

  • A bug or a missing dependency in the app. Logs with --previous usually say so, often as a stack trace or a "connection refused" to a database that isn't there.
  • Missing or wrong configuration. A typo like this one, a variable renamed in one place and not the other, a config file mounted at the wrong path, or a value that's fine in staging and wrong in production.
  • Not enough memory. Exit code 137 with Reason: OOMKilled in describe. Raise the limit or fix the leak, but find out which one first.
  • A liveness probe that kills a healthy app. The app starts, the probe fails (too strict, wrong path, too short a delay for a slow start), and the kubelet restarts the container. The events say Liveness probe failed.
  • The container never really starts. A wrong command or args, an image built for another CPU architecture, a missing binary. Here the logs are often empty, because nothing ran long enough to write any. describe and its events carry the message instead.

One extra tip from the docs on finding why a pod failed: set terminationMessagePolicy: FallbackToLogsOnError on your containers. When a container fails without writing a termination message, Kubernetes then copies the last lines of its log into the pod status, so describe shows the error even after the logs are gone.

The short version

When a pod is in CrashLoopBackOff, this order gets you to the cause quickly, whatever the cause turns out to be:

  1. kubectl get pods shows the symptom and the restart count.
  2. kubectl get rs tells you whether anything is still serving, which decides how urgent this is.
  3. kubectl logs <pod> --previous gives you the dead container's last words.
  4. kubectl describe pod <pod> gives the exit code, the reason and the events.

Then fix the thing the pod was copied from, not the pod, and let rollout status tell you when it's really done.

title: A Software Factory on Kubernetes: Gemini Builds, jev Decides (Genkit + senro in Go)
description:
Introduction

The previous article put Genkit flows in Kubernetes pods with senro and let jev, a decision model, route a support ticket. The decisions there were small: which team, how urgent, send or hold.

This one hands jev something bigger to judge: software. A software factory takes a feature request and produces a Go module: a design, a plan, the code, a green build, passing tests and a pull request description. Gemini writes every one of those. jev decides, at every gate, whether the work moves on, goes back, or stops for a human. Each stage runs as a pod, each stage is a Genkit flow, and the whole thing is a few hundred lines of Go.

Everything below ran against the real Gemini API (gemini-3.8-flash) and the real TypeSafe API (jev-latest), on Genkit Go v1.14.0, senro v1.4.5 and a local kind cluster. The code is in genkit-k8s-flows-jev-software-factory.

Why a factory needs a judge, not a second writer

The usual way to review model-written code is to ask another chat model. It works, up to a point. The reviewer writes a paragraph, you parse the paragraph, the paragraph is sometimes wrong in the same way the code is, and a well-written pull request description can talk the reviewer into "looks good to me".

A decision model does not write. It takes a state (the request, the plan, the code, the test log) and answers typed questions with probabilities, in a few hundred milliseconds. There is no prose to parse and nothing to be talked into: BuildGreen is a number, and a red test log drags it down whatever the pull request says.

Chat model as reviewer Decision model as reviewer
Verdict A paragraph you parse Choice[CodeVerdict]: ship, rework or human, with a probability each
Evidence Mentioned, maybe A Noul per question: covers the request, tests are meaningful, build is green
Feedback for the next round Whatever it felt like writing Each question that scored "yes" is one line of feedback
Latency and cost Seconds, thousands of output tokens Milliseconds, tokens for the state only
Can be persuaded by the author Yes No: it never reads instructions, only state

The split that falls out of this is the whole design: Gemini builds, jev decides. And senro is what gives each build step a pod, a workspace, a log, a retry policy and a secret, and each decision a place in the graph.

What we are building

A feature request goes in. A reviewed Go module comes out, or a brief for a human saying why not.

The factory is three senro pipelines and a small state machine over them:

Run Step Where Who What it leaves behind
design clean coordinator none an empty workspace with request.md in it
design design pod Gemini and jev, in a loop design.json, DESIGN.md and one record per review round
design plan pod Gemini plan.json, PLAN.md
implement implement pod Gemini the module's files
implement vet, test pod go vet, go test vet.log, test.log and their exit codes
implement review pod jev review.json: ship, rework or human
rework fix, then vet, test, review pod Gemini, Go, jev the same, after a fix
finish pr then publish pod, coordinator Gemini PR.md and the module under out/<request>/src
finish brief then notify pod, coordinator Gemini BRIEF.md for a human

jev decides three times. Inside the design step, it reviews each design Gemini writes and the loop revises until jev says ready, says reject, or three rounds are up. After test, it reviews the code with the logs in hand and picks ship, rework or human. And the state machine in main turns each verdict into the next senro run, with rework bounded at two.

What you need

  • Go 1.27 or newer, Docker, kind and kubectl
  • GEMINI_API_KEY and TYPESAFE_API_KEY in your environment
  • the senro CLI if you want the terminal UI (optional) 
go get github.com/firebase/genkit/go@v1.14.0
go get github.com/xavidop/senro@v1.4.5
go get github.com/xavidop/mamori

Step 1: a cluster and an image with a Go toolchain

The cluster setup is the one from the previous article: kind, a namespace, a ServiceAccount with the permissions senro's Kubernetes executor needs (including get on pods/exec), and three environment variables, since senro never reads your kubeconfig. The repo's scripts/cluster-up.sh does it and source scripts/cluster-env.sh exports them.

The one difference is the image. A func step needs only sh and tar in the pod, but this factory also runs go vet and go test as plain command steps, so every step uses the official Go image, pinned to its digest as senro requires:

const stepImage = "docker.io/library/golang:1.27-alpine@sha256:f2c872bcee949b7be9c490efd02b48a8a2fbf947cdf533f1c58525ec9d8170fd"

func pods() senro.ExecutorTarget {
    return k8s.Pod(stepImage,
        k8s.Namespace("factory"),
        k8s.Resources(
            map[string]string{"cpu": "500m", "memory": "512Mi"},
            map[string]string{"cpu": "2", "memory": "2Gi"},
        ))
}

Your pipeline binary is still not in that image. senro cross-compiles it and sends it into each pod, exactly as before.

Step 2: the design loop, with jev inside the flow

The first gate is the one that saves the most money: a bad design produces bad code, a green build and a confident pull request. So the design is reviewed before anything is planned, and the review is a loop inside one Genkit flow.

The questions are a Go type. Every yes/no question is one a revision can act on: a "yes" becomes a line of feedback for the next round.

type DesignVerdict string

func (DesignVerdict) Criteria() map[DesignVerdict]string {
    return map[DesignVerdict]string{
        "ready":  "Complete, unambiguous, scoped to the request, and testable as described",
        "revise": "The right direction, with gaps a revision can close",
        "reject": "The request is too vague or too large to design from; a human has to clarify it first",
    }
}

type Risk int

func (Risk) Levels() []string { return []string{"Low", "Medium", "High"} }

type DesignReview struct {
    Verdict        systemonex.Choice[DesignVerdict] `json:"verdict" jsonschema_description:"Is this design ready to implement?"`
    RequestClear   systemonex.Noul                  `json:"request_clear" jsonschema_description:"Does the request say what to build precisely enough that two engineers would build the same thing?"`
    ScopeCreep     systemonex.Noul                  `json:"scope_creep" jsonschema_description:"Does the design add things the request did not ask for?"`
    Underspecified systemonex.Noul                  `json:"underspecified" jsonschema_description:"Is any component described too loosely to implement without guessing: missing fields, signatures, edge cases or error behaviour?"`
    MissingTests   systemonex.Noul                  `json:"missing_tests" jsonschema_description:"Does the test plan leave any requirement of the request untested?"`
    Risk           systemonex.Score[Risk]           `json:"risk" jsonschema_description:"How risky is implementing this design as written?"`
}

And the loop. Gemini designs; jev reviews; if the verdict is revise, Gemini gets the previous design plus the feedback and tries again:

f.Design = genkit.DefineFlow(g, "designFeature", func(ctx context.Context, request string) (DesignResult, error) {
    var res DesignResult
    feedback := ""
    for round := 1; round <= maxDesignRounds; round++ {
        prompt := "Request:\n" + request
        if round > 1 {
            prompt += "\n\nYour previous design:\n" + asJSON(res.Design) + "\n\nReviewer feedback:\n" + feedback
        }
        d, _, err := genkit.GenerateData[Design](ctx, g,
            ai.WithModelName("googleai/gemini-3.8-flash"),
            ai.WithSystem("You are a senior Go engineer writing a short design for exactly what the request asks. "+
                "Stay inside the request: no extra features. Components are the Go types and functions you will create. "+
                "The test plan names concrete, deterministic test cases. Be brief."),
            ai.WithPrompt("%s", prompt))
        if err != nil {
            return res, err
        }
        res.Design = *d

        out, resp, err := genkit.GenerateData[DesignReview](ctx, g,
            ai.WithModelName("typesafe/jev-latest"),
            ai.WithSystem("The state has a feature request and a design written for it."),
            ai.WithPromptParts(ai.NewDataPart(map[string]any{"request": request, "design": res.Design})))
        if err != nil {
            return res, err
        }

        // jev's verdict, then our rules on top.
        verdict := string(out.Verdict.Choice)
        var notes []string
        if out.RequestClear.Probability < 0.4 {
            verdict = "reject" // nobody should design from a request two engineers would read differently
        }
        if out.ScopeCreep.Probability >= 0.5 {
            notes = append(notes, "remove everything the request did not ask for")
        }
        if out.Underspecified.Probability >= 0.5 {
            notes = append(notes, "specify every component fully: fields, signatures, edge cases and error behaviour")
        }
        if out.MissingTests.Probability >= 0.5 {
            notes = append(notes, "add a test case for every requirement in the request")
        }
        if verdict == "ready" && len(notes) > 0 {
            verdict = "revise"
        }
        res.Rounds = append(res.Rounds, DesignRound{Round: round, Verdict: verdict,
            Ready: out.Verdict.Probabilities["ready"], Feedback: notes /* ... */})
        res.Verdict = verdict
        if verdict != "revise" {
            break
        }
        feedback = fmt.Sprintf("The reviewer rated the design %q (probability of ready %.2f). Do the following:\n- %s",
            verdict, out.Verdict.Probabilities["ready"], strings.Join(notes, "\n- "))
    }
    return res, nil
})

Two things to notice. The verdict is jev's, but the rules around it are yours: a request that two engineers would read differently is rejected whatever the design looks like, and a design with a flagged problem is not ready even if jev leaned that way. And the feedback is built from the questions, not from prose: a decision model never writes a sentence, so the sentences live in your code, one per question, and the next round gets exactly the ones that applied.

The whole loop is one flow, so it is one senro step, one pod, one log, with every round recorded in design.json.

Step 3: plan, implement, and let Go have its say

The plan and the implementation are ordinary Gemini calls with typed outputs: a Plan with files and steps, then a Code with every file in full. The step writes the files into the workspace, refusing anything that would escape it:

type Code struct {
    Files []File `json:"files"`
    Notes string `json:"notes,omitempty"`
}

func writeCode(ctx senro.Ctx, code Code) error {
    root := wsPath(ctx, ".")
    for _, f := range code.Files {
        rel := filepath.Clean(f.Path)
        if rel == "." || strings.HasPrefix(rel, "..") || filepath.IsAbs(rel) || strings.HasPrefix(rel, factoryDir) {
            return fmt.Errorf("refusing to write outside the module: %q", f.Path)
        }
        path := filepath.Join(root, rel)
        if err := os.MkdirAll(filepath.Dir(path), 0o755); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if err := os.WriteFile(path, []byte(f.Content), 0o644); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        fmt.Fprintf(ctx.Stdout(), "wrote %s (%d bytes)\n", rel, len(f.Content))
    }
    return nil
}

Then the compiler and the tests run, as command steps in the same pod image, with no model anywhere near them:

func goStep(w *senro.WorkflowBuilder, id, after, cmd string, ws *senro.WorkspaceRef) *senro.StepBuilder {
    script := "mkdir -p .factory; " + cmd + " > .factory/" + id + ".log 2>&1; echo $? > .factory/" + id + ".exit; " +
        "cat .factory/" + id + ".log; exit $(cat .factory/" + id + ".exit)"
    return w.Step(id, exec.Command("sh", "-c", script)).
        Needs(after).
        Mount(ws.At("/repo", senro.RW)).
        WorkDir("/repo").
        Env("HOME", "/tmp").
        Env("GOCACHE", "/tmp/gocache").
        Env("GOFLAGS", "-mod=mod").
        Env("GOPROXY", "off").
        Env("GOTOOLCHAIN", "local").
        Env("CGO_ENABLED", "0").
        Timeout(stepTimeout).
        Retry(3, retry.OnInfra()).
        ContinueOnError()
}

goStep(code, "vet", "implement", "go vet ./...", ws)
goStep(code, "test", "vet", "go test -count=1 ./...", ws)

Each one leaves its output and exit code under .factory/ in the workspace, so the reviewer can read them. GOPROXY=off and GOTOOLCHAIN=local keep the pod honest: the request said standard library only, and the pod cannot download anything to pretend otherwise. And ContinueOnError is the important one: a red test is a failed step, but the review still runs. jev gets to see why the build failed, which is exactly the evidence a rework needs.

Step 4: the code review gate

The second gate reads everything a human reviewer would open: the request, the plan, every source file, and what go vet and go test printed.

type CodeVerdict string

func (CodeVerdict) Criteria() map[CodeVerdict]string {
    return map[CodeVerdict]string{
        "ship":   "Builds, tests pass, does what the request asked, no obvious defects",
        "rework": "Fixable problems: failing or missing tests, a missed requirement, sloppy code",
        "human":  "Something a model should not decide: security, data loss, or the request was misunderstood",
    }
}

type Quality int

func (Quality) Levels() []string { return []string{"Poor", "Acceptable", "Good", "Excellent"} }

type CodeReview struct {
    Verdict         systemonex.Choice[CodeVerdict] `json:"verdict" jsonschema_description:"Should this change ship?"`
    Quality         systemonex.Score[Quality]      `json:"quality" jsonschema_description:"How good is the code?"`
    CoversRequest   systemonex.Noul                `json:"covers_request" jsonschema_description:"Does the implementation do everything the request asked for?"`
    TestsMeaningful systemonex.Noul                `json:"tests_meaningful" jsonschema_description:"Do the tests exercise the behaviour the request cares about, rather than just compile?"`
    BuildGreen      systemonex.Noul                `json:"build_green" jsonschema_description:"According to the logs and exit codes, did go vet and go test both pass?"`
}

The flow sends the whole ReviewInput as a data part, reads the answers, and applies the factory's rules on top. A red build never ships, whatever the overall verdict:

f.Review = genkit.DefineFlow(g, "reviewChange", func(ctx context.Context, in ReviewInput) (Review, error) {
    out, resp, err := genkit.GenerateData[CodeReview](ctx, g,
        ai.WithModelName("typesafe/jev-latest"),
        ai.WithSystem("The state has the feature request, the implementation plan, every source file, "+
            "and the output and exit codes of go vet and go test. Exit code 0 means success."),
        ai.WithPromptParts(ai.NewDataPart(in)))
    if err != nil {
        return Review{}, err
    }
    r := Review{
        Verdict:         string(out.Verdict.Choice),
        Confidence:      out.Verdict.Confidence,
        Quality:         out.Quality.Label(),
        CoversRequest:   out.CoversRequest.Probability,
        TestsMeaningful: out.TestsMeaningful.Probability,
        BuildGreen:      out.BuildGreen.Probability,
        Model:           systemonex.ResponseInfo(resp).Model,
    }
    if in.VetExit != 0 {
        r.Reasons = append(r.Reasons, "go vet failed")
    }
    if in.TestExit != 0 {
        r.Reasons = append(r.Reasons, "go test failed")
    }
    if r.CoversRequest < 0.6 {
        r.Reasons = append(r.Reasons, "the implementation does not cover the request")
    }
    if r.TestsMeaningful < 0.5 {
        r.Reasons = append(r.Reasons, "the tests do not exercise the requested behaviour")
    }
    if out.Quality.Level() == 0 {
        r.Reasons = append(r.Reasons, "code quality is poor")
    }
    if r.Verdict == "ship" && len(r.Reasons) > 0 {
        r.Verdict = "rework"
    }
    return r, nil
})

The Reasons are what the fix flow gets, together with the logs. Again: the decision model decides, your code says it in words.

Step 5: three pipelines and a state machine

The module under construction lives in a persistent workspace, so every run of one request works on the same tree. senro insists a persistent workspace is bounded, and refuses one without both bounds:

func repo() *senro.WorkspaceRef {
    return senro.Workspace("factory-repo",
        senro.Scope(senro.ScopePersistent),
        senro.MaxAge(24*time.Hour),
        senro.MaxSize(256<<20))
}

The three pipelines are short. Every AI step gets the same shape through a helper, with only the secrets it needs:

func aiStep(s *senro.StepBuilder, ws *senro.WorkspaceRef, secrets ...string) *senro.StepBuilder {
    s = s.Mount(ws.At("/repo", senro.RW)).Timeout(stepTimeout).Retry(3, retry.OnInfra())
    for _, name := range secrets {
        s = s.SecretEnv("SENRO_"+name, name)
    }
    return s
}

func buildPipeline(outDir string, rework bool) *senro.Pipeline {
    name, fn := "implement", "factory/implement"
    if rework {
        name, fn = "rework", "factory/fix"
    }
    p := senro.New(name)
    ws := repo()

    code := p.Workflow("code", senro.On(pods()))
    aiStep(code.Step(name, senro.Func(fn, NoParams{})), ws, "Gemini")
    goStep(code, "vet", name, "go vet ./...", ws)
    goStep(code, "test", "vet", "go test -count=1 ./...", ws)
    aiStep(code.Step("review", senro.Func("factory/review", NoParams{})), ws, "TypeSafe").Needs("test")

    handoff := p.Workflow("handoff", senro.Needs("code"), senro.On(senro.Local()))
    handoff.Step("collect", senro.Func("factory/collect", DirParams{Dir: outDir})).
        Mount(ws.At("/repo", senro.RO))

    return p
}

finish declares both endings and lets a run parameter pick one, the same senro.When pattern as the previous article:

func finishPipeline(outDir, reason string) *senro.Pipeline {
    p := senro.New("finish")
    ws := repo()

    ship := p.Workflow("ship", senro.On(pods()), senro.When(senro.ParamIs("verdict", "ship")))
    aiStep(ship.Step("pr", senro.Func("factory/pr", NoParams{})), ws, "Gemini")

    publish := p.Workflow("publish", senro.Needs("ship"), senro.On(senro.Local()),
        senro.When(senro.ParamIs("verdict", "ship")))
    publish.Step("publish", senro.Func("factory/publish", DirParams{Dir: outDir})).
        Mount(ws.At("/repo", senro.RO))

    escalate := p.Workflow("escalate", senro.On(pods()), senro.When(senro.ParamIs("verdict", "human")))
    aiStep(escalate.Step("brief", senro.Func("factory/brief", BriefParams{Reason: reason})), ws, "Gemini")
    // ...and a notify workflow on the coordinator that collects BRIEF.md
    return p
}

And main is the state machine. Each run ends with a record jev produced, and the record picks the next run:

state, reason, reworks := "design", "", 0
for {
    switch state {
    case "design":
        if err := run(designPipeline(request, out)); err != nil {
            exit(err)
        }
        var d DesignResult
        read(out, "design.json", &d)
        if d.Verdict == "ready" {
            state = "implement"
        } else {
            state, reason = "human", fmt.Sprintf("the design review ended %q after %d round(s)", d.Verdict, len(d.Rounds))
        }

    case "implement", "rework":
        // A red vet or test is a failed step, so the run is partial; the
        // review still ran (ContinueOnError) and its verdict is what counts.
        if err := run(buildPipeline(out, state == "rework")); err != nil && !partial(err) {
            exit(err)
        }
        var r Review
        read(out, "review.json", &r)
        switch r.Verdict {
        case "ship":
            state = "ship"
        case "rework":
            if reworks >= *maxRework {
                state, reason = "human", fmt.Sprintf("jev asked for rework %d times: %v", reworks+1, r.Reasons)
            } else {
                reworks++
                state = "rework"
            }
        default:
            state, reason = "human", fmt.Sprintf("the code review ended %q: %v", r.Verdict, r.Reasons)
        }

    case "ship", "human":
        if err := run(finishPipeline(out, reason), senro.WithParams(senro.Params{"verdict": state})); err != nil {
            exit(err)
        }
        return
    }
}

Every arrow in the state diagram is one of those cases, and every run is a directory under runs/ with its plan, its events and one log per step.

Step 6: run it

The first request is a token-bucket rate limiter, the kind of package every service ends up with:

# Feature request: a token-bucket rate limiter package

We need a small, dependency-free Go package `ratelimit` (module path
`github.com/acme/ratelimit`) that other services can import.

- `New(rate float64, burst int) *Limiter`: `rate` is tokens added per second,
  `burst` is the bucket capacity.
- `(*Limiter) Allow() bool`: takes one token if available, otherwise returns false
  without blocking.
- `(*Limiter) AllowN(n int) bool` for batches.
- Safe for concurrent use from many goroutines.
- Time must be injectable so tests are deterministic (no sleeping in tests).
- Standard library only. Tests included, run with `go test ./...`.

go run . -request requests/token-bucket.md

The first run is the design. Read back with senro attach --run <id> --ui=plain:

clean succeeded
design stdout | round 1: jev-1.13.0 decided "revise" (p_ready 0.44) request_clear=0.62 scope_creep=0.36 underspecified=0.56 missing_tests=0.38 risk=Low
design stdout |   - specify every component fully: fields, signatures, edge cases and error behaviour
design stdout | round 2: jev-1.13.0 decided "ready" (p_ready 0.57) request_clear=0.57 scope_creep=0.49 underspecified=0.28 missing_tests=0.34 risk=Low
design succeeded
plan stdout | module github.com/acme/ratelimit, 3 files, 11 steps
plan succeeded
collect succeeded
run succeeded

Two rounds. jev found the first design underspecified (0.56), the feedback said so in one sentence, and the second design named every field, signature and edge case. The ready probability moved from 0.44 to 0.57, and the design that came out of it is the one Gemini implemented; this is its component list in DESIGN.md:

## Components

- type Limiter struct { mu sync.Mutex; rate float64; burst float64; tokens float64;
  last time.Time; now func() time.Time } - concurrency-safe state tracking ...
- func New(rate float64, burst int) *Limiter - public constructor delegating to
  newWithClock using time.Now; clamps negative rate to 0.0 and negative burst to 0 ...
- func newWithClock(rate float64, burst int, now func() time.Time) *Limiter - internal
  constructor enabling time injection for tests; ... panics if now is nil.
- func (l *Limiter) Allow() bool - convenience method returning l.AllowN(1) ...
- func (l *Limiter) AllowN(n int) bool - thread-safe token deduction; edge cases: returns
  true immediately if n <= 0 without modifying state; returns false immediately if
  n > int(l.burst); advances tokens by elapsed.Seconds() * l.rate capped at l.burst ...

The plan turns that into three files and eleven steps, and the second run executes it.

implement stdout | wrote go.mod (42 bytes)
implement stdout | wrote ratelimit.go (1371 bytes)
implement stdout | wrote ratelimit_test.go (3172 bytes)
implement succeeded
vet succeeded
test stdout | ok    github.com/acme/ratelimit   0.009s
test succeeded
review stdout | jev-1.13.0 decided "ship" (confidence 0.66) quality=Excellent covers_request=0.87 tests_meaningful=0.95 build_green=0.98
review succeeded
collect succeeded
run succeeded

Gemini wrote the module, go vet and go test ran in the pod against it, and jev read the three files and the logs and said ship, with the build at 0.98 and the tests at 0.95. The module it reviewed:

// AllowN reports whether n tokens can be consumed immediately.
func (l *Limiter) AllowN(n int) bool {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()

    if n <= 0 {
        return true
    }
    if float64(n) > l.burst {
        return false
    }

    curr := l.now()
    elapsed := curr.Sub(l.last)
    if elapsed > 0 {
        l.tokens += elapsed.Seconds() * l.rate
        if l.tokens > l.burst {
            l.tokens = l.burst
        }
        l.last = curr
    }

    if l.tokens >= float64(n) {
        l.tokens -= float64(n)
        return true
    }
    return false
}

with six tests beside it: clamping, a nil clock panic, burst capacity, AllowN edge cases, deterministic replenishment against an injected clock, and a race test over concurrent goroutines. No sleeping anywhere, as the request demanded.

The third run has both endings declared and runs one:

pr stdout | # Implement token-bucket rate limiter package
pr stdout | ## Summary
pr stdout | Introduces `github.com/acme/ratelimit`, a thread-safe, zero-dependency token-bucket rate limiter. ...
pr stdout | ## Tests
pr stdout | ok      github.com/acme/ratelimit   0.009s
pr stdout | ## Risk
pr stdout | Low. Mutex contention under high concurrency is mitigated by keeping critical sections limited to basic in-memory arithmetic. ...
pr succeeded
publish stdout | published 3 files to .../out/token-bucket/src
publish succeeded
brief skipped_condition
notify skipped_condition
run succeeded

Three senro runs, seven pods, two Gemini designs, two jev design reviews, one implementation, one vet, one test, one jev code review and one pull request, in a little over a minute and a half. out/token-bucket/ holds every record and the module under src/.

Step 7: when jev says no

The second request is the kind every team gets:

# Request

The app feels slow lately, especially in the afternoon. Can you make it faster?
Nothing specific, just whatever you think is best. Thanks.

go run . -request requests/make-it-faster.md

clean succeeded
design stdout | round 1: jev-1.13.0 decided "reject" (p_ready 0.13) request_clear=0.05 scope_creep=0.87 underspecified=0.70 missing_tests=0.79 risk=Low
design stdout |   - remove everything the request did not ask for
design stdout |   - specify every component fully: fields, signatures, edge cases and error behaviour
design stdout |   - add a test case for every requirement in the request
design succeeded
plan stdout | design ended "reject", nothing to plan
plan succeeded
collect succeeded
run succeeded

Gemini did what a chat model does with a vague request: it invented a feature, in this case pprof routes and a latency middleware. jev put the probability that the request is clear at 0.05, and the factory's rule turned that into reject in the first round, before a plan, a line of code or a second model call. The finish run then takes the other ending:

pr skipped_condition
publish skipped_condition
brief stdout | ### What was asked
brief stdout | A user submitted a vague performance complaint stating the app "feels slow lately, especially in the afternoon" and asked to "make it faster" without providing specific endpoints, metrics, or reproduction steps.
brief stdout | ### Why it stopped
brief stdout | The design was rejected on Round 1 (Readiness: 13%, Clarity: 5%). The factory attempted to introduce Go `net/http/pprof` diagnostic routes and custom in-memory latency middleware, triggering a rejection for high scope creep (87%) ...
brief stdout | ### What a human should decide
brief stdout | 1. **Clarify the issue:** Contact the user to identify affected routes, user workflows, and target latency SLOs.
brief stdout | 2. **Authorize observability work:** Determine if the team should prioritize a dedicated ticket for production profiling/metrics ...
brief succeeded
notify succeeded
run succeeded

The brief is written by Gemini, from the record jev produced. The two models keep their jobs even in the failure path.

A request jev cannot be talked into

The third request is a glob matcher: *, **, ?, character classes with ranges and negation, backslash escapes, and an error for an unterminated class. It is precise, it is testable, and the factory never got to write it:

clean succeeded
design stdout | round 1: jev-1.13.0 decided "revise" (p_ready 0.39) request_clear=0.68 scope_creep=0.35 underspecified=0.49 missing_tests=0.32 risk=Medium
design stdout | round 2: jev-1.13.0 decided "revise" (p_ready 0.39) request_clear=0.65 scope_creep=0.40 underspecified=0.34 missing_tests=0.22 risk=Medium
design stdout | round 3: jev-1.13.0 decided "revise" (p_ready 0.47) request_clear=0.59 scope_creep=0.66 underspecified=0.33 missing_tests=0.20 risk=Medium
design stdout |   - remove everything the request did not ask for
design succeeded

Gemini's design transpiles the glob into a Go regular expression. jev never called it ready, the ready probability never crossed 0.5 in three rounds, and in two of those rounds none of the specific questions crossed the line either, so the feedback Gemini got was the generic "tighten the approach". The loop cannot converge on a complaint it has no question for, and after three rounds the factory stops and writes the brief:

## What was asked
Implement a standard-library Go package (`github.com/acme/glob`) providing `Compile(pattern string)
(*Glob, error)` and `(*Glob) Match(path string) bool`. ...

## Why it stopped
The design review failed after 3 rounds, ending in a "revise" verdict (`p_ready` plateaued at 0.46).
Automated reviewers flagged persistent specification risks and scope creep regarding the chosen
approach (transpiling globs into Go `regexp`), specifically around complex regex metacharacter
escaping and separator handling in negated character classes.

## What a human should decide
1. **Architecture:** Approve regex transpilation (accepting edge-case escaping risks) or mandate a
   dedicated AST/rune-based glob parser.
2. **Path boundaries:** Explicitly define exact semantics for `**` edge cases and `/` exclusions
   inside negated classes.

That brief is the factory working as designed. A decision model only answers the questions you ask, and when it keeps saying no without any of them firing, the honest move is to stop and ask a person, with the evidence attached. The fix for the next version of the factory is one more field on DesignReview: a question about the approach itself, so that "this should be a parser, not a regex" becomes a sentence Gemini can act on.

What the combination gives you

Concern Who handles it
Design, plan, code, fix, pull request text Gemini, through genkit.GenerateData and GenerateText
Is the design ready, should the code ship jev, through the same GenerateData call with a decision type
Feedback for the next round Your code, one sentence per question jev answered "yes"
Compiling and testing go vet and go test, as command steps in the pod, with no model involved
A red build reaching the reviewer ContinueOnError on the Go steps
The module between runs A bounded persistent workspace
Which ending runs senro.When(senro.ParamIs("verdict", ...))
Credentials mamori resolves, senro delivers a file per pod, per step
Evidence runs/<id>/ per run, plus .factory/ records that travel with the code

Conclusion

A software factory is not one big agent. It is a handful of small, typed calls with a judge between them, and the judge is the part most people leave out. jev makes that part cheap: a design review is one call that answers six typed questions in a few hundred milliseconds, and the questions are Go fields you choose. Put the loop inside a Genkit flow, the flow inside a senro step, the step in a pod, and the verdict in a run parameter, and the factory is a state machine you can read in one screen.

title: I rewrote VS Code's Live Server in Rust: one 3 MB binary, no Node.js
description:
I like VS Code's Live Server: click Go Live, the page opens, save a file and it reloads. What I didn't like was everything behind it: a Node.js process, a node_modules tree, and about 230 MB of memory to serve a few HTML files.

So I rewrote it in Rust. live-serve is a single binary of about 3 MB that serves a folder, reloads the page when a file changes, and swaps stylesheets in place without reloading.

Try it 

brew install nguyentruong354/tap/live-serve   # macOS, Linux
scoop install live-serve                      # Windows (after: scoop bucket add nguyentruong354 https://github.com/NguyenTruong354/scoop-bucket)
cargo install live-serve                      # anywhere with Rust

live-serve --open

In VS Code, install the extension live-serve-rs (also on Open VSX for VSCodium, Cursor and Windsurf). It bundles the binary, so nothing else needs installing; click Go Live in the status bar.

What it does

  • Live reload over a WebSocket; saving a stylesheet swaps only the sheets from your own origin
  • --https with a self-signed certificate made on the fly, or --cert/--key for one from mkcert
  • --proxy /api=http://localhost:3000 so a static frontend can call a local backend without CORS
  • --spa for single-page apps, --host 0.0.0.0 to open it on your phone
  • Refuses requests from other websites (DNS rebinding, cross-origin reads) and hides .env and .git
  • live-serve init vscode / init zed adds an editor task to the project

Numbers

Against live-server, the package VS Code's Live Server runs, on the same machine and folder (median of six rounds; method):

live-serve live-server
Folder listing, 1,200 entries 2.0 ms ~48 ms
HTML page with the reload script 0.50 ms 0.7–1.5 ms
First response after start 44 ms ~1.4 s
Memory 11 MB ~230 MB

Static files cost about the same for both: reading the file and the loopback connection dominate. The difference is everything around the files.

Things that were harder than they looked

The watch dies with the folder. Build tools love rm -rf dist && build. A file watcher on dist stops when dist is deleted, so after the first rebuild nothing reloads anymore. live-serve also watches the parent folder and re-arms the watch when the folder comes back. macOS made this fun: FSEvents can report the folder's creation late, after the removal, so "created" alone can't mean "it's back".

Two programs on one port. On Windows and macOS, one program can listen on 0.0.0.0:5500 while another binds 127.0.0.1:5500, and both succeed. live-serve used to "take" localhost away from a server that was already running. It now checks the other kind of address before binding and moves to the next port.

HTTPS without setup. --https makes an ECDSA certificate with rcgen for localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1 and, with --host 0.0.0.0, your network address, keeps it in a cache folder and renews it before it expires. TLS is rustls with ring, which added about 1.2 MB to the binary. A plain http:// request to the HTTPS port gets a redirect instead of a confusing error.

CSS swaps and editors. Many editors save by writing a temporary file and renaming it. The reload script has to recognise that the stylesheet changed (not that some random .tmp appeared) and swap only the sheets from the page's own origin, so a stylesheet from a CDN or Google Fonts isn't fetched again on every save.

It's built on axum, tokio and notify.

How it was built

I wrote the core myself and used Claude (an AI assistant) for parts of the HTTPS, proxy and file-watching work, the tests and the release pipeline. I reviewed every change before merging.

Feedback welcome

The code is MIT-licensed on GitHub: https://github.com/NguyenTruong354/live-serve

I'd especially like to hear how the file watching behaves with your build tool, and whether the HTTPS setup works on your machine. Issues and PRs are welcome.

title: CSS Logical Properties: How Browsers Translate Them to Physical Styles
description:
You’ve probably hit this subtle bug before: you write some CSS using logical properties like margin-inline-start, expecting your layout to just work regardless of text direction. But then you flip your app to RTL or switch writing modes, and suddenly things don’t line up as you expected. Margins that should shift to the left stay put, or worse, shift in the wrong direction.

I ran into this during a recent localization sprint. Our UI had mixed LTR and RTL content, and rather than duplicating styles or using awkward hacks, I leaned on CSS logical properties. They’re supposed to abstract away physical directions like left/right and top/bottom. But debugging why my margins weren’t behaving as I imagined forced me to dig under the hood , how exactly do browsers turn these logical properties into physical ones?

Logical vs Physical CSS Properties: The Basic Idea

Traditional CSS uses physical directions:

margin-left: 10px;
padding-top: 5px;

These are fixed to the box’s edges, regardless of the document’s writing mode (LTR or RTL) or layout direction (horizontal or vertical).

Logical properties, introduced in CSS Logical Properties and Values Module, let you specify styles based on the writing mode and flow:

  • margin-inline-start applies margin at the start of the inline flow
  • padding-block-end applies padding at the end of the block flow

So in a left-to-right language, margin-inline-start equals margin-left. In right-to-left, it maps to margin-right. This makes your CSS more adaptable without duplication.

But here’s the kicker: browsers do this mapping internally, translating your logical properties to physical ones at layout time. Understanding that translation explains many layout quirks.

How Browsers Translate Logical Properties

When the browser’s CSS engine parses a rule like:

.my-box {
  margin-inline-start: 16px;
}

it doesn’t leave it as margin-inline-start. Instead, it figures out the physical edge corresponding to "inline start" for the element’s writing mode and direction.

For example, suppose your document is LTR horizontal:

  • inline direction goes left to right
  • inline start is left

The browser will apply the margin as margin-left: 16px internally. But if the same element is in RTL horizontal:

  • inline direction is right to left
  • inline start is right

Now the browser applies margin-right: 16px.

This mapping happens during style computation, after resolving the element’s writing-mode and direction but before layout.

What about vertical writing modes?

When the writing mode is vertical (like Japanese or Mongolian vertical text), "inline" and "block" directions swap:

  • Inline flows top to bottom or bottom to top
  • Block flows left to right or right to left

So margin-inline-start could map to margin-top or margin-bottom depending on writing-mode and direction. This can be surprisingly confusing if you only think in LTR horizontal terms.

Behind the Scenes: The Browser’s Style Computation Pipeline

In the browser’s rendering engine (think Blink, Gecko, or WebKit), style computation is a multi-step process:

  1. Parsing CSS , The engine parses your CSS, creating a style tree where each node has declarations like margin-inline-start.

  2. Resolving Computed Styles , The engine resolves computed values for each property. For logical properties, it uses the element’s computed writing-mode and direction to map logical properties to physical ones.

  3. Applying Physical Styles , The engine applies these physical styles to layout boxes, which then participate in the box model and flow layout calculations.

This means that from the layout engine’s perspective, it never really sees margin-inline-start; it only sees margin-left or margin-top, etc., depending on context.

Why This Matters for Debugging Layout Issues

  1. Unexpected Margins on RTL or Vertical Text

If your app flips to RTL but some margins don’t move as expected, check if you’re mixing logical and physical properties. Physical properties like margin-left don’t adapt, so your layout breaks.

  1. Overriding Logical Properties with Physical Ones

Sometimes, authors override logical properties with physical ones elsewhere in CSS. Because physical properties have the same specificity and cascade rules, the last one wins. This can cause logical properties to be silently ignored.

  1. DevTools Show Physical Properties

Inspecting elements in browser DevTools often shows the physical properties after translation, not the logical ones you wrote. This can confuse you into thinking your CSS isn’t applied.

Practical Tips When Using Logical Properties

  • Always use logical properties consistently in your CSS for layout margins, paddings, borders, and positioning.

  • Be mindful of writing mode. If your app supports vertical writing modes, test your layouts carefully. Logical properties behave differently there.

  • Check DevTools carefully. Don’t expect to see margin-inline-start in computed styles. Look for the mapped physical properties.

  • Use computed styles and layout debugging tools. Some browsers let you visualize box model edges and directions, which can help understand how logical properties translate.

  • Avoid mixing physical and logical properties for the same edge. This reduces cascade confusion.

A Real Debugging Example

I had a sidebar that used:

.sidebar {
  padding-inline-start: 20px;
  border-inline-end: 1px solid #ccc;
}

It looked perfect in LTR, but in RTL, the padding stayed on the left, and the border appeared on the left instead of the right. Turns out, somewhere else in the stylesheet, there was a physical property:

.sidebar {
  padding-left: 10px;
}

Because padding-left came after in the cascade, it silently overrode the logical padding on the physical left edge.

Removing the physical property and relying solely on logical properties fixed the problem.

Wrap-up

CSS logical properties are a powerful way to write adaptable, locale-friendly styles. But they’re not magic. Browsers internally translate them to physical properties based on the element’s writing mode and direction, and understanding that helps you debug those sticky layout issues in multilingual or vertical writing layouts.

Next time your margin-inline-start feels stubborn, remember: it’s actually a margin-left or margin-right in disguise, chosen based on your document’s flow.

Happy styling!

title: vlac: A lossless audio codec for voice, written in Rust
description:
vlac: A lossless audio codec for voice, written in Rust

I built vlac, a lossless audio codec designed specifically for 16kHz mono voice audio. It uses an Order-4 LPC predictor and Zstandard with trained dictionaries.

It's written in Rust for memory safety.

How it works

  1. Predict the next sample using the previous three.
  2. ZigZag encode the residuals.
  3. Split the residuals into High and Low bytes (so Zstandard can compress the zero-padded High bytes efficiently).
  4. Compress with Zstandard.

Benchmarks

On a 10.75-second voice memo (337 KB WAV):

  • Original WAV: 337 KB
  • FLAC (ffmpeg default): 151 KB
  • vlac: 163 KB

vlac currently produces files 8% larger than FLAC on general voice audio. However, it is 100% bit-perfect (verified via MD5 hash on the raw PCM data) and compiles to WebAssembly. The architecture allows for domain-specific dictionary training, which FLAC cannot do.

Repo: https://github.com/pngz-dev/vlac.git

title: A status icon has a bright border: why can its meaning still disappear?
description:
Disclosure: This draft was generated with AI and checked against the cited primary sources, with a separate AI editorial review. It was prepared for the FrameSprite team, which has a commercial interest in FrameSprite. Proposed examples are not executed tests unless explicitly identified as recorded fixture results.

Identify the part of a status icon that actually conveys its meaning, then check that part against adjacent colors. A bright outer border does not rescue a faint interior symbol if the player needs the symbol to distinguish poison from protection.

Key Takeaways

  • Evaluate essential shapes rather than the most visible decoration.
  • Inspect adjacent colors in every relevant interface state.
  • Keep icon meaning, selection, and disabled appearance distinct.

The decorative border can pass the wrong test

W3C's non-text contrast guidance addresses meaningful visual information and relevant adjacent colors. It is not a rule that every pixel in an illustration must contrast with every background.

For a browser review tool or game interface, first describe what the user must recognize. If the central droplet distinguishes poison from a shield, the droplet's boundary matters. Measuring only a high-contrast outer frame answers a different question.

Mark the essential visual parts

Create an annotated copy naming the meaningful silhouette, any required internal distinction, and optional ornament. Ask whether removing a detail changes the status interpretation. This is a design exercise, not proof that all players perceive the remaining shape.

Check text labels separately using minimum text contrast guidance. Do not apply text-size exceptions to a tiny pictogram merely because the icon sits beside a label.

Inspect normal, selected, pressed, disabled, and overlapping-status states relevant to your interface. Some states change the background, opacity, or border. A source PNG inspected on white does not represent all of them.

Example: poison and ward icons

Two status icons share a bright square border. Poison uses a thin purple droplet; ward uses a thin blue shield. At their smallest display size, both interiors fade into the dark slot, leaving identical bright squares.

A repair could strengthen the meaningful interior silhouette, simplify detail, or provide a persistent readable status name. Keep the shared frame only for its actual purpose. If it indicates selection, it should not also be the only clue to status identity.

Do not solve the problem by increasing saturation alone. The required shape can remain low contrast against its immediate background even when the hue looks vivid.

Acceptance in the actual interface

Microsoft's multiple-cue guidance supports using more than a single information channel. Decide which text or other supported cue accompanies the icon when the status affects a player's decision.

Proposed acceptance tasks include distinguishing the two statuses, identifying the selected one, and understanding a disabled state at the actual display size. Record the tested background and scale. A numerical contrast check supports the task but does not replace user evaluation.

This is a source-informed inspection method, not a tested accessibility result or a blanket standards claim about artistic game sprites. No icon was measured or evaluated with participants for this article. Apply the relevant standard to the actual interface and its essential information.

Related workflow

title: Why do sprite review labels and approval controls disappear at browser zoom?
description:
Disclosure: This draft was generated with AI and checked against the cited primary sources, with a separate AI editorial review. It was prepared for the FrameSprite team, which has a commercial interest in FrameSprite. Proposed examples are not executed tests unless explicitly identified as recorded fixture results.

Let review labels and controls reflow around a sprite that may need its own pan or zoom surface. A large two-dimensional image does not justify clipping the approval button, metadata, or correction link when the browser is zoomed. Separate the artwork viewport from the surrounding document layout.

Key Takeaways

  • Preserve all review actions when text grows or the viewport narrows.
  • Keep image navigation distinct from page navigation.
  • Check reflow and text resizing as related but different tasks.

The canvas can hide a layout failure

W3C reflow guidance includes scope and exceptions for content requiring two-dimensional layout. Apply those carefully. A sprite contact sheet may have a spatial purpose, while its labels and controls often can reflow normally.

Do not place the entire review interface in one fixed-width bitmap or clipped container. That couples readable text, interaction, and image inspection to the same scaling decision. An artist may need a large image without wanting tiny labels.

Separate the review regions

Use a bounded artwork viewport for panning or zooming the source. Place action names, revision, metadata, and approval controls in normal responsive document layout. Keep the relationship between the selected image and its details explicit.

The text-resize guidance concerns preserving content and functionality when text is enlarged. Browser zoom, text resizing, and an in-image zoom slider are not interchangeable tests.

Make scroll behavior predictable. A user should understand whether a wheel, arrow key, or drag moves the image or the page. Avoid trapping them inside the artwork area when they want to reach the next field.

Example: an approval button below a clipped panel

A review page uses a fixed-height side panel aligned with a large sprite canvas. At normal scale, the panel shows action metadata and Approve. When text grows, longer labels occupy more lines and push Approve below the panel's clipped edge.

Making the source image smaller does not repair the control layout. Allow the detail panel to grow or scroll appropriately, and preserve a clear route to its actions. On a narrow viewport, move details below the image rather than overlaying essential text across it.

Check that the selected frame remains identified after layout changes. Reflow should not reset selection or associate metadata with a different thumbnail.

Verify the full task

Use keyboard guidance to review access without a pointer. At the intended zoom and text sizes, select a frame, read its revision, enter a correction, reach approval, and leave the image viewport.

Record the browser, viewport, zoom, and text settings. Check long action names and translated labels as well as short defaults. A single narrow screenshot can reveal clipping but does not prove the whole interaction works.

This is a proposed browser-review test, not an executed responsive-layout or standards-conformance result. It does not require shrinking the sprite's production resolution; the repair concerns presentation and access to the review controls.

Related workflow

See sprite team review contact sheet not preview for the adjacent task. Carry the animation handoff checklist with the release, and use the art reference board to retain visual intent.

title: Why does a sprite selection border disappear in Windows high contrast?
description:
Disclosure: This draft was generated with AI and checked against the cited primary sources, with a separate AI editorial review. It was prepared for the FrameSprite team, which has a commercial interest in FrameSprite. Proposed examples are not executed tests unless explicitly identified as recorded fixture results.

Make sprite selection and focus survive the user's forced-colors mode. A shadow-only selection ring can disappear when the browser replaces author colors or suppresses shadows. Adapt the controls narrowly instead of disabling the user's display preference for the whole gallery.

Key Takeaways

  • Use structural cues for selection and visible focus.
  • Inspect controls in the actual forced-colors environment.
  • Keep the artwork's presentation separate from control affordances.

A decorative shadow can carry essential state accidentally

The MDN forced-colors reference documents browser adjustments, including shadow handling. An interface that relies entirely on a glow can lose its only visible selection cue.

This does not imply every raster sprite is recolored by the browser. Inspect the actual elements and properties involved. The state indicator surrounding the image may fail while the image itself remains unchanged.

Distinguish selection from focus

Selection tells the reviewer which frame or action will be acted on. Focus identifies the current keyboard location. Both can matter at once. The W3C visible-focus guidance addresses the latter; it does not automatically implement selection.

Use a visible border, outline, text label, or other supported cue that remains perceivable. Avoid relying only on the difference between two custom background colors. Prefer native semantic controls when they fit the task.

Review the meaningful boundary against its actual adjacent colors with non-text contrast guidance. The relevant colors can differ from the normal theme after the user's preference is applied.

Example: the selected attack card

A card uses a teal box shadow when selected. Its plain border is intentionally transparent. In forced colors, the shadow no longer provides the expected cue, so the reviewer cannot tell whether Walk or Attack will be downloaded.

A proposed repair keeps a real border for the selected state and a separate visible focus treatment. A textual Selected label can reinforce the distinction. Test whether moving focus to the download button leaves the selected action understandable.

Do not broadly apply a forced-color opt-out to restore the original design. That can remove display adjustments the user relies on. If the artwork needs a controlled preview surface, isolate that requirement and retain the surrounding controls' support.

Acceptance with user preferences active

Run the review task using the supported operating-system and browser combination. Select a frame, move focus away, switch actions, and activate a control. Verify that both selection and focus are understandable rather than judging a static screenshot alone.

Record the environment and any targeted CSS adjustment. A normal dark theme is not the same test as a real forced-colors mode, and a screenshot with simulated recoloring does not establish equivalent behavior.

This is a proposed browser-interface check. No operating-system setting, CSS change, or keyboard task was executed for this article. It does not claim standards conformance from one visual cue or recommend changing the production sprite's palette to repair a review-control defect.

Related workflow

title: Can reviewers understand added and deleted sprite changes without red and green?
description:
Disclosure: This draft was generated with AI and checked against the cited primary sources, with a separate AI editorial review. It was prepared for the FrameSprite team, which has a commercial interest in FrameSprite. Proposed examples are not executed tests unless explicitly identified as recorded fixture results.

Label added, removed, and changed sprite regions with text or distinct marks as well as color. A red-green overlay can be quick for some reviewers, but hue alone makes the review meaning fragile. Keep annotation meaning separate from the artwork's own palette.

Key Takeaways

  • Name each review state directly.
  • Make annotations distinguishable without their hue.
  • Preserve an unmarked source view for judging the art.

Review color is a second visual language

W3C's use-of-color guidance explains why information should not depend only on color. An art-review overlay is an interface conveying decisions, even when the underlying sprite is decorative content.

A red region might mean removed pixels in one tool and newly painted pixels in another. State the legend beside the comparison. Do not assume reviewers share a convention or can distinguish every overlay against the sprite.

Separate evidence from annotation

Retain the previous and candidate frames unchanged. Generate a distinct annotation layer that can be toggled off. This lets a reviewer inspect the actual silhouette without confusing a diagnostic tint with a proposed palette.

Use a readable label such as Added, Removed, or Changed, and consider distinct outline or hatch treatments. Review essential marks against adjacent colors using non-text contrast guidance. Decorative highlights and essential indicators have different responsibilities.

Keep selected-frame state visually separate from change type. A selection border should not make a removed region look approved or a changed region look like an error.

Example: red armor in a red deletion overlay

A character wears dark red shoulder armor. A review tool tints removed pixels red and added pixels green. The deletion region becomes hard to see against the armor, while a green weapon glow appears similar to the addition overlay.

A useful comparison offers an unmarked before/after view, a labeled change list, and annotation marks distinguishable by shape or pattern. The reviewer can identify a removed shoulder pixel without knowing whether its tint is red.

If the tool can only generate a color heatmap, accompany it with specific frame coordinates and a textual description. Do not claim that a grayscale screenshot alone establishes usability.

Review the task, not merely the legend

Ask a reviewer to locate a described removal, identify the candidate frame, and state whether the change is intentional. Record where the annotation causes confusion. This is a proposed task check, not a completed participant study.

Microsoft's additional-cue guidance provides broader context for redundant communication in game interfaces. Apply that principle to the review workflow without presenting it as certification of the exported game.

Accept the comparison when the intended states remain understandable, unmarked art is available, and comments identify the correct revision. Changing review annotations should not alter production pixels.

This procedure concerns an art-review interface. It does not redesign the game's item-rarity system or prove accessibility through a single simulated view. No review tool or participant test was executed here.

Related workflow

See game item rarity icons without color only for the adjacent decision. Keep the animation handoff checklist with the deliverable and preserve the art reference board for visual intent.
