title: One line removes our app menu, and on macOS that is also the line that removes Cmd+V
description:
Notifio is a one-window desktop app that watches rental searches and tells you when a listing appears. It lives in the tray, it has no documents, no tabs and no zoom, so the first thing it does after ready is throw away the menu Electron gives you for free:

// Remove the default application menu
app.on('ready', () => Menu.setApplicationMenu(null));

I wrote that line for a good reason. Electron's default menu is built for an editor: File, Edit, View with Reload and Toggle Developer Tools in it, Window, Help. On Windows it renders as a visible strip of chrome across the top of a window that is one panel of status rows. Both windows also carry the matching option for the platforms where that strip exists:

mainWindow = new BrowserWindow({
  width: 1000,
  height: 800,
  autoHideMenuBar: true,
  // ...
});

Two settings aimed at two platforms, both in service of the same thing: an app that looks like a utility rather than a word processor.

On macOS that line does something I did not think about, because the Mac does not put the menu in the window. It puts it in the system menu bar, and the menu bar is where the keyboard owns its commands.

What the Edit menu actually is on a Mac

Cut, Copy, Paste, Select All, Undo and Redo on macOS are not keyboard handling in the usual sense. They are menu items with key equivalents. The system matches the keystroke against the menu, and the menu sends the command on. Electron knows this, which is why its menu roles exist at all:

role?: ('undo' | 'redo' | 'cut' | 'copy' | 'paste' | 'pasteAndMatchStyle' | 'delete'
  | 'selectAll' | 'reload' | 'forceReload' | 'toggleDevTools' | ...
  | 'appMenu' | 'fileMenu' | 'editMenu' | 'viewMenu' | ...);

That list is from electron.d.ts in our own node_modules. The whole reason there is a bundled editMenu role, one word that expands into the standard six items, is that an app with no menu has no clipboard shortcuts on macOS and the usual fix is to put exactly that submenu back.

Set the application menu to null and there is nothing to match the keystroke against. On Windows and Linux the same keys are delivered by Chromium inside the web contents, so the shortcuts keep working there. This is a macOS-only hole, which is also why it can sit in a codebase for months without anyone noticing: it works on the machine you tested it on, and it works for the half of your users who are on the other platform.

Six text fields, and one of them says Paste

I went and counted what is actually on screen. The renderer has eight <input> elements across four components. Two are checkboxes. The other six are text fields, and they are not decorative:

// ActivationScreen.tsx, the first screen any new user sees
<input id="email" type="email" placeholder="you@example.com" ... />
<input id="token" type="text" placeholder="NTFIO-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX" ... />

The activation token arrives by email as NTFIO- and twelve characters from a deliberately unambiguous alphabet, which is a design I have written about before. The reason that alphabet has no O, 0, I or 1 in it is to make the token safe to read and retype. It should not have to be retyped. It is in an email, two keystrokes away from being in the field.

And then there is this one, in the form where you add a search:

<input
  placeholder="Paste your search results page URL"
  value={newUrl}
  onChange={(e) => setNewUrl(e.target.value)}
/>

The product's own instruction to the user is the word "paste". A search URL from a rental portal with filters on it is sixty to two hundred characters of query string. Nobody is typing that.

There is no second route either

The usual fallback for a missing shortcut is right-click, and Electron does not give you a context menu for free. A text field in a BrowserWindow has no Cut, Copy or Paste item unless the app handles the context-menu event on webContents and builds one. I grepped ours:

$ grep -rn "context-menu\|before-input-event\|globalShortcut" src/

Nothing. No context menu, no before-input-event interception mapping keys onto webContents.paste(), no registered shortcuts. The menu was the only path and the menu is null.

The window where this stings most is not even the main one. Notifio opens a real browser window with no automation in it so you can sign in to a rental site yourself, by hand, in a session the app then reuses. There are no browser extensions in an Electron window, so a password manager cannot fill that form. Paste is how a long generated password gets into it, and that window inherits the same empty application menu as every other window in the app.

The fix is one template, and it is platform-shaped 

app.on('ready', () => {
  // macOS keeps the menu in the system bar, and the Edit submenu is where the
  // clipboard shortcuts come from. Windows and Linux get no menu at all.
  Menu.setApplicationMenu(
    process.platform === 'darwin'
      ? Menu.buildFromTemplate([{ role: 'appMenu' }, { role: 'editMenu' }])
      : null
  );
});

Two roles, no items of my own, and the original goal survives: there is still no File menu, no View menu and no Toggle Developer Tools in a shipped build. The window chrome on Windows stays exactly as bare as it was.

The second half is a context menu, which is worth adding on every platform because right-click on a text field doing nothing is its own small wrongness:

contents.on('context-menu', (_event, props) => {
  if (!props.isEditable) return;
  Menu.buildFromTemplate([
    { role: 'cut' }, { role: 'copy' }, { role: 'paste' }, { type: 'separator' }, { role: 'selectAll' },
  ]).popup();
});

What makes this one uncomfortable is that Menu was already imported and already in use. The tray menu a few lines further down is built with Menu.buildFromTemplate, with a Show Window item and a Quit item, because the window's close button hides rather than quits. The API I needed was on screen while I wrote the line that broke the clipboard.

I found this by reading, not from a support email, and the fix is not shipped yet, so the honest status is: if you are on a Mac, this is the current behaviour. It is also the cheapest thing in the world to check in your own app. Launch it, click into a text field, press Cmd+V. If nothing happens, your menu is the reason, and it is two roles away from being fixed.

The app itself is on the download page as a Mac DMG for each architecture and a Windows installer, the first-run walkthrough is in the help pages, and the search-adding step with that placeholder in it is described per site on the supported sites pages, for example the Kamernet one. It is a one-time licence, which means the activation screen with the two text fields on it is a screen every single customer sees exactly once, on their first launch, and it is the screen this bug lands on hardest.

title: A webmanifest cannot read a CSS variable, so our brand colour is spelled twice: once as OKLCH and once as hex
description:
Nakodo's stylesheet is 865 lines long and contains no hex colours at all: 98 of those lines declare an oklch() value. Every colour is an OKLCH ramp step, and everything else is a semantic alias pointing at one:

--color-paper-0: oklch(0.993 0.005 85);
--color-paper-50: oklch(0.972 0.012 85);
--color-paper-100: oklch(0.952 0.013 85);
...
--background: var(--color-paper-50);

There is a grep ban on raw palette classes and on hex values outside that file, written into the brand document. Then there is this, which is 20 lines of TypeScript and contains the same colour twice, written out by hand:

// Served at /manifest.webmanifest. Icons are in public/.
export default function manifest(): MetadataRoute.Manifest {
  return {
    name: BRAND.name,
    short_name: BRAND.name,
    description: BRAND.description,
    start_url: "/campaigns",
    display: "standalone",
    background_color: "#f9f5ed",
    theme_color: "#f9f5ed",
    icons: [
      { src: "/icon-192.png", sizes: "192x192", type: "image/png" },
      { src: "/icon-512.png", sizes: "512x512", type: "image/png" },
      { src: "/icon.svg", sizes: "any", type: "image/svg+xml" },
    ],
  };
}

A webmanifest is JSON read by the operating system. There is no cascade in it, no var(), no computed value, and nothing in it is ever resolved by a browser engine against a stylesheet. The same is true of the theme-color meta tag, our Open Graph image renderer and our email layout, so the full count of places that know this colour as a hex string is five:

$ grep -rn "f9f5ed" src/
src/app/layout.tsx:48:export const viewport: Viewport = { ..., themeColor: "#f9f5ed" };
src/app/manifest.ts:12:    background_color: "#f9f5ed",
src/app/manifest.ts:13:    theme_color: "#f9f5ed",
src/lib/seo/og.tsx:13:const PAPER = "#f9f5ed";
src/lib/email/layout.ts:15:  page: "#f9f5ed", // paper-50

Every one of those is a boundary where CSS stops: the OS, the OS again, the browser chrome, a PNG renderer, and a mail client. The comment on the last line is the only thing in the repository that says which ramp step the string is supposed to be.

The two spellings are the same colour, and nothing enforces it

#f9f5ed is not approximately --color-paper-50. It is exactly it. You can check that without trusting me, by converting the OKLCH value by hand:

import math
L, C, H = 0.972, 0.012, 85
a, b = C * math.cos(math.radians(H)), C * math.sin(math.radians(H))
l_, m_, s_ = L + 0.3963377774*a + 0.2158037573*b, L - 0.1055613458*a - 0.0638541728*b, L - 0.0894841775*a - 1.2914855480*b
l, m, s = l_**3, m_**3, s_**3
r  =  4.0767416621*l - 3.3077115913*m + 0.2309699292*s
g  = -1.2684380046*l + 2.6097574011*m - 0.3413193965*s
bl = -0.0041960863*l - 0.7034186147*m + 1.7076147010*s
f = lambda x: 12.92*x if x <= 0.0031308 else 1.055*x**(1/2.4) - 0.055
print("#%02X%02X%02X" % tuple(round(f(max(0, min(1, v))) * 255) for v in (r, g, bl)))
# #F9F5ED

So the real state of this codebase is: one colour, two notations, five copies of the second notation, and no test. Nudge the ramp step a thousandth of a lightness and the app's background moves while the Android splash screen, the browser's address bar tint, the social card and every email stay where they were. That drift would be invisible in the pull request and faintly visible in real life, as a seam where the browser chrome meets the page.

The fix is not to delete the hex, because nothing on those five boundaries can consume OKLCH. It is to have one of them: a single exported constant that the manifest, the viewport, the card renderer and the email layout all import, with one test asserting it matches the ramp step's conversion. That is maybe thirty lines including the conversion, and it is now on the list. Writing the post is what put it there, which is most of why I write them.

Two of the five already behave: name, short_name and description in the manifest come from the BRAND constant rather than being typed, so the string in an install prompt is the same string as the meta description on the home page.

Next links the manifest without being told to

Our root layout's metadata export has no manifest key in it. It sets a title template, a description, Open Graph defaults, Twitter card type and the icons, and that is all. The manifest link tag still ships on every page:

$ curl -s https://nakodo.app/ | grep -o '<link rel="manifest"[^>]*>'
<link rel="manifest" href="/manifest.webmanifest"/>

That comes from the file convention: app/manifest.ts exists, so the route exists and the tag is injected. Which is convenient and worth knowing precisely, because it means deleting a manifest key from your metadata does not unlink the manifest, and the thing to delete is the file.

It also means the manifest is linked from every public page, including the marketing pages a stranger lands on, which leads to the next part.

The installed app opens a sign-in form 

start_url: "/campaigns",

/campaigns is the signed-in app. It is not public, and our proxy says so:

$ curl -sI https://nakodo.app/campaigns | grep -i '^http\|^location'
HTTP/2 307
location: /login?next=%2Fcampaigns

So: a visitor reads the pricing page, the browser offers to install Nakodo because the page links a manifest with icons over https, they install it, they open the icon, and they get a sign-in form.

I have thought about this one for a while and I am keeping it. For the case the installed app exists for, a customer who uses Nakodo weekly, start_url: "/campaigns" is exactly right: an installed window that opens on the marketing home page would be absurd, and a standalone window shares the browser profile's cookies, so a signed-in customer goes straight to their campaigns. For the stranger case, the redirect carries ?next=%2Fcampaigns, so signing in lands them where the icon said it would. The first run is one screen longer than it should be and it is not a dead end.

What I would not do is point start_url at /. That trades a correct destination for every real user against a tidier first launch for someone who installed an app they have no account for.

The one honest criticism left is that the install prompt is offered at all on a page where the product cannot be used. Chrome decides that, not us, from the manifest and the icons, and the manifest is link-tagged site wide by the convention above. Scoping the tag to the signed-in area would mean dropping the file convention and setting metadata.manifest per route group, which is a larger change than the problem.

Standalone, with no service worker, on purpose 

display: "standalone",

There is no service worker in this app. No sw.js, no caching layer, no offline page:

$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://nakodo.app/sw.js
307

That is the sign-in redirect answering for a file that does not exist, which is its own small joke.

standalone without a service worker is a legitimate combination and it is the one I want. It gives an installed window with no tab strip and no address bar, which is the whole benefit anybody gets from installing a dashboard. What it does not give is offline, and offline is meaningless here: every screen in Nakodo is a server render of live state, and the work it does happens on a cron while nobody is looking. An app shell cached on a phone would show a brand their campaign exactly as stale as the last time they opened it, which is worse than telling them the truth about the network.

If a service worker ever shows up in this repository it will be for web push, not for caching.

The icons, and the one the manifest does not own

Three entries, 192 and 512 PNGs plus the SVG at sizes: "any". The PNGs exist because Android's launcher and the install prompt want raster at known sizes, and 192 and 512 are the two the specification and Chrome's install criteria actually look for.

The apple touch icon is not in the manifest at all. It is in the page metadata:

icons: {
  icon: [
    { url: "/favicon.ico", sizes: "16x16 32x32 48x48" },
    { url: "/icon.svg", type: "image/svg+xml" },
  ],
  apple: "/apple-touch-icon.png",
},

iOS does not take home screen icons from a webmanifest's icons array, and it does not accept an SVG for apple-touch-icon either. So that one is a 180 by 180 PNG, sitting in public/, and if it were missing or an SVG, iOS would quietly use a screenshot of the page instead. That is the kind of bug nobody files, because the person affected assumes it is normal.

The .ico has explicit sizes for a smaller reason: without them, Chrome prefers the .ico over the SVG favicon, and the SVG is the one that follows the colour scheme.

What the file is worth

Twenty lines, of which four are decisions: where an installed window opens, what the splash screen looks like before the first paint, what display mode the window has, and which icons the OS gets. The colour duplication in it is not a mistake in the manifest, it is the shape of every boundary a design system has to cross, and the only real sin is that we cross it five times with five string literals instead of one.

The manifest is public if you want to read the whole of it, and the pricing page is where a browser will probably offer to install it.

title: How do I approve sprite readability across changing scene backgrounds?
description:
Disclosure: This draft was generated with AI and checked against the cited primary sources, with a separate AI editorial review. It was prepared for the FrameSprite team, which has a commercial interest in FrameSprite. Proposed examples are not executed tests unless explicitly identified as recorded fixture results.

Approve a transparent sprite against the scene conditions where its important features must remain readable. One neutral checkerboard cannot represent bright snow, dark interiors, overlays, and changing lighting. Define a small, deliberate background review set before deciding the asset needs repainting.

Key Takeaways

  • Choose backgrounds by the information the player must perceive.
  • Check the final composite at the actual display scale.
  • Distinguish interface contrast requirements from artistic silhouette judgment.

Transparency makes the background part of the result

The PNG specification defines alpha separately from color. A partially transparent edge participates in a composition rather than acting like an opaque outline.

That makes the target background relevant to visual review. It does not mean every sprite requires a universal contrast ratio. W3C non-text contrast guidance concerns relevant meaningful graphical information and interface components; apply its scope carefully.

Build the background set from real scenes

List the situations where the player must identify the character or a specific feature. Select representative backgrounds that stress those tasks: a pale environment behind white hair, dense foliage behind a green weapon, or a dark overlay during a menu.

Include lighting and interface states that actually occur. Do not create dozens of arbitrary color swatches and call that complete scene coverage. A smaller set tied to real conditions gives the art and engineering teams actionable evidence.

Render the complete composition. If a shader, outline, or selection marker provides essential separation, include it. Inspect both the source asset and the supported presentation path so responsibility for the visible result is clear.

Example: the snowfield companion

A companion's white scarf identifies them in a crowded party. The scarf reads clearly in a gray asset viewer but disappears against a snowfield. Increasing the entire character's darkness would also damage the intended armor palette.

Possible repairs include a carefully placed local outline, a different scarf value, or a supported identity marker. Choose the smallest change that preserves the intended information in the real scene. Check the same repair against the dark interior so it does not introduce a new failure.

The scenario is illustrative. No scarf, outline, or scene was rendered for this guide.

Keep meaning separate from color preference

W3C use-of-color guidance is relevant when a feature's hue carries information. If the scarf indicates party role, give that role another perceivable cue rather than relying only on its color.

Record the task, background state, scale, and presentation settings for each proposed check. A pass should describe what was recognizable, not merely that a screenshot looked attractive.

Accept the delivery when required visual cues work in the reviewed scene conditions and any remaining gaps are explicit. This is a proposed review set, not an executed scene benchmark or a claim of complete accessibility. New backgrounds, lighting changes, and equipment can require another targeted review.

Related workflow

See game asset blind review scene acceptance for the adjacent decision. Keep the animation handoff checklist with the deliverable and preserve the art reference board for visual intent.

Prepared by the FrameSprite Workflow Team. Editorial method · Corrections. Primary documentation checked 2026-10-20.

title: How can an artist inspect a large sprite contact sheet without a mouse?
description:
Disclosure: This draft was generated with AI and checked against the cited primary sources, with a separate AI editorial review. It was prepared for the FrameSprite team, which has a commercial interest in FrameSprite. Proposed examples are not executed tests unless explicitly identified as recorded fixture results.

Choose an explicit keyboard model for the contact sheet instead of making every frame a mouse-only target. A simple list of frame buttons and an interactive grid are different interfaces. Use the simpler model unless two-dimensional navigation materially helps the review task.

Key Takeaways

  • Keep frame identity stable while sorting or filtering.
  • Make selection and keyboard focus distinct.
  • Implement the complete chosen interaction model.

A visual grid is not automatically an accessible grid

The WAI-ARIA grid pattern describes a composite interaction model with keyboard responsibilities. Adding a grid role to a group of thumbnails does not implement those behaviors.

For a small contact sheet, ordinary labeled buttons in a meaningful document order may be easier to maintain. For a large sheet, a grid can support efficient directional movement if navigation, focus management, and semantics are implemented together.

Define what each command does

Write down how a reviewer enters the sheet, moves between frames, selects a frame, opens details, and returns to the surrounding controls. Decide what arrow keys do at row boundaries and after filtering.

The keyboard criterion concerns operating functionality without requiring a pointing device. A reviewer should be able to inspect a frame and reach approval controls through the supported keyboard path.

Keep the focused frame identifiable using visible-focus guidance. A selected frame may remain selected while focus moves to a download button. Showing only one of those states makes navigation confusing.

Example: sorting by an error score

A contact sheet initially displays frames in playback order. The reviewer focuses frame 17, then sorts by an alignment score to inspect outliers. If focus remains at the same array position, it can now refer to a different frame.

Track focus by stable frame identity, not by the previous visual index. If the focused frame remains present, restore focus to its new location. If filtering removes it, move to an appropriate remaining control and make that change understandable.

Keep playback order available even when visual review uses another order. Sorting thumbnails must not silently change the exported sequence.

Test the real review path

A proposed task sequence is to enter the sheet, reach a named frame, inspect its metadata, filter results, restore the original view, and leave the sheet. Test with keyboard alone and then with the assistive technologies the tool claims to support.

Check focus after asynchronous thumbnail loading and after removal of a frame. A browser's default focus handling may not preserve the user's place when the focused element is replaced.

Acceptance should record the chosen interaction model and demonstrate that every review action remains reachable. Avoid describing a grid as accessible solely because it has ARIA attributes or a visible border.

This is a proposed browser-review workflow, not an executed keyboard or screen-reader test. It extends the content of a contact sheet into its interaction contract; it does not alter the underlying sprite frames.

Related workflow

See sprite team review contact sheet not preview for the adjacent task. Carry the animation handoff checklist with the release, and use the art reference board to retain visual intent.

Prepared by the FrameSprite Workflow Team. Editorial method · Corrections. Primary documentation checked 2026-10-20.

title: Our proposal screen arrives already written, and every part of it has a Change button instead of an empty field
description:
Nakodo emails creators and businesses on a brand's behalf, which means somewhere in the product the brand has to say what it wants and what it gives in return. A fee, a product, a trial, a commission, a free month. That screen started life as the usual thing: a card with two textareas labelled "What you'd like" and "What they get", a save button, and a blank page.

That version is easy to build and hard to finish, because it asks somebody to write marketing copy from a standing start, in a product they signed up to five minutes ago, before they have seen a single creator. The standing rule in this codebase is now the opposite:

Anything readable off the brand's own site is found automatically and shown as found, with a Change button. Never an empty box.

This post is the 941 lines that rule turned into, and the five pieces of state that carry it.

Nothing is asked for that can be read

The editor is one client component, opened from two places: the campaign setup flow and the outreach tab of a running campaign. Its props are the whole world it needs, including what we already know about the brand:

export type ProposalEditorProps = {
  campaignId: string;
  kind: CampaignKind;
  domain: string;
  platforms: Platform[];
  range: { min: number; max: number }; // the brief's follower range
  currency: Currency;
  saved: Proposal | null; // the brand's own, once there is one
  suggestion: ProposalSuggestion | null;
  pricing: string; // the brand's prices as found on its site, for what a customer is worth
  suggest: boolean; // ask for a suggestion when there's neither
  fits: Audience[]; // the campaign's good fits so far
  approval: "review" | "auto";
  mode: "setup" | "outreach";
};

saved and suggestion are the two sources, in that order of authority, and startingDraft is the whole merge:

function startingDraft(p: ProposalEditorProps): Draft {
  const creators = p.kind === "creators";
  const s = p.saved ?? p.suggestion;
  if (!s) return { idea: "", ask: "", offer: "", terms: creators ? plainTerms(p.range, p.currency) : null };
  return {
    idea: s.idea ?? "",
    ask: creators ? "" : s.ask ?? "",
    offer: creators ? "" : s.offer ?? "",
    terms: creators ? (s.terms ?? plainTerms(p.range, p.currency, s.ask, s.offer)) : null,
  };
}

The interesting line is the last one. Creator campaigns used to have one ask and one offer for everybody; now they have a set of terms per size of creator. Rather than migrating a jsonb column, the old shape is upgraded on read: plainTerms(range, currency, s.ask, s.offer) builds a tier per size and seeds every one of them with the single ask and offer that were saved before tiers existed. A brand that saved a proposal in September opens this screen and sees their own words, repeated across the sizes, ready to differ where they want them to.

A migration in a component is not a thing to be proud of in general. It is right here because the old shape is still a legal shape for a business campaign, so the code has to understand both anyway, and the alternative is a database rewrite plus a component that understands both.

The first open writes the whole thing while you wait

With nothing saved and nothing suggested, the screen does not render a form. It asks for a suggestion immediately, once:

const [writing, setWriting] = useState(!saved && !props.suggestion && props.suggest);
const asked = useRef(false);

// No proposal and no suggestion: ask for one straight away, once.
useEffect(() => {
  if (!writing || asked.current) return;
  asked.current = true;
  askForSuggestion();
}, []);

The ref rather than the empty dependency array is what makes that safe. An effect with no dependencies still runs twice in React's development mode, and this one spends real money, so the guard has to be a value that survives a second run.

While it works, the screen is an honest wait rather than a spinner:

<EmptyState illustration={<Notebook size="m" className="illo-loop" />} title="Writing your proposal.">
  Nakodo is working out what to ask {w.many} for and what to offer them, from what it read on {domain}. This usually takes 10 to 20 seconds.
  <Asides lines={creators ? WRITING_ASIDES : BUSINESS_ASIDES} className="mt-1" />
</EmptyState>

Three things in there are deliberate. The domain is named, because "from what it read on acme.com" tells the reader where the answer is coming from and sets up the Change buttons they are about to use. The estimate is a range with a unit, because "10 to 20 seconds" is a promise the code can keep and "please wait" is not. And Asides rotates a few lines of genuinely useful context, which is the only honest thing to put in a wait that long:

const WRITING_ASIDES = [
  "Smaller creators often say yes to the product and commission. Bigger ones expect a fee.",
  "Fees come from each creator's typical views at market rates, not from their follower count.",
  "A business buyer is usually worth a little more per viewer than a shopper.",
];

Failure has its own branch, with two ways out rather than one: try again, or write my own. A screen whose only recovery is a retry button is a screen that can trap somebody behind a provider outage.

A suggestion that is only on screen is not saved 

// Nothing saved yet counts as unsaved: a suggestion only takes effect once saved.
const [dirty, setDirty] = useState(!saved);

This is the most important line in the file. The suggestion arrives, fills the screen, and reads exactly like a finished document, so it would be entirely reasonable for the reader to assume it is already in effect. It is not: nothing is written to the campaign until Save. Initialising dirty from !saved means the bar at the bottom says "You have unsaved changes" from the first paint, and the browser asks before the tab closes:

// Leaving with unsaved edits asks first.
useEffect(() => {
  if (!dirty || writing) return;
  const warn = (e: BeforeUnloadEvent) => e.preventDefault();
  window.addEventListener("beforeunload", warn);
  return () => window.removeEventListener("beforeunload", warn);
}, [dirty, writing]);

!writing in the guard because a half-written proposal that does not exist yet is not something worth warning about, and the warning would land while the reader is watching a progress state they did not cause.

Facts, with Change on them

Each part of the proposal is a card. Closed, it is a description list. Open, it is fields with a Done button. The state is one union:

// What's open for changing: the idea, a business's ask and offer, or a size.
type Open = "idea" | "business" | CreatorSize | null;

One union rather than a boolean per section, so only one thing is ever open and the rest of the page stays readable while you type. The closed view:

<dl className="space-y-3">
  <Fact label="Ask">{draft.ask.trim() ? cap(draft.ask.trim()) : <Unset />}</Fact>
  <Fact label="They get">{draft.offer.trim() ? cap(draft.offer.trim()) : <Unset />}</Fact>
</dl>

Unset is 1 line and exists to be rare:

export const Unset = () => <span className="text-muted-foreground">Not set yet</span>;

It is what "never an empty box" looks like when the box genuinely is empty: still a sentence, in the muted colour, in the same layout as a filled fact, rather than an input waiting for you.

The Change button carries the distinction the reader cares about:

<Button variant="ghost" size="sm" onClick={onClick} aria-label={`${empty ? "Add" : "Change"} ${label}`}>
  <PencilIcon />
  {empty ? "Add" : "Change"}
</Button>

aria-label spells out which thing is being changed, because fifteen buttons on one page all named "Change" are useless in a list of landmarks, and the visible label stays short because the card's title is right next to it.

Section, ChangeButton, Editing, Fact, Unset and Segmented live in one 122-line file, imported by four screens: the proposal, the campaign details, the reply settings and the setup flow. That is the whole reason those three screens feel like one screen.

Segmented controls in there are real radios with no JavaScript:

<label className="cursor-pointer rounded-md px-3 py-1.5 text-sm text-muted-foreground has-checked:bg-card has-checked:font-medium has-checked:text-foreground has-focus-visible:outline-2">
  <input type="radio" name={name} value={o.value} checked={value === o.value} onChange={() => onChange(o.value)} className="sr-only" />
  {o.label}
</label>

The input is visually hidden rather than replaced, inside a fieldset with a legend, so arrow keys, the focus ring and the accessible name all come from the platform. has-checked: and has-focus-visible: do the styling that a custom toggle would otherwise need state for.

Typing something by hand changes the rules for that field

This is the detail that took three tries to get right. Each creator size has a content format (a mention, a dedicated video, a Reel) and an ask written in words. Choosing a different format should update the words, because the words describe the format. But if you wrote your own ask, a format change must not throw your sentence away:

// Sizes whose ask was typed by hand: a new format no longer replaces it.
const [typedAsks, setTypedAsks] = useState<Set<CreatorSize>>(() => new Set(saved ? draft.terms?.tiers.map((t) => t.size) : []));

const chooseFormat = (tier: Tier, format: AskFormat) => {
  const suggested = suggestion?.terms?.tiers.find((t) => t.size === tier.size);
  editTier(tier.size, {
    format,
    ...(!typedAsks.has(tier.size) && { ask: suggested?.format === format ? suggested.ask : DEFAULT_ASKS[format] }),
  });
};

Two rules in four lines. A size the reader has typed into is left alone for ever. A size they have not gets new words, and if the format they just picked is the one that was originally suggested, the words that come back are the suggested ones rather than the generic default, so clicking away and clicking back is not destructive.

The initial value of that set is the other half of it: when a proposal was loaded from the database, every tier counts as typed by hand, because we have no idea which parts of it the brand wrote and have to assume all of it.

Reasons expire when the draft stops resembling the suggestion

The preview panel beside the editor shows the suggestion's reasoning: why this ask, why this offer. Those sentences are about the suggestion, so they stop being true once the proposal has been rewritten:

// Whether the draft still mostly says what Nakodo suggested, so its reasons
// still apply.
function followsSuggestion(d: Draft, s: ProposalSuggestion): boolean {
  if (d.idea === s.idea) return true;
  if (!d.terms) return d.ask === s.ask || d.offer === s.offer;
  return d.terms.tiers.some((t) => s.terms?.tiers.find((x) => x.size === t.size)?.ask === t.ask);
}

reasons={suggestion && followsSuggestion(draft, suggestion) ? suggestion.reasons : []}

It is a deliberately loose test: any one part still matching counts. A strict equality check would drop the explanation the moment somebody fixed a typo, and the explanation is most useful precisely while they are editing. The honest failure mode of loose is an explanation that outlives one of the three things it explains, which is better than an explanation that vanishes when you touch anything.

One level of undo, in one piece of state

There is a "Suggest again" button, which throws the current proposal away and asks for a new one. That needs an undo, and undo in a form usually turns into a history stack nobody asked for:

const [undo, setUndo] = useState<Draft | null>(null);

// in askForSuggestion:
setUndo(replacing ? draft : null);

One slot. It holds the draft as it was immediately before the replacement, and the button only exists while it is full:

{undo && (
  <Button variant="ghost" onClick={() => { setDraft(undo); setUndo(null); }}>
    <Undo2Icon /> Undo
  </Button>
)}

The draft is a plain object of strings and small arrays, so storing a copy of it costs nothing and restoring it is one setState. The first suggestion sets undo to null, because there is nothing to go back to and a disabled Undo button is a worse answer than no Undo button.

Saving, and the question that only exists on one of the two routes 

const [saving, runSave] = useAction();

const next = mode === "setup" ? `/campaigns/new/${campaignId}` : `/campaigns/${campaignId}/outreach`;

const save = () =>
  runSave(
    () => saveProposalAction(campaignId, asInput(draft)),
    (r) => {
      setDirty(false);
      setOpen(null);
      if (mode === "outreach" && r.redraft) setRedraft(r.redraft);
      else router.push(next);
    },
  );

useAction is an 18-line file over useTransition that runs a server action, turns its result into a toast, and calls onOk only on success. Every mutating button in the app goes through it, which is why the whole codebase has one idea of what "saving" looks like.

mode decides where Cancel and a successful save go, so the same component is a step in a wizard on one route and a settings screen on another, without either route knowing about the other.

And then the case that only exists in the running-campaign route. Changing the proposal while emails are already drafted and waiting means those drafts were written from details that are now out of date, so instead of navigating away, the save opens a dialog:

Rewrite the 7 emails waiting to go out?

They were written from your old details. Rewritten emails wait for your approval again. It takes about a minute.

with a checkbox that only appears if some of those drafts were edited by hand:

{edited > 0 && (
  <Label htmlFor={id}>
    {edited === total ? `Replace your own edits too (you edited all ${edited})` : ...}
  </Label>
)}

Default off. The thing a person typed is the thing a bulk action must not quietly destroy, which is the same rule as typedAsks, two screens apart.

What the shape is worth

Five pieces of state carry all of it: draft, open, dirty, typedAsks and undo. No form library, no reducer, no field-level validation layer. The reason that stays manageable is that the screen is not really a form. It is a document that arrives written, with the parts you can change marked, and a single save at the bottom.

If you want the public version of the thinking behind the numbers in it, the sponsorship cost calculator is the same arithmetic with nothing hidden, and the pricing page describes what Nakodo does with a proposal once it is saved. The suggestion's own instructions and the fee tables stay in the app, where they belong.

title: Why do SDL3 nine-grid UI corners look wrong after resizing a panel?
description:
Disclosure: This draft was generated with AI and checked against the cited primary sources, with a separate AI editorial review. It was prepared for the FrameSprite team, which has a commercial interest in FrameSprite. Proposed examples are not executed tests unless explicitly identified as recorded fixture results.

SDL3 SDL_RenderTexture9Grid takes source-pixel border sizes and a separate corner scale. The destination rectangle controls the panel's overall size; it does not redefine which pixels belong to its corners. Measure the source cuts before tuning the destination. The official nine-grid reference defines each argument.

Key Takeaways

  • Border widths refer to the selected source region.
  • Corner scale and panel dimensions are separate choices.
  • Stretching and tiling the panel center produce different results.

Mark the actual source rectangle

If a panel is packed into an atlas, first verify its source rectangle with an ordinary textured draw. A nine-grid operation cannot repair a source region that already includes the neighboring icon.

Use temporary marks at the four border cuts. For an illustrative 64 by 64 source panel with eight-pixel decoration, the inner area begins after those source cuts. Do not express them as percentages of a changing destination width.

The sheet preparation guide covers atlas dimensions and source organization. Keep those packing choices independent from the display-size decision.

Supply explicit corners and destination

An example configuration is:

/* SDL 3.2+ fragment; not compiled or run here. */
SDL_FRect source = {0, 0, 64, 64};
SDL_FRect destination = {20, 20, 240, 96};
if (!SDL_RenderTexture9Grid(
        renderer, panel_texture, &source,
        8, 8, 8, 8, 1.0f, &destination)) {
    SDL_Log("Nine-grid draw failed: %s", SDL_GetError());
}

These are constructed dimensions for a symmetrical panel. Measure asymmetric ornamentation separately. A left border of eight pixels is inappropriate if a flourish extends farther into the source.

The documented scale parameter controls how source corners are transformed into destination corners. Do not increase it merely to make the center pattern larger. That changes the decorative frame as well.

Decide whether the center may stretch

A flat fill often tolerates stretching. A grid, fabric weave or repeated rivet pattern may need repetition instead. SDL provides SDL_RenderTexture9GridTiled for the related tiled operation starting in SDL 3.4.0. A build targeting only SDL 3.2 cannot assume this additional function is available.

For a baseline comparison, SDL_RenderTexture draws the source as a single scaled image. Showing that beside the nine-grid result makes it easier to see which corner distortion the split actually addresses.

Panel content Inspection priority
Flat center, ornate corners Border placement and corner scale
Repeated center pattern Pattern size under resize
Illustration crossing every cut Separate illustration from scalable frame
Small destination Room for borders and readable content

The UI button-state checklist covers appearance across interaction states. Nine-grid drawing does not generate those states or define their clickable regions.

Acceptance at minimum size

Draw narrow, wide and tall destinations and inspect all four corners. Test the smallest supported panel, not only the attractive large version. Keep text and icons outside border decorations through explicit layout rules.

Repeat with an atlas-packed source to ensure the cuts remain relative to that region. Record source rectangle, border pixels, corner scale and minimum destination in the delivery checklist.

No SDL rendering run was performed here. The main operation is documented since SDL 3.2.0; related newer operations must be checked against the actual linked runtime.

Measure a content-safe inset separately

Define the panel's content-safe area independently of the source border cuts. Decorative corners may extend inward beyond the simple cut line, leaving less usable room for text or a portrait. Check the longest supported label and the smallest intended panel before approving the asset. If content cannot fit, provide a larger minimum size or a simpler compact frame. Do not shrink every corner until the label fits without reviewing whether the visual design remains readable. Nine-grid sampling and interface layout solve different parts of the task.

Sources and editorial ownership

Primary references checked on October 20, 2026:

  • Nine-grid source borders and corner scale
  • Related tiled nine-grid operation
  • Ordinary scaled source comparison

Editorial owner: FrameSprite Workflow Team. Editorial and verification policy. Report a documentation correction.

title: One picker for seven conditions and fourteen allergies, and its hardest rule is that nothing you selected may hide
description:
Munchable asks you two questions before it can answer anything: which digestive conditions you are eating for, and which allergies you need flagged. The seven conditions are listed on munchable.app/conditions, each with its own guide, for example GERD and reflux. The allergies are the fourteen that labels are legally required to declare.

Both questions are the same screen, twice, in onboarding and again in settings. One component renders all of it, and almost every line of it is about one of two problems: a list long enough to be a scroll instead of a choice, and a choice that disappears.

A list is split only when splitting pays 

/**
 * The list is only split once it is long enough that scanning it costs
 * something. Below this every item is simply a row, which is what the seven
 * conditions want; the fourteen allergies get the common set and a search.
 */
const SPLIT_AT = 9;

Seven conditions render as seven rows with no search field at all. Fourteen allergies render the seven with the highest adult prevalence in UK and US surveys, a search, and a "Show 7 more" disclosure.

That threshold is the only configuration either screen passes about layout. Everything else about the shape of the list is derived, so adding an eighth condition one day changes the screen without anybody deciding it should.

Search has to match the word you would actually type

The search runs over three fields: the title, the one-line helper, and a hidden keyword list that is never displayed.

keywords: ['heartburn', 'acid', 'reflux', 'gord', 'oesophageal'],
keywords: ['fodmap', 'irritable bowel', 'bloating'],
keywords: ['bile', 'bile acid', 'diarrhoea', 'diarrhea'],

People do not search for the name of their condition in the form a product team wrote it. They search for the symptom, for the abbreviation they were given at the clinic, and for whichever of two spellings their country uses. Both spellings of diarrhoea are in there for exactly that reason, and so is the British spelling of the reflux acronym, GORD, next to the American GERD.

Matching folds diacritics as well as case, so an accent typed or not typed makes no difference:

/** Lowercase and strip diacritics, so "coeliac" finds "Coeliac" and "é" finds "e". */
function fold(s: string): string {
  return s.normalize('NFD').replace(/[̀-ͯ]/g, '').toLowerCase();
}

The item arrays are built once at module scope rather than inline in the screens, because three screens render the same list and the search is a useMemo whose dependency is that array. A fresh literal per render means the memo is decorative.

Nothing you chose is allowed to hide

Here is the bug that drove most of this component. Select something from the bottom of the expanded list, collapse the list, and your selection is now behind a disclosure you have to remember to open. The screen says you picked four things and shows three.

So selected rows get pinned into view:

// Hidden items that are selected get pinned into view, so nothing the user
// has chosen is ever behind a disclosure they would have to remember to open.
const [pinned, setPinned] = useState<Set<Id>>(() => new Set(selected));

Then three subtleties, each of which was a real moment of the thing feeling wrong.

Pinning happens when the list closes, not when the item is tapped, because closing is the moment something could go out of sight. While the list is open nothing is pinned at all: every row is already on screen in its own place, and hoisting the row you just tapped up the page moves the thing under your finger.

Selecting from the collapsed list or from a search result pins immediately, because clearing a search is the other way a just-made choice can vanish.

And deselecting does not unpin. The row stays exactly where it is until the next time the screen is opened. Tapping a checkbox should never make the row you are looking at disappear, even when your tap means "not this one".

While a search is running, anything selected that the query does not reach gets named underneath rather than silently dropped:

{missed.length > 0 ? (
  <Text variant="caption" muted>Also selected: {missed.map((i) => i.title).join(', ')}.</Text>
) : null}

The empty state names the edge of the list

A search that matches nothing is the one place a picker can leave somebody stuck, so it does not say "no results":

export const CONDITIONS_NOT_LISTED =
  'Munchable checks seven digestive conditions today. If yours is not here, it cannot be checked yet.';

export const ALLERGIES_NOT_LISTED =
  'Munchable checks the 14 allergens that labels must declare. If yours is not here, it cannot be checked yet.';

Both are deliberately flat. Searching for a condition Munchable does not cover is a real answer and the user has learned something true about the product in one sentence. The alternative, a cheerful "try another search", wastes the only moment where the honest answer is useful.

The clear button sits in the field the whole time, so the way out of an empty result is one tap and is visible before you need it.

The accessibility details are in the labels, not the look

The visible disclosure says "Show 7 more". Its accessibility label says the noun too:

accessibilityLabel={showRest ? `Show fewer ${noun}` : `Show ${hiddenItems.length} more ${noun}`}
accessibilityState={{ expanded: showRest }}

The noun prop exists for that string alone, which is why the component takes "allergies" and "conditions" as text. "Show 7 more" is clear when you can see what it sits under and meaningless read on its own. The clear button announces "Clear allergies search" for the same reason. Rows are role="checkbox" with their selected state attached, rather than a styled pressable that looks chosen.

The only non-visual feedback is one haptic tick per toggle. The app ships no sound files at all, so a selection confirms itself by feel or not at all.

Open the conditions page and you are looking at the same seven items, the same titles and the same one-line helpers the picker shows, just rendered as pages instead of rows. The list is short enough to read in full, which is the whole reason the picker can afford to tell you when your condition is not on it.

title: One palette in a package, 28 CSS variables beside it, and the file that calls itself the source of truth is still green
description:
Munchable is a barcode scanner for people with digestive conditions. You point a phone at a pack and it answers for your own set of conditions. The whole product is one look, which the team notes call "Cookie and Cream": a cream base, cocoa ink, cookie gold and caramel for the playful parts, one pink pop for sprinkles.

You can see it on the landing page, in a condition guide like the IBS and low FODMAP one, and on a recipe page such as gentle rice congee. Keep one of those open, because the point of this post is that a repository can hold several descriptions of its own colours, and only the live pages tell you which description won.

Three surfaces, one look

Three things have to look like Munchable: the Expo app, the marketing site, and the Remotion compositions that render a phone running Munchable for social video.

The third one is why a token package exists at all. The reels used to carry a hand-copied palette under a comment promising it mirrored the app:

/**
 * The reels' look is the app's look.
 *
 * The palette, the scales and the verdict vocabulary are IMPORTED from
 * @munchable/design-tokens ... They used to be hand-copied here under a
 * comment promising they mirrored the app, which is exactly the arrangement
 * that drifts: changing the caution colour or the "Can't assess" label in the
 * app left the reels rendering the old one with no type error.
 */

That is the failure worth designing against. Nothing breaks, nothing fails to compile, and the marketing video shows last month's product.

So packages/design-tokens holds the platform-free half: the palette, spacing, radii, the type scale as sizes only, and the verdict vocabulary. apps/mobile/src/theme/tokens.ts re-exports all of it and adds the parts that need React Native, which are the motion curve, the shadow, and the font-family names Expo loads. The reels import the same module. App code still has one import path, and a phone in a video is painted from the real values.

Two decisions in that file are worth pulling out.

The contrast ratio of every pairing is written next to the value, so a colour cannot be nudged without reading what it costs:

text: '#3B2314',       // cocoa, cream 13.9:1
textMuted: '#7F5F47',  // warm brown, cream 5.5:1
link: '#9A5F1C',       // deep caramel, cream 4.9:1
accent: '#FF8FAB',     // decoration only: it fails contrast as text

And there is exactly one palette:

/** The one and only palette. Munchable is light mode only. */
export const palette: Palette = light;

No dark object, no theme switch, no useColorScheme. A light-only product is a real decision with real costs, and writing it as one exported constant means nobody has to wonder whether the dark half is missing or unfinished.

The website does not import any of it

The site is plain CSS. Its colours live in 28 custom properties at the top of a 3,144-line stylesheet:

:root {
  --primary: #5c3417;
  --ink: #3b2314;
  --bg: #fff8ec;
  --bg-warm: #f5ead8;

  --good: #15803d;
  --caution: #b45309;
  --avoid: #dc2626;

  --r-sm: 12px;
  --r: 18px;
  --r-lg: 28px;
}

That is defensible. Custom properties are the web's own token mechanism, cascade into every rule for free, and pulling a TypeScript module into a stylesheet means adding a codegen step and a generated file to review. The cost is that agreement between the site and the app is now a convention rather than a type.

So I audited it while writing this, and the result is split cleanly in two.

Every colour agrees, exactly. --bg is the package's bg, --ink is text, --primary is primary, and the three verdict colours match to the digit.

The radii do not agree at all. The package says 8, 12, 16, 22. The stylesheet says 12, 18, 28. Those are not roundings of each other, and no comment in either file claims the site is deliberately rounder than the app. The site's cards are physically bigger, so a bigger radius may well be the right call, but right now the only evidence that it was a call is that somebody typed it.

There is also a colour the site does not have. The package defines four verdict colours, and the fourth one carries a rule:

/** Solid verdict colour. `unknown` is deliberately grey, never green. */

The stylesheet has three. The marketing pages never render the fourth state, so nothing was missing, but it does mean the one verdict colour with a written-down rule attached is the one living in a single file.

The third copy, which is not a copy of anything

While looking, I found a docs/design-tokens.json. It opens like this:

"description": "Poppy, fresh-produce-energy design system for the Munchable
  gut-health app. Machine-readable source of truth; codegen'd into the RN
  theme."

And docs/DESIGN-SYSTEM.md beside it says, in bold, that when the two disagree the JSON wins and the prose is stale.

Its palette is green. bg is #FBFDF6, text is #152318, primary is #0A8049, and the avoid colour is described in the prose as a friendly watermelon coral. It is a complete, carefully reasoned design system for a product that now looks nothing like it, from before the cookie mark existed.

My favourite part is that the shipped palette has a comment forbidding precisely what the stale file prescribes:

// The brand primary is deliberately not green so a button never reads as "good".

Nothing generates anything. grep -rl design-tokens.json over the repository returns exactly one file: the Markdown document that points at it. There is no codegen step, there never was one in this repository, and the React Native theme it claims to produce is a hand-written file importing a TypeScript package.

What I take from it

A token package is worth it for the surface it can actually reach. Moving one palette out of the app and into a package deleted a whole class of silent drift between the app and the video renderer, and it did it with types rather than vigilance.

It cannot reach a stylesheet, and the honest version of that is to say so, which is why the radius mismatch is in this post rather than quietly fixed in the same commit. The fix I want is a test that reads both files and asserts the shared values, not a migration of the site onto a JavaScript theme.

The JSON is worse than the mismatch. A document claiming to be generated reads like a build step, so the next person to touch the design either edits the wrong file or stops trusting documents. Two sources of truth that disagree is a bug. A third that lies about being generated is a trap, and deleting it is one line in a commit nobody will miss.

Open munchable.app and you can settle which palette shipped in about three seconds. That is the part a repository cannot argue with.

title: Building a Zero-Dependency Interactive T-Shirt Size Calculator (S-5XL) in Vanilla JavaScript
description:
One of the highest-friction moments in online apparel e-commerce is the size selector. Most stores still rely on a static table of numbers that leaves shoppers guessing whether they should measure their body or an existing shirt — and whether a unisex Medium will still fit after its first trip through the dryer.

While building the sizing tooling for Tshirts I Want (Wear what you're really into. — an online store for original graphic apparel printed on demand in the USA), we wanted a fast, zero-dependency, client-side tool that solves both individual fit questions and bulk group orders (family reunions, charity 5Ks, school drama casts, and company teams).

You can try the live tool here:
Live Demo: Interactive T-Shirt Size Calculator (S-5XL)

1. The Domain Problem: Garment Width vs. Body Chest Circumference

When shoppers read a size chart, two completely different measurements often get confused:

  1. Flat-Lay Half-Chest Width (Armpit-to-Armpit): Measured across a shirt lying flat on a table, 1 inch below the armholes.
  2. Full Body Chest Circumference: Measured around the fullest part of the wearer's chest with a flexible tape.

A classic adult unisex crewneck (sizes S through 5XL) needs 2 to 4 inches of ease over body chest circumference for a standard everyday fit, less ease for a tailored silhouette, and more ease for a relaxed streetwear drape.

To document the underlying garment specifications clearly, we paired the calculator with four reference guides:

  • Unisex T-Shirt Size Chart: Chest, Length & Fit Guide (S-5XL)
  • How Should a T-Shirt Fit? Shoulder Seam, Chest, Sleeve & Length Checkpoints
  • Men's vs. Women's vs. Unisex T-Shirt Sizing Compared
  • Does Cotton Shrink? Ringspun Cotton vs. Heavy Cotton vs. Cotton-Poly Blends

2. Modeling the S-5XL Garment Measurement Matrix in Vanilla JS

Rather than loading a heavy third-party sizing widget that blocks main-thread rendering or requires external API calls, we modeled the S-5XL size chart as a deterministic lookup table in vanilla JavaScript:

const UNISEX_SIZE_MATRIX = [
  { size: "S",   flatWidthIn: 18.0, lengthIn: 28.0, chestMinIn: 34, chestMaxIn: 37 },
  { size: "M",   flatWidthIn: 20.0, lengthIn: 29.0, chestMinIn: 38, chestMaxIn: 41 },
  { size: "L",   flatWidthIn: 22.0, lengthIn: 30.0, chestMinIn: 42, chestMaxIn: 45 },
  { size: "XL",  flatWidthIn: 24.0, lengthIn: 31.0, chestMinIn: 46, chestMaxIn: 49 },
  { size: "2XL", flatWidthIn: 26.0, lengthIn: 32.0, chestMinIn: 50, chestMaxIn: 53 },
  { size: "3XL", flatWidthIn: 28.0, lengthIn: 33.0, chestMinIn: 54, chestMaxIn: 57 },
  { size: "4XL", flatWidthIn: 30.0, lengthIn: 34.0, chestMinIn: 58, chestMaxIn: 61 },
  { size: "5XL", flatWidthIn: 32.0, lengthIn: 35.0, chestMinIn: 62, chestMaxIn: 65 }
];

function recommendByFlatShirt(flatWidthInches, lengthInches, fitOffset = 0) {
  const targetWidth = flatWidthInches + fitOffset;
  for (const row of UNISEX_SIZE_MATRIX) {
    if (row.flatWidthIn >= targetWidth - 0.5 && row.lengthIn >= lengthInches - 1.0) {
      return row;
    }
  }
  return UNISEX_SIZE_MATRIX[UNISEX_SIZE_MATRIX.length - 1];
}

Handling Fit Preference & Cotton Shrinkage Buffers

As detailed in our Does Cotton Shrink? laundering study, 100% ringspun and heavy cotton tees typically shrink 3% to 5% when tumble-dried on medium-to-high heat. When a shopper lands on the boundary between two sizes (for example, a 41-inch chest sitting right between M and L) and plans to machine-dry their shirts, the calculator surfaces a boundary recommendation so they can size up confidently.

3. Zero-Latency UX & Accessibility Details

  • Instant Unit Conversion (in to cm): Every input and table cell converts dynamically using 1 in = 2.54 cm without page reloads.
  • Dual Input Modes: Users can switch between Compare My Favorite Shirt (Flat-Lay) and Body Chest + Height + Fit Preference depending on whether they have a measuring tape or an existing tee handy.
  • Shareable URL for Group Orders: Event organizers collecting shirt sizes for a reunion, club, or race can link directly to https://tshirtsiwant.com/tools/size-calculator/ inside Google Forms or registration pages.

Check out the live calculator at tshirtsiwant.com/tools/size-calculator/ and explore our full graphic apparel collection at tshirtsiwant.com.

title: Why can a Bevy camera see a character body but not its child equipment?
description:
Disclosure: This draft was generated with AI and checked against the cited primary sources, with a separate AI editorial review. It was prepared for the FrameSprite team, which has a commercial interest in FrameSprite. Proposed examples are not executed tests unless explicitly identified as recorded fixture results.

Check RenderLayers on both the camera and each renderable entity when a Bevy character body appears but its child equipment does not. RenderLayers are not inherited from the parent. The camera and renderable must share a layer. This is separate from hierarchy visibility and image loading, as documented in the Bevy 0.17.2 layer implementation.

Key Takeaways

  • Parent-child ownership does not copy a render layer to equipment.
  • Confirm an actual camera/entity layer intersection.
  • Keep the body and equipment visible in a minimal single-camera scene first.

List the renderable entities

A character root may be only a gameplay entity. Its body, sword and shadow can be separate Sprite children. Inspect the component on the Sprite entity itself, not just on the root shown at the top of the hierarchy.

Create a short inventory with entity ID, parent ID, image handle, Visibility and RenderLayers. For the intended camera, record its layers and target. This makes an invisible sword a concrete mismatch to investigate rather than a reason to regenerate the PNG.

If the image is still loading, first follow the Bevy dependency-readiness guide. An absent image and a layer mismatch can produce similar screenshots but need different fixes.

Align the camera and selected drawables

A small setup fragment illustrates a dedicated preview layer:

// Bevy 0.17.2, unexecuted setup fragments.
commands.entity(preview_camera).insert(RenderLayers::layer(1));
commands.entity(body).insert(RenderLayers::layer(1));
commands.entity(weapon).insert(RenderLayers::layer(1));

Do not paste this into every entity indiscriminately. A portrait camera may intentionally exclude world shadows, and a main camera may intentionally exclude preview equipment. Decide which renderables belong to the view, then assign the shared layer.

The official pixel-grid example uses camera and layer separation in a render-to-texture setup. It is useful evidence of the mechanism, not a ready-made policy for your character hierarchy.

Test visibility and layers independently

Visibility can still hide a correctly layered drawable. The visibility implementation describes hierarchy-related visibility separately. Temporarily use a simple visible root and a known loaded image when testing the layer intersection.

Body Weapon Preview camera Interpretation
Layer 1 Layer 0 Layer 1 Weapon has no shared layer
Layer 1 Layer 1 Layer 1 Inspect loading, visibility, position and target
Layers 0 and 1 Layer 1 Layer 0 Body may appear while weapon is excluded

Avoid inferring a layer problem from a single successful frame. Switch the active camera or open the preview and gameplay views together. A drawable assigned to both may appear twice if both cameras render into the same final view.

Preserve the asset contract

Layer selection should not change frame order, alpha or the position of the weapon inside its source image. The equipment-layering guide explains the artwork tradeoff; this procedure addresses which renderable a particular camera draws.

Store the camera-layer policy with the sprite delivery checklist, especially when a preview feature creates a second camera.

Acceptance requires the intended body, weapon and shadow to appear in the correct views and remain absent from excluded views. Test after reparenting equipment. This is a source-based diagnostic for Bevy 0.17.2; the setup has not been executed here.

Check newly attached equipment

Test equipment created after the initial character setup, not only parts spawned at startup. A system that assigns layers to existing children once can miss a sword attached later. Put the intended view assignment in the equipment creation or attachment path and validate it when that path runs. When an item is moved between world and preview views, update the layer policy deliberately. Copying a layer from an arbitrary sibling is fragile because that sibling may serve a different camera or represent an intentionally excluded shadow.

Sources and editorial ownership

Primary references checked on October 20, 2026:

  • RenderLayers inheritance and intersection
  • Official layered camera example
  • Visibility propagation implementation

Editorial owner: FrameSprite Workflow Team. Editorial and verification policy. Report a documentation correction.

title: Why does a Bevy sprite preview image stay blank when used as a camera target?
description:
Disclosure: This draft was generated with AI and checked against the cited primary sources, with a separate AI editorial review. It was prepared for the FrameSprite team, which has a commercial interest in FrameSprite. Proposed examples are not executed tests unless explicitly identified as recorded fixture results.

A Bevy image used as a camera target must support render attachment usage. If the same image is later displayed by a Sprite, it also needs texture binding usage. A preview can remain blank even though its handle exists and its PNG sources loaded. The Bevy 0.17.2 pixel-grid example shows the producer camera and displayed canvas.

Key Takeaways

  • World-retention flags and GPU texture usages are separate settings.
  • Render the preview before the camera that displays its image.
  • Keep the preview camera from drawing its own output sprite.

Create an image for the target role

An ordinary imported sprite image is not automatically the right render destination. Start with a purpose-built target of known dimensions and an explicit format supported by your rendering path.

Bevy 0.17.2 provides a helper for that role:

// Configuration fragment, not executed here.
let canvas = Image::new_target_texture(
    256,
    256,
    TextureFormat::Bgra8UnormSrgb,
);
let canvas_handle = images.add(canvas);

The Bevy Image helper implementation sets texture binding, copy destination and render attachment usages. If you construct the descriptor manually, preserve the capabilities required by your use instead of copying only its size and format.

Do not confuse those flags with RenderAssetUsages. The latter controls main-world/render-world retention, as defined in the asset usage source. Retaining a CPU image does not give a GPU texture permission to act as a render attachment.

Separate producer and consumer

The preview camera produces the image. A second view displays a Sprite using that handle. Give the producer an earlier render order than the consumer and assign appropriate layers to both views.

Inspect the pinned example's Camera.order and RenderTarget::Image configuration rather than assuming startup system order determines rendering order. A source sprite may exist before both cameras while the cameras still need an explicit rendering relationship.

Keep the canvas Sprite outside the preview camera's selected layers. Otherwise the preview may sample the image it is currently producing or form an unintended recursive display. The intended result is the isolated character, not an image of its own monitor.

Diagnose with a solid clear color

Use a conspicuous preview clear color and one simple source Sprite. If the displayed image shows only the clear color, the target may be working while the source sprite is excluded or outside the camera view. If it stays unchanged after the clear color changes, inspect the target handle, consumer Sprite and camera execution.

Result Next boundary
Target creation reports a validation error Texture descriptor and format capabilities
Clear color visible, character absent Layers, framing, image readiness and visibility
Previous preview persists Producer execution or target/handle replacement
Scene appears inside its own preview Producer/consumer layer separation

The Bevy loading guide covers source readiness. The mobile texture-budget guide helps bound target dimensions; a larger preview is not a free fix.

Acceptance after resize and replacement

Open and close the preview repeatedly, replace the character, and resize the target deliberately. Confirm both camera target and displayed Sprite use the intended handle after a replacement. Keep export/readback as a separate requirement.

Record the target size, camera order and layer policy in the handoff checklist. This is a source-grounded Bevy 0.17.2 recipe. No GPU validation or rendering run was performed here.

Keep a replacement target coherent

If resizing creates a new image handle, treat the camera target and the displayed canvas as one small replacement set. Updating only one makes the producer write into an image the consumer no longer displays. Keep the old valid pair until the new pair is ready, then publish both references through the same transition owner. Include any export or thumbnail consumer in that inventory. This recommendation concerns handle coordination; it does not assert that creating an image synchronously means every downstream GPU operation has already completed.

Sources and editorial ownership

Primary references checked on October 20, 2026:

  • Official camera-to-image and canvas example
  • Target image capabilities
  • World-retention flags

Editorial owner: FrameSprite Workflow Team. Editorial and verification policy. Report a documentation correction.
