title: Design v ADHD
description:
ADHD is a complex and common mental disorder which changes how the person processes information, behaves, and functions in society. Common recommendations for “ADHD-friendly design” include reducing clutter, avoiding distractions, and simplifying information architecture. I argue that these suggestions do not constitute “ADHD-friendly design”, and that the real solution is more sophisticated and challenging, if not impossible, to implement.

In 2014, Ethan Zuckerman, a renowned media scholar and Internet activist, apologised for his role in inventing the Internet’s most hated marketing tool: the pop-up ad.

All of us have screwed up situations in our lives so badly that we’ve been forced to explain our actions by reminding everyone of our good intentions. It’s obvious now that what we did was a fiasco, so let me remind you that what we wanted to do was something brave and noble.

In the late 1990s, Zuckerman led a team at tripod.com — a popular service which allowed users to launch their own websites for free. Zuckerman had tried countless ways to fund the growing business until concurring that the only way to keep the company afloat was to bring in advertisers. The format invented by his team — a pop-up ad — would not only boost tripod.com’s revenue but change the Internet once and for all.

With the advent of the pop-up ad came the boom of intrusive, aggressive, and persistent advertising. The industry has weaponised our lack of attention and filled every corner of the Internet with meaningless distractions and quick rewards. Pop-ups embodied everything wrong about the advertiser-centric approach: it appeared out of thin air and demanded attention like a capricious baby, no matter what was on the user’s mind or what they were occupied with. Pop-ups reduced users to targets for the omnipresent advertisers.

The Internet today is the realm of noise and chaos. Advertisers are more vicious than their predecessors, and ads themselves have transformed to appear more organic and blend into the content until it is impossible to tell them apart. Users continue to limp around this inaccessible desert, constantly bombarded with emails and notifications informing them of special offers, keeping them up to date with what their friends have been up to, and begging them to return for more mindless entertainment.

How does someone with an already disrupted attention span find the strength to concentrate when the entire world around them is vying for their attention? How do they make decisions, resist temptations, and struggle to conform in an environment that does not suit someone like them at all?

In this article, we will discuss people with ADHD, what it means to live with this condition, and why existing design frameworks for neurodivergent users address the wrong problem.

Understanding Attention Deficit and Hyperactivity Disorder

ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition that affects a person’s ability to concentrate and control emotions and actions. Despite being commonly associated with hyperactivity (hence the name), there are several distinct types of ADHD: hyperactive and impulsive (rather self-descriptive), inattentive (characterised by distractibility and lack of attention), and combined (the most prevalent type); each manifesting differently in each individual patient. Most commonly, people (especially adults) with ADHD have problems concentrating on the task at hand, be it a work assignment or a lengthy conversation.

MRI studies of patients with ADHD show various dysfunctions in dopamine and noradrenaline transmissions. The disorder particularly impacts the prefrontal cortex, the area of the brain involved in regulating attention, motivation, and emotion, which in turn affects the patient’s ability to concentrate, control, and shift attention.

Children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder show prominent abnormalities in the inferior PFC and its connections to striatal, cerebellar, and parietal regions.

ADHD is not curable but its symptoms can be reduced and managed. There are essentially two paths to regulating attention deficit: medication and therapy. Medication is commonly prescribed to children with ADHD to address the biological mechanisms of the disorder and regulate noradrenaline and dopamine transmission in the brain. Cognitive behavioural therapy is widely used to enable self-regulation and form coping strategies. This duality, however, is a mere reflection of a wider conversation around how ADHD should be viewed and addressed. Should we side with the biomedical discourse of ADHD and choose to view it primarily as a medical category, or should we focus on addressing the flaws in a system that punishes disobedience?

It is hard to deny that ADHD affects — at times, quite severely — the patient’s ability to exist and function within complex social structures that require discipline, obedience, and compliance. Children with ADHD achieve less in school than their peers and face a higher likelihood of engaging in criminal activities. ADHD is positively correlated with anxiety and depression. Adults with ADHD struggle with employment and marital problems. Suicide rates among both children and adults with attention deficit are higher on average than in the general population.

A popular interpretation of the positivist biomedical paradigm may suggest stimulants as the most appropriate answer to curbing “undesirable behaviour”. Medication’s proven ability to improve daily functioning benefits the patient as much as an institution that will gladly drug “children into docility…in the service of a tacit project of social control”. However, acknowledging that the system obsessed with producing identical, obedient workers has little tolerance for defiance does not require viewing stimulants as a tool for enforcing cooperation. Medication is not the only way to manage the symptoms of ADHD, and it is not always the most appropriate as similar, if not more powerful, effects can be achieved with individual and systemic tools.

A more balanced take suggests viewing ADHD as the product of a complex interaction between biological and social-environmental factors. It would recognise and address the biomedical mechanisms and create opportunities for people with ADHD to function, express themselves, and realise their potential in social scenarios. This take dismisses neither medication nor therapy: it views them as valid and effective tools in their own right, but offers a reframing of what is viewed as a problem in modern society.

Take, for instance, students with ADHD, who are talkative, distracted, hyperactive. Such students are only problematic if we choose to view them as such and refuse to make the necessary adjustments to leverage, not curb, their inattentiveness. A teacher who prioritises classroom discipline is a teacher who disregards the evidence that pupils with ADHD perform significantly better when given clear instructions and expectations. The teacher’s focus on obedience and order blinds them to a multitude of opportunities to maximise student performance without disrupting the learning process: for instance, by using pupils with ADHD as peer educators. By framing attention deficit as a condition associated with some deeply problematic, anti-social, disruptive behaviours, we unwittingly set pupils with ADHD up to fail in place of a far better simple solution:

Optimal pupil performance is associated with brevity and clarity of sequences of instruction, the accompaniment of verbal instructions with visual cues and the availability of resources that pupils can refer to for reminders of direction and expectations.

The same, of course, applies to other areas of life impacted by ADHD. Building sustainable relationships, pursuing meaningful careers, enjoying the simple joys of everyday living, demand adjustments — not only from the person with ADHD but from the system itself. Reasonable accommodations are not synonymous with special treatment: they are designed to empower people who are otherwise deprived of the opportunity to function in society, not to absolve them of the need to put in effort. Such accommodations create welcoming environments where people contribute to common goals in the ways that suit them best, and where their needs and challenges are acknowledged and addressed.

ADHD v Technology

The relationship between modern technology and ADHD is complex. On the one hand, smartphones, wearable devices, and other gadgets are becoming increasingly prominent in health management and emotional regulation, complementing therapeutic and medicinal treatments with handy personalised tools. To-do lists and AI chat-bots, remote symptom tracking and online testing — adults with ADHD have plenty to choose from depending on what they wish to achieve. In addition to that, the Internet has played a big role in raising awareness of ADHD and reducing stigma around the disorder. ADHD diagnoses have increased in recent years — which, considering that women are far more likely to remain undiagnosed than men, is a positive development. Technology makes it possible for people to discover ADHD, better understand its symptoms, exchange experiences, and receive treatment.

On the other hand, the digital world is a ruthless, fast-paced, overwhelming space that is neither welcoming nor kind to people with ADHD. The rates of “Internet addiction” (which stood at 14% of children and 20% of adolescents in 2006 and has since increased) are astronomical, and neurodivergent individuals who are known to have issues with substance abuse and addiction are among the groups most affected by the phenomenon. In people with ADHD, Internet addiction is positively correlated with inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. Social media is especially harmful: engineered to maximise engagement, these platforms use all sorts of tools to make it nearly impossible to quit or even reduce screen time. Excessive use of social media in particular opens the door to a range of side effects, such as low self-esteem, feelings of inadequacy and underachievement, and increased social isolation.

However, it wouldn’t be fair to blame it all on social media alone. Most modern applications are designed for engagement and employ a wide range of tools to attract and retain users. One such tool is gamification — a popular technique that uses game mechanics in non-gaming settings to reward certain behaviours and entice continuous and regular use. As research demonstrates, rewards make even the most routine tasks far more exciting, allowing users to do chores, learn languages, and socialise with ease. For people with ADHD, however, gamification is a double-edged sword: while it certainly helps make learning more enjoyable, it also exacerbates ADHD symptoms. Instant gratification makes stimulation easy to achieve, forcing the user to seek more and turning mindful gamified experiences into never-ending quests for novelty. It is worth noting that because ADHD comprises at least two major domains — inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity — the same technology that severely influences one may have little impact on the other. For example, this 2026 study found a positive correlation between the use of short video platforms and inattention but not hyperactivity-impulsivity.

The digital age has revolutionised how we create, distribute, and consume knowledge, making it far more accessible and affordable than ever before. The influx of new information and the ever-increasing speed at which new content is produced have transformed the way we live, amplified our anxieties and feelings of overwhelm. The abundance of options has further contributed to turning attention into an especially scarce and valuable resource. Today’s digital world is a terrifying place that takes users’ time and mental wellness in exchange for occasional dopamine hits. It is not designed with the neurodivergent user in mind, but it profits from their struggles: from encouraging fast, mindless interactions to enabling impulsive decisions.

Wouldn’t it be great if we could do something about this?

Why designing for ADHD is so hard

When it comes to designing for users with ADHD, recommendations commonly include reducing cognitive load, avoiding distractions, and relieving users of the need to rely on memory — solid tips that are little more than general UX principles, adjusted ever so slightly for the neurodivergent audience. These principles cannot replace a comprehensive design framework. As a complex disorder, ADHD poses multiple challenges: from social disability and academic and occupational problems to physical and psychological issues and risky behaviours. To design for ADHD means to address all these challenges at a fundamental level and, importantly, to understand why addressing them is essential in the first place.

In the book “Against Technoableism: Rethinking Who Needs Improvement”, Ashley Shew describes how most solutions are designed for people with disabilities but never with them: “[universal] design employs and imagines our bodies […] while rarely (if ever) simply asking us what we need”. What is worse, many of these solutions are built to correct or conceal disabilities rather than accommodate them. Our products, services, and environments are not simply built for the able-bodied — they force people with disabilities to adjust, to adopt particular ways of using and existing in them with the help of technology, to pretend that their disabilities are fixed or cured. Let’s medicate an inattentive student. Let’s use therapy to subdue them. Let’s agree on a design principle like “avoid clutter” in theory but allow a neurotypical middle manager to break it as they and their overlords please.

Take Bionic Reading — a method developed by Renato Casutt, a Swiss typographic designer, that emboldens the first letters of each word in a sentence to improve readability by guiding the reader’s eyes. Bionic fonts are sold for $79 per package of 10, and the company offers many other paid apps and products as well. Bionic Reading is a premium product with good advertising. It spread like wildfire in 2022, often positioned as the best possible solution for people with ADHD, dyslexia, and cognitive impairments.

Does Bionic Reading actually work? The company’s original testing method involving 12 participants (which, to the founder’s own admission, produced mixed results) does not withstand scrutiny. A real scientific test involving eye tracking on a large cohort of participants revealed that “the selective bolding of characters within words does not facilitate more efficient word identification or enhance overall reading performance in skilled adult readers”. Other tests show similar results. Bionic Reading claims that it keeps the reader’s mind focused, but in reality, it is a commercial product that tries to force a neurodivergent brain to act normally. As Daniel Lavelle at The Guardian asks: “Maybe having a wandering mind isn’t such a bad thing?” Would a better way to increase comprehension be to encourage neurodivergent people to read slowly?

So, what would it really take to design better products for people with ADHD? The process begins, unsurprisingly, with inclusion. A 2025 paper, “Towards Inclusive Guidelines for Web Design for Adults with ADHD”, describes co-designing such a framework with a panel of neurodivergent and neurotypical users. The recommendations produced by the panel varied from general UX tips (avoid complex menus, limit the number of options, keep navigation similar to other products) to ADHD-specific guidance:

  • Avoid stock photos and decorative illustrations;
  • Avoid components that may be confused with ads;
  • Restrict scrolling to vertical only;
  • Avoid non-standard hover effects and decorative animations;
  • Indicate external links and buttons.

The paper assessed these guidelines, by having two designers with ADHD put together a prototype. Nearly all suggestions yielded promising results: users with ADHD found it significantly easier to navigate the prototype designed according to these principles and discover relevant information. In the neurotypical cohort, the results were relatively moderate, although non-ADHD users, too, benefited from simplified navigation, clear information hierarchy, and other improvements. Interestingly, the only design choice that was not well received was to use the Bionic Reading method, which reportedly reduced readability in non-ADHD participants.

Does that mean that checking the boxes above will make your product ADHD-friendly?

The answer is no.

Although structured layouts and simplified navigation definitely make products easier to digest, and rewards and incentives indeed keep users with ADHD engaged, these principles alone do not amount to an ADHD-friendly framework. By narrowing the recommendations down to a short list of checkboxes, we design for people with ADHD instead of designing with them. We attempt to make them “normal” rather than empowering them to be themselves.

Product-focused approach addresses the wrong problem. It simultaneously sands down a square peg and turns a round hole into a rectangle: both parts somewhat fit one another, and everyone pretends that they are not deformed and misshapen. It does not dare to challenge the system that produces square pegs and round holes: its job is to mitigate the damage, not ask questions. Its job is to make a pop-up ad less annoying, not to find a sustainable alternative. It is to have a phone number people in wheelchairs can call for assistance instead of building accessible urban environment.

Meanwhile, designing with ADHD is the process of co-creation, of mutual learning and exchange between neurodivergent and neurotypical partners. It entails, first and foremost, transforming the environment in which the collaboration occurs. A design framework for ADHD must therefore go beyond product considerations to inform product creation itself: from establishing healthy routines and enabling productive collaboration and reflection to protecting critical decisions against corporate interference.

Under this framework, a product team could add rewards to encourage daily usage, but cannot leverage anxiety and the fear of missing out that such rewards can create. This framework would suggest the team to apply the same principles to their work as well: set short-term, achievable goals, engage and reward team members, and respect each other’s time, space, and ways of working. This framework would ensure that the product is co-designed with neurodivergent users, not tested against some vaguely defined criteria. This framework would never give rise to another pop-up ad.

Is it such a surprise that this framework does not exist?

Pop-up ads are dead. The disdain for them was so strong that by 2004, when 6.2% of all ads on the Web were pop-ups, at least 20% of all Internet users had a pop-up blocker installed. Advertisers and tech corporations they funded did not cave in until new and improved formats came along. Pop-ups did not die because the public hated them. They died because something better was on the horizon.

Pop-ups are dead, but their story, their demise, and their complicated legacy make me dread the future even more than I already do. Corporations wish to cultivate users who conform, consumers who neither demand systemic changes nor require small accommodations. In the absence of regulation and external pressure, what could possibly motivate tech giants to consider people with disabilities, let alone involve them in making important decisions?

Pop-ups are dead, but people who pushed them into existence remain in charge: not the Ethan Zuckermans who inadvertently created monsters but decision-makers who breathed life into these creatures and set them loose. So long as they remain in power, so long as growth takes priority over customer experience and care, there will be no room for human-centric thinking or accessibility. So long as they continue to reduce all users to identical numbers in a spreadsheet, any considerations that do not immediately translate into revenue will remain an afterthought, forever postponed, abandoned at the bottom of the backlog.

Two years ago, a young, moderately stressed-out PhD student wrote an article about pursuing a doctoral degree while living with ADHD. In that article, the author discussed the struggles that people with ADHD face in academia, how bureaucracy and formalities are designed, as if intentionally, to crush all hope and excitement in neurodivergent people, and how simple accommodations and small adjustments may significantly impact someone’s career. That student was optimistic about the future — his own as a neurodivergent researcher, his peers’, and the tech industry’s.

In the time since, he “toughened up”. He filled out countless ethics forms, amendment requests, and research milestone reports. He completed standardised tests, passed exams, and handed in assignments. He faced every deadline, every requirement, every expectation head-on. There was nothing that could alleviate the pressure. The system itself was not interested in changing, so he changed his ways of doing things. He succeeded at some (not all) endeavours, though in the process, lost his passion for many things he had once adored. He became timid, dull, complacent.

Back then, he was excited about things to come. Today, I no longer see him in the mirror.

What to read

  • HealthDirect. Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).
  • ADDA. Types of ADHD in Adults: Understanding the Differences.
  • Paul Cooper, 2008. Like Alligators Bobbing for Poodles? A Critical Discussion of Education, ADHD and the Biopsychosocial Perspective.
  • Paul Cooper, Fintan O’Regan. Educating Children with AD/HD. A Teacher’s Manual.
  • Louise C. Druedahl & Sofia Kälvemark Sporrong, 2019. A Foucauldian perspective on treating ADHD with medicine.
  • Gyöngyi Fekete & Andrés Lucero, 2019. P(L)AY ATTENTION! Co-designing for and with Children with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD).
  • Ashley Shew, 2023. Against Technoableism: Rethinking Who Needs Improvement.
  • David Skidmore. Inclusion: The Dynamic of School Development.
  • Margaret D Weiss et al., 2011. The screens culture: impact on ADHD.
  • Linda Wheeler, 2010. Critique of the article by Visser and Jehan (2009): ‘ADHD: a scientific fact or a factual opinion? A critique of the veracity of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder’

About the author

Kristian Mikhel is a PhD Candidate at the University of Tasmania, a product designer and a founder of Paper and Pain, a design agency for good, an accessibility advocate, and the author of the free newsletter, “The Accessibility Apprentice”.

Design v ADHD was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Launch HN: Alter (YC S25) – Access control for multi-user agents
description:
Hi HN! We’re Srikar and Kevan, founders of Alter – https://alterauth.com/. We’re building access control for agents that can take actions on behalf of multiple users.

If you’ve built an internal agent people use through Slack, you may have experienced this scenario: everyone signs in with their own account, but the agent connects to the CRM or billing system with one shared API key, so the agent can do anything that the key can do. User-level authentication in Slack does nothing to control what the agent can do in an external system like the CRM or billing system.

Here’s what Alter does:

-It acts as a proxy and manages downstream credentials for every API request that an agent takes;

-It takes identity into account for every action the agent does. Automatically take into account the end user identity of the person that the agent is taking actions on behalf of.

-It enforces fine grained runtime policies and records compliance grade audit logs.

Here’s a demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9ZqPU14ipGE

We started this because we saw first hand how hard it is to build agents in regulated industries. To unlock the true benefits of agents we need to allow agents to take actions, sometimes actions on behalf of end users. I (Srikar) was working at Goldmans and I saw how prohibitively expensive it was for me as a developer to write my own custom auth to enable multi-tenancy in agents and to allow agents to have strict policy controls as they act on behalf of end users. My co-founder, Kevan, is a second time founder and was previously working on a database startup. He has experience building and selling deep tech into highly regulated environments. So this problem seemed like a natural fit for the both of us.

Building and maintaining custom auth for multi tenant agents was challenging. But so was ensuring that the solution we developed was secure, scalable and keeping track of security grade audit logs. As a result we realized there needs to be a separate product category for this that enables developers to easily build secure multi user agents that can actually take actions in an enterprise. Some of the real-world use cases we’ve seen include:

We have built a multi user open claw for our own team using Alter that saved us countless hours on our GTM effort. Link here:https://github.com/AlterAIDev/openclaw-alter-plugin

We have multiple startups who have used our platform to build their own secure internal agents for everything ranging from SRE agents to back office agents dealing with Quickbooks and payroll platforms like Rippling. It has saved developers countless hours both in terms of building and maintenance. We also have a defense contractor building air gapped agents for marine corp using Alter.

Under the hood, the value that we provide is that we do a lot of the plumbing that no one wants to do. We support hundreds of providers, all manually tested end to end. Reliability is our biggest priority. We have built this in a way to allow developers to custom build their agents however they see fit. Everything ranging from custom policies, agent delegation, user attribution, audit logs needed for compliance to a LLM gateway with guardrails (Coming soon)

Building a security product is hard. We have learnt that in order to build a truly secure product, security thinking has to pervade every part of the development process. We have embraced shift left security. Every PR that is pushed out is continuously checked for supply chain attacks, potentially dangerous code patterns etc.

Our business plan revolved around usage based pricing. There is a free tier up to 10k requests and then a pricing tier starting beyond that. We would love it if people configured their APIs and OAuth credentials, tried out the policies and actually built agents that can take actions with alter!

If you’ve built an agent that acts for multiple users, how are you handling permissions today? We’d especially like to hear what you’ve had to build yourself.

https://alterauth.com/

title: 5 Free React UI Libraries to Escape Generic AI Designs
description:
Ever built something with AI that worked perfectly but looked like every other SaaS product?

Same cards. Same gradients. Same boring layouts.

Here are five React UI libraries worth exploring if you want to break the pattern and build something that actually feels different.

  1. Dither UI — Give Your AI Better Building Blocks

AI coding agents can build your UI, but the results often feel repetitive.

Dither UI is a collection of interactive, motion-first React components built with Framer Motion, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui.

Copy the source into your project and give your AI coding agent better building blocks for creating animated cards, interactive buttons, and more distinctive interfaces.

🔗 ditherui.dev

  1. beUI — Make Your Interfaces Feel Alive

Static components are fine, but thoughtful animations can make an interface feel much more polished.

beUI offers free, open-source animated React components built with Motion and Tailwind CSS, from interactive cards to more expressive form controls.

Copy the code, customize the interactions, and make the components fit your product.

🔗 beui.dev

  1. Beautiful UI — Built for AI Interfaces

Building an AI product involves more than putting a chat window on a page.

Beautiful UI focuses on AI-native components, including streaming text, thinking states, tool chips, approval cards, and agent interfaces.

If you're building an AI assistant or an agent-powered product, these patterns can save you from reinventing common AI interactions.

🔗 beautifului.dev

  1. Cult UI — For More Expressive Interfaces

Sometimes, a few well-designed components can completely change how a product feels.

Cult UI offers motion-rich React components for shadcn/ui projects, including animated buttons, creative hero sections, AI prompt inputs, and interactive cards.

Add a component, customize the source, and give your interface a little more personality.

🔗 cult-ui.com

  1. ObsidianUI — Add More Character to Your UI

It's often the little details that make an interface memorable.

ObsidianUI offers animated, interactive React components built with Tailwind CSS and Motion, including draggable marquees, text animations, and interactive visual elements.

Explore the live previews, find something that fits your design, and customize it for your next project.

🔗 obsidianui.dev

Stop Settling for Generic UI

AI has made building products easier than ever. But making your product feel distinct still takes thoughtful design choices.

These libraries are a great starting point. Experiment with different components, customize them to match your vision, and give your AI coding agent better building blocks to work with.

If you're looking for motion-first React components, check out Dither UI.

Now I'm curious: What's your go-to UI library when building with AI? Drop it in the comments. I'd love to discover more tools worth exploring.

Happy building! 🚀

title: October 20, 2026
description:
Apigee X

Announcement

On October 20th, 2026, we began maintenance updates of Apigee instances configured for maintenance windows.

If you set a preferred window for maintenance for your instance, and your instance version is below 1-18-0-apigee-6, your instance will be updated to 1-18-0-apigee-6 within the next seven to 21 days. A notification containing the expected date of upgrade will be sent within the next two business days.

Note: Instances that meet either of the following two criteria will not be updated:
  • Your instance has a DNS misconfiguration, as described in Known Issue 445936920.
  • Your instance uses an Apigee Java Library that has been removed, as described in Apigee release notes dated October 16, 2025.

For more information on participating in scheduled maintenance windows, see Maintenance overview and Manage Apigee instance maintenance windows.

Cloud SDK

Breaking

590.0.0 (2026-10-20)

Breaking Changes

  • (Google Cloud CLI) Removed the gcloud-man-pages component. Use --help for full command documentation.
  • (App Engine) Removed the app-engine-grpc component from the Google Cloud CLI.
  • (Cloud Build) Removed the Cloud Build Local Builder component (cloud-build-local) from the Google Cloud CLI.

Google Cloud CLI

  • Updated bundled Python on Linux and Windows, and in the Alpine-based Docker images, to pyOpenSSL 26.4.0 and cryptography 50.0.1. 32-bit Windows uses pyOpenSSL 26.2.0 and cryptography 48.0.1, the newest releases that support it.

AI

  • Updated gcloud beta ai endpoints deploy-model to request automatic resources for Gemini deployments on GDC connected endpoints.
    • If no replica counts are specified, the minimum replica count defaults to 1 only for gemini-2.5-flash.
    • Specifying flags that apply only to dedicated resources, such as --machine-type or --accelerator, now prints a warning and deploys with dedicated resources.

Agent Identity

  • Added gcloud beta agent-identity auth-providers resolve-authorization command.

AlloyDB

  • Added --enable-public-dns flag to gcloud beta alloydb instances create|update.

Apigee

  • Fixed an issue where gcloud apigee commands would fail with an UnauthorizedRequestError for users who authenticate using Mutual TLS (mTLS).

App Engine

  • Updated gcloud beta app migrate-to-run to default to the App Engine application's region instead of us-central1 when neither --region nor the run/region property is set.

BigLake

  • Promoted --federated-catalog-identity-mode for gcloud biglake iceberg catalogs create to GA.
  • Promoted --federated-catalog-identity-mode for gcloud biglake iceberg catalogs update to GA.
  • Promoted --metadata-service-directory-name for gcloud biglake iceberg catalogs create to GA.
  • Promoted --metadata-service-directory-name for gcloud biglake iceberg catalogs update to GA.
  • federated value for --catalog-type flag of gcloud biglake iceberg catalogs create is now supported.

Certificate Authority Service

  • Added --filter flag to gcloud privateca subordinates list. The flag is able to allow filtering results based on specified boolean expression.

Cloud Bigtable

  • Build with 1.26.4 to resolve CVE-2026-39820.

Cloud Bigtable Emulator

  • Rebuild cbt-emulator for CVE-2026-39820.

Cloud Dataflow

  • Promoted gcloud dataflow config-store-settings to GA.

Cloud Dataplex

  • Fixed gcloud dataplex dbt metadata-jobs create so that dbt resources whose names contain a dot, such as tests on a model with a decimal version, are no longer rejected by the import job.
  • Fixed gcloud dataplex dbt metadata-jobs create so that two dbt resources that map to the same Dataplex entry ID no longer fail the whole import job. The first is imported and a warning names the other.

Cloud IAM

  • Added --vendor-type flag to gcloud iam workforce-pools providers create-oidc, create-saml, update-oidc, and update-saml commands.

Cloud Resource Manager

  • Promoted gcloud resource-manager capability-configs to GA.
  • Promoted gcloud resource-manager boundary-configs to GA.
  • Promoted gcloud resource-manager boundaries to GA.

Cloud Run

  • Added --dry-run flag to gcloud beta run domain-mappings create to validate a domain mapping, including whether the domain is available, without creating it.

Cloud SQL

  • Added POSTGRES_19 to --database-version flag of gcloud sql instances create and gcloud sql instances patch.
  • Added --no-replication-lag-max-seconds-for-recreate flag to gcloud beta sql instances patch to disable recreating a lagging MySQL read replica.
  • Updated 'cloud-sql-proxy' packaged component to use 2.26.2 of the Cloud SQL Proxy.

Cloud Spanner

  • Improved error output when gcloud spanner cli runs an incompatible spanner-cli binary found on PATH instead of the spanner-cli component; users are now directed to install the component.

Cloud Workstations

  • Added enable-automatic-failover to --boost-config flag in gcloud beta workstations configs create and gcloud beta workstations configs update.

Compute Engine

  • Added compute instance-templates export command to all release tracks.
  • Removed WORKLOAD_IDENTITY choise in --identity-type flag.
  • Promoted --instance-flexibility-policy flag and min CPU platform and disk overrides to GA for gcloud compute instance-groups managed create and update.
  • Added compute instance-templates import command to all release tracks.

Database Migration

  • Added --failback flag to gcloud database-migration migration-jobs promote command to promote a migration job from destination back to source during the FAILBACK phase.

GKE Hub

  • Promoted --view, --memberships, --filter, and --sort-by flags on gcloud container fleet|hub config-management describe command to GA.

  • Updated gcloud container fleet|hub memberships register to allow skipping the Connect agent installation on non-GKE clusters via the --no-install-connect-agent flag.

Kubernetes Engine

  • Added the reservedSystemCpus kubelet config option to the gcloud container clusters create, gcloud container node-pools create, and gcloud container node-pools update commands. This option specifies the list of CPUs reserved for host system services.
  • Added ltsc2025 option to --windows-os-version flag of gcloud container node-pools create and gcloud container node-pools update to create or update Windows node pools using the Windows Server 2025 (LTSC2025) image.
  • Updated default kubectl to 1.35.9.
  • Additional kubectl versions:
    • 1.31.14
    • 1.32.13
    • 1.33.13
    • 1.34.12
    • 1.35.9
    • 1.36.5
    • 1.37.1
  • Allowed --num-nodes=0 for gcloud container clusters create to create a cluster without a default node pool on GKE versions that support it. Flags that only configure the default node pool, such as --machine-type and --enable-autoscaling, can't be used with --num-nodes=0.

Network Connectivity

  • Added --purpose flag to gcloud network-connectivity internal-ranges create to specify the purpose of the internal range.

Network Security

  • Promoted --wildfire-analysis-profile flag of gcloud network-security security-profile-groups create and gcloud network-security security-profile-groups update commands to GA.
  • Promoted gcloud network-security security-profiles wildfire-analysis command group and its create, delete, describe, list and update commands to GA.
  • Promoted add-submission-rule, delete-submission-rule, add-inline-cloud-analysis-rule and delete-inline-cloud-analysis-rule commands of gcloud network-security security-profiles wildfire-analysis to GA.

Service Extensions

  • Created a new set of commands for gcloud service-extensions extension-bindings (alpha and beta).
  • Added gcloud beta service-extensions cdn-edge-extensions command group to manage CdnEdgeExtension resources.

Subscribe to these release notes at https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/google-cloud-sdk-announce.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Antigravity Enterprise Gateway support

Antigravity Enterprise Gateway lets organizations route model inference requests from the Antigravity app, Antigravity CLI, and Antigravity for IDEs through a centralized enterprise gateway before forwarding them to Google Cloud. This deployment enables organizations to inspect and audit model traffic, enforce custom security and network egress policies, and authenticate developers through a gateway API key without requiring individual Google Account sign-in.

Requests routed through Antigravity Enterprise Gateway use a centralized Google Cloud service account and are billed on a pay-as-you-go (PAYG) consumption basis through the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. This deployment model doesn't use your Gemini Enterprise seat-based subscription quotas (such as included Standard or Plus monthly allowances). You can't use a gateway and sign in with a Google Account at the same time. If you want to use your included subscription quota instead, disable the enterprise gateway and sign in with your Google Account.

This feature is generally available (GA).

For more information, see:

  • Deploy Antigravity Enterprise Gateway
  • Connect Antigravity to an Enterprise Gateway.

Breaking

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 2.5 Pro discontinued in Canada and Japan

Gemini 2.5 Pro has been discontinued for in-country Gemini Enterprise app deployments in Canada and Japan. Agents and chat sessions in these regions that previously used Gemini 2.5 Pro automatically switch to in-country Gemini 3.5 Flash.

Gemini 2.5 Pro remains available in the global, us, and eu regions.

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise and Manage web app features.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Fixed

A security issue in GKE fleet management that could have allowed unauthorized configuration changes to clusters registered to a fleet has been resolved. The fixes are rolled out to all regions, and no action is required.

Fixed

This is an update to the release note regarding the Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver issue published on October 2, 2026.

This issue has been resolved. You can upgrade your cluster control plane to the following versions to fix the issue for ubuntu_containerd and older cos_containerd node pools:

  • 1.36.5-gke.1032000 or later

  • 1.37.1-gke.1552000 or later

  • Specific 1.36.4 mitigation patches: 1.36.4-gke.1247001, 1.36.4-gke.1247002, 1.36.4-gke.1391001, 1.36.4-gke.1391003, 1.36.4-gke.1495001, 1.36.4-gke.1495003, 1.36.4-gke.2046001, 1.36.4-gke.2202002

Spanner

Feature

Spanner supports approximate aggregate functions for both GoogleSQL and PostgreSQL dialects. These functions produce statistical estimates of distinct counts, allowing you to compute results faster and save resources on large datasets compared to exact aggregation.

For more information, see approximate aggregate functions (GoogleSQL and PostgreSQL), HyperLogLog++ functions, and Sketches.

title: October 15, 2026
description:
Apigee Edge for Private Cloud

Announcement

Released Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Designated Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.00 a long-term support (LTS) release: 18 months of full support ending April 2028, then 18 months of maintenance ending October 2029. After October 2029, 4.54.00.00 receives no software updates, security mitigations, or technical support.

Installing a later 4.54 minor release or patch does not change those dates. To extend the support lifecycle, upgrade to the next LTS release.

For the support lifecycle phases, release cadences, and version numbering, see Apigee Edge for Private Cloud release and lifecycle policy.

Announcement

This release replaces Java 8 with Java 17 and Java 21, removes the Classic UI and the apigee-sso component, and updates the bundled Cassandra, Postgres, OpenLDAP, ZooKeeper, Qpid Broker-J, Nginx, and Consul versions. These changes are not backward-compatible.

For the 4.54.00 versions and the 4.53.01 versions they replace, see Supported software and supported versions.

Before upgrading, read Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00, then Update Apigee Edge 4.53.00 or 4.53.01 to 4.54.00 or New installation overview. For known issues, see Known issues with Edge for Private Cloud.

Announcement

Replaced the Classic UI (edge-ui) with the New Edge UI (edge-management-ui).

The New Edge UI is the only management UI in 4.54.00 and is installed by default. Deployments running the Classic UI must transition to it before upgrading. Custom Classic UI properties do not carry over automatically. The default port also changes from 9000 to 3001, configurable with conf_uebe_port, so firewall rules and load balancer target ports that point at 9000 fail until they are updated.

For the migration steps and the supported feature list, see Migrate to the New Edge UI and What features are supported?.

Breaking

In deployments with Apigee SSO enabled, an integrated OIDC identity broker in apigee-openldap replaces the standalone apigee-sso component and Apache Tomcat 9.0.x. Before upgrading, take a complete and validated LDAP backup; existing apigee-sso configurations do not migrate automatically. Deployments not using Apigee SSO require no action.

For migration prerequisites, validation checks, and rollback constraints, see Option 2: Upgrade UI (with Apigee SSO).

Breaking

4.54.00 runs Java in mixed mode: Java 17 for Cassandra and ZooKeeper, Java 21 for the Management Server, Message Processor, Router, and Qpid Broker-J. Both Oracle JDK and OpenJDK are supported at those versions.

Oracle JDK 8 and OpenJDK 8 are no longer supported.

API proxies with custom JavaCallout policies or custom resource JARs can break on Java 21. For details, see Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Change

Upgraded Nginx on the Edge Router to 1.30.0.

If you are upgrading from Nginx 1.20.x, see Nginx 1.30 changes in Apigee Edge 4.54.00 for the full list of changes.

Change

Changed the TLS defaults on Message Processors to the Java 21 cryptographic baseline.

Message Processors run on Java 21, which enables TLS 1.3 by default (JEP 332) and prefers it for outbound backend connections, falling back to TLS 1.2. No configuration change is required if your target servers and load balancers negotiate TLS 1.3, or negotiate TLS 1.2 with forward-secret (ECDHE) cipher suites.

Java 21 also disables the non-forward-secret static RSA key-exchange suites (TLS_RSA_*). If you have overridden conf_http_HTTPTransport.ssl.cipher.suites.whitelist or conf_message-processor-communication_local.http.ssl.ciphers with static RSA suites only, backend calls fail with no cipher suites in common and the Router cannot complete a TLS handshake with the Message Processor. Replace the TLS_RSA_* entries with modern cipher suites and restart the Message Processor.

For the remediation path, see Legacy backend requirements and remediation.

Feature

Added Basic authentication to the New Edge UI, which lets you sign in without configuring an identity provider.

The New Edge UI supports Basic authentication without additional configuration. You can also configure Apigee SSO, or an external identity provider such as SAML or OIDC. This feature is generally available in 4.54.00.

Feature

Added automated pre-flight validation checks to apigee-setup and apigee-service, which surface environment configuration problems before a component is installed.

This feature is generally available in 4.54.00.

Security

Fixed multiple security vulnerabilities in Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

These fixes ship as part of the component upgrades in this release; see Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Change

Changed the default garbage collector on Message Processors to the Garbage-First garbage collector.

Message Processors set useG1GC=true and useStringDeduplication=true by default in 4.54.00. In 4.53.01 neither was set by default. To configure garbage collection, see Configure the garbage collector for Message Processors.

Apigee Edge for Public Cloud

Announcement

On October 15, 2026, we began releasing Single Sign-On (SSO) updates for Apigee Edge for Public Cloud.

Fixed

Bug ID Component Description
560310696 SSO Fixed an issue where the Portal SSO endpoint inadvertently accepted deprecated TLS 1.1 connections. The endpoint now strictly enforces TLS 1.2+.

Apigee Integrated Portal

Announcement

On October 15, 2026, we released a new version of the Apigee integrated portal.

Fixed

Bug ID Description
560310696 Fixed an issue where the Portal SSO endpoint inadvertently accepted deprecated TLS 1.1 connections. The endpoint now strictly enforces TLS 1.2+.

Apigee X

Fixed

Bug ID Description
466116259 Updated the startup script for the managed instance group (MIG) that routes external traffic to Apigee. net.ipv4.ip_forward is now written to /etc/sysctl.d/, so an instance no longer stops forwarding traffic when a reboot or an OS update resets it. The script does not change unrelated iptables NAT rules. Instances pick up the change the next time they are restarted or recreated.

BigQuery

Feature

You can copy tables across regions. This feature is now generally available (GA).

Feature

You can now use reusable column aliases in GoogleSQL. This feature lets you define an alias for an expression in the SELECT clause of a SQL query and immediately reference that alias within the same SELECT list or in the WHERE clause of the same query block.

Reusable column aliases also streamline the migration of workloads from other data warehouses such as Snowflake and Teradata, by supporting their syntax.

This feature is generally available, and is opt-in only. To use reusable column aliases, you must first enable the feature.

Feature

You can export a conversational analytics agent's answer, including text, visualizations, tables, and citations, to a PDF or CSV file. This feature is generally available (GA).

Cloud Vision

Deprecated

Face detection model update

The emotion label response in the Cloud Vision API is deprecated. Going forward, the Cloud Vision API face detection (FACE_DETECTION feature) will return UNKNOWN for all emotion-related labels.

Compute Engine

Feature

Preview: You can create regional disks, including Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability volumes, by cloning a zonal boot disk.

For more information, see Duplicate a disk with clones.

Change

If you try to create an on-demand reservation or increase the number of reserved Compute Engine instances in a reservation when the zone has reached its reservation capacity limit for your requested machine family, then the request fails with a RESERVATION_CAPACITY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED error. For more information, see Reservation capacity limit exceeded.

Feature

Generally available: The storage-optimized Z4M machine series is generally available for Compute Engine. Powered by fifth generation Intel Emerald Rapids Xeon Scalable processors and Titanium offload processors, Z4M instances are purpose-built for workloads that require larger storage capacity, such as:

  • Parallel file systems to support AI/ML workloads
  • I/O intensive workloads such as SQL, NoSQL, and vector databases
  • AI/ML training and inference workloads such as checkpointing and distributed Key-Value (KV) cache

The Z4M machine series delivers up to 1,536 GB of memory and 168,000 GiB of local Titanium SSD capacity. Z4M also supports up to 400 Gbps of network bandwidth using two physical NICs. Z4M instances use Titanium and Cloud RDMA to help enable higher levels of networking performance, isolation, and security.

For more information, see Storage-optimized machine family.

Dataflow

Feature

Dataflow Auto VM Selection now supports 4th generation Compute Engine machine series. When Auto VM Selection is enabled, the service prioritizes these newer generation VMs for improved performance. If 4th generation VMs are unavailable at startup, the service automatically falls back to widely available 2nd generation machine families to ensure that your jobs can start without unnecessary delays.

For more information, see Auto VM Selection.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Anthropic models are available in the Gemini Enterprise app

Administrators can make Anthropic models—Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5—available to users in the Gemini Enterprise app. After an administrator turns on a model in the Enable third-party models section of the Feature Management tab, users can select the model in the model selector. Claude models are available in the global location and the us and eu multi-regions, and are charged on a pay-as-you-go basis.

This feature is generally available. For more information, see Enable third-party models.

Looker

Feature

The Looker 26.18 features have begun to be enabled for Looker (Google Cloud core) instances.

NetApp Volumes

Announcement

Google Cloud NetApp Volumes now supports the Flex Unified service level, including custom performance, in the following region:

  • europe-west8 (Milan)

For more information about available regions, see Supported regions.

Security Command Center

Feature

To increase the precision of attack path analysis and provide attack exposure scores that help you prioritize confirmed internet exposures, Risk Engine attack path simulations support the EXTERNALLY_EXPOSED_VM_INSTANCE External Exposure finding category (Preview). This finding category identifies Compute Engine or Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) resources with a direct public IP address that allows host OS access.

For more information, see Detect exposed resources, Risk Engine feature support, and Overview of attack exposure scores and attack paths.

Video Intelligence API

Deprecated

We are deprecating the emotion label response in the API. Going forward, the API will return UNKNOWN for all emotion related labels.

title: WebSocket support is now generally available
description:

Since the public beta launched in late June, Vercel CDN has served 300 million WebSocket connections, and now serves 15 million per day.

Customers use WebSockets for AI chat, streaming, and realtime multiplayer apps. WebSockets also power AI Gateway's realtime models.

WebSocket connections follow the same limits and pricing as other Function invocations. With Active CPU pricing, CPU is billed only for the time spent processing messages.

Get started at the documentation.

Read more

title: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is now available in Token Pass
description:
Token Pass now includes DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, alongside Kimi K3 and GLM 5.3, each accessed through its preferred provider, with more models to come. The DeepSeek model uses the latest weights (1017).

Token Pass is a $30/month subscription on Pro teams that grants $80 in monthly credit and runs through AI Gateway. Use it with any coding agent such as fx, Pi, Cline, Command Code etc. or build your own with the AI SDK, with Zero Data Retention enabled by default.

Add DeepSeek V4.1 Flash from the Token Pass page in your team's AI Gateway dashboard, or read the Token Pass documentation for setup.

Read more

title: Making every harness durable
description:
Developers are familiar with running coding agents locally through harnesses like Pi, Claude Code, and others. They are reliable daily drivers for generating code, but keeping agents running around the clock requires your computer to be on and awake, which led to the laptop lid memes and Mac mini demand spike.

Running harnesses in the cloud

Harness workloads are moving to the cloud. Individual developers are deploying always-on coding agent workflows, projects like OpenWork and HanaAgent use open-source harnesses as the engines behind the apps, and engineers are building their own harness products.

These harnesses are designed for long-lived processes that keep the session in memory, and agent tasks commonly run for minutes or hours. Locally, a harness has direct, continuous access to the workspace and session history on the same disk, so resuming interrupted work only requires a simple prompt.

In the cloud, you can replicate that setup with a VM and persistent storage, but the VM doesn't automatically record which model and tool calls completed or resume interrupted turns after a crash. A failed turn or network error means lost work.

Also, not every agent task executed through a harness needs a sandbox. Database queries and API calls can run securely in functions, and that also means required credentials never have to enter the sandbox.

Making every harness durable

We built eve and fx to run durably in the cloud out of the box, and today we are introducing durable-harness, which extends that durability to any harness, including Pi, OpenCode, Codex, and Claude Code. It uses the same machinery that powers Workflow SDK to survive crashes and function timeouts.

With durable-harness, you can:

  • Run any of these harnesses durably on Vercel

  • Self-host a harness with your own Postgres instance

  • Make your local harness workflow durable

  • Build your own durable harness

Sessions that survive a crash mid-turn

Take the example of a coding agent adding a pricing page to an existing app. The agent reads the existing page, writes a new one, opens a pull request, and waits for CI to finish before reporting back.

What happens if its function times out while CI is still running?

Kill the function or drop the connection in the demo below to compare how the two agents recover and which work is repeated.

Without durability, the agent stops work until it is manually restarted, and completed work is repeated unnecessarily.

With durable-harness, a new function reads completed results from the log and resumes the turn. If the browser disconnects, the agent keeps running, and reconnecting catches up from the log.

Logs and queues

durable-harness is the newest package in our open source portfolio. It’s a set of adapters and utilities that let the harnesses you already use keep their sessions in a World, the Workflow SDK’s durable backend.

It writes each step of a turn to a durable log. Before a model call or tool call runs, it records an intent, and when the call finishes, it records the outcome. The turn itself is backstopped with a queue message, so if its function dies, the queue hands the turn to a new function that reads the log and continues where it left off.

After a crash, the log says what finished, what was running, and what never started:

  • Completed calls never run again because their results are read from the log, so you’re never billed twice for a finished model call’s tokens.

  • Models remember their previous calls rather than repeating them.

  • Interrupted tools marked replay: 'safe' run again. Any other tool comes back to the model as possibly run, and the model decides whether to check.

Harnesses that keep their own session files, like Claude Code's transcript, Codex's rollout, and OpenCode's event store, have every record mirrored into the log, so a new function or Sandbox rebuilds them from it.

Pick your harness

fx and eve are durable on their own. For the rest, durable-harness adds durability from the outside, without changing the harness.

For the full setup guide for each harness, check the docs.

Runs everywhere

Durable agents need a log of each step, a way to resume a turn when its process dies, and a stream for whoever is watching.

Workflow SDK ships all three behind one interface, a World.

durable-harness writes to that interface, so you can move the same agent from one World to another without changing its code:

  • On Vercel, it uses the Vercel World.

  • In development, it uses files on your machine.

  • On your own servers, it uses Postgres, MongoDB, Redis, or Turso.

Two variables move every agent using durable-harness to Postgres.

For more control, such as setting a namespace or recovering sessions when your server starts, create the World in code and pass it to your agent:

Check the self-hosting docs for more details.

See every session in Agent Runs

Agent Runs on Vercel shows the trace for every session, including each model call and tool call. Turns that resumed after a crash appear in the same trace, so you can see exactly where a turn stopped and picked back up.

Tools

An agent has only the tools you give it, and they run in your function. Each tool says what should happen if a crash interrupts it. A 'safe' tool, such as a lookup, can run again. A 'never' tool, such as a refund, never runs twice: the model is told the call may have happened, so it can check before it tries again.

Here’s how the coding agent from the demo above might define its tools:

  • A tool that reads a file or checks CI status is marked as 'safe' so it can run again automatically.

  • A tool that posts a PR comment is marked as 'never' so that comments aren't posted twice.

The following example defines a tool for each policy using the example of an agent processing a refund:

For each harness’s built-in tools, like its shell and file editing, read on.

Files

When a harness needs a shell and files, it’s not safe to run them directly on a shared serverless function host. Many sessions can share the same function, and its filesystem isn’t guaranteed to persist between invocations.

To address this, durable-harness gives you a few options:

  • virtual() keeps the files in the session’s log, with a bash-compatible shell that can’t reach your function’s files or the network. It suits short tasks and small workspaces without starting an entire sandbox.

  • virtual({ durable: false }) keeps the files in memory for scratch work and clears them at the end of every turn.

  • sandbox() gives the session its own Vercel Sandbox, with /workspace on a Drive that outlives every sandbox and every function. It suits real projects and long-running work.

Compare the three side by side in the docs.

Each harness’s built-in tools run on the workspace you choose. With Pi, CodingTools installs Pi’s own read, write, edit, and bash, and virtualEnv() or sandboxEnv() gives them a workspace:

For OpenCode, pass the workspace as workspace, and for fx, pass it to fxTools(). Claude Code and Codex always run in a Vercel Sandbox, since they expect a real shell and filesystem, and aren’t safe for multi-tenant use. Their built-in tools work on the session’s Drive once you turn them on with builtins: true. Each harness guide lists its built-in tools.

Documents

Some state belongs with the session but isn’t part of the conversation, such as a to-do list, a plan, or a form the agent fills in. A document is typed JSON that lives in the session’s log, so it survives a crash and moves with the session.

Tools can edit documents through io.docs, and each edit commits to the log alongside the tool’s result, so the document’s durable state stays consistent with the tool calls themselves:

Your app can read and edit the same document without a database of its own, and the chat route can even stream every change to your UI:

In fact, the virtual() workspace from earlier is built on documents: its file tree is a document in the session’s log, and each tool call’s changes commit with its result.

Learn more about tools, files, and documents and how to keep your agent secure.

Wrapping up

Developers choose a harness for the choices it makes about prompts, tools, and context. How it survives a crash shouldn’t be one of them. With durable-harness, a turn that loses its function partway through continues from the log on a new one, without a manual retry and without repeating what already finished. Self-hosting and portability work out of the box by building on top of the Workflow SDK’s World interface.

durable-harness is open source on GitHub.

Read more

title: AI Gateway logs now show session affinity
description:
AI Gateway logs now have a Sessions view that groups requests into sessions and shows how session affinity routed each one. Each row shows the coding agent or app that ran the session, such as Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor, along with its cost, models, providers, and how much of its input was cached across every turn.

Open a session to see its cache hit rate, duration, and path. The path lists each turn with its model and timing, and names the provider serving the session along with any earlier ones. Session affinity sends each turn to the provider that served the one before it, so the provider already has most of the prompt in cache. A session that stays on one provider reads more of each prompt from cache.

Filter sessions by turns, client, model, provider, authentication, or cost. Single-turn sessions are hidden until you clear the minimum turns filter.

Session affinity runs by default on text and chat requests. To group requests yourself, send the same sessionId in providerOptions.gateway, or the same x-session-id header, on every request in a conversation. Requests without one are grouped by a fingerprint of the conversation's opening and appear as fingerprinted sessions.

Read the session affinity documentation for more information on how AI Gateway identifies sessions.

title: Findings from the $1M Vercel Sandbox challenge
description:
In August, we launched the $1M hacker challenge for Vercel Sandbox, inviting security researchers to try and escape Vercel Sandbox. We also coordinated with cybersecurity experts Trail of Bits to review the source code and security architecture.

Here is a summary of the challenge:

  • 1,285 reports over two weeks

  • $242,000 in bounties paid out

  • One Linux kernel zeroday vulnerability uncovered

No reports showed anyone accessing customer data in Vercel Sandbox. The most severe finding was the defect in the upstream Linux kernel.

The kernel zero day

The program's most important report arrived on day three.

Paulos Yibelo (pwn.ai), a HackerOne researcher working from a standard sandbox with no special access, found a defect in the Linux kernel's networking stack. Paulos discovered that specially crafted packets sent from within the microVM enabled three different attacks:

  1. Leak host memory over the network

  2. Crash the host machine

  3. Execute code on the host

Leaking host memory

In the first attack, memory from the host, the machine your sandbox shares with other tenants, shows up in packets the guest sends over the internet. This can happen continuously, for as long as the guest keeps sending.

This attack was demonstrated against Vercel production sandboxes.

Crashing the host and executing code on the host

The researcher also found that by sending specific packets, they could compromise the host.

First, by sending two packets, the researcher crashed the host machine, shutting down every sandbox running on it. Second, using the same flaw, they were able to run commands with full administrator privileges on the host, breaking out of the sandbox’s isolation boundary.

The packet-related crash and code execution attacks were demonstrated on the researcher’s own KVM and Firecracker machines matching Vercel Sandbox configuration.

Responsibly disclosing the kernel vulnerability

Almost every major cloud provider isolates customer workloads on this same layer of the Linux kernel, so any defect is shared-infrastructure risk.

Immediately after being notified, we collaborated with the researcher to understand and mitigate the vulnerability, working with AWS and other industry partners to prioritize a fix, and ensuring that Vercel customers and other developers using the kernel were safe.

The researcher also contacted the kernel maintainers and worked with them to create candidate patches. Fixes are under private review and CVEs are pending, so we are not publishing additional details until the patches are public. We are disclosing the existence of the vulnerability because it was separately disclosed in public.

Our approach to pressure-testing Vercel Sandbox

The HackerOne challenge made bounties available to any researcher, but we also extended our program to include internal evaluations and an independent investigation.

Before launching the public bounty, we performed live security assessments internally with full source access and support from the engineers who created and maintain Vercel Sandbox. We also engaged Trail of Bits, bringing on two engineers to evaluate our security architecture.

Not every finding came from the outside. Marcos Hernanz, a Vercel intern, found a cross-tenant data leak in the Linux device-mapper storage layer. This vulnerability let any sandbox read recycled disk blocks from previously deleted sandboxes.

The white-box deep dive

Trail of Bits spent four engineer-weeks inside our source code, with full access to the repositories and two enterprise test teams. They delivered 20 findings, and each was tested, confirmed, and referenced to the exact code.

They also performed an architectural review and concluded that our virtualization boundary is sound. Each sandbox runs on its own Firecracker microVM with a dedicated guest kernel, and the device model is deliberately tiny. No guest shares a running kernel with the host, or with another tenant.

On top of that foundation, they gave us three structural recommendations, which we implemented:

  • Find and eliminate all trust in the guest. Our control plane accepted values returned by software running inside the microVM, and every one of those values is tenant input. Anything that crosses the boundary should be derived server-side or signed with a key the guest cannot reach.

  • One policy, one decider. Egress enforcement was split across subsystems that each parsed the same network policy independently, and they did not always agree. We now use one canonicalization routine per data type, one component per decision, and revalidate connections when policy changes.

  • Assume the next zero day. We strengthened the protections around each sandbox to limit the damage if an attacker exploits the virtualization software. We keep host kernels up to date, have disabled nested virtualization, and use Firecracker’s jailer to run each microVM process with restricted permissions and isolate it from the rest of the host.

Vercel Sandbox findings

We received 1,285 reports in two weeks. This volume is only possible because researchers now hunt at AI speed.

Here is a breakdown of reports by category:

  • 877 duplicates

  • 319 not applicable

  • 57 valid

  • 32 informative

In our report triage we have validated:

  • 1 Critical finding

  • 5 High findings

  • 9 Medium findings

  • 42 Low findings

  • 32 Informative findings

We have paid out $242,000 in bug bounties.

The medium, Low, and Informative findings are small policy-boundary gaps, like a firewall rule that behaved differently than documented and a field that trusted the guest more than it should.

The most severe finding was the Linux kernel zero day defect, and no reports showed anyone reading a customer’s files, secrets, or application data.

We were most impressed with the heterogeneity of the reports. It was clear that researchers used different setups and have different obsessions. Some clearly know Linux namespaces and steered their agents straight at the kernel boundary. Others went after the network policies, and many went after areas we didn’t think to put on the menu.

That variety is what you're funding with a public challenge. Here's one of the more interesting findings it produced.

Cross-tenant disk snapshot restore (with limits)

Filed on day one of the challenge, this report is our favorite example of why we run a public bug bounty, even after internal assessments and a white-box engagement.

When you snapshot a sandbox, the control plane has to record where the snapshot data landed: {storage_url, size, checksum}. The flaw the researcher found was subtle: that answer came from software running inside the guest, and services running on the host trusted it. That is a trust-boundary violation. The guest is where our customers (and hackers) run untrusted code, so the host can never take its word as authoritative.

The researcher combined a known, documented container-escape primitive with this trust flaw. They intercepted the snapshot response inside their own sandbox and rewrote it, swapping the storage objects of two snapshots belonging to two separate accounts they owned. That meant restoring "your" snapshot materialized the other account's entire filesystem.

The researcher demonstrated that each account could read and modify the other’s files, verified the results using hashes, and preserved the test resources so we could independently reproduce the findings.

The limits of this attack matter. Aiming the swap at a specific victim required knowing that victim's internal snapshot storage key, a random 96-bit identifier the platform generates per snapshot and never exposes through the API. The only place that key appears is inside the victim's own sandbox. The researcher owned both accounts, which is what made the proof possible; there was no demonstrated path for a stranger to target another tenant. We still treated it as a priority fix, because a boundary that depends on a secret staying secret is not a boundary.

Trail of Bits independently flagged the same root cause in their assessment, which told us the finding was real, important, and discoverable from two completely different angles.

The fix shipped within a week, and the control plane now binds every snapshot object to the project that created it and rejects anything else. Snapshot creation moved out of the guest-reachable environment into a host-side service, and storage paths are project-scoped with strictly validated URLs.

Thank you to the research community

We would like to thank every researcher who filed a report, whether their finding was a zero day or a duplicate. Every technique discovered in the challenge informs how we protect the workloads running on Vercel Sandbox.

Thank you also to Trail of Bits for your comprehensive internal investigation and guidance.

Read the original challenge announcement and learn more about Vercel Sandbox in the documentation.

Read more

title: $1 million hacker challenge for Vercel Sandbox
description:
Agents need to run untrusted code, and the microVM has become the standard way to do it: a dedicated guest kernel per workload, isolated from the host and from every other workload on the same machine.

But recent security research and real-world incidents have revealed that agents running untrusted code do not need to cross a VM boundary to escape containment; they only need one network path the security model failed to account for, which we explained in our post A sandbox without a network boundary is only half a sandbox.

Isolation only holds if both sides of it hold: the Firecracker microVM and the host-side network controls. Recently our CTO pointed an open-weight model with no safeguards at Vercel Sandbox. It did not escape, but it mapped the guest kernel, built a VM to reproduce its ideas, and wrote a fuzzer.

Defenders have first-mover advantage, but it won't last forever, and the choice is when to test the boundaries (we strongly encourage building a scanning program, which you can do on any budget with an open-source tool like deepsec and AI Gateway).

We are proactively choosing to test Vercel Sandbox on our own schedule, not an attacker's, and we are doing it in the open, with the best researchers in the world.

So for two weeks, we are paying up to $1,000,000 USD to the researchers who can escape a Vercel Sandbox.

The challenge

Starting today, Vercel is running a two-week public HackerOne program focused on Vercel Sandbox isolation.

  • Program: Public HackerOne program, open to all eligible researchers

  • Window: Tuesday, August 18 to Tuesday, September 1, 2026, or earlier if the reward pool is exhausted

  • Max per report: $50,000 USD, for a vulnerability that lets a threat actor read or modify another Vercel tenant's data

  • Total pool: Up to $1,000,000 USD in total payouts

Bounties are paid per report, scoped to a single root cause, and assigned by Vercel triage based on the maximum demonstrable impact. The full bounty table, detailed scope, and the list of known-duplicate classes are on the HackerOne program page.

How Vercel Sandbox is built

Vercel Sandbox runs on bare-metal EC2 hosts. Each sandbox gets its own Firecracker microVM with a dedicated guest kernel, and inside that microVM a Linux container runs the operator's code. The microVM, not the container, is the security boundary, so operator-supplied code runs two layers removed from the host. We assume that code is fully hostile: root inside the container, full kernel access inside the microVM, and motivated to reach the host or another tenant.

The network side of the boundary is enforced on the host, outside the microVM, where code inside the sandbox cannot modify or disable it. The sandbox firewall intercepts outbound TCP and DNS, checks each connection against the operator's domain and CIDR policies, and can inject credentials at the boundary so they never enter the microVM.

What we're looking for

In short: anything that breaks the sandbox boundary.

  • Compute boundary: Escaping the Firecracker microVM to the EC2 host, or reaching another tenant's sandbox through the compute layer (reading, modifying, or executing code in it), or crashing another tenant's sandbox from within another sandbox

  • Network boundary: Defeating the sandbox firewall without crossing the microVM: reaching destinations the operator did not authorize, exfiltrating data, or retrieving brokered credentials

Container namespace escapes that only reach the Firecracker guest OS are not in scope. Namespaces are a developer-experience feature, not the security boundary.

Bounties

Severity

Bounty

Critical

$25,000 – $50,000

High

$10,000 – $25,000

Medium

$5,000 – $10,000

Low

$1,000 – $5,000

The full bounty table, with example vulnerability classes for each tier, is on the HackerOne program page.

How to participate

The program is open now and closes on Tuesday, September 1, 2026, or earlier if the $1,000,000 USD reward pool is exhausted. Reports go through the HackerOne program page.

To reproduce a finding, boot a sandbox with the @vercel/sandbox SDK and demonstrate the impact with a live proof of concept. The default sandbox OS is enough for most reports; bring a custom image from the Vercel Container Registry only if your PoC needs extra tooling. We will not reward static-analysis-only findings; to issue a payout, we need to see the boundary break.

Full rules, eligibility, the complete scope and bounty table, and the submission process are on the HackerOne program page.

Results and payouts

We will triage reports from the day the program opens through one month after it closes. As findings are confirmed, we will pay bounties, ship fixes, and credit every researcher whose report holds up. The techniques discovered during this program will become permanent additions to the sandbox boundary, protecting every workload on Vercel long after the challenge ends. After the program closes, we will publish a follow-up writeup of the techniques and the fixes we shipped.

Thanks to HackerOne for standing up the program, and to the researchers who will spend the next two weeks trying to break what we built.

title: The Vercel Sandbox CLI is now more agent-friendly
description:
The Sandbox CLI version 4.0.1 ships four output and error improvements:

  • New sandboxes point users towards how to connect into them.

  • A sandbox not found error shows where to look for existing sandboxes.

  • Common mistakes, like typing a command after sh, redirect to the command that was intended.

  • Outdated installs show an update notice when they create a new sandbox.

Each of these messages now carries the action to take next instead of leaving you to work it out.

New sandboxes tell you how to connect

create and fork output now ends with a connect hint, so a fresh sandbox never leaves you wondering what to type next.

Not found errors point you to your sandboxes

When a command references a sandbox that does not exist, the error is quiet and actionable instead of a raw API dump. Setting DEBUG=sandbox:errors restores the request detail for debugging.

A misused command explains the right one

sh opens a plain interactive shell, so it takes no command of its own. The CLI can now return precise answers that rewrite the attempt into the command that does what you meant, whatever the command is.

Outdated installs warn you at creation time

create, sh, and run check for a newer published CLI and print an update notice when the install is behind. The check is cached to a file and refreshed at most once per hour; when a lookup does run it happens concurrently with the creation request, so it adds no latency. Creation defaults, such as the base image, are chosen client side, so an outdated global install silently keeps old defaults. Prerelease versions skip the check, and SANDBOX_SKIP_VERSION_CHECK=1 disables it.

Learn more in the Sandbox CLI documentation.

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.
