title: Introducing Agent Plugins
description:
Today, Agent Plugins 1.0.0 is publicly available. Agent Plugins is an open, vendor-neutral standard for plugins that extend AI agents.

Agent Skills provide reusable instructions and resources for AI agents. MCP servers connect agents to tools and services. Both can be reused across clients, but clients often package and discover them differently.

Agent Plugins gives compatible clients a common format: a directory with a plugin.json manifest and fixed locations for its components. The format is intentionally small and easy to implement, and it leaves installation, distribution, policy, user experience, and client-specific capabilities to each client.

One package for the portable parts

Extension authors often adapt the same component to several client formats. Even though the underlying Skill or MCP server is identical, clients often expect different top-level metadata, discovery paths, or MCP configuration.

Agent Plugins gives those shared components one predictable, structured home:

A minimal JSON manifest (plugin.json) identifies the specification version and names the plugin:

Those two fields are the minimum requirement for the manifest, and the rest of the contract is represented in the file structure of the directory itself. A reusable component should not need to be repackaged for every client, so the format specifies only what a client needs to discover and load what is inside.

Every compatible client checks for plugin.json at the plugin root. Clients that support Skills discover them under skills/. Clients that support MCP servers read their configuration from mcp.json. A client can support either component type or both. After the client validates the manifest, components are validated independently, so one invalid component does not disable unrelated ones.

For plugin authors, that means fewer client-specific conventions for the same component. For client implementers, the specification defines a small, deterministic contract for discovery, validation, and loading.

Small on purpose

Agent Plugins defines the portable contract for a plugin and leaves the behavior of the client up to each client.

Version 1 focuses that contract on two component types: Agent Skills and MCP servers. Both already have specifications and meaningful adoption of their own, and Agent Plugins does not attempt to redefine them. Agent Plugins provides a shared definition of how clients find the components together in a distributable plugin.

Other components, such as commands, hooks, and agents, remain with clients. The Technical Steering Committee may consider additional component types in future versions as semantics converge and a demonstrated portability need emerges.

Keeping the boundary small makes the format easier to implement and gives the ecosystem room to converge before adding more portable surface area.

Clients retain flexibility

Clients need freedom to innovate while a shared format evolves, so Agent Plugins includes a namespaced extension mechanism for client-specific data and files.

Extensions remain outside the portable contract. Each client defines its own namespace, and other clients ignore it. This prevents client-specific behavior from leaking into the common format or blocking adoption of the shared components. A client-specific capability can remain client-specific until there is reason and consensus to standardize it.

An open, multi-vendor project

Vercel initiated the proposal, which representatives from Amazon Web Services (AWS), Anysphere, GitHub, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Vercel refined collaboratively into Agent Plugins 1.0.0.

The initial Technical Steering Committee includes Core Maintainers from AWS, Cursor, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Vercel.

The project is openly licensed, and its maintainers, contribution process, and technical decisions are public. No single company's product roadmap sets the format's direction.

Build with Agent Plugins 1.0.0

The specification, its JSON Schemas, and guides for plugin authors and client implementers are available at agent-plugins.org. Governance and the contribution process live in the Agent Plugins specification repository on GitHub.

If you author agent extensions, you can use the specification to package Skills and MCP servers behind one portable manifest. If you build an agent client, the specification's conformance checklist defines the minimum requirements for discovering and loading Agent Plugins.

At launch, Agent Plugins are supported across:

  • ChatGPT and Codex

  • Cursor

  • GitHub Copilot

  • Kiro

  • VS Code

Plugin authors can package components once, and their plugin will automatically carry between supporting clients.

Agent Plugins is a contract between the authors who build extensions for agents and the clients that load them. That contract is now defined and open for both sides to shape.

Read more

title: Seedance 2.5 now available on Vercel AI Gateway
description:
Seedance 2.5 from ByteDance is now available on AI Gateway. It can generate up to 30-second clips with synchronized audio, and takes up to 50 reference inputs in one request, spanning images, video, audio, and style.

A single clip holds camera movement and continuity without stitching shots together in post, and short clips can be extended, carrying over character, scene, and camera movement. Prompts work in more than ten languages.

Seedance 2.5 can also edit a finished video in place, swapping backgrounds, products, or characters while the frame, camera, and pacing stay fixed, so one shoot yields several variants.

Generating a video

Set model to bytedance/seedance-2.5 and call generateVideo from the AI SDK:

Adding image references

Pass image URLs in inputReferences and point at them in the prompt with [Image 1], [Image 2]. Tag each entry with its media type. Seedance treats an untagged URL as an image.

Combining reference types

Mix videos and images in the same request to pull different qualities from each: motion and camera work from a clip, a subject's appearance from a still.

Videos go in the same inputReferences array as images, tagged with a video media type. Numbering runs per type so the first video is [Video 1] and the first image is [Image 1], and both can appear in one prompt.

Editing a video

Referencing and editing use the same setup, so the prompt decides which you get. Ask the model to follow a clip's camera movement and it builds a new video from scratch. Ask it to change something in the clip and it edits the video you gave it.

You can reference and edit in one prompt, though results get less predictable, so it helps to be explicit about what each asset is for.

For the playground and API reference, see the model page, or browse every video model on AI Gateway.

Its central goal is to help readers build knowledge they can apply in everyday financial decisions.
Section 1: Understanding Verified Binance Accounts
1.1 Account Structure and Essential Features
A Binance account is a digital profile through which an eligible user can access the platform's available services. Its structure may include personal profile information, account preferences, identity verification status, transaction records, and settings relevant to the services available in the user's jurisdiction.
Verification is a process through which a platform checks information about an account holder. Depending on the applicable requirements, this process may involve identifying information, identity documents, or additional checks. The precise requirements can change according to jurisdiction, account type, and platform policy.
Understanding these components helps users recognize that an exchange account is more than a username and password. It connects an individual's identity, access permissions, financial activities, and records within a digital service.
A verified status indicates that certain verification requirements have been completed. It does not automatically establish financial expertise, guarantee access to every feature, or demonstrate that an individual will make sound investment decisions.
1.2 Digital Identity and Financial Significance
Digital identity is increasingly important in modern financial services. Banks, payment providers, investment platforms, and cryptocurrency exchanges may use identity checks to understand who is accessing their services and to meet applicable regulatory obligations.
For cryptocurrency users, understanding digital identity can improve their ability to navigate financial applications. It encourages them to read account requirements, maintain accurate personal information, understand transaction records, and recognize the relationship between identity verification and access to regulated services.
A verified account should be understood as one part of a broader financial identity. Other important elements include financial literacy, responsible decision-making, accurate records, and familiarity with the platform's terms.
The distinction between account ownership and account access is particularly important. Verification is generally tied to the person whose identity was checked. Users should therefore learn how to complete the applicable process for themselves instead of assuming that another person's verification can simply be transferred.
Section 2: Practical Applications
2.1 Everyday Uses of Cryptocurrency Exchange Accounts
Cryptocurrency exchange accounts can support several practical activities when the relevant services are available and the user meets the applicable eligibility requirements. Their usefulness depends on the individual's objectives, understanding of digital assets, and ability to manage financial decisions responsibly.

For example, a person who learns to review transaction histories may become more organized when tracking household expenses. Someone who studies identity verification may better understand why financial institutions request particular documents.

Organized documentation can make it easier to review spending, investigate discrepancies, and prepare information for personal or professional accounting.

Its age alone cannot establish the accuracy of its information or the quality of its owner's decisions. For this reason, the educational focus should be on legitimate account ownership, accurate information, clear documentation, and consistent compliance with applicable requirements. 4.2 Key Factors That Support Credibility Several habits can help individuals maintain a clear and credible digital financial profile. Accurate personal information: Information provided during account registration and verification should be truthful and consistent with applicable requirements. Consistent account management: Users should keep relevant account details current through the platform's authorized procedures and review important notifications. Documented financial activity: Maintaining transaction records and understanding account statements can help users explain and review their financial activities. Knowledge of platform rules: Reading applicable terms and verification requirements helps users understand which actions are permitted and which services are available. Responsible communication: When discussing financial activity with an accountant, adviser, or other appropriate professional, clear records and accurate explanations support productive conversations. Independent evaluation: Financial claims should be assessed using credible documentation rather than relying solely on an account's apparent age or status. These principles apply to cryptocurrency exchanges as well as online banking, investment accounts, and payment applications. Ultimately, credibility is built through accurate information, transparent practices, and responsible behavior. It should not be treated as something that can be established solely by obtaining an account with a particular history. Section 5: Productivity and Workflow 5.1 How Structured Account Management Improves Efficiency Digital financial tools can simplify recordkeeping and make information easier to review. However, these benefits are most apparent when users adopt a consistent workflow. A structured approach begins with understanding the account's purpose. Someone studying cryptocurrency markets may need a different set of records from a person who is organizing digital asset transactions for personal accounting. Once the purpose is clear, the user can identify the information they need, establish a regular review schedule, and organize relevant documentation. For example, reviewing transaction records periodically can help a person identify unfamiliar entries, understand how balances have changed, and prepare information for budgeting. Keeping notes about educational activities can also help learners track progress without confusing study exercises with actual financial transactions. 5.2 Actionable Productivity Tips The following practices can make digital financial management more organized. Create a simple recordkeeping system. Maintain a consistent location for relevant statements, transaction exports, and notes. Use clear file names and dates. Schedule regular reviews. Set aside time to examine financial records, account notices, and any changes to applicable platform requirements. Separate learning from financial activity. Use educational materials, demonstrations, or practice exercises where available before making decisions involving real money. Read instructions before beginning. Reviewing the requirements in advance can reduce confusion and help users prepare the information they need. Use official documentation. Platform help centers and published policies are useful references when questions arise about verification, account settings, or available features. Keep financial goals realistic. Learning about cryptocurrency does not require frequent trading or constant monitoring of market prices. A defined learning schedule can prevent digital finance from becoming an unnecessary distraction. Record important decisions. Brief notes about why a financial decision was made can help users review their reasoning later. A productive workflow should reduce unnecessary effort while improving understanding. It should not encourage people to bypass account requirements or treat account access as a substitute for financial knowledge. Section 6: Case Studies and Examples The following illustrative scenarios demonstrate how the principles of account verification, financial education, and organized digital workflows can apply in everyday situations. They are hypothetical examples rather than reports of independently verified individuals or specific outcomes. Example 1: A Student Learning About Cryptocurrency A university student is interested in blockchain technology and wants to understand how cryptocurrency exchanges operate. Initially, the student assumes that obtaining an account is the main step toward learning about the subject. After reviewing educational materials, the student realizes that account registration and identity verification are only parts of the broader process. The student begins by studying blockchain fundamentals, transaction fees, market terminology, and the role of exchanges in digital asset markets. The student also reviews the platform's official documentation to understand eligibility requirements and available educational resources. Where account access is appropriate, the student follows the authorized registration and verification procedures. Over time, the student develops a glossary of financial terms and keeps notes about the differences between exchanges, wallets, and blockchain networks. Learning point: Practical financial education begins with understanding concepts and requirements. Account access alone does not provide the knowledge needed to evaluate digital assets. Example 2: A Freelancer Organizing Financial Records A freelance designer receives payments through several digital services and wants to improve personal bookkeeping. The designer studies how transaction histories and downloadable statements can support financial organization. Instead of concentrating on account age or status, the designer creates a monthly recordkeeping routine. Relevant statements are stored by date, and income entries are categorized for later review. The designer also learns that different services may use different fee structures, transaction formats, and reporting methods. Keeping these differences documented makes it easier to compare records and prepare information for an accountant. When researching cryptocurrency exchanges, the designer examines the applicable account requirements and considers whether the platform's services meet the intended purpose. Learning point: Organized records and an understanding of transaction documentation can improve financial administration. These benefits do not depend on purchasing an established account. Example 3: A Small Business Owner Exploring Digital Finance A small business owner wants to understand whether cryptocurrency could become relevant to future business operations. Before considering any financial activity, the owner researches accounting requirements, applicable regulations, transaction documentation, and the availability of services in the business's jurisdiction. The owner creates a comparison sheet covering platform features, fees, reporting tools, and eligibility conditions. The business also consults an appropriate accounting professional about the implications of digital asset transactions. Rather than treating a verified account as evidence that a platform is suitable, the owner evaluates the business's objectives and documentation needs. The result is a more structured assessment process. Even if the business ultimately decides not to use cryptocurrency, the research provides useful knowledge about financial technology and recordkeeping. Learning point: Sound financial decisions depend on evaluating practical requirements, costs, and objectives instead of focusing on a single account feature. Example 4: An Adult Learner Improving Digital Literacy An adult learner wants to become more comfortable with online financial services. The learner starts by studying the account settings, verification terminology, transaction records, and customer support documentation commonly found on financial platforms. The learner practices recognizing official help resources and distinguishing platform requirements from general advice published elsewhere. When encountering unfamiliar instructions, the learner checks the relevant documentation rather than relying on assumptions. The learner also establishes a routine for reviewing financial records and writing down questions before contacting customer support. These habits gradually become useful across other digital services, including online banking and payment applications. Learning point: Understanding one financial platform can help develop transferable digital skills, including careful reading, documentation, independent research, and organized problem-solving. Taken together, these examples show that the main educational benefits come from knowledge, consistency, and informed decision-making. None requires the purchase of an account that was verified for someone else. Section 7: Step-by-Step Guide to Understanding Binance Account Verification The following six steps provide a practical framework for learning about account verification and applying that knowledge responsibly. Step 1: Define Your Learning Objective Begin by identifying what you want to understand. Your objective might be learning cryptocurrency terminology, reviewing digital financial records, studying exchange operations, or understanding identity verification. A clear objective helps you choose relevant educational resources and avoid spending time on features that do not support your goals. Write down two or three questions you want to answer. For example, you might want to understand what identity verification involves, how transaction histories work, or which services are available in your jurisdiction. Step 2: Review Official Platform Information Visit the official Binance website and locate the relevant help center or account documentation. Read the current information about registration, identity verification, eligibility, supported jurisdictions, and available account features. Requirements can change, so current documentation is more useful than relying entirely on older articles. If you consult general informational resources such as usasvcit, compare important statements with official documentation before treating them as authoritative. Step 3: Understand Identity Verification Requirements Learn what the platform requires from individuals seeking access to its services. Depending on the applicable rules, the process may include submitting identifying information, providing an accepted identity document, or completing additional verification steps. Make sure you understand the relationship between the account holder and the identity being verified. Verification should be completed through the platform's authorized process using the account holder's own accurate information. Do not assume that an account verified for another individual can be treated as your own verified account. Step 4: Prepare Accurate Information Before starting an authorized registration or verification process, read the instructions carefully and identify the information required. Ensure that your information is accurate and consistent with the platform's stated requirements. If a document is not accepted or a detail needs clarification, consult the official instructions or appropriate support channels. Preparing in advance can make the process easier to understand and reduce avoidable errors. Step 5: Learn the Account's Available Features After completing the applicable requirements and receiving access, familiarize yourself with the available account interface. Study profile settings, transaction histories, fee information, account statements, and educational resources. Feature availability may differ according to location, eligibility, and platform policies. Take notes about unfamiliar terms and look for official explanations before relying on your interpretation. Step 6: Establish a Regular Review Routine Create a simple schedule for reviewing account information and maintaining relevant financial records. For example, a monthly review might include checking transaction histories, organizing statements, reading important platform notices, and updating personal financial records. Use this process to reinforce your understanding of digital finance. The objective is to develop a sustainable habit of informed account management rather than simply completing a registration procedure. Following these steps creates a foundation for understanding cryptocurrency services, identity verification, and responsible digital financial administration. Section 8: Frequently Asked Questions
  6. What does a verified Binance account mean? A verified Binance account is an account for which the platform has completed the applicable identity verification requirements. The exact process and available services depend on current platform policies, jurisdiction, and eligibility. Verification does not guarantee investment success or access to every feature.
  7. Why is identity verification important on cryptocurrency platforms? Identity verification can help financial platforms meet applicable legal and regulatory obligations, establish account-holder information, and determine eligibility for particular services. Understanding these procedures helps users navigate digital financial systems more effectively.
  8. Is purchasing a previously verified Binance account the same as verifying my own account? No. A previously verified account may be associated with another individual's identity. Purchasing it does not establish that the buyer has completed the platform's verification requirements. The appropriate educational and practical approach is to understand the current rules and follow the authorized process for your own account.
  9. Can learning about Binance help with everyday financial management? Yes. Studying exchange interfaces, transaction histories, fees, and financial terminology can help develop recordkeeping, analytical thinking, and digital literacy. These skills may also be useful when working with online banking and other financial applications.
  10. What should beginners learn before using a cryptocurrency exchange? Beginners should understand basic cryptocurrency concepts, market volatility, transaction fees, account requirements, financial recordkeeping, and the services available in their jurisdiction. They should also review official documentation and avoid making financial decisions based on unfamiliar terminology or assumptions.
  11. Where can I find reliable information about Binance account verification? The official Binance website and help center are appropriate starting points for current account requirements and procedures. General educational resources, including usasvcit, may provide additional context, but important requirements should be checked against official documentation and applicable regulations. Conclusion Understanding the topic of buying verified Binance accounts provides an opportunity to explore a much broader subject: the role of identity, financial literacy, and responsible account management in the digital economy. A cryptocurrency exchange account is not simply a digital profile. It can connect an individual's identity, financial records, platform access, and interactions with digital asset markets. Understanding these connections helps users approach financial technology with greater clarity and confidence. The most valuable lessons concern accurate information, legitimate account ownership, identity verification, organized recordkeeping, and informed decision-making. These principles are useful not only for cryptocurrency exchanges but also for online banking, investment applications, and other digital financial services. Practical education should focus on understanding how account verification works, what requirements apply, and how financial information can be managed effectively. Purchasing an account verified under another person's identity does not replace the process of establishing one's own eligibility and completing the platform's required procedures. Beginners can make meaningful progress by studying official documentation, learning basic cryptocurrency terminology, reviewing transaction records, and developing consistent financial habits. Additional educational resources, including usasvcit, can serve as starting points for research when their information is evaluated alongside authoritative sources. Ultimately, digital financial competence is built through knowledge and practice. Understanding the systems behind an account is more valuable than focusing solely on its age or verification status. By applying the principles in this guide, readers can develop transferable skills, improve their understanding of digital finance, and make better-informed decisions about the financial technologies they encounter in everyday life. Call to Action Take the next step by strengthening your understanding of cryptocurrency and digital financial services. Start with the official Binance help center, review the identity verification requirements that apply to your location, and explore introductory educational materials about blockchain technology, transaction fees, and financial recordkeeping. Create a personal learning checklist, keep notes about unfamiliar concepts, and set aside time each week to review what you have learned. If you consult additional resources such as usasvcit, verify important procedural details against current official documentation. Focus on developing knowledge, maintaining accurate records, and understanding legitimate account procedures. These practical habits can support long-term digital literacy and help you approach financial technology with greater confidence.

title: One Developer + One AI Bot: Building an SSH Client in 45 Self-Iterating Rounds
description:
I'm building AI-SSH-Pro, an open-source SSH client with a built-in AI assistant (Electron + React + TypeScript): terminal, SFTP, command history and AI chat in one window.

The unusual part is the team. It's me plus one AI bot. I treat the bot as a whole product team — product manager, UX/UI designer, developer, QA, and retro lead — and let it iterate round after round on its own. My job is direction, feedback, and deciding when to ship.

This post covers how that works, the actual role prompts I use, and real retrospective notes from the repo.

The numbers

All of these come straight from git log and the docs folder, as of 2026-10-21:

  • 405 commits in total (first commit on 2026-04-02), 319 of them in just two days (Oct 20–21).
  • 45 rounds of continuous self-iteration completed since Oct 20; round 46 is in progress.
  • 124 design docs under docs/iterations/.
  • 407 regression tests, all green on the latest full npm test run.
  • 11 retro entries in docs/retro.md, distilled into 17 rules in docs/dev-rules.md.

The loop: one bot, five hats

Every round follows the same pipeline:

Product → UX/UI design → Development → QA → Retro

  • Product proposes just 3 small items per round, focused on what people use every day: connecting, the terminal, SFTP, history, AI chat.
  • Design screenshots the real UI first, then writes a design doc.
  • Development commits in small steps — one item, one commit.
  • QA adds regression tests; nothing is done until the full suite passes.
  • Retro turns every mistake into an actionable rule that the next round reads first.

A round takes roughly 30 minutes. Any bug I report jumps the queue.

The role prompts

These are the prompts I actually use, lightly trimmed. Feel free to copy them.

Shared context (always first)

Project: AI-SSH-Pro, an AI SSH client (Electron + React + TypeScript).
Rules: commit locally only; push only for releases. npm test must be fully green.
Use theme components and spacing tokens, never native <select>.
Production hosts show a banner but are not blocked; read-only hosts block writes.
AI-generated commands are only prefilled — the user presses send.
Redact anything before it is sent to the AI.

Product

You are the product manager. Only propose high-frequency, everyday features;
niche ideas go to the backlog. Before proposing, grep docs/iterations and src
to dedupe — never re-propose something already built.
Each round: 3 small items, each with the user scenario, what feels awkward today,
and the change the user will actually notice.

UX / UI design

You are the UX/UI designer. Screenshot the real UI first, then write a design doc.
Cover empty, disabled (explain why) and error states, shortcuts, and both
light and dark themes. Principles: dense but not cramped, symmetric layouts,
icon buttons over text buttons, and never drop an existing feature.

Development

You are the developer. Implement the design doc in small steps, one commit per item,
no pushing. Toggle-style state must read the latest value from a ref.
Render popovers into document.body so they never get clipped.

QA

You are QA. Every item gets a regression test covering rapid repeated clicks,
acting after switching tabs, and edge cases. Run the full npm test on the final
HEAD — it must be all green. Capture before/after screenshots.

Retro

You are the retro lead. After every round and every bug fix, append an entry to
docs/retro.md: time (planned vs actual), where it got stuck, what went wrong,
root cause, and how to avoid it next time (as an actionable rule).
Promote general rules to docs/dev-rules.md. Read them before each round starts.

Self-iteration (one line to start it)

Iterate continuously: product → design → dev → QA → retro, round after round,
without asking me. ~30 minutes per round; bugs I report jump the queue.
End each round with a 3–5 line report.

Quick request / bug (the one I use most)

[screenshot] This doesn't respond / this looks messy — designers, please fix it.
State the root cause or design rationale first, then fix, test, commit, and write a retro entry.

Before and after

Split view: from a dedicated toolbar to pane headers

The old split toolbar ate a whole row, used a native dropdown, and had a cryptic "left/right" button. Now the controls live in each pane's header, primary and secondary panes are clearly labeled, and broadcast input is a real toggle.

The split button in the top-right became a menu: off, side-by-side, or stacked, with the current mode checked.

Snippets: one line each, built-ins grew from 3 to 26

Each snippet used to be a tall card. Now it's a single row, action buttons appear on hover, and double-click or Enter only prefills the command — it never runs it. Risky commands like delete or reboot are deliberately left out of the built-in list.

SFTP header: it started with one screenshot

This is the screenshot I sent the bot: the breadcrumb duplicated the path input, the two sides didn't match, and too many text buttons wrapped onto a second line. The bot came back with a design and shipped it: one symmetric row per side, click the address bar (or press Ctrl+L) to type a path, and rarely used actions tucked into a "More" menu.

AI chat panel

Real retros

Each of these is taken from docs/retro.md and matches a real incident.

1. "The split button doesn't respond"

  • What I saw: the split toggle worked only sometimes; clicking it again after enabling often did nothing.
  • Root cause: a missing useCallback dependency meant the closure read stale state. Tests only covered a single click.
  • Rule: toggle callbacks that fire repeatedly always read the latest value from a ref. Toggle tests must cover two clicks in a row, three rapid clicks, and acting after switching tabs.

2. The split redesign took an hour

  • What I saw: a 30-minute task took about 60.
  • Root cause: the requirements changed mid-way with no new estimate; the full test suite ran after every small edit; the screenshot script kept turning split view off.
  • Rule: run only related tests while iterating and the full suite once on the final HEAD; re-estimate before acting on a requirement change; screenshot scenarios must be idempotent.

3. A wall of script after connecting to a server

  • What I saw: connecting to a test server echoed the shell-integration bootstrap script into the terminal.
  • Root cause: it was only verified on the demo host, which has no real TTY, so the echo was invisible.
  • Rule: anything written into a remote shell must be checked once in a real interactive bash session for echo and history. Anything meant to be hidden needs an explicit end marker and a render-layer gate.

4. "All tabs" flashes and disappears

  • What I saw: clicking "All tabs" showed the list for a split second.
  • Root cause: the auto-close condition was "close when tabs don't overflow", but the button had since been made always visible — the condition was never updated.
  • Rule: popovers may auto-close only on a state transition, never on the current state; when changing an entry point's visibility, grep every effect on that state; every popover needs a "stays open after opening" test.

5. Product kept re-proposing finished features

  • What I saw: the product role repeatedly suggested things that already existed.
  • Root cause: different wording from the existing implementation, and dedupe relied on memory.
  • Rule: every proposal must grep docs/iterations, the backlog and src with at least two synonyms, and list the search terms and hits in the proposal.

6. A context menu covering a modal

  • What I saw: the tab context menu stayed on top of the host-key dialog.
  • Root cause: the fix assumed all menus shared one close path, but the tab menu had its own state in App.
  • Rule: before touching popover behavior, grep every popover implementation and list its owner; closing goes through a single broadcast event that every menu must listen to; layering fixes must be verified with an "after" screenshot.

What the human actually does

In this setup I do three things:

  • Direction: decide where the product goes — for example, "only build high-usage features".
  • Feedback: use the app, take a screenshot, and say "this is messy" or "this doesn't respond".
  • Release decisions: when to cut a test build and when to push is my call.

Breaking down requirements, design, code, tests and retros are all handled by the bot. The retro loop means each mistake is (ideally) made only once — the rulebook keeps growing, and iterations keep getting steadier.

Try it

  • Website: https://guoshuaipeng.github.io/ai-ssh-pro
  • Download: https://github.com/guoshuaipeng/ai-ssh-pro/releases

Feedback is very welcome — and if you're also letting an AI drive your development, I'd love to hear how you run it.

title: I Tested a Map-Based AI 3D Generator on the Bay Bridge: Notes and Limits
description:
I needed a quick 3D blockout of the San Francisco–Oakland Bay Bridge for a lighting and camera test. Hand-modeling 4.5 miles of bridge was out of the question. I wanted something rough enough to answer scale questions in an afternoon, not a survey asset.
So I tried a map-first approach: select the area, generate a model, then fix what the generator cannot know.

TL;DR

  • A selection covering both spans and the island produced a usable massing model in minutes.
  • Scale was close enough for camera blocking, not for measurement.
  • Cables and tunnel portals needed manual work.
  • Good for silhouette and fog tests, bad for structural detail. ## The actual constraint This was previsualization. I wanted cameras at deck level, tower base, and on a hillside, then to see how fog separated the layers. I needed the footprint, deck heights, tower positions, and a rough city backdrop. Not rivets or lane markings. That distinction matters. A model that is wrong about a bolt can still be right about a silhouette. A model that is wrong about deck height cannot. ## Step 1: define the selection I used GenAnywhere, which works by drawing an area on a map and generating a 3D model from that selection. My first selection was too tight, just deck and towers, and the result floated in empty space. The second included the corridor from the San Francisco anchorage to the Oakland touchdown, open water on both sides, Yerba Buena Island, and a thin strip of waterfront. That produced a much better base. The selection is the most important input: too small and the model has no context; too large and you spend an hour deleting buildings you do not need. ## Step 2: generate, then audit scale The first export looked convincing until I put a camera at deck level. The eastern tower read too short relative to the roadway. I checked known dimensions, roughly 160 meters for the tower and 624 meters for the main span, and scaled the tower group. After that, proportions matched well enough for blocking. I also counted the towers. The western span has two; the eastern span has one. A quick count catches more errors than it should. ## Step 3: repair the geometry The generator gave me a massing model, not an engineer's model. Three fixes took most of the time:
  • Cables. The eastern span's fan came in as straight segments. I replaced it with curves and a radial array, then adjusted the anchor points.
  • Suspenders. The western span needed vertical ropes at regular intervals. An array modifier handled it.
  • Tunnel portals. The entrances were merged into the terrain. I cut two openings and added simple concrete surrounds. None of this is hard, but it is not automatic. Budget for it.

Step 4: block the cameras

I set three: bay trail at eye level, under the western span looking up at the truss, and East Bay hills with a long lens. The hillside shot immediately showed a problem: the model's city blocks were too tall and blocked the bridge. I scaled the backdrop down and moved the camera.
That is the point of a blockout. You find composition problems before materials.

Where it earns its place

Fast coverage of a large, complex site. Useful silhouettes for fog and lighting tests. Easy iteration on the selection. Enough context to judge how the bridge sits in the bay.

Where it falls apart

Cable topology is approximate, especially on the self-anchored suspension span. Textures are flat at close range. Railings and road markings are missing. Nothing here is suitable for structural analysis, clearance checks, or construction documents.
I would not hand this to an engineer. I would hand it to a layout artist.

When not to use it

If you need measured accuracy, use survey data, CAD, or photogrammetry. If you need a hero close-up of a cable band, model it by hand. The map-first workflow is for the wide shot, the camera plan, and the early look-development pass.

What I would change next time

Split the selection into two runs: eastern span, then western span plus island. Each half had different geometry problems, and fixing them together was messy. Two smaller models joined in Blender would have been faster.
The blockout took an afternoon. Most of that was cable repair, not generation. Fair trade for a scene I would otherwise have skipped.

title: Why Security Reviews Stall Procurement — and How to Answer Them Faster
description:
A Toronto-based SaaS vendor gets within one signature of a six-figure enterprise deal. Then procurement routes the contract to security review. Three weeks later, the champion who fought for you internally is fielding questions about data residency, database access, and audit trails that nobody on your team can answer without pulling an engineer off the roadmap for a day. The deal doesn't die — it just stalls, quarter after quarter, until the buyer moves on.

This is the quiet tax on growth at mid-size Canadian software and services firms: the product sells itself, but the security questionnaire doesn't. And the questions are rarely about your roadmap. They're about whether a vendor's AI or support tooling can reach a live production database, and whether you can prove, in writing, what happened during an incident.

Why security reviews stall procurement

Most review delays come down to one unanswerable question: can this system touch our data, and if something breaks, can you show us exactly what changed and who approved it? Vendors who rely on broad database access for support or diagnostics have no clean answer. Vendors who can say a tool never connects to a live database at all — and that every fix is logged as a reviewable pull request — end that conversation in one meeting instead of three.

This matters more in regulated and semi-regulated Canadian sectors — finance in Toronto, health tech in Montreal, logistics and natural resources in Vancouver — where procurement teams are explicitly trained to ask for a data-flow diagram before they ask for a demo. If your production-support process depends on a developer or AI tool holding live credentials, that diagram becomes the reason the deal sits in legal for another month.

The real cost of a stalled review

The slow procurement cycle isn't the only cost. When a production incident does hit, the clock is just as unforgiving — industry estimates put the median cost of downtime for large enterprises at roughly US$9,000 per minute. A security review that takes weeks because nobody can explain your incident-response architecture is bad enough; an incident that takes hours to diagnose because the same architecture lacks a clear root-cause trail is worse, and it's the exact scenario a sharp-eyed procurement reviewer is trying to screen out.

Layer on the talent market: skills gaps are reported by around 90% of organisations in the Gulf and an estimated 57% of firms in Europe can't find qualified developers. Canadian teams are competing in the same global hiring pool, and senior engineers who can trace a production bug to the exact file and line under pressure are the scarcest, most expensive hires on the team. A lean Canadian operation — ten developers instead of thirty — cannot afford to keep that kind of diagnostic depth on call around the clock, and procurement teams increasingly know it, which is part of why they ask so many questions about your support model in the first place.

How to answer security reviews faster

Corporate AI 365 is built around the sentence that ends most security reviews early: it never hosts your code and never connects to a live database. It reasons over your source code and a scripted database schema — not live rows, not a connection string. When a genuine need for live data comes up, it writes a read-only query for your own developer to run; the result never leaves your environment and never comes back to us. That's not a policy promise buried in a contract appendix — it's the architecture, and it's the line that lets a reviewer check the box and move on.

The rest of the workflow is built for the same scrutiny. Anyone in the company — not just engineers — can describe a problem in plain language through the Employee support portal. The AI diagnoses root cause down to file, class, and line, with a confidence score and a proposed fix, and the analysis is reproducible: cached against a hash of the issue, the code snapshot, and the model, so the same report always produces the same answer. That reproducibility is what makes an approval gate meaningful instead of theatrical.

From there, the fix moves through real git branches and pull requests — Developer, QA, approval, production — each gate a permission, each transition an audit record, with a one-click revert if something still goes wrong. Your own CI confirms what shipped. When procurement asks for an audit trail, you hand them one that already exists, rather than reconstructing it from Slack threads.

Across GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and Azure DevOps, with 41 composable permissions and a real org hierarchy, the same governed pipeline works whether you're a ten-person team in Vancouver or a 200-person department in Toronto. Face Off then scores delivered work across developers, teams, and departments, with an AI umpire naming the actual bottleneck — useful internally, and a credible answer when a buyer asks how you keep a lean team accountable without a stack of senior hires you can't find.

title: Declarative Go CLIs with Commandment
description:
Over the last seven years in IT consulting, I have built more than 50 CLIs for customers and projects. I spent a lot of that time refining workflows around Cobra and Viper, trying to make CLI authoring feel as clean and idiomatic as the rest of the Go around it. I never quite got the workflow I wanted.

There was no single breaking point. The same kinds of friction just kept showing up. I wanted flags and arguments to become ordinary Go values once they reached the application. I got tired of defining the same idea again because help, completion, configuration, or tests needed it. I wanted new capabilities to fit the CLI instead of feeling bolted on. Setup order should only matter when order is actually part of the CLI's meaning.

I also spend a lot of time with Kubernetes and Terraform, so declarative systems were already a natural way for me to think. You declare relationships, validate them, and let the system derive the consequences. After years of trying to improve my CLI workflow, I stopped thinking the remaining friction was another convention I had failed to discover. I thought the underlying authoring model was the constraint.

That line of thinking became Commandment, a declarative CLI framework for Go.

Meet alienctl

I'll use a small fictional CLI called alienctl throughout the article. It has two commands.

$ alienctl scan mars
scanning mars

$ ALIEN_BEAM_STRENGTH=2 alienctl abduct --beam-strength 4 cow
abducting cow with beam strength 4

BeamStrength has a static default of 1. The host environment can contribute 2 through ALIEN_BEAM_STRENGTH. The user can contribute 4 through --beam-strength. The accepted value must also be between 1 and 10.

That one value captures the broader problem I kept running into. The flag spelling can live in parser setup, help and completion can need their own description of it, configuration can separately decide whether the flag beats the environment, and tests can encode the same precedence again. Each piece can be reasonable on its own while the same fact ends up with several owners.

Commandment takes a different approach. Application code declares semantic relationships in ordinary Go. Compile validates them and produces an immutable Application, and later operations read from that application instead of rebuilding the CLI's meaning. That's what I mean by declarative here. It does not mean YAML or struct tags, and it does not replace ordinary Go control flow.

Definition -> Compile -> immutable Application

type abductConfig struct {
    Target       string
    BeamStrength int
}

abductCmd := cli.Command[abductConfig]{
    Name: "abduct",
    Declare: func(cb *cli.CommandBuilder[abductConfig]) {
        cb.Arguments.String(&cb.Config.Target, "target")

        beamStrength := cb.Values.Int(&cb.Config.BeamStrength)
        cb.Values.Default(beamStrength, 1)
        cb.Values.Environment(beamStrength, "ALIEN_BEAM_STRENGTH")
        cb.Flags.ValueFor(beamStrength).Long("beam-strength")
        cb.Rule.Between(beamStrength, 1, 10)
    },
    Run: func(_ context.Context, cfg *abductConfig) error {
        fmt.Printf(
            "abducting %s with beam strength %d\n",
            cfg.Target,
            cfg.BeamStrength,
        )
        return nil
    },
}

The root also declares a simpler scan command.

type scanConfig struct {
    World string
}

var definition = cli.Definition[struct{}]{
    Name: "alienctl",
    Declare: func(cb *cli.CommandBuilder[struct{}]) {
        scanCmd := cli.Command[scanConfig]{
            Name: "scan",
            Declare: func(cb *cli.CommandBuilder[scanConfig]) {
                cb.Arguments.String(&cb.Config.World, "world")
            },
            Run: func(_ context.Context, cfg *scanConfig) error {
                fmt.Printf("scanning %s\n", cfg.World)
                return nil
            },
        }
        cb.Subcommands.Command(scanCmd)
        cb.Subcommands.Command(abductCmd)
    },
}

The separate scanConfig and abductConfig types are deliberate. Each command owns the Go state its handler actually needs instead of contributing fields to one universal root configuration. Commandment's declarations stay ordinary, statically typed Go. The design does not depend on reflection-driven struct or tag decoding.

The process entrypoint is ordinary Go too.

app, err := cli.Compile(definition)
if err != nil {
    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
    os.Exit(1)
}

if err := app.RunFromProcess(context.Background()); err != nil {
    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
    os.Exit(cli.ExitCode(err))
}

For that invocation, the same destination has three candidate values.

static default  -> 1
environment     -> 2
flag            -> 4
resolved value  -> 4

The handler never sees a parser object or a bag of raw strings. It gets an ordinary int. That was one of the things I wanted from the start. The CLI boundary is textual, but application code should work with typed Go values.

int is only the built-in case. An application-defined Go type can use a ValueCodec[T] to define how it crosses the textual CLI boundary. Flags, environment input, defaults, resolution, and inspection can all work with that typed destination instead of inventing separate string representations.

The default, environment variable, flag, and range rule all point at the same typed destination. There is no second BeamStrength definition for configuration or validation.

Help and completion use the compiled application

The compiled application already has enough information to render help.

$ ./alienctl --help
Usage:
  alienctl [flags] <command>

Commands:
  scan
  abduct
  help        Show help.
  completion  Generate shell completion source

Flags:
  --help  Show help.
  -h      Show help.

The abduct command is available through the intrinsic help action as well.

$ ./alienctl help abduct
Usage:
  alienctl abduct [flags] <target>

Arguments:
  <target>

Flags:
  --beam-strength VALUE, --beam-strength=VALUE

I did not define a second command-and-flag model for help. The compiled application already knows the command, positional argument, and flag spelling, so help can present them without another description of the CLI.

Completion uses the same grammar. With incomplete input ab, the application can determine what can legally come next.

completion, err := app.Complete(ctx, cli.CompletionRequest{
    Args: []string{"ab"},
    Cursor: cli.CompletionCursor{
        Argument: 0,
        Byte:     2,
    },
})

For this application, the completion result contains abduct.

abduct

The completion request is not tied to a shell. Shell integration adapts the semantic result for a concrete client without defining another command language.

The compiled application still has the grammar, so execution, help, and completion all use it.

Cobra already does this part well

If you use Cobra, this part should be familiar. Cobra already gives Go applications an executable command model with arguments and flags, generated help, and shell completion.

Viper can sit alongside it as a configuration registry, binding command-line flags and environment variables and resolving multiple configuration sources with an explicit precedence order. In the example above, Cobra + Viper can also resolve the effective value to 4.

Commandment is not a feature-for-feature replacement for Viper. Its boundary is the CLI's semantic model. Broader application configuration can stay in ordinary application code. When external configuration affects CLI semantics, it crosses that boundary as typed input instead of becoming another model of the CLI.

What pushed me toward Commandment was the authoring model. After years of writing CLIs, I was tired of carrying setup knowledge across declarations, follow-up mutations, bindings, lifecycle hooks, and initialization timing. Cobra and Viper can be wrapped and organized carefully. I wanted the relationships themselves to be the source of truth.

Commandment validates those relationships during compilation. Order affects behavior only when order is part of the model. Dependencies between semantic values are declared too, so Commandment can validate scope and cycles and derive evaluation order from the dependency graph instead of callback timing.

A typical Cobra + Viper arrangement separates those responsibilities roughly like this.

Cobra / pflag
    command grammar
    flags
    help
    completion

Viper
    configuration sources
    precedence
    effective configuration

application code
    application-specific policy

             versus

Commandment

BeamStrength destination
    <- default 1
    <- environment ALIEN_BEAM_STRENGTH
    <- flag --beam-strength
    <- rule Between(1, 10)

             Compile
                |
                v
      immutable Application
                |
       +--------+--------+
       |        |        |
      Run    Inspect   Complete
                |
          semantic tests

Both approaches can produce 4. With Commandment, the application still knows why 4 won.

Inspecting why the flag won 

$ ALIEN_BEAM_STRENGTH=2 alienctl abduct --beam-strength 4 cow
abducting cow with beam strength 4

A terminal-output test can prove that the program printed 4, but it cannot distinguish normal flag precedence from an ignored environment value, a handler overwrite, or a fallback that happened to produce the same integer.

Because Commandment retained the invocation semantics, Inspect can analyze explicit invocation input without executing the selected handler. The clitest package can assert those observations directly.

func TestBeamStrengthFlagWins(t *testing.T) {
    t.Parallel()

    app := clitest.Compile(t, definition)
    beamStrength := clitest.Command("abduct").Flag("--beam-strength").Value()
    request := cli.InspectionRequest{
        Env: cli.Env{{
            Name:  "ALIEN_BEAM_STRENGTH",
            Value: "2",
        }},
        Args: []string{"abduct", "--beam-strength", "4", "cow"},
    }
    clitest.Inspect(t.Context(), app, request).Require(t,
        clitest.InspectionReady(),
        beamStrength.Text("4"),
        beamStrength.ContributedBy(cli.ValueProducerKindFlag),
    )
}

That test proves both the effective value and the winning producer.

effective value  = 4
winning producer = flag

The default, environment input, and flag are three producers for one semantic destination. Resolution chooses the effective contribution and retains its provenance.

The test does not recreate Commandment's precedence rules. It asks the compiled application what happened.

Parsing does not erase the reason behind the result. Inspect can explain it later without running the handler or inferring semantics from presentation text.

One semantic authority does not mean one representation

One semantic authority does not require one giant data structure or one implementation path for everything.

Help, completion, inspection, diagnostics, schema, reference data, and runtime value state have different consumers and different lifetimes. They deserve different representations.

A semantic fact should still have one authority. Other operations and artifacts can project that fact for their own purpose, but they should not silently redefine it.

Definition
    |
    | Compile
    v
immutable Application
    |
    +-- Run / RunFromProcess --> execution and intrinsic actions such as help
    +-- Complete -----------> semantic completion
    +-- Inspect ------------> invocation-specific observation
    `-- Schema -------------> detached static artifact

Execution, help, completion, inspection, and schema need different representations, but they should agree on the command and value semantics they share.

That is the design I had been trying to get to. Handlers receive typed Go values, each CLI fact has one owner, and help, completion, inspection, and tests reuse the compiled model. Setup order only matters when the model says it matters.

When would I use this instead of Cobra?

Cobra fits well when the main job is an executable command tree with commands, arguments, flags, dispatch, help, and completion. Pairing it with Viper can also provide configuration through environment variables, defaults, files, and explicit precedence.

Commandment is aimed at CLIs where the command tree is only part of the problem. Typed resolution, provenance, and policy may also need to stay coherent across execution, completion, diagnostics, tooling, and tests.

Cobra can implement the behavior shown in this article. The decision is whether a command tree plus configuration registry is enough semantic authority for the CLI you are building.

For a CLI dominated by routing, flags, help, and completion, Cobra is probably the smaller choice. Commandment starts to earn its extra machinery when you need to ask the compiled CLI why a value resolved the way it did, project the same accepted semantics into tooling, or test those semantics without recreating them.

At that point, I would rather have one source of CLI meaning feeding several views than several reasonable systems that can slowly drift apart.

Commandment RC1

Commandment is now in its RC1 review period and requires Go 1.27.1. I am using this release-candidate period to get the API in front of people building real Go CLIs before I finalize v1.0.0.

The source, examples, and documentation are all in the Commandment repository.

If you try Commandment on an existing Go CLI, I'd especially like to hear what gets simpler, what stays awkward, and anything in the API that you think should change before v1.0.0 is finalized.

title: Google Hotels Printed $17 for a Stay It Itemised at $16.66
description:
I run a visa agency in Bali. The other half of my week goes into scrapers on Apify, and one of them reads Google Hotels: a place and two dates in, one row per property out.

A row carries four price numbers for the stay. totalPrice, priceBeforeTaxes, taxesAndFees, totalWithTaxes. Google labels none of them, because Google doesn't ship them as named fields — they come out of an unnamed array, and what each slot means is something you work out or guess.

I guessed. My own README said totalPrice includes taxes and fees. Then a $17 homestay made me go and count.

The row that didn't add up

Liang Homestay and Hostel, Ubud, two nights, 20–22 November 2026:

{
  "name": "Liang Homestay and Hostel",
  "pricePerNightDisplay": "$8",
  "pricePerNight": 8.33,
  "totalPriceDisplay": "$17",
  "totalPrice": 17,
  "priceBeforeTaxes": 13.77,
  "taxes": 0,
  "fees": 2.89,
  "totalWithTaxes": 16.66,
  "nights": 2,
  "currency": "USD"
}

The headline total is above the all-in total. $17 against $16.66.

That is not a parsing bug and it is not a hotel doing something clever. It is two different numbers from two different places in the same response. Google's displayed total is a formatted string with its value next to it — "$17", 17 — rounded to the whole dollar. The itemisation is a separate four-number array that is not rounded at all: 13.77 + 0 + 2.89 = 16.66. Round 16.66 to the nearest dollar and you get the headline back.

Fourteen rows in my sample landed this way, every one of them a sub-$20 stay where a 34-cent rounding step is 2% of the price. On a $300 stay the same rounding is invisible. That is exactly why this bug class survives: it only shows up at the bottom of the price range, where nobody is testing.

The useful part wasn't the rounding. It was that 13.77 + 0 + 2.89 is not how I had described the fields.

755 rows, one rule, no exceptions

So I pulled every hotel row from 35 production runs between 14 and 21 October 2026 — 757 rows across Ubud, Barcelona, Bali-wide, Bangkok, Singapore, Tokyo, Paris and Lisbon, in USD, EUR and GBP. 755 of them carried both a headline total and a full itemisation.

Two rules held in 755 of 755:

totalPrice        == priceBeforeTaxes + fees
totalWithTaxes    -  totalPrice        == taxes

Not "mostly". Not "within a tolerance that lets me claim mostly". Every row, every city, every currency, at a tolerance of one unit of currency or 0.6%, whichever was larger — the slack is there only to absorb the whole-dollar rounding described above.

Read that as plain English and it's a design decision, not an accident. Google's four-number array is [base, taxes, fees, total], and the price it prints on the card is base plus fees, with the tax slot left outside. Whatever Google files under fees is inside the number you see; whatever it files under taxes is not. I am not going to tell you which real-world charge landed in which slot, because Google ships two unlabelled integers and I would be guessing.

Which means the one field people build their spreadsheet on, totalPrice, is systematically short by whatever is sitting in taxes. Here is how much that is:

Destination Rows taxes as share of all-in, median Max Rows with zero tax
Ubud, Bali 552 9.9% 20.0% 41
Barcelona 158 17.6% 30.4% 1
Bali (wide) 10 16.7% 17.4% 0
Singapore 10 12.1% 16.6% 0
Tokyo 5 9.2% 20.0% 1
Paris 5 16.1% 25.9% 0
Lisbon 5 14.8% 15.8% 0
Bangkok 10 9.1% 15.0% 0

712 of 755 rows had a non-zero tax slot. 277 had non-zero fees, and 238 had both.

A fresh run this morning, 21 October 2026, two locations, five hotels each, to make sure none of this is a historical artifact: 10 rows out of 10 had the tax outside the headline. Casa Gràcia in Barcelona came back at $128 headline, $170.41 all-in — a 24.9% gap, which on three nights is most of an extra night. The same run had Pita Maha Resort in Ubud at $208 headline against $249.98.

What it does to a ranking

I expected the sort order to fall apart. It mostly doesn't, and the reason is boring: inside one city the tax rate is near-constant, so a near-constant multiplier barely reorders anything. Across 14 Ubud runs with 37–40 distinct hotels each, moving from headline-per-night to all-in-per-night flipped 0.3% to 3.8% of all hotel pairs, and the membership of the top 10 and the top 20 survived 26 of 28 checks.

The one place it does bite is the single row anybody actually looks at. In 9 of those 14 runs the cheapest hotel changed identity:

  • Cheapest by headline: Arjuna Homestay Ubud, $4.61/night — all-in $5.62
  • Cheapest all-in: Santun Homestay, $5.08/night headline — all-in $5.54

Arjuna is 9% cheaper on the card and 1.4% dearer to actually stay in. The same pair came back the same way on four separate days, which is what convinced me this is a tax-rate difference between two properties rather than noise.

Cross-city is where the whole thing breaks, and it breaks badly. Bangkok's median tax share is 9.1%; Barcelona's is 17.6%. Build a "cheapest city for three nights" chart on the headline price and you have quietly handed Barcelona an 8-point discount it does not get.

What I changed

My README said totalPrice includes taxes and fees. It doesn't — it includes fees and excludes taxes, in all 755 rows I can check. That sentence is being replaced, and the column note now says which slot is outside the headline, because the alternative is a buyer summing the wrong column and finding out from their accountant.

The fields themselves I left alone. The temptation was to make totalPrice the all-in number so the obvious column is the correct one. I didn't, for the same reason I ship Booking.com's unnamed charge codes as integers instead of guessing names: if the dataset says $208 and the Google page says $208, a buyer can check me in ten seconds. If my totalPrice says $249.98 and the page says $208, every cross-check fails and the honest number looks like a bug. The headline stays the headline. totalWithTaxes sits next to it.

So the honest total is a one-liner on your side:

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("<APIFY_TOKEN>")
run = client.actor("lergassy/google-hotels-scraper").call(run_input={
    "locations": ["Barcelona, Spain"],
    "checkIn": "2026-11-20",
    "checkOut": "2026-11-22",
    "adults": 2,
    "currency": "USD",
    "maxHotelsPerLocation": 40,
})

rows = [r for r in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items()
        if r.get("type") == "hotel" and r.get("totalWithTaxes") is not None]

for r in sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r["totalWithTaxes"]):
    headline, allin = r["totalPrice"], r["totalWithTaxes"]
    print(f'{r["name"][:34]:34} {headline:8} -> {allin:8.2f}'
          f'  ({(allin / headline - 1) * 100:+.1f}%)')

Note the is not None filter rather than an or fallback. Two rows in my 757 were priceless — Google listed the property and quoted no rate for the dates, so totalPrice, priceBeforeTaxes and totalWithTaxes all came back null together. I deliberately do not paper over that by copying one field into another. A null makes you decide what to do with a property Google won't price. A quietly copied number makes your average look fine and your worst row wrong.

The same logic in curl, if you'd rather not install a client:

curl -s -X POST \
  "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/lergassy~google-hotels-scraper/run-sync-get-dataset-items?token=$APIFY_TOKEN" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"locations":["Lisbon, Portugal"],"checkIn":"2026-11-20","checkOut":"2026-11-22","maxHotelsPerLocation":20}' \
| jq -r '.[] | select(.type=="hotel")
         | [.name, .totalPrice, .totalWithTaxes, (.taxes // 0)] | @tsv'

The scraper is Google Hotels Scraper if you want to reproduce the table above; the inputs in this post are the inputs I used.

When this is the wrong tool

Three cases where I'd tell you to look elsewhere.

You need the rate a specific hotel charges on its own site. Google's number is the cheapest offer it found across sellers for your dates, and the per-seller breakdown on the hotel page is quoted for Google's own default stay — roughly two weeks out — not the dates you asked for. The row stamps which dates those offers belong to, which is me admitting the limitation rather than hiding it, but it is still a limitation.

You need room-level detail. Bed type, cancellation policy, board basis, occupancy beyond adults-in-one-room: none of that is in the Google Hotels search response. Go to the seller.

You need a tax figure you can file. taxes and fees are Google's split for a display card. They are good enough to rank a market honestly and not good enough to be a line in a VAT return.

What they are good for is the thing I actually needed: knowing that the $128 on the card and the $170.41 you pay are both in the row, and knowing which one is which.

title: I Built a Small LLM From Scratch — Here’s What I Finally Understood About Transformer
description:
I used to understand Large Language Models mostly from the outside.

I knew terms like:

  • Transformer
  • Attention
  • Embeddings
  • Tokens
  • Fine-tuning
  • GPT
  • LLM

But knowing the terminology is very different from understanding what actually happens inside a model.

So instead of only reading about LLMs, I decided to build a small language model from scratch using PyTorch.

The goal wasn't to build the next ChatGPT.

The goal was much more important for me as a learner:

What I Built

The model starts with Shakespeare text and learns to predict the next character.

The basic pipeline is:

Text
  ↓
Character Tokenization
  ↓
Token Embeddings
  ↓
Transformer Blocks
  ↓
RMSNorm
  ↓
Grouped Query Attention + RoPE
  ↓
SwiGLU Feed Forward Network
  ↓
Final Normalization
  ↓
Language Model Head
  ↓
Next-token prediction

The model configuration I worked with was:

Vocabulary size:       65
Embedding dimension:   256
Transformer blocks:     4
Query heads:            8
KV heads:               2
SwiGLU hidden size:     680
Context length:         256

The important thing is that these aren't just names in a diagram. I implemented the pieces and followed the tensors through the model.

1. First Problem: How Does Text Become Numbers?

Neural networks don't understand strings directly.

So the first step was tokenization.

For this project, I used a character-level tokenizer.

For example:

"Hello"

can become something like:

[20, 43, 50, 50, 53]

The tokenizer maintains two mappings:

char_to_idx = {
    character: integer
}

idx_to_char = {
    integer: character
}

Then:

def encode(s):
    return [char_to_idx[c] for c in s]

def decode(ids):
    return "".join([idx_to_char[i] for i in ids])

The important lesson for me was simple:

Before a model can learn language, language has to become numerical data.

The training examples are created by shifting the sequence by one position.

For example:

Input:  To be o
Target: o be or

So the model is continuously learning:

Given previous characters → predict the next character

This turns one sequence of length N into N next-token prediction examples.

2. RMSNorm — A Simpler Way to Normalize Activations

One component I learned about was RMSNorm (Root Mean Square Normalization).

Traditional LayerNorm performs operations involving the mean and standard deviation.

RMSNorm simplifies this.

Conceptually:

x
 ↓
calculate RMS
 ↓
normalize x
 ↓
learnable scale

The implementation is roughly:

rms = torch.sqrt(
    x.pow(2).mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True) + eps
)

output = (x / rms) * weight

The interesting part is that RMSNorm only needs a learnable scale vector.

My takeaway:

Normalization isn't just a mathematical trick. It helps keep the values flowing through a deep network under control.

The material compares RMSNorm with LayerNorm and notes its use in modern architectures such as LLaMA, Mistral, and Gemma.

3. RoPE — How Does a Transformer Know Where a Token Is?

This was one of the concepts I found most interesting.

A transformer needs positional information.

One approach is to add positional embeddings.

RoPE — Rotary Positional Embeddings — takes a different approach.

Instead of simply adding a position vector, RoPE rotates the Query and Key vectors.

The important intuition is:

Position 3 → Position 5
distance = 2

Position 7 → Position 9
distance = 2

RoPE allows the attention mechanism to capture this kind of relative positional relationship.

At a high level:

Query + position
Key + position
       ↓
rotations
       ↓
attention

The rotation is applied to pairs of dimensions:

(d0, d1)
(d2, d3)
(d4, d5)
...

and each pair gets its own rotation frequency.

The biggest lesson I took from this:

Position isn't just “where is this token?” — attention can benefit from understanding how far apart tokens are.

4. GQA — Reducing Attention Memory

Next came Grouped Query Attention (GQA).

This was especially useful because it showed me that modern LLM architecture isn't only about making models bigger.

It's also about making them more efficient.

Instead of giving every Query head its own Key and Value heads, GQA allows multiple Query heads to share KV heads.

In my model:

Query heads = 8
KV heads    = 2

So four Query heads share each KV head.

Conceptually:

Q0 ─┐
Q1 ─┤
Q2 ─┤──→ K0, V0
Q3 ─┘

Q4 ─┐
Q5 ─┤
Q6 ─┤──→ K1, V1
Q7 ─┘

This significantly reduces the size of the KV cache.

The implementation first projects Q, K and V, reshapes them into heads, applies RoPE to Q and K, and then expands the KV heads to match the Query heads.

This taught me an important engineering lesson:

AI engineering isn't only about model accuracy. Memory usage and inference efficiency matter too.

5. Causal Attention — Why Can't the Model See the Future?

During training, the model shouldn't be allowed to cheat.

Suppose we're predicting:

The cat sat

When predicting the next token after "The", the model shouldn't be able to look at "cat".

That's why causal masking is used.

Conceptually:

       T0 T1 T2 T3

T0     ✓  ✗  ✗  ✗
T1     ✓  ✓  ✗  ✗
T2     ✓  ✓  ✓  ✗
T3     ✓  ✓  ✓  ✓

Each token can attend to itself and previous tokens, but not future tokens.

The attention computation looks roughly like:

scores = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) * scale

scores = scores.masked_fill(
    mask,
    float("-inf")
)

weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)

out = weights @ v

This made the phrase “next-token prediction” much more concrete for me.

6. SwiGLU — The Feed-Forward Part Isn't Just ReLU

Another component I implemented was SwiGLU.

A traditional feed-forward network can look like:

Input
  ↓
Linear
  ↓
ReLU
  ↓
Linear
  ↓
Output

SwiGLU introduces a gating mechanism.

It has two paths:

             ┌──→ SiLU ──┐
Input ───────┤            × ──→ Linear ──→ Output
             └──→ Up ────┘

The core operation is:

gate = F.silu(self.w_gate(x))
up = self.w_up(x)

output = self.w_down(gate * up)

The gate learns which information should be emphasized or suppressed.

The training material describes this as a gated dual-path feed-forward network, with SiLU on the gate path and element-wise multiplication controlling information flow.

7. Putting Everything Together

A transformer block in my implementation follows this pattern:

Input
  │
  ├── RMSNorm
  │
  ├── GQA + RoPE
  │
  └── Residual Add
          ↓
        x'
          │
          ├── RMSNorm
          │
          ├── SwiGLU
          │
          └── Residual Add
                 ↓
               Output

In code:

x = x + self.attention(
    self.attn_norm(x),
    rope_cos,
    rope_sin
)

x = x + self.ffn(
    self.ffn_norm(x)
)

This is a pre-norm + residual architecture.

The residual connection means the block learns a change to the existing representation instead of having to completely rebuild it at every layer.

8. The Complete Mini LLM

The complete model then becomes:

Character IDs
     ↓
Token Embedding
     ↓
Transformer Block × 4
     │
     ├── RMSNorm
     ├── GQA
     │    └── RoPE
     ├── Residual
     ├── RMSNorm
     ├── SwiGLU
     └── Residual
     ↓
Final RMSNorm
     ↓
Language Model Head
     ↓
Logits
     ↓
Softmax
     ↓
Next Character

The model uses weight tying between the token embedding and language-model head.

The complete architecture in the project uses 4 transformer blocks, 8 Query heads, 2 KV heads, and a 256-dimensional representation.

9. Training the Model

Once the architecture was ready, the next question was:

How does it actually learn?

The training loop follows the familiar deep-learning pattern:

Get batch
   ↓
Forward pass
   ↓
Calculate loss
   ↓
Zero gradients
   ↓
Backward pass
   ↓
Gradient clipping
   ↓
Optimizer step

The project used:

Batch size:      64
Learning rate:   3e-4
Optimizer:       AdamW
Training steps:  3000

The training code follows:

xb, yb = get_batch(...)

logits, loss = model(xb, yb)

optimizer.zero_grad()

loss.backward()

torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(
    model.parameters(),
    max_norm=1.0
)

optimizer.step()

Gradient clipping is used to reduce the risk of exploding gradients during training.

10. Training Loss vs Validation Loss

One thing I don't want to overlook when building ML models is evaluation.

A model getting better on training data doesn't automatically mean it's generalizing well.

So we can compare:

Training loss
      vs
Validation loss

A growing gap between them can be a signal of overfitting.

During evaluation, dropout is disabled and gradients aren't needed:

@torch.no_grad()
def estimate_loss():
    model.eval()
    ...
    model.train()

The training material uses the train/validation loss gap as an indicator for overfitting.

11. Finally: Generating Text

After training, the model can generate new text.

The process is autoregressive:

Prompt
  ↓
Model
  ↓
Predict next token
  ↓
Append token
  ↓
Model again
  ↓
Predict next token
  ↓
Repeat...

For example:

"ROMEO:"

gets encoded into token IDs.

The model predicts the next character, adds it to the sequence, and repeats the process.

The generation code takes the logits from the last position, converts them into probabilities using softmax, samples the next token, and appends it to the sequence.

12. Temperature Controls Randomness

Another concept that became much clearer after implementing generation was temperature.

Lower temperature:

More predictable
Less random

Higher temperature:

More diverse
More random

For example:

T = 0.3 → conservative
T = 0.8 → balanced
T = 1.5 → creative

So temperature doesn't make the model “smarter”.

It changes how we sample from its probability distribution.

What I Actually Learned From This Project

The biggest lesson wasn't memorizing what RMSNorm, RoPE, GQA and SwiGLU stand for.

It was understanding how the pieces connect.

Before this project, I could say:

“Transformers use attention.”

Now I can explain:

Text
 ↓
Tokens
 ↓
Embeddings
 ↓
Q / K / V
 ↓
RoPE
 ↓
Causal Attention
 ↓
GQA
 ↓
Residual Connection
 ↓
SwiGLU
 ↓
Repeated Transformer Blocks
 ↓
Logits
 ↓
Probability Distribution
 ↓
Next Token

That difference is important.

Knowing the vocabulary is not the same as understanding the system.

Why I Built This Instead of Only Using an LLM API

As someone preparing for an AI/ML engineering role, I think there is value in going one layer deeper.

Using:

response = client.chat(...)

is useful.

But understanding what happens underneath gives me a stronger foundation for:

  • debugging ML systems
  • reading research papers
  • understanding model architectures
  • optimizing inference
  • experimenting with transformers
  • explaining technical decisions during interviews

I don't expect a small Shakespeare model to qualify me for an LLM engineering role by itself.
