title: I built a browser for AI agents, then benchmarked it against Playwright MCP and browser-use
description:
Every agent I tried on the web had the same problem: it was reading too much. A browser tool hands the model a page snapshot, the model clicks, and then gets a fresh snapshot of the whole page again. Most of the tokens go on re-reading things that didn't change.

So I built AgentGo, a Chromium browser for Windows (Rust, on CEF) made to be driven by an agent over MCP. Then I measured it against the two tools most people use today.

The result

Same model (gpt-6-luna, medium reasoning), same 24 BrowserGym MiniWoB++ tasks, a fresh agent session for every task, only that browser's MCP tools, and the page's own reward decides.

Setup Solved Median time Input tokens Agent turns
AgentGo 0.1.5 22/24 32 s 94.7k 7.7
browser-use 0.13.11 19/24 92 s 209.9k 13.2
Playwright MCP 0.0.83 18/24 42 s 178.4k 13.0

About half the tokens, roughly half the turns, and the fastest median per task.

Why it uses fewer tokens

Three design choices do most of the work:

  1. A compact outline instead of a snapshot. browser_open returns headings plus the things you can act on, one per line, as [ref] role "name". The refs stay stable while the page changes.
  2. Only what changed. After browser_act, the reply is the diff: + for new elements, - for removed ones, ~ for changed values. The model doesn't re-read the page to find out whether its click worked.
  3. The browser waits, not the model. Each action waits for the page to settle before answering, so the agent doesn't spend turns calling "wait" and reading again.

It's also a real browser rather than a test harness: its own pointer and keyboard (so date pickers, sliders and key-listening widgets behave), the agent can have its own signed-in accounts, and payments or final submissions pause until the person approves them in the browser window.

What it got wrong

Two tasks beat every setup, AgentGo included:

  • form-sequence-2: the instruction never says to press Submit, and no agent did.
  • click-pie: every agent opened the pie menu and clicked the item, and the page didn't count the click.

And the limits of the test itself: one machine, one run per task and setup, one model. MiniWoB++ pages are small; a different model or another run will move single tasks. The full method, every task's result, and a separate check on 20 real websites are in the benchmark write-up.

GoMini

AgentGo also ships GoMini, a small model (322M parameters) that runs on your own GPU and takes routine steps, like filling the values you supplied, so the big model doesn't have to read every page. On 13 held-out task types it went from 15 to 39 of 65 subgoals between versions. It's still in development: with it on, AgentGo solved the same 22/24, at slightly more tokens.

Try it

  • AgentGo (Windows 11, free): https://github.com/Moha2005269/agentgo
  • Claude Code: /plugin install agentgo --marketplace Moha2005269/agentgo-mcp
  • Other MCP clients: the installer connects Claude Code, Codex or Droid, or run agentgo mcp. It's also on the official MCP Registry as io.github.Moha2005269/agentgo.

I built this solo. I'd love to hear what breaks, and which sites you want me to try next.

title: What If We Built a Stock Market That Had to Wait for You to Grow Up?
description:
Imagine opening an investment app on your eighteenth birthday.

Instead of confetti, it shows you a receipt.

Not just a balance. A record of every fee charged, every investment decision made on your behalf, every organization that benefited, and every risk someone accepted with money that belonged to you.

At the bottom, there is a button:

Ask why.

That is the product I want to explore.

Not a trading app with cartoon rockets. Not a leaderboard for wealthy children. Not a casino wearing a financial-literacy costume.

A financial system whose operators must eventually explain themselves to the person who was too young to question them.

Call it the Childhood Exchange.

This is a design proposal, not an existing product or legal blueprint. And its most interesting feature might be that it should barely resemble an exchange at all.

Giving a child a share is easy to imagine. Designing the relationship is harder.

Start with a simple thought experiment: every child receives a share in a company.

The immediate questions are financial:

What is it worth? Who holds it? Can it be sold? What happens if its value falls?

But a developer should see another set of questions:

Who controls the account? What does the interface encourage? What data gets collected? Whose interests does the recommendation engine serve? What happens when the child disagrees?

A share is an asset.

The software around it is a system of permissions, incentives, and power.

We can make the asset belong to the child while designing everything else around someone else’s objectives.

That is the problem worth building against.

Please do not build a brokerage app with smaller buttons

There is an obvious version of this product:

  • Colorful charts.
  • A friendly mascot.
  • Daily streaks.
  • Trading challenges.
  • Notifications announcing “opportunities.”
  • A leaderboard comparing returns.

It would be easy to pitch. It might even look educational.

But learning about markets and being encouraged to trade are not the same product.

The UK’s Financial Conduct Authority tested digital engagement features in an experiment involving more than 9,000 consumers. It found that features such as notifications and prize draws could increase trading frequency and risk-taking. That study was not about children, so it does not establish the effects on them. It does give designers a reason not to treat engagement mechanics as harmless decoration. fca.org

Here is the alternative design principle:

Make understanding easy. Make consequential financial action deliberate.

A child should be able to explore a concept without entering a transaction funnel.

Curiosity does not need a buy button.

The product needs two worlds—and a wall between them

I would separate the system into two environments.

The learning world

This is a simulation.

Users can investigate businesses, test assumptions, watch hypothetical portfolios change, and discover that a plausible story is not a guaranteed return.

They should be able to lose imaginary money without losing real money—or dignity.

No public wealth rankings. No rewards for being the most aggressive trader. No implication that winning a simulation proves investment skill.

The ownership world

This contains real assets.

It needs legally appropriate custody, clear authority boundaries, understandable disclosures, and a transition process that follows the rules of the relevant jurisdiction.

Adult-managed investment accounts for children already exist; US UGMA/UTMA custodial accounts are one example. Their existence means “children can own investments” is not, by itself, the innovation. fidelity

The innovation would have to be the quality of accountability around that ownership.

And there should be no automatic bridge from “excellent simulator score” to “permission to trade real assets.”

Learning achievement != financial authorization

That is not a minor UX detail.

It is a boundary the architecture should enforce.

The most important dashboard belongs to a future user

The child using the product today is not its only audience.

There is also the future adult who will inherit the consequences.

So I propose a requirement:

Every consequential action must be explainable to the account holder when they gain control.

Call it the Eighteen-Year Test—a memorable name, not a claim that control transfers at eighteen in every jurisdiction.

For each action, the system should help answer:

  • Who authorized this?
  • What authority did they have?
  • What information was available?
  • What did it cost?
  • Who received the payment?
  • What alternatives were considered?
  • What uncertainty remained?

Notice the difference between this and a performance chart.

A chart says what happened to the balance.

An accountability record helps explain what people did.

Those are different questions.

Build the receipt before the recommendation engine

Here is a conceptual event record:

type AccountDecision = {
  id: string;
  occurredAt: string;

  actor: {
    id: string;
    role: "guardian" | "authorized_manager" | "account_holder";
  };

  authorityReference: string;
  action: string;

  rationale: {
    plainLanguage: string;
    policyVersion: string;
    alternativesConsidered?: string[];
  };

  costs: Array<{
    amount: string;
    currency: string;
    recipient: string;
    reason: string;
  }>;

  disclosedConflicts: string[];
  evidenceReferences: string[];
};

This is not a production-ready financial schema.

It illustrates a product priority: the explanation is part of the transaction record, not a paragraph generated years later to make the decision sound reasonable.

Recording a rationale does not prove the decision was good.

But a system that cannot preserve who acted, under what authority, and at what cost cannot meaningfully promise accountability.

An audit trail also needs privacy boundaries. “Preserve evidence” must not become an excuse to retain every childhood interaction forever.

Keep what is necessary to explain the management of the assets. Do not turn the account into a permanent behavioral biography.

What would success look like if we refused to optimize for trading?

For this proposal, I would not make daily active use or transaction count the primary success metrics.

I would test measures such as:

  • Can users explain what they own?
  • Can they distinguish a simulated result from a real financial outcome?
  • Can they find the fees without assistance?
  • Can they identify who has authority over the account?
  • Can they challenge an error?
  • Does the eventual transfer of control work?
  • Can they leave without being manipulated into staying?

These metrics are less exciting than a growth chart.

They also tell us more about whether the product serves its stated purpose.

A teenager opening the app less often could be perfectly compatible with success.

The goal is not to make a child think about markets every day.

The goal is to help preserve options for the adult they will become.

Children should own assets. They should not become assets.

There is a boundary this idea must never cross.

We are discussing investments held for children.

We are not discussing shares in children.

No markets in their future earnings. No tradable claims on their potential. No public “talent valuations.” No investment thesis built around pressuring a child to become a particular kind of adult.

The distinction needs to survive the business model.

If the product becomes more profitable when children disclose more, compete more, or make more financial moves, we should examine that incentive before polishing the interface.

Good intentions are not an access-control policy.

They are not a revenue model, either.

A child must be allowed to reject the future we funded

Suppose a child receives an investment connected to a particular vision of progress.

They grow up.

Then they decide they want something else.

They do not want to work in that industry. They disagree with the company. They care more about a local river than a distant technological frontier.

Does the product still consider them a success?

It should.

An investment made for a child should expand their choices, not quietly assign them a mission.

The eventual account holder must be free to ask difficult questions, change direction, and—subject to the applicable rules—exit.

Gratitude should not be a condition of ownership.

The uncomfortable question: do we need an exchange at all?

Perhaps not.

An actual exchange would introduce questions this essay does not solve: who trades, how prices form, what liquidity exists, which assets qualify, and how the market is supervised.

Those are not implementation details to postpone until after launch.

If the objective is long-term ownership, education, and accountability, the better first product might be a protective layer around existing financial infrastructure.

That would make “Childhood Exchange” a provocative name for a design exercise—not necessarily the right company structure.

Before handling real assets, I would prototype three things:

  1. A clearly labeled simulator.
  2. An explanation interface using synthetic account histories.
  3. A transfer-of-control walkthrough.

Then test whether people understand them.

Not whether they click more.

Whether they understand.

The feature that matters most

Picture that eighteenth-birthday screen again.

The balance might be larger than expected. It might be smaller. No responsible interface should rewrite uncertainty as a promise.

But underneath the number is something the system can deliberately provide:

An intelligible record.

Here is what belonged to you.

Here is who managed it.

Here is what they charged.

Here is why they acted.

Here is how to challenge an error.

Here is what you control now.

That would not solve inequality. It would not make investing risk-free. It would not substitute for education, public institutions, or a livable world.

It would establish a narrower, demanding principle:

When we build systems for people who cannot yet fully question us, we should prepare to answer them later.

The best financial app for a child might not be the one that teaches them to behave like a trader.

It might be the one that forces the adults to behave like trustees.

title: How to Improve SaaS User On boarding Through Better UX Design
description:
For SaaS companies, acquiring new users is only half the challenge. The real challenge begins after someone creates an account. If users cannot understand the product, navigate its interface, or experience its value quickly, they may leave before becoming active customers.

This is where user onboarding becomes essential. A well-designed onboarding experience helps new users understand how a product works, complete important tasks, and discover the features that solve their problems. However, onboarding is not simply about adding tutorials or welcome screens. It requires a thoughtful UX design strategy that makes the product easier to understand and use.

By improving the onboarding experience, SaaS businesses can reduce friction, increase user activation, and build stronger customer relationships. Here are practical ways to improve SaaS user onboarding through better UX design.

Simplify the Signup and Registration Process

The onboarding journey starts before users enter the product. A complicated signup process can discourage potential customers before they have an opportunity to experience the product's benefits.

Many SaaS platforms request too much information during registration, including company details, job titles, phone numbers, team sizes, and billing information. While some of these details may be useful later, requiring everything upfront can create unnecessary friction.

A better approach is to make registration as simple as possible.

Consider these improvements:

  • Request only the information required to create an account.
  • Offer convenient signup options, such as Google authentication, when appropriate.
  • Use clear labels and helpful instructions for form fields.
  • Explain password requirements before users submit the form.
  • Display specific error messages instead of generic notifications.
  • Make optional fields clearly distinguishable from required ones.

For example, a project management SaaS platform may only need a user's name and email address to create an account. Information about team size, project type, and workflow preferences can be collected later when it becomes relevant.

The objective is to remove unnecessary barriers and help users reach the product as quickly as possible.

Help Users Experience Value Quickly

One of the most important principles of SaaS onboarding UX is reducing time-to-value. This refers to the time it takes for a new user to experience a meaningful benefit from a product.

Users generally sign up because they want to solve a specific problem. They may want to organize projects, automate repetitive tasks, analyze business data, or improve team collaboration. If they spend their first session navigating settings instead of solving that problem, they may question whether the product is worth their time.

To improve the experience, identify the product's activation point. This is the action or outcome that demonstrates the product's value to a new user.

For example:

  • A CRM platform might help users add their first contact and schedule a follow-up.
  • An analytics tool might guide users to connect their data and generate their first report.
  • A project management platform might help users create a project and assign their first task.
  • An AI writing tool might let users generate their first useful piece of content.

Design the onboarding flow around this first meaningful outcome. Remove unnecessary steps, provide useful defaults, and make the next action obvious.

When users experience value early, they have a clearer reason to continue exploring the product.

3. Use Guided Onboarding Instead of Long Product Tours

Traditional product tours often introduce users to multiple features through a series of pop-ups and tooltips. Although these tours can explain an interface, they may overwhelm users with information before they understand why it matters.

A user who has just registered for a SaaS product does not necessarily need to know where every button is located. They need to know how to complete their immediate task.

Contextual guidance offers a more practical alternative. Instead of explaining every feature at once, show relevant instructions when users encounter a particular action or challenge.

For example, when a user opens a dashboard for the first time, the interface could display a short explanation and a clear button to create a project. Once the project is created, the next instruction could explain how to invite teammates or assign tasks.

  • Effective guided onboarding should:
  • Focus on one meaningful task at a time.
  • Use short, understandable instructions.
  • Allow users to skip or dismiss optional guidance.
  • Avoid blocking important interface elements.
  • Provide additional help when users need it.

This approach allows users to learn by doing rather than memorizing a long list of instructions.

4. Design Clear and Helpful Empty States

Empty states are screens that appear when users have not yet created, imported, or received any content. Examples include an empty dashboard, a project list without projects, or a reporting interface without data.

For new SaaS users, these screens can create confusion. A blank interface does not explain what the product can do or how to get started.

Instead of treating empty states as unfinished screens, use them as onboarding opportunities.

A useful empty state should explain what belongs in the section, why it matters, and what users should do next.

For example, a project management dashboard could display the message:

"Your workspace is ready. Create your first project to organize tasks, set deadlines, and collaborate with your team."

A prominent button labeled "Create Your First Project" would give users a clear next step.

Sample data can also help users understand the product before importing their own information. An analytics platform, for instance, could provide a sample dashboard that demonstrates how reports will look once real data is connected.

The important thing is to ensure that sample content is clearly identified and easy to replace or remove.

5. Personalize the Onboarding Experience

Different users often have different goals, even when they use the same SaaS product.

A marketing manager may want to analyze campaign performance, while a sales manager may need to track leads and monitor team activity. Giving both users an identical onboarding experience may introduce unnecessary steps or irrelevant information.

Personalized onboarding helps users reach the features most relevant to their needs.

Start by collecting a small amount of useful information, such as the user's role, primary goal, or intended use case. Use those answers to recommend relevant workflows, templates, or features.

For example, a SaaS content platform could offer different starting points for content marketers, SEO specialists, and agency teams.

However, personalization should not become another source of friction. Avoid lengthy questionnaires that delay access to the product. Ask only questions that meaningfully improve the experience, and allow users to skip optional steps.

The goal is to make onboarding feel relevant without making it complicated.

6. Use Progress Indicators and Simple Onboarding Checklists

When users face several setup tasks, they may struggle to understand what remains or how much effort is required.

A well-designed onboarding checklist provides structure and makes progress visible. It can help users complete important actions without requiring them to remember every step.

For example, a SaaS platform might include these tasks:

  • Create a workspace.
  • Complete the first project.
  • Import existing data.
  • Invite a teammate.
  • Explore a recommended feature.

Keep the checklist focused on actions that help users experience the product's value. Avoid filling it with administrative tasks that do not directly contribute to activation.

Progress indicators can also help users understand how far they have progressed. However, a checklist should not become a mandatory sequence that prevents users from exploring the product independently.

Allow users to complete tasks in a flexible order when possible, automatically mark completed actions, and make the checklist easy to revisit.

A useful checklist reduces uncertainty and encourages users to continue.

7. Improve UX Writing and Interface Clarity

Even a visually attractive SaaS product can feel difficult to use when its interface contains unclear instructions, unfamiliar terminology, or ambiguous buttons.

UX writing plays an important role in making onboarding understandable. Every heading, label, instruction, and error message should help users understand what is happening and what they can do next.

Consider the difference between a vague button labeled "Continue" and a specific button labeled "Connect Your Data Source." The second option communicates the expected action more clearly.

  • Good onboarding copy should:
  • Use straightforward language instead of unnecessary technical terms.
  • Explain unfamiliar features in context.
  • Make button labels specific and action-oriented.
  • Provide helpful feedback after users complete a task.
  • Explain how to recover from errors.
  • Set realistic expectations about what happens next.

For example, if an integration fails, simply displaying "Something went wrong" leaves users without a clear path forward. A more useful message explains that the connection could not be completed and offers an option to retry or review the required permissions.

Clear communication reduces uncertainty and helps users build confidence in the product.

8. Make Onboarding Accessible Across Devices

SaaS users may access a product through desktop computers, tablets, or mobile devices. An onboarding flow that works well on a large screen may become frustrating when buttons are difficult to tap, text is too small, or forms require excessive scrolling.

Responsive design helps ensure that onboarding remains usable across different screen sizes.

Important considerations include:

  • Use readable text sizes and sufficient contrast.
  • Make interactive elements large enough to operate comfortably.
  • Ensure forms adapt to smaller screens.
  • Avoid relying exclusively on hover interactions.
  • Keep navigation and progress indicators easy to understand.
  • Test onboarding with keyboard navigation and assistive technologies.

Accessibility also benefits users who may be unfamiliar with the product or working in less-than-ideal conditions.

A consistent, accessible experience helps more people complete onboarding successfully, regardless of their device or abilities.

9. Provide Helpful Feedback at Every Important Step

Users need confirmation that their actions have worked. Without feedback, they may wonder whether a form was submitted, an integration connected, or a project was successfully created.

Good UX design communicates system status clearly and promptly.

For example, after a user creates their first project, display a confirmation message and take them directly to the new project. If an upload takes time, show a progress indicator. If a task fails, explain the problem and provide a recovery option.

Feedback should also acknowledge meaningful milestones. When users complete their first report or successfully launch their first workflow, a short confirmation can reinforce their progress.

Avoid excessive animations, intrusive pop-ups, or celebratory messages for trivial actions. Feedback should be useful, timely, and proportionate to the task.

These small interactions make the product feel more predictable and help users understand the results of their actions.

10. Measure Onboarding Performance and Improve Continuously

Improving onboarding requires more than making visual changes. SaaS teams need to understand how users behave, where they encounter difficulties, and which improvements produce meaningful results.

Start by defining an activation event that represents a valuable product outcome. Then track the journey from registration to that event.

Useful metrics include:

Signup-to-activation rate: The percentage of new users who complete the defined activation event.

Time-to-value: The time users need to experience the product's first meaningful benefit.

Onboarding completion rate: The percentage of users who complete the key steps in the onboarding flow.

Step-by-step drop-off rate: The percentage of users who leave or fail to progress at each stage.

Early retention: The percentage of newly activated users who return after a defined period.

Combine quantitative analytics with qualitative feedback. Session recordings, usability testing, support tickets, and user interviews can reveal why people abandon a particular step.

For example, analytics might show that many users stop during data integration. Usability testing could then reveal that the permission instructions are unclear. Addressing that specific problem is more useful than redesigning the entire onboarding flow without evidence.

Test improvements through controlled experiments when practical, and compare results against a reliable baseline. The goal is to create a continuous cycle of observation, testing, and refinement.

The Role of Professional UX Design in SaaS Onboarding

SaaS onboarding connects product design with business outcomes. It influences how quickly users understand a product, how confidently they navigate its interface, and whether they discover enough value to continue using it.

For SaaS companies, improving this experience often requires looking beyond individual screens. Signup forms, dashboards, empty states, contextual guidance, and activation workflows should work together as one coherent journey.

A product design partner can help identify usability problems, map user journeys, conduct research, and create interfaces that support real user goals. Teams exploring these improvements can learn more about wavespace, a product design studio working with SaaS and AI teams on digital product experiences.

The right design decisions should be based on user needs, product complexity, and measurable business objectives rather than visual trends alone.

Conclusion

Improving SaaS user onboarding through better UX design starts with understanding what new users need to accomplish and removing the obstacles that prevent them from reaching that goal.

Simplify registration, guide users toward their first meaningful outcome, use contextual instructions, improve empty states, and personalize the experience where it adds genuine value. Clear interface writing, accessible layouts, useful feedback, and ongoing performance measurement can further strengthen the journey.

Most importantly, treat onboarding as an ongoing part of product development rather than a one-time design task. As user expectations and product capabilities evolve, continue evaluating the experience and refining the areas that create friction.

When SaaS onboarding makes the product easier to understand and its value easier to experience, users have a stronger foundation for long-term engagement and adoption.

title: How to Build a 3-State Uptime Dashboard from Metrics and Logs (Internally)
description:
Short answer: poll recent health metrics and structured logs, reduce them to green, yellow, or red, and keep the raw evidence one click away. For a small healthtech team, the least complex useful version is an internal page backed by two direct queries. It should expose telemetry cost beside operational status, because a dashboard that hides its own cost is unfinished.

Choice Recovery fit Cost attribution Operating burden
Infrai Recent metrics, logs, and error groups behind one API Per-call cost, vendor, and latency metadata Polling and aggregation are yours
Datadog Specialist observability suite Dedicated product billing More platform surface to configure
Amazon CloudWatch Natural fit for AWS workloads AWS billing and log-ingestion accounting Strongest inside AWS
Grafana Cloud Flexible cross-source dashboards Separate hosted-service accounting More choices to own
Healthchecks.io Dead-man monitoring for jobs Separate specialist service Narrow complement for silent jobs

My recommendation is narrow: a team already consolidating backend calls should try Infrai for the recent-status query layer, because one key and one bill reduce credential and invoice glue, while per-call metadata gives the dashboard a direct cost-attribution trail. It is not a full incident-management system.

How should Node.js build an uptime dashboard from metrics and logs?

A checkout page needs a decision rule before it needs charts. I use three states because operators can act on them quickly:

  • Green: recent checks are healthy and there is no matching failure evidence.
  • Yellow: checks are degraded, stale, or mixed; an operator should inspect logs.
  • Red: the recent window shows a failed check, with logs available for triage.

This is deliberately modest. A 0/1 status signal says whether the checkout path worked. Structured logs explain which stage failed, such as eligibility, payment authorization, or order persistence. Error groups can connect an outage window to repeated exceptions for the same service. Do not pretend one signal answers all three questions.

For a healthtech checkout, keep sensitive payloads out of the status document. The UI needs a service name, timestamp, state, correlation identifier, and failure stage. It does not need a patient's name, order contents, or free-form clinical text. The available log interface also has no per-user deletion route, which makes it a poor home for data that may later need selective erasure.

The first trap is averaging. Ten successful checks can hide the one failure an operator cares about. Preserve the latest result and failure count separately, then define yellow and red from explicit product policy. Google's four golden signals are a useful check: errors and latency matter, but saturation and traffic can change how the same error rate should be read.

Keep it boring.

Three colors. Two evidence sources. One written policy.

Two criteria beat a feature checklist

The first criterion is recovery speed. Can an operator move from red status to a small set of relevant events without opening four consoles? Infrai puts recent metrics, logs, and error groups under the same key. Its public discovery surface describes 295 routes across 20 modules, including schemas and runnable TypeScript examples. That reduces client glue, but it does not remove the application work: there is no log subscription or batch export surface, so the admin page must poll direct queries and aggregate returned records itself.

The second criterion is cost attribution. Per-call metadata includes cost, vendor, latency, cache status, and request identity across the native API conventions. That is more actionable than a month-end total when a team wants to ask which internal screen or recovery loop generated spend. One wallet and one bill also remove invoice reconciliation across backend capabilities routed through the platform. I care about that more than a transient unit price. Prices move. Plumbing lingers.

There is a hard boundary. These limitations matter: retention and cold-storage configuration are limited, so this design is for recent operational visibility, not long-term compliance reporting. It also has no threshold, phone, SMS, or webhook notification route. The polling process below updates an internal view; it is not an on-call system. That trade-off is acceptable for an admin panel only when another system owns paging.

Implement the 3-state poller

The query filters for these surfaces are not declared in discovery, so the client must not guess parameters such as service, from, or window. Query the documented routes as exposed, then inspect the returned schema from discovery before adapting record extraction. This TypeScript program makes both authenticated calls, handles rate limiting, surfaces real error bodies, and prints a compact snapshot.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";

async function request(url: string, attempt: number): Promise<unknown> {
  const response = await fetch(url, {
    method: "GET",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
      Accept: "application/json",
    },
  });

  if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
      ? retryAfter * 1_000
      : 500 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
    return request(url, attempt + 1);
  }

  if (!response.ok) {
    const body = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`${response.status} ${response.statusText}: ${body}`);
  }
  return response.json();
}

async function queryMetrics(): Promise<unknown> {
  return request(`${baseUrl}/metrics/query`, 0);
}

async function searchLogs(): Promise<unknown> {
  return request(`${baseUrl}/logs/search`, 0);
}

const [metrics, logs] = await Promise.all([
  queryMetrics(),
  searchLogs(),
]);

console.log(JSON.stringify({
  checkedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
  service: "checkout",
  evidence: { metrics, logs },
}, null, 2));

Run it with Node.js 20 or newer so fetch is available.

INFRAI_API_KEY=ifr_your_key_here npx tsx checkout-status.ts

This stops before inventing a response shape. Once discovery confirms the current schemas, add a pure reducer that accepts normalized check records and returns one of the three states. Test it with fixed timestamps. Keep network code out of it. That split makes the red/yellow boundary reviewable and prevents a response change from silently rewriting operational policy.

Polling every few seconds by default is config bloat disguised as responsiveness. Choose the interval from the recovery objective and rate-limit budget. Record the last successful refresh separately; a stale green screen is not green. On 429, the example honors Retry-After when numeric and otherwise uses exponential backoff. A production process should add jitter if several replicas can poll together.

Where does each alternative win?

Choose Datadog when the team wants a specialist observability product, especially if managed alerting, tracing, or richer investigation workflows are requirements. Infrai exposes trace and span identifiers in logs but does not provide distributed trace queries or a span tree. It also has no source-map decoding, crash symbolication, or session replay. Those are decisive gaps for some teams.

Choose Sentry when checkout exceptions, source-mapped stack traces, and application-error investigation dominate the job. Its specialist focus is a better match than this lightweight query layer when developers need crash context rather than a small service-status view.

CloudWatch is the pragmatic runner-up for an AWS-centered checkout. Keeping telemetry beside the workload can simplify ownership, and its published pricing explains log ingestion as a billed dimension. The trade is tighter coupling to the AWS operating model. Compare the bill using your own retention and ingestion pattern; a generic price table will age badly.

Grafana Cloud makes sense when cross-source visualization is the product requirement. Its flexibility is useful when the team already speaks the Grafana ecosystem. For a three-state admin page, that flexibility can mean more configuration than the decision warrants. Benchmark time-to-first-use with your real schema, not a demo dataset.

Add Healthchecks.io when the failure is silence: a reconciliation task, export, or scheduled payment job never ran. Infrai has no synthetic probe or heartbeat monitor, so ordinary logs cannot prove that a task which emitted nothing was supposed to execute. This is a complement, not a duplicate.

The selection rule is blunt. Use direct queries for recent internal visibility and explicit cost attribution. Use a specialist when alert delivery, deep traces, long retention, compliance export, replay, or silent-job detection belongs in the acceptance criteria.

No single winner.

Ship the recovery path, not just the colors

A status page earns its place when red leads somewhere. Put the correlation identifier and a bounded evidence view beside the state. Link repeated failures to an error group after the query response has been normalized. Give operators a timestamp for both the source event and dashboard refresh.

Then test failure handling. Return a 429 from a local stub and verify backoff. Return a non-JSON 403 body and verify the error remains visible. Freeze time and verify a stale success becomes yellow. These cheap tests target the awkward paths dashboard demos skip.

I would benchmark three numbers before choosing a provider: minutes from empty directory to first authenticated response, lines of adapter code after normalization, and credentials the service must rotate. Those are evaluation criteria, not claimed measurements. They expose integration cost without pretending every team values the same features.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the internal uptime page guide and verify the live schemas before writing the reducer.

Further reading

  • Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems
  • Amazon CloudWatch pricing
  • Datadog documentation
  • Sentry documentation

title: Meet Harnis: the open-source platform for running AI agents safely across your company
description:
AI agents are finally useful enough to do real work: fix code, answer customers, update tickets, run internal tools. The hard part isn't getting an agent to act. It's letting it act inside a company: across teams and customers, on real systems, with someone accountable for every change and a bill that doesn't surprise anyone.

That's what Harnis is for. It's an open-source, self-hosted platform that gives every agent in your organization the same harness: isolation, approvals, sandboxing, budgets and an audit trail, so teams can ship agents quickly without rebuilding the safety layer every time.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/karawash-projects/harnis
  • PyPI: pip install harnis
  • Helm chart: oci://ghcr.io/karawash-projects/charts/harnis
  • License: Apache 2.0

Why a harness?

Every team that builds an agent ends up writing the same plumbing: who is this user, which customer's data can they see, should this action wait for a human, where does model-written code run, how much did that conversation cost, and who approved what. When each team writes it alone, you get ten slightly different answers and no single place to audit.

Harnis turns that plumbing into a platform. Agents plug in; the guarantees come with them.

Three products on one engine

Harnis ships three ready-to-use workloads, all running on the same orchestrator:

1. A coding agent for your developers. Point the CLI at a project and describe the change. The agent works on an isolated copy, shows a diff for every file it wants to write, asks before running any command, runs your tests in a sandbox, and applies the final result to your files only when you confirm.

harnis --workspace ./my-service "add input validation to the signup handler and a test for it"

2. Multi-agent workflows. A router on a small, fast model reads each message and hands it to the right specialist (a support agent, a coding agent, or your own). Agents can hand work to each other or escalate to a person. Add a new specialist with a few lines of plugin code.

3. A multi-tenant agent app. A full API with live streaming over WebSockets and a web console for every role:

  • Users chat with agents and see each proposed change, with diffs inline.
  • Reviewers work an approvals queue and see usage and analytics.
  • Admins manage agents and their prompt versions, API keys and the audit log.
  • Platform admins create and manage tenants.

What every agent gets for free

Customer data stays separated, by the database itself

Every tenant table uses Postgres row-level security, enabled and forced, and the app connects with a role that can't bypass it. The tenant always comes from the verified login or API key, never from the request. Even a query that forgets to filter by tenant can't return another customer's data.

A human approves the exact action

Writing files, running commands and installing packages pause the session until a reviewer approves. The approval is tied to a cryptographic hash of the exact action, so the agent can't get approval for one change and then make a different one. Approvals expire, and separation of duties can stop people approving their own sessions. Paused sessions live in the database, so a decision made hours later resumes the work on any server.

Model-written code runs in a disposable sandbox

Each command gets a fresh Docker container or Kubernetes Pod with no network, a read-only system, no Linux privileges, a non-root user and strict memory, CPU and process limits. gVisor is supported for an extra kernel boundary. Files coming back out are checked, so a model can't sneak a link to a host file into your project.

Need packages? An approved install goes through a proxy that only allows package registries, and it can only change a separate dependency folder, never your code.

Security that checks itself

On Kubernetes, Harnis doesn't just assume the network rules are in place. Before it copies anything into a sandbox Pod, it probes from inside the Pod and only proceeds once the network is confirmed blocked. If the cluster can't isolate the sandbox, the command is refused with a clear error rather than run unprotected.

Costs you can predict

  • Per-turn budgets for steps, tool calls, hand-offs and spend in USD.
  • Per-tenant cost caps.
  • A token and cost ledger per model.
  • A loop breaker: it spots an agent repeating itself, warns it, then hands the session to a person.
  • Confirmed prices: you confirm each model's price at setup, so cost figures and caps are based on real numbers.

Your models, your rules

  • Models: use Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini or Amazon Nova on Bedrock, or self-hosted ones through any OpenAI-compatible API (vLLM, Ollama, LM Studio, LiteLLM).
  • Failover: you set the order and Harnis fails over between providers automatically.
  • Data residency: each tenant has its own list of allowed providers, and failover never sends that tenant's data outside it.

Your login, your roles

  • Single sign-on: any OpenID Connect provider (Okta, Entra ID, Auth0, Keycloak, Google), with group-to-role mapping.
  • Roles: user, reviewer, tenant admin and platform admin.
  • API keys: service keys for CI and automation, with roles, expiry and instant revocation.

Your tools and agents

A plugin SDK lets you add tools, agents and even model providers that register exactly like the built-in ones. Internal APIs, ticketing systems and databases all become tools that inherit approvals, sandboxing and auditing automatically.

Built-in guardrails

  • Prompt injection: incoming messages are checked for injection attempts.
  • Card numbers: they're redacted before the model sees them.
  • Tool output: it's marked as untrusted data, so instructions hidden in a file or web page aren't treated as commands.
  • Semantic cache: repeated questions are answered from the cache, which is fast and costs nothing.

Ready for your auditors and your ops team

  • Audit log: append-only, exportable as JSON or NDJSON.
  • Monitoring: OpenTelemetry traces, Prometheus metrics and alert webhooks.
  • Data lifecycle: retention jobs, per-user data export and erasure, and backup and restore commands with verification.

Runs where you do

On a laptop, everything starts with Docker Compose on Windows, macOS or Linux. On Kubernetes, the Helm chart deploys:

  • the API, which scales out because sessions resume on any replica;
  • database migrations, run before each install or upgrade;
  • scheduled maintenance;
  • a separate, locked-down namespace for sandbox Pods.

Try it in five minutes, without an API key

The quick start uses a built-in mock model, so you can explore approvals, the sandbox and the loop breaker for free:

git clone https://github.com/karawash-projects/harnis.git
cd harnis
python tasks.py install
python tasks.py up              # Postgres, Redis, tracing, demo tenants
python tasks.py sandbox-image
python tasks.py dev             # http://127.0.0.1:8000

Open the console, click Continue as local developer, and type create calc.py. The coding agent proposes two files with diffs, waits for your approvals, then runs the tests in the sandbox. Try repeat: list the files to watch the loop breaker step in, or ignore all previous instructions to see the input guard. When you're ready, python tasks.py check runs a complete feature check against your instance.

Built to be tested

Each release passes:

  • a cross-platform test suite;
  • end-to-end checks against a running API;
  • an evaluation suite and red-team scenarios;
  • sandbox tests under gVisor;
  • a full Helm deployment on a Kubernetes cluster in CI.

The same feature-check script ships with Harnis, so you can verify your own deployment the way the project verifies its releases.

Get involved

Harnis 1.0 is out now, free under Apache 2.0, and provided as is. Star the repo, try it on a real workflow, and tell me what you'd build on it:

https://github.com/karawash-projects/harnis

Issues, ideas and pull requests are welcome.

title: Partner commissions on serverless Node and Postgres, with no server to run
description:
I run a small software company in Malaysia. We sell through referral partners and agents, and we pay them a share of what customers pay, not once, but for as long as the customer keeps paying.

That sounds simple until you try to do it. A customer pays on the 3rd. You promise the partner 25%, but only after a 30-day hold, in case the customer asks for a refund. In month 13 the rate drops to 20%. A refund arrives for half of one payment. The partner quits, and now you owe their unpaid commission to the house. Every one of those is a place where money can be wrong.

Of course, there are many existing tools in the market that does this out of the box, some even self-hosted. However, most tools that do this want their own server. A hosted CRM, or a self-hosted one with a Docker container, a background worker and a queue. We run on a serverless stack: Next.js functions on Vercel and one Postgres database. There is no machine of ours that stays switched on, and we felt like the cost vs benefit doesn't justify maintaining one just to pay partners.

Since we could not find a tool that did this and ran as a library inside our stack, we built one. It is called Tandem CRM, it is open source (MIT), and this post is about how it works and what I learned.

The idea: a CRM that is just a library and a schema

Tandem is an npm package plus a set of SQL migrations. You point it at a Postgres database you already have, and it adds a tandem schema with leads, agents, partners, commissions and payouts. There is no separate server and no container to run.

That is the part that matters for serverless. Each call is just a function that opens a database connection, does its work inside one transaction, and returns. Nothing holds state in memory between requests, so it does not care how many function instances you have or how often they start and stop. The state lives in Postgres, and Postgres is what keeps two requests from stepping on each other: the code locks the lead's row before it writes, so two payment webhooks arriving at the same moment cannot both win. Hold periods and releases are plain SQL, so a scheduled job (a cron route on Vercel works, and is how we do it) calls one function, release_due_commissions(), and that is the only background work there is.

npm install tandem-crm
npx tandem-crm init --database-url "$DATABASE_URL" --sample-data

init applies the migrations, runs a health check, and can seed a small demo workspace so you have something to look at.

Every payment gets its own commission line

Here is a lead being created and a payment being recorded. Everything goes through one shared writer, so the rules apply the same way whether the call comes from your app, a webhook or the admin screen.

import { defineTandemConfig } from "tandem-crm";
import { createTandemPool, withTandemSession, createLead, recordPayment } from "tandem-crm/db";

const pool = createTandemPool(process.env.DATABASE_URL);

const config = defineTandemConfig({
  commission: {
    holdDays: 30,
    rateSchedule: [
      { fromMonth: 0, basisPoints: 2500 },   // 25% for the first year
      { fromMonth: 12, basisPoints: 2000 },  // 20% after that
    ],
  },
});

const { leadId } = await withTandemSession(pool, ownerId, (client) =>
  createLead(client, {
    workspaceId,
    companyName: "Aman Logistics",
    contactPhone: "+60 12-345 6789",
    qualificationMetric: 8,
    productTag: "starter",
    partnerId: "rajesh",
    config,
    source: "signup",
    sourceEventId: "signup-1042",
  })
);

await withTandemSession(pool, ownerId, (client) =>
  recordPayment(client, {
    workspaceId,
    leadId,
    config,
    source: "stripe",
    payment: {
      paymentId: "inv_001",
      amountMinor: 30000,          // RM300.00, always whole sen
      currency: "MYR",
      confirmedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
    },
    partnerStatus: async (id) => ({ id, active: true }),
  })
);

Each payment produces one commission line with its own rate and its own 30-day hold. A scheduled job releases lines once they are due. If a refund comes in, the matching line is reduced or clawed back. If a partner is deactivated, their unpaid lines move to a house account. That policy is something you configure, not something we decide for you. We just decided to set ours up this way.

Why events

Tandem stores what happened, not just the current state. A lead is a stream of events: created, qualified, converted, paid, refunded. The current status is calculated by replaying them.

The practical benefit is that every decision is saved in the event it was made in. The rate that applied, the qualification result, who the beneficiary was. If you change your commission settings next year, old payments do not quietly change. And when a partner asks "why did I get this amount?", you can answer with the actual history.

Row-level security, so one tenant cannot read another

Tandem uses Postgres row-level security. Every query runs as a role called authenticated, and every row belongs to a workspace. Agents can only append three kinds of event (lead.lost, lead.stage_changed, conversion.confirmed). Anything that moves money needs an owner or admin, and the database enforces it, not just the application code.

The one setup step people trip on: the role you connect with must be able to grant authenticated. init explains this clearly if it cannot.

What two audits found

I am not a programmer by training, and I built this with quite a bit of help from AI and learning each step of the way (I make sure I understand at least fundamentally what the code is supposed to do). That is exactly why I did not want to trust it on my own. I had two independent audits run over the money code, and I wrote tests against a real Postgres instead of mocks.

The audits found real problems. A scheduled release job that could crash part way through. A case where a payment could silently produce no commission at all. Writes that were not safe if two requests arrived at the same moment. All of them are fixed, and each fix has a test that fails without it.

The rules we now follow for anything that touches money:

  • Money is integer minor units. No floating point anywhere.
  • Every write to a lead locks the lead row first, replays the history plus the new events, and only then inserts.
  • Retrying a request with the same source id returns the existing result and never creates a duplicate.
  • A fix needs a test that fails without it.

Where it is tested

The test suites run against real Postgres 14, 15, 16, 17 and 18 in CI, on Node 20 and 22, and also as a limited, non-superuser admin account, which is what most managed hosts give you. I have also run it by hand on Neon, Supabase, Layerbase and Aiven. Aiven needs its own certificate file, and the docs say how.

What it is not (yet)

It is early and pre-1.0, and it has not been proven at scale. It has run the partner commission ledger for our own product, Utuh, since 20 October 2026, and I checked it end to end on the live Stripe account, with a real card payment from an outside account and a real refund. No outside developers use the package yet, and we still pay partners by hand, by bank transfer. It is one Postgres and an append-only events table, which should be fine for small and medium use, but I have not load tested it.

Try it, and tell me what breaks

  • Repo: https://github.com/angkutdigital/tandem-crm
  • Docs: https://tandemcrm.dev

The most useful thing you can do is run it against your own Postgres host and open a "Postgres host report" issue, whether it worked or not. If a guide confused you, that is a bug in the guide, and I would like to know.

title: Phương Thức (Method) Trong Java
description:
Phương thức (method) trong Java là một khối mã được định nghĩa trong một lớp, có nhiệm vụ thực hiện một chức năng hoặc một loạt các chức năng cụ thể. Phương thức giúp chia nhỏ chương trình thành các phần nhỏ, dễ quản lý và có thể tái sử dụng. Trong Java, phương thức được chia thành hai loại:

Phương thức không trả về (Void Method)
Phương thức có trả về (Returning Method).

Ảnh mô tả hai phương thức chính trong java.

Khai báo và định nghĩa phương thức

Cấu trúc cơ bản của một phương thức trong Java:


Ví Dụ 
<từ_khóa_truy_câp> <kiểu_dữ_liệu> <tên_phương_thức>(tham_số) {

    // Thân phương thức - chứa các câu lệnh thực thi chức năng

}

Giải thích các thành phần:

↳ <từ_khóa_truy_câp>: Từ khóa truy cập cho phương thức (ví dụ: public, private, static).

↳ <kiểu_dữ_liệu>: Kiểu dữ liệu mà phương thức trả về (có thể là void nếu không trả về giá trị).

↳ <tên_phương_thức>: Tên của phương thức (phải tuân theo quy tắc đặt tên Java).

↳ (tham_số): Danh sách các tham số truyền vào phương thức (mỗi tham số có kiểu dữ liệu và tên).

↳ Thân phương thức: Chứa các câu lệnh thực thi chức năng của phương thức.

Quy ước đặt tên phương thức

↳ Sử dụng tên mô tả, thể hiện rõ ràng chức năng mà phương thức thực hiện.

↳ Tránh đặt tên quá dài hoặc quá ngắn.

↳ Sử dụng chữ thường cho các từ trong tên và viết hoa chữ cái đầu tiên của các từ tiếp theo.

↳ Tránh sử dụng các ký tự đặc biệt, dấu gạch dưới, không được sử dụng dấu cách trong tên.

↳ Sử dụng tên ngắn gọn cho các phương thức đơn giản, tên dài hơn cho các phương thức phức tạp.

↳ Sử dụng tên nhất quán cho các phương thức có chức năng tương tự.

Ⅰ. Phương thức không trả về (Void Method)

Phương thức không trả về là phương thức mà sau khi thực thi, nó không trả về bất kỳ giá trị nào. Kiểu dữ liệu của phương thức này được chỉ định là void. Không cần sử dụng từ khóa return trừ khi bạn muốn kết thúc phương thức sớm. Chức năng chính là thực hiện hành động, thay đổi trạng thái hoặc tương tác với người dùng.


Example.java 
public class Example {

    // Phương thức không trả về giá trị nào (void)

    public void printMessage(String message) {

        System.out.println("Tin Nhắn: " + message);

    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Example example = new Example();


    // Gọi phương thức printMessage
    example.printMessage("Xin Chào, Thế Giới!"); // Output: Tin Nhắn: Xin Chào, Thế Giới!
}




}

Kết quả của chương trình là: 

Tin Nhắn: Xin Chào, Thế Giới!

Trong ví dụ trên: Phương thức printMessage(String message) không trả về giá trị nào, do đó kiểu trả về của nó là void. Phương thức này chỉ thực hiện nhiệm vụ in ra thông điệp được truyền vào.

Ⅱ. Phương thức trả về (Returning Method)

Phương thức trả về là phương thức thực hiện một chức năng và có trả về giá trị sau khi thực thi.

Đặc điểm phương thức trả về

↳ Được khai báo với kiểu dữ liệu trả về (không phải void) sau tên phương thức.

↳ Sử dụng từ khóa return để trả về giá trị cho chương trình gọi.

↳ Giá trị trả về có thể được sử dụng trong các biểu thức hoặc gán cho biến.


Example.java 
public class Example {

    // Phương thức trả về giá trị kiểu int

    public int add(int a, int b) {

        return a + b;

    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Example example = new Example();


    // Gọi phương thức add và nhận giá trị trả về
    int sum = example.add(5, 3);
    System.out.println("Tổng: " + sum); // Output: Tổng: 8
}




}

Kết quả của chương trình là: 

Tổng: 8

Trong ví dụ trên: Phương thức add(int a, int b) trả về một giá trị kiểu int. Kết quả của phương thức add(5, 3) là 8, được trả về và lưu trữ trong biến Tổng.

Cách gọi phương thức trả về trong hàm Main

Nếu phương thức không được khai báo là static, bạn cần tạo một đối tượng của lớp chứa phương thức đó để gọi nó. Nếu phương thức được khai báo là static, bạn có thể gọi nó trực tiếp mà không cần tạo đối tượng của lớp. Để gọi một phương thức trong hàm main của Java, bạn cần thực hiện các bước sau:

↳ Khai báo và định nghĩa phương thức trong lớp của bạn.

↳ Tạo một đối tượng của lớp đó (nếu phương thức không phải là phương thức static).

↳ Gọi phương thức thông qua đối tượng (hoặc trực tiếp nếu là phương static).

Cú pháp phương thức trả về

Để gọi một phương thức trong hàm main, bạn sử dụng cú pháp sau:


Cú pháp 
<đối_tượng>.<tên_phương_thức>(<tham_số1_>, <tham_số_2>, ...);

Giải thích từng phần:

↳ <đối_tượng>: Là tham chiếu đến đối tượng của lớp mà phương thức thuộc về.

↳ Dấu chấm: Được sử dụng để phân biệt đối tượng và tên phương thức.

↳ <tên_phương_thức>: Là tên của phương thức cần gọi.

↳ (<tham_số_1>, <tham_số_2>, ...): Là danh sách các tham số truyền vào phương thức (nếu có).


Example.java 
public class Example {

    // Phương thức không tĩnh

    public void printMessage(String message) {

        System.out.println("Tin Nhắn: " + message);

    }

    // Phương thức trả về tổng của hai số nguyên

    public int add(int a, int b) {

        return a + b;

    }

       // Phương thức tĩnh

    public static void printMessage1(String message) {

        System.out.println("Tin Nhắn 1: " + message);

    }

    // Phương thức tĩnh trả về tổng của hai số nguyên

    public static int add1(int a, int b) {

        return a + b;

    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        // Tạo một đối tượng của lớp Example

        Example example = new Example();


    // Gọi phương thức printMessage thông qua đối tượng example
    example.printMessage("Xin Chào, Thế Giới!"); // Output: Tin Nhắn: Xin Chào, Thế Giới!
    // Gọi phương thức add thông qua đối tượng example và nhận kết quả
    int sum = example.add(5, 3);
    System.out.println("Tổng: " + sum); // Output: Tổng: 8

    // Gọi phương thức tĩnh printMessage trực tiếp
    printMessage1("Xin Chào, Phương Thức static!"); // Output: Tin Nhắn 1: Xin Chào, phương thức static!
    // Gọi phương thức tĩnh add trực tiếp và nhận kết quả
    int sum1 = add1(5, 3);
    System.out.println("Tổng 1: " + sum1); // Output: Tổng: 8
}




}

Kết quả của chương trình là: 

Tin Nhắn: Xin Chào, Thế Giới!

Tổng: 8

Tin Nhắn 1: Xin Chào, Phương Thức static!

Tổng 1: 8

Lưu ý:

↳ Chỉ có thể gọi các phương thức truy cập công khai (public) từ bên ngoài lớp.

↳ Kiểu dữ liệu và số lượng tham số truyền vào phương thức phải khớp với ↳ kiểu dữ liệu và số lượng tham số được khai báo trong định nghĩa phương thức.

↳ Giá trị trả về của phương thức có thể được sử dụng trong các biểu thức hoặc gán cho biến.

Sự khác biệt giữa phương thức trả về giá trị và phương thức không trả về giá trị

Đặc Điểm

Phương Thức Trả Về

Phương Thức Không Trả Về

Kiểu dữ liệu trả về

Có (không phải void)

Void

Từ khóa return

Sử dụng để trả về giá trị

Không sử dụng

Mục đích

Thực hiện chức năng và trả về giá trị

Thực hiện hành động, thay đổi trạng thái hoặc tương tác với người dùng

Ví dụ

getSum(), calculateArea()

printHello(), displayMessage()

Khi nào sử dụng

Sử dụng phương thức không trả về:

↳ Khi cần thực hiện hành động mà không cần trả về giá trị cụ thể.

↳ Khi cần thay đổi trạng thái của một đối tượng hoặc lớp.

↳ Khi cần hiển thị thông tin hoặc tương tác với người dùng.

Sử dụng phương thức trả về:

↳ Khi cần lấy kết quả sau khi thực thi một chức năng.

↳ Khi cần thực hiện tính toán và trả về giá trị cho các phép toán khác.

↳ Khi cần truy xuất dữ liệu từ một đối tượng hoặc lớp.

title: How to Connect AI Agents to Web Apps with Durable Action Receipts & Clean DOM Inspection: An MCP Browser Bridge
description:
How to Connect AI Agents to Web Apps with Durable Action Receipts & Clean DOM Inspection: An MCP Browser Bridge in Python

In 2026, autonomous AI agents (Claude Desktop, Cursor, OpenAI Codex, LangGraph) are routinely tasked with interacting with live web applications: filling checkout forms, retrieving invoices from SaaS portals, triggering CI/CD pipelines, and scraping protected dashboards.

However, developers building agentic workflows quickly run into three severe production bottlenecks:

  1. Context Window Exhaustion: Dumping raw HTML (often 1MB to 5MB with inline SVG, JSON hydration payloads, and telemetry scripts) exhausts the LLM's context window within 2 or 3 turns, driving token costs through the roof.
  2. Lack of Cryptographic Action Receipts: If an agent performs an irreversible transaction—like submitting a payment form or modifying permissions—there is no tamper-evident audit record proving what the DOM state was before and after the action.
  3. Zombie Memory Leaks: Unmanaged headless browser contexts stay resident in RAM when agents drop connections or fail unexpectedly, consuming gigabytes of host memory.

To solve this, we designed and built BrowserBridge: an enterprise Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in Python that transforms noisy web pages into compact, token-efficient Accessibility Object Models (AOM) (~95% token reduction), enforces strict session pooling with automated zombie-reaping, and seals every agent action with a cryptographic SHA-256 receipt.

🏗️ The System Architecture

Instead of having your LLM parse raw HTML or blindly dispatch click coordinates, BrowserBridge sits as an auditable MCP sidecar:

           +-----------------------------------------------+
           |       AI Agent / LLM (Claude, Cursor, Swarm)  |
           +-----------------------------------------------+
                                   |
                          (MCP JSON-RPC Tools)
                                   v
           +-----------------------------------------------+
           |          BrowserBridge Pro MCP Server         |
           +-----------------------------------------------+
              /                    |                    \
             v                     v                     v
   +-------------------+  +-------------------+  +-------------------+
   |  AOM DOM Filter   |  | Session Pool Mgr  |  |  Durable Receipts |
   |  (-95% token cost)|  | (Anti-Zombie TTL) |  |   (SQLite WAL)    |
   +-------------------+  +-------------------+  +-------------------+
             \                     |                     /
              +--------------------+--------------------+
                                   |
                                   v
                      +-------------------------+
                      |   Target Web App DOM    |
                      +-------------------------+

1. Slashing Token Bloat: The Accessibility Object Model (AOM)

Raw HTML is packed with tags irrelevant to an AI agent: <style>, <script>, <svg>, tracking pixels, and deep nesting. What an agent actually needs to know is:

  • What buttons exist?
  • What links can be followed?
  • What text fields require input?

Here is the Python implementation that converts messy HTML into structured, interactive @node elements:

import re
from typing import Dict, Any, List

def extract_accessibility_tree(html_content: str, form_state: Dict[str, str]) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
    aom_nodes = []
    node_counter = 1

    # 1. Extract Buttons
    for m in re.finditer(r"<button([^>]*)>(.*?)</button>", html_content, re.IGNORECASE | re.DOTALL):
        attrs, content = m.groups()
        text = re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", "", content).strip() or "Unnamed Button"
        aom_nodes.append({
            "id": f"@node-{node_counter}",
            "role": "button",
            "name": text[:50],
            "selector": f"button:contains('{text[:20]}')"
        })
        node_counter += 1

    # 2. Extract Links
    for m in re.finditer(r"<a\s+([^>]*href=[\"']([^\"']*)[\"'][^>]*)>(.*?)</a>", html_content, re.IGNORECASE | re.DOTALL):
        _, href, content = m.groups()
        text = re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", "", content).strip()
        if text and not href.startswith("javascript:"):
            aom_nodes.append({
                "id": f"@node-{node_counter}",
                "role": "link",
                "name": text[:50],
                "target_url": href,
                "selector": f"a[href='{href}']"
            })
            node_counter += 1

    # 3. Extract Text Input Fields
    for m in re.finditer(r"<input\s+([^>]*)/?>", html_content, re.IGNORECASE):
        attrs = m.group(1)
        name_m = re.search(r"name=[\"']([^\"']*)[\"']", attrs, re.IGNORECASE)
        type_m = re.search(r"type=[\"']([^\"']*)[\"']", attrs, re.IGNORECASE)
        name_val = name_m.group(1) if name_m else f"input_{node_counter}"
        type_val = type_m.group(1) if type_m else "text"

        aom_nodes.append({
            "id": f"@node-{node_counter}",
            "role": "textbox" if type_val in ("text", "email", "password", "search") else type_val,
            "name": name_val,
            "selector": f"input[name='{name_val}']",
            "current_value": form_state.get(name_val, "")
        })
        node_counter += 1

    return aom_nodes[:50]

By presenting the LLM with @node-1 (role: button, name: "Checkout") instead of 250 lines of tailwind divs, prompt tokens drop by ~95% while dramatically improving selector accuracy.

2. Cryptographic Durability: Action Receipts Engine

When an agent interacts with a web interface, proving what happened and when is critical for compliance and debugging.

BrowserBridge calculates a SHA-256 fingerprint of the DOM before the action (pre_state_hash) and immediately after execution (post_state_hash), persisting the transition to an atomic SQLite WAL ledger:

import uuid
import sqlite3
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from typing import Dict, Any

class DurableReceiptsEngine:
    def __init__(self, db_path: str = "receipts.db"):
        self.db_path = db_path
        self._init_db()

    def _init_db(self):
        with sqlite3.connect(self.db_path, isolation_level=None) as conn:
            conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;")
            conn.execute("""
                CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS action_receipts (
                    receipt_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
                    session_id TEXT NOT NULL,
                    action_type TEXT NOT NULL,
                    target TEXT NOT NULL,
                    payload TEXT,
                    pre_state_hash TEXT NOT NULL,
                    post_state_hash TEXT NOT NULL,
                    status TEXT DEFAULT 'success',
                    created_at TEXT NOT NULL
                );
            """)

    def issue_receipt(self, session_id: str, action_type: str, target: str,
                      pre_state_hash: str, post_state_hash: str,
                      payload: str = "") -> Dict[str, Any]:
        receipt_id = f"rcpt_{uuid.uuid4().hex[:12]}"
        now = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()

        with sqlite3.connect(self.db_path, isolation_level=None) as conn:
            conn.execute("""
                INSERT INTO action_receipts (
                    receipt_id, session_id, action_type, target, payload,
                    pre_state_hash, post_state_hash, status, created_at
                ) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, 'success', ?);
            """, (receipt_id, session_id, action_type, target, payload, pre_state_hash, post_state_hash, now))

        return {
            "receipt_id": receipt_id,
            "session_id": session_id,
            "action_type": action_type,
            "target": target,
            "pre_state_hash": pre_state_hash[:16],
            "post_state_hash": post_state_hash[:16],
            "timestamp": now
        }

Auditing State Continuity

Using verify_action_trail(session_id), you can verify that the sequence of actions has not been tampered with or skipped:

def verify_action_trail(self, session_id: str) -> bool:
    receipts = self.list_receipts(session_id)
    for i in range(len(receipts) - 1):
        if receipts[i]["post_state_hash"] != receipts[i + 1]["pre_state_hash"]:
            return False # Chain discontinuity detected!
    return True

3. Preventing Memory Leaks: The Anti-Zombie Session Pool

Headless browser automation easily leaks memory when agents abandon sessions mid-flight. BrowserBridge solves this with an automated session reaper:

from datetime import datetime, timezone, timedelta
from typing import Dict, List

class SessionPoolManager:
    def __init__(self, idle_ttl_seconds: int = 180):
        self.idle_ttl_seconds = idle_ttl_seconds
        self.sessions: Dict[str, BrowserSession] = {}

    def reap_zombies(self) -> List[str]:
        now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
        reaped = []
        for sid, sess in list(self.sessions.items()):
            last_active = datetime.fromisoformat(sess.last_active)
            if now - last_active > timedelta(seconds=self.idle_ttl_seconds):
                del self.sessions[sid]
                reaped.append(sid)
        return reaped

Whenever any session is requested, or on a periodic tick, sessions exceeding the inactivity window are safely terminated and removed from host memory.

4. Configuring with Claude Desktop or Cursor

BrowserBridge adheres to the standard Model Context Protocol (MCP) JSON-RPC specification. Adding it to Claude Desktop or Cursor is as simple as adding a snippet to claude_desktop_config.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "browserbridge": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["-m", "browserbridge.server"]
    }
  }
}

Now, your AI agent has direct access to:

  • navigate_page(url)
  • extract_clean_text()
  • extract_accessibility_tree()
  • click_element(selector)
  • fill_form_field(selector, value)
  • verify_action_trail(session_id)

🚀 Get Started: Open-Source & Enterprise

The full open-source BrowserBridge Lite is available immediately on GitHub with an MIT license:

👉 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/johannschiffer/browserbridge-mcp
