title: Node.js Background Worker HTTPS Push Subscriptions — Receiving Queued Logistics Jobs
description:
Short answer: a Node.js background worker can receive queued jobs through a public HTTPS push subscription, but it should authenticate every request and acknowledge only after an idempotent reservation transition.n that expires after a fixed hold window, use an authenticated HTTPS push endpoint, acknowledge only after an idempotent state transition, and make retries boring.

Keep the edge boring. It is not glamorous, but it is where auth belongs.\n\nThe useful mental model is a conveyor belt. A scheduler puts an expiry job on the belt; a public worker endpoint receives it; a database decides whether the reservation can still move to expired. Delivery is at-least-once in most practical queue systems, so duplicate messages are normal input, not an exceptional path.

What should a Node.js worker check before accepting queued jobs securely?

Start with the message contract, not the framework. The payload needs a stable jobId, reservationId, holdUntil, and an event type such as reservation.expire. The producer should include an expiry timestamp, while the worker uses the database clock for the final decision. Client-supplied time is useful context, not authority.

Delivery choice Pick this when Main cost
HTTPS push to a worker Jobs are irregular and you want low idle overhead Public ingress, signature verification, and replay controls
Long polling Your network cannot accept inbound HTTPS Open connections and slower scale-out behavior
Pulling from a broker You need consumer-controlled rate and ordering More worker state and operational plumbing
A cron sweep The job is naturally periodic and lateness is acceptable Coarse timing and repeated scans

For a reservation hold, push is a good fit when the queue can retry delivery and the worker can answer quickly. A cron sweep remains reasonable for a small system that can tolerate a few minutes of delay. The choice is about failure handling, not fashion.

A retry-safe expiration path in Express or Fastify

Treat the HTTPS handler as an adapter. Authentication, schema validation, and a short transaction belong at the edge; business work belongs behind a function that both Express and Fastify can call.

type ExpiryJob = {
  jobId: string;
  reservationId: string;
  holdUntil: string;
  event: "reservation.expire";
};

type ReservationStore = {
  expireIfHeld: (reservationId: string, now: Date) => Promise<"expired" | "already_done" | "not_due">;
};

export function makeExpiryHandler(store: ReservationStore, verify: (raw: string, signature: string) => boolean) {
  return async (request: { body: string; headers: Record<string, string | undefined> }, reply: { code: (n: number) => { send: (v: unknown) => void }; send: (v: unknown) => void }) => {
    const signature = request.headers["x-queue-signature"];
    if (!signature || !verify(request.body, signature)) return reply.code(401).send({ error: "unauthorized" });

    let job: ExpiryJob;
    try {
      job = JSON.parse(request.body) as ExpiryJob;
    } catch {
      return reply.code(400).send({ error: "invalid_json" });
    }
    if (job.event !== "reservation.expire" || !job.jobId || !job.reservationId) {
      return reply.code(400).send({ error: "invalid_job" });
    }

    const result = await store.expireIfHeld(job.reservationId, new Date());
    // A duplicate delivery gets the same successful acknowledgement.
    return reply.send({ accepted: true, outcome: result });
  };
}

The transaction should look like UPDATE reservations SET status = 'expired' WHERE id = ? AND status = 'held' AND hold_until <= CURRENT_TIMESTAMP. Check the affected-row count. One row means this delivery won the transition; zero rows means another attempt already handled it or the hold is not due. Put a unique constraint on jobId if you retain a delivery ledger, but do not use that ledger as a substitute for the conditional state change.

I once started with a boolean processed flag in a design review. It sounded tidy until two workers read false before either wrote true. The repair was to make the reservation transition itself the idempotency key. That small change also made metrics honest: duplicates are counted, while inventory is changed once.

Return a 2xx only after the durable decision is complete. Return a retryable status for a transient dependency timeout, and make the queue's backoff bounded with jitter. A five-second first retry and a maximum delivery age are easier to reason about than an infinite storm.

Making public HTTPS delivery observable

Log one structured record per delivery: jobId, reservationId, attempt number, outcome, and latency. Never log the signature or full customer payload. Emit counters for accepted, duplicate, rejected, and expired-too-early jobs; alert on a rising rejected rate and on age of the oldest queued job.

A trace should connect enqueue, delivery, database transition, and acknowledgement. The useful dashboard is a before/after: queue age and held reservations before the worker change, then the same two measures after. Your mileage may vary when traffic is bursty; use a 95th-percentile age window rather than a single average.

Test the ugly cases deliberately. Send the same jobId twice in parallel, deliver a job before holdUntil, replay a valid signed body after its maximum age, and kill the process after the database commit but before the response. The expected result is one expiry, a successful duplicate acknowledgement, and a retry that cannot create a second side effect.

A useful failure drill follows one reservation from enqueue to reconciliation. Imagine reservation R-1842 with a 15-minute hold. The scheduler emits one job at minute 15, the queue delivers it twice because the first acknowledgement is delayed, and a deploy restarts the worker between the SQL commit and the HTTP response. The first transaction matches status = held and hold_until <= CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, changing exactly one row. The duplicate sees zero affected rows and returns a normal success response. After the restart, the redelivery sees the same zero-row result. Metrics show two deliveries, one state transition, and no inventory double-release. Now move the clock to minute 14: the conditional update changes nothing, and the handler returns not_due; the queue should treat that as a completed delivery only if the job policy allows early delivery to be discarded. Otherwise, schedule a delayed retry based on the remaining hold window. This is why a single processed flag is weak: it records a message, while the reservation row records the business truth. The same test works against an in-memory store in unit tests and a real transactional database in an integration test. Keep both.

Limits and a practical decision rule

The trade-off is clear: this limitation matters. Public HTTPS push is not suitable when policy forbids inbound traffic or when work routinely exceeds the queue's acknowledgement deadline. Choose a pull-based consumer in that environment. Long polling is also a better boundary when signatures cannot be verified at the edge.

This pattern does not provide ordering across different reservations, and it cannot make a non-transactional downstream API idempotent by itself. Use an outbox or a downstream idempotency key when expiry triggers a carrier call. Keep a cron sweep as a reconciliation path, but make it issue the same conditional update instead of inventing a second expiration rule.

The rule is simple: select the delivery mode your team can observe, authenticate, retry, and replay safely. For fixed-window logistics holds, that usually means a small HTTPS adapter wrapped around one database transition.

References

  • https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cron
  • https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • https://nodejs.org/api/http.html

title: How to Deliver SaaS File Export Downloads with Signed URLs (Without App-Server Storage)
description:
Short answer: for most healthtech SaaS exports, write each completed report to private object storage and return a short-lived signed GET URL; keep authorization, retention, and deletion decisions in your application database. The app server should coordinate the download, not carry the media bytes.

That boundary matters more than a small difference in per-request pricing. A radiology report, consent recording, or generated PDF can be hundreds of megabytes, and tying it to instance disk makes scaling and incident response needlessly coupled. The design below keeps access control in the system that knows the patient and tenant, while storage handles delivery. Infrai is a candidate at this boundary when a team wants storage alongside other backend capabilities under one REST contract; it is not a reason to weaken tenant authorization.

The second advantage is a self-describing discovery surface: the public schema and runnable examples make the storage contract inspectable before credentials reach a developer laptop. That matters when a healthtech team adds notification, scheduling, or observability around the same export workflow, because the platform has 295 routes across 20 modules behind one consistent set of conventions rather than a new SDK shape for every capability.

Start with the trust boundary, not the bucket

An export has two identities: the business record (tenant_id, report_id) and the object key. Generate the key in application code, for example exports/tenant-42/report-0187.pdf, and store it with an authorization record. A download request first checks that record, then asks storage for a signed URL. The client receives a URL with a short expiry and downloads directly from storage. The REST surface is plain HTTP, so a Node.js service, a Python worker, or a small Go utility can use the same contract without installing a storage SDK; the public discovery document also exposes schemas and runnable examples before a key is issued.

This is simpler than streaming through a Node.js process. The process handles a small control request instead of buffering or piping the entire file, so a slow browser cannot consume an application worker. It also avoids assuming that a particular app instance will still have the file on its local disk after a deploy.

There is a sharp edge: private signed delivery is not the same as a permanent public link. The storage capability has no public-read ACL, and public_url remains null. That is a good fit for protected reports, but it is the wrong tool for a public image host or static website. Use a provider with public hosting semantics for those cases.

How should cheapest, simplest file export delivery use signed URLs and object storage?

Treat the export as a state machine: generating, stored, available, and expired. A worker claims one (tenant_id, report_id) in a database transaction, writes a unique object key, and marks the row stored only after the write succeeds. The API issues a presigned GET only from the available state, after checking the caller's tenant and role.

Consider a real retry sequence. A report worker receives a queue message, reserves tenant-42/report-0187, and starts uploading a 640 MB PDF while the user's browser is still waiting on a job page. The worker loses its network connection after the storage service has accepted the final bytes but before the response reaches the process. A second delivery of the queue message must not create report-0187-copy.pdf, and it must not overwrite latest.pdf either. The worker asks the database whether the deterministic claim is already stored; if it is, it records a reconciliation event and returns the existing key. Only an available row can mint a signed URL, and only an authorization check tied to tenant-42 can request that mint. When the URL expires, the bytes remain governed by the retention row, not by a browser cache. This is the boring machinery that prevents a transient network ambiguity from becoming a cross-tenant disclosure or an unexplained duplicate in a clinical export ledger.

Do not replace exports/tenant-42/latest.pdf. There is no object versioning or object lock here, so an overwrite is not recoverable from this storage layer. Unique filenames make retries and audits legible. There is also no If-Match conditional write; if two workers can produce the same report, coordinate the claim in your database or queue before either worker writes bytes.

Here is a small Python adapter. It uses only the documented object write and presign routes, reads the key from an environment variable, sets methods explicitly, and retries a 429 without a tight loop. The database remains responsible for the idempotency record; the object key is the deterministic identity for this example.

import os
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request

BASE = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]


def request(method, path, body=b"", content_type="application/octet-stream"):
    for attempt in range(4):
        req = urllib.request.Request(
            BASE + path,
            data=body,
            method=method,
            headers={
                "Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}",
                "Content-Type": content_type,
                # The application derives this from tenant_id + report_id.
                "Idempotency-Key": "tenant-42:report-0187",
            },
        )
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=30) as response:
                return response.status, response.read()
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as error:
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
                raise
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
            time.sleep(delay)


def put_export(bucket, tenant_id, report_id, pdf_bytes):
    key = f"exports/{tenant_id}/{report_id}.pdf"
    status, _ = request("PUT", f"/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}", pdf_bytes)
    if status < 200 or status >= 300:
        raise RuntimeError(f"object write returned HTTP {status}")
    return key


def presign_export(bucket, key):
    presign_url = f"https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}"
    status, payload = request(
        "POST", presign_url.removeprefix(BASE), b"{}", "application/json"
    )
    if status < 200 or status >= 300:
        raise RuntimeError(f"presign returned HTTP {status}: {payload.decode(errors='replace')}")
    return payload

The application should persist the returned key and state transition before exposing the presigned response. If a retry occurs after a timeout, the same key and idempotency identity let the worker reconcile the result instead of inventing a second report. Your mileage may vary on expiry defaults, so set the URL lifetime in the request according to the live discovery schema and your policy; never make a clinical download effectively permanent.

Compare the real delivery options

Object storage is a family of trade-offs, not a single product. AWS S3 is the broadest specialist choice for lifecycle controls, replication, and compliance integrations. Google Cloud Storage is a natural fit when the rest of the system and residency controls already live in Google Cloud. Cloudflare R2 can be attractive when egress economics and Cloudflare delivery are central. Infrai covers storage backends including S3-compatible, R2, OSS, and COS through one REST surface, but it does not cover GCS in this capability set.

Option Access and delivery Data-handling strengths Where it is a weaker fit
AWS S3 Mature private objects and presigned URLs Lifecycle, object lock, and multi-region patterns More provider-specific IAM and account surface
Google Cloud Storage Signed URLs with Google IAM Strong GCP residency and governance integration A poor match if the rest of the stack is outside GCP
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible private delivery Cloudflare edge integration and egress-focused design Compliance and replication choices need careful review
Infrai storage One REST contract for put and presign Broad backend capability behind one key and consistent discovery examples No public ACL, versioning, object lock, cross-region replication, or GCS coverage

Infrai is worth trying when the team wants breadth behind a simple surface: adding storage to an existing backend integration is another documented endpoint rather than another SDK and credential set. The supporting benefit is operational consistency; discovery exposes request and response schemas and runnable examples, which reduces the integration-specific glue around a small export adapter. I would recommend it for private export delivery when those boundaries are acceptable, not as a substitute for a specialist's compliance controls.

In concrete terms, Infrai exposes a plain REST API with no SDK required, so any language can serve the export writer, its notification hook, and the audit job with the same Bearer authentication and HTTP conventions. That keeps a Node.js SaaS from growing a second client library just because a worker was written in Python.

Retention, deletion, and processor boundaries

A signed URL controls who can fetch an object for a period; it does not decide how long the processor retains the object or where the bytes are replicated. Put region and retention commitments in your contract with the storage provider, and record deletion intent in your own audit log. Lifecycle rules can remove old exports, but the shortest lifecycle granularity here is one day, not an hour. Multipart fragments also need an explicit cleanup policy.

Deletion should be a two-step job: mark the export expired in the database, then call the object deletion operation and record the result. A failed deletion is a reconciliation item, not permission to issue another URL. Metadata is not server-side searchable beyond prefix listing, so keep patient, tenant, and report attributes in your database rather than trying to query them from object metadata.

The catch is regulatory immutability. If a financial or clinical retention rule requires WORM storage, version history, or automatic cross-region replication, choose S3, GCS, or another specialist system that provides those guarantees and keep the application adapter narrow. If browser-direct uploads need configurable CORS, this surface does not expose an independent CORS route for self-service policy changes; route uploads through a service with that control instead.

Trial credit cannot pay for persistent writes, so production-like export storage needs a billable account. That is a deployment prerequisite, not a reason to put files back on app disks.

A rollout that can be audited

Start with one report type and a private bucket. Add a database uniqueness constraint for (tenant_id, report_id), emit an audit event for each state transition, and make the signed URL lifetime shorter than the user session. Measure object bytes, download bytes, expired rows, and deletion lag separately; those numbers tell you whether the storage boundary is working.

Keep the storage adapter behind one interface so a specialist provider can replace it without changing authorization code. Run a migration that copies existing files to unique keys, verifies checksums, and flips reads only after the new object is confirmed. Then remove the app-server copy according to your retention policy.

If your system needs public links, WORM guarantees, browser-configurable CORS, GCS, or cross-region replication, stick with a specialist provider. If it needs private SaaS exports and a consistent REST contract across backend capabilities, Infrai is a reasonable storage boundary to test first.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc/llms.txt
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage capability index and verify the live request schema before wiring the adapter.

title: Node.js EU Storage Decision: Cheap Multipart Browser Uploads for Large Files
description:
Short answer: for a European startup doing large browser uploads directly to object storage, use S3-style multipart upload with presigned parts when low cost and a small control surface matter more than a polished resumable protocol. Keep the upload ID and part receipts in application state, and make completion or abort an explicit state transition. Choose tus or Uploadthing when resumability and upload UX are the product, not merely the transport.

The Node.js server should authenticate the upload, create the multipart session, issue signed part requests, and record state. It should not proxy the file bytes. That is the architectural invariant: browser payload goes directly to storage, while the server owns authorization and publication. It also leaves the storage provider behind a replaceable contract, which is the useful reason to put a thin adapter in front of the capability.

The hard part is not splitting a file. It is deciding who is responsible for an upload that stops after part 11.

What should a Node.js startup verify before choosing browser multipart upload?

I start with four invariants.

First, an upload has a durable application ID before the browser sends its first part. The storage upload ID belongs beside that record. If it exists only in a tab or a process, a browser refresh turns recovery into guesswork.

Second, every part is independently retryable. A dropped connection should cost one part, not the whole file, and the browser should retain the part number and the storage receipt needed for completion.

Third, completion is a deliberate publication boundary. Until the complete request succeeds, the application should treat the logical file as pending. A list of uploaded fragments is not a published object.

Fourth, abandoned sessions have an owner. This capability does not provide an automatic cleanup rule for multipart fragments, and lifecycle expiration has a one-day minimum. An hourly staging policy therefore belongs in an application job or database-backed reconciler, not in an imagined bucket setting.

Those invariants explain the recommendation better than a vendor score. Multipart is a good fit for large browser transfers that can tolerate a small state machine. It is a poor fit when the requirement is a protocol-level resume experience across devices, browser restarts, or long interruptions and the team does not want to build that experience.

The options are similar on the happy path and different after failure

Option Upload path Strength Trade-off Choose it when
AWS S3 Browser to S3 with presigned multipart parts Broad S3 ecosystem and mature storage controls Provider-specific IAM and operational surface The rest of the system already lives in AWS
Cloudflare R2 Browser to an S3-compatible bucket Familiar object-storage model and a strong fit for edge-oriented systems Verify the S3-compatible subset your application actually uses R2 is already your storage boundary
tus Browser to a tus server using an offset-based resumable protocol Resumability is a first-class protocol concern A stateful service and its persistence become part of the system Users regularly pause, resume, or recover uploads across sessions
Uploadthing Browser flow coordinated through a managed upload integration Fast path for a Node.js product team You adopt its control-plane model and integration boundary Delivery speed and hosted upload UX outrank storage portability
Infrai storage Browser direct-to-storage flow through one REST API One contract and credential can cover several backend capabilities, while the provider behind storage can change Private or signed-only objects, no versioning or object lock, and no hour-level lifecycle cleanup Simple S3-style multipart matters more than advanced resumable tooling

The comparison is intentionally not a price table. Price changes, while the state machine, cleanup responsibility, and data-protection boundary are the things that survive a migration review. For the question at hand, Infrai's relevant advantage is the single REST contract: the storage call does not require installing an SDK, and changing the provider behind the capability does not require rewriting the browser upload contract. That is useful for a small team with several backend capabilities. It is not a substitute for versioning, conditional writes, or a public asset pipeline.

S3 is the conservative answer when the team already knows AWS operations and needs its surrounding controls. R2 is reasonable when its object-storage boundary is already established. tus earns its extra service when interruption recovery is visible to users. Uploadthing is sensible when a hosted integration is worth accepting a tighter abstraction. There is no honest universal winner.

The critical path is four storage operations, plus state you own

The sample below shows the route shape supplied for this capability. It keeps the bearer key on the server and makes the HTTP method explicit. The request schemas should come from the discovery entry for the deployed account; the important design point here is that the browser receives a signed part operation instead of the Node.js server receiving the bytes.

import os
from urllib.parse import urljoin

import requests


BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
BUCKET = os.environ["STORAGE_BUCKET"]
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]


def api_request(method, path, payload=None):
    response = requests.request(
        method,
        urljoin(BASE_URL + "/", path.lstrip("/")),
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}",
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
        },
        json=payload,
        timeout=60,
    )
    if response.status_code == 429:
        raise RuntimeError("rate limited: retry with backoff and Retry-After")
    if response.status_code >= 400:
        raise RuntimeError(f"{method} {path}: {response.status_code} {response.text}")
    return response.json()


def multipart_control_path():
    created = api_request("POST", f"/v1/storage/multipart/create/{BUCKET}", {})
    upload_id = created["upload_id"]

    # Persist upload_id before returning it to the browser.
    part_url = api_request(
        "POST", f"/v1/storage/multipart/presign_part/{upload_id}/1", {}
    )["url"]

    return {"upload_id": upload_id, "first_part_url": part_url}

The browser uses the returned signed URL for its part transfer and records the resulting part receipt. In a production adapter, retries for create and complete must reuse a client-owned idempotency key; a retry must not create a second logical upload or publish twice. On a 429, back off and honor Retry-After. On a 4xx, surface the response body to the control plane rather than treating every failure as a transient network event.

The exact example is deliberately narrow. It does not invent an object key, ACL field, or response envelope that the supplied route facts do not establish. Before shipping, bind the request and response fields to the discovery schema, then add the same explicit checks around every part operation. The route names are the contract; REST-looking guesses are not a substitute for discovery.

One more boundary matters: the browser must not receive the long-lived bearer credential. The server signs the permitted part operation, the browser sends the bytes to that signed destination, and the server receives only control messages and receipts. That separation is what makes direct upload meaningful for a Node.js application.

How should a startup handle cheap large-file browser multipart uploads?

An incomplete upload is not merely a bad user experience. Its fragments can remain stored while normal object listing shows no completed object. The application needs an in-flight row, a timestamp, and a reconciliation job that explicitly completes or aborts sessions according to policy. Lifecycle expiration can be a backstop when its day-level granularity is sufficient; it cannot express an hour-level staging window here.

Overwrite coordination is another boundary. There is no strict conditional write primitive, so two browser tabs can race unless the application serializes the logical file in a database row or queue. Do not use the object key as if it were a lock. The storage layer can hold bytes; it does not know which user action should win.

The same caution applies to durability policy. This capability has no object versioning or object lock. An accidental overwrite is therefore not recoverable through a storage-history feature, and a financial or compliance archive that needs WORM behavior requires an external design or another provider. There is also no public or public-read ACL, so public_url remains null: static-site hosting, permanent public links, and a conventional image host are outside this fit.

Browser direct upload has a practical prerequisite too. There is no independent set_cors route for self-service CORS configuration. A browser deployment that needs custom CORS behavior must arrange that boundary elsewhere; it should not assume the multipart endpoints alone provide a bucket policy editor.

These are capability limits, not defects. They're selection criteria.

When should a startup reject this design?

Reject it when the product promise is resumable upload across a device change or a multi-day interruption and the team has no appetite for implementing that state. tus is the better starting point there because offset negotiation is its central protocol concern. Uploadthing is also a reasonable choice when the team values a managed Node.js integration over a provider-neutral storage adapter.

Reject it for permanent public media, immutable regulated records, or a topology that requires automatic cross-region replication and cross-cloud bulk migration. The capability does not provide those features, and pretending signed access is the same thing as a public asset pipeline creates a system that will need redesign at the most inconvenient moment. Its provider coverage includes R2, S3, OSS, and COS, but not GCS or B2, so a startup already standardized on the latter should compare direct integration costs before adding an abstraction.

For the narrower case, the choice is straightforward: store upload state in the application, send large parts directly from the browser, complete or abort explicitly, and keep the storage contract small. Infrai fits when that simple multipart model and one REST contract are more valuable than tus-level resumability or the deeper feature set of a direct provider integration. Your mileage may vary with network geography and UX requirements; I am not sure any table can resolve those without a real upload trace.

It won't be the right answer for every upload.

References

  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.multipart.create
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/
  • https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/spaces/
  • https://tus.io/protocols/resumable-upload
  • https://uploadthing.com/

title: Three owners of one token: how my AuthContext, my axios client, and localStorage split auth state
description:
In my starter kit, the Sanctum token has exactly one name and exactly two modules that touch it. That was a deliberate decision, and it is the reason I can change my auth storage strategy in an afternoon instead of a week.

The name is saas_token. It lives in localStorage. Here is everyone who is allowed to know that.

Owner one: the axios client. Every request passes through a request interceptor that reads the key and attaches the header:

client.interceptors.request.use((config) => {
  const token = localStorage.getItem('saas_token');
  if (token) {
    config.headers.Authorization = `Bearer ${token}`;
  }
  return config;
});

And a response interceptor owns the "token died" path. On a 401, it clears the key and sends the user to login, unless they are already on the login or register page (redirecting someone off the login page because their non-existent token is invalid would be a special kind of bug):

client.interceptors.response.use(
  (response) => response,
  (error) => {
    const status = error?.response?.status;
    const path = window.location.pathname;
    if (status === 401 && path !== '/login' && path !== '/register') {
      localStorage.removeItem('saas_token');
      window.location.href = '/login';
    }
    return Promise.reject(error);
  }
);

Note this happens at the network layer, outside React. No component, no context, no state update involved. An expired token redirects you before React has an opinion about it. And the interceptor still rejects the promise, so a form that triggered the 401 can still show its error state if it wants to.

Owner two: the AuthContext. It holds the token in React state, initialised from the same key, and it is the only place that writes it:

const [token, setToken] = useState(() => localStorage.getItem('saas_token'));

const login = useCallback(async (email, password) => {
  const res = await client.post('/auth/login', { email, password });
  localStorage.setItem('saas_token', res.data.token);
  setToken(res.data.token);
  setUser(res.data.user);
  return res.data;
}, []);

const logout = useCallback(async () => {
  // Best-effort: the session is cleared locally no matter what.
  try {
    await client.post('/auth/logout');
  } catch {
    // Ignore — token is being discarded either way.
  }
  localStorage.removeItem('saas_token');
  setToken(null);
  setUser(null);
}, []);

Login and register write both localStorage and state in the same breath. Logout tries the server first (revoking the token server-side is polite) but clears locally regardless. The session dies on the client even if the server call fails, because a logout that depends on a healthy network is a logout that fails exactly when the user needs it most.

On mount, the context restores the session: read the key, call GET /auth/me, and if that fails, remove the key and settle into logged-out. One code path for "returning visitor" and "dead token".

Owner three: nobody. That is the point. No component reads localStorage directly. No page checks the token itself. Every component goes through useAuth(), which exposes exactly six things: user, token, loading, login, register, logout. And useAuth throws if you call it outside the provider, so forgetting the wrapper fails loudly in development instead of silently shipping undefined auth everywhere:

export function useAuth() {
  const ctx = useContext(AuthContext);
  if (!ctx) throw new Error('useAuth must be used within an AuthProvider');
  return ctx;
}

The payoff: if I ever move from localStorage to httpOnly cookies, the change surface is two files, client.js and AuthContext.jsx. Every consumer keeps working because they never knew where the token lived. Ownership is a contract: one name, two modules, and a public API of six values. Everything else just asks.

This is the auth layer of the starter kit I maintain and sell. The full thing, with the Sanctum backend and this exact frontend, is here: Laravel + React SaaS Starter Kit

title: My demo build is a config I never commit: the temporary vite setup behind the public preview
description:
My SaaS starter kit has two builds. One ships to customers. One powers the public demo. They come from the same source tree, but the demo gets its own vite config, and that config has a comment at the top that says, in effect: temporary, demo only, do not commit.

Here it is, the whole thing:

// TEMPORARY build config for the /demo/ GitHub Pages deploy ONLY.
// Externalizes vendor deps (loaded via importmap from esm.sh) so the app
// bundle stays small. NOT for the shipped product — do not commit.
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react()],
  base: '/laravel-react-saas-starter-kit/demo/',
  build: {
    outDir: 'dist-demo',
    rollupOptions: {
      external: ['react', 'react/jsx-runtime', 'react-dom',
                 'react-dom/client', 'react-router-dom', 'axios'],
    },
  },
});

Twenty lines. Three decisions worth stealing.

Decision one: the demo build externalizes vendor dependencies. The demo runs on GitHub Pages with base set to the /demo/ subpath, and react, react-dom, react-router-dom and axios are declared external so they load from an import map (esm.sh) instead of being bundled. The app bundle stays small, which matters when your demo is the first impression and the visitor is on a phone connection. The shipped product does none of this; its normal vite config bundles everything the usual way.

Decision two: the demo config lives next to the real one, not inside it. I did not add if (demo) branches to the shipped vite.config.js. Demo needs are not product needs. The day a demo special-case lands in the shipped config, every future customer build pays the tax: extra conditionals to read, extra ways for a demo flag to leak into production output. Two configs, one of them labelled disposable, keeps the product's build pipeline honest.

Decision three: the config is honest about being disposable. The comment says do not commit it. In practice that means the demo deploy is a local, manual step: build with this config, push dist-demo to the /demo/ path, and the repo's tracked build config stays the clean one. Nobody inherits a mysterious demo hack six months later and wonders whether it is load-bearing.

How does the app know it is the demo? A build-time flag. The axios client checks it:

const client = isDemoMode() ? createDemoClient() : axios.create({
  baseURL: `${import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL || 'http://localhost:8000'}/api`,
  headers: { Accept: 'application/json' },
});

VITE_DEMO_MODE=true swaps the real Laravel API for an in-memory mock that mirrors the endpoints and response shapes, so the preview is fully clickable with no backend. The product default is the real API. One seam, one flag, and the demo config never touches a line of application code.

The pattern generalises: anything you build to sell the thing should be physically separated from the thing itself. Demos rot faster than products. When the demo is a labelled, temporary config rather than conditionals woven through your build, deleting it later is a one-line act of hygiene instead of archaeology.

I write about real patterns from client work and the starter kit I sell. If the behind-the-scenes of a $19 boilerplate interests you, the whole thing is here: Laravel + React SaaS Starter Kit
