title: What Android App Testers Actually See in a Google Play Closed Test
description:
When a closed test stalls, most of us debug it from Play Console. Tester count, release status, the Testers tab. If the number sits below what you expected, it's easy to assume people just didn't bother.

Often they did bother. They got stuck on a screen you never see as the developer, usually because of the wrong Google account or a step nobody told them about.

So this post is the tester's side of Google Play closed testing: what your Android app testers actually see, the four screens they go through, where each one breaks, and the message I now send before anyone taps the link.

TL;DR

  • Testers go through four screens: opt-in page, Play listing, install, private feedback.
  • Most "my testers aren't counting" bugs come from the wrong Google account or a Google Group nobody joined.
  • The rule is 12 testers opted in for 14 continuous days. Tell people that in plain words, more than once.
  • There's a copy-paste tester message near the end.

Step 0: check which Google account they're on

Google says a tester needs a Google Account or a Google Workspace account. What the docs don't spell out for testers is that it has to be the same account in two places.

  • The opt-in happens on a web page, under whatever account the browser is signed into.
  • The install happens in the Play Store app, under whatever account is active there.

If those differ, the tester has joined your test with one account and is trying to install with another. They'll often see the app as unavailable, and you'll see one fewer tester than you expected.

Two more things to check before anything else:

  • Google Group on the track? The tester has to join the group first, then opt in. Play Console's help says so, and it's a very common silent failure.
  • Opted in to your internal test before? They aren't eligible for the closed test until they opt out of internal. A user in internal testing only gets the internal version.

Screen 1: the opt-in page

This is the link from the Testers tab of your closed track. The tester opens it in a browser, sees a short explanation of what being a tester means, and taps a button to join. You can't opt in for them. Each person does it themselves.

Things that trip people up here:

  • The link isn't live yet. It only appears once the release is published, and right after the first publish it can take several hours to work. Sending it at midnight and expecting installs by 12:05 doesn't go well.
  • No feedback contact. The feedback email or URL you set on the Testers tab shows on this page. Leave it blank and testers have nowhere obvious to write.
  • Searching instead of tapping. After opting in, the page shows a link to the app on Google Play. Testers should tap it. A closed test app doesn't appear in Play search before you have a public release.


The tester's side of a closed test in five checkpoints, with the thing that most often breaks at each one.

Screen 2: your Play Store listing

From the opt-in page, the tester lands on your listing in the Play Store app. If everything lines up, there's a normal Install button. If there isn't, go back to Step 0 before you debug anything else.

One surprise for paid apps: closed testers have to buy them. Only internal testers get paid apps for free.

Screen 3: install and updates

The install comes straight from Google Play. No APK file, no other store. After that:

  • Their copy updates to your test version automatically.
  • Every new release on the closed track reaches them as a normal app update.
  • They don't have to opt in again.

Google also tells testers that some usage data, like device info and app usage, is shared with the developer during a test. That's why I check Android vitals and crash reports in Play Console every day of the test, not just at the end. Closed testing is still mobile app testing, even if the main goal is the 14 days.

Screen 4: private feedback

Testers can't leave public reviews on a test version. Instead, your Play Store page shows them a "Private feedback to developer" section with a Write feedback button. It asks for a star rating and a short note, and only you can read it.

On your side it lands in Play Console under Monitor and improve > Ratings and reviews > Testing feedback. You'll want a summary of it for the production access form later, so tell testers it exists. Most of them have never seen it.

The 14 days, from the tester's phone

The rule, from Google's Play Console Help page on testing requirements: personal developer accounts created after November 13, 2023 need at least 12 testers opted in continuously for at least 14 days before applying for production access.

  • A tester who opts out before 14 days doesn't count.
  • If they rejoin, their 14 days have to be consecutive again.

On the phone, leaving is one tap, and people do it while tidying up their apps. Google's own advice is to tell testers to stay opted in for at least 14 days, so say it plainly.

I also ask testers to keep the app installed. That's my own practice, not a Google rule: I haven't seen anything in the docs saying an uninstall ends the opt-in. But an app that isn't installed isn't being used, and Google can ask for more testing if engagement was low.


Four tester-side mistakes that quietly lower your opted-in count in Google Play closed testing, and the fix for each.

The message I send testers

Copy it, fill in the brackets, send it with the link:

Hi! Thanks for testing [App name] on Google Play. A few steps:

1. Use the same Google account on the link below AND in your Play Store app.
   (Play Store > tap your profile picture to check which one is active.)
2. [Only if you use a Google Group] Join this group first: [group link]
3. Open this link and tap the button to become a tester: [opt-in link]
4. Then tap the Google Play link on that page and install from there.
   Don't search for the app. It won't show up.
5. Please stay in the test for at least 14 days, and keep the app installed.
   If you leave early, Google doesn't count you.
6. Feedback: on the app's Play Store page, scroll to
   "Private feedback to developer" > Write feedback. Or email me at [email].

This week, could you try: [task 1], [task 2], [task 3]?

The tasks at the bottom matter more than they look. "Try the app" gets one session. "Create an account and add your first item" gets a session and usually a bug report.

Quick debug list when the count is low

Before you message anyone, run through this:

  1. Is the release on the closed track actually published?
  2. Does your opt-in link open for a fresh account?
  3. If you use a Google Group, are the missing people in it?
  4. Are any of them still opted in to internal testing?
  5. Did anyone install from a shared APK instead of from Play?
  6. Has anyone left and rejoined, restarting their 14 days?

If headcount is the real problem

The message fixes confusion. It doesn't fix headcount. If how to get 12 testers for 14 days is the part you're stuck on, that's what we built TestMyApps for.

We run 14 Google Play testers on physical Android phones for 16 days, so there's a buffer above Google's minimum. They join through your opt-in link, usually within 6 hours, and you get a production-access report at the end. Plans start from $15. If production access isn't approved, you get a free retest, and if that still isn't approved, a refund. We've tested 400+ apps with a 99.9% approval rate, but Google makes the call, so read that as a track record and not a promise.

Whichever way you find your testers, check the Google account question first. It saves more closed tests than anything else here. Details are on the 12 testers for 14 days page.

title: Designing Internal Service Status from Metrics and Logs (For AI Agent Loops)
description:
An uptime page for a media AI agent loop has a stricter constraint than a general monitoring console: an editor needs to know whether a publishing job can finish correctly, while an operator needs enough evidence to reconstruct why it did not. Displaying every metric and log line satisfies neither need. The right first version is a small, read-only projection built from bounded metrics, correlated terminal events, and an explicit freshness rule.

TL;DR: model the loop as a state machine, expose one aggregate snapshot to the internal admin UI, and keep raw logs behind drill-down links. Show availability, end-to-end latency, error ratio, and an estimated usage unit for each workflow class. Mark stale data as unknown rather than healthy. This preserves the distinction between service reachability and completed editorial work, which is where many simple status pages become misleading.

How should a Node.js uptime dashboard combine metrics and logs?

A media workflow may accept a story brief, retrieve background material, call one or more models, run a policy check, and persist a draft. A process-level health check can succeed while that sequence repeatedly times out or produces no publishable result. For an internal page, the unit of health should therefore be the completed workflow, not the HTTP process.

Start with four questions derived from the latency, traffic, errors, and saturation signals described in the Google SRE monitoring chapter: are workflows finishing, how long do they take, how much work is arriving, and is a constrained dependency accumulating pressure? The dashboard can present those questions without pretending that one green badge captures them all.

For each workflow class, such as article-draft or caption-rewrite, define a terminal success event and a terminal failure event. Require both to carry the same opaque run identifier, policy version, and workflow class. The identifier is the audit key. It also makes retries visible: a retry is another attempt attached to the same logical run, not a second successful publication.

Exactly-once processing is not something a dashboard can confer on the underlying pipeline. Its projection can still adopt an exactly-once mindset. Deduplicate terminal events by (run_id, attempt_id, terminal_state), reject contradictory duplicates from the aggregate, and retain enough evidence for reconciliation. If a success counter says 100 while the terminal-event ledger contains 99 unique successful runs, the page should report an integrity discrepancy instead of averaging the disagreement away.

Retries lie.

Unknown matters.

A snapshot older than the agreed collection interval is not evidence of availability. It is unknown, with its observation timestamp shown plainly. That single rule prevents a frozen collector from leaving a reassuring green panel on screen.

Derive the projection before choosing storage

The status view needs a compact contract. The example below uses a 5-minute window for fast operational feedback and a 24-hour window for context; those are example policy choices, not universal thresholds. The response separates observed values from decisions so a later threshold change does not rewrite history. A Node.js admin application can consume the same JSON contract even when the aggregation worker is written in another language.

package status

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "net/http"
    "time"
)

type Window struct {
    DurationSeconds int64   `json:"duration_seconds"`
    Completed       uint64  `json:"completed"`
    Failed          uint64  `json:"failed"`
    P95LatencyMs    float64 `json:"p95_latency_ms"`
    UsageUnits      float64 `json:"usage_units"`
}

type Snapshot struct {
    Workflow      string    `json:"workflow"`
    Status        string    `json:"status"`
    ObservedAt    time.Time `json:"observed_at"`
    FreshUntil    time.Time `json:"fresh_until"`
    Recent        Window    `json:"recent"`
    Daily         Window    `json:"daily"`
    IntegrityGaps uint64    `json:"integrity_gaps"`
}

type SnapshotReader interface {
    Read(r *http.Request) (Snapshot, error)
}

func Handler(reader SnapshotReader, now func() time.Time) http.Handler {
    return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        snapshot, err := reader.Read(r)
        if err != nil {
            http.Error(w, "status snapshot unavailable", http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
            return
        }
        if now().After(snapshot.FreshUntil) {
            snapshot.Status = "unknown"
        }
        w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        w.Header().Set("Cache-Control", "no-store")
        if err := json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(snapshot); err != nil {
            return
        }
    })
}

UsageUnits should use the stable unit the pipeline actually records, not a currency estimate silently mixed across model contracts. Currency conversion belongs in a separately versioned rule with its effective time and source. This is the same discipline a ledger projection needs: preserve the immutable observation, then apply a reviewable interpretation.

The aggregate store may be a relational table, a time-series database, or an in-memory cache backed by durable events. The status contract does not depend on that choice. What does matter is atomic publication: calculate a complete snapshot off to the side, validate its counts and timestamps, then replace the visible version in one operation. Readers should never see the five-minute latency from one calculation paired with the daily failure count from another.

This design has a clear limitation: a precomputed projection favors predictable reads and auditable states over open-ended exploration. It is not suitable as a replacement for a metrics explorer or restricted log-search system. The trade-off is deliberate because an incident-facing status page must remain cheap to read and easy to reconcile, while deeper diagnosis can tolerate a separate, slower path with tighter access controls.

Join metrics and logs without turning the page into a log viewer

Metrics answer trend questions efficiently. Logs explain individual runs. Joining them on the page is useful only if the join is deliberate: an aggregate row links to a filtered set of terminal events for the same workflow and time window, and an individual run links to its attempts. Do not ship raw prompts, generated copy, credentials, or personal data into a broad admin view. Retention and access must follow the organization's compliance policy, and access to the status page should itself leave an audit record.

The useful event is small. A terminal record needs the run and attempt identifiers, workflow class, terminal state, start and finish timestamps, policy version, usage unit, and a bounded error category. Free-form error text belongs in restricted logs, not in a label or aggregate key. Unbounded labels create noise and make the metric series harder to reason about.

This division also controls ingestion volume. Log services commonly charge according to ingestion volume; the CloudWatch pricing page, for example, documents per-GB log ingestion dimensions. The architectural response is not to make price the main criterion. It is to emit fewer, higher-value events, keep high-cardinality evidence out of metrics, and choose retention according to investigation and compliance needs.

A compact admin table can then carry the information operators actually compare:

Workflow State Last observed 5m completions 5m failures p95 latency Integrity gaps
Article draft Healthy 14:05 UTC 82 1 18,400 ms 0
Caption rewrite Unknown 13:54 UTC 0 0 - 0
Policy review Degraded 14:05 UTC 77 9 6,200 ms 2

These values are illustrative data, not benchmark claims. Notice that zero traffic is not automatically an outage, and stale observation is not converted into zero. The integrity column also remains separate from runtime failure: a workflow may finish while its evidence trail is incomplete.

Set decisions that resist alert noise

A dashboard and an alert have different jobs. The page can show every supported workflow class; a page-worthy alert should represent an actionable breach sustained for a defined window. One failed run may deserve a visible count and a drill-down link without waking anyone. Conversely, an integrity gap may require immediate investigation even while the completion ratio looks normal.

Use a decision table owned in version control. For example, a team might classify a workflow as degraded when its error ratio breaches a reviewed threshold in two consecutive five-minute windows, or when its p95 latency exceeds a workflow-specific objective with enough completed samples to make the percentile meaningful. The exact threshold must come from the service objective and traffic profile. No source can supply it generically.

Three distinctions keep the signal honest:

  1. Separate unknown from healthy; missing telemetry cannot prove success.
  2. Separate logical runs from attempts; retries must not inflate throughput or erase the original failure.
  3. Separate operational errors from audit-integrity gaps; each has a different owner and response.

Test those rules with deterministic fixtures before testing the HTML. Feed the projector duplicate terminal events, late arrivals, a retry that succeeds, contradictory terminal states, an empty window, and a snapshot beyond fresh_until. Assert both the aggregate and the retained reconciliation record. Then load-test the read path independently, because an internal page that runs expensive ad hoc log queries can compete with the collection path during the incident it is meant to explain.

Roll out the view without losing audit continuity

Begin in shadow mode. Produce snapshots, compare their completed and failed counts with the terminal-event ledger, and publish the discrepancies only to the implementation team. Once reconciliation remains within the team's explicit acceptance rule, expose the page read-only to operators; alerting can follow after the display has earned trust.

During migration, version the snapshot schema and keep the prior projector available until consumers have moved. Deploy decision-rule changes with an effective timestamp, record who approved them, and annotate the page when a rule changes. A latency graph that crosses a newly changed threshold is then explainable rather than mysterious.

The final acceptance test is intentionally plain: given a run identifier, an operator can trace every attempt to one terminal outcome, reproduce the aggregate row for its window, and explain the displayed state from a versioned rule. If any link is missing, the page is decoration, not an operational control.

Sources

  • Google SRE Book, "Monitoring Distributed Systems": https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/
  • Amazon CloudWatch pricing: https://aws.amazon.com/cloudwatch/pricing/

title: Node.js Broadcast Polls: Aggregate Votes into a Reconnect-Safe Interval Tally
description:
Short answer: keep vote ingestion separate from interval publication, assign every published tally a monotonic revision, and let a reconnecting viewer request the newest snapshot after the last revision it applied. For a live media poll, the least complex dependable design is one authoritative aggregator per poll, a durable vote log or database behind it, and disposable realtime connections in front of it. The five-second ticker is presentation cadence, not correctness.

The page that should fire is tally_revision_stalled, scoped to one poll and accompanied by the last accepted vote position, the last published revision, connected viewers, and publish age. The on-call does not need a bright chart saying connections are down 8%. They need to know whether votes are still being accepted while viewers are seeing an old result, because that is the split-brain experience an audience will notice during a broadcast.

This design also answers the Node.js implementation question without tying correctness to an Express process timer. Express can validate and accept a vote; a serialized poll worker owns aggregation; a scheduler asks that worker to publish; and the transport delivers a versioned snapshot. If a process restarts or a viewer reconnects, both resume from durable positions instead of guessing what happened during the gap.

What should page the on-call?

Imagine the alert arriving with only WebSocket disconnect rate high. That signal is noisy by construction: mobile viewers roam between networks, laptops sleep, and browsers close. A disconnect is an event, not yet an incident. The actionable failure is narrower: accepted votes have advanced beyond the input position represented by the most recent published tally, and that gap has remained open longer than the promised publication interval plus a small scheduling allowance.

The alert payload should make the failure legible without dashboard archaeology:

  • poll and broadcast identifiers
  • latest durable vote position
  • input position included in the latest tally
  • tally revision and publication timestamp
  • worker lease owner, if ownership is leased
  • publish attempts and delivery failures

Ask one blunt question: what page fired? If the answer is merely CPU, open connections, or queue depth, the team still has to infer user impact. Page on a sustained publication lag while votes are arriving. Ticket or graph the rest.

The earlier signal is accepted_position - published_position, measured per poll. Publication age alone cannot distinguish a quiet poll from a stuck worker. Vote throughput alone cannot show that viewers are stale. The position gap joins the two sides of the contract, so it should fire before audience reports arrive.

How should Node.js aggregate votes and publish each interval tally?

A vote command needs a stable identifier, poll identifier, selected option, and an authoritative position assigned when the command becomes durable. Reject choices outside the poll definition before appending. Deduplicate by the stable vote identifier according to the product's voting rule; a rule allowing one active choice per account requires an identity and replacement policy, while an anonymous multiple-choice poll has a different state transition. Do not pretend those policies are interchangeable.

The aggregator consumes commands in position order and produces a complete snapshot. A snapshot carries the poll identifier, counts, the highest included input position, and a monotonic tally revision. Complete snapshots cost more bytes than deltas, but they make reconnect recovery bounded: the client can replace local state after verifying that the revision is newer. Deltas demand gap detection and replay, and one lost increment can poison every later display. For a small option set, the snapshot trade-off is easier to operate.

That is the invariant.

The state transition below is Go because the important part is ownership and revision, not a framework API. A Node.js service should preserve the same single-writer semantics through one queue partition, a database transaction, or another explicit serialization boundary.

package tally

import (
    "errors"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type Vote struct {
    ID       string
    Option   string
    Position uint64
}

type Snapshot struct {
    PollID           string         `json:"pollId"`
    Revision         uint64         `json:"revision"`
    IncludedPosition uint64         `json:"includedPosition"`
    PublishedAt      time.Time      `json:"publishedAt"`
    Counts           map[string]int `json:"counts"`
}

type Aggregator struct {
    mu       sync.Mutex
    pollID   string
    allowed  map[string]bool
    seen     map[string]bool
    counts   map[string]int
    position uint64
    revision uint64
}

func (a *Aggregator) Apply(v Vote) error {
    a.mu.Lock()
    defer a.mu.Unlock()

    if !a.allowed[v.Option] {
        return errors.New("unknown poll option")
    }
    if a.seen[v.ID] {
        return nil
    }
    if v.Position <= a.position {
        return errors.New("non-monotonic input position")
    }
    a.seen[v.ID] = true
    a.counts[v.Option]++
    a.position = v.Position
    return nil
}

func (a *Aggregator) Publish(now time.Time) Snapshot {
    a.mu.Lock()
    defer a.mu.Unlock()

    a.revision++
    copied := make(map[string]int, len(a.counts))
    for option, count := range a.counts {
        copied[option] = count
    }
    return Snapshot{
        PollID: a.pollID, Revision: a.revision,
        IncludedPosition: a.position, PublishedAt: now.UTC(),
        Counts: copied,
    }
}

The mutex makes this sample internally coherent, but it does not make two processes one writer. That trap matters. If every Express replica runs its own interval and holds its own counts, viewers can receive alternating realities; adding a distributed transport spreads the contradiction faster. Elect or partition one owner for a poll, persist the consumed position and snapshot atomically, and treat publication as retryable delivery of already committed state.

Timers are not authority.

How does reconnect and backfill stay boring?

A client stores the greatest tally revision it has applied. On connection, it sends that revision as resume metadata. The server returns the current snapshot when the stored revision is absent or older; if the client already has the current revision, no tally transfer is necessary. A late message with a lower revision is discarded. An equal revision is idempotent. A higher revision replaces the displayed counts.

That rule is intentionally dull.

WebRTC data channels are one possible transport, and the WebRTC specification defines data channels for bidirectional arbitrary data, but transport choice does not remove the application-level revision contract. The same contract can sit above WebSocket, server-sent events for downstream delivery, or periodic HTTP retrieval. Keep vote submission on an authenticated request path with explicit acknowledgement rather than assuming a transient viewer connection proves a vote became durable.

Backfill does not need to mean replaying every five-second publication. A viewer wants the latest correct tally, so one current snapshot is enough unless the interface exposes historical movement. Analytics is different: if producers need the full time series, retain committed snapshots or derive them from the durable vote log under a stated retention policy. Do not overload reconnect recovery with an analytics requirement most viewers never use.

Incoming revision Client action Operational meaning
lower than applied discard delayed or reordered delivery
equal to applied ignore safely duplicate delivery
exactly one higher replace snapshot normal interval update
more than one higher replace and record a gap reconnect or missed delivery

Recording a gap is useful telemetry, but a gap between complete snapshots is not a reason to freeze the UI. The newer snapshot is authoritative. This distinction keeps recovery fast while leaving evidence for investigation.

Instrument the contract, then test failure

Start with four measurements: accepted vote position, aggregated position, committed tally revision, and delivered revision acknowledgements sampled from clients. The first three locate a server-side stall. The last reveals an audience segment that is connected but not advancing. Include broadcast and poll identifiers in logs, but avoid attaching voter identity to high-cardinality metrics.

Emit one structured record at each boundary using the same poll identifier and positions: vote committed, vote applied, snapshot committed, publication attempted, and client revision observed. This creates an alert-to-action trace. An operator can move backward from a stale client revision to a failed delivery, an unpublished committed snapshot, a stalled aggregator, or an ingestion gap without correlating unrelated panels by eye.

Test the trace with failures. Kill the aggregation owner immediately after snapshot commit and before delivery. Deliver revision 42 after revision 43. Submit the same vote identifier twice. Disconnect a client for three publication intervals, then resume it with revision 39 while the server holds 43. Restart an Express replica and verify that its local timer cannot create a second authority. Each test should assert displayed counts and positions, not merely that a callback ran.

Deployment needs the same discipline. Introduce revision fields as optional readers first, then publish them, then require them after old clients age out. During rollback, a previous server must not emit an unversioned message that a newer client mistakes for fresh state. Schema compatibility belongs in the incident plan because reconnects surface older client builds.

The threshold can create its own incident

A five-second publication interval should not translate into a page at 5.001 seconds. Runtime pauses, scheduler jitter, and temporary delivery retries exist, while a quiet poll can legitimately publish no changed tally if that behavior is documented. Define the alert around a sustained position gap across more than one expected publication opportunity, and validate it under the slowest supported deployment conditions. The exact allowance is a service objective decision, not a universal constant.

Too loose, and viewers watch stale numbers while votes accumulate. Too tight, and every brief pause wakes someone who can take no useful action; repeated false positives train the team to distrust the one page that matters. Track how often the alert corresponds to an actual breached viewer-freshness objective, then revise either the threshold or the instrumentation when it does not.

The operational conclusion is compact: make vote acceptance durable, serialize aggregation per poll, publish complete versioned snapshots, and recover reconnects by revision. The interval controls how often the picture changes. It must never be the only place the truth lives.

Further reading

  • W3C, WebRTC 1.0: Real-Time Communication Between Browsers: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: From DevSecOps to Operational Resilience: 26 Engineering Improvements Across Cloud, Kubernetes and ML Infrastructure
description:
*From Security Scanning to Operational Resilience: Engineering Improvements Across DevSecOps, Cloud and ML Infrastructure *

Lessons from integrating security into CI/CD, strengthening observability, automating recovery, modernising API gateways and improving production operations.

Modern platform engineering is not just about deploying applications faster. It is about building secure, reliable, recoverable and maintainable systems while reducing manual operational effort.

In a multi-cloud environment supporting pharmaceutical SaaS applications, API platforms, Kubernetes clusters and machine learning services, operational excellence requires a combination of DevSecOps, observability, automation, capacity management and disciplined change control.

Over time, I have worked on a series of engineering improvements across CI/CD pipelines, on-premises infrastructure, Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), API gateways, databases, monitoring platforms and ML workloads.

These improvements share a common objective: shift operational practices from reactive troubleshooting towards proactive controls, repeatable automation and evidence-based engineering decisions.

This article explores the key improvements, the engineering considerations behind them and the operational value they bring.

1. Integrating Gitleaks with CI/CD: Bringing Secret Detection into the Development Workflow

Security vulnerabilities can enter a production environment long before deployment. Hard-coded credentials, API tokens, passwords and private keys committed to source control are examples of risks that should be detected as early as possible.

To address this, I integrated Gitleaks into the CI/CD workflow to identify potential secrets in source code and related repository content.

Why this matters

When credentials are committed to a repository, the risk extends beyond the immediate application. Credentials may be copied into build logs, cached artifacts, cloned repositories or downstream environments. Removing the secret from the latest commit does not necessarily remove it from the repository's history or eliminate the need to rotate it.

Engineering approach

The integration introduces secret scanning into the software delivery process, allowing findings to be identified closer to the point where code changes are introduced.

A mature implementation should include:

  • Scanning code changes and, where appropriate, repository history.
  • Reviewing findings to distinguish genuine secrets from false positives.
  • Assigning ownership for remediation.
  • Rotating exposed credentials rather than relying solely on deleting them from source code.
  • Defining severity-based handling and exception procedures.
  • Retaining scan results and remediation evidence according to policy.

The next level of maturity is to enforce pipeline failure for confirmed policy violations, subject to an agreed exception process. Detection and build-blocking enforcement are separate controls and should be implemented and verified independently.

Operational value: Earlier detection of credential exposure, improved security awareness in development workflows and a foundation for policy-driven DevSecOps.

2. Strengthening Security Visibility with Wazuh Across On-Premises Servers

Security controls are more effective when infrastructure events can be observed centrally.

I worked on installing Wazuh across on-premises servers to improve security monitoring and centralise visibility into relevant host events.

Key considerations

A successful deployment involves more than installing an agent. It requires attention to:

  • Agent connectivity and health.
  • Collection of relevant security events.
  • Alert rules and severity classification.
  • Investigation and escalation procedures.
  • Ownership of findings and remediation.
  • Monitoring of agent coverage and reporting gaps.

The operational objective is to make security events visible to the appropriate teams and provide a consistent basis for investigation.

A useful follow-up measure is coverage: the number of in-scope servers reporting successfully compared with the total number of servers that should be monitored. Additional measures can include alert investigation time and the age of unresolved high-priority findings.

Operational value: Improved security visibility across the on-premises server estate and a stronger basis for operational risk monitoring.

3. Evaluating Root-Access Changes Through a Proof of Concept

Privileged access is one of the most sensitive areas of infrastructure administration. Excessive or poorly controlled root access can increase the impact of accidental changes, compromised credentials and unauthorised activity.

I worked on a proof of concept for changing root-access practices, with broader rollout identified as a subsequent step.

A controlled approach to privileged access should consider:

  • Whether administrative access can be performed through named accounts and approved privilege elevation.
  • Authentication and authorisation requirements.
  • Audit logging for privileged commands and sessions.
  • Emergency access procedures.
  • Service dependencies that may require special treatment.
  • A tested rollback and recovery approach.

A proof of concept should validate compatibility with existing administration procedures before wider deployment. Production rollout should include a staged migration, clear ownership, exception handling and a method to recover access if the new controls fail.

Operational value: A structured path towards stronger privileged-access governance without introducing avoidable operational disruption.

4. Upgrading Trivy to Improve Vulnerability-Scanning Currency

Container and infrastructure security scanning must evolve alongside the tools, libraries and vulnerabilities they are intended to detect.

I upgraded Trivy from version 0.58.1 to 0.64.1 as part of maintaining the security tooling used in the engineering environment.

Tool upgrades are an important operational activity, but the upgrade alone does not establish that vulnerabilities have been eliminated.

A sound upgrade process should include:

  1. Reviewing release notes and compatibility considerations.
  2. Testing the new version against representative images and repositories.
  3. Validating vulnerability database access and scan output.
  4. Comparing findings and investigating material differences.
  5. Confirming that CI/CD integrations continue to operate correctly.
  6. Documenting the deployed version and the upgrade outcome.

The broader objective is to ensure that scanning remains a dependable part of the delivery process and that findings can be prioritised and remediated.

Operational value: Updated vulnerability-scanning tooling and a stronger foundation for maintaining consistent container security checks.

5. Resolving Certificate Trust Issues Between On-Premises Containers and OCI OpenSearch

Secure communication between distributed systems depends on correct certificate trust configuration.

An SSL connectivity issue was encountered when on-premises containers communicated with OCI OpenSearch. The issue was resolved by adding the required CA certificate to the operating system on the OCI server.

This illustrates an important troubleshooting principle: TLS failures are not always caused by application code or network connectivity. They can arise from certificate chains, trust stores, hostname verification, certificate expiry or configuration differences between environments.

A systematic investigation should validate:

  • The certificate presented by the remote endpoint.
  • The certificate chain and relevant CA certificates.
  • The trust store used by the client process.
  • Hostname and certificate validity checks.
  • Certificate expiry and renewal procedures.
  • Connectivity and TLS negotiation using approved diagnostic tools.

The durable fix should also be documented and incorporated into configuration management where appropriate, rather than relying on manual changes that may be lost during rebuilds.

Operational value: Restored secure connectivity and a clearer understanding of certificate trust dependencies between environments.

6. Improving Cloud Hygiene by Removing Unused Route 53 Records

Cloud resources and DNS records can remain after services are migrated, retired or replaced. Unused records create unnecessary configuration complexity and may introduce security, ownership or troubleshooting risks.

I removed unused Route 53 URLs after identifying records that were no longer required.

DNS cleanup should be performed carefully because a record that appears unused may still support a legacy integration, scheduled job, external client or certificate-validation workflow.

A controlled cleanup process should include:

  • Identifying the record owner and associated service.
  • Reviewing traffic and dependency evidence where available.
  • Confirming that the target service has been decommissioned or migrated.
  • Checking certificate, redirect and integration dependencies.
  • Recording the change and retaining a recovery path where appropriate.
  • Validating service behaviour after removal.

Operational value: Reduced DNS clutter and improved configuration maintainability, provided that dependency checks and post-change validation are completed.

7. API Gateway Modernisation: WSO2, Kong, Azure API Management and OCI API Gateway

API gateways are critical infrastructure components because they sit on the path between clients and backend services. Their configuration, availability and migration strategy can directly affect application connectivity.

My API gateway improvement work included WSO2-to-Kong migration activities, Kong failover-related implementation, API migration from Azure API Management to OCI API Gateway and work involving migration of services to Standard API Manager from Basic SKU.

Addressing OCI API Gateway service limits

During the migration to OCI API Gateway, a service configuration constraint involving the limit of 50 APIs per service required attention. The engineering team reduced the number of APIs configured per service to remain below that limit.

This is an example of adapting API architecture to the constraints of the target platform instead of treating migration as a direct copy of the source configuration.

Resolving Jasper API compatibility issues

Jasper APIs that were invoked from Azure did not function as expected after the move to OCI API Gateway. OCI Functions were used to address the integration issue.

The broader engineering lesson is that API migration requires functional validation, not just successful deployment. Differences in request handling, authentication, integration behaviour, routing and platform capabilities can affect API compatibility.

Reliability and failover

Kong failover implementation and related proof-of-concept activities were also part of the improvement work.

A robust failover implementation should verify:

  • Health detection and failure thresholds.
  • Routing to the correct healthy endpoint.
  • Connection and session behaviour.
  • Authentication, rate limiting and TLS configuration.
  • Recovery when the original node becomes healthy again.
  • Logging, alerting and operational ownership.

A failover design should be tested under controlled failure scenarios before it is treated as production-ready.

Operational value: Improved migration readiness, more deliberate gateway architecture and a structured approach to API availability and failover.

8. Automating Kong API Manager Administration

Manual API management can become difficult to maintain as the number of services, configurations and environments grows.

I developed an automated script for managing Kong API Manager activities.

Automation is especially useful for repeatable administrative tasks when it reduces configuration inconsistency and improves execution speed. However, API-management automation must also protect against accidental changes to routes, credentials, upstream services or access policies.

A reliable automation workflow should include:

  • Validated inputs and environment selection.
  • Authentication using appropriately protected credentials.
  • Pre-change checks and configuration validation.
  • Logging of actions and results.
  • Error handling and safe failure behaviour.
  • Change traceability and controlled permissions.
  • Post-change verification.

Operational value: A foundation for more repeatable API administration and reduced reliance on manual configuration steps.

9. Building a More Reliable Backup and Recovery Practice

Backups are only useful when they are available, consistent and recoverable when required.

I implemented automated backup processes across several infrastructure and data platforms, including:

  • Zabbix
  • Kong
  • Grafana
  • Prometheus
  • Weaviate
  • Dgraph
  • Legal-Elastic
  • Redis
  • PostgreSQL
  • MLflow

Additional work included automated PostgreSQL database backups and the use of an NFS server on separate box to receive backups from the five-node Elasticsearch cluster on Master Node.

The objective was to make backup execution more repeatable and reduce dependence on manual intervention.

Backup automation is only the first step

A production-ready backup process should also monitor completion, validate backup integrity, control access, manage retention and verify that the recovery process works.

Key questions include:

  • Did the backup complete?
  • Does the backup contain the expected data?
  • Is it protected from accidental or unauthorised deletion?
  • Can it be restored independently of the production failure?
  • Can the service be recovered within its agreed RTO?
  • Is the amount of data lost within the agreed RPO?

These checks are essential because a successful backup job is not proof of recoverability.

Operational value: More repeatable backup execution across a diverse technology stack and a foundation for better recovery readiness.

10. Restoring Legal-Elastic and Weaviate Data

Backup processes become more meaningful when recovery is demonstrated.

As part of the operational work, I restored Legal-Elastic on Backup Server and restored Weaviate data on Master node.

These activities provided practical experience with data restoration and the operational dependencies involved in bringing data services back into service.

A restoration procedure should validate more than whether a process starts. Depending on the platform, verification may include:

  • Database or index health.
  • Expected collections, indices or records.
  • Data consistency and application connectivity.
  • Authentication and access controls.
  • Application-level queries.
  • Evidence that the restored service is fit for its intended use.

The next maturity step is to formalise recurring restore tests, record the duration and results, and compare them against recovery objectives.

Operational value: Demonstrated restoration capability for the specific systems involved and a basis for improving recovery procedures.

11. Recovering a 2 TB Disk Snapshot for a UAT Environment

A disk recovery activity involved using a 2 TB disk snapshot to create and mount a disk on the UAT virtual machine on Azure. The restored data was checked with Ayan, after which the original 2 TB disk was depleted and decommissioned.

This activity highlights the importance of managing the complete lifecycle of recovered storage—not just creating the disk.

A controlled process should confirm:

  1. The correct snapshot and recovery point were selected.
  2. The restored disk was attached and mounted safely.
  3. The expected data was available and validated by the relevant owner.
  4. The UAT environment could access the required data.
  5. The original disk was no longer required before decommissioning.
  6. The storage change and decommissioning were documented.

The principle is simple: validate the recovery target and data before retiring the original resource.

Operational value: Recovered storage and validated data availability for the UAT environment, followed by the removal of the original disk after confirmation.

12. Expanding Elasticsearch Cluster Capacity

I added Node 4 and Node 5 as Elasticsearch nodes to an existing cluster having 3 nodes.

Adding nodes can increase available capacity and provide more flexibility in distributing data and workload. However, node addition must be accompanied by cluster-health and capacity validation.

Important checks include:

  • Cluster health before and after the change.
  • Node discovery and membership.
  • Shard allocation and rebalancing.
  • Disk utilisation and storage watermarks.
  • Heap utilisation, CPU and query latency.
  • Replication and recovery activity.
  • Any application impact during rebalancing.

Operational value: Expanded the cluster's node footprint, creating additional capacity potential. The actual performance or capacity improvement should be established from before-and-after metrics.

13. Resource Optimisation Through Pod and Docker Profiling

Infrastructure capacity decisions should be based on observed workloads rather than assumptions.

I carried out proof-of-concept work for pod profiling and then profiled pods across Development, QA, Sales and UAT Kubernetes clusters. I also performed Docker profiling for ML services.

Profiling helps identify:

  • CPU and memory utilisation patterns.
  • Workloads with excessive or insufficient resource requests.
  • Potential memory leaks or unexpected growth.
  • Containers that frequently restart or encounter OOM termination.
  • Opportunities for resource right-sizing.
  • Workloads that may benefit from isolation or separate scaling policies.

This is particularly important for ML workloads, where resource demand can vary significantly between model types and execution patterns.

Profiling should cover normal usage as well as peak periods. Reducing resource allocations based only on average usage can introduce instability during traffic spikes or concurrent workloads.

Operational value: Better evidence for capacity planning and resource optimisation across Kubernetes and containerised ML services.

14. ML Service Rationalisation and Ollama Configuration

I worked on ML service deprecation activities, Ollama configuration changes for ML services and Ollama model availability on GPU hosts.

These activities relate to managing an evolving ML infrastructure footprint and aligning deployed services and models with operational requirements.

For service deprecation, a controlled process should verify service ownership, consumer dependencies, traffic usage, replacement availability and rollback requirements before a service is retired.

For model and GPU-host configuration, important operational considerations include:

  • GPU and memory utilisation.
  • Model compatibility and loading behaviour.
  • Concurrent request capacity.
  • Model-serving latency and error rates.
  • Process health and recovery.
  • Version consistency and configuration management.

The objective is to maintain a service footprint that is operationally supportable while ensuring that active workloads continue to meet their functional requirements.

Operational value: Improved management of ML service and model configurations. Quantified resource savings or inference-performance improvements should be reported only after measurement.

15. Automating ML Service Deployment

I completed proof-of-concept work for ML service deployment automation, with broader automation across all ML services identified as a next step.

ML deployment automation can reduce manual configuration, improve repeatability and help maintain consistency across multiple environments.

A mature workflow should cover:

  1. Versioned deployment configuration.
  2. Validation of required secrets and environment variables.
  3. Image and dependency checks.
  4. Resource configuration and health probes.
  5. Deployment execution with appropriate permissions.
  6. Post-deployment smoke tests and service validation.
  7. Failure handling and rollback.
  8. Audit-friendly records of what was deployed and when.

The important distinction is between a working proof of concept and a fully operationalised deployment framework. Broader rollout should include testing, documentation, ownership and support procedures.

Operational value: A foundation for consistent ML deployment and a path towards reducing manual deployment effort.

16. Operational Resilience Through Swap Configuration

Swap configuration was standardised based on available host memory:

  • Hosts with 8 GB RAM: 4 GB swap.
  • Hosts with 16 GB RAM: 8 GB swap.
  • Hosts with 32 GB RAM: 8 GB swap.

Swap can provide a buffer during memory pressure, but it is not a replacement for adequate physical memory. Excessive swapping can also degrade application performance, especially for latency-sensitive services.

A production implementation should monitor swap usage, memory pressure, OOM events and application response times. It should also consider workload characteristics and the performance implications of swapping.

Operational value: More consistent swap configuration across the specified host sizes, with the actual reliability benefit dependent on workload behaviour and monitoring evidence.

17. Safer Service Isolation and Environment Segregation

I worked on separating the vigilance data service by deploying vigilance-qa in the QA cluster and vigilance-prod in the Prod cluster. I also worked on service-ner environment segregation.

Separating services by environment can improve operational isolation, reduce the risk of accidental cross-environment interaction and make deployment ownership clearer.

However, segregation requires more than separate deployment names. It should also consider:

  • Namespace and cluster boundaries.
  • Service accounts and permissions.
  • Network access.
  • Environment-specific secrets and configuration.
  • Database and external-service connectivity.
  • Monitoring, logging and alert routing.
  • Deployment and rollback procedures.

Operational value: Clearer environment separation and a more controlled foundation for managing service configurations across QA and Sales.

18. Improving Kubernetes Deployment Safety with Health Probes and Strategies

I updated deployment.yaml configurations with liveness probes, readiness probes and deployment strategies for backend services across Development, QA and Prod environments.

These controls address different aspects of application availability.

  • Readiness probes help prevent traffic from reaching pods that are not ready to serve requests.
  • Liveness probes help detect applications that need to be restarted.
  • Deployment strategies control how application versions are rolled out and how old and new instances coexist during a change.

Correct configuration is critical. A liveness probe that is too aggressive can cause restart loops, while an inadequate readiness probe can expose users to an application that has started but is not ready.

Deployment validation should cover normal startup, slow startup, dependency failures, rolling updates and rollback scenarios.

Operational value: Stronger deployment-level health controls and a more structured approach to managing backend service updates.

19. Liquibase CI/CD for Database Changes

Database changes require a controlled approach because schema modifications can affect application compatibility, data integrity and recovery.

I worked on Liquibase CI/CD for database delivery.

A well-designed database deployment pipeline should include:

  • Version-controlled migration scripts.
  • Review and approval of changes.
  • Validation against the target database.
  • Controlled execution in the appropriate environment.
  • Compatibility checks between application and schema versions.
  • Verification after migration.
  • A documented recovery or forward-fix strategy.

Database rollback requires special consideration. Not every schema or data transformation can be safely reversed, so the recovery strategy must be designed for the specific change.

Operational value: A foundation for repeatable, traceable database changes and closer integration between application and database delivery processes.

20. Jenkins Upgrade and Deployment Hygiene

I upgraded Jenkins from version 2.479.2 to 2.504.3.

CI/CD infrastructure is itself a critical production dependency. An upgrade should therefore include plugin compatibility checks, configuration and job validation, backup verification, access-control review and post-upgrade testing.

I also updated deployment scripts to automatically delete TAR files from 52 hosts after deployment, and backed up deployment scripts from those hosts to Bitbucket.

These activities address two operational concerns: managing deployment artefacts after use and retaining version-controlled copies of operational scripts.

A strong implementation should verify that:

  • The artefact is no longer needed by the running application or rollback process.
  • Cleanup only targets the intended files and directories.
  • Script failures are logged and surfaced.
  • The deployment outcome is not reported as successful when required cleanup or validation fails.
  • The version-controlled script is accessible to authorised maintainers.

Operational value: More consistent deployment cleanup and improved version-control coverage for deployment scripts.

21. Standardising the Linux Operating-System Baseline

I worked on upgrading Ubuntu from version 20.04 to 22.04.

Operating-system upgrades require a balance between security maintenance, application compatibility and service availability. A safe upgrade process should include dependency assessment, testing, backup validation, change approval, rollback planning and post-upgrade health checks.

For production systems, I would also verify monitoring-agent compatibility, service startup behaviour, network configuration, scheduled jobs and application dependencies.

Operational value: Progress towards a more current operating-system baseline for the systems included in the upgrade.

22. Managing ML Automation with Locking Controls

I worked on a lock script for ML automation.

Concurrent automation can create conflicts when multiple jobs attempt to modify the same resource, deploy the same service or run an operation that should only have one active execution.

Locking controls can help prevent duplicate execution, but they must handle stale locks, abnormal termination, ownership and safe release.

A production-ready implementation should define:

  • What resource is protected.
  • How lock ownership is established.
  • How stale locks are detected and recovered.
  • How concurrent execution attempts are handled.
  • What happens when a job fails midway.
  • How execution is logged and monitored.

Operational value: A mechanism for controlling concurrent ML automation and reducing the risk of conflicting operations, subject to the lock implementation and its failure handling.

23. Infrastructure Connectivity and Network Resilience

Network availability is a fundamental dependency for monitoring, application connectivity and operational support.

I changed the primary ISP from ACT to TATA after the ACT Fair Usage Policy threshold was exceeded and firewall bandwidth dropped to 3 Mbps.

The change addressed an operational connectivity constraint. It also illustrates why network-provider performance should be evaluated against actual business requirements rather than assumed service capacity.

Useful follow-up measurements include:

  • Available bandwidth and utilisation.
  • Packet loss and latency.
  • Connection stability.
  • VPN and remote-access performance.
  • Incident frequency and duration.
  • Failover capability and recovery time.

Where possible, network changes should be validated against representative workloads and documented alongside the associated firewall and routing configuration.

Operational value: A change in primary ISP to address a bandwidth limitation affecting operational connectivity.

24. Observability with OpenTelemetry

I worked on introducing an OpenTelemetry pod in AKS.

OpenTelemetry provides a common approach for collecting telemetry such as traces, metrics and logs through supported instrumentation and collectors. Its value comes from making it easier to correlate application behaviour across distributed components.

For a production rollout, I would validate:

  • Which telemetry signals are collected.
  • Whether the instrumentation covers the required services.
  • Exporter and collector configuration.
  • Access controls and protection of sensitive telemetry.
  • Sampling, retention and data-volume implications.
  • Collector health and telemetry delivery.
  • Integration with the organisation's observability platform.

Operational value: A foundation for more consistent telemetry collection and cross-service troubleshooting, with the actual observability improvement depending on instrumentation coverage and integration.

25. Resolving an Infrastructure Capacity Constraint in the Network Path

The network-provider change from ACT to TATA also illustrates a broader operational principle: infrastructure capacity issues can originate outside the application or server layer.

When firewall throughput falls, application symptoms can resemble a backend problem—slow requests, timeouts, unstable remote sessions or delayed monitoring data.

A layered investigation should therefore examine the full service path, including the local network, firewall, ISP, VPN, routing and remote endpoint.

Operational value: A practical reminder to correlate application symptoms with network performance before making unnecessary changes to application infrastructure.

26. Bringing the Improvements Together

The individual changes become more valuable when managed as part of a coherent operational improvement programme.

I group this work into six engineering themes:

Security and control

  • Gitleaks integration with CI/CD.
  • Wazuh deployment across on-premises servers.
  • Trivy upgrade.
  • Root-access change proof of concept.
  • Certificate trust remediation.
  • DNS hygiene.

Reliability and recovery

  • Automated backups across multiple platforms.
  • Legal-Elastic and Weaviate restoration.
  • Disk snapshot recovery for UAT.
  • Elasticsearch cluster expansion.
  • Kong failover-related implementation.
  • Kubernetes health probes and deployment strategies.

Automation and engineering consistency

  • Kong API Manager automation.
  • Liquibase CI/CD.
  • Jenkins upgrade.
  • ML deployment automation proof of concept.
  • ML automation locking.
  • Deployment-script cleanup and version control.

Cloud and API modernisation

  • WSO2-to-Kong migration work.
  • Azure API Management to OCI API Gateway migration.
  • OCI API configuration-limit remediation.
  • Jasper API integration remediation using OCI Functions.
  • API migration work involving Standard API Manager.

Capacity and platform optimisation

  • Pod and Docker profiling.
  • ML service rationalisation.
  • Ollama configuration and GPU model management.
  • Swap configuration.
  • Elasticsearch node expansion.

Operational hygiene and environment management

  • Linux OS upgrades.
  • Service segregation across environments.
  • Removal of unused DNS records.
  • Network-provider change to address bandwidth constraints.
  • OpenTelemetry deployment work.

27. Measuring Operational Improvement

Engineering changes should ultimately be evaluated using evidence. For this programme, I would track a focused set of measures.

Improvement area Useful measure
Secret scanning Repositories covered, findings triaged and remediation time
Security monitoring Server coverage, agent health and high-priority finding age
Vulnerability scanning Scan coverage, finding severity and remediation status
Backup and recovery Backup success, restore-test success, RPO and RTO
API gateway reliability Availability, request errors, latency and failover test results
Kubernetes operations Pod restarts, OOM events, deployment failures and readiness failures
Capacity optimisation Resource utilisation, headroom and cost per workload
Automation Manual effort avoided, automation failures and repeat-ticket reduction
Database delivery Migration success, rollback or forward-fix events and post-deployment validation
Network performance Latency, packet loss, throughput and connectivity incidents

I would establish a baseline before claiming a percentage improvement. Where measurements are unavailable, the correct approach is to describe the engineering change and its intended benefit without inventing an outcome.

Conclusion: Engineering Operations as a Continuous Improvement Discipline

These improvements demonstrate how DevSecOps, observability, automation, infrastructure management and recovery planning work together.

Security scanning helps identify risks earlier. Monitoring makes operational behaviour visible. Backup and restoration processes support recovery. Kubernetes health controls improve deployment management. API gateway and infrastructure changes address platform constraints. Automation reduces repetitive work, while capacity profiling provides evidence for optimisation.

The next level of maturity is to connect these activities to measurable operational outcomes: fewer recurring incidents, faster and safer recovery, more reliable deployments, stronger security-control coverage and better use of infrastructure resources.

For me, the central principle is straightforward:

Operational excellence is not the absence of incidents. It is the ability to detect problems early, recover safely, learn systematically and engineer the conditions that make the next incident less likely.

That is the direction I continue to pursue across DevSecOps, cloud platforms, API infrastructure and ML operations.

title: Day 17/60: Testing HTTP handlers - Go Backend Engineering
description:
Day 17/60: Testing HTTP handlers

60 Day Go Backend Engineering Challenge

Today I focused on making testing http handlers feel like request flow design rather than just handler boilerplate. The strongest checkpoints were name the request boundary, validation step, and response contract before writing handler code, keep routing and middleware explicit enough that ownership of each concern is obvious, and make serialization and status codes follow the service contract rather than handler convenience.

The mistake I wanted to avoid was mixing validation, orchestration, and transport formatting in one handler. The day felt better once the service boundary stayed visible and each component had one job.

The goal for tomorrow is simple: keep the rule clear enough that the next service still feels related to the same design idea. I also want to keep tracing one request path end to end because it exposes weak assumptions faster than a larger demo.

title: Day 17/60: Matrix operations in Rust - Rust DSA
description:
Day 17/60: Matrix operations in Rust

60 Day Rust DSA Challenge

Today I focused on making matrix operations in rust work with Rust slices, strings, and indices without losing correctness. The strongest checkpoints were decide early whether bytes, chars, or slices are the right representation in Rust, keep the transformation or scan state explicit instead of mixing index tricks together, and use iterators and owned buffers deliberately so UTF-8 handling does not become accidental.

The mistake I wanted to avoid was mixing byte indexing and character assumptions in UTF-8 text. The day felt better once the invariant stayed visible and each update had one job.

The goal for tomorrow is simple: keep the rule clear enough that the next variation still feels related to the same idea. I also want to keep tracing tiny examples because they expose weak assumptions faster than large random tests.

title: AWS Secrets Manager: Rotation, IAM Scoping, and Production Gotchas
description:
Day 17: AWS Secrets Manager

Secrets Manager charges $0.40/secret/month but gives you something Parameter Store does not: automatic credential rotation with pre-built Lambda functions for RDS, Redshift, and DocumentDB.

Retrieving Secrets in Go 

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go-v2/config"
    "github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go-v2/service/secretsmanager"
)

type DBCreds struct {
    Username string `json:"username"`
    Password string `json:"password"`
    Host     string `json:"host"`
}

func getSecret(ctx context.Context, name string) (*DBCreds, error) {
    cfg, _ := config.LoadDefaultConfig(ctx, config.WithRegion("us-east-1"))
    client := secretsmanager.NewFromConfig(cfg)
    result, err := client.GetSecretValue(ctx, &secretsmanager.GetSecretValueInput{
        SecretId: &name,
    })
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to retrieve secret: %w", err)
    }
    var creds DBCreds
    json.Unmarshal([]byte(*result.SecretString), &creds)
    return &creds, nil
}

Key Tips

  • Name secrets as env/app/purpose for clean IAM wildcard scoping
  • Always pin the AWS region -- cross-region secret injection is a real attack
  • Rotation Lambda needs VPC + NAT gateway access to reach RDS
  • Cache secrets in-app (1hr TTL default) to reduce costs
  • Cross-account access needs BOTH a resource policy AND a KMS key grant

Tomorrow: AWS Systems Manager and Parameter Store.

title: Day 17/90: Lifetimes and lifetime annotations - Rust Engineering
description:
Day 17/90: Lifetimes and lifetime annotations

90 Day Rust Challenge: Zero to Production

Today I wanted lifetimes and lifetime annotations to feel like a real engineering decision, not a syntax demo. The useful shift was making lifetimes and lifetime annotations readable in terms of ownership, borrowing, and lifetime boundaries.

The checks that mattered were which borrowed data must outlive what, how signatures communicate that constraint, and where owned data is simpler than another annotation.

The failure mode I was actively trying to avoid was fighting the borrow checker without first deciding which value should actually own the state. I wanted lifetimes and lifetime annotations to feel like something I could explain at a whiteboard or in a code review, not just something I recognized from docs.

That is the bar I want from this track: code that stays readable when requirements move, not just code that compiles today.

title: I Built a Fake Linear So My Agents Could Fail in Private 🫠
description:
Hey tech adventurers! 👋

Confession: I'm building a tool where agents pick up Linear issues, do the work, and open PRs. It's called Paws. And testing that against a real Linear workspace is a great way to teach your coworkers what an agent sounds like at 3am. 😅

So I did the reasonable thing and built my own Linear. Locally. In a few hours. Like a normal person.

Mocks lie, and agents believe them 🤥

The usual move is to mock the API. Stub issue.update, return some JSON, call it a day.

Except agent workflows don't really live in single calls. They live in the stuff between calls. A webhook shows up twice. A delivery fails and retries an hour later. An OAuth token rotates mid-session. A human answers the agent's question in a comment thread. Mocks happily skip all of that, and then production finds it for you.

I didn't want a fake that agrees with me. I wanted one that argues back.

Meet Finear 🏠

Finear is a local, Linear-compatible server for integration tests. Bun, SQLite, done.

The part I'm weirdly proud of: it runs the unchanged @linear/sdk against real GraphQL. My code doesn't know it's being lied to. It just points apiUrl somewhere else.

What's actually in there:

  • Issues, projects, sub-issues, labels, threaded comments 📋
  • OAuth consent, PKCE, refresh rotation, revocation 🔐
  • Signed, durable webhooks with retries 📬
  • Agent delegation, sessions, activities, and the human prompts in between 🤖
  • Deterministic fixtures and a reset button 🧽

I can fast-forward time now ⏰

Real webhook retries wait a minute, then an hour, then six hours. Waiting six hours to watch a test fail is not a personality I want.

So Finear has a virtual clock. Advance it, and due retries fire in order, instantly. Inspect every delivery and every attempt. Reset the whole world when you're done.

It's the closest I'll ever get to time travel, and I used it to debug webhooks. 🫠

The agent part 🐕

This is why it exists. Delegate an issue to an app and Finear creates an agent session. The agent can post thoughts, take actions, ask the human a question, and finish with a response or an error. The questions and answers show up as normal comment threads, like you'd expect.

That's exactly the loop Paws lives in. Now I can break it as many times as I want, on my laptop, without a single "hey, why is a bot commenting on my issue?" DM.

The fine print 🧾

Finear is a test harness, not a Linear replacement. It binds to 127.0.0.1 on purpose, and it isn't affiliated with Linear in any way. Please don't run your team on it. I'm begging you.

How to set it up lives in the README. This post is just me admitting I built a whole issue tracker so my agents could fail in private.

P.S. If your integration tests mostly test your mocks, I'm not judging. I was there two weeks ago. 🍕
