title: Unknown Is Not Zero: Modeling Evidence in a Fan-Made Game Wiki
description:
Most game wikis I've used have the same failure mode: every cell is filled. Drop rate? A precise percentage. Pet speed? A precise number. Codes? A long list, all "working". Half of those numbers came from one video, a Discord screenshot, or a guess that got copied enough times to look like a fact.

While working on a fan guide for the Roblox game Ride A Pet, we took the opposite approach: a value is only shown if we can say where it came from and when. That sounds like an editorial rule, but it turned out to be mostly a data-modeling problem. Here's what that looks like in practice and what we'd do the same way again.

1. Give every fact an evidence status, not just a value

The eggs reference doesn't have one "source" column. Each row carries a label for how we know it:

  • Recorded screen: the name is visible in gameplay footage we can rewatch (e.g. an Aurora Egg growing at a ranch nest).
  • Reported: a dated third-party source says it (e.g. Blackhole and Cherub Eggs being searched for around the Giant Tree and a waterfall cave).
  • Official artwork: the name appears in promotional art (Flame Egg, Dragon Egg). That proves the name exists, not that it's buyable today.

The UI consequence is small but important: a "Reported" row reads differently from a "Recorded" row, and a reader can see why the page is hedging.

A sketch of the shape:

type Evidence =
  | { kind: "recorded"; source: string; timestamp: string }   // e.g. "SpaceQT", "2:57"
  | { kind: "reported"; source: string; checkedOn: string }   // ISO date
  | { kind: "official-art"; source: string }
  | { kind: "unknown" };

interface Fact<T> {
  value: T | null;          // null when unknown, never 0
  unit?: string;            // "$/s", "stock", ...
  evidence: Evidence;
}

2. null is not 0, and the UI should say so

The pets page has a line I like a lot: an unmeasured stat remains unknown; it should not be entered as zero.

That's a classic data bug wearing a game costume. If a comparison tool defaults an empty field to 0, every pet nobody measured looks terrible, and readers draw conclusions from your defaults. So:

  • Missing values render as "Unknown", not as 0 or -.
  • A number is always shown with its unit. The game shows a lightning label, a clover label, and a dollar-per-second label next to pets; a big number alone doesn't tell you whether it's movement, luck, or income.
  • Comparisons only happen between the same field on two pets.

The same idea shows up in the game-pass table. Four passes (Instant Hatch, Infinite Radar, Infinite Backpack, Auto Collect) have a known purpose from published guides, but the exact rules and prices aren't confirmed. Instead of guessing, the table has a column literally called "function detail still needed for a purchase decision". Writing down what you don't know is more useful than a confident row that's wrong.

3. Snapshots get a date and a source timestamp

Shop data in a live game is volatile. A recorded Gears shop frame shows Royal Radar marked Legendary at $20K with x3 stock, and Magic Radar out of stock. That's useful for recognizing the row, and useless as a price list a week later.

So every snapshot keeps:

  • the creator and video timestamp it came from (SpaceQT at 3:07, ItzVexo at 5:45),
  • a note that "$" is the game's own price display, not US dollars,
  • and a page-level "Checked" date plus a separate "last substantive edit" date.

Two dates sound redundant until you need them. "Checked" means "we re-read the sources on this day." "Edited" means "the content actually changed." Mixing them hides whether a page is stale or just stable.

4. The best page on the site is an empty list

Codes pages are where game wikis lose the most trust. The fan guide's answer is a page whose main content is: no verified codes, with a timestamp (24 September 2026, 03:07 UTC), the official page that was checked, and two dated third-party reports that also found none.

What makes it work as a data page is that "verified" has a definition. A code record needs four fields before it's published:

  1. the exact string,
  2. the announced reward,
  3. a redemption control that actually exists in the current game,
  4. a successful redemption check.

If any one is missing, the record doesn't exist yet. A failed attempt can't tell you whether a code expired, was mistyped or never existed, so on its own it doesn't move a row anywhere. You can see the whole structure on the Ride A Pet codes checklist; it's a nice reference if you're designing any "status" page where the honest answer is often "nothing yet".

5. Separate states that look the same

Another modeling lesson from the eggs page: a world listing, a radar target, and an egg in your basket are three different states, even though a player might call all of them "my egg". The page maps each screen to the one question it answers:

Screen Question
Track What is listed in the world?
Radar marker Where is this search's target?
Egg Basket What am I carrying?
Hatch screen What stage is this egg at?
Index: Eggs What have I collected?

If you've ever debugged an order system where "in cart", "paid" and "shipped" got collapsed into one boolean, this will feel familiar.

6. Keep personal state on the client, and say so

The egg-locations page has a small run-notes checklist: an optional target name (up to 60 characters) and seven checks, from "prepare a rideable pet" to "place it in a nest and confirm hatching". It's one checklist per browser, not synced to a game account, and the page states that the component doesn't send notes to analytics.

The "report a problem" form is similarly scoped: it sends the page address and a category (outdated, unclear, video problem, missing info), and nothing else. Writing the data boundary next to the control costs one sentence and removes a whole class of "what are you collecting?" questions.

What I'd take to any reference site

  • Model evidence explicitly. A value without a source is a draft.
  • Default to null, render "Unknown", keep units attached.
  • Store "checked" and "edited" dates separately.
  • Define what "verified" means as required fields, and let the empty state be a real, dated page.
  • Put the privacy boundary of a widget right next to the widget.

None of this needs a fancy stack. It's mostly refusing to let a table cell be filled just because the layout has room for it.

title: What Stays Intact When the Model Changes? Paper 2 on Externalized Intelligence
description:
I have published the second paper in the Artificial Deterministic Intelligence research series: Externalized Intelligence and Model Substitution.

The question is deliberately narrower than “are smaller models as intelligent as larger models?” They are not assumed to be. The question is whether a bounded operational contract can remain intact when authoritative task state is maintained outside model weights and the inference model changes.

In synthetic first-party studies, a frozen governed package was tested across 8B to 35B, 35B to 8B, and same-model restart controls. All 120 confirmatory handoff trials retained the measured policy contract and task correctness. The study also compares governed scoped context, authorized metadata-filtered lexical retrieval, and an oracle authorized-context ceiling. Each completed 90 of 90 trials under the shared frozen contract; conventional lexical retrieval had the lower measured retrieval-component time.

Those findings do not establish general model equivalence, production readiness, universal continuity, a universal safety guarantee, or retrieval superiority. The companion retains non-acceptances, timeouts, an incomplete scoped study, and a non-confirming cross-environment replication attempt.

Read the Version 2 preprint and evidence companion: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23523687

The public-safe supplementary evidence package provides aggregate outcomes, claim boundaries, hashes, and a verifier without disclosing Cortex, HOPE OS, raw prompts, worker packages, or private implementation.

I welcome technical criticism, alternative experimental designs, and independent work that can challenge these bounded findings.

title: The 12-Factor App Methodology in the Cloud-Native Era
description:
title: "The 12-Factor App Methodology in the Cloud-Native Era"
published: true
published_at: "2027-01-29T09:00:00+05:30"
description: "A practical engineering guide to The 12-Factor App Methodology in the Cloud-Native Era. Learn core mechanics, production tradeoffs, and best practices."
tags: [architecture, devops, softwareengineering, cloud]
ai_disclosure_level: some_ai

In modern software development, The 12-Factor App Methodology in the Cloud-Native Era is a critical subject that every serious engineer must understand. Whether building distributed backend systems, designing scalable databases, or optimizing developer productivity, mastering the underlying mechanics separates junior developers who guess from senior engineers who deliver reliable architectures.

In this deep dive, we break down why The 12-Factor App Methodology in the Cloud-Native Era matters, examine common failure modes in production, and walk through concrete implementation patterns.

The Problem: Why Naive Approaches Fail

In earlier development workflows or smaller-scale projects, teams frequently overlook the subtleties of software engineering architectures.

When systems scale, common bottlenecks emerge:

  1. Unpredictable Latency & Resource Starvation: High concurrency and unoptimized execution pipelines exhaust system resources, leading to degraded response times and thread pool stalls.
  2. Hidden Failure Cascades: Unhandled edge cases and lack of defensive invariants create silent data corruption that propagates across microservices.
  3. High Cognitive Overhead: As codebases evolve, poorly structured domain abstractions become difficult to maintain, test, and refactor.

To resolve these challenges, engineering teams must implement disciplined patterns focusing on:

  • Examining Each Factor (Config In Environment: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Stateless Processes: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Port Binding: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Concurrency: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.

Under the Hood: Architectural Overview

Understanding how The 12-Factor App Methodology in the Cloud-Native Era functions beneath high-level abstractions is essential for diagnosing production anomalies.

+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| System Workflow: Software engineering Architecture                    |
|                                                              |
| [Incoming Workload] ---> [Validation & Boundary Layer]       |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                     [Optimized Core Execution]               |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                  [Resilient State / Output Store]            |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

When designing systems around this pattern, prioritize:

  • Isolation of Concerns: Keep business invariants decoupled from transport protocols and third-party drivers.
  • Deterministic Resource Management: Bound memory allocations, connection pools, and worker concurrency to prevent out-of-memory crashes.
  • Observability & Metrics: Expose granular latency histograms, error rates, and throughput metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.

Practical Implementation

Here is a clean, production-oriented pattern demonstrating these principles in action:

import asyncio
import logging
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ExecutionContext:
    task_id: str
    payload: dict
    retries: int = 3

class ResilientProcessor:
    """Production-ready processor addressing: Examining each factor (Config in environment, Stateless processes, Port binding, Concurrency, Disposability) through modern containerized application architectures."""

    def __init__(self, concurrency_limit: int = 10):
        self.semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency_limit)

    async def execute_with_guardrails(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> Optional[dict]:
        async with self.semaphore:
            for attempt in range(1, ctx.retries + 1):
                try:
                    logger.info(f"Processing task {ctx.task_id}, attempt {attempt}")
                    result = await self._process_task(ctx)
                    return result
                except (ConnectionError, TimeoutError) as ex:
                    backoff = 2 ** attempt
                    logger.warning(f"Transient error on {ctx.task_id}: {ex}. Retrying in {backoff}s...")
                    await asyncio.sleep(backoff)
                except Exception as ex:
                    logger.error(f"Permanent failure processing {ctx.task_id}: {ex}")
                    raise
            return None

    async def _process_task(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> dict:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        return {"task_id": ctx.task_id, "status": "completed", "meta": ctx.payload}

Production Gotchas to Avoid

When deploying this architecture at scale, keep these three operational realities in mind:

  1. Beware of Unbounded Queues: Always place hard limits on in-memory buffers and connection queues. An unbounded queue simply hides backpressure until the process encounters an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash.
  2. Set Aggressive Timeouts: Never make external network or storage calls without explicit connection and read timeouts. A single hanging dependency can exhaust worker pools system-wide.
  3. Ensure Idempotency: Network packets get dropped and clients retry. Ensure that mutating operations can be executed multiple times safely without producing duplicate side-effects.

Summary Checklist

  • [x] Validate at the boundary: Ensure invalid states never penetrate deep domain layers.
  • [x] Enforce bounded resource limits: Protect memory, connections, and CPU threads against unexpected spikes.
  • [x] Log structured telemetry: Attach correlation IDs to log records for rapid root-cause analysis during outages.
  • [x] Design for failure: Always provide graceful fallbacks and fast-failure mechanisms when dependencies degrade.

title: Blueprints, Not Prompts: Using TLA+ to Guide AI-Written Code
description:
Code used to be where a team's understanding of a system lived. Now that LLMs write most of it, that understanding is quietly eroding. Here's why we're exploring formal methods at Mulga, specifically TLA+, to build better systems with AI without losing our grip on what we're building, with a real AWS EBS spec as an example.

The real contribution isn't code

It is my sincere belief that shared understanding and curated mental models are the primary artifact produced by a great engineering team.

For many, the act of sitting down to write the code was the critical step where their understanding of the problem space would SLOWLY be formalized, picked apart, and rearranged. The codebase simply provided a consistent and objective way to distribute the fruits of individual reasoning efforts to the wider team. The design discussions, frantic bug hunts, and PR reviews were core activities that served to deepen a team's understanding of how their particular problem could, and should, be solved.

At the end of it all, yes, the codebase "did the thing" (ideally). Hooray. The more important outcome was that there was now a formalized solution to the original problem, and likely many adjacent issues. Such a repository of distilled technical intent enabled later generations of engineers within the same company/group/project/community to leverage the hard-won mental models of their forebears, and ultimately drive forward the collective understanding.

Where it all went wrong

Since AI-written code became "good enough" to feasibly reach production in early 2026, many of us have been aware of the slow decline of this feedback loop that sustains our industries, livelihoods, and passions. For most of us, days now consist of prompting an LLM to produce code that satisfies a particular business need. Usually via written English. I can't speak for the entire development community, but I can personally attest to this having degraded my ability to write code by hand.

One could play devil's advocate and say something along the lines of: if LLMs can write all the code now, then why does it matter if we lose the ability to do so ourselves? To which I would say: it shouldn't really matter, provided we are able to maintain the cycle of capturing individual understanding in a manner that may be easily consumed by peers.

At last, we arrive at the core of the problem. By degrading/losing the ability to write code, we become disconnected from the act of translating ideas and intent into verifiable formalized logic that is useful to others.

The problem with natural language

How many of us regularly chat to our LLMs using the most horrendous, broken English we can possibly conceive out of sheer laziness? I'm definitely guilty! Even if you are one of the few who maintain a high quality of communication in your prompts, written/spoken language is a famously imprecise method of communication (cough synonyms cough cough).

I challenge you to try to write a system specification in your language of choice that makes explicit all assumptions and ignored details, yet leaves no room for alternate interpretations of the details that are captured. It is unlikely that you will succeed to a degree that allows you to hand that specification to an LLM and get a result that satisfies your intent.

If your system is simple enough that you do achieve an initially satisfactory result, you will inevitably discover some edge case that needs addressing. At that point, you could either adjust the written specification and have AI regenerate the implementation from scratch, which would likely resolve the issue, but also leave you with an entirely different system (unless your written spec is absurdly long and detailed).

Or you could simply ask the LLM to patch the change into the existing implementation via a quick prompt. A prompt whose core ideas are never properly understood, refined, and formalized into the collective human understanding of the project. Even if you do take the time to update the specification, fixing the edge case in isolation from the rest of the system introduces drift that severely degrades (even destroys) the spec's trustworthiness.

To illustrate the hilarity of the current prevailing approach to software specification, imagine an architect giving a construction team nothing more than a written description of the building! If natural language were precise enough to facilitate proper specifications, we wouldn't need lawyers to disambiguate the legal system for us average folk.

Formal methods and TLA+

So what do we do? How do we plug the AI-shaped hole in the bottom of the bucket that used to hold the collective knowledge of our field? Honestly, I don't know. However, my desire for a solution to this conundrum has led me deep into the formal methods rabbit hole over the past year. On my journey, I've picked up a few techniques/tools that have begun to help me address my concerns with LLM-assisted development.

One such tool that has been especially beneficial is TLA+. It was originally created by Leslie Lamport, and proves once again just how far ahead of his time he was. I'm not going to dive into an explanation of TLA+ here as it's already been done far better than I ever could, by the man himself. I highly recommend taking a moment to read Lamport's high-level view of TLA+ over on his website before proceeding. For those of you who will not heed my advice (shame), TLA+ is a language based on formal mathematical notation that allows one to create precise models of anything that can be represented as a state machine (everything, with a bit of creativity). It ships alongside TLC, which can be used to exhaustively explore logical paths within your models, and find design issues.

TLA+ is NOT code; it is mathematics. Before you recoil in disgust, here's an excerpt from Lamport's website that explains why this is so:

TLA+ teaches you that math is inherently more expressive than programming languages because it can describe a value without having to describe how the value is computed.  For example, it can describe the greatest common divisor (GCD) of two numbers as the largest positive integer that divides both numbers. This makes it possible to write a model for a specific purpose, abstracting away irrelevant details such as how to calculate the GCD. (Putting code in a procedure doesn't abstract it away; it just makes you go elsewhere to read the code, requiring that you understand the semantics of procedure call as well as the code.)

In the context of a world in which AI writes the code, this is enormously important. It gives us a language in which we can elegantly capture our intent, without getting bogged down in implementation details that ultimately don't matter to the use case. A well-written TLA+ spec is a human-readable artifact that forces the author to reason through the system they are designing in a constrained and logical format, is easy for peers to digest and iterate upon, and is objectively machine checkable (via TLC) so that LLMs are given a concrete benchmark that implementations may be evaluated against.

The TLA+ model is the architectural blueprint that the design team argues over, iterates upon, and hands to the next generation as learning material, just as the codebase used to be. The code itself becomes a concern of the construction team (coding agents). The details of the implementation can be tied to the spec, preventing drift, with the use of strategies such as trace-checking and refinement mapping. I liken these processes to the surveyor who measures a new build against the numbers in the plans to ensure conformance.

Many readers might be thinking something along the lines of "if TLA+ is so great, why haven't I heard of it before?". TLA+, and the discipline of formal methods as a whole, has largely flown under the radar of the wider software engineering community, with the exception of niche teams within resource-rich industry titans such as Google and AWS. As far as I can tell, this is mostly due to the barrier to entry.

Engineers are trained to write code. Most gave their discrete mathematics classes only the bare minimum attention needed to pass their exams, then promptly forgot the skills once they entered the workforce. From the perspective of an engineering executive: why would I have my team spend time writing a model in TLA+ (or another specification language), when I could have them build the real solution in [insert programming language of choice]? Someone would have to write the code eventually anyway...

At the time, such arguments were perfectly reasonable. No matter how precise your formal spec, someone still has to write the executable code. Or rather, someTHING! Enter LLMs. On February 5th of this year (2026), Anthropic released Opus 4.6. It is widely considered the turning point for AI-assisted development; models could finally write code that was at least somewhat reasonable. We live in a world where, if we can produce testable specifications that sufficiently constrain the details of a system that matter to the use case, we can give AI an "abstract" model and receive a working implementation with very little human babysitting.

This is MUCH easier said than done, but TLA+ is an incredible step in the right direction. And given that so many engineers are no longer writing code themselves, one could argue that improving the quality and accuracy of our specifications is a core part of the job, in a way that it never was before. I have a hunch that this mentality shift will go a long way towards breaking down the perceived "barrier to entry" that has so limited the usefulness of formal methods to the wider software engineering community.

A TLA+ specification of the AWS Elastic Block Store API

My attention at Mulga is largely focused on the storage components of our stack, Predastore (S3-compatible object storage) and Viperblock (EBS-like virtual disks). In such projects, details are extraordinarily important, and ambiguity is to be avoided at all costs. When a user engages with something claiming to be a storage service, they assume that their data is in good hands and won't be carelessly lost. On top of this responsibility, the systems are complex and easy to lose track of under the tidal wave of AI-generated contributions.

I recently used TLA+ to write a specification of the observable behavior of a subset of AWS's EBS API. The intent was to solidify my understanding of the EBS volume lifecycle state machine, so that I can ensure Spinifex (our AWS-compatible control plane) is properly adhering to the behaviors expected by the AWS CLI for the EBS operations it exposes.

For the curious reader, the specification is open source and is available to read in the Viperblock GitHub repository. It's only ~400 lines (as of now), across 4 files! This is rather notable, considering the relevant (English) technical documentation published by AWS for these operations extends across 13 separate web pages, and still manages to leave a vast amount of detail up to the reader to discern. The specification's brevity makes sense as, naturally, a written description of a building would take up far more space than a blueprint capturing the relevant details! Some request/response fields, possible error codes, and features have been abstracted out of this initial version, of course, but the core volume/attachment status state machines are captured very clearly. You do not need to be a career mathematician to make fantastic use of TLA+!

A common question I receive is "can't AI just write the TLA+ too?". Well, yes... technically. However, I'd argue there's not really any value in doing things that way. If an AI writes it, you're right back to relying on prompts that nobody has rigorously thought through, and that are invisible to colleagues and mentees.

TLA+ is ultimately a tool for the communication of ideas, in the same way that the legal system uses a constrained version of natural language to avoid confusion and mathematicians use formal notation. The power in a specification language built upon said mathematical notation is its innate ability to be applied effectively at any level of abstraction. If all you have is a vague idea of how the system you wish to build should appear to a user, that is enough to write a solid specification. There is plenty of room later to refine, and add detail that was missed (or deemed unimportant) on the first pass. This can extend as far down as the electrons themselves, if such detail is relevant to your problem space.

To illustrate this idea, here is the part of my EBS specification that captures the subset of the observable behavior of the CreateVolume operation that I was particularly interested in:

\* A client requested a new volume.
CreateVolume(req, res) ==
  /\ req \in CreateVolumeRequests
  /\ LET PossibleErrors(db) == Errors({})
         PossibleRecords    == [status             : {"creating"},
                                \* After enabling encryption by default, CreateVolume may still
                                \* see a stale value from another replica for a short window.
                                encrypted          : {db.encryptedByDefault : db \in VisibleDBs},
                                multiAttachEnabled : {FALSE}]
        \* The request was accepted.
     IN \/ /\ PossibleErrors(CurrentDB) = {}
           /\ \E vId \in VolumeIds \ usedIds, record \in PossibleRecords :
                /\ Commit([CurrentDB EXCEPT !.volumes = InsertKey(@, vId, record)])
                /\ res = [vId |-> vId] @@ record
        \* The request was rejected, possibly by a stale replica.
        \/ /\ \E db \in VisibleDBs : res \in PossibleErrors(db)
           /\ UNCHANGED vars

Some information to aid in reading this excerpt: /\ and \/ can be read as AND and OR respectively; curly braces represent a set; == is a definition; = is a comparison; the lines that begin with \E are checking whether an element exists in a target set that satisfies the condition after the :. The comments give enough of the gist that the rest of the syntax can be glossed over. Specifics can be found at learntla.com. It helps to think of a TLA+ spec as one big condition in an if statement that you would find in a traditional programming language.

This operator (an action in TLA+ terms) contains very little detail about how exactly a volume is created. In fact, throughout my entire spec, the concept of a "volume" being a virtual disk that bytes can be read from and written to is not captured anywhere! This is because it was not relevant to the control plane operations that I was concerned with at the time. I simply abstracted it away.

A final anecdote: while writing the EBS control plane model, I found myself unable to glean all of the information required to get a good picture of the possible volume status transitions from the AWS docs. This drove me to run some tests myself, and led to the discovery that a volume whose status is "creating" can immediately transition to "deleting" without first passing through "error" in certain cases. This is undocumented behavior that is extremely valuable to me in the design of Viperblock.

What's next?

At the time of writing, the spec only captures a few particularly important EBS API endpoints. I'm currently working on using TLC to trace-check my model against the real EBS API to verify that it is correct. The plan is to then trace-check Spinifex's EBS API implementation against the verified model, and fix the divergences that will inevitably be surfaced! From there I will extend the model to capture all EBS API operations that Spinifex supports, and repeat the trace-checking process.

This was not the article I initially set out to write. I'd intended to cover far more technical detail and dive deeper into the structure of the spec itself, the trace-checking methodology, and my ideas around how formal specification may be feasibly brought into the industry as a standard practice. However, in explaining my experiences to friends and colleagues, I realized that such content would not be very useful to the engineering community if I didn't first attempt to give the "why" behind the methods. Alas, the rest will have to wait for future articles.

If I have sufficiently piqued your interest, rest assured that you will not be waiting long for the next installment in this saga. So stay tuned. Until next time!

Bryn

title: We pointed AI testing agents at our own apps. 36/100, 79 issues. Here is what they found and what we fixed.
description:
Disclosure first: I'm on the team behind Preetest, an AI website-testing platform built by Yamama Software (Saudi Arabia). This post is about running that platform on Yamama Software's own apps. These are our own apps scanned with our own platform, not an independent audit. Every number below comes from a real report; the report links are public (they open behind a cookie-consent prompt you can decline, so I have also put a screenshot of each report's summary page below). This write-up was drafted by the AI assistant that runs our testing and fixes, from those reports, at the founder's direction.

What Preetest is, in one paragraph

Preetest is a platform, not a company. You give it a URL (and a login if the app needs one). It runs AI testing agents, each with a specialty (accessibility, performance, security headers, mobile layout, SEO, forms, caching and so on; the platform lists 17 specialties, and each of the standard runs below used 9 agents covering 8 of 14 aspects), and writes one report: a score out of 100, every issue with severity and the element it was found on, and a fix prompt per issue that you can paste into Cursor, Claude Code or whatever you build with.

Run 1: our internal office suite

A 10-page signed-in scan of the staff suite we use ourselves (documents, mail, calendar, chat).

Score: 36/100. 79 issues: 0 critical, 3 high, 31 medium, 45 low, 0 info. Known-screen coverage 44 %.
Report: https://app.preetest.com/r/z1LctGGKyBvPlZIcTkeh4w

The findings that mattered:

  • Every static file was served with Cache-Control: max-age=0. Every visit re-downloaded every script. High severity, and correct.
  • The cross-app sign-in put the user's email and name in a GET ?t= parameter. Medium. Also correct; that lands in server logs and browser history.
  • The "export all my data" action was a plain GET link with no confirmation. Medium.
  • Bottom navigation at 390 px wide cut off the "Mail" label. Low, but it is the first thing a phone user sees.

Run 2: the same app, after two small fixes. The score went down.

We fixed the export confirmation and one accessible-name issue, re-ran with the same settings, and got 29/100. 101 issues: 0 critical, 8 high, 35 medium, 57 low, 1 info (the report's issue card shows 100, because it does not count the info item). Known-screen coverage 51 %.
Report: https://app.preetest.com/r/AIykp03BiPhDdXf2jn-Lww

Why worse? The second run reached more screens (the calendar, the staff guide, the privacy and download pages), so it found more. Coverage is budget-based: each run stops when its token reservation runs out, and the two runs stopped at different pages. So this is not a clean before/after, and I am not going to present it as one. What the second run added was the most useful finding of the day:

  • The calendar had 49 column-header cells with no role="row" parent, and 42 day buttons using aria-pressed, which their role does not support. Plus text at 4.12:1 contrast where 4.5:1 is required.
  • LCP of 4.7 s on the documents page. The assistant greeting waited on about 1.5 MB of scripts.

Run 3: a small Expo web app

Score: 53/100. 27 issues: 0 critical, 5 high, 11 medium, 10 low, 1 info (the issue card shows 26 for the same reason). 100 % known-screen coverage, 143 tokens used.
Report: https://app.preetest.com/r/BTlW0oUUg-ybJZQxCpPyKA

  • Unknown URLs returned 200 instead of 404 (soft 404). High.
  • No header / main / footer / nav landmarks. High.
  • The onboarding "Next" control was not exposed as a button to screen readers. High.
  • sitemap.xml served as HTML; a JSON data file served with no caching.

What we changed, and how much of it is proven

Plainly: none of the fixes below has been confirmed by a Preetest re-run yet. The only full rescan we did after fixing anything is run 2 above, and it scored lower because it covered more screens. There is no improvement to show, implied or otherwise. What follows is what we changed and how we checked each change ourselves.

Changed, and verified by us (not by the platform):

  • Calendar ARIA: headers and weeks now sit inside role="row", day cells use aria-selected, arrow keys move between days. Verified with axe-core on that page: 92 ARIA violations plus 33 contrast failures before, 0 after.
  • Contrast: the faint purple went from #7c6fd6 (4.12:1) to #5a4cc0 (6.5:1). Verified by computing the ratio.
  • Mobile bar: five apps plus a "More" button. Verified with our own screenshots at 360, 390 and 412 px; nothing cut off.
  • Caching: versioned JS/CSS now sent with a one-year cache header. Verified by reading the response headers; a repeat visit to the documents page renders in under a second in our timing.
  • Expo app: unknown URLs now return a real 404 status, the page has landmarks, "Next" has a real button role, sitemap.xml is served as XML, versioned files get a long cache. Verified with HTTP requests and a DOM check, not with a rescan.
  • A bug the 404 fix exposed: 19 icon font files had been missing from the deploy the whole time. The old catch-all returned an HTML page with status 200 for them, so nothing ever errored. Restored and checksum-checked. Soft 404s hide real breakage; that one finding paid for the run.

Not fixed, or not proven:

  • The documents page first load is still about 4 s. Only repeat visits got faster.
  • We moved the sign-in token out of the URL, but have not yet tested a real signed-in hop between apps with a staff account, so I am not calling it fixed.
  • No Preetest rescan since the bigger fixes, so there is no "after" score. When there is one, I will add it here, whichever way it goes.

Where the agents were wrong

  • It flagged /api/config on the Expo app as "returns private data with no auth". It returns public settings (app name, support links, public client ids). False positive.
  • It flagged a missing aria-current on the docs sidebar. The source already renders it on the active button.
  • It flagged noindex on the internal editor as high. That is intended; it is a staff tool.

So: a sharp junior QA that works at 3 a.m., not an oracle. Read the report, do not paste every fix prompt blindly.

Pricing, honestly

The free plan is 50 tokens. Our smallest real run above used 143, so the free tokens get you a project set up and a look at the flow, not a full inspection. A standard inspection is roughly 1,000 tokens, which is the $29/month plan. The platform also refuses to scan its own domain, so you cannot run it on preetest.com.

If you try it on your own app, I would genuinely like to hear where it was wrong. That list above is the one we work from.

Honest reviews wanted (from the Preetest team)

We are collecting reviews from people who actually used Preetest, good or bad.

Try it on your own site, then write a review on Trustpilot: https://www.trustpilot.com/evaluate/preetest.com. We give one month of the Starter plan ($29) free for a published review. The month is for writing a review, not for a rating: a 1-star review with real reasons gets it exactly like a 5-star one. Please say in the review that you received free access.

To have enough tokens for a full scan, sign up through https://app.preetest.com/register?ref=KJZDCYB4 (adds 300 bonus tokens to the 50 free ones once you confirm your email).

Email preetest.team@mail.tab.bot with the address you signed up with and the link to your review.

title: TIL: GBase Database Silent Installation Doesn't Mean the Instance Is Ready
description:
A silent installation of GBase Database(GBase 8s) can finish successfully without leaving you with a database instance that's ready for use.

This is an easy detail to overlook when automating database deployment. The installer may complete the software installation, but instance configuration and initialization depend on the installation method and the steps defined in your deployment workflow.

What Happens After Silent Installation?

Before treating a GBase Database installation as complete, review these areas:

1. Configure environment variables

Set the environment variables required by the target instance. Confirm that the installation directory and instance-specific settings point to the correct locations.

2. Review onconfig

Check the instance configuration file and make sure its settings are appropriate for the target server.

3. Configure sqlhosts

Verify the connection definitions, including the server name, protocol, and configured service or port.

4. Initialize and start the instance if required

If your installation procedure does not already create and initialize the instance, follow the documented initialization process using the designated database operating system account.

For example, oninit -ivy is an initialization command used in applicable GBase Database(GBase 8s) procedures. Do not run it blindly on an existing or already initialized instance; confirm the correct procedure for your installation method first.

Automate the Entire Workflow

The important distinction is between installing database software and delivering a usable database service.

For batch deployment, your automation should account for every required stage:

  • Software installation
  • Environment configuration
  • Instance configuration
  • Instance initialization, where necessary
  • Startup and connectivity checks
  • Error handling and deployment logging

A successful installer exit code alone does not prove that the database can accept client connections.

After deployment, verify the instance status and test connectivity before reporting the server as ready. If any validation step fails, capture the relevant logs and stop the workflow rather than silently marking the deployment successful.

The Takeaway

Silent installation makes GBase Database(GBase 8s) deployment more repeatable, but the installer is only one part of the process.

True deployment automation covers the entire workflow, from software installation to a validated, usable database instance.

When automating GBase Database deployment, does your script stop after the installer finishes, or does it also verify instance readiness?

title: TIL: How to Record a Response File for GBase Database Silent Installation
description:
Writing a response file manually for GBase Database(GBase 8s) can be error-prone. A misspelled parameter or an unsupported value may cause problems when you automate the installation.

Fortunately, the installer can record your choices during an interactive installation and save them to a response file.

Record Your Installation Choices

Run the following command from the directory containing the installer:

./ids_install -r /opt/bundle.properties

Follow the interactive installation prompts as usual. The installer records the supported installation settings in /opt/bundle.properties, which you can then review and reuse for silent installation.

Depending on the installer version, the recorded settings may include the installation directory, selected components, and other installation options.

Why Record Instead of Starting from Scratch?

This approach offers three practical benefits.

1. Fewer manual errors

You don't have to guess every parameter name or construct the entire response file from memory.

2. A useful starting point

The response file is generated from an actual installation workflow, giving you a practical configuration to review before automating deployment.

3. Easier customization

After recording the file, you can inspect it and adjust the settings required for your target environment.

One important caveat: a recorded response file is not automatically guaranteed to work on every server. Review the parameters, confirm any required license-acceptance setting, and check for paths or options that differ between environments.

A Practical Workflow for GBase Database

For batch deployment of GBase Database(GBase 8s), use this sequence:

  1. Record a representative interactive installation.
  2. Review the generated response file.
  3. Adjust and validate the required parameters.
  4. Test silent installation on a single target machine.
  5. Reuse the validated configuration for additional servers.

The key idea is simple: record first, review second, automate third.

This workflow reduces unnecessary manual editing and provides a more reliable starting point for repeatable database deployment.

Have you tried recording an installation response file, or do you usually build yours manually?

title: Declared value is an allowlist sum, not a total you defend
description:
A valuation service that adds up invoice lines is implementing the wrong shape. 19 CFR 152.103 builds dutiable value from a base plus a fixed set of additions, and the regulation says the additions cover those items and no others, counted only to the extent they are not already inside the base. That is an allowlist with a de-duplication rule, which is a very different data structure from a sum.

The model 

type ChargeKind =
  | 'goods'
  | 'packingBuyer'          // 152.103(b)(1)(i)
  | 'sellingCommissionBuyer' // (ii)
  | 'assist'                 // (iii)
  | 'royaltyConditionOfSale' // (iv)
  | 'resaleProceedsToSeller' // (v)
  | 'foreignInlandFreight'   // excluded only under 152.102(a)(5) conditions
  | 'internationalFreight'
  | 'merchantDiscount'
  | 'unclassified';

type Charge = {
  kind: ChargeKind;
  amount: number;
  currency: 'USD';
  separatelyStated: boolean;
  incurredBy: 'buyer' | 'seller';
  evidence?: 'throughBillOfLading' | 'other';
};

The unclassified member is the honest one. Any charge the ingestion step cannot name lands there, and the pipeline must fail rather than silently include or exclude it. A model with no unknown bucket is a model that guesses.

The additions are a closed set 

const ADDITIVE: ReadonlySet<ChargeKind> = new Set([
  'packingBuyer', 'sellingCommissionBuyer', 'assist',
  'royaltyConditionOfSale', 'resaleProceedsToSeller',
]);

function dutiableValue(charges: Charge[]): number {
  const base = charges.filter((c) => c.kind === 'goods').reduce((n, c) => n + c.amount, 0);
  let value = base;
  for (const c of charges) {
    if (c.kind === 'unclassified') throw new Error('UNCLASSIFIED_CHARGE: cannot value');
    if (!ADDITIVE.has(c.kind)) continue;
    if (c.incurredBy !== 'buyer' && c.kind !== 'resaleProceedsToSeller') continue;
    value += c.amount;
  }
  return value;
}

Two details in that loop come straight from the text rather than from taste. The buyer-incurred test is there because the packing and selling commission items are worded as costs incurred by the buyer, while the royalty item is worded as a fee the buyer is required to pay as a condition of the sale for export. And the base already contains whatever the parties priced in, so an addition that is inside the invoice total should not be added twice. If the ingestion step cannot tell which case it has, the charge belongs in unclassified.

Freight is a documentation predicate

A foreign inland freight line does not become excludable just because someone typed it on its own row. Under 152.102(a)(5) the exclusion needs two facts at once. The charge has to appear as a separate item, and it has to arise after the goods were sold for export to the United States and handed to a carrier for through shipment. Proof of that second fact runs through a through bill of lading, with other paperwork available only where using one clearly would have been impossible.

function freightExcludable(c: Charge, seq: { soldForExportAt: Date; handedToCarrierAt: Date }): boolean {
  if (!c.separatelyStated) return false;
  if (seq.handedToCarrierAt < seq.soldForExportAt) return false;
  if (c.evidence === 'throughBillOfLading') return true;
  return false;   // 'other' needs the impossibility record, which is a human call
}

The last branch returns false on purpose rather than trusting a string. The impossibility route exists, but it is a documented exception rather than a document type, and a service that treats other as equivalent to a through bill of lading has quietly deleted the condition.

Note the direction of the correction as well. The same section points the other way too. If checking reveals that a foreign inland freight figure, or an equivalent international shipment charge, was padded, the appraiser can still add the difference back into dutiable value. Overstating a deductible line is not conservative. It is a different error with the same endpoint.

The order of methods is a resolver chain

152.101(b) fixes the sequence: transaction value, then identical merchandise, then similar, then deductive, then computed, then a residual method consistent with the subpart's principles. A resolver that lets an operator pick a method has modeled a preference rather than a rule.

const METHOD_ORDER = ['transactionValue', 'identical', 'similar', 'deductive', 'computed', 'residual'] as const;

function resolve(charges: Charge[]): { method: typeof METHOD_ORDER[number]; value: number } {
  try { return { method: 'transactionValue', value: dutiableValue(charges) }; }
  catch { /* fall through to the next method only because this one could not be determined */ }
  throw new Error('MANUAL_METHOD_SELECTION_REQUIRED');
}

The fallbacks each have their own inputs, and none of them is "the number we would like". 152.108 removes the convenient bases outright, including the US selling price of domestically produced goods, any system that appraises at the higher of two alternative values, and the price in the exporter's domestic market. A shop-floor shortcut like "use the Amazon price minus a margin" is the first of those with extra steps.

What the warehouse layer contributes

FulfillNexa by SBT (fulfillnexa.com) records weights, counts and packing configuration per SKU at receipt across three sites, the largest being Suzhou at 13,000 square meters, then Dongguan at 8,000 and Shenzhen at 3,000. That record is evidence rather than a valuation. It lets a packing cost be identified separately and dated, which is the condition the exclusion turns on. The declared number stays the seller's, and the log is what makes it defensible rather than merely stated.

title: A lab acceptance is a validity range per rule, not a flag on the vendor
description:
Most systems that store test records model laboratory status as a boolean on a vendor row. is_accredited = true. That column is wrong in a specific way: 16 CFR part 1112 grants acceptance per rule or test method, the scope can be extended later, and it can be suspended for one slice of the scope while the rest stands. A boolean cannot represent any of that.

The correct shape is a range table keyed by rule, with the test date checked against it.

The schema 

CREATE TABLE cab (
  id            BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  legal_name    TEXT NOT NULL,
  address       TEXT NOT NULL,
  -- independent | firewalled | government, per 1112.11
  cab_kind      TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (cab_kind IN ('independent','firewalled','government'))
);

CREATE TABLE cab_acceptance (
  id            BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  cab_id        BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES cab(id),
  cpsc_rule_id  TEXT NOT NULL,           -- the rule, not a product category
  accepted_from DATE NOT NULL,
  accepted_to   DATE,                    -- NULL means currently open
  status        TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('active','suspended','withdrawn','discontinued')),
  source_url    TEXT NOT NULL,           -- where the listing said so
  observed_on   DATE NOT NULL            -- the day this row was read, not asserted
);

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX acceptance_one_open_window_per_rule
  ON cab_acceptance (cab_id, cpsc_rule_id, COALESCE(accepted_to, DATE '9999-12-31'));

The observed_on column is the one people skip. Section 1112.19 has the Commission maintain a listing and update it as scopes change, so every row here is an observation with a date attached, not a fact about the world. A pipeline that overwrites observed_on with now() on every write has thrown away the only field that lets you reconstruct what was known on the test date.

The test record 

CREATE TABLE test_record (
  id            BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  product_id    BIGINT NOT NULL,
  cpsc_rule_id  TEXT NOT NULL,
  tested_on     DATE NOT NULL,
  prime_cab_id  BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES cab(id),
  -- 1112.25: subcontracted work must be identifiable in the prime report
  performed_by  JSONB NOT NULL DEFAULT '[]',   -- [{cab_id, tests: [...]}]
  report_uri    TEXT NOT NULL
);

The gate query

A test result counts only if the body held acceptance for that rule on that date. That is a join with a range predicate, and it has to run before the certificate row is considered complete.

SELECT t.id
  FROM test_record t
 WHERE NOT EXISTS (
         SELECT 1
           FROM cab_acceptance a
          WHERE a.cab_id = t.prime_cab_id
            AND a.cpsc_rule_id = t.cpsc_rule_id
            AND a.status = 'active'
            AND a.accepted_from <= t.tested_on
            AND (a.accepted_to IS NULL OR a.accepted_to >= t.tested_on)
       );

Zero rows is the pass condition. A non-empty result means the file cites a test whose scope line does not cover the rule, or covers it on a date outside the window. Both look identical in a system that stores is_accredited.

The same predicate is what catches a suspension that lands later. Refresh the acceptance windows on a schedule, rerun the query against existing certificates, and a report that was valid when issued can surface as invalid now. That is not a bug in the file. It is the file being current.

Subcontracting

performed_by exists because 1112.25 requires the prime contractor's report to identify which tests a CPSC-accepted body acting as a subcontractor performed. A single PDF from a trading company that consolidated three laboratories does not satisfy that as data. Model it as an array of (cab_id, tests) and let the same range predicate run over each entry rather than only over the name on the cover page.

type Attribution = { cabId: number; tests: string[] };

function unresolvedParts(t: TestRecord, windows: AcceptanceWindow[]): string[] {
  const covered = new Set<number>();
  for (const w of windows) {
    if (w.status === 'active' && w.acceptedFrom <= t.testedOn &&
        (w.acceptedTo === null || w.acceptedTo >= t.testedOn)) covered.add(w.cabId);
  }
  return t.performedBy
    .flatMap((a: Attribution) => a.tests.map((name) => ({ cabId: a.cabId, name })))
    .filter((row) => !covered.has(row.cabId))
    .map((row) => `${row.name}@${row.cabId}`);
}

unresolvedParts().length === 0 is the assertion worth putting in CI for the ingestion job, because the failure mode is silent. A missing attribution reads as a complete report.

Retention, and what it is not

Section 1112.25 makes the laboratory hold its own test reports and technical records for section 14 tests for at least five years from the date the test was conducted. That is the lab's duty on its own copies. It is not a license to delete your side after five years, and it is not a statement that a report older than five years is unusable. The date that starts the clock is the test date rather than the shipment date, so a slow-moving SKU can carry a report whose retention window closed while the goods were still on the shelf.

FulfillNexa by SBT (fulfillnexa.com) runs the inbound scan at three China facilities, floor area 13,000 square meters in Suzhou, 8,000 in Dongguan and 3,000 in Shenzhen, where one carton resolves to one product identifier before it resolves to a test file. That is the same join in the other direction. Whatever the storage layer looks like, the question at the dock is identical to the question in the query above. Which body ran this test, against which rule, on which date.

title: TIL: GBase Database Silent Installation Requires License Acceptance
description:
Today, I ran a silent installation of GBase Database(GBase 8s), only to have it fail on the first attempt. The cause? The license acceptance parameter was missing.

It is a small configuration detail, but it can stop an unattended installation before deployment gets anywhere.

Why Does License Acceptance Matter?

Unlike an interactive installation, silent installation has no graphical prompt where an operator can review and accept the license during execution. The required acceptance must be provided explicitly through the supported installation parameters.

For a GBase Database(GBase 8s) silent installation, the response file may contain:

LICENSE_ACCEPTED = TRUE

Alternatively, you can pass the parameter directly in the installation command:

./ids_install -i silent \
  -f /opt/bundle.properties \
  -DLICENSE_ACCEPTED=TRUE

Confirm the exact parameter name and syntax against the documentation for your installation package, and make sure the applicable license terms have actually been reviewed and accepted before setting the value to TRUE.

Make It Part of Your Deployment Standard

When deploying GBase Database across multiple servers, a missing parameter can cause repeated failures and unnecessary troubleshooting.

To avoid this:

  • Include the required license-acceptance setting in your response file template.
  • Validate the response file before running a batch deployment.
  • Test the complete installation procedure on one machine first.
  • Check the installer logs and exit status rather than assuming the installation succeeded.

The broader lesson goes beyond licensing: every confirmation required by an interactive installation must be handled explicitly in an unattended workflow.

For reliable GBase Database deployment automation, small prerequisites deserve the same attention as installation paths, component selection, and post-installation configuration.

Have you ever lost time debugging a silent installation because of one missing parameter?

title: Batch Deploying GBase Database with a Response File
description:
Deploying GBase Database(GBase 8s) across multiple servers can become repetitive if every installation requires manual interaction. A response file provides a more consistent approach by defining installation parameters once and reusing them across deployment targets.

Combined with shell scripts and remote execution tools such as SSH, silent installation can become part of a repeatable database deployment workflow.

The goal is not simply to install software faster. It is to make the deployment process easier to validate, maintain, and reproduce.

1. Prepare the Response File

Start by preparing a bundle.properties response file using the template supplied with your GBase Database installation media or by recording a supported interactive installation.

Review the installation directory, selected components, license-acceptance settings, and any other required parameters.

Before deploying to multiple machines, test the response file on one representative server. Confirm that the installation succeeds and that the resulting database instance can be configured and started correctly.

Keep environment-specific settings separate where necessary. Different servers may require different paths, resource configurations, or connection definitions.

2. Create a Reusable Installation Script

The following Bash example checks for the response file and installer before starting silent installation.

#!/bin/bash
set -Eeuo pipefail

RESP="/opt/bundle.properties"
INSTALLER="/opt/ids_install"

# Verify required files
[[ -f "$RESP" ]] || {
    echo "ERROR: Missing response file: $RESP" >&2
    exit 1
}

[[ -x "$INSTALLER" ]] || {
    echo "ERROR: Installer is missing or not executable: $INSTALLER" >&2
    exit 1
}

# Run silent installation
"$INSTALLER" -i silent \
    -f "$RESP" \
    -DLICENSE_ACCEPTED=TRUE

echo "Silent installation command completed."

Save the script as install_gbase.sh and make it executable:

chmod +x install_gbase.sh

The script uses set -Eeuo pipefail to help detect command failures and prevent certain errors from being silently ignored.

The installer command shown here is an example. Confirm its supported options and license-acceptance requirements against the documentation for your specific installation package.

Also note that a successful installer exit does not necessarily mean the database instance is ready for application connections. Post-installation configuration and validation remain necessary.

3. Execute the Installation on Multiple Servers

For a small environment, SSH and SCP can distribute the response file and execute the installation script remotely.

For example:

#!/bin/bash
set -Eeuo pipefail

RESP="/opt/bundle.properties"
SCRIPT="/opt/install_gbase.sh"
HOSTS=(node1 node2 node3)

[[ -f "$RESP" ]] || {
    echo "ERROR: Missing response file" >&2
    exit 1
}

[[ -f "$SCRIPT" ]] || {
    echo "ERROR: Missing installation script" >&2
    exit 1
}

for host in "${HOSTS[@]}"; do
    echo "Deploying to $host..."

    scp "$RESP" "$SCRIPT" "root@$host:/opt/"

    ssh "root@$host" \
        "bash /opt/install_gbase.sh"

    echo "Installation command completed on $host."
done

This example processes the hosts sequentially, which makes execution easier to follow and failures easier to isolate.

Before using it, ensure that SSH authentication, host-key verification, remote permissions, and installation prerequisites are configured correctly.

The example also assumes that the installer is already available at /opt/ids_install on every target server. If it is not, include distribution and verification of the installation media in the deployment workflow.

Important: Running the installer as root should follow the supported installation procedure. Instance initialization may require switching to the designated database account, such as gbasedbt. Do not assume installation and initialization use the same account.

4. Add Post-Installation Configuration and Validation

Batch installation should not stop when the installer exits.

A complete GBase Database deployment workflow should also address:

  • Environment variables: Configure the required instance-specific environment.
  • Configuration files: Review onconfig and sqlhosts for the target server.
  • Instance initialization: Run the documented initialization procedure using the appropriate operating system account.
  • Service validation: Confirm that the instance starts and client connections succeed.
  • Logging: Record the host, installation result, and relevant diagnostic output.

These steps should be implemented according to the selected installation method and the requirements of your environment.

Avoid reporting a server as successfully deployed until the required validation checks have passed.

5. Make Batch Deployment Reproducible

For larger deployments, consider a few additional safeguards.

Version-control the response file and scripts. Review changes before they are used in production.

Protect sensitive configuration. Do not store passwords, private keys, or other secrets in ordinary response files or source repositories.

Control deployment concurrency. Start with sequential execution. Introduce parallel deployment only after validating resource requirements and failure handling.

Make reruns safe. Check whether a target already has an installation or running instance before executing the installer again. A failed deployment should not automatically trigger an unsafe reinstall.

Maintain a recovery procedure. Record installation logs and define how failed or partially completed deployments will be investigated and corrected.

For larger fleets, configuration-management tools can provide better inventory management, controlled concurrency, and centralized execution reporting than a collection of ad hoc shell commands.

Conclusion

Batch deployment of GBase Database(GBase 8s) starts with a validated response file and a reliable installation script. SSH and SCP can extend that workflow across multiple machines, while configuration management and automated checks help maintain consistency as the environment grows.

The essential principle is simple: standardize the installation inputs, validate the results, and make failures visible.

How does your team manage database deployments across multiple servers: shell scripts, SSH automation, or a configuration-management platform?

title: How to Give Claude & Cursor Safe Database Access Without Crashing Production (Zero-Trust MCP Guard in Python)
description:
How to Give Claude & Cursor Safe Database Access Without Crashing Production (Zero-Trust MCP Guard in Python)

Giving an AI assistant or autonomous agent access to a live database is one of the most powerful workflows for modern software teams: Claude Desktop, Cursor, or Windsurf can write complex analytics queries, optimize slow joins, and inspect schemas in seconds.

However, granting raw database credentials to an LLM is dangerous:

  • Accidental Disasters: One misaligned prompt or prompt injection can lead the agent to execute DROP TABLE, TRUNCATE, or unconstrained UPDATE / DELETE queries.
  • Production Freezes: A query missing a WHERE clause or missing an index on a million-row table can trigger a full sequential table scan, consuming 100% CPU and locking transactions.
  • PII Exposure: Raw customer records (plaintext emails, password hashes, credit cards) get pulled into prompt contexts and third-party LLM server logs.

The modern, standardized solution is to place a Zero-Trust Model Context Protocol (MCP) guard between your agent and the database engine.

In this guide, we will walk through how PgSafe MCP was engineered in Python to provide secure, read-only database exploration, forced LIMIT injection, real-time PII redaction, and dry-run mutation simulation.

The Zero-Trust MCP Architecture

Rather than connecting Claude directly to Postgres or SQLite with an unrestricted superuser connection, the MCP server acts as an intelligent firewall:

[ AI Agent: Claude / Cursor / Antigravity ]
                      │  JSON-RPC 2.0 (stdio)
                      ▼
             [ PgSafe MCP Server ]
                      │
           [ ReadOnlyGuard (AST Analysis) ]
           ├─ Blocks DROP, TRUNCATE, DELETE, ALTER
           └─ Blocks Semicolon Chaining
                      │
           [ CostAnalyzer (LIMIT Guard) ]
           ├─ Forces max 1,000 row limits
           └─ Warns on missing WHERE clauses
                      │
            [ Database Connection ]
            (PostgreSQL / SQLite / MySQL)
                      │
             [ Real-Time PII Masker ]
           ├─ Redacts emails (u***@domain.com)
           ├─ Masks credit cards (****-****-****-1234)
           └─ Redacts password hashes
                      │
                      ▼
[ Clean, Safe JSON-RPC Output to Agent ]

1. Enforcing Read-Only SQL Lexical Validation

A secure read-only guard must inspect every statement before it ever reaches the database cursor, stripping comments and blocking destructive keywords:

import re

BLOCKED_KEYWORDS = [
    r"\bDROP\b", r"\bTRUNCATE\b", r"\bDELETE\b",
    r"\bUPDATE\b", r"\bINSERT\b", r"\bALTER\b",
    r"\bCREATE\b", r"\bGRANT\b", r"\bREVOKE\b"
]

class ReadOnlyGuard:
    @staticmethod
    def validate(sql: str) -> tuple[bool, str]:
        # Disallow multi-statement injection (semicolon chaining)
        statements = [s.strip() for s in sql.split(";") if s.strip()]
        if len(statements) > 1:
            return False, "Semicolon chaining disallowed."

        # Verify query begins with read-only keyword
        first_word = statements[0].split()[0].upper()
        if first_word not in {"SELECT", "EXPLAIN", "WITH", "PRAGMA", "SHOW"}:
            return False, f"Statement '{first_word}' is forbidden."

        for pattern in BLOCKED_KEYWORDS:
            if re.search(pattern, sql, re.IGNORECASE):
                return False, "Destructive SQL operation detected."

        return True, "Query verified safe."

2. Dynamic LIMIT Injection

Runaway SELECT * FROM audit_logs queries can crash your client's memory. PgSafe intercepts every query and caps row limits:

import re

def enforce_limit(sql: str, default_limit: int = 100, max_limit: int = 1000) -> str:
    cleaned = sql.strip().rstrip(";")
    match = re.search(r"\bLIMIT\s+(\d+)\b", cleaned, re.IGNORECASE)
    if match:
        limit_val = int(match.group(1))
        if limit_val > max_limit:
            return re.sub(r"\bLIMIT\s+\d+\b", f"LIMIT {max_limit}", cleaned, flags=re.IGNORECASE)
        return cleaned
    return f"{cleaned} LIMIT {default_limit}"

3. Real-Time PII Redaction Before Agent Ingestion

When the query returns data, sensitive columns (password_hash, ssn, token) and customer PII are redacted on the fly:

import re

EMAIL_REGEX = re.compile(r"\b([A-Za-z0-9._%+-])[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]*@([A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Z|a-z]{2,})\b")
CARD_REGEX = re.compile(r"\b(?:\d{4}[-\s]?){3}(\d{4})\b")

def redact_pii(text: str) -> str:
    text = CARD_REGEX.sub(r"****-****-****-\1", text)
    text = EMAIL_REGEX.sub(r"\1***@\2", text)
    return text

4. Configuring Claude Desktop & Cursor

Add the server to your claude_desktop_config.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "pgsafe": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["-m", "pgsafe.server"],
      "cwd": "/path/to/pgsafe-mcp",
      "env": {
        "DATABASE_URL": "postgresql://user:pass@localhost:5432/my_db"
      }
    }
  }
}

Now you can prompt Claude:

"Inspect the orders table, find the top 5 customers with pending invoices, and suggest indexes to speed up this query."

Enterprise Edition: Dry-Run Mutation Simulation Harness

When agents need to draft data mutations or migrations, the Enterprise Pro edition includes an isolated simulation harness:

  • Executes INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE queries within an isolated transaction.
  • Returns row diffs, affected count, and execution time.
  • Guarantees auto-ROLLBACK: changes are never committed to your database.
  • Includes automatic index recommendation advisors and Docker Compose setups.

Downloads and Packages:

  • Lite Version (Open Source): Read-only guard and SQLite/Postgres schema inspection.
  • Enterprise Pro Edition ($14.99): PII masking, dry-run mutation simulation, index advisor, Docker Compose, and automated test suite.
