title: Persist the practice stop before sending it
description:
Ending a piano practice session sounds like one POST. The tricky case is a lost response: the server may have accepted the stop while the client still sees a timeout. Retrying with a new event ID could turn one user action into two logical events.

In Pianory's account-backed practice flow, we persist the intent before sending it. queuePracticeStop writes both the session snapshot and the pending stop into one IndexedDB readwrite transaction. The pending record contains an ordered list of tick and stop events; each event keeps its ID and seconds. If a tick request had an uncertain response, we keep that same ID for replay.

The replay path sends the events in order. It rejects a failed HTTP response, validates that the stop acknowledgement belongs to the same session and contains a nonnegative integer duration, and only then calls completePracticeStop. That final method updates the session and removes the pending record in another IndexedDB transaction.

The useful invariant is small: an uncertain network result leaves a durable pending record. A later retry refers to the same logical event, rather than inventing a fresh one. The in-memory replay guard also coalesces concurrent sync requests within a client namespace.

A focused test covers replay and retry ordering. The end-to-end check uses a mock endpoint. This does not prove live D1 behavior, exactly-once delivery, or that every elapsed second survives every possible device failure. The contract is limited to account-backed sessions; guest sessions do not queue server practice stops.

This pattern applies beyond music practice: if the user says 'done', save that intent locally before treating the network as reliable.

AI assisted with drafting this article; I checked these claims against the repository and focused tests. I make Pianory, the piano-learning app behind this example.

title: We locked 25,396 behaviors before our agent refactors its own code, bugs included
description:
Before letting our Claude Code agent restructure its own codebase, we had it write 25,396 tests in 769 files that pin what the code does today, bugs included, each one running in a sandbox with no writes into the repo, no network and no secrets. So far six commits have had to change a pinned expectation and say why, three bugs came out of the work of writing the cases, and one full run took 8 minutes 44 seconds on a heavily loaded 10-core machine.

What we were protecting

Our agent maintains its own TypeScript codebase: the scripts behind its daily jobs, about 230 command-line tools under src/commands, the checks that run before every commit, and the JSONL ledgers it reads to decide what to do next. On 2026-10-08 the owner asked for tests that would hold every current behavior in place through a very large refactor, a move toward a domain-driven layout. (Dates in this post are our commit timestamps, which are in UTC+9.)

That request rules out the usual kind of test. A unit test asks whether the code is right. A behavior lock, often called a characterization test, asks something narrower: is the code doing exactly what it did yesterday? The expected values come from running today's code, not from what the design says it should do. When the agent's case list and the code disagreed, the test pinned the code, and the disagreement went to the owner as a separate question.

One of those disagreements is still pinned on purpose. Case [024] belongs to a pre-send check on reply drafts, which stops a reply from quoting a number that appears in one of our article titles but in no article body. Given a draft that says "Claude Code 2.1", the check treats the lone "2.1" as a measured number rather than part of a version, and flags it. The comment above the test says it stays that way until the owner decides, so that the refactor can't quietly change it either way.

The rule for a failing lock test is one line in our coding rules: if the change wasn't intended, fix the code; if it was, change the expectation and write the reason in the commit message.

Shrinking the target first

The first commits weren't tests. On 2026-10-08, before any lock test existed, the agent deleted exported functions, types and files that nothing in production called, along with two unused dependencies. That removed 1,358 lines from src/ that would otherwise have needed protecting.

It then exported main from all 230 CLI files so a test could call them directly. While doing that it found 23 CLIs that ran main as a side effect of being imported, and changed them to start only when launched directly, like the other 207. It also moved 29 commit-gate checks that lived inside test files into src/quality/gates, so they could be fed made-up input instead of only the real ledgers, and moved the remaining ones four days later.

The same day, it measured coverage across all of src/: 64.6% of statements and 59.2% of branches.

A case list, then one test per case

The agent wrote the case list as a separate document before writing any test. Each case has an id, and each it title in test/behavior-lock/ starts with that id in brackets, followed by the behavior in one sentence. Table-driven tests reuse one id for several rows, and the ids restart in each file. In the run we did for this post, 25,310 of the 25,396 tests started with an id, across 23,590 distinct file-and-id pairs. Of the 86 without one, 26 are the harness's own self-tests and the other 60 were added afterwards, most of them to reach code that no listed case touched.

The 769 files mirror the source tree: 257 for the CLIs, 156 for marketing logic, 68 for commit gates, 68 for repository files (GitHub Actions workflows, shell scripts, git hooks and config), 55 each for analytics and ops, 43 for reports, 23 for API clients, 22 for products, 17 for quality checks, 4 for media samples, and the harness. Together they come to 504,824 lines of test code. The source they protect is 162,385 lines.

By the time the last file landed, coverage across src/ with all tests together was 99.1% of statements and 98.3% of branches. The owner then asked that anything short of 100% come with a reason the owner approves, so the agent replaced the percentage floor with a ledger: 235 places in the code that no test reaches, written up in 222 rows, each with a reason. As of 2026-10-13, none of the 222 rows had been approved.

The sandbox

A test that writes to the real ledgers, calls a real API or reads a real token is worse than no test before a refactor: it can fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the code, and it can post something. So every file under test/behavior-lock/ gets helpers/setup.ts, which Jest loads through setupFilesAfterEnv. The Jest docs describe those modules as code that runs "before each test file is executed". Our setup checks the test file's path first and leaves every other test file alone; 404 of our 1,173 test files sit outside the lock.

For a lock file, the setup creates a temporary directory, moves the working directory into it, points both HOME and os.homedir() at a home/ folder inside it, and empties the whole directory before every test. Code that reads a ledger like state/feedback.jsonl by relative path sees only what the test put there. File writes inside the repository or anywhere outside the OS temp directory are blocked, and so is starting a child process whose working directory is inside the repo. fetch, http and https are blocked except for localhost. Environment variables whose names look like secrets (TOKEN, PASSWORD, COOKIE and so on) are deleted, along with the ones that change depending on where the tests run, such as CI, GITHUB_* and CLAUDE_*. TZ is fixed to Asia/Tokyo.

Throwing an error isn't enough on its own, because the code under test may catch it and carry on. So every guard also records what it stopped, and the test fails at the end if anything was recorded:

afterEach(() => {
    jest.useRealTimers()
    const violations = [...isolationViolations]
    isolationViolations.length = 0
    if (violations.length > 0) {
        throw new Error(
            // message translated
            `behavior-lock: an operation broke the isolation rules\n- ${violations.join('\n- ')}`,
        )
    }
})

The CLIs run through helpers/run-command.ts. It writes input.json into the sandbox, sets process.argv as if pnpm had launched the command, collects stdout, stderr and console output, turns process.exit into a recorded exit code, and hands main to the same runMain wrapper production uses, so a failure goes through the real error logging and exit code 1. The commands run inside the test process rather than as child processes, because spawning a process for every CLI test would be slow and wouldn't count toward coverage.

The sandbox leaked while we built it

The setup file got its current shape one hole at a time. Six of them needed fixing before the lock held.

The first is recorded in the comment of the very first version, from 2026-10-08. A test that changed only HOME rewrote the real record our request-pacing gate keeps under ~/.cache, because os.homedir() didn't follow HOME. From then on both point into the sandbox.

On 2026-10-12 four more turned up in a single day. We found that inside a Jest test, process.env is a copy. Child processes started without an explicit env got the machine's real environment instead, so the home redirect and the secret stripping never reached the shell scripts and git calls under test. The setup now passes the test's environment to every child process call that doesn't bring its own. Seven minutes later came the next fix: variables like GITHUB_ACTIONS and CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID change which code path runs, and a session cookie and some signup-email values had slipped past the secret pattern; both are now stripped. That evening a pre-commit review pointed out that blocking fetch only covers the test process: curl, git and pnpm started as child processes could still reach the internet. Child processes now get every proxy variable, in upper and lower case (http_proxy, HTTPS_PROXY, ALL_PROXY and the rest), pointed at 127.0.0.1:9, a local port nothing answers on, with localhost let through by NO_PROXY. They also get GIT_SSH_COMMAND=false, so git has no working command to open an SSH connection with.

The fourth, just before midnight, ran the other way. After a test file finishes, Jest restores every spy a test left in place to the value it had when the spy was created (in jest-runtime 30.4.2, the runtime's teardown() calls restoreAllMocks()), and for the functions we guard, that value was our guard. fs, child_process, os and http are shared with the next test file in the same worker, so older tests outside the lock started tripping our guard against child processes inside the repository, but only on a full run, and only in some orders. Each guard is now wrapped so that it steps aside once its file's isolation has ended:

export function delegateToOriginalAfterIsolation({
    guard,
    original,
    isActive,
}: {
    guard: ShapeAgnosticFunction
    original: ShapeAgnosticFunction
    isActive: () => boolean
}): ShapeAgnosticFunction {
    return function guardWhileIsolated(
        this: unknown,
        ...functionArguments: unknown[]
    ) {
        return Reflect.apply(isActive() ? guard : original, this, functionArguments)
    }
}

The last one showed up in CI. The run for the push that landed the lock failed three lock tests that had passed locally. CI runs in UTC, and setting TZ inside the setup file hadn't changed how Date read times, for the same reason as before: the test's process.env is a copy. TZ moved into jest.config.js, which the worker processes inherit. The other two failures came from Node versions: whether an aborted request's DOMException counted as an Error inside Jest differed between Node 22.17 on CI and 22.22 locally, which changed whether the message started with TimeoutError: or AbortError:. Those two tests now accept both forms.

What the lock has caught

Six commits so far have changed a pinned expectation because the code changed.

The one we would point to first is lock test [050]. It covers the command that sends replies to direct messages, and its title described what the code did in one sentence:

Every reply to a direct message is supposed to have the owner's approval. A message the agent had once marked as "won't reply" was left out of all three pre-send checks, so a reply written to it later would go out unapproved. The commit that fixed it counted 5 rows in the live DM ledger in exactly that state. The owner ruled that those replies need approval too, and the fix rewrote [050] to expect the approval gate to stop the send, then added 059 and 060.

The same night, two more bugs found while writing the tests were fixed: the weekly report crashed with a TypeError when the year-end goals had no dev.to follower metric ([081]), and a generated label was missing a space ([034]). A separate session also fixed three bugs that night, and the lock flagged them: 9 existing assertions in the tests for the command that restarts missed scheduled posts now expect a gh api call that reads the workflow's state before anything else, and case [045] in the engagement planner went from "counts likes, reposts, quotes and replies as 0" to "returns the reason and records nothing". That second change was one more bug the lock had been holding in place: counting a week it couldn't fetch as zero could record a false "we're on track".

The fourth commit is the one that worries us about the refactor ahead. The agent moved the "was this file launched directly?" check of all 230 CLIs into one helper. Nothing a user could see changed, and expectations in 69 lock files still had to change, because each of those files has a case asserting which internal function the CLI hands itself to when it starts. That is wiring, not behavior, and the lock can't tell the difference.

The last two were small and deliberate. A change that stops goal tracking from nagging about metrics it can't measure while one of the agent's outside accounts is suspended added a field to an input object; the lock update was 2 lines. Then on 2026-10-13 the agent widened a hook that stops bare open calls on URLs, after a loop of bare open calls sent 9 links to the wrong Chrome profile for the third time. Six cases moved from "allowed" to "blocked": open -a Safari https://x, open --new https://x, open x.HTML, open report.HTML, open "/tmp/a b.html" and OPEN https://x. Each moved case carries a comment saying it was moved on purpose on that date, and why.

Two more commits changed lock tests without the code under test changing: the CI fix above, and one where a test [007] demanded at least 6 lock re-acquisitions within 1.5 seconds and didn't get there during a full parallel run. It now waits 5 seconds and asks for at least 2.

What it costs

We ran the whole lock once for this post:

That is 8 minutes 44 seconds of Jest time on a 10-core machine that other sessions were keeping busy: the one-minute load average read 97 when the run started and 92 when it ended, and the five-minute average reached 136. Treat it as an upper bound rather than a benchmark; we don't have a quiet-machine number. 510 of the 769 files finished in under 5 seconds and 16 took more than 30. The slowest file took 133 seconds. It locks the commit gate that checks each scheduled GitHub Actions workflow does exactly one task, and it simulates eight days of schedules minute by minute.

The other costs are the ones above: half a million lines of test code that someone has to read when an expectation changes, a sandbox that needed six fixes before it held, and tests that pin wiring as firmly as behavior.

What we don't know yet

The refactor itself hasn't started. Since the lock landed, two commits have touched src/, both small fixes for while an outside account is suspended, and one of them is the goal-tracking change above. The question we can't answer yet is how many of the 25,396 tests assert wiring rather than behavior. The 69-file commit suggests the answer isn't small: a change that nobody outside the code would notice still moved 69 files. Under our rule, every changed expectation needs a reason in the commit message, and a domain-driven restructuring moves a lot of wiring. We may have to split the wiring cases out before the refactor, so that a failing lock test means what it is supposed to mean.

If you have locked a codebase's behavior before a big refactor, we'd like to know how it went. Did your expected values come from the code or from the spec? How did you stop the tests from pinning which function calls which, and was it worth separating those cases from the behavioral ones? And how did you keep tests from touching anything real? Tell us in the comments below; we'll answer each one there.

title: "Design a Calendar System" Looks Easy. Here's Where Candidates Fail in the Interview
description:
"Design Calendar System" sounds simple. Create a meeting, invite people, show a grid of boxes.

It isn't. Underneath sit some of the most interesting problems in system design: a read-heavy workload with a fan-out on every write, notifications that must reach every invitee, reminders that must fire at an exact minute for hundreds of millions of people, and recurring events that never really end.

This walkthrough follows the structure we coach for a 45–60 minute interview: requirements, estimates, APIs, data model, high-level design, then the deep dives where the real signal is, and finally the AI follow-up more interviewers now ask.

1. Requirements

Functional

  • Create, read, update and delete meetings.
  • Invite people by email, including people who don't use the product.
  • Show a user's calendar for a day, week or month.
  • Notify invitees when a meeting is created or changed.
  • Remind participants a few minutes before a meeting (e.g. 15 minutes).

Nice to have: find a free slot across several people (free/busy), recurring meetings, time zones.

Non-functional

  • Highly available: 99.99%. A calendar that's down means missed meetings.
  • Low latency: calendar views in well under 500 ms (p99).
  • Read-heavy: people look at their calendar far more often than they change it.
  • Scalable: hundreds of millions of daily users.
  • Consistency: eventual consistency is fine for invitees, but the organizer must see their own change immediately (read-your-writes).

Interview tip: say why each requirement matters. "Eventually consistent, except read-your-writes for the organizer" shows judgement; "eventually consistent" alone is a buzzword.

2. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumptions:

  • 2B users
  • 500M daily active users (DAU)
  • 20% of DAU create 2 meetings a day, and 30% create 1
  • New meetings / day → 0.2 × 500M × 2 + 0.3 × 500M = 350M
  • ~4 participants per meeting → ~1.4B invites per day
  • Calendar views / day → ~10 opens per DAU → 5B

QPS planning:

  • Write QPS → 350M / 86,400 ≈ 3.5K/s average, ~10.5K/s peak
  • Read QPS → 5B / 86,400 ≈ 50K QPS average, ~150K/s peak
  • Read : write ratio ~15 : 1, so read-heavy

Capacity planning:

  • 1 KB meeting + ~100 Bytes per participant ≈ 1 KB + 4 × 100 Bytes = 1.4 KB
  • 1.4 KB × 350M ≈ 0.5 TB/day ≈ ~180 TB/year before replication (no media)

Interview tip: The numbers tell us where to spend effort: optimise reads, make writes reliable, and design the fan-out carefully.

3. APIs 

POST   /meetings                      create (title, start, duration, tz, invitees)
                                      + recurrence?, Idempotency-Key header
GET    /users/{id}/calendar?start&end  meeting summaries for a day/week/month (paginated)
GET    /meetings/{id}                 full details
PATCH  /meetings/{id}                 update only the changed fields (If-Match: version)
DELETE /meetings/{id}                 cancel
POST   /meetings/{id}/invitees        add invitees
DELETE /meetings/{id}/invitees/{uid}  remove an invitee
POST   /meetings/{id}/rsvp            accept / decline / maybe
GET    /free?users&start&end          free blocks only (for slot finding)

Two details interviewers notice:

  • The calendar view returns summaries, not just IDs. Returning IDs and then fetching details is an extra round trip on the hottest path.
  • Updates carry a version (optimistic locking). Even if only the owner can edit, they can edit from two devices at once.

How an update works. The client sends only the fields that changed, never the whole meeting row. Moving a meeting 30 minutes later looks like this:

PATCH /meetings/m_123
If-Match: "7"
Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json
{ "start": "2026-10-20T10:30:00Z" }
  • Partial update. Fields that aren't sent stay as they are, and null clears a field. The payload is tiny, and a client can't accidentally overwrite a field it never touched.
  • Version check. If-Match: "7" means "apply this only if the meeting is still at version 7". The Meeting Service runs a conditional write: UPDATE meetings SET start_utc = …, version = 8 WHERE meeting_id = 'm_123' AND version = 7. If another device changed the meeting first, nothing is updated and the API returns 412 Precondition Failed. The client refetches, shows the user the newer meeting, and lets them retry. The response to a successful update returns the whole updated meeting with its new version (ETag: "8").
  • Invitees have their own endpoints. Adding or removing people writes participant rows and sends notifications, so it isn't hidden inside a generic PATCH.

4. Data model

Users

  • user_id (PK) → Shard Key
  • email (unique)
  • metadata

Meetings

  • meeting_id (PK) → Shard Key
  • owner_id
  • title
  • description
  • start_utc
  • duration
  • version
  • metadata
  • list

Participants

  • user_id → Shard Key
  • meeting_id
  • start_utc
  • duration
  • status (invited / accepted / declined)
  • PK(user_id, start_utc, meeting_id)

Why two tables? The two hottest queries want different partitioning:

  • "Show my week" → all of one user's meetings in a time range → partition by user_id, sort by time. One range scan on one shard. Once you get meeting_id, you can easily fetch meeting details based on meeting_id from meetings table.
  • "Change this meeting" → one meeting and all its participants → partition by meeting_id.

The participants table denormalises the start time so the calendar view never has to join. The cost: moving a meeting rewrites one participant row per invitee. Writes are rare and reads are hot, so that's a good trade.

Interview tip: Tables in the same DB can have different shard keys.
To fetch meeting details for a user, don't perform join between participants and meeting table, instead first fetch all the meeting Ids for the user within a day/week and then issue a separate query to DB to fetch meeting details. The Calendar Service does this server-side, so the client still gets summaries in one call.
Optimization → Cache meeting details for the current and next week. Older meetings are rarely read, so caching them wastes memory.

5. High-level design


Async path for notification. Every change in the participants table is captured with change data capture (CDC) into an event queue. Downstream consumers react to it:

  • Event Subscriber Service subscribes to a change and put notifications in a queue.
  • Change notifications (new invite, time changed, cancelled) are sent with immediately delivery to the delay queue. Delay queue with immediate delivery behaves as a FIFO queue.
  • The Reminder Notifications are scheduled with delay delivery.

Using CDC instead of having the Meeting Service publish events directly is deliberate. The database is the single source of truth, so an event can't be lost because a service crashed between "write the DB" and "publish the event".

What if the Participant table can't be updated in the same transaction as meetings table.

Use CDC to update participants table asynchronously.

6. Deep dive: keeping invitees up to date

When a meeting changes, invitees should see it if online. Two options:

Pull (periodic refresh)

  • Simple to build.
  • Wasteful: most refreshes return nothing new, and at 500M DAU that's a lot of empty requests.
  • Changes appear late.

Push

  • Precise and cheap on the network.
  • The server sends a tiny message, "meeting X changed", over Server-Sent Events or WebSocket to open web clients.
  • The client then fetches only what changed.

Use push, and keep a light pull on app open as a safety net (pushes can be missed when a device is offline).

7. Deep dive: reminders 15 minutes before

This is where strong candidates separate themselves. We need to fire hundreds of millions of reminders a day, at the right minute, exactly once, even when meetings move or get cancelled.

8. Where agentic AI fits, and where it doesn't

Interviewers now often add a follow-up: "How would you use AI here?" In agentic AI system design rounds it's sharper: "Which parts of this would you hand to an agent?" The strong answer starts by drawing a line.

Keep the core deterministic. The Calendar DB, CDC, the event queue, fan-out and the delay queue must be exact, fast and cheap. An LLM call takes a second or more, costs real money per request, and can answer the same input differently twice. Nobody wants a reminder that fires "probably around 9:45", or a fan-out that decides which invitees deserve a notification. None of these components should be replaced by an agent.

Put agents at the edges, where the input is human. The good fits are jobs that today need a person to read, judge or negotiate:

  • Finding a time: open everyone's calendar, compare, propose. With Agent → "Find 30 minutes with Priya and Alex next week, mornings, not Friday" → it checks free, ranks slots and drafts the invite
  • Rescheduling after a decline or a new conflict With Agent → Proposes new times to everyone, collects the replies and books the slot that works.
  • Empty meeting descriptions With Agent → Drafts an agenda from the email thread or last meeting's notes.

9. Common mistakes

  • One table for everything, so "show my week" becomes a scatter-gather across shards.
  • Not creating Participants table and read fetch meetings created but not invited. Participants table is required and Invitees, organizer both should be added as participants.
  • Relying on Redis key expiry for reminders.
  • Doing the maths and not using it. Estimates should drive decisions (read-heavy → denormalize data).
  • Putting an LLM in the core path, for example letting an agent decide who gets notified, or giving it direct database access.

Wrapping up

A great answer isn't the biggest diagram. It's a clear story: the numbers say it's read-heavy, so we shape the data for reads; writes fan out asynchronously through CDC; and reminders use a delay queue that survives retries and reschedules. AI belongs at the edges, where people talk to the system, not inside its core. Then you show you know where it breaks.

Preparing for system design interviews, from classic designs like this to agentic AI systems? Crack Tech offers private 1:1 coaching and realistic mock interviews scored the way a hiring committee reads them. Book a free 15-minute call at cracktech.app.

title: I built a 30 MB API client with Tauri and Rust (Postman is 214 MB)
description:
use an API client every single day. And for a long time, every single day it was the heaviest app on my machine.

So I built my own. It's called Elisa, it's free, and its Windows installer is 30 MB.

Client Windows installer
Elisa 30 MB
Bruno 122 MB
Postman 214 MB
Insomnia 525 MB

Official installers of each stable version as of October 19, 2026.

This post is about how it gets there, and what I learned building it.

Why not Electron?

Almost every API client is built on Electron. That's not a bad choice: it's mature and it lets you ship one codebase everywhere. But every Electron app ships its own full copy of Chromium, plus Node.js. That's where most of those megabytes go, and it's why five Electron apps open at once feel like five browsers.

Tauri takes the opposite approach: it uses the web engine your OS already has (WebView2 on Windows), and the backend is Rust instead of Node.

For Elisa that means:

  • A much smaller download.
  • It opens faster and uses less memory, so it can sit next to your editor, your browser and Docker without your laptop complaining.
  • A real native backend for the heavy lifting.

The frontend is plain React 19, built with Rsbuild. The same frontend also runs as a web app, so you can try it in the browser with nothing to install.

What Rust does under the hood

The fun part of Tauri is that the Rust side isn't just a wrapper. In Elisa it does real work:

Requests go out from Rust. On desktop, requests are sent with reqwest, not from the browser. That means no CORS, real cookie handling, multipart uploads, timeouts and custom certificates. If you've ever had to tell someone "it works in curl but not in the browser", you know why this matters for an API client.

Scripts run in a sandbox. Pre-request and test scripts run in QuickJS through rquickjs, with a pm.*-style API. Postman collections with scripts can come along when you import them.

Load tests stream live. The load tester runs in Rust with Tokio and streams progress to the UI through a Tauri Channel, so the chart updates while the test runs instead of waiting for the end.

A mock server, for real. You can serve any collection as a local API. It's a small hyper server that answers with your saved examples. A browser can't open a port on your machine, so this one is desktop only.

A real terminal. The built-in terminal uses portable-pty (ConPTY on Windows), the same idea VS Code uses.

Local-first, not cloud-first

The other thing I cared about: your collections are yours.

Everything is stored on your machine first, in IndexedDB. Elisa works with no account and no internet. If you want to work with your team, you can sign in and sync to the cloud in real time, but that's optional, not the price of opening the app.

When you're offline, changes go into a queue and sync on their own when the connection comes back.

What else it does

Lightweight doesn't have to mean basic:

  • REST, GraphQL and MCP. You can test MCP servers with auto-generated forms, or turn on "Elisa for agents" so Claude Code or Cursor can read your collections (every change asks for your permission).
  • Flows: drag requests onto a canvas and chain them. Capture the login token once and the rest of the flow uses it.
  • Code and types from any response: TypeScript, Zod, Go, Rust, Python, C#, Java, Kotlin, Swift and Dart.
  • Import from Postman, Insomnia, OpenAPI, HAR or a cURL command.
  • Git: save a collection to a folder and commit, branch and push from the app.

What I learned

  • Tauri is not "free" size. You give up a bundled browser, so you have to respect the system web engine. Testing on the real WebView matters.
  • Moving work to Rust pays off twice: it's faster, and it removes whole classes of bugs, like CORS, that a pure web app can't fix.
  • Local-first changes how you design everything. Every feature has to answer "what happens offline?" before it ships.

Try it

Elisa is free, with no account needed:

👉 elisa.develoops.dev

You can import your Postman collection in seconds and see the difference on your own machine.

I'm building it on my own, end to end: the app, the Rust engine and even the little mascot. So feedback means a lot. What's the one thing that annoys you most about your current API client? Let me know in the comments 🙂

title: Reactive Spring Applications: Architecture, Trade-offs, and Production Realities
description:
This article covers fundamentals of Spring WebFlux, blocking dependencies, backpressure and resilience.

Imagine a backend service receiving thousands of concurrent requests. Each request performs a small amount of computation but spends most of its lifetime waiting for a database query, a remote API, or another microservice to respond. The service is not necessarily CPU-bound. Its resources are tied up waiting for work to complete.

A traditional Spring MVC application handles requests using a thread-per-request model. This is straightforward and works well for many workloads, but concurrency can become expensive when large numbers of threads remain occupied by blocking I/O. Threads consume memory and scheduling resources, and increasing the thread pool indefinitely is not a sustainable way to handle growing concurrency.

Spring WebFlux approaches this problem differently. Instead of requiring a dedicated application thread to remain occupied while every I/O operation completes, it uses non-blocking I/O and reactive composition to allow execution to progress when results become available.

That sounds like an obvious improvement, but there is an important distinction: non-blocking execution can improve resource efficiency without necessarily making an individual request faster. A database query still takes as long as the database needs. A remote service still introduces network latency. Reactive programming changes how the application manages waiting, composes asynchronous work, and responds to demand.

Understanding that distinction is essential to deciding whether reactive Spring is the right architectural choice.

1. Why Reactive Spring Exists

The conventional thread-per-request model is attractive because its execution flow closely resembles the business process. A controller calls a service, the service queries a database, and the result is returned to the caller. When a method performs blocking I/O, however, the executing thread waits until that operation completes.

At modest concurrency, this is rarely a problem. As concurrent requests increase, more threads may spend their time waiting rather than doing useful work. Increasing the thread pool can help up to a point, but it also increases resource consumption and scheduling overhead. The actual bottleneck may eventually move to the database connection pool or a downstream service rather than the application threads themselves.

Spring WebFlux is designed for workloads where many concurrent operations spend significant time waiting on I/O. Its non-blocking execution model allows a relatively small number of event-loop threads to coordinate a much larger number of in-flight requests, provided the application and its dependencies do not block those threads.

Reactive programming also introduces Reactive Streams backpressure, which provides a mechanism for consumers to signal how much data they are ready to receive. This becomes useful when producers can generate data faster than downstream consumers can process it.

Neither capability guarantees lower latency or higher throughput in every application. A CPU-intensive service may benefit little from non-blocking I/O, while a conventional CRUD service using blocking JPA calls may gain complexity without removing its primary bottleneck.

The architectural question is therefore not whether reactive programming is more modern. It is whether the workload benefits from non-blocking concurrency, asynchronous composition, or controlled data flow enough to justify the associated complexity.

2. Reactive Foundations: Mono, Flux, and Reactive Streams

Project Reactor, the reactive library commonly used with Spring WebFlux, provides two fundamental publisher types: Mono and Flux.

A Mono<T> represents an asynchronous computation that can produce zero or one value, followed by completion, or terminate with an error. A Flux<T> represents a sequence that can produce zero to many values, followed by completion or an error. These types describe the shape of the result; they do not, by themselves, guarantee that the underlying work is asynchronous or non-blocking.

Consider a reactive repository:

Mono<Customer> customer =
    customerRepository.findById(customerId);

Flux<Order> orders =
    orderRepository.findByCustomerId(customerId);

The first publisher represents an optional customer result. The second represents a stream of orders associated with that customer.

Reactive Streams defines the interaction between publishers, subscribers, and demand. A subscriber can request a certain number of elements, allowing a compliant publisher to regulate how much data it emits. This is the foundation of backpressure, although its effectiveness depends on how the entire pipeline and its external dependencies handle demand.

Another important characteristic is that Reactor pipelines are generally lazy. Declaring a publisher does not necessarily execute the work it describes. Execution is initiated when something subscribes to the publisher, or when a framework component such as WebFlux subscribes as part of handling an HTTP request.

Mono<Customer> customer =
    customerRepository.findById(customerId)
        .map(this::enrichCustomer);

This declares a pipeline. In a typical WebFlux controller, returning the Mono allows the framework to manage subscription and response handling. Application code generally should not introduce arbitrary manual subscriptions inside request processing, because doing so can detach work from the request lifecycle and make error propagation and cancellation harder to manage.

The important point is that Mono and Flux are not simply replacements for ordinary Java return types. They represent computations whose execution, completion, failure, and demand are managed through a reactive protocol.

3. How Spring WebFlux Executes Requests

WebFlux commonly uses an event-loop-based execution model, particularly with Reactor Netty. A small number of event-loop threads process network activity and advance reactive pipelines as I/O operations complete. When a properly non-blocking operation is waiting for network data, the thread can process other work instead of remaining blocked on that operation.

A simplified request lifecycle looks like this:

Incoming HTTP Request
         |
         v
   WebFlux Handler
         |
         v
   Reactive Pipeline
         |
         +---- Non-blocking I/O
         |          |
         |          v
         |    Thread is available
         |    for other work
         |          |
         |          v
         |    I/O completion signal
         |          |
         +----------+
                    |
                    v
             HTTP Response

The key benefit is not that one thread performs every operation. It is that the application avoids occupying threads while waiting for supported non-blocking I/O.

This is also why blocking operations are particularly dangerous on event-loop threads. If a handler calls a synchronous database driver or waits on a blocking SDK, the event-loop thread cannot progress other work assigned to it until that call returns. A single blocking dependency can therefore undermine the concurrency model the application was designed to exploit.

Reactor provides publishOn and subscribeOn to influence execution context. publishOn changes the scheduler used for subsequent downstream operators, while subscribeOn influences where subscription and upstream execution begin. Their exact effects depend on the pipeline and source.

Neither operator transforms a blocking API into a non-blocking API. Scheduling a blocking call on an event loop still blocks that event loop. Moving it to a dedicated scheduler can isolate the impact, but the operation remains blocking and still consumes a thread while it waits.

That distinction should guide design reviews: thread switching is an execution decision, not a substitute for understanding the blocking behavior of dependencies.

4. Building a Reactive Request Flow

Consider an Order Summary API that retrieves an order and then uses the order's customer identifier to retrieve customer details. The second request depends on the first, so the pipeline should express that dependency explicitly.

public Mono<OrderSummary> getOrderSummary(String orderId) {
    return orderClient.getOrder(orderId)
        .flatMap(order ->
            customerClient.getCustomer(order.customerId())
                .map(customer ->
                    new OrderSummary(order, customer)
                )
        );
}

The flatMap operator composes the asynchronous customer lookup after the order response becomes available. The customer request is not started until the order provides the required customer identifier. The resulting Mono<OrderSummary> represents the complete operation.

This is more than a different syntax for nested callbacks. The dependency is visible in the pipeline, and failures from either request can propagate through the composed result.

Now consider a product view that requires inventory and pricing information. If the two calls are independent, they can be composed without waiting for one to finish before starting the other:

public Mono<ProductView> getProductView(String productId) {
    return Mono.zip(
        inventoryClient.getInventory(productId),
        pricingClient.getPrice(productId)
    ).map(tuple ->
        new ProductView(tuple.getT1(), tuple.getT2())
    );
}

When the returned publisher is subscribed to, both source publishers can progress independently. The combined result becomes available when both have produced their required values. This can reduce the time spent waiting sequentially, but only when the calls are genuinely independent and the underlying clients support asynchronous execution.

Reactive composition does not remove the need to define failure behavior. If either call fails, the combined publisher normally fails unless the pipeline explicitly handles that failure. If pricing is optional, for example, the application might choose a fallback value rather than fail the entire response.

Timeouts and cancellation matter for the same reason. A request that has already exceeded its useful deadline should not continue consuming downstream capacity unnecessarily. At the same time, cancellation of a reactive publisher does not guarantee that every external operation can be forcibly stopped. The client, protocol, and downstream service must support the relevant cancellation semantics.

The design objective is to make dependencies, concurrency, and failure behavior explicit—not merely to express ordinary business logic with reactive operators.

5. The Hidden Complexity: Blocking Dependencies and Data Access

The largest architectural mistake in reactive applications is adopting WebFlux at the HTTP layer while leaving the rest of the application predominantly blocking.

Consider a service that uses WebFlux controllers but relies on Spring Data JPA and JDBC for persistence. These technologies are built around blocking database access. Wrapping a repository call in a Mono does not change the behavior of the JDBC driver or turn the database interaction into non-blocking I/O.

For a genuinely reactive persistence path, Spring Data R2DBC provides database access through Reactive Streams-based APIs and supported reactive drivers. That can allow database operations to participate in a non-blocking pipeline, but it does not automatically guarantee better performance. Database capacity, connection limits, query efficiency, transaction behavior, and downstream contention still determine the practical outcome.

The same issue arises with third-party SDKs, legacy clients, filesystem operations, and libraries that expose only synchronous APIs. Sometimes replacing these dependencies is not feasible. In that case, blocking work can be isolated on an appropriate scheduler:

Mono<Data> data =
    Mono.fromCallable(() -> legacyClient.fetchData())
        .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic());

This schedules the callable on Reactor's bounded-elastic scheduler, which is intended for blocking work. It protects event-loop threads from directly executing the blocking call, but it does not eliminate the cost of waiting or create unlimited capacity. Scheduler saturation, queueing, and downstream limits still need to be considered.

The escape hatch is useful when blocking work is unavoidable. It is not a strong reason to make an entire application reactive while retaining blocking persistence and most of its existing execution model.

Connection pools introduce another constraint. Non-blocking execution can support many concurrent in-flight requests, but the database cannot necessarily execute thousands of queries concurrently. If the connection pool has limited capacity, additional requests may queue for connections. Increasing application concurrency without managing database capacity can move the bottleneck rather than remove it.

This is why Spring MVC can be the more appropriate choice for conventional applications built around blocking JPA/JDBC access. A coherent blocking architecture is often easier to understand and operate than a partially reactive one.

6. Backpressure, Errors, and Resilience

Reactive Streams backpressure provides a mechanism for consumers to communicate demand to publishers. This can help control data flow in streaming pipelines, particularly when the producer and consumer can coordinate how many elements are requested and emitted.

However, backpressure is not an automatic, end-to-end guarantee across every system in an application. A database, HTTP client, message broker, or external API may have its own buffering and flow-control behavior. If a producer cannot slow down, the application must decide whether to buffer, drop, reject, or fail work. Unbounded buffering simply converts a throughput mismatch into a memory problem.

Resilience also requires deliberate error and timeout policies. Consider a downstream status lookup:

return paymentClient.fetchStatus(paymentId)
    .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
    .retryWhen(
        Retry.backoff(2, Duration.ofMillis(100))
            .filter(this::isTransientFailure)
    );

This example applies a two-second timeout and retries selected transient failures with backoff, allowing up to two retries under the configured policy. The exact overall deadline depends on the timeout's placement and the time consumed by retries, so production code should define the intended request deadline explicitly.

Retries are not inherently safe. If a request triggers a side effect and the client times out before receiving the response, the operation might already have succeeded remotely. Retrying it can duplicate that effect unless the operation is idempotent or protected by an idempotency mechanism. During an outage, aggressive retries can also amplify load on an already struggling dependency.

Cancellation, circuit breakers, and bulkheads address related concerns. Cancellation can stop unnecessary downstream work when supported. Circuit breakers can prevent repeated calls to a failing dependency, while bulkheads limit how much capacity one dependency or workload can consume.

Reactive programming provides tools for composing these policies, but it does not choose the correct policies for the business. Those decisions still depend on deadlines, retry safety, downstream capacity, and the consequences of partial failure.

7. Reactive Spring vs. Spring MVC with Virtual Threads

Java 21 introduced virtual threads, giving Spring MVC applications another way to handle high concurrency while retaining an imperative programming model. Virtual threads are lightweight threads managed by the JVM, making it practical to support many concurrent blocking tasks without the same platform-thread cost associated with traditional thread-per-request designs.

This changes the decision between WebFlux and Spring MVC. Reactive programming is no longer the only option worth considering when a service needs to support many concurrent I/O-bound requests.

Consideration Spring WebFlux Spring MVC with Virtual Threads
Programming model Reactive composition Imperative, blocking-friendly
Concurrency approach Non-blocking I/O Lightweight virtual threads
Backpressure Reactive Streams support Requires other mechanisms where applicable
JDBC/JPA integration Blocking calls require careful isolation Natural fit for blocking APIs
Streaming Strong fit for reactive streaming Depends on API and workload
Complexity Higher learning and debugging cost Often simpler for conventional business workflows

Virtual threads reduce the cost of blocking threads; they do not make blocking I/O non-blocking. Nor do they remove database connection limits, downstream bottlenecks, or the need to manage concurrency. A service can create many virtual threads while still overwhelming a database with too many concurrent queries.

WebFlux remains attractive when the application benefits from non-blocking clients, streaming, reactive composition, or explicit demand management. Spring MVC with virtual threads can be a better fit when the application is primarily request-response business logic built around blocking libraries and the team values a straightforward imperative flow.

Neither option is universally superior. The decision should reflect the dependency stack, workload characteristics, operational requirements, and the team's ability to debug and maintain the chosen model.

8. Production Observability and Testing

Reactive code that passes unit tests can still fail under contention, slow downstream responses, scheduler saturation, or connection-pool exhaustion. Production validation must therefore cover more than successful responses.

Track latency, throughput, error rates, timeout rates, and connection-pool saturation. For WebFlux applications, investigate blocked event-loop threads and scheduler saturation. Distributed traces should preserve request context across asynchronous boundaries so that a slow dependency can be identified without reconstructing the entire execution path from logs.

Reactor's StepVerifier can test publisher behavior, including emitted values, completion, errors, and time-dependent behavior when configured appropriately. Those tests are useful for validating reactive logic, but they do not replace integration tests against real databases, brokers, and network clients. The integration layer should validate the behavior that unit tests intentionally simulate.

Load tests are equally important. Benchmark with realistic downstream latency, representative concurrency, meaningful payload sizes, and realistic resource limits. Compare the same workload and infrastructure when evaluating WebFlux against MVC or virtual threads. Synthetic benchmarks that exclude the actual bottleneck can make an architectural choice appear better without demonstrating a production benefit.

The outcome to measure is not the number of reactive operators or the number of requests a test can generate. It is whether the chosen architecture improves the service's resource efficiency, throughput, latency distribution, or resilience under the workload it actually serves.

9. A Practical Decision Framework

Before adopting reactive Spring, ask whether the workload is predominantly I/O-bound, whether its important dependencies support non-blocking access, and whether streaming or backpressure solves a real problem. Evaluate whether the team can operate and debug reactive pipelines effectively, and compare the design with Spring MVC using virtual threads where appropriate. Finally, use representative load tests to demonstrate a measurable improvement before accepting the additional complexity.

Reactive programming is valuable when its execution model matches the workload and the surrounding infrastructure supports it. It is not a universal performance upgrade, and Mono and Flux are not evidence of a scalable architecture by themselves.

Choose reactive programming because the workload benefits from non-blocking composition and flow control—not because Mono and Flux look more modern than imperative Java.

title: Fixing "Hydration failed because the server rendered text didn't match the client" from dates in Next.js (tested repro, Next 16 + React 19.3)
description:
If your AI-built (or hand-built) Next.js app throws Hydration failed because the server rendered text didn't match the client in the browser, a common culprit is a date formatted with toLocaleDateString() or toLocaleString() and no locale or time zone. The server and your visitor's browser print different text, and React refuses to hydrate.

We reproduced it on a small synthetic app, applied the smallest fix, and checked it in headless Chrome set to a different locale and time zone than the server. Below: the exact error, the cause, the fix, how we verified it, and what we did not test.

The exact error

In development (next dev), from our headless-browser run:

Hydration failed because the server rendered text didn't match the client. As a result this tree will be regenerated on the client. This can happen if a SSR-ed Client Component used:

- A server/client branch `if (typeof window !== 'undefined')`.
- Variable input such as `Date.now()` or `Math.random()` which changes each time it's called.
- Date formatting in a user's locale which doesn't match the server.
...
<time id="placed" dateTime="2026-01-13T23:30:00Z">
+  14.1.2026
-  1/13/2026

The + line is what the browser rendered; the - line is what the server sent.

In production (next build + next start) the same problem shows only as:

Minified React error #418; visit https://react.dev/errors/418?args[]=text&args[]= for the full message

Older React/Next versions word this differently, for example "Text content does not match server-rendered HTML" (the title of the official Next.js page). We did not run those versions.

Versions we used

Item Version
Node.js 20.19.2
next 16.4.2 (Turbopack)
react / react-dom 19.3.1
Browser Google Chrome, headless, via playwright-core 1.64.1
Server time zone UTC
Browser locale / time zone de-DE / Europe/Berlin
OS Linux, single machine

Cause

Even a "use client" component is rendered twice: once on the server to make the HTML, and again in the browser to make it interactive ("hydration"). React requires the two results to match.

new Date(x).toLocaleDateString() with no arguments uses whatever locale and time zone the current machine has. Our server was in UTC with US English, so it printed 1/13/2026. The browser was in Berlin with German, where the same moment (2026-01-13T23:30:00Z) is already 14 January, so it printed 14.1.2026. Same code, two answers, hydration error.

The same thing happens with Date.now(), new Date(), Math.random(), or typeof window checks used during render. We reproduced only the locale/time-zone date case.

Smallest working fix

Pass an explicit locale and time zone, so the server and every browser format the date identically.

Before (hydration error): app/OrderRow.js 

"use client";
import { useState } from "react";

export default function OrderRow({ id, createdAt }) {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);
  return (
    <div>
      <span>Order {id} placed </span>
      <time id="placed" dateTime={createdAt}>{new Date(createdAt).toLocaleDateString()}</time>
      <button onClick={() => setOpen(!open)}>{open ? "Hide" : "Details"}</button>
      {open && <p id="details">Synthetic details</p>}
    </div>
  );
}

After (no hydration error)

Change the <time> line to call formatDate(createdAt) and add this at the bottom of the file:

// Same locale and time zone on the server and in every browser,
// so the first browser render matches the server HTML.
function formatDate(iso) {
  return new Date(iso).toLocaleDateString("en-US", { timeZone: "UTC" });
}

Pick the locale and zone that fit your business (for example "en-US" and "America/Phoenix"). The trade-off: every visitor sees that same zone's date. If you need each visitor's own local date, the usual pattern is to render a neutral value first and switch to local formatting in useEffect after hydration. That is documented on the Next.js hydration page, but we did not test that variant.

Prompt for your AI coding tool 

My Next.js App Router app shows "Hydration failed because the server rendered text didn't match the client" in the browser console. Find every place that formats dates, times, numbers or prices during render using toLocaleString, toLocaleDateString, toLocaleTimeString or Intl.DateTimeFormat/Intl.NumberFormat without an explicit locale and timeZone, and every place that uses Date.now(), new Date() with no argument, or Math.random() during render. For the formatting cases, pass an explicit locale and timeZone (use "en-US" and "UTC" unless I tell you otherwise). For the clock/random cases, compute the value on the server and pass it as a prop, or set it in useEffect. Do not change anything else, and show me the diff.

Review the diff yourself. We did not test this prompt in any AI tool.

How we verified

All runs on 2026-10-20 on a small synthetic app. Server started with TZ=UTC; headless Chrome set to locale de-DE and time zone Europe/Berlin.

  1. Both builds pass: npx next build exited 0 for before and after. The bug does not show at build time.
  2. Before, production (next start): the browser threw Minified React error #418 ... args[]=text. Server HTML had 1/13/2026; after hydration the page showed 14.1.2026.
  3. Before, dev (next dev): the browser threw the full "Hydration failed ..." message with the + 14.1.2026 / - 1/13/2026 diff shown above.
  4. After, production and dev: no hydration error or React error in the console; server HTML and the hydrated page both showed 1/13/2026.
  5. Button still works: in every run, clicking "Details" showed the details paragraph.

Both runs also logged one unrelated 404 resource error, most likely the missing favicon; we did not confirm which file it was.

Not verified

To be upfront about the limits:

  • Other browsers (Firefox, Safari), real phones, and real visitors' settings; we simulated one locale/time zone in headless Chrome.
  • The useEffect "show local time after load" variant.
  • The other causes in the error message (Date.now(), Math.random(), typeof window, invalid HTML nesting, browser extensions). Same family, not reproduced.
  • Other Next.js/React/Node versions, including older "Text content does not match" wording, and the Pages Router.
  • Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare or other hosts (host server time zones may differ from ours).
  • Code generated by Cursor, Lovable, Bolt or v0; our app is hand-written and synthetic. We did not measure how often AI tools produce this pattern.
  • Whether the AI prompt produces a correct diff in any tool.

Quick troubleshooting

  • Only see "Minified React error #418": run npm run dev and open the page; the dev overlay shows the full message with the +/- diff that points to the exact text.
  • Error goes away on your machine but users report it: your computer and server may share a time zone. Test with a browser set to a different time zone or language.
  • The diff points to an attribute, not text, or you have a password manager/translate extension: try a private window with extensions off; extensions can cause this too (not tested by us).
  • Prices like 1,234.50 vs 1.234,50: same cause; pass a locale to toLocaleString / Intl.NumberFormat.

Security: no secrets are involved. Don't "fix" this by disabling server rendering for whole pages without understanding the SEO and performance cost.

The original guide, with the before/after files, is on The Agent Ledger: Hydration mismatch from date locale: Next.js fix.

AI disclosure: This article was written with the help of AI. The reproduction and the before/after browser runs described above were actually performed and checked against the logs before publishing.

title: Encapsulation and Visibility in Java: Protecting Your Objects
description:
When writing Java code, it’s easy to focus on making a program work. But good object-oriented design is also about controlling how that program can be used.

That’s where encapsulation and visibility come in.
What Is Encapsulation?
Encapsulation means protecting an object’s internal state and providing controlled ways to interact with it.
Instead of allowing other classes to change a field directly, we can make it private and expose methods that enforce the object’s rules.



public class BankAccount {
    // Private state: cannot be changed directly from outside the class.
    private double balance;

    public BankAccount(double initialBalance) {
        if (initialBalance < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Balance cannot be negative");
        }
        this.balance = initialBalance;
    }

    // Public API: exposes only the information callers need.
    public double getBalance() {
        return balance;
    }

    // Public behavior: validates changes and protects the object's rules.
    public void deposit(double amount) {
        if (amount <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Deposit must be positive");
        }
        balance += amount;
    }

    public void withdraw(double amount) {
        if (amount <= 0 || amount > balance) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid withdrawal");
        }
        balance -= amount;
    }

    // Package-private: available only to classes in the same package.
    void applyMonthlyFee(double fee) {
        if (fee < 0 || fee > balance) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid fee");
        }
        balance -= fee;
    }

    // Protected: available to subclasses and classes in the same package.
    protected boolean hasMinimumBalance(double minimum) {
        return balance >= minimum;
    }

    // Private: internal implementation detail.
    private void resetBalance() {
        balance = 0;
    }
}

title: Unix Timestamp Converter: Why My Logs Said 1970-01-21 (and the Seconds vs Milliseconds Fix)
description:
Unix Timestamp Converter: Why My Logs Said 1970-01-21 (and the Seconds vs Milliseconds Fix)

I spent a solid forty minutes last Tuesday staring at a billing page that claimed every subscription in our system had expired on 1970-01-21.

Not 1970-01-01, the date everyone learns to recognize instantly. 1970-01-21, a much more specific flavour of wrong. That particular wrongness has exactly one cause: a millisecond timestamp got handed to code that expected seconds.

The API was fine. My frontend was not.

If you have ever debugged a date that landed in 1970, or a "today" that showed up eight hours early, this is the checklist I wish I had taped to my monitor. Three ways to convert a Unix timestamp, then three traps I keep stepping in.

Method 1: Python 3.11.1

Server side, datetime.fromtimestamp() is the whole job. The one argument that matters is the second one.

# Python 3.11.1
import datetime

ts = 1761000000

utc = datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp(ts, datetime.timezone.utc)
print(utc.isoformat())
# 2025-10-20T22:40:00+00:00

print(datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp(ts).isoformat())
# 2025-10-21T06:40:00   <- same instant, my laptop is UTC+8

Skip the timezone argument and you get a naive datetime silently rendered in local time. That is where off-by-eight-hours bugs are born.

Going the other direction, build an aware datetime and read .timestamp():

# Python 3.11.1
import datetime

d = datetime.datetime(2026, 10, 21, 0, 0, 0, tzinfo=datetime.timezone.utc)
print(int(d.timestamp()))
# 1792540800

print(datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).isoformat())
# 2026-10-21T01:47:19.575814+00:00

I always store UTC and format at the edge. The Python datetime docs spell out the naive-vs-aware rules better than I can, and they are worth reading once.

Method 2: Node.js 22.13.1

JavaScript's Date constructor takes milliseconds. Full stop. It does not guess, and it does not warn.

// Node.js 22.13.1
const seconds = 1761000000;

console.log(new Date(seconds).toISOString());
// 1970-01-21T09:10:00.000Z   <- wrong, this is my bug from Tuesday

console.log(new Date(seconds * 1000).toISOString());
// 2025-10-20T22:40:00.000Z   <- correct

Backwards is Date.now() (milliseconds) or Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) when the backend wants seconds:

// Node.js 22.13.1
console.log(Date.now());
// 1792547248983

console.log(Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000));
// 1792547248

MDN's Date page is the reference I keep open, especially the section on date-string parsing, which never behaves the way people assume.

When I am already in a terminal, GNU date is faster than opening an editor:

TZ=UTC date -d @1761000000 '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %Z'
# 2025-10-20 22:40:00 UTC

TZ=UTC date -d "2026-10-21 01:47:19" +%s
# 1792547239

Method 3: paste it into a browser

Sometimes I am reading a stranger's log line and do not want to boot anything. A free online Unix timestamp converter handles both directions in one input box, and shows UTC and local time side by side, which is the part I actually care about when the number came from a server in another region.

I keep this browser-based timestamp converter bookmarked for exactly that. Nothing is uploaded, the arithmetic happens in the page, and I can hand the link to a support engineer who has never opened a REPL.

Three traps worth memorizing

1. Seconds versus milliseconds. Symptoms: a date in January 1970, or a year around 57000. In Node, new Date(1761000000) returns 1970-01-21T09:10:00.000Z. In Python, passing the millisecond value straight in does not degrade gracefully, it throws:

>>> datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp(1761000000000)
ValueError: year 57773 is out of range

That traceback is a gift. It means milliseconds, and the fix is to divide by 1000.

2. Timezone drift on round trips. A date-only string is parsed as UTC, but a date-time string without an offset is parsed as local. On Node 22.13.1 with TZ unset on a UTC+8 box:

new Date('2026-10-21').toISOString()
// 2026-10-21T00:00:00.000Z
new Date('2026-10-21T00:00:00').toISOString()
// 2026-10-20T16:00:00.000Z

Python mirrors the trap in reverse. datetime.datetime(2026, 10, 21, 0, 0).timestamp() returned 1792512000.0 on my machine, while the same value marked UTC returned 1792540800.0. Eight hours apart, because a naive datetime is interpreted in local time. Set TZ explicitly in CI, or your tests pass locally and fail in the container.

3. The 2038 ceiling and 32-bit storage. 2147483647 is 2038-01-19T03:14:07Z. Store timestamps in a 64-bit column or as bigint, because a signed 32-bit int wraps one second later. Postgres integer and legacy MySQL INT columns are the usual offenders, and they will not complain until they do.

I also stopped trusting shell date syntax across machines. GNU wants date -d @1761000000; macOS and BSD want date -r 1761000000. Run the GNU form on a BSD box and you get:

date: 1761000000: No such file or directory

Same command, same number, completely different parsing. Any script that might run on a laptop needs the branch.

Task Python 3.11.1 Node.js 22.13.1 Shell
Epoch to UTC datetime.fromtimestamp(ts, timezone.utc) new Date(ts * 1000) TZ=UTC date -d @$ts
Date to epoch int(aware_dt.timestamp()) Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) TZ=UTC date -d "$str" +%s
Unit seconds, float milliseconds seconds
Main trap naive datetime reads local seconds treated as ms BSD date -r vs GNU date -d

Two habits fixed this class of bug for me: I name every timestamp field with its unit (expires_at_s, created_ms), and I never let a naive datetime cross a function boundary. When I do need to eyeball a number fast, the timestamp converter at utilvy shows both directions at once, which is usually enough to confirm whether I am off by a factor of 1000.

More free browser-based utilities at utilvy.com
