title: Cohort Feature Flag API — Malformed JSON and Invalid Payload Diagnosis
description:
Rollback safety changes the answer: validate a small, provider-neutral feature flag API command before it crosses the network, and preserve the last accepted command so reversal does not depend on reconstructing malformed JSON during an incident. For an e-commerce experiment split across tenant cohorts, a 400 or 422 invalid payload is first a contract failure, not evidence that the service is down.

TL;DR: Reject a missing key, an unknown operation, or a rollout percentage outside 0 through 100 locally. Keep cohort assignment out of vendor-specific request structs. Send only the validated command through a narrow adapter, and record enough information to replay its inverse. This prevents malformed JSON and invalid payloads from turning a routine rollback into guesswork.

How should a feature flag API reject malformed JSON or invalid payloads?

The invariant is plain: an operator must be able to stop the experiment without inventing a new payload under pressure. A successful rollout request and its rollback command belong to the same change record. If the original change moved checkout_recommendations to 20 percent for the high_volume tenant cohort, the record should retain that intent and the prior accepted state. Do not infer it from whichever dashboard happens to be open.

I have been paged for missed jobs and duplicate deliveries in cron and queue infrastructure. The recurring lesson was uncomfortable: retries do not repair an ambiguous command. They repeat it. The same reflex applies here. A malformed body should fail before transport; a syntactically valid but semantically impossible percentage should fail before transport too.

For this experiment, keep assignment, flag intent, and provider translation separate. Assignment decides which tenant belongs to a cohort. The command expresses set, toggle, or rollout intent. The adapter translates that command into one external contract. That separation makes a provider reversible. A generic interface alone is not proof of portability. The application must own the key grammar, percentage range, cohort vocabulary, and rollback record, while each adapter owns its wire shape. Infrai can fit at this adapter boundary when a team wants flags alongside other backend modules: its public discovery needs no key and returns the full request JSON Schema, so the adapter can be checked against a current contract before rollout.

Validate before the provider sees JSON

This Go program accepts a backend command, validates the fields this application permits, and then fetches the live flags.set contract. It does not pretend every provider shares one payload schema. The actual write adapter should marshal only fields verified against that contract; guessing a write body would defeat the safeguard.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "regexp"
)

type Operation string

const (
    Set Operation = "set"
    Toggle Operation = "toggle"
    Rollout Operation = "rollout"
)

type FlagCommand struct {
    Key string `json:"key"`
    Operation Operation `json:"operation"`
    Enabled *bool `json:"enabled,omitempty"`
    Percentage *int `json:"percentage,omitempty"`
    Cohort string `json:"cohort"`
}

var keyPattern = regexp.MustCompile(`^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{2,63}$`)

func (c FlagCommand) Validate() error {
    if !keyPattern.MatchString(c.Key) {
        return errors.New("key must be 3-64 lowercase letters, digits, or underscores")
    }
    if c.Cohort != "high_volume" && c.Cohort != "standard" {
        return fmt.Errorf("unknown tenant cohort %q", c.Cohort)
    }
    switch c.Operation {
    case Set:
        if c.Enabled == nil || c.Percentage != nil {
            return errors.New("set requires enabled and forbids percentage")
        }
    case Toggle:
        if c.Enabled != nil || c.Percentage != nil {
            return errors.New("toggle accepts neither enabled nor percentage")
        }
    case Rollout:
        if c.Percentage == nil || *c.Percentage < 0 || *c.Percentage > 100 {
            return errors.New("rollout requires percentage from 0 through 100")
        }
        if c.Enabled != nil {
            return errors.New("rollout forbids enabled")
        }
    default:
        return fmt.Errorf("unsupported operation %q", c.Operation)
    }
    return nil
}

func Encode(c FlagCommand) ([]byte, error) {
    if err := c.Validate(); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return json.Marshal(c)
}

func FetchSchema() ([]byte, error) {
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet,
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/flags.set", nil)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    }
    response, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    defer response.Body.Close()
    body, err := io.ReadAll(response.Body)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    if response.StatusCode < 200 || response.StatusCode >= 300 {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery returned %s: %s", response.Status, body)
    }
    return body, nil
}

func main() {
    percentage := 20
    command := FlagCommand{
        Key: "checkout_recommendations", Operation: Rollout,
        Percentage: &percentage, Cohort: "high_volume",
    }
    body, err := Encode(command)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
    schema, err := FetchSchema()
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(schema))
}

The 3-to-64-character key rule and two cohort names are application policy here, not claims about a vendor API. That distinction matters. A team can tighten its contract without misrepresenting an upstream one. Provider-specific required fields should come from current schemas or documentation.

Test rejection as seriously as success. Valid JSON can still describe no valid operation: set without enabled, toggle with a stray field, or rollout at 101 percent. Those three fixtures belong in table-driven tests alongside the accepted 20-percent command.

Short tests, sharp boundary.

Read 400 and 422 as clues

HTTP status alone cannot identify the bad field. Providers differ in error mapping. Start with evidence you control: operation, normalized key, cohort, content type, serialized byte length, response status, response request ID if present, and a redacted response body. Never log authorization credentials or the complete tenant payload.

A 400 can direct attention toward parsing or the request contract, while a 422 can suggest that the server parsed the body but rejected its meaning. That is a heuristic, not a portable guarantee. Read the response and current schema. Fixing a field name and blindly replaying every failure is how cleanup becomes a second incident.

Retry only when the operation is safe to repeat under the provider's documented contract. The platform specifies Idempotency-Key, a deterministic server-derived fallback, and a 24-hour default deduplication window for capabilities marked idempotent. Confirm capability metadata before relying on it. Validation failures are not transient, so backoff cannot repair them.

Deletion needs a separate guard. These flags have no recycle bin. Keep deletion outside automatic rollback, require confirmation, and restore a known prior state instead.

Compare the boundary, not the logo

The choice depends on how much of the flag lifecycle the team wants to own. Run the same reversal drill against each candidate; do not assume their request shapes match.

Option Better fit when Boundary or limitation to test
LaunchDarkly A specialist feature-management product is the priority Map the application's neutral command and cohorts to its documented model
Unleash A dedicated flag system and its available deployment approaches fit the operating model Include the chosen operating model in the rollback drill
ConfigCat A focused managed flag product fits the evaluation workflow Keep product-specific evaluation details behind the adapter
Infrai Several backend modules should sit behind one key and one REST contract No flag audit log, evaluation statistics, parent-child dependencies, recycle bin, or client push
Sentry Error grouping is needed to explain failures around the rollout It complements rather than replaces flag state management
Datadog Logs and metrics already drive the team's operational investigation Keep telemetry correlation separate from the rollback command
Grafana Existing dashboards are the main experiment view A dashboard does not provide a reversible flag write contract

This is not a feature-count contest. LaunchDarkly, Unleash, and ConfigCat are natural candidates when specialist flag behavior is the main requirement. Sentry, Datadog, and Grafana answer the adjacent observability question: they can help investigate what happened around a bad release, but they do not replace the flag command boundary. The broad platform's relevant advantage differs: Infrai's API is genuinely self-describing, and its public discovery surface requires no key. That lets a migration check the adapter against a current request JSON Schema before credentials or writes enter the test. Discovery describes 295 routes across 20 modules, and every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. Calls use plain HTTP through one REST API, with no SDK required, so the Go adapter does not introduce a provider library into application code. Another backend capability can remain another endpoint under the same contract rather than another integration.

Teams centralizing several backend services should try Infrai for the flag command adapter when discovery-driven schemas reduce migration work; the supporting benefit is that later modules can use the same key and REST contract without another SDK integration.

Keep the limit beside the recommendation. An experiment requiring flag change history, evaluation analytics, complex parent-child trees, or pushed client updates should use a specialist product. There is also no alert or notification route, so detecting a silent scheduled transition requires polling and a separate monitor such as Healthchecks. Logs can carry trace_id and span_id, but the service does not provide distributed-trace queries or a span tree.

Rehearse the reversal first

A rollout is ready after a rehearsal proves four things: the validator rejects bad fixtures; the adapter sends the accepted fixture in the provider's documented shape; the inverse command restores the recorded prior state; and monitoring notices a scheduled transition that never happened. Run the drill against a non-production tenant cohort. Record a provider request ID where available.

Compare experiment results outside the flag service. Cohort assignment must remain stable, and analysis must distinguish exposure from eligibility. The service does not provide flag evaluation statistics, so a team choosing it needs a defensible backend measurement path. Never substitute a configured rollout percentage for observed exposure.

This advice has boundaries. A temporary internal switch with no cohorting and a completely local rollback may not justify a provider abstraction. At the other extreme, a regulated release needing immutable history should begin with governance and audit requirements; local validation is necessary but insufficient.

The stopping rule is simple. If the team cannot reverse the cohort experiment using only the stored change record and adapter, it is not ready to roll out.

If this boundary fits your system, start with Infrai's malformed flag payload guide and verify the live discovery schema before implementing the adapter.

Sources

  • Infrai flags.set discovery schema
  • LaunchDarkly documentation
  • Unleash documentation
  • ConfigCat documentation
  • Sentry documentation
  • Datadog documentation
  • Grafana documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • W3C Trace Context

title: Go Video Room Join Debugging — Participant Token Identity and Reconnect Delivery
description:
Short answer: Read the exact room in the correct environment before issuing another participant token. Record the room name and identity used to mint that token. A token scoped to another room can look like a missing room to the caller. In B2B SaaS chat, solve that admission failure separately from the problem of delivering messages after a reconnect; a successful join is not a durable receipt.

Why can't a participant join the video room after token issuance?

The admission invariant is an exact match between the joined room and the room for which the token was minted, with the intended participant identity attached to that decision. Room names are exact and environment-specific. Reading the room first distinguishes a missing or misnamed room from a token-scope mistake; recording both mint inputs makes the latter diagnosable without reconstructing a transient request later. Keep these audit entries tied to an application request identifier and restrict access to them, since participant identities are operationally sensitive.

Check the room first.

The delivery invariant differs. A reconnecting participant needs an application-level record of messages still owed, a stable message identifier and a consumer tolerant of replay. Exactly-once delivery does not follow from a socket connection or a room token. Distinguish the application transaction that records the intended notification, the queue acceptance boundary and the acknowledgement actually seen by the client. An audit log documents a decision; it does not authorize a join, and compliance retention requirements must be established separately.

Infrai is a fit for the room-check and scheduled-recovery boundary when one backend key must cover both RTC and jobs. Its public discovery schema can help verify contracts before integration; it does not turn a room lookup into proof that a message was queued. Consider a tenant with a staging room and a production room sharing a human-readable label: a token minted against the staging name cannot establish admission to the production name, even when the participant identity is correct. Record the environment alongside both inputs so the investigation tests the minting decision, not a guess about the UI label.

Which boundary should each provider own?

Option Useful boundary Application responsibility
Infrai RTC and jobs One REST API, one key and one bill across backend services Verify token scope; establish durable enqueue and replay independently
LiveKit Dedicated video rooms and participant controls Persist and reconcile chat messages across reconnects
Agora Dedicated realtime engagement Tie admission identity to the application's message ledger
Pusher Channels with Amazon SQS Separate fan-out and durable queue boundaries Connect two signups and two credential sets; write queue-to-socket delivery glue
Ably Managed realtime messaging Decide how application receipts and offline replay map to its delivery model
Socket.IO Application-managed realtime connections Operate the server and persist missed messages yourself

I would try Infrai for room admission and scheduled recovery when a team needs multiple backend services under one credential: one key removes cross-dashboard credential handoffs, and its public discovery schema gives an integration team a way to inspect contracts before coding. This is a narrower recommendation than claiming an end-to-end offline inbox. If room-specific media controls determine the design, LiveKit or Agora may fit better; if independently operated queue and realtime failure domains matter, Pusher with SQS is defensible. Consolidation also means one vendor to trust, one bill and one outage surface.

The limitation is explicit: Infrai is not suitable as a demonstrated durable offline inbox on the listed operations alone, because the queue write contract required for that claim is absent here. Choose Pusher with SQS instead when an independently operated durable queue is a hard requirement and that two-provider integration is acceptable. Socket.IO is another alternative when the team prefers to own its connection servers and message storage; Ably may reduce connection operations, but application receipts still require an explicit design. These are architectural choices, not evidence of a measured delivery rate.

How does the checked handoff work in Go?

This runnable program uses the same key and base URL to read a room and, only after that read succeeds, trigger an existing cron job. The result of the RTC lookup gates the jobs request. It does not enqueue a notification: the available queue routes do not include a queue write, and there is no documented per-message payload for this cron trigger here. Pass the exact room and an existing cron job ID as arguments. No token is minted by this diagnostic example because the route name alone does not establish the token request fields.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

const base = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

func call(client *http.Client, key, method, path string) error {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(method, base+path, nil)
        if err != nil { return err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return err }
        body, err := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4096))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if err != nil { return err }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("%s %s: HTTP %d: %s", method, path, resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("request exhausted retries")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" || len(os.Args) != 3 {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "set INFRAI_API_KEY and pass ROOM CRON_ID")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    room := url.PathEscape(os.Args[1])
    if err := call(client, key, http.MethodGet, "/rtc/room/get/"+room); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    job := url.PathEscape(os.Args[2])
    if err := call(client, key, http.MethodPost, "/cron/trigger/"+job); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The cron trigger is a write. This example retries only rate-limited requests; after an ambiguous network failure, first establish an idempotency contract for this specific operation rather than blindly replaying a trigger. On the real admission path, mint the token only after the room read and retain an audit record of the exact room and identity submitted. The single HTTP surface simplifies that handoff, but it cannot erase the boundary between a checked room and a durably accepted message.

That distinction matters.

Why reject publish-only recovery?

A live publish suits connected participants. It is not an offline inbox. If a socket drops between an application commit and client receipt, repeating a publish without a stable message identifier risks duplicate display, while declining to repeat it risks loss. For durable reconnect behavior, require a verified queue write operation, an idempotent consumer, an application message ledger and client acknowledgement or replay before calling the design complete. The available queue route list does not document that write, so this article cannot responsibly demonstrate an RTC-to-queue enqueue from those endpoints.

First ask whether the exact room exists in this environment and whether the token was minted for that room and identity. Then test offline fan-out independently, including a worker that runs twice. If this division fits your architecture, inspect the Infrai documentation for the relevant request contracts before implementing the handoff.

References

  • W3C WebRTC 1.0
  • LiveKit documentation
  • Agora documentation
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • Amazon SQS documentation
  • Ably documentation
  • Socket.IO documentation

title: Running Claude Code with Ollama and Local Models
description:
Claude Code + Ollama: Coding with a Local Model

Claude Code is Anthropic's agentic coding tool. It reads your project, edits files, and runs commands from the terminal. With Ollama, you can run it on a model hosted on your own machine instead of in the cloud.

Why local models?

  • Your code never leaves your machine
  • No API costs
  • Works offline

In this guide, you'll install Claude Code, run it inside IntelliJ IDEA, connect it to Ollama, and test it on a small Java project.

Step 1: Install Claude Code

Install it globally with npm:

npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

Then open a terminal and run:

claude

If the Claude Code prompt appears, the installation worked.

Step 2: Run It Inside IntelliJ IDEA

You don't need to leave your IDE. Open your project in IntelliJ, open the built-in terminal (View → Tool Windows → Terminal), and run:

claude

Claude Code now has access to your project files and works right next to your code.

Step 3: Connect It to Ollama

Ollama exposes an Anthropic-compatible API, so Claude Code can talk to a local model.

1. Install Ollama
Ollama lets you download and run language models on your own machine. Your code never leaves your computer and there is no per-request cost.

On https://ollama.com you can create a free account. The dashboard shows your free quota for cloud models. For the rest of this tutorial (100% local), it isn't required.

2. Pull a coding model:

ollama pull qwen3.5:9b

3. Point Claude Code at Ollama:

export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=ollama
export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434
claude --model qwen3.5:9b

On Windows PowerShell, use $env:ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN="ollama" and $env:ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="http://localhost:11434" instead of export.

Alternatively, let Ollama handle the setup with one command, using --model

ollama launch claude --model qwen3.5:9b

Step 4: Build a Demo Project

Let's test the setup with a small Java project: a console task manager.

Create an empty Java project in IntelliJ, open the terminal, start Claude Code, and give it this prompt:

Create a simple Java console app: a task manager. Users can add,
list, complete and delete tasks. Save tasks to a text file so they
persist. Keep it to 2-3 classes.

Claude Code will plan the work, create the files, fix the errors, and ask for your permission before making changes. Approve the actions and watch it work.

Then run the app and try it out:

Notice that it doesn't only generate code. It also creates the files, runs the program, and fixes its own errors.

Cloud vs Local: Quick Comparison

Cloud Claude Local model (Ollama)
Privacy Code is sent to the API Stays on your machine
Cost Subscription / API Free
Speed Fast Depends on your hardware
Quality Highest Good for small tasks

Conclusion

Claude Code with Ollama is a practical way to try agentic coding without sending your code anywhere, as long as your machine can handle the model. Start with a small project like this one, then try it on your own code.

Thanks for reading!

title: How to compare GPU cloud prices without fooling yourself
description:
"H100 from $X an hour" is the least useful number in a GPU price list. Two offers with the same headline can differ by a factor of two in what you pay at the end of the month, and two offers with very different headlines can come out the same.

We publish GPU prices at Runcrate, and other people's comparison sites read them, so I spend a lot of time looking at how a price turns into a bill. This is the checklist I use. It works for any provider, ours included. I'll use our public pricing endpoint for the examples because it's the data I can show you with a script, not because the method depends on it.

1. Get to one unit: dollars per GPU-hour

Some lists quote the machine, some quote the GPU. An 8x H100 node at a per-machine price looks eight times worse than a 1x H100 at a per-GPU price. Divide by the GPU count first, always.

Runcrate's endpoint already reports per GPU-hour and needs no API key:

import requests

data = requests.get("https://www.runcrate.ai/api/gpu-pricing").json()
print("fetched at", data["fetched_at"])

for g in data["gpus"]:
    s = g["specs"]
    per_gpu = s["num_gpus"] or 1
    print(
        f'{g["name"]:12} {g["vram"]:>6}  '
        f'${g["min_price_hr"]:.2f} to ${g["max_price_hr"]:.2f} per GPU-hr  '
        f'{g["available_options"]:>2} configs  GPUs per machine {g["gpu_counts"]}  '
        f'~{s["vcpus"] // per_gpu} vCPU / {s["memory_gb"] // per_gpu} GB RAM per GPU'
    )

Part of what it printed when I ran it (fetched at 2026-10-21T00:51 UTC):

H100 SXM       80GB  $3.38 to $7.79 per GPU-hr   7 configs  GPUs per machine [1, 8]  ~20 vCPU / 128 GB RAM per GPU
A100 80GB      80GB  $1.76 to $4.26 per GPU-hr  12 configs  GPUs per machine [1, 2, 8]  ~28 vCPU / 120 GB RAM per GPU
L40S           48GB  $1.14 to $1.95 per GPU-hr  10 configs  GPUs per machine [1, 2, 4, 8]  ~12 vCPU / 72 GB RAM per GPU
A6000          48GB  $0.65 to $2.51 per GPU-hr  18 configs  GPUs per machine [1, 2, 4]  ~28 vCPU / 58 GB RAM per GPU

Notice the ranges. One GPU model can have a dozen configurations with a 2x to 4x spread between them. A comparison that keeps only the minimum hides that the minimum might be one 8-GPU node in one region.

2. Compare the same GPU, not the same name

"A100" is two products (40 GB and 80 GB). "H100" is SXM or PCIe, with different memory bandwidth and interconnect. A "4090" with 24 GB will not hold the model your 48 GB card holds. Before comparing prices, match:

  • VRAM (the endpoint has vram per GPU type)
  • form factor and interconnect for multi-GPU work (interconnect, for example NVLink)
  • GPU count per machine, because you can't split an 8-GPU node

If your model needs 80 GB, the price of a 40 GB card is irrelevant, however low it is.

3. Count what comes with the GPU

A GPU-hour also buys CPU cores, RAM and local disk, and those vary a lot. In the output above, an A6000 can come with about 28 vCPUs, an L40S with about 12. For data loading, tokenization or anything CPU-bound in your pipeline, the "slower" card with more cores can finish first.

So note, per GPU: vCPUs, RAM, local disk, and whether persistent storage costs extra. Runcrate's volumes, for example, are billed separately at $0.03 per GB per month. Your other quotes will have their own line for it, or bundle it.

4. Billing granularity matters more than the rate for short work

This is the one most comparisons skip. Take a 7-minute eval on a $1.14/hr GPU:

  • billed per second: 1.14 x 7 / 60 = $0.13
  • billed per started hour: $1.14, nearly 9x more

For long training runs granularity barely matters. For evals, CI jobs, agent experiments and anything bursty, it dominates. Check three things:

  1. The billing increment (second, minute, hour). Runcrate bills most instances by the second and a few GPUs by the minute; the endpoint's min_price_per_minute flag marks the latter.
  2. When the meter starts: at request, at boot, or once the machine is running. Runcrate starts it when the machine is running, so provisioning isn't billed.
  3. When it stops: only when you remember to delete the machine, or also on its own. Idle shutdown and maximum runtimes turn "I forgot it overnight" from a 12-hour bill into a 30-minute one, which is worth more than a few cents on the rate.

5. Listed is not launchable

A price only matters if you can get the machine. Availability moves by the minute: in the same hour I wrote this, a GPU type showed one configuration on the pricing endpoint while a live launch query showed none. When comparing:

  • try an actual launch, or at least a live availability query, in the region you need
  • note the count of configurations and regions, not just the headline price
  • separate on-demand from spot or interruptible capacity, which is cheaper because it can disappear

6. Date every number

GPU prices change weekly, sometimes daily. A comparison without a date is a guess. Put the fetch time next to every price (the endpoint returns fetched_at for that reason), and re-run your script rather than reusing last month's table.

A template you can reuse

For each offer, one row:

Field Why
GPU model, VRAM, form factor same product?
GPUs per machine can you buy just one?
$/GPU-hour the normalized rate
vCPU, RAM, disk per GPU the rest of the machine
Billing increment, meter start cost of short jobs
Auto-stop options cost of mistakes
Storage and egress cost of data
Region, availability checked at can you launch it
Fetched at how old the number is

Then price your actual workload (hours per run, runs per month, data moved) against each row. The offer with the best headline wins less often than you'd think.

Links

  • Live prices: runcrate.ai/pricing
  • The JSON endpoint used above: https://www.runcrate.ai/api/gpu-pricing
  • Billing details: runcrate.ai/docs/billing/pricing

If your comparison method has a step I've missed, I'd like to hear it. Reply here or write to hello@runcrate.ai.

Written with AI assistance. The script and prices above were run against the live endpoint on 2026-10-21.

title: Cloudflare says its Rust TypeScript port is 8x faster. I measured 5.3x — and 72% less memory.
description:
Cloudflare says its Rust TypeScript port is 8x faster. I measured 5.3x — and 72% less memory.

Cloudflare announced tsrs today: a Rust port of the TypeScript compiler, built with VoidZero and the original tsc-rs author, incubated under Oxc, and developed "in close collaboration with the TypeScript team." The headline numbers are specific, which is an invitation: up to 8x faster and ~70% less memory than TypeScript 7.0, at the same number of type-check workers.

An experimental release is on npm, so the claim is checkable the way all compiler claims should be checked — by installing both and timing them. I did. The short version: the memory claim landed almost exactly, the speed claim is real but "up to" is doing some work, the diagnostics matched perfectly, the emitted JS was byte-identical — and the exit code wasn't.

The setup 

npm install tsrs typescript
tsrs        0.18.0-ts7.1.0-dev.20260929
            reports: Version 7.1.0-dev.20260930.4 (microsoft/TypeScript@b85298b)
typescript  7.0.2   (the "TypeScript 7.0" baseline from the claim)
machine     2 vCPU Linux VM, Node v24.20.0

One fairness note, because Cloudflare is honest about it in the post and you should be too when quoting me: tsrs tracks TypeScript 7.1 dev, and the post itself says TypeScript 7.1 beta is already up to 2.5x faster than 7.0, partly from optimizations upstreamed from tsrs. So this is not a clean "Rust vs Go, same compiler version" race. It's the race a user actually gets today: the two packages you can npm install right now, run with defaults on the same project. That's the comparison that decides whether you switch.

The corpus is synthetic but not trivial: 400 TypeScript files, 35,199 lines, generated deterministically — a chain of modules, each defining a generic interface, 28 generic functions doing Map construction over typed arrays, and Pick/& type aliases, all under strict: true with skipLibCheck. Both compilers ran tsc --noEmit / tsrs --noEmit, three runs each, timed externally with peak RSS from wait4 rusage (the compiler's own peak, not the npm shim's).

The numbers 

clean project, 400 files / 35,199 lines, --noEmit, defaults
              run 1     run 2     run 3     median    peak RSS
tsc 7.0.2     3.400s    2.508s    1.936s    2.508s    ~392 MB
tsrs 0.18.0   0.581s    0.474s    0.385s    0.474s    ~110 MB

Median-to-median that's 5.3x faster; best-to-best it's 5.0x; first (cold) runs give 5.9x. I couldn't coax out 8x on this box and corpus — but this is a 2-vCPU VM and a mid-size synthetic project, not Cloudflare's benchmark suite, and their wording is "up to." What I can say is that a 5x type-check speedup is not a rounding error or a cherry-picked microbenchmark. It's the difference between a check you run on save and a check you run on commit.

Memory is where it gets almost boring: ~110 MB vs ~392 MB peak is 72% less, against a claim of "~70% less." Reproduced, nearly to the digit. On a laptop that number is trivia; in the environments Cloudflare cares about — Wasm sandboxes, browser-hosted toolchains, Workers — it's the whole argument, and their post makes it explicitly: a Go binary compiled to Wasm carries its garbage collector with it, a Rust one doesn't have one to carry.

Startup overhead, for the small-project case (a one-file project, 5 runs each):

tsc    0.825  0.860  0.552  0.525  0.514   (seconds)
tsrs   0.450  0.354  0.247  0.209  0.217

Even where there's almost nothing to compile, tsrs starts in roughly half the time. Both are dominated by process startup at this size; the ratio is the story, not the absolutes.

Does it agree with tsc?

Speed is worthless if the port quietly checks a slightly different language. I seeded the same project with four errors across two files — two bad assignments, a call to a nonexistent function, and a method call on a number:

tsc:  exit=1, 4 errors
tsrs: exit=2, 4 errors
  src/mod10.ts(89,14):  error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.
  src/mod10.ts(90,14):  error TS2322: Type 'number' is not assignable to type 'string'.
  src/mod10.ts(91,1):   error TS2304: Cannot find name 'nonexistentFunction'.
  src/mod200.ts(89,42): error TS2339: Property 'toUpperCase' does not exist on type 'number'.

The four diagnostics are identical in file, line, column, code, and message — in this run even the order matched, though Cloudflare warns diagnostic order is a known current difference, so don't build tooling that depends on it. Then I compiled the clean project to JS with both: 400 output files each, and diff -rq found zero differences — byte-identical emit on this corpus.

The one real divergence I found is small and exactly the kind that breaks a CI script at 2 a.m.: on type errors, tsc exits 1 and tsrs exits 2. Any script doing if [ $? -eq 1 ] instead of -ne 0 will treat a failed tsrs check as success-shaped. It's an experimental release (the version string is a dev build, 0.18.0-ts7.1.0-dev), so this is a "file it and move on" difference, not a scandal — but it's the sort of detail the announcement's "compiles like tsc" framing glosses over, and now you know to grep for it.

Verdict

Reproduced, with one qualifier each:

  • "~70% less memory" — yes: 72% less on my corpus.
  • "Up to 8x faster" — I measured 5.3x median on a 2-vCPU VM with a 35k-line synthetic project, against a baseline (7.0.2) that tsrs's own upstream (7.1) is already much faster than. Treat 8x as a ceiling, 5x as plausible, and measure your own repo — the gap will move with project shape and core count.
  • Faithful port — on everything I threw at it: identical diagnostics, identical emit. One exit-code difference to check in your scripts.

The more interesting claim in Cloudflare's post isn't a number at all: it's that frontier models now make ports like this feasible in days, so the maintenance strategy is an agent that reads upstream TypeScript diffs every morning and regenerates a compatibility matrix every night. If that process holds, tsrs stays faithful; if it slips, tsrs becomes a fork with good benchmarks. The 5.3x I measured is real today. Whether it's still the same language in a year is a process question, and for once the vendor said so themselves.

Sources: Cloudflare's announcement (published today, October 20; HN 329 points), the tsrs npm package (0.18.0-ts7.1.0-dev.20260929). All timings, memory figures, diagnostics, and emit comparisons above were measured locally today; the corpus generator and benchmark script are deterministic (seed 42).

title: How to Build Retrieval Audit Logs for Internal Engineering PDFs in Go (Grounded)
description:
Short answer: build retrieval audit logs as an evidence ledger, not a transcript. For every answer over the PDF folder, pin the corpus revision, preserve the ordered chunk IDs returned by retrieval, record the citations selected by generation, and withhold any answer whose citations cannot be joined to that request's retrieval set.

Suppose the page fires at 02:17. The on-call sees a user report that an internal documentation answer cites release-runbook.pdf, page 18, but the active PDF has only 16 pages. CPU is quiet, latency is inside its objective, and the generator returned fluent prose. None of those signals answers the operational question: which indexed revision and which passages were allowed to support this answer?

The earlier signal should have been a failed evidence join.

Retrieval-augmented generation combines generated output with retrieved non-parametric memory, and the original RAG paper identifies provenance as a benefit of that arrangement. An application still has to turn provenance into an enforceable release rule. For this system, I would make citation validity a separate SLO from request availability — a response can be fast and syntactically valid while being unsuitable for release.

How should retrieval architecture govern audit logs for internal engineering documentation?

Start with governance, before picking an index or writing an event struct. Decide who may inspect a question, who may inspect retrieved PDF passages, how long each class of record survives, and which fields must remain usable after a serving component is replaced. A useful audit event needs enough information to reproduce the evidence boundary without copying every sensitive question, answer, and PDF passage into a second data store. Record a request ID, authenticated actor or calling service, event time, corpus snapshot ID, query digest, retrieval-policy version, ordered chunk IDs and scores, prompt-template version, answer digest, cited chunk IDs, validation result, latency, and final disposition.

Names are display data, not identity. release-runbook.pdf can be replaced while keeping the same filename, so derive a source revision from its content digest. A chunk identifier should also bind the source revision to a page range, chunking-policy version, and ordinal. That gives the evidence ledger stable handles across index rebuilds and makes a corpus snapshot a concrete manifest rather than a timestamp someone hopes is close enough.

Don't log credentials, authorization headers, or unrestricted extracted text. Auditability does not justify widening access to internal engineering documentation. If retention policy prohibits raw questions and answers, their digests plus access-controlled references can still support correlation and replay checks; if investigators must inspect content, keep that content behind the same authorization boundary as the source PDFs.

The retention classes don't have to match. Operational metrics can expire quickly, evidence events can remain for the investigation window, and source content can follow the documentation system's own policy. What matters is preserving the join keys for as long as the organization claims an answer is auditable. Deleting a PDF passage while retaining an event that points to it may satisfy an event-retention rule, but it no longer permits substantive replay; that limitation should be explicit.

Define a portable evidence contract in Go

The key invariant is deliberately narrow: every citation on a released answer must identify a chunk retrieved for that same request under the pinned corpus snapshot. This catches fabricated identifiers, stale cross-request citations, and broken correlation. It does not prove that the prose accurately represents the cited passage. That requires a separate evaluation of support, which is why one green citation_valid field must never be presented as total answer quality.

Keep that contract in application-owned fields rather than opaque component state. The following Go program hashes text that should not be copied into the event, checks citation membership and duplication, and emits one append-oriented JSON record. The sample data is illustrative; the invariant and portable identifiers are the parts to carry into production.

package main

import (
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "os"
    "time"
)

type RetrievedChunk struct {
    ID    string  `json:"id"`
    Score float64 `json:"score"`
}

type GeneratedAnswer struct {
    Text      string   `json:"text"`
    Citations []string `json:"citations"`
}

type AuditEvent struct {
    RequestID        string           `json:"request_id"`
    OccurredAt       time.Time        `json:"occurred_at"`
    CorpusSnapshot   string           `json:"corpus_snapshot"`
    RetrievalPolicy  string           `json:"retrieval_policy"`
    QueryDigest      string           `json:"query_digest"`
    Retrieved        []RetrievedChunk `json:"retrieved"`
    Citations        []string         `json:"citations"`
    AnswerDigest     string           `json:"answer_digest"`
    CitationValid    bool             `json:"citation_valid"`
    FinalDisposition string           `json:"final_disposition"`
}

func digest(value string) string {
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(value))
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
}

func validateCitations(retrieved []RetrievedChunk, citations []string) error {
    if len(citations) == 0 {
        return errors.New("answer has no citations")
    }

    allowed := make(map[string]struct{}, len(retrieved))
    for _, chunk := range retrieved {
        allowed[chunk.ID] = struct{}{}
    }

    seen := make(map[string]struct{}, len(citations))
    for _, citation := range citations {
        if _, ok := allowed[citation]; !ok {
            return fmt.Errorf("citation %q was not retrieved", citation)
        }
        if _, duplicate := seen[citation]; duplicate {
            return fmt.Errorf("citation %q is duplicated", citation)
        }
        seen[citation] = struct{}{}
    }
    return nil
}

func main() {
    retrieved := []RetrievedChunk{
        {ID: "runbook-digest:page-18:chunk-2:v3", Score: 0.84},
        {ID: "policy-digest:page-4:chunk-1:v3", Score: 0.79},
    }
    answer := GeneratedAnswer{
        Text:      "Production changes require the documented approval step.",
        Citations: []string{"runbook-digest:page-18:chunk-2:v3"},
    }

    validationErr := validateCitations(retrieved, answer.Citations)
    disposition := "released"
    if validationErr != nil {
        disposition = "withheld"
    }

    event := AuditEvent{
        RequestID:        "req-7f31",
        OccurredAt:       time.Now().UTC(),
        CorpusSnapshot:   "corpus-a17",
        RetrievalPolicy:  "hybrid-v3",
        QueryDigest:      digest("What approval is required for production changes?"),
        Retrieved:        retrieved,
        Citations:        answer.Citations,
        AnswerDigest:     digest(answer.Text),
        CitationValid:    validationErr == nil,
        FinalDisposition: disposition,
    }

    if err := json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout).Encode(event); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    if validationErr != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, validationErr)
        os.Exit(2)
    }
}

Run it with:

go run main.go

Withholding is intentional. If the user interface must always return something, return a non-answer such as “No supported answer was found in the indexed documents” and record that disposition; don't let an uncited fallback bypass the same release rule. The catch is that strict withholding is not suitable when the workflow explicitly values partial discovery over a supported answer, such as exploratory search where users inspect source pages themselves. In that case, label the result as search output, expose the passages, and don't represent generated prose as grounded.

Make migration a replay test

A retrieval migration is acceptable only if old and new paths can be compared through the same evidence contract. Feed both paths the same pinned corpus snapshot and approved question set, then compare candidate membership, citation validity, and disposition. Score values may not be comparable across implementations, so don't declare a migration safe because two arbitrary decimals are close; compare the decisions the scores produce and retain each policy version.

The same replay gives the 02:17 responder a map. Group the affected audit events by corpus snapshot and retrieval-policy version, then compare those groups with the prior healthy window. If an impossible citation ID is absent from its request's ordered retrieval set, investigate request correlation and the release validator. If the expected page is absent from every candidate set, move earlier in the pipeline: PDF extraction, chunk identity, snapshot publication, or retrieval policy. If the page appears in the candidates but the answer does not cite it, move later: prompt assembly and support evaluation. These paths have different owners and rollback decisions. A single “RAG quality” alarm is weak operationally because it asks someone to reconstruct all of them under time pressure.

Build the replay suite from approved question-to-source-page mappings. Measure candidate-set success separately from answer support: did retrieval include an acceptable page, and did each released claim remain inside its cited evidence? A fluent answer can hide poor retrieval, while a good candidate set can be squandered later. Keeping the stages separate makes the alert actionable and keeps component owners from arguing over one blended score.

Migration exposes lock-in in a measurable way. If corpus snapshots, chunk identities, and audit events use an application-owned schema, the serving implementation can change without erasing historical meaning. If those identities exist only inside one index, migration requires preserving two interpretation systems or abandoning replay for older answers. Decide which loss is acceptable before ingestion starts.

One more trap deserves a short rule.

Don't replay against “latest.” Replay against the snapshot that served the request.

Budget retention and ownership before choosing components

Capacity planning follows the evidence path. Estimate ingestion demand from changed PDF bytes and pages per revision, index size from chunks per page and representation size, query demand from peak requests and candidates considered, and ledger retention from events per request times retained fields. Load-test publication separately from query serving. A large documentation update and a query spike consume different resources, and one shared concurrency limit couples two failure domains that the architecture can keep apart.

The build-versus-buy decision then follows the evidence contract rather than preceding it. A managed component can remove index operations from the team's on-call load; a self-hosted component can give the team tighter control over placement, retention, and change timing. Neither choice supplies auditability by itself.

Boundary Build and operate Managed component Decision test
PDF extraction and identity Control digest and chunk rules; own parser drift Reduce parser upkeep; accept the offered identity model Can an unchanged source revision reproduce the same chunk IDs?
Retrieval index Control placement and rollout; own capacity and recovery Transfer more operations; verify event export and version semantics Can a served result be tied to a pinned snapshot?
Evidence ledger Control schema, retention, and access; own durability Reduce storage operations; validate portability and deletion controls Can an investigator replay the join after the serving system changes?
Release validator Keep the invariant in application code Delegate only if behavior is testable and observable Can unsupported output be withheld before it reaches a user?

Stick with managed infrastructure when it exports the identifiers and version context the ledger requires, and the reduction in on-call work matters more than tuning freedom. Build or self-host the boundary when retention, placement, deterministic identity, or replay access cannot be met by the managed contract. A team with no capacity to operate an index should not self-host merely to gain theoretical control; an ownership boundary that routinely misses its SLO is not safer.

Set the page after the policy is testable

Only now is the alert definition defensible. Emit bounded state transitions such as retrieval_started, retrieval_completed, citation_validation_completed, answer_released, and answer_withheld. Outcome and policy version can be metric labels when their value sets are controlled. Request IDs, filenames, and chunk IDs should remain in traces or audit storage rather than metric labels because their value sets grow with requests and the corpus.

The instrumentation change is small: add the evidence-join result and its version context at the release boundary, then carry the same request ID through retrieval, validation, and disposition. The page can now say which invariant failed and which policy state served it. Earlier indicators — rising zero-result rate, a shift in candidate scores after a retrieval-policy change, or a snapshot falling behind its source manifest — belong in a non-paging warning path until replay evidence shows that they predict the release SLO.

I'm not sure any universal numeric threshold for citation-valid answers is defensible. Traffic volume, the base rate of questions the PDFs can answer, and the cost of withholding all change the paging trade-off. What resolves that uncertainty is replaying known questions against real corpus snapshots, observing the failure distribution, and choosing a window that corresponds to an action the on-call can actually take.

Page on sustained user harm: a breach in the objective for releasable, citation-valid answers. A single rejected answer should be withheld and counted, but paging on each rejection imposes a false-positive cost during sparse traffic and trains responders to ignore the signal.

This returns us to the page. A threshold set too tightly wakes the on-call for isolated, correctly withheld requests; one set too loosely lets a sustained grounding regression reach users before anyone acts. The right alert is the narrowest sustained breach that maps to a documented rollback, snapshot repair, or policy rollback — and the audit ledger is what tells the responder which action fits.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401

Building Query Conditions In JooqTemplate
description:
Using JooqTemplate requires no code generation and no XML configuration.

Add Dependency

gradle:

implementation 'net.sf.sprtool:sprtool-jooq:1.7.0'

maven:

<dependency>
    <groupId>net.sf.sprtool</groupId>
    <artifactId>sprtool-jooq</artifactId>
    <version>1.7.0</version>
</dependency>

Inject JooqTemplate 

import static net.sf.sprtool.jooq.JooqFields.*;

import net.sf.sprtool.jooq.JooqTemplate;

@Autowired
private JooqTemplate jt;

Using JooqTemplate

Method 1: conditions() — Field-Value Pair Varargs (Recommended)

conditions(Object... fieldValuePairs) takes arguments in pairs of "field name, value"; the operator is written directly after the field name string, and when no operator is written the default is ==. It returns a List<Condition>, and conditions whose values are null are automatically ignored:

// name = 'Smartphone' and price > 1000 and status = 'on_sale'
List<Condition> conds = jt.conditions(
        "name", "Smartphone",
        "price>", 1000,        // the > operator follows the field name
        "stock<=", 50,         // the <= operator
        "status", "on_sale");  // default operator ==

// You can also separate the field and operator with a colon: "price:>"
List<Condition> conds2 = jt.conditions("price:>", 1000);

When a parameter value is null, that condition is ignored — ideal for dynamic queries: if the frontend doesn't send a value, no filter is applied:

// When nameParam is null, no name condition is generated
List<Condition> conds = jt.conditions("name", nameParam, "category", categoryParam);

You can also mix native jOOQ Condition objects directly into the varargs:

Condition other = DSL.field("price").ge(1000);
List<Condition> conds = jt.conditions("category", "Electronics", other);

Method 2: and() / or() — Directly Returning a Single Combined Condition

and(...) and or(...) take arguments exactly like conditions(); the difference is the return value: multiple conditions are merged with AND / OR into a single Condition, and null is returned when there are no conditions at all:

// AND: name = 'John' and age > 30 and status = 'active'
Condition cond = jt.and("name", "John", "age>", 30, "status", "active");

// OR: name like 'Soph%' or name like 'Fra%'
Condition cond2 = jt.or("name:%l", "Soph", "name:%l", "Fra");

// Empty arguments return null
Condition empty = jt.and();   // null

Find two users with OR (corresponding to the user_table example in JooqTemplateOrTest):

// name = 'John' or name = 'Lee'
Condition cond = jt.or("name", "John", "name", "Lee");
List<LowerCaseRecord> records = jt.queryLowerCaseRecord("user_table", cond);

Method 3: condition() — Single-Condition Method

condition(Name fieldName, String operator, Object[] values) accepts a jOOQ Name, an operator string, and a value array, and generates a single Condition. The number of values must match what the operator requires, otherwise an IllegalArgumentException is thrown:

import org.jooq.Condition;
import org.jooq.Name;
import org.jooq.impl.DSL;

// Equality: == requires 1 value
Condition c1 = jt.condition(DSL.name("name"), "==", new Object[]{"Smartphone"});

// Comparison: > requires 1 value
Condition c2 = jt.condition(DSL.name("price"), ">", new Object[]{1000});

// in: requires 1 value, and the value must be a Collection or Object[]
Condition c3 = jt.condition(DSL.name("category"), "in",
        new Object[]{Arrays.asList("Electronics", "Appliances", "Apparel")});

// between: requires 2 values
Condition c4 = jt.condition(DSL.name("created_at"), "between",
        new Object[]{beginDate, endDate});

// isnull: requires 0 values
Condition c5 = jt.condition(DSL.name("remark"), "isnull", new Object[]{});

This method also follows the null rules: a null value returns null (ignored); wrapping with ND(null) generates is null; a null field name or operator returns null; an invalid operator throws IllegalArgumentException:

// Value is null → returns null, condition ignored
Condition c = jt.condition(DSL.name("name"), "==", new Object[]{null});   // null

// ND wrapping null → generates name is null
Condition c2 = jt.condition(DSL.name("name"), "==", new Object[]{ND(null)});

// Value count mismatch → throws IllegalArgumentException("Operator require value count is 1")
Condition c3 = jt.condition(DSL.name("name"), "==", new Object[]{});

not() — Negating a Condition

not(Condition) negates an existing condition and returns null when the input is null:

Condition original = jt.and("status", "disabled");
Condition notDisabled = jt.not(original);   // not (status = 'disabled')

orOne() — Multiple Fields Matching the Same Value

orOne(Object... sameOneValues) starts with several "fields" (single-value operators), and the last argument is the shared value, generating field1 op value or field2 op value .... A typical "global keyword search" scenario:

// name = 'Apple' or nick_name = 'Apple' or remark = 'Apple'
Condition cond = jt.orOne("name", "nick_name", "remark", "Apple");

Null Fallback for between

between / notbetween take 2 values; when either end is null, it automatically falls back to a one-sided comparison, and when both ends are null the whole condition is ignored:

// Both begin and end are non-null: price between 100 and 500
jt.conditions("price:between", 100, 500);

// begin=100, end=null: price >= 100
jt.conditions("price:between", 100, null);

// notbetween fallback: begin=null, end=500 → price > 500
jt.conditions("price:notbetween", null, 500);

Operator Reference

Condition operators (written after the field name or passed to condition(); all are case-insensitive):

Operator Value Count Meaning
== (default) 1 Equal to
<> 1 Not equal to
> >= < <= 1 Comparison
% / like 1 Contains %value%
%l / llike 1 Prefix match value%
%r / rlike 1 Suffix match %value
in / notin 1 Value is a Collection or Object[]
between / notbetween 2 Range; a null end falls back automatically
isnull / isnotnull 0 Null check

Sort operators (only used in the order part of a query or in orders()): asc, ascnf (nulls first), ascnl (nulls last), desc, descnf, descnl.

Null handling rules:

  • In queries (conditions() / and() / or() / condition()), a null value → the condition is ignored.
  • A value wrapped with ND(null) → generates field is null.
  • In UPDATE / DELETE, a null value → generates field is null.

title: Crafting a Professional Services Website RFP: A Comprehensive Guide
description:
Crafting a Professional Services Website RFP: A Comprehensive Guide

In the digital age, a well-crafted Request for Proposal (RFP) is essential for professional services firms seeking to build a website that truly reflects their expertise and meets their unique needs. However, many firms fall short by relying on generic templates, which often fail to address the specific challenges and requirements of their industry. This guide outlines why standard RFPs are inadequate and provides actionable insights to ensure your RFP stands out.

Why Off-the-Shelf Templates Fall Short

1. Lack of Customization

Generic RFPs are one-size-fits-all solutions that rarely align with the specific needs of professional services firms. These templates often overlook critical aspects such as showcasing expertise, managing client confidentiality, and presenting complex service offerings.

2. Insufficient Technical Depth

Professional services websites often require advanced functionalities like secure client portals, project management tools, and custom reporting. Off-the-shelf RFPs lack the technical depth needed to address these requirements, potentially leading to underwhelming results.

3. Poor User Experience Focus

The user experience (UX) is crucial for professional services websites, as they aim to inspire trust and professionalism. Generic templates often fail to emphasize the importance of a seamless, intuitive UX, which can hinder user engagement and retention.

Engineering Takeaways for a Tailored RFP

1. Start with User Personas

Begin by defining detailed user personas for your website. This includes potential clients, existing clients, and internal stakeholders. Understanding their needs, pain points, and behaviors will help you craft an RFP that addresses their specific requirements.

2. Prioritize Technical Architecture

Ensure your RFP includes a detailed technical architecture section. This should outline the necessary backend systems, integration points, and security measures. By doing so, you can attract vendors who can deliver a robust, scalable solution.

3. Include Detailed UX Requirements

A professional services website must offer a seamless and intuitive user experience. Specify UX requirements such as navigation structure, content hierarchy, and mobile responsiveness. Consider including wireframes or mockups to provide a clear vision.

Conclusion

Inspired to submit your own? Rank about ten proposals you'd like to see prioritized. The Firefox team says that's enough to provide useful input.

Would You Let Your AI Agent Grade Its Own Homework? — Agents write code faster than ever. They even review their own work. But who’s reviewing them? Dropbox, Notion & ElevenLabs don’t take the risk. With Meticulous, every change is exhaustively verified, with zero developer effort.

Meticulous sponsor

🗳️ The State of HTML 2026 — The annual survey returns to measure the awareness and adoption of HTML features and browser APIs. This year covers Web Components, progressive enhancement, AI, and more. It takes less than 15 minutes and you can learn new things just by taking it.

Devographics

Safari Blocks 'Identity Resolution' Tracking Infrastructure — Cross-site cookies are long gone in Safari, so trackers moved to 'identity resolution' where third parties get the email address you type into forms and turn it into a cross-site, cross-device tracking ID. Safari now blocks them at the domain level.

Wilander, Wolfe, and Finkel (WebKit)

  • 🌐 Chrome 157 is in beta with corner shorthands, a <string> value for text-overflow, and anchor-valid. Chrome 156 went stable this week with CSS random().

  • 🚫 Chrome has finished deprecating the unload event: handlers no longer fire by default, so use pagehide or visibilitychange instead.

📙 Articles, Opinions & Tutorials

JPEG XL vs AVIF for Web Use-Cases — Now that JPEG XL has landed in all major browsers, Jake took the format for a spin, benchmarking it against AVIF. There's a lot of detail here with some good takeaways. You might also be surprised at what you can cram in under 200 bytes with JPEG XL.

Jake Archibald

Embracing Playful Imperfection with CSS's random() Function — A look at how to approach adding some randomness into our projects, and whether it makes sense on the web. The demos here show off some ideas, like organic typography, bouncing letters, and splayed cards.

Brecht De Ruyte

Photorealistic 3D in the Browser Without the Rendering Overhead — Learn how radiance fields and spatial streaming bridge real-time photorealistic 3D to the web with just 2 lines of Three.js.

Miris sponsor

Fitting an Element's Height to Its Background Pattern with calc-size() — A repeating pattern cut off at the bottom is a classic annoyance. Ahmad uses calc-size() (Chromium only for now, Safari soon) with round() to snap an element's auto height to a multiple of the tile height.

Ahmad Shadeed

Core Web Vitals Now (Experimentally) Count Soft Navigations — Most sites won’t notice, but navigation-heavy SPAs should see scores improve, with Search Console switching over when it goes stable next year.

Annie Sullivan (Google)

Using Math to Balance Your Heading Styles — Craig outlines a simple system for styling heading levels using a modular scale.

Craig Abbott

▶  Do We Really Need alpha()? — We now have three ways to lower the opacity of a color in CSS. Kevin has the details, highlighting what the alpha function brings to the table in particular.

Kevin Powell

WCAG 3: A Different Future for Accessibility — Why binary pass/fail made WCAG 2 a ceiling, and how WCAG 3 aims to make conformance a floor.

Phil Eaton

Do Web Components Have a Future If Nobody is Writing Them?
Nolan Lawson

📊 Chartist 2.0: This Lightweight SVG Charting Library Is Back — A freshly modernized SVG charting library that you style with CSS. It originally popped up in 2014, but "went stale". It's back with a composable API, server-side rendering, and still remains small. There's a migration guide for existing users.

Gion Kunz et al.

Mobile AI Infrastructure for Web Devs Who Code with Agents — Point the agent you use for the web at iOS and Android. Expo takes care of the native builds and the trip to the stores.

pour: A Free Accessibility Checker & WCAG Audit Tool — Available as a browser extension or bookmarklet. Run it on any page to see an overlay with violations categorized as critical, serious, moderate, minor, etc.

title: Give your coding assistant a design brief, not just a screenshot
description:
A screenshot can show a coding assistant the shape of a design. A short brief with actual colors, typography and spacing gives it values it can work with. You can collect those values with browser DevTools; a CSS inspection extension can reduce some of the clicking.

Disclosure: I'm working on Stylegrab, the extension used in the accompanying demo. The workflow below also works manually.

Editorial disclosure: this article was prepared with AI assistance. The examples and product demo use our own sample page; the extension does not call an AI model.

Choose the part of the reference that matters

Start with a page you own or have permission to reuse. Pick one component and a small set of visual rules: a page background, text and accent colors, body and heading type, common spacing and corner radii. Keep your own product's content and identity.

Read rendered values as well as source rules

The declaration with the highest selector specificity doesn't always win. Cascade layers, importance and other parts of the cascade come first. In DevTools, use the Computed panel to check the final value before copying it. For a tool, this is a useful regression test:

@layer base, overrides;
@layer base { #example { color: red; } }
@layer overrides { .example { color: blue; } }

For <div id="example" class="example">, the normal declaration in the later layer wins: blue. A copier that sorts only by selector specificity will give you the wrong starting point.

Write a compact brief 

Use these reference values for our settings panel:
Background #0E1016; surface #171B24.
Text #E7E9EE; secondary text #A6ACBA; accent #7C6CFF.
Body: system sans-serif, 16px, line-height 1.5.
Heading: 28px, weight 700.
Spacing: 8px / 16px / 24px. Cards: 12px radius.
Keep our own copy and product identity.
Verify contrast and keyboard focus.
Check the result at 390px and 1280px widths.

These are illustrative values. Replace them with the values you actually need, and compare them with your project's existing design tokens.

Export a component as a starting point

A static HTML/CSS export can help with a button or card. It doesn't bring along the application's state, JavaScript interactions or all responsive rules. Check asymmetric borders and radii too: four different corners cannot be represented by one uniform rounded class.

Verify in the destination page

Check the narrow layout, focus and hover states, text contrast, and the influence of your own theme. With Tailwind, make sure the generated classes are included in your build and that your theme hasn't changed the meaning of a named utility.

The Stylegrab guide includes the workflow and demo. Its free inspection tools and Pro trials are being prepared for the Chrome Web Store release; the page shows the current installation and payment availability.

title: Announcing Amazon ECS Gateway, a managed ingress solution for your ECS services
description:
AWS announces Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) Gateway, a new resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized applications by dynamically provisioning and managing Application Load Balancers (ALBs) and their supporting resources directly in your account.

With ECS Gateway, platform teams define organizational networking standards once on a gateway and associate it with one or more clusters, giving organizations a centralized way to govern how traffic reaches their ECS services. Application teams simply opt in to inherit those standards without requiring networking expertise. ECS Gateway offers host-based routing, allows up to 25 services to share an ALB to optimize infrastructure costs, and gives each service a unique Domain Name System (DNS) hostname. ECS manages the full lifecycle of the underlying infrastructure, provisioning the first ALB when your first service connects, adding more ALBs when capacity is reached, and removing them when no longer needed. You can inspect these resources and the gateway route to each service to see exactly how requests reach your applications. For traffic and health monitoring, you can use standard ALB metrics in Amazon CloudWatch and target health information from Elastic Load Balancing.

To get started, create an ECS Gateway, associate it with a cluster, and opt in your ECS service by adding the gateway connector parameter using the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, API, AWS SDKs, or AWS CloudFormation. ECS Gateway is available for ECS services using the awsvpc network mode across all launch types. It is available now in all commercial AWS Regions at no additional charge. You pay only for the underlying infrastructure provisioned in your account when your services connect to the gateway. To learn more, refer to the AWS News blog and our documentation page.

title: Getting Started with AWS S3: Creating a Bucket, Uploading an Object, and Understanding Why the Object URL Says Access Denied
description:
Introduction

I'm starting a new series on AWS, and this first article covers Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service), one of the most widely used services on AWS. I did this lab in my own personal AWS free-tier account, and I'll explain every term as it comes up.

By the end, you'll know how to:

  • Create an S3 bucket with a consistent naming convention
  • Read the bucket's ARN and properties
  • Upload a file to the bucket
  • Find an object's URL, and understand why opening the image works while opening the Object URL doesn't

What is Amazon S3?

Amazon S3 is an object storage service. Instead of organizing data in a traditional disk with a file system, S3 stores data as objects inside buckets. You can store and retrieve any amount of data from anywhere, and you pay only for what you use.

Three terms to know first:

  • Bucket: a container for your data. Every object in S3 lives inside a bucket.
  • Object: the thing you store. It's the file itself plus its metadata (size, type, last modified date and so on).
  • Key: the object's unique name inside the bucket. For my file, the key is datacenter.png.

Step 1: Open the S3 service

In the AWS Management Console, I typed S3 into the search bar and selected S3 (Scalable Storage in the Cloud) from the results.

This opens the Amazon S3 landing page, where Create bucket is the first thing you see.

Step 2: Create a bucket

I clicked Create bucket, and the only thing I had to provide was the bucket name. The region was already set for me (more on that below), and I left everything else at the defaults to keep things simple.

Region

I didn't pick the region on this page. The Create bucket page shows it as plain text, not a dropdown: Europe (Stockholm) eu-north-1. That's because S3 creates a bucket in whichever region your console is currently set to, and mine was already set to Stockholm. If you want a different region, switch it with the region selector in the top bar of the console before you click Create bucket.

A region is a physical geographic location where AWS runs data centers. Your bucket's data stays in the region it was created in, and the region affects latency (how close the data is to your users) and pricing.

Bucket type

I kept General purpose, which AWS recommends for most use cases. The other option, Directory, is for low-latency workloads that use a single Availability Zone.

Bucket namespace

I kept Global namespace. A namespace is the set of names in which yours has to be unique. In the global namespace, a bucket name must be unique across all AWS accounts, in every region. If someone else already has my-bucket, you can't use it. The console also offers an Account Regional namespace (labelled "recommended"). Buckets created there are unique only within your own account, so no other AWS account can ever claim the same name. I stayed with the global namespace for this lab.

Bucket name and the prefix naming convention

I named my bucket aws-lab1-rahimah.

The aws-lab1- part is a prefix I chose as a naming convention. A consistent prefix gives you three things:

  • It keeps names unique, since adding your own name or project helps avoid clashes in the global namespace.
  • It groups related resources together (aws-lab1-..., aws-lab2-...).
  • It makes resources easy to find and to clean up later.

S3 bucket names must be 3 to 63 characters long, can contain only lowercase letters, numbers, periods and hyphens, and must begin and end with a letter or number.

Default encryption

Further down the page, Default encryption was already set to Server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3). This means S3 automatically encrypts every new object at rest, using keys that AWS manages for you. You don't have to do anything. I left it as it was and clicked Create bucket.

S3 confirmed with a green banner: Successfully created bucket "aws-lab1-rahimah". The Objects tab shows Objects (0) because the bucket is empty.

Step 3: Look at the bucket's properties and ARN

I opened the Properties tab. The Bucket overview shows three things:

  • AWS Region: Europe (Stockholm) eu-north-1
  • Creation date: October 20, 2026
  • Amazon Resource Name (ARN): arn:aws:s3:::aws-lab1-rahimah

What is an ARN?

An Amazon Resource Name (ARN) is the unique identifier AWS gives every resource. It's how you point at a specific resource in IAM policies, logs and other services. The general shape is:

arn:partition:service:region:account-id:resource

For S3 buckets, the region and account sections are empty, which is why you see three colons in a row (:::). The bucket name is the final part.

The Properties tab also shows two settings that were off by default:

  • Bucket Versioning: Disabled. Versioning keeps multiple versions of an object, so you can recover from accidental overwrites or deletions. With it disabled, uploading a file with the same key replaces the old one.
  • Multi-factor authentication (MFA) delete: Disabled. This extra layer of security requires MFA before you can permanently delete object versions.

Step 4: Upload a file to the bucket

Back on the Objects tab, I clicked Upload.

On the Upload page, I clicked Add files and picked an image called datacenter.png from my Downloads folder. You can also drag and drop files, or use Add folder to upload a whole folder.

The page then listed the file as 1 total, 2.4 MB, type image/png, with the destination shown as s3://aws-lab1-rahimah.

Scrolling down, you'll see two collapsed sections:

  • Permissions: where you can grant public access and access to other AWS accounts.
  • Properties: where you can set the storage class, encryption settings and tags.

I left both alone and clicked Upload.

The next page showed Upload succeeded, with a summary of 1 file, 2.4 MB, 100% succeeded and 0 failed.

Back in the bucket, Objects (1) now lists datacenter.png, size 2.4 MB, and storage class Standard.

Storage class controls how your data is stored and what it costs. Standard is the default and is meant for frequently accessed data. Other classes, such as Glacier, are cheaper for data you rarely need to retrieve.

Step 5: Explore the object's details

I clicked datacenter.png to open its details. The Object overview shows:

  • Owner: the canonical ID of the AWS account that owns the object
  • AWS Region: eu-north-1
  • Last modified, Size and Type
  • Key: datacenter.png
  • S3 URI: s3://aws-lab1-rahimah/datacenter.png
  • ARN: arn:aws:s3:::aws-lab1-rahimah/datacenter.png
  • Entity tag (ETag): an identifier for this specific version of the object's content
  • Object URL: https://aws-lab1-rahimah.s3.eu-north-1.amazonaws.com/datacenter.png

Two of these are easy to confuse:

  • The S3 URI (s3://bucket/key) is what AWS tools like the AWS CLI and SDKs use to refer to an object.
  • The Object URL is the HTTPS address of the object on the internet, in the form https://bucket-name.s3.region.amazonaws.com/key.

The ARN here is the bucket's ARN with the object key added on the end.

Step 6: Open the image vs. use the Object URL

This is the part that surprised me, and it taught me the most. There are two ways to view the uploaded image, and they behave differently.

Option 1: Click "Open"

Clicking the Open button displays the image in a new browser tab. The address bar shows a very long URL that carries extra parameters such as X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256.

That is a presigned URL. When you click Open, the console uses your own credentials to generate a temporary, signed link that grants access to the object for a short time. S3 sees the signature, confirms that a permitted user created it, and serves the file.

Option 2: Paste the Object URL

When I copied the plain Object URL into the browser, I got this:

<Error>
  <Code>AccessDenied</Code>
  <Message>Access Denied</Message>
  ...
</Error>

Why the difference?

The Object URL is an unauthenticated request. When you paste it into a browser, there's no signature and nothing that tells S3 who you are, so S3 treats you as an anonymous visitor. S3 buckets and objects are private by default, and only the owner can access them unless permissions are explicitly granted. So the anonymous request is refused with AccessDenied.

The error is not a bug. It shows S3's security model working as designed: nothing is public until you deliberately make it so.

Making objects public

If you need public access, for example to host images on a website, you'd have to change two things: turn off the relevant Block Public Access settings on the bucket, and then grant read access through a bucket policy or object permissions. Only do this for data that's genuinely meant to be public. For private files, presigned URLs are a safer way to share something temporarily.

Key Takeaways

  • A bucket is a container and an object is a file inside it, identified by its key.
  • Bucket names must be globally unique, so a naming prefix like aws-lab1- helps keep names unique and organized.
  • The region determines where your data physically lives.
  • An ARN uniquely identifies any AWS resource, and an object's ARN is its bucket's ARN plus the key.
  • The S3 URI is for AWS tools, while the Object URL is the HTTPS address.
  • S3 is private by default. Opening an object from the console works because it uses a presigned URL, while the plain Object URL returns AccessDenied.

Clean up

To avoid unexpected charges, delete what you created. You must empty a bucket before you can delete it:

  1. Select datacenter.png and click Delete. Make sure you tick it, so that the Delete button is not greyed out.


Then confirm deletion.

  1. Go back to the bucket list, select aws-lab1-rahimah and click Delete.

Conclusion

In this first lab, I created an S3 bucket, uploaded an object, and learned why access to it is blocked by default. Next in the series, I'll build on this with more S3 features and other AWS services.

If you're learning AWS, let me know in the comments which service I should cover next.
