title: Autonomous LLM Agents as Dynamic Decision Nodes in Temporal Sagas
description:
Modern core banking platforms are increasingly adopting generative AI and Large Language Model (LLM) agents to handle complex operational reasoning—such as assessing unstructured trade finance documents, triaging complex fraud cases, and resolving cross-border exception processing. However, introducing autonomous AI agents into core banking workflows presents a fundamental architectural contradiction: Temporal Sagas demand absolute determinism, whereas LLM reasoning is inherently non-deterministic.

Temporal workflows achieve fault tolerance through event-sourced execution replay. If a workflow definition behaves non-deterministically during history replay, execution drifts, state corruption occurs, and replay validation fails. Conversely, LLMs generate probabilistic outcomes influenced by temperature settings, floating-point variance across hardware inference clusters, and model version shifts.

Under the Xenon Architecture Standards, core banking platforms resolve this tension by encapsulating autonomous LLM agents inside isolated Temporal Activities bounded by strict JSON schema contracts, formal validation guardrails, and deterministic fallback paths. This paper evaluates the operational boundaries, dynamic task planning topologies, mathematical reliability models, and compensation patterns required to deploy autonomous LLM agents as dynamic decision nodes in distributed core banking Sagas.

💡 Explore the Xenon Architecture Standard For comprehensive architectural blueprints, BIAN service domain mappings, and dual-orchestration integration patterns, visit the official Xenon Architecture Guide. To inspect reference code, infrastructure templates, and open-source banking modules, explore the VecPay-Tech GitHub Organization.

Architectural Boundaries across BIAN Service Domains

Not all decision nodes within a Banking Industry Architecture Network (BIAN) ecosystem require LLM autonomy. Integrating AI agents into deterministic Sagas must be strictly categorized by domain risk and exception frequency.

BIAN Service Domain Capability Mapped to LLM Node Autonomy Level Primary Risk Boundary Fallback Mechanism
Trade Positioning LC (Letter of Credit) document clause verification Semi-Autonomous Operational Exception Human-in-the-Loop Approval
Fraud Evaluation Suspicious transaction triage & contextual analysis Autonomous Decision False Positive Risk Default Deterministic Rule Engine
Customer Onboarding Unstructured Identity Exception Handling Semi-Autonomous Compliance / Regulatory Re-route to Compliance Officer Task
Payment Execution Automated Payment Clearing & ISO20022 Routing Strict Deterministic (No LLM) High Financial Risk N/A (Hardcoded / DMN Engine Only)
Position Keeping Double-Entry Ledger Posting Strict Deterministic (No LLM) Balance Integrity Risk N/A (Static Microservice Logic)

The Determinism Isolation Pattern

To prevent non-deterministic LLM behavior from corrupting Temporal's execution history, LLM agent reasoning must never execute directly within a Temporal Workflow Definition. Instead, the workflow definition maintains absolute determinism, while the LLM execution logic is fully encapsulated inside a Temporal Activity.

                  THE DETERMINISM ISOLATION ARCHITECTURE

  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | TEMPORAL WORKFLOW ENGINE (100% Deterministic Event History Execution)          |
  |                                                                                 |
  |  [Start Workflow] ---> [Execute Activity: RunAgentActivity] ---> [Branch Logic] |
  +-----------------------------------|---------------------------------^-----------+
                                      |                                 |
                           1. Invoke Activity Payload        4. Return Deterministic
                              (Structured Context)              Structured JSON Output
                                      |                                 |
  +-----------------------------------|---------------------------------|-----------+
  | TEMPORAL ACTIVITY WORKER LAYER    v                                 |           |
  | (Non-Deterministic Sandbox)                                         |           |
  |                                                                     |           |
  |  +---------------------------------------------------------------+  |           |
  |  | LLM AGENT REASONING LOOP                                      |  |           |
  |  |                                                               |  |           |
  |  |  [Construct Prompt] ---> [LLM Inference Engine (OpenAI/Ollama)]|  |           |
  |  |                                  │                            |  |           |
  |  |                                  ▼                            |  |           |
  |  |  [JSON Guardrail Validation] ◄── [Tool Call / Re-Act Loop]     |  |           |
  |  +----------------------------------│----------------------------+  |           |
  |                                     |                               |           |
  |                          2. Return Output Schema                    |           |
  |                             (Passed or Rejected)                    |           |
  +-------------------------------------│-------------------------------+-----------+
                                        v
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | IMMUTABLE EVENT STORE & STATE AUDIT                                             |
  |  [ Persists Prompt Hash, Token Cost, Confidence Score, and Decision Payload ]  |
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Key Architectural Rules

  1. Replay Immutability: Temporal records the activity output payload (the LLM's final structured JSON decision) into the workflow's Event History. During workflow replay, Temporal does not re-invoke the LLM activity; it simply reads the recorded decision payload from history.
  2. Deterministic Branching: The workflow evaluates the structured decision payload using standard deterministic logic (if/else or switch statements) to dispatch downstream machine Sagas or human tasks.
  3. Idempotency & Retry Safety: LLM activities must implement strict idempotency keys (derived from WorkflowID + RunID + ActivityTaskID) to prevent duplicate inference costs or repeated side effects during network retries.

Mathematical Model: Agent Decision Reliability & Guardrail Probability

The reliability of an LLM agent operating as a dynamic decision node within a distributed financial Saga depends on schema adherence, hallucination rates, and downstream transaction commitment.

The probability of a successful autonomous decision node commit Pnode-success​ across an agentic execution path is defined as:

Pnode-success​=Pschema-valid​×(1−Phallucination​)×Psaga-commit​

Where:

  • Pschema-valid​ is the probability that the LLM output conforms strictly to the target JSON schema on attempt k (where k≤MaxRetries ).
  • Phallucination​ is the probability that the agent generates a factually incorrect decision despite schema validity.
  • Psaga-commit​ is the probability that the downstream distributed machine Saga succeeds without compensation.

If the agent's confidence score falls below a pre-configured threshold θconfidence​ , or if Pschema-valid​=0 after maximum retries, the system triggers a Deterministic Fallback Override, shifting control to a standard rule engine or human user task.

Technical Implementation: Agentic Activity & Temporal Workflow

1. Structured Output Decision Schema (Java DTOs) 

package com.xenon.banking.ai.model;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonProperty;
import java.util.List;

public record TradeExceptionDecision(
    @JsonProperty(required = true) String decisionOutcome, // "APPROVE_EXEMPTION", "REJECT_EXEMPTION", "ESCALATE_HUMAN"
    @JsonProperty(required = true) double confidenceScore, // 0.0 to 1.0
    @JsonProperty(required = true) String reasoningSummary,
    @JsonProperty(required = true) List<String> verifiedClauseIdentifiers,
    @JsonProperty(required = true) String recommendedCompensatingAction
) {}

2. Temporal Activity Encapsulating the LLM Reasoning Loop

This Java activity executes an agentic reasoning loop using structured function calling. If the LLM generates invalid JSON or fails validation constraints, the activity retries locally up to a bounded threshold before returning an explicit failure state.

package com.xenon.banking.ai.activity;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import com.xenon.banking.ai.model.TradeExceptionDecision;
import io.temporal.activity.Activity;
import io.temporal.activity.ActivityExecutionContext;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.util.Map;

@Component("tradeAgentActivity")
public class TradeAgentActivityImpl implements TradeAgentActivity {

    private final HttpClient httpClient = HttpClient.newHttpClient();
    private final ObjectMapper objectMapper = new ObjectMapper();

    @Override
    public TradeExceptionDecision evaluateTradeException(String documentText, String exceptionCode, double transactionAmount) {
        ActivityExecutionContext ctx = Activity.getExecutionContext();
        String workflowId = ctx.getInfo().getWorkflowId();

        System.out.println("Executing Agentic Decision Node for Workflow: " + workflowId);

        // Construct System & User Prompt for Structured Function Calling
        String promptPayload = buildPromptJson(documentText, exceptionCode, transactionAmount);

        int attempts = 0;
        int maxRetries = 3;

        while (attempts < maxRetries) {
            attempts++;
            try {
                // Call LLM Inference Endpoint (OpenAI / Internal Enterprise Model API)
                HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
                        .uri(URI.create("https://ai-gateway.internal.xenon/v1/chat/completions"))
                        .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
                        .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + System.getenv("AI_GATEWAY_KEY"))
                        .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(promptPayload))
                        .build();

                HttpResponse<String> response = httpClient.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());

                // Parse Structured Output Response
                String rawJsonResponse = extractStructuredJsonFromResponse(response.body());
                TradeExceptionDecision decision = objectMapper.readValue(rawJsonResponse, TradeExceptionDecision.class);

                // Validation Guardrail: Enforce minimum confidence threshold
                if (decision.confidenceScore() < 0.85) {
                    System.out.println("Agent confidence score (" + decision.confidenceScore() + ") below threshold. Escalating.");
                    return new TradeExceptionDecision("ESCALATE_HUMAN", decision.confidenceScore(), 
                            "Low confidence score in automated evaluation.", decision.verifiedClauseIdentifiers(), "NONE");
                }

                return decision; // Successfully evaluated and validated

            } catch (Exception e) {
                System.err.println("Attempt " + attempts + " failed to parse LLM structured decision: " + e.getMessage());
                if (attempts >= maxRetries) {
                    // Fail-safe default returned to Workflow
                    return new TradeExceptionDecision("ESCALATE_HUMAN", 0.0, 
                            "LLM execution failed structural validation after retries.", List.of(), "NONE");
                }
            }
        }

        return new TradeExceptionDecision("ESCALATE_HUMAN", 0.0, "Execution exhausted retries.", List.of(), "NONE");
    }

    private String buildPromptJson(String documentText, String exceptionCode, double amount) {
        // Formats prompt enforcing JSON Schema output constraints
        return """
            {
              "model": "xenon-financial-agent-v2",
              "messages": [
                {"role": "system", "content": "You are a specialized risk evaluation agent. You must output JSON conforming strictly to the TradeExceptionDecision schema."},
                {"role": "user", "content": "Evaluate document: %s under exception code: %s for amount: %.2f"}
              ],
              "response_format": {"type": "json_object"},
              "temperature": 0.0
            }
            """.formatted(escapeJson(documentText), exceptionCode, amount);
    }

    private String extractStructuredJsonFromResponse(String responseBody) throws Exception {
        var node = objectMapper.readTree(responseBody);
        return node.path("choices").get(0).path("message").path("content").asText();
    }

    private String escapeJson(String input) {
        return input.replace("\"", "\\\"").replace("\n", " ");
    }
}

3. Temporal Workflow Definition (Deterministic Branching)

The workflow invokes the agent activity. Depending on the agent's structured decision, it deterministically dispatches an automated downstream machine Saga or suspends for human review.

package com.xenon.banking.ai.workflow;

import com.xenon.banking.ai.activity.TradeAgentActivity;
import com.xenon.banking.ai.model.TradeExceptionDecision;
import io.temporal.activity.ActivityOptions;
import io.temporal.workflow.Workflow;
import io.temporal.workflow.WorkflowInterface;
import io.temporal.workflow.WorkflowMethod;

import java.time.Duration;

@WorkflowInterface
public interface TradeResolutionWorkflow {
    @WorkflowMethod
    void processTradeException(String tradeId, String documentText, String exceptionCode, double amount);
}

public class TradeResolutionWorkflowImpl implements TradeResolutionWorkflow {

    private final TradeAgentActivity agentActivity = Workflow.newActivityStub(
            TradeAgentActivity.class,
            ActivityOptions.newBuilder()
                    .setStartToCloseTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(30))
                    .setRetryOptions(io.temporal.common.RetryOptions.newBuilder()
                            .setMaximumAttempts(3)
                            .build())
                    .build()
    );

    @Override
    public void processTradeException(String tradeId, String documentText, String exceptionCode, double amount) {

        // 1. Invoke Isolated LLM Agent Activity (Non-deterministic code runs safely inside activity)
        TradeExceptionDecision agentDecision = agentActivity.evaluateTradeException(documentText, exceptionCode, amount);

        // 2. Deterministic Workflow Execution Path based on Activity Event History
        switch (agentDecision.decisionOutcome()) {
            case "APPROVE_EXEMPTION" -> {
                // Trigger automated machine Saga step (e.g., Ledger Release)
                Workflow.getLogger(TradeResolutionWorkflowImpl.class).info("Agent approved exception. Executing release Saga.");
                executeAutomatedReleaseSaga(tradeId, amount);
            }
            case "REJECT_EXEMPTION" -> {
                // Trigger automated cancellation & compensation Saga
                Workflow.getLogger(TradeResolutionWorkflowImpl.class).info("Agent rejected exception. Executing compensation Saga.");
                executeCompensatingCancellationSaga(tradeId);
            }
            case "ESCALATE_HUMAN" -> {
                // Halt workflow deterministically and await Human-in-the-Loop Signal
                Workflow.getLogger(TradeResolutionWorkflowImpl.class).warn("Agent requested human escalation. Awaiting signal.");
                awaitHumanReviewSignal(tradeId, agentDecision.reasoningSummary());
            }
            default -> throw new IllegalStateException("Unexpected agent decision outcome: " + agentDecision.decisionOutcome());
        }
    }

    private void executeAutomatedReleaseSaga(String tradeId, double amount) {
        // Standard deterministic machine Activity calls
    }

    private void executeCompensatingCancellationSaga(String tradeId) {
        // Standard deterministic compensating Activity calls
    }

    private void awaitHumanReviewSignal(String tradeId, String reasoning) {
        // Suspend workflow execution until human approval signal arrives
    }
}

Transactional Consistency and Saga Compensation Scenarios

When an autonomous LLM agent decides to approve an operational exception, it triggers forward transactions (e.g., balance holds or ledger postings). If a downstream microservice fails after an LLM agent decision has been rendered, the Temporal orchestrator automatically executes standard Compensating Actions.

  AGENT DECISION SAGA COMPENSATION FLOW

  +-----------------------+        1. Approve Exception        +-----------------------+
  |  LLM Agent Activity   | ---------------------------------> | Temporal Saga Manager |
  | (Evaluates Document)  |                                    | (Workflow History)    |
  +-----------------------+                                    +-----------+-----------+
                                                                           |
                                   2. Execute Step 1 (Ledger Debit)        |
                                                                           v
  +-----------------------+        3. Step 2 Fails (API Timeout) +-----------------------+
  | Downstream Services   | <----------------------------------| Executing Machine     |
  | (Ledger / Risk Engine)| ---------------------------------> | Activities            |
  +-----------------------+        4. Trigger Compensation     +-----------+-----------+
                                                                           |
                                   5. Execute Rollback Activity            |
                                      (Revert Ledger Debit)                v
                                                               +-----------------------+
                                                               | Audit Log & Escalate  |
                                                               | to Human Desk         |
                                                               +-----------------------+

Compensation Safety Rules

  1. Non-Reversible Actions: An LLM agent must never execute uncompensable real-world actions (such as dispatching an external Fedwire SWIFT MT103 message) directly from within its reasoning loop.
  2. Two-Stage Authorization: The agent activity may only modify internal staging state or emit execution intents. The actual final settlement step must be gated by a secondary deterministic activity or a human approval check if the transaction value exceeds strict monetary limits.

Observability, Prompt Lineage, and Auditability

Financial regulators (such as OCC, EBA, and MAS) require complete lineage for AI-assisted operational decisions. Storing only the final decision payload is insufficient; the system must retain full cryptographic lineage of the agent's context.

Audit Metadata Record Structure

For every LLM decision node invocation, the activity writes an immutable audit record to the centralized log storage layer, linked to the Temporal WorkflowID and RunID:

{
  "auditId": "AUDIT-2026-902183",
  "temporalWorkflowId": "TradeResolution-TR-9902",
  "temporalRunId": "b182f4e8-421d-405a-a309-88f2b7190012",
  "bianDomain": "TradePositioning",
  "llmProvider": "Azure-OpenAI-Internal",
  "modelDeployment": "gpt-4o-financial-v2",
  "promptHash": "e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855",
  "inputTokenCount": 1420,
  "outputTokenCount": 185,
  "rawOutput": "{\"decisionOutcome\":\"APPROVE_EXEMPTION\",\"confidenceScore\":0.94,\"reasoningSummary\":\"Clause 4b matches standard ICC UCP 600 rules.\",\"verifiedClauseIdentifiers\":[\"CLAUSE-4B\"],\"recommendedCompensatingAction\":\"NONE\"}",
  "confidenceScore": 0.94,
  "schemaValidationPassed": true,
  "executionTimestamp": "2026-09-16T11:56:28Z"
}

Integrating autonomous LLM agents into Temporal Sagas bridges the gap between flexible AI-driven reasoning and rigid financial reliability. By strict application of the Determinism Isolation Pattern—confining non-deterministic LLM execution inside structured Temporal Activities while keeping the orchestration workflow fully deterministic—core banking platforms achieve intelligent operational automation without sacrificing transactional integrity, fault tolerance, or regulatory auditability across BIAN service domains.

title: Amazon DynamoDB global tables now support disassociating replicas
description:
Amazon DynamoDB global tables now support disassociating a replica without deleting its table or data. Global tables provide fully managed, multi-Region, multi-active replication. You can now stop replication to and from a replica and continue using the same table as a single-Region table.

An account can leave a shared multi-account global table and continue using its table independently. You can also stop replication to a Region while keeping its table for local workloads, validation, or audit, without creating a replacement table or copying data.

DynamoDB supports disassociating replicas in all AWS Regions for same-account and multi-account global tables that use multi-Region eventual consistency (MREC).

To get started, use the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, DynamoDB API, or AWS CloudFormation. For more information, see Disassociating replicas in the Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide.

title: Hibernate Under the Hood. Part 2: Entity Lifecycle and the Persistence Context
description:
This is arguably the most important topic in Hibernate. If you understand entity states and what happens inside the Persistence Context, 80% of Hibernate-related bugs cease to be a mystery.

What is the Persistence Context

The Persistence Context is a container of managed entities within a Session/EntityManager. Its key properties are:

  1. It is a first-level cache. All loaded entities live here until the session is closed.
  2. It guarantees identity. Within a single session, calling get(User.class, 1L) twice will return the exact same Java object instance (Identity Map pattern).
  3. It tracks changes. Upon flush, Hibernate compares the current state of entities with their snapshot and generates an UPDATE only for the modified fields (dirty checking).
  4. It implements write-behind. save/persist do not write to the DB immediately — changes are accumulated and synchronized upon flush. 
User u1 = session.get(User.class, 1L);
User u2 = session.get(User.class, 1L);
System.out.println(u1 == u2); // true — the exact same object instance

This is not "optimization for the sake of optimization". It is a semantic guarantee: within a single unit of work, you always work with the same object instance, preventing the scenario of "two objects, both representing User with id=1, one with name='A' and the other with name='B'".

The Four Entity States

1. Transient (New / Unmanaged)

The object is created via new, but Hibernate knows nothing about it.

User user = new User();  // Transient
user.setName("Alice");

This is a regular Java object created with the new operator. It is not associated with the database or the current Hibernate session.

  • Database connection: None. No corresponding record exists in the database.
  • Identifier (ID): Usually null (unless set manually, but Hibernate will ignore it).
  • Tracking: Hibernate does not track changes to its fields. If you modify a field and do nothing else, nothing goes to the DB.
  • Analogy: A document draft written on your desk. It is not yet registered in the archive.

How to transition to another state:

  • To Persistent: call session.save() or session.persist().
  • To Detached: (rarely done directly; usually, the object is saved first, and then the session is closed).

2. Persistent (Managed) 

session.persist(user);   // user is now Persistent
user.setName("Bob");     // changes are tracked
// upon flush, Hibernate will generate an UPDATE

The object is managed by the current session. It has a representation in the database (it is already saved there or will be upon flush).

  • Database connection: Direct. The object corresponds to a row in the table.
  • Identifier (ID): Must have a value (the ID from the DB).
  • Tracking: Hibernate closely monitors the object (via Dirty Checking). If you modify any field of this object, Hibernate will notice and automatically generate and execute an UPDATE SQL query on the next flush().
  • Analogy: A document you pulled from the archive, opened in the system, and are editing. The system sees all your changes and will save them when you click "Save" (flush).

How to get into this state:

  • From Transient: session.save(), session.persist().
  • From Detached: session.update(), session.saveOrUpdate(), session.merge().

How to leave this state:

  • To Detached: close the session (session.close()), clear it (session.clear()), or evict the object from the session cache (session.evict()).
  • To Removed: call session.delete() or session.remove().

3. Detached 

session.close();
// all previously loaded entities are now Detached

The object was in the Persistent state (it has an ID and exists in the DB), but lost its connection to the current session (the session was closed or the object was evicted from it).

  • Database connection: The object exists in the database.
  • Identifier (ID): Must have a value.
  • Tracking: Hibernate does not track it. If you modify a Detached object's field, nothing goes to the DB until you "re-attach" it to a session.
  • Analogy: A document you physically took from the archive to your desk. You can read and even change it, but the archive system knows nothing about it. To apply changes to the archive, the document must be returned (via merge/update).

How to get into this state:

  • From Persistent: close the session (session.close()), clear the cache (session.clear()), or evict the object (session.evict()).

How to transition to another state:

  • To Persistent: call session.update(), session.saveOrUpdate(), or session.merge() (in a newly opened session).

4. Removed 

session.remove(user);  // Removed
// upon flush → DELETE FROM users WHERE id = ?

The object is marked for deletion. It is still associated with the session, but "doomed".

  • Database connection: The record still exists in the DB but is marked for deletion.
  • Tracking: On the next flush() or commit(), Hibernate will generate a DELETE SQL query and remove the row from the database.
  • Analogy: A document stamped with a red "DESTROY" mark. It is still in the system, but at the end of the workday (upon commit), it will be sent to the shredder.

How to get into this state:

  • From Persistent: call session.delete() or session.remove().

Key Takeaway

The most common beginner mistake is attempting to modify a Detached object and expecting it to update in the DB automatically.

Remember: changes are automatically pushed to the DB only from the Persistent state. If an object becomes Detached (e.g., you fetched it from the DB in one method, but are trying to update it in another where the session is already closed), you must explicitly "re-attach" it via merge() or update().

persist() vs save()

Feature persist() (JPA) save() (Hibernate)
Returns void Serializable (the generated ID)
INSERT timing Deferred (upon flush) Can be immediate (if the ID is needed)
Outside a transaction Throws an exception Works (but it's a bad practice)
For detached objects Throws an exception May create a new object (or throw an error if ID exists)

Use persist() if you are working via the JPA API. It is the standard.

merge() vs update()

Feature merge() (JPA) update() (Hibernate)
What it does Loads the current state from the DB, copies changes into a new managed object, and returns it "Re-attaches" the passed detached object to the session
Returns A managed copy void
Original object Remains detached Becomes persistent
If the record was deleted Creates a new record Throws an exception

Crucial note: merge() does not make the passed object managed. It returns a different managed copy.

User detached = ...;               // Detached
User managed = session.merge(detached);
// detached — remains Detached
// managed — is now Persistent

get() vs load()

Feature get() load()
DB query Immediate Lazy (returns a proxy)
If not found Returns null Throws EntityNotFoundException upon access
Returns Real object or null Proxy or real object

load() returns a proxy — Hibernate provides a subclass that will fetch the actual data upon the first access to any field (except the ID).

Other Key Methods

  • refresh(): Reloads the object's state from the DB, overwriting it in memory. Useful if data might have been changed externally (another process, native SQL). 
session.refresh(user);  // user is reloaded from the DB
  • evict() / detach(): Removes the object from the Persistence Context. The object becomes Detached. 
session.evict(user);  // user is no longer managed
  • clear(): Completely clears the Persistence Context. All objects become Detached. 
session.clear();  // 1st-level cache is empty
  • flush(): Synchronizes the Persistence Context with the DB. It does not commit the transaction — it only executes INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE statements. 
session.flush();  // SQL is executed, but the transaction is not committed

When does automatic flush occur?

  • Before a transaction commit.
  • Before executing a query that might affect tables containing "dirty" entities (auto-flush).
  • Upon an explicit flush() call.
  • Upon session.close() (if uncommitted, it triggers a rollback).

Dirty Checking — How Hibernate Detects Changes

When loading an entity, Hibernate saves a snapshot — a copy of all its fields. Upon flush, it compares the current state with the snapshot.

@Transactional
public void rename(Long id, String newName) {
    User u = session.get(User.class, id);  // snapshot is saved
    u.setName(newName);                    // modified in memory
    // flush on commit: snapshot.name != u.name → UPDATE users SET name = ?
}

What this provides:

  • No need to call update() — changes are picked up automatically.
  • Generates an UPDATE only for modified fields (unless disabled).
  • If nothing changed, no UPDATE is executed at all.

Dirty checking triggers on flush, not on set. If you modify a field and roll back the transaction, the change won't reach the DB (which is correct). However, if you modify a field and don't commit, it remains in the object's memory.

Write-behind — Why save Doesn't Write Immediately

persist() does not execute an INSERT immediately. It registers the entity in the Persistence Context, and the SQL is generated upon flush.

Why:

  • Batching: Hibernate can collect several INSERTs and send them as a single batch (hibernate.jdbc.batch_size).
  • Operation ordering: Hibernate automatically sequences INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE statements to avoid violating foreign key constraints.
  • Efficiency: If the transaction rolls back, the INSERT was never actually executed against the DB.

Exception: If the ID generation strategy is IDENTITY (auto-increment), Hibernate is forced to execute the INSERT immediately to obtain the generated ID. This breaks batching.

Identity Map — The Uniqueness Guarantee

User u1 = session.get(User.class, 1L);
User u2 = session.get(User.class, 1L);
assert u1 == u2;  // true

How it works: The Persistence Context is essentially a Map<EntityKey, Object>, where the key is (entityClass, id). Upon get, Hibernate first checks the map. If the object is there, it returns it. If not, it loads it from the DB and puts it in the map.

Why it's needed:

  • Consistency guarantee: Prevents having two different objects with the same ID in memory.
  • Performance: Repeated get calls do not hit the DB.
  • Accurate dirty checking: Hibernate knows exactly which object instance to track.

The identity map lives only within a session. Across sessions, these are different objects.

// Session 1
User u1 = session1.get(User.class, 1L);
session1.close();

// Session 2
User u2 = session2.get(User.class, 1L);
assert u1 != u2;  // different object instances, both with id=1

Typical Mistakes and Pitfalls

1) LazyInitializationException

@Transactional
public User getUser(Long id) {
    return session.get(User.class, id);  // returns managed
}
// session is closed, user is now Detached

// in the controller:
user.getOrders().size();  // LazyInitializationException!

Solution: Fetch required data within the transaction (JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph), or use DTO projections.

2) merge() does not make the original object managed

User detached = ...;
session.merge(detached);
detached.setName("new");  // NOT tracked! detached is still Detached

Solution: Work with the result of merge():

User managed = session.merge(detached);
managed.setName("new");  // NOW tracked

3) Modifying a detached object without merge()

@Transactional
public void update(User user) {  // user came from outside (detached)
    user.setName("new");
    // NOTHING happens — user is not managed
}

Solution: Use session.merge(user) or reload the entity and modify the managed instance.

4) save() vs persist() with an existing ID
If a transient object already has an ID (e.g., assigned manually), save() might assume the object is detached and execute an UPDATE instead of an INSERT. persist() will throw an exception in this situation, which is safer.

5) Long session → Memory Leak
The Persistence Context grows with every loaded entity. If a session is kept open for the entire HTTP request (OpenSessionInView) and loads thousands of objects, memory will leak.

Solution: Do not keep the session open longer than necessary; periodically flush() + clear() during batch processing.

6) flush() does not commit

session.flush();  // SQL is executed, but not committed
// if an exception occurs next — it will roll back

Solution: Remember: flush() is for synchronization, commit() is for finalizing.

7) Auto-flush before queries
Hibernate performs a flush before createQuery() if the query affects tables containing "dirty" entities. This can lead to unexpected UPDATEs in the middle of a method.

Solution: Understand this behavior; if necessary, configure FlushMode.MANUAL or COMMIT.

Example: All States in Action 

@Transactional
public void demo() {
    // 1. Transient
    User user = new User();
    user.setName("Alice");

    // 2. Transient → Persistent
    session.persist(user);
    // upon flush → INSERT

    // 3. Persistent (managed)
    user.setName("Bob");  // dirty checking will pick this up on flush

    // 4. Persistent → Detached
    session.evict(user);
    user.setName("Charlie");  // NOT tracked

    // 5. Detached → Persistent (via merge)
    User managed = session.merge(user);
    // managed is now Persistent, user remains Detached

    // 6. Persistent → Removed
    session.remove(managed);
    // upon flush → DELETE
}

Summary

  1. Persistence Context = 1st-level cache + identity map + dirty checking + write-behind. It is the heart of the Session.
  2. Four states: Transient, Persistent, Detached, Removed. Transitions are managed via session methods.
  3. persist() ≠ save(), merge() ≠ update(). Understand the difference.
  4. merge() returns a copy; the original object remains detached.
  5. Dirty checking triggers on flush, not on set.
  6. flush() does not commit; it only synchronizes.
  7. After session closure, objects are Detached → lazy fields are inaccessible.
  8. The identity map lives only within a session — across sessions, objects are different instances.
  9. Long session = memory leak. Do not keep it open longer than necessary.
  10. LazyInitializationException is a symptom of improper state management, not a "Hibernate bug".

title: Mastering Flexbox: The Ultimate Stress-Free Guide to Modern Web Layouts
description:
Mastering Flexbox: The Ultimate Stress-Free Guide to Modern Web Layouts

When you start learning HTML, everything makes complete sense until you try to position elements on a screen. For years, beginners struggled with floats, display: inline-block, and complex margin calculations just to put a sidebar next to a main content column. It was messy, unpredictable, and caused massive styling ling stress.

Enter Flexbox (The Flexible Box Layout). Flexbox is a modern CSS layout system designed to align items dynamically, distribute space evenly, and make responsive design completely effortless.

In this guide, we will look at how Flexbox works and the only 4 properties you need to master to build stunning layouts on your phone or computer.

**The Core Concept: Parent vs. Child

Before writing Flexbox code, you must understand its golden rule: Flexbox is applied to the container (the Parent), but it controls the layout of the elements inside it (the Children).

Imagine a standard HTML structure like this:

Box 1 Box 2

Box 3

By default, block elements like

stack vertically on top of each other. To activate Flexbox and tum them into an automatic horizontal row, you only need one magic line of CSS on the parent class:

.container

display: flex;

As soon as you type display: flex;, the child boxes instantly jump to line up side-by-side in a horizontal row.

The 4 Properties You Need to Know

Once Flexbox is activated, you use these 4 core properties on the parent container to control exactly how the child elements move and stretch.

⚫ flex-direction (Controlling the Layout Track): By default, Flexbox aligns items horizontally. You can change the main axis instantly using flex-direction: row; (side-by-side) or flex-direction: column; (stacked vertically).

⚫ justify-content (Horizontal Alignment): This property controls how space is distributed along the horizontal axis. It features configurations like center (packs everything in the middle), space-between (pushes items to far edges), and space-around (equal space on both sides).

⚫ align-items (Vertical Alignment): Centering items vertically used to require massive layout hacks. Flexbox solves this completely with align-items: center;, which aligns elements to the vertical midpoint of the parent.

⚫ flex-wrap (Handling Overflows): If you run out of space on a row, Flexbox defaults to shrinking your items until they look squished. Adding flex-wrap: wrap; allows items to automatically wrap cleanly onto new lines.

The Ultimate Cheat Sheet to Center Anything

.center-box {

If you ever need to center a button, text, or a login form perfectly dead-center on a page, copy and paste this

universal 3-line Flexbox setup onto the parent container:

display: flex: justify-content: center; align-items: center;

}

Conclusion

Flexbox eliminates the guesswork and stress from CSS layouts. By applying display: flex to a container and adjusting how its children align, you can create fully responsive, professional mobile layouts with minimal lines of code.

title: Data Residency vs Data Sovereignty: Cloud Architecture Guide 2026
description:
Data residency is about where data is physically stored and processed. Data sovereignty is about whose laws and whose access apply to it. Meeting both comes down to pinning workloads and data to approved locations, controlling who can reach them, and keeping evidence, while still running in more than one location so an outage does not take you down.

TL;DR

Customers and auditors now ask where the data lives, who can access it, and how it stays available during an outage.

  • Define the requirement first. Residency, sovereignty, and localization are different obligations. Name the framework, the data class, and the jurisdiction before choosing a region.
  • GDPR restricts transfers outside the EEA. It does not by itself require EU storage. Contracts, sector rules, and national laws often add stricter location terms.
  • Primary data is the easy part. Backups, replicas, logs, traces, metrics, keys, support access, and AI inference are where data leaves the approved boundary by accident.
  • One region per jurisdiction answers residency but creates an availability risk. Run active-active across two or more approved locations in the same jurisdiction, so failover stays inside the boundary.
  • Match the pattern to the requirement: single region, multi-region in one jurisdiction, per-tenant cells, on-premises or local-provider locations, or a hyperscaler sovereign offering.
  • Keep evidence current: location configuration, access logs, an audit trail, data flow diagrams, subprocessor lists, and certifications.
  • Confirm obligations with counsel. This guide describes architecture and links primary sources. It is not legal advice.

Control Plane runs each workload active-active in every location of a Global Virtual Cloud, so you build one GVC per jurisdiction and failover never leaves it. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations, which can be two regions in the same jurisdiction.

Residency vs sovereignty vs localization

Data residency is a location constraint: a regulation, contract, or policy says a dataset must be stored or processed in a defined geography, such as a country or the EU.

Data sovereignty adds legal jurisdiction and operational control: which country’s laws apply, which authorities can compel access, and who can administer the systems that hold the data. Data can be resident in the EU and still be subject to another country’s legal reach if the provider or operator is based elsewhere.

Data localization is residency required by law rather than by contract, usually national, and it is often stricter than contractual terms, for example by prohibiting offshore copies or processing.

A sovereign cloud is an architecture and operating model built to enforce a named set of residency, jurisdiction, access, and operational requirements together. A design that satisfies one public-sector framework may not satisfy a financial-services requirement.

Term What it controls What drives it What it means for architecture
Data residency Where data is stored and processed Contracts, customer requirements, regulations Pin workloads, databases, backups, and logs to approved locations
Data sovereignty Which laws apply and who can compel or perform access Jurisdiction of the provider, operator, and data location Control administrative access, keys, and the legal exposure of every party in the stack
Data localization Mandatory in-country storage or processing National law or sector regulator Use in-country locations, sometimes on infrastructure you operate or a local provider
Sovereign cloud A bundle of residency, jurisdiction, access, and operational controls A named framework, data class, and jurisdiction Design placement, isolation, keys, access, telemetry, and operations together, then map each control to evidence

The rules that shape architecture

Each row states what the primary source says. Confirm your obligations with counsel.

Rule What the primary source says Architecture implication
GDPR, Chapter V Article 44 says a transfer of personal data to a third country takes place only if the conditions in that chapter are met. Article 45 allows a transfer where the Commission has decided the country ensures an adequate level of protection, with no specific authorisation required. GDPR conditions transfers; these articles do not say data must be stored in the EU. Map every flow that leaves the EEA and name its legal basis.
Adequacy decisions The Commission’s list includes Canada (commercial organisations), Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States for commercial organisations participating in the EU-US Data Privacy Framework. Personal data can flow to those countries without further safeguards. Adequacy can make a transfer lawful. Check that US vendors participate in the framework, and keep a fallback transfer mechanism.
Standard contractual clauses Contractual clauses ensuring appropriate safeguards can be a ground for transfers to third countries. The Commission issued modernised SCCs on 4 June 2021. SCCs govern the transfer; they do not change where data sits.
UK GDPR transfers (ICO) The ICO publishes guidance on restricted transfers, adequacy regulations, and safeguards including the UK IDTA and Addendum. UK customers may need UK-specific transfer paperwork in addition to EU paperwork.
GDPR Article 48 (EDPB Guidelines 02/2024) The European Data Protection Board explains how foreign court judgments and administrative decisions requiring disclosure interact with GDPR transfer rules. Data center location and provider jurisdiction are separate variables.
EU Data Act Applicable from 12 September 2025, with switching charges, including certain data-egress charges, phased out from 12 January 2027 (Article 29). Article 32 requires providers to take all adequate technical, organisational and legal measures, including contracts, to prevent third-country governmental access to non-personal data held in the Union where it would conflict with EU or Member State law. Expect questions about government access controls and switching. Portability planning matters.
US CLOUD Act The DOJ describes the Act, enacted in March 2018, as speeding access to electronic information held by US-based global providers and authorizing bilateral agreements; it lists agreements with the UK and Australia. Sovereignty reviews ask about the legal jurisdiction of every provider in the stack, not only the data center location.
HIPAA and cloud (HHS) A covered entity or business associate may use a cloud service for ePHI with a business associate agreement, and both must conduct risk analyses. A provider holding only encrypted ePHI without the key is still a business associate. Location decisions belong in your documented risk analysis and your BAA.
PCI DSS A baseline of technical and operational requirements to protect payment account data, for entities that store, process, or transmit cardholder data. Validation requirements are set by payment brands, acquirers, or other program managers. Scope the cardholder data environment tightly and ask your acquirer and assessor whether any location requirement applies.
Australia, My Health Records Act 2012, s77 Prohibits the System Operator and registered repository, portal, and contracted service providers that hold My Health Record records, or have access to related information, from holding, taking, or processing them outside Australia, or causing or permitting another person to do so, with a narrow exception for non-identifying data. An example of localization written into health law, applying to the providers the Act names.
India, RBI payment data directive The 6 April 2018 directive requires payment system providers to store the entire data relating to the payment systems they operate only in India; data for the foreign leg of a transaction can also be stored abroad. An example of localization in payments that needs in-country locations.

A requirement to keep data in the EU can apply even where GDPR does not impose it. Customer contracts, public-sector procurement rules, sector regulators, and Member State laws can all set stricter location terms, so read the contract, not just the regulation.

Data residency checklist: what has to stay in region

Teams pin the production database to an approved region and consider the job done. Auditors then find copies in other places. Check each item for every workload covered by a residency requirement:

  • Primary data: databases, object storage, and file stores.
  • Backups and snapshots: backup targets and disaster recovery copies can move regulated data outside the boundary even when primary storage is correct.
  • Replicas: read replicas, cross-region replication, and caches.
  • Logs and traces: application logs, request traces, and error reports often contain personal data, tokens, and query parameters.
  • Metrics and analytics: product analytics, session replay, and metrics with user identifiers.
  • Secrets and encryption keys: where keys are held and who can authorize decryption is a sovereignty question.
  • Support and administrative access: who can reach production, from where, under what approval, and with what logging.
  • Processing: compute location matters as much as storage, including AI inference and embedding calls that send customer data to a model endpoint.

Logs, backups, and observability pipelines are frequent sources of accidental cross-border transfers. A centralized logging or monitoring service in another jurisdiction can create a transfer even when production data never moves, so check where each telemetry pipeline sends data first.

Architecture patterns

Single-region deployment per jurisdiction

Run the full stack in one region inside the approved jurisdiction, with a separate copy for each other jurisdiction.

When to use it. Early-stage products, small footprints, and workloads where a short regional outage is acceptable.

Tradeoffs. The simplest way to prove residency and the weakest on availability: a regional outage takes the whole jurisdiction down, and backups kept in the same region share that risk.

Multi-region within one jurisdiction, active-active

Run the same workload in two or more regions inside one jurisdiction, for example two EU regions, and serve live traffic from all of them.

When to use it. Production workloads with both a residency requirement and an availability commitment.

Tradeoffs. It needs data replication that stays inside the boundary, health-based routing, and headroom in each location to absorb a failed one. Every location serves live traffic, so you are not paying for a standby that serves nothing. The active-active high availability guide covers the design.

Cell-based or per-tenant deployments

Deploy independent cells, each holding a set of customers, and route each customer to the cell in their jurisdiction.

When to use it. B2B software with customers in several regulated regions, where some customers contractually require a specific location.

Tradeoffs. Cells give a clear residency story per customer and limit the blast radius of a failure, but every cell needs deployment, monitoring, and upgrades, and a misrouted request is a residency incident. Run all cells with the same tooling.

Hybrid, on-premises, and local-provider locations

Run the strictest workloads in your own data centers or with a national or local provider, and join those locations to cloud regions under one management layer.

When to use it. Localization laws, highly sensitive data, customers who require infrastructure under their own control, and regions where hyperscalers have no suitable location.

Tradeoffs. You gain control over who operates the hardware and where it sits, and you take on capacity planning unless a provider handles it. The common failure is running those locations as a separate stack; see adding a neocloud without running a second stack and hybrid cloud platforms.

Hyperscaler sovereign offerings

Each major provider publishes sovereignty options, described here from their own pages:

  • AWS: the AWS European Sovereign Cloud is described as a new, independent cloud for Europe for stringent data residency, operational autonomy, and resiliency requirements, alongside Dedicated Local Zones placed in a customer-specified location.
  • Microsoft: the EU Data Boundary commits to processing and storing EU and EFTA customer data in region, and Microsoft Sovereign Cloud includes a Sovereign Private Cloud for hybrid or fully disconnected environments with Azure Local.
  • Google Cloud: Google Cloud’s sovereign cloud offerings include a Data Boundary that stores core customer data in the chosen region with logged administrative access, Google Cloud Dedicated run by a local partner (S3NS in France), and Google Distributed Cloud for on-premises use, connected or air-gapped.

Tradeoffs. These address placement and operations inside one provider’s ecosystem. If you also need other providers or your own data centers, you still need a layer that manages them together; see how to avoid cloud vendor lock-in.

Data residency and high availability together

A single-region deployment is a residency answer and an availability risk. When that region fails, the options are to wait or to fail over somewhere that may break the residency commitment, and teams under pressure often choose the second. Active-standby inside the jurisdiction helps, but the standby bills for capacity that serves no traffic and is often not tested under real load.

Active-active across two or more approved locations in the same jurisdiction removes that tradeoff. Every location is proven under production load, and when one becomes unhealthy, traffic shifts to locations that are already inside the boundary, so a failover never becomes a residency exception. Keep replication, backups, logs, and keys inside the same boundary. For what each design can deliver, see five nines availability architecture.

Proving it

Auditors and customer security teams ask for evidence, and they ask repeatedly, so build the evidence trail as you build the system.

Evidence What it shows How to keep it current
Location configuration The approved locations each workload can run in Store it as code and review changes like any other change
Access logs Who accessed systems and data, and from where Centralize inside the boundary and set retention to match contracts
Audit trail Every administrative action, tamper-resistant Generate it automatically
Data flow diagrams Where data moves, including backups, logs, and third parties Update with each architecture change and review quarterly
Subprocessor list Every vendor that touches the data and where it operates Review on onboarding and vendor changes, and notify customers as contracts require
Certifications and reports Independent assessment of controls Track expiry, scope, and version, and confirm the scope covers the service you use

Treat the location configuration as the source of truth and generate diagrams from it where you can. Then test the boundary: try to deploy a workload to an unapproved location in staging and confirm it is refused.

How Control Plane helps with data residency and sovereignty

Control Plane is the platform for running unbreakable apps and agents. It combines any cloud, neocloud, on-premises, and bare-metal location into one Global Virtual Cloud (GVC).

  • You choose the locations. A workload deployed to a GVC runs only in that GVC’s locations, active-active in every one, and a global endpoint routes each request to the nearest healthy location. Build each GVC from locations in one jurisdiction, and use separate GVCs for separate jurisdictions.
  • Residency and resilience in one design. Every location in a GVC serves live traffic, so you get active-active failover inside your boundary without paying for idle standby capacity. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations, and those locations can be two regions in the same jurisdiction, on one provider or on different providers.
  • Proven in an outage. During the October 2025 AWS us-east-1 outage, 20% of Control Plane customers had us-east-1 in their Global Virtual Clouds. Their workloads were active and running in healthy locations within 10 seconds, with no customer downtime, according to Control Plane internal incident telemetry.
  • Infrastructure you control. Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK) and Managed Kubernetes let your own clusters, your own servers, on-premises data centers, or a local or national provider join a GVC as locations, managed alongside cloud regions.
  • Use regional cloud services in place. Universal Cloud Identity gives workloads short-lived, least-privilege access to 600+ AWS, GCP, and Azure services, with no long-lived cloud keys in your code, so workloads can use databases and key management services you keep in the same jurisdiction.
  • Controls that produce evidence. Mutual TLS between workloads, secrets management, fine-grained access policies, and a tamper-proof audit trail, plus autoscaling, readiness-gated rollouts, automatic TLS certificates, and unified logs, metrics, and traces, with no Kubernetes cluster you have to operate.
  • Compliance. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant, so the platform layer comes with its own compliance evidence to add to yours.

FAQ

What is data residency?

A requirement that data be stored or processed in a specific geography, such as a country or the EU. It comes from regulations, contracts, or internal policy, and it applies to every copy of the data, including backups, replicas, and logs.

What is the difference between data residency, data sovereignty, and data localization?

Residency is where data is stored and processed, sovereignty is which laws apply and who can compel access, and localization is residency required by national law.

What is a sovereign cloud?

An architecture and operating model that enforces a named set of residency, jurisdiction, access, and operational requirements together. AWS, Microsoft, and Google Cloud publish sovereign offerings, and you can also assemble one from regional locations, local providers, and infrastructure you operate.

Does a sovereign cloud require dedicated, single-tenant infrastructure?

Not always. The framework, data class, jurisdiction, and threat model decide whether shared regional infrastructure is acceptable or dedicated infrastructure under your control is required.

How do I keep customer data in the EU on AWS, GCP, or Azure?

Choose EU regions for every workload and data store, apply the same rule to backups, replicas, telemetry, and keys, and use each provider’s policy controls to block deployment outside approved regions. On Control Plane, a GVC built from EU locations keeps every workload replica in those locations, across one provider or several.

Does GDPR require data to stay in the EU?

GDPR’s transfer articles set conditions for moving personal data to third countries, such as adequacy decisions and standard contractual clauses; they do not require EU storage. Contracts, sector rules, and national laws can.

Can I have data residency and high availability at the same time?

Yes. Run active-active across at least two approved locations in the same jurisdiction so failover stays inside the boundary. Control Plane’s 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations, which can be two regions in the same jurisdiction.

What data residency requirements apply to healthcare and payments data?

HIPAA guidance centers on a business associate agreement and a documented risk analysis, and PCI DSS sets security requirements with validation set by acquirers and payment brands. Some countries add localization law, such as Australia’s My Health Records Act and India’s RBI payment data directive.

How do I prove data residency to an auditor or customer?

Provide location configuration, data flow diagrams that include backups and telemetry, access logs, an audit trail of administrative actions, a subprocessor list with locations, and current certifications, matched to the framework being tested.

Can I add a region for a new market without rebuilding my application?

Yes, if your platform treats locations as configuration. On Control Plane you add an approved location to a GVC or create a new GVC for that jurisdiction, and the workload definition does not change. Plan data replication and telemetry for the new jurisdiction.

Next step: bring your residency requirements and current architecture, and the Control Plane team will map them to a GVC layout per jurisdiction that stays up when a region fails. Talk to the Control Plane team or sign up free.
