title: Cloud Cost Optimization in 2026: 10 Levers That Cut Your Compute Bill
description:
Most cloud compute waste comes from paying for capacity your workloads do not use: over-provisioned requests, idle nodes, standby capacity, and per-service add-ons. The biggest savings come from changing how capacity is reserved and packed, not only from discounts or dashboards.

TL;DR

If you already hold reserved instances or savings plans and run a FinOps dashboard, your unit rate is likely fine and your unit count is the problem. Pull these levers in this order:

  1. Right-size CPU and memory from observed usage.
  2. Pack workloads densely onto fewer, fuller nodes.
  3. Autoscale on real signals and scale idle workloads down.
  4. Stop paying for idle standby; in active-active, failover capacity also serves live users.
  5. Commit after you shrink, against the smaller baseline.
  6. Use spot capacity for fault-tolerant work only.
  7. Control egress between zones, regions, and the internet.
  8. Count the add-ons: load balancers, NAT gateways, observability.
  9. Count the platform team that operates Kubernetes.
  10. Use capacity across providers and neoclouds where price or availability is better.

Control Plane applies right-sizing, autoscaling, active-active without idle standby, and built-in day-two operations at the platform layer, on one cloud or several, with no Kubernetes cluster you have to operate. Customers typically cut compute costs 30 to 50 percent compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure.

Sources of avoidable compute spend

Source of spend Why it happens Lever
Over-provisioned CPU and memory requests Teams set requests high to avoid incidents and never lower them 1
Low node utilization and idle nodes Pods do not fit together well, or autoscalers leave spare nodes running 2, 3
Standby and duplicate environments Disaster recovery, staging, and preview environments run all the time 4
Data transfer and egress Traffic crosses zones, regions, clouds, or the internet 7
Managed add-ons billed separately Load balancers, NAT gateways, observability, certificates, and secrets each bill per unit 8
People cost of operating Kubernetes Clusters, upgrades, and add-ons need engineers and on-call time 9

Why Kubernetes bills run high

Kubernetes schedules pods by their requests, not by what they use. The Kubernetes resource management docs explain that the scheduler places a pod on a node only if the sum of resource requests, including the new pod’s, stays within the node’s capacity, even when actual usage is low. A pod that requests 2 vCPU and uses 0.3 still blocks 2 vCPU, and across hundreds of pods the cluster needs far more nodes than the real load requires.

The CNCF’s 2023 Cloud Native and Kubernetes FinOps microsurvey found that “Kubernetes has driven cloud spend up for nearly half (49%) of those surveyed…” and that “Over-provisioning came first by a long way at 70%” among causes of overspending. It drew just over 100 responses, so treat it as directional.

The 10 levers

1. Right-size CPU and memory

What it is. Compare each workload’s requests to its actual usage over a full business cycle, then set requests to match with headroom. The Kubernetes project documents the Vertical Pod Autoscaler, an add-on you install separately, for this purpose.

Effort. Low to measure, medium to change across teams, and recurring, because usage drifts as code and traffic change.

What it can save. Often the largest single lever: over-provisioning was the top cause of overspending in the CNCF survey, and every unit you stop requesting lowers the number of nodes needed to hold it.

Reliability risk. Medium if done by hand. Memory limits below peak usage cause out-of-memory kills, and memory requests below real usage make pods eviction candidates when a node runs short. Use a high percentile of usage over several weeks and change a few services at a time.

On Control Plane, Capacity AI right-sizes CPU and memory between a minimum and maximum you set, based on historical usage, on both Control Plane-provided and customer-provided compute.

2. Pack workloads densely

What it is. Bin-packing places pods so nodes run close to full. Utilization can be measured as requested (the share of a node’s allocatable CPU and memory that pods request) or actual (the share pods use); low numbers on either mean you pay for instances that do little.

Effort. Medium. Right-size first, since packing inflated requests only packs the waste more tightly, then tune node sizes and consolidation.

What it can save. Fewer nodes for the same workload, compounding with right-sizing.

Reliability risk. Medium. Dense nodes raise the blast radius of a node failure. Spread critical replicas across nodes and zones, and set pod disruption budgets to limit how many replicas voluntary evictions, such as consolidation, can remove at once.

On Control Plane-provided compute, you pay for the CPU and memory reserved for each workload, by the millicore and the megabyte, rather than for whole nodes, so node packing is not your cost to manage.

3. Autoscale on real signals

What it is. Horizontal autoscaling adds and removes replicas as load changes. Requests per second, latency percentiles, and queue depth track demand better than CPU for many services, and KEDA extends Kubernetes autoscaling to event and custom metrics, including scaling to zero.

Effort. Medium: pick a signal, set minimum and maximum replicas, and load test.

What it can save. Capacity follows demand instead of peak, and workloads that scale down when idle stop billing for unused replicas.

Reliability risk. Medium. Scaling too slowly under a spike hurts latency, so keep a sensible minimum for user-facing services.

On Control Plane, workloads scale on requests per second, a latency percentile, or custom metrics through KEDA. Serverless workloads scale to zero natively, and standard and stateful workloads do so through KEDA.

4. Stop paying for idle standby

What it is. Active-passive disaster recovery keeps a second copy of your stack running, or ready to start, in another region or cloud. That copy bills for compute, databases, load balancers, and NAT gateways whether or not it serves a request, and staging, QA, and preview environments add to the pattern.

Effort. High if you redesign it yourself: active-active needs workloads that run in several places at once, routing to a healthy location, and a data strategy, covered in how to build active-active high availability.

What it can save. In active-active, every location serves live traffic, so failover capacity is also production capacity. Each location still needs headroom to absorb a failed location’s traffic (1/(N-1) of its normal load: 100% with two locations, 50% with three), and autoscaling can add that capacity when needed instead of holding it idle, as long as quotas are confirmed in advance.

Reliability risk. Lower than standby when done correctly, because failover is continuous and tested by real traffic, while a standby environment that has never carried production load often fails during the failover itself.

On Control Plane, a workload deployed to a Global Virtual Cloud runs active-active in every location of that GVC, and a global endpoint routes each request to the nearest healthy location, so you get active-active failover without paying for idle standby capacity. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations.

5. Commit after you shrink

What it is. Commitments trade flexibility for a lower rate over one or three years. AWS Savings Plans and Standard Reserved Instances save up to 72% compared with On-Demand. Google Cloud committed use discounts discount a committed level of resources or spend, with overage charged at the on-demand rate. Azure reservations save up to 72% on virtual machines and the Azure savings plan for compute up to 65% on select services, compared with pay-as-you-go.

Effort. Low to buy, high to manage well, since commitment utilization must stay high.

What it can save. A lower rate on steady usage; these are provider maximums, and your result depends on term, payment option, and how much of your usage is steady.

Reliability risk. None to uptime. Commitments bought before right-sizing can go unused, with limited exchange or resale options depending on provider and type, so commit to a conservative share of the reduced baseline.

6. Use spot capacity for fault-tolerant work

What it is. Providers sell spare capacity at a discount and reclaim it on short notice: AWS Spot Instances (up to 90% off On-Demand, two-minute notice), Google Cloud Spot VMs (about 30 seconds to shut down), and Azure Spot Virtual Machines (about 30 seconds’ notice).

Effort. Medium. Workloads must handle shutdown signals and checkpoint their work.

What it can save. A much lower rate on interruptible capacity.

Reliability risk. High for stateful or latency-sensitive services, low for batch jobs, CI runners, and stateless workers with retries.

7. Control egress

What it is. Providers charge per gigabyte for traffic that leaves a region or goes to the internet, and AWS and Google Cloud also charge for traffic between zones in the same region. Inbound traffic is free, and each provider includes a small monthly free tier for internet egress. Check AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure rates.

Effort. Medium: find the top flows by volume, keep chatty services together where reliability allows, cache at the edge, and compress.

What it can save. For data-heavy services, egress can rival the compute bill.

Reliability risk. Low to medium. Pinning traffic to one zone saves money but reduces zone redundancy.

8. Count the add-ons

What it is. Many managed services bill separately from the compute they support. NAT gateways on AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure charge for the gateway and for data processed. AWS Elastic Load Balancing bills per load-balancer hour plus capacity units, Google Cloud Load Balancing for forwarding rules and data processed, and Azure Load Balancer per rule-hour plus data processed. Observability usually bills by volume, and secret stores per secret or request.

Effort. Low to medium: share load balancers where safe, move NAT traffic to private endpoints, and set log retention and sampling.

What it can save. Small per item, large across dozens of services.

Reliability risk. Low, if you keep redundancy where it matters.

On Control Plane, load balancing through a global endpoint, automatic TLS certificates, secrets management, and unified logs, metrics, and traces are part of the platform for no additional cost.

9. Count the platform team

What it is. Running Kubernetes means operating clusters, planning upgrades, keeping versions compatible, and maintaining ingress, certificate, secrets, logging, and autoscaling add-ons. To estimate the cost, list every engineer who spends time on cluster operations, multiply their time share by loaded cost, and add it to the compute and add-on bill.

Effort. Low to measure, high to reduce: keep operating clusters, use a managed offering, or move to a platform with no Kubernetes cluster you have to operate. The Kubernetes alternatives guide compares the options, and how to cut cloud compute costs without rewriting your apps covers the move itself.

What it can save. Engineer hours spent on upgrades, add-on maintenance, and cluster on-call, which for many teams cost more than the infrastructure they maintain.

Reliability risk. Depends on the option; moving off clusters is a migration, so plan it service by service.

10. Use capacity across providers and neoclouds

What it is. Prices and capacity differ by provider, region, and hardware. Neoclouds and bare-metal providers can offer lower prices or capacity a hyperscaler region lacks, and several providers reduce dependence on one vendor, as covered in how to avoid cloud vendor lock-in.

Effort. High if each provider needs its own stack, low on a platform that treats each provider as a location; see how to add a neocloud without running a second stack.

What it can save. A lower rate on part of your capacity, plus capacity you cannot get elsewhere.

Reliability risk. Medium, since each provider adds failure modes; a global endpoint that routes to the nearest healthy location reduces that risk.

On Control Plane, Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK) and Managed Kubernetes let existing clusters or your own servers join a Global Virtual Cloud as locations, so you can use capacity you already own or buy it from a neocloud.

Where FinOps tools fit

Cost visibility and allocation tools show where money goes and who owns it, and some recommend or automate changes. Listed in no specific order:

Tool What its own pages say it does
AWS Cost Explorer AWS’s cost analysis tool, including Savings Plans recommendations
Google Cloud Billing reports Reports for viewing and analyzing Google Cloud costs
Microsoft Cost Management Cost analysis and management for Azure (formerly Azure Cost Management)
IBM Kubecost Kubernetes cost allocation by cluster, team, namespace, and workload, with automated actions such as request sizing and namespace turndown
Vantage Cost reporting across providers, autopilot purchasing of AWS Savings Plans, Kubernetes rightsizing, anomaly detection, and budgets
CloudZero Cost allocation across cloud, Kubernetes, and AI spend, with unit costs such as cost per customer
Cast AI Kubernetes optimization that sets requests from observed usage, bin-packs pods, and moves eligible workloads to spot; you can start read-only and turn on automation later

Native tools give a first pass at no extra tooling cost, allocation tools add showback by team or customer, and automation tools apply recommendations. Standby copies, per-service load balancers, and cluster operations stay on the bill until the platform underneath changes.

A 30-day plan

Week Focus Actions Done when
1 Measure Tag spend by team and service, pull requested versus used CPU and memory, list idle and duplicate environments, and list the top network flows and add-on charges You can rank the top ten sources of waste
2 Right-size Lower requests on the most over-provisioned services a few at a time, keep memory headroom, and shut down idle environments Requested capacity is close to used capacity on the top services
3 Pack and autoscale Consolidate nodes, add pod disruption budgets, scale on request rate, latency, or queue depth, and scale dev and batch workloads down when idle Node count follows load
4 Commit and decide Buy commitments against the smaller baseline, fix the top egress and add-on charges, and decide whether to keep operating clusters or move to a platform with no Kubernetes cluster you have to operate Commitments cover a conservative share of steady usage and the platform decision is written down

Change one tier of services at a time and watch error rate and latency after each change.

How Control Plane cuts compute costs

Control Plane is the platform for running unbreakable apps and agents. It combines any cloud, neocloud, and bare metal into one Global Virtual Cloud and cuts over-provisioning, idle standby, and per-service add-ons at the platform layer. The savings do not depend on running several clouds: one provider is enough.

  • Right-sizing: Capacity AI right-sizes CPU and memory between a minimum and maximum you set, based on historical usage.
  • Billing: on Control Plane-provided compute, you pay for the CPU and memory reserved for each workload, by the millicore and the megabyte, with no contracts or minimums, and Capacity AI sets that reservation. See Control Plane pricing.
  • No idle standby: every location of a Global Virtual Cloud serves live traffic, and the 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations.
  • Day-two operations included: autoscaling, readiness-gated rollouts, load balancing through a global endpoint, automatic TLS certificates, secrets management, unified logs, metrics, and traces, mutual TLS, and a tamper-proof audit trail, with no Kubernetes cluster you have to operate.
  • Keep your managed services: Universal Cloud Identity gives workloads short-lived, least-privilege access to 600+ AWS, GCP, and Azure services, with no long-lived cloud keys in your code.
  • Cost visibility: a Cost and Usage view shows spend per org and per resource, with a projected total.

Result: Customers typically cut compute costs 30 to 50 percent compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure.

FAQ

How do I reduce my AWS costs?

Measure requested versus used CPU and memory first, since paying for capacity workloads do not use is the main source of waste. Then right-size, pack workloads onto fewer nodes, autoscale on real signals, and shut down idle environments before buying Savings Plans or Reserved Instances. Control Plane applies right-sizing, autoscaling, and active-active without idle standby at the platform layer, and customers typically cut compute costs 30 to 50 percent compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure.

What is the right order for cloud cost optimization?

Reduce the capacity you pay for before you reduce the rate: right-size, pack, autoscale, and remove idle standby, then apply commitments and spot capacity to what remains.

How do I lower my Kubernetes bill?

Kubernetes schedules by requests, so inflated requests force extra nodes. Right-size requests, consolidate nodes, and scale idle workloads down. On Control Plane there is no Kubernetes cluster you have to operate, and Capacity AI right-sizes CPU and memory automatically.

How do I stop over-provisioning CPU and memory?

Base requests on measured usage over several weeks, keep headroom for memory, and automate the review so it does not drift. Control Plane’s Capacity AI does this between a minimum and maximum you set, using historical usage.

Are reserved instances and savings plans worth it?

Yes, for steady usage you have already right-sized. Bought before right-sizing, they lock in waste for the term, with limited exchange or resale options.

How much does running Kubernetes cost, including the platform team?

Add compute, add-ons, and the loaded cost of the engineers who operate clusters, handle upgrades, and maintain add-ons; the people cost never appears on a cloud invoice. A platform with no Kubernetes cluster you have to operate, such as Control Plane, removes most of that people cost.

What are hidden cloud costs?

Charges that scale with traffic or service count instead of compute: egress, NAT gateway processing, per-service load balancers, observability volume, and idle capacity, which is often the largest because it looks like ordinary instance spend. Control Plane includes load balancing, automatic TLS, secrets management, and unified observability in the platform.

What FinOps tools show where cloud spend goes?

Control Plane removes waste at the platform layer: Capacity AI right-sizes CPU and memory, billing on Control Plane-provided compute follows reserved millicores and megabytes, active-active runs without idle standby, and a Cost and Usage view shows spend per org and per resource. For visibility on hyperscaler bills, use AWS Cost Explorer, Google Cloud Billing reports, and Microsoft Cost Management, and add Kubecost, Vantage, CloudZero, or Cast AI for allocation, recommendations, or automation.

When should I use spot instances?

For fault-tolerant work that handles shutdown signals: batch jobs, CI runners, and stateless workers with retries. Keep stateful and latency-sensitive services on on-demand or committed capacity, since AWS gives two minutes’ notice and Google Cloud and Azure about 30 seconds.

title: Workload Identity Federation: Cloud Access Without Keys (2026)
description:
Workload identity replaces stored cloud keys with an identity the platform proves for each workload. The cloud exchanges that proof for short-lived, least-privilege credentials at runtime, so there is no long-lived key to leak, rotate, or copy.

Workload identity federation extends the same idea across environments: a workload on a Kubernetes cluster, another cloud, an on-premises server, or a CI pipeline presents a signed token from an identity provider the target cloud trusts, and the cloud returns temporary credentials.

TL;DR

  • Static keys are the weak point. Access keys and service account key files leak through source code, CI logs, images, and laptops, and they stay valid until someone disables or rotates them, unless an expiry is enforced by policy.
  • Workload identity and secrets management solve different problems. Secrets managers hold secrets that must exist; workload identity removes the cloud credential from the secret store entirely.
  • Each cloud has a native mechanism: IAM roles and IAM Roles Anywhere on AWS, Workload Identity Federation on Google Cloud, and managed identities and Microsoft Entra Workload ID on Azure.
  • Cross-cloud access works through trust, not keys. Each target cloud trusts a token issuer, and the setup repeats for each provider and often for each cluster.
  • Identity must follow the workload. Credentials tied to one cloud or one cluster can break a failover even when the workload itself starts.

Control Plane gives each workload one identity that works in every cloud and location. Universal Cloud Identity gives workloads short-lived, least-privilege access to 600+ AWS, GCP, and Azure services, with no long-lived cloud keys in your code, and the same identity keeps working when a workload fails over to another location.

Why long-lived keys are the problem

A static access key or service account key file is a bearer credential: anyone who holds the string can act as the identity, from anywhere, until the key is disabled. Google Cloud’s best practices for managing service account keys state that “Service account keys can become a security risk if not managed carefully” and tell readers to “choose a more secure alternative for authentication whenever possible.” Keys end up in predictable places:

  • Source code and config files. A key committed once stays in version history.
  • CI logs and environment variables. Pipelines print and pass credentials to many steps.
  • Container images. A key baked into an image travels with every copy.
  • Laptops. A developer downloads a key to debug and never deletes it.

Two public incidents show the downstream cost. Codecov’s Bash Uploader update listed as affected “any credentials, tokens, or keys that our customers were passing through their CI runner that would be accessible when the Bash Uploader script was executed.” CircleCI’s January 2023 incident report urged customers to rotate and revoke secrets. In both cases, customers had to find and replace every credential that might have been exposed.

Rotation rarely happens because it is manual: create a new key, update every consumer, confirm nothing broke, and delete the old key. A missed consumer causes an outage. AWS’s IAM best practices tell readers to “Require workloads to use temporary credentials with IAM roles to access AWS” and treat long-term access keys as the exception.

A shared key breaks least privilege. It must carry the union of everything its services need, so one compromise exposes all of it, and every action appears under the same identity in audit logs. Separate identities per workload grant exactly what each needs and show exactly what each did.

Secrets management vs workload identity

A secrets manager stores a secret that has to exist and controls who can read it. Examples include HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secret Manager, and Azure Key Vault. Workload identity answers a different question: how a workload proves who it is to a cloud without a stored credential.

Secrets management Workload identity
What it handles Secrets that must exist: third-party API tokens, database passwords, signing keys
Where the credential lives In the secret store, then in the workload’s memory
Rotation Scheduled or automated rotation of stored values
Typical examples Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault
Main risk it reduces A secret leaking from code, config, or logs

Most teams need both: workload identity for cloud services, and a secrets manager for credentials cloud IAM cannot replace, such as a payment processor token. The secrets manager benefits too, since the workload can authenticate to it without a stored credential of its own.

How each cloud does it natively

AWS

  • IAM roles for EC2. Amazon EC2 uses an instance profile as a container for an IAM role, and the application retrieves temporary credentials through the instance metadata service.
  • IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA). On EKS, an OIDC JSON web token is passed to STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, which returns temporary role credentials. AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity works with any OpenID Connect-compatible provider.
  • EKS Pod Identity. EKS Pod Identity grants pods access to AWS services; the Pod Identity Agent on each node issues the credentials to the SDKs.
  • IAM Roles Anywhere. IAM Roles Anywhere gives workloads outside AWS temporary credentials using X.509 certificates from your certificate authority, registered as a trust anchor, so you don’t manage long-term AWS credentials for them.

Google Cloud

  • Attached service accounts. Applications using client libraries automatically use the attached service account, with credentials from the metadata server.
  • Workload Identity Federation for GKE. The GKE metadata server uses Security Token Service to exchange the Kubernetes JWT for a short-lived federated access token.
  • Workload Identity Federation for other environments. Workload Identity Federation lets on-premises or multicloud workloads use federated identities instead of a service account key, from X.509 certificates, AWS, Azure, on-premises Active Directory, GitHub, GitLab, or any OIDC or SAML 2.0 provider.
  • Blocking keys. Google lists credential leakage, privilege escalation, information disclosure, non-repudiation, and malicious credential configurations as the main key threats, and the iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation constraint disables creation of new external service account keys.

Azure

  • Managed identities. Microsoft’s managed identities overview says: “Manual handling of secrets and certificates are a known source of security issues and outages. Managed identities eliminate the need for developers to manage these credentials.” They come as system-assigned or user-assigned identities.
  • Microsoft Entra Workload ID on AKS. Workload ID on AKS uses federated identity credentials on a managed identity.
  • Workload identity federation for external workloads. Workload identity federation lets a user-assigned managed identity or app registration trust tokens from an external identity provider such as GitHub or Google, for software running in places like on-premises Kubernetes or GitHub Actions.

Cross-cloud and hybrid access

The harder case is a workload in one environment calling another. The pattern is the same in every cloud:

  1. Choose a token issuer: an OIDC issuer or certificate authority on the workload’s platform, such as a Kubernetes cluster, a cloud metadata service, or a CI system.
  2. Configure trust in the target cloud: which issuer to trust and which claims map to which role or identity.
  3. Exchange the token: the workload presents its token at runtime and receives short-lived credentials.
  4. Scope the permissions: the role, service account, or app registration holds only what that workload needs.
Workload runs on Target cloud Native path
GCP or Azure AWS An OIDC identity provider plus STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, or IAM Roles Anywhere with X.509 certificates
AWS or Azure Google Cloud Workload Identity Federation with an AWS or Azure provider
AWS or Kubernetes Azure A federated identity credential on a managed identity or app registration
On premises Any of the three The cloud’s federation feature, backed by an OIDC issuer or X.509 certificates

Every cloud, cluster, and location adds setup. Three clouds and four clusters mean many issuers, trust configurations, and role mappings, each with its own limits and console. Drift between them causes outages that look like authentication errors, and moving a workload means repeating the setup there. That operational load is a main reason teams fall back to static keys.

SPIFFE and SPIRE

SPIFFE, the Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone, is an open standard for workload identity; the project describes SPIFFE and SPIRE as providing “strongly attested, cryptographic identities to workloads across a wide variety of platforms.” SPIFFE defines how an identity is named and carried in an X.509 certificate or JWT, and SPIRE attests workloads and issues those identities. SPIFFE identities can be federated into AWS, Google Cloud, or Azure through the mechanisms above, and teams that run SPIRE take on operating it.

CI federation

CI pipelines are a common source of leaked keys. GitHub’s OpenID Connect documentation says you won’t need to duplicate cloud credentials as long-lived GitHub secrets: configure OIDC trust on your cloud provider and have workflows request a short-lived token. All three clouds support this, and it is often the easiest first migration.

Why cloud credentials break failover

A pod identity bound to one cluster’s issuer stops working when the workload moves to a cluster with a different issuer, unless the cloud also trusts that issuer. The workload starts in the new location, tries to read from S3 or write to BigQuery, and fails with an access error: the failover succeeded and the application is still down.

Teams often find this during an incident, because failover tests check that the workload starts, not that it reaches its dependencies. The fix is identity that follows the workload into every location it runs in, so access depends on who the workload is, not where it runs. That belongs on the checklist for active-active high availability, where every location serves live traffic.

Best practices checklist

  • Inventory every static key across code, pipelines, images, and secret stores.
  • Use short-lived credentials for workloads; automatic expiry removes manual credential rotation and limits the value of a stolen credential.
  • Give each workload its own identity to limit blast radius and keep audit logs readable.
  • Apply least privilege and review permissions on a schedule.
  • Federate CI pipelines instead of storing cloud keys as pipeline secrets.
  • Block new keys by policy. Google Cloud offers the iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation constraint. On AWS, a service control policy can deny iam:CreateAccessKey. In Microsoft Entra ID, app management policies can block new client secrets and cap credential lifetimes.
  • Keep a secrets manager for third-party tokens and database passwords.
  • Audit access and alert on unused or unexpected access.
  • Remove old keys after migrating: disable first, watch for failures, then delete.
  • Test credentials during failover: move a workload to another location and confirm it still reaches every cloud service it uses.
  • Document the exceptions with an owner, a reason, and a removal date.

How Control Plane handles workload identity

Control Plane is the platform for running unbreakable apps and agents. It combines any cloud, neocloud, on-premises, and bare-metal location into one Global Virtual Cloud (GVC) and runs workloads active-active in every location of a GVC. Removing long-lived keys matters on a single cloud too, because a static key carries the same leak risk on one cloud or three.

  • What it does. Universal Cloud Identity covers 600+ AWS, GCP, and Azure services through short-lived, least-privilege credentials issued at runtime.
  • How it works. You attach one identity to a workload. Giving the identity a cloud access rule provisions one principal for it inside your own cloud account: an IAM role on AWS, a service account on GCP, and an app registration on Azure. Per cloud, you either list the permissions for Control Plane to create that principal, or name an existing role or service account to attach to. Control Plane serves the provider’s own instance metadata endpoint inside the workload, so an unmodified cloud SDK finds short-lived credentials exactly where it already looks. Applications that use the cloud SDK’s default credential lookup need no code changes.
  • One identity across clouds. An identity can hold access to one AWS account, one GCP account, and one Azure account at once, so a workload that reads from Amazon S3 and writes to BigQuery uses a single identity.
  • The same identity in every location. Access works the same on compute Control Plane provides, on your own Kubernetes clusters through Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK), and on Managed Kubernetes locations, including on premises, so a workload fails over between locations or clouds without changing its credentials. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations.
  • Proven in an outage. During the October 2025 AWS us-east-1 outage, 20% of Control Plane customers had us-east-1 in their Global Virtual Clouds. Their workloads were active and running in healthy locations within 10 seconds, with no customer downtime, according to Control Plane internal incident telemetry.
  • Built-in secrets management. Third-party API tokens and database passwords live in Control Plane secrets. A workload reads one only when a policy grants its identity reveal on that secret, and references it as cpln://secret/NAME, so the value never appears in the workload definition. Teams with an existing secrets manager can keep using it alongside the platform.
  • Traffic and audit. Every workload talks to other workloads over mutual TLS with a certificate unique to that workload, with no certificate management required, and a tamper-proof audit trail records every action.
  • Day-two operations included: autoscaling, readiness-gated rollouts, automatic TLS certificates, and unified logs, metrics, and traces, with no Kubernetes cluster you have to operate; see the Kubernetes alternatives guide.
  • Compliance. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant; for regulated data placement, see the data residency guide.

FAQ

What is workload identity?

A way for software, not a person, to prove who it is to a cloud or service. The platform running the workload vouches for it, and the cloud returns short-lived credentials scoped to that workload, so no long-lived key is stored in the application.

What is workload identity federation?

It lets a workload in one environment access another by presenting a token from an identity provider the target trusts; the target validates it and issues temporary credentials. AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure each document a federation path.

How do I stop using long-lived AWS access keys in my applications?

Use IAM roles: an instance profile on EC2, IRSA or EKS Pod Identity on EKS, and IAM Roles Anywhere or an OIDC provider with AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity outside AWS. Remove the old keys once nothing uses them.

How do I access AWS from GCP or Azure without storing keys?

Create an IAM OIDC identity provider in AWS that trusts the workload platform’s token issuer, create a role that trusts specific claims from it, and exchange the token through AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. IAM Roles Anywhere is the alternative for workloads with X.509 certificates from your own CA.

How do I access GCP or Azure from AWS or Kubernetes without service account keys?

For Google Cloud, configure Workload Identity Federation with an AWS, Azure, or OIDC provider. For Azure, add a federated identity credential to a managed identity or app registration that trusts your cluster’s or provider’s tokens.

What is the difference between secrets management and workload identity?

Secrets management stores and rotates secrets that must exist, such as third-party API tokens; workload identity removes the need to store a cloud credential at all.

Does workload identity keep working during failover?

Only if the identity is not bound to one cluster or cloud. On Control Plane, the identity belongs to the workload’s Global Virtual Cloud (GVC) and follows it to every location, so a workload that fails over keeps its AWS, GCP, and Azure access.

What are the best practices for secrets management in 2026?

Remove static cloud keys, use short-lived credentials, give each workload its own identity, and apply least privilege. Keep a secrets manager for non-cloud secrets with restricted reads, rotation, and audit, and block new long-lived keys by policy.

How do I manage cloud credentials across multiple clouds?

Federate trust instead of distributing keys, and attach one identity per workload that holds access to each cloud. On Control Plane, a single identity covers one AWS, one GCP, and one Azure account.

What tools help with workload identity and secretless access?

Native options are AWS IAM roles, IRSA, EKS Pod Identity, and IAM Roles Anywhere, Google Cloud Workload Identity Federation, and Azure managed identities with Microsoft Entra Workload ID; SPIFFE and SPIRE are the open standard. Control Plane’s Universal Cloud Identity provides access to AWS, GCP, and Azure services across every location of a GVC, with no long-lived cloud keys in your code.

Next step: start with an inventory of your static keys, then see how one identity can replace them across clouds and locations. Talk to the Control Plane team or sign up free.

title: AI doesn’t care about your job title
description:
Exposure to artificial intelligence runs through the tasks you do each week, not the role on your badge. Here’s how to measure yours and lower the risk.

My mom doesn’t understand my job, and it isn’t her fault. The closest I’ve ever come to explaining it is “I design how it works,” which is true and tells her almost nothing about my day.

It also works best when I’m wearing a black turtleneck and holding an iPhone, channeling my inner Steve Jobs.

That’s the curse of knowledge, and I’ve never directly defined my role in many of the places I’ve worked. Over decades I’ve managed design, product management, and engineering, and more than once I started without a job description. It wasn’t about my job title, it was about judgement applied through my experience building software.

Artificial intelligence doesn’t care about your job title or mine. It’s probabilistically predicting an outcome without looking at your LinkedIn.

In GPTs are GPTs, published in 2023, researchers from OpenAI and the University of Pennsylvania scored occupations task by task. They estimated that 80% of U.S. workers could see at least a tenth of their tasks affected, and about 19% could see at least half.

Those averages hide what matters for one person. Your exposure depends on how much of your week can be specified briefly and checked quickly, and seniority protects you only when it changes that mix.

For her work, she’s not exposed even though she’s in the models. From Claude:

The main trace of Jean Neeman in the art world is a single, well-documented piece: a teapot titled “Tea on the Go,” made in 1994 by Jean Neeman (American, b. 1948) from silver, copper, brass, and cocobolo wood, measuring about 8.4 x 7.75 x 4.5 inches. That puts her work alongside some serious company.

She doesn’t have to measure her risk because she’s an artist. I measure mine all the time so I can add value that AI can’t add, and that’s judgement.

The five steps below show how to measure yours, each with a prompt to run in Claude.

List Your Actual Tasks

Start with a week, not a job description.

List everything you spent more than half an hour on: the usability readout, the stakeholder review, the status update nobody read. Note the hours, how often each task repeats, and who reviews the result.

Also leave room for the white space between tasks.

Unblocking a teammate, the quick answer that saves someone a day, the thinking before a hard review: none of it shows up in a job description or on a calendar. It also goes unseen when people judge what you do, whether that’s a manager at review time or a researcher scoring tasks for exposure.

It’s often where you absorb complexity that, as Tesler’s Law puts it, can be moved but never removed.

Write it down anyway.

For a checklist, O*NET OnLine, the Labor Department’s occupational database, lists 31 tasks for Web and Digital Interface Designers. In Putting Tasks to the Test: Human Capital, Job Tasks and Wages, a 2009 paper, economists David Autor and Michael Handel found that tasks vary substantially within occupations, enough to predict wage gaps among people who hold the same job.

In Toil and Technology, written for the International Monetary Fund in 2015, economist James Bessen showed how automated teller machines took over dispensing cash and taking deposits. The tellers needed to run an average urban branch fell from 20 to 13 between 1988 and 2004, but banks opened 43% more urban branches, so the jobs held.

The title stayed the same while the job underneath it was rebuilt.

My own title changed in March, from director to senior principal designer. Neither title would tell you which of my tasks a model can do, but my calendar would.

Try It in Claude

Run these prompts in one Claude conversation. The first one drafts your week from your role, so you correct a list instead of writing one, and you can check its tasks against O*NET OnLine.

To map my exposure to artificial intelligence, don’t read my calendar or connected accounts, or ask me to describe my week. If you don’t know my title, ask once. Name the O*NET occupation you matched, and say if you’re recalling its tasks from memory. Draft 15 to 20 tasks from it, plus the undocumented work between them, for a normal week. Give hours, frequency, and reviewer for each, marked as guesses. Then have me correct it, including whether I manage anyone.

Score Each Task’s Exposure

Difficulty is a poor guide to exposure. In a 2023 experiment for Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier, a team led by Fabrizio Dell’Acqua gave 758 Boston Consulting Group consultants realistic work.

With the model, they did far better on 18 tasks inside its abilities but were 19 percentage points less likely to get the right answer on one task outside them. Coauthor Ethan Mollick calls this the jagged frontier in Centaurs and Cyborgs on the Jagged Frontier: tasks that look equally hard can sit on opposite sides of an invisible wall.

Score each task with two questions instead. I call it the spec-and-check test.

  • Specify the result. Ask whether you could describe a finished version in two sentences that someone else could follow.
  • Check the output. Ask whether someone could confirm it’s right in less time than it took to make.
A task that’s quick to specify and quick to check is exposed, whatever your title says.

Twenty variations of an empty state pass both questions. Deciding which of three problems to fund this quarter fails both, and for now that decision stays yours.

Then weight the list by hours, because the Pareto Principle usually holds and a few tasks fill most of the week. A task that passes both and fills two days a week is where your risk sits.

When leadership reviews a pie chart of where a team’s hours go, you don’t want to be on the wrong side of it.

Passing the test means a model could do the task, not that one already does. In Labor market impacts of AI: A new measure and early evidence, from its own March 2026 usage data, Anthropic found Claude covering about 33% of computer and math tasks, against 94% rated feasible in GPTs are GPTs.

So the prompt below has Claude try one.

Try It in Claude

Paste this after the task table. It ends with Claude attempting your most exposed task, so you judge real output instead of a forecast.

Score each task in my table: could a finished version be described in two sentences, and checked faster than it took to make? Answer yes, partly, or no for each. Then say honestly if you could do each task today, fully, partly, or not yet, and why. Mark tasks with two yeses as exposed, sort by hours, and tell me what share of my week is exposed. Offer to try my top exposed task so I can judge it.

Check Your Career Stage

In the August 2026 revision of Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence, Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab found no economy-wide job displacement in payroll data. Employment for workers ages 22 to 25 in exposed occupations, though, sits 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers, mostly because companies are hiring fewer young people.

Experienced workers show no comparable gap, and the authors call these early indicators, not proof of cause.

Entry-level work is often the most specified on a team, handed down with clear instructions and reviewed by someone senior, which is where a model does best. Experience protects through judgment and context that rarely fit in a two-sentence spec.

A senior title over a week of status decks is junior exposure with a bigger paycheck.

If you’re early in your career, ask to own one small decision from start to finish. If you’re senior, hand your juniors judgment calls along with tasks.

Management will also change because there will be smaller teams.

Melvin Conway observed in 1968 that organizations build systems that copy their communication structures, which I cover in Conway’s Law. My extension is that much of management exists to carry that communication, so a smaller team needs less of it. Four people share six possible pairs, while 10 people share 45.

The flattening predates these tools. For The Manager Mass Exodus: How SMBs Are Flattening the Org Chart, Gusto studied payroll at about 8,500 small and midsize businesses. The share of their workers who manage anyone fell from just under 25% in 2019 to about 15% by late 2024. If you manage, move your hours from relaying information toward the decisions and coaching a smaller team still needs.

Try It in Claude

This prompt compares your task list against your experience. Correct it if it gets your background wrong.

Based on my title and experience, split my tasks into entry-level work (well specified and reviewed by others) and judgment work only I can do. If you don’t know my years of experience, ask once. Give the share of hours in each and, if I manage, how much goes to relaying information. Name the knowledge I bring that you could supply without my judgment. Tell me plainly if my week looks junior for my title, and suggest one decision I could own this quarter.

Deepen Your Domain Expertise

Knowing your field pays off more than knowing your tools. For Agentic coding and persistent returns to expertise, published in June 2026, Anthropic studied about 400,000 Claude Code sessions.

People made about 70% of the planning decisions — that’s human agency — and the agent made about 80% of the execution decisions.

The researchers rated expertise task by task and said it differs from job title: a senior engineer asking a first question about the Rust language counts as a beginner at Rust. Expert sessions succeeded about twice as often as novice ones, and a working grasp of the domain captured most of that gain, the same early-steep curve as the Power Law of Practice.

The person who understands the problem and not the model gets more out than the person who understands the model and not the problem.

Knowledge on its own doesn’t protect you anymore: If what you know can be pulled from a large language model without judgment to apply it, you’re at risk.

Companies don’t need you to tell them something they already know, they need the person who knows which answer fits this customer and this quarter, and the person who acts as connective tissue between people, building trust and getting decisions made rather than relaying status.

If you’re neither, your expertise is a search ot an AI Assistant result.

For designers, the domain is the user’s world and the business around it. Get closer to your users’ domain than your product manager is: read the regulations your customers follow, sit with support for a day, and learn how the money moves.

Try It in Claude

Answer the way you would with a new manager, without polishing. Short, unsure answers show the gaps fastest.

If you don’t know what my company sells, ask once. Tell me in one sentence who my product serves, and let me correct it. Ask me eight to 10 questions, one at a time, about their regulations, money, metrics, and workflow; “not sure” is a fine answer. Rank my knowledge gaps by how much they’d change my design decisions, suggest one way to close the top gap in 30 days, and revise the decision you suggested earlier.

Rebuild Your Portfolio

Employers expect 39% of workers’ core skills to change by 2030, according to the World Economic Forum’s The Future of Jobs Report 2025. A portfolio of polished final screens puts the fastest-changing part of your job up front and hides the part that holds its value.

Rebuild it around decisions: the problem you chose and the ones you turned down, the tradeoff and why, and what happened after launch. Show one case where you directed a model, caught its mistake, and shipped the fix.

Show the work a model couldn’t have done without you.

Look sideways too.

O*NET lists 10 related occupations for the same designer category, from software developers to graphic designers, and jobs overlap where their tasks do. As I wrote in We’ve Seen This Movie Before: Desktop Publishing Already Showed Us How AI Prototyping Plays Out, typesetting effectively ended as a profession while graphic design grew into web, motion, and product design. They all adjusted, and we’re seeing this move now too.

Whole economies have also made this move before.

The agricultural revolution let fewer people grow more food, and the industrial revolution absorbed the workers it freed. In 1900, 41% of American workers farmed, and by 2000 fewer than 2% did, according to The 20th Century Transformation of U.S. Agriculture and Farm Policy from the USDA’s Economic Research Service.

The adjustment wasn’t gentle, though.

In Engels’ Pause, economic historian Robert Allen found that British wages stalled for roughly half a century in the early industrial era while output per worker kept climbing.

People adjusted, but it took a generation, and the ones who fared best moved toward the new work instead of waiting for it to reach them.

The good news is that employers now have software to map those overlaps, something Henry Ford never had. When Ford ended the Model T in 1927, about 60,000 workers were laid off, according to Last Day of Model T Production at Ford from HISTORY. Skills platforms such as Skills Cloud, from my employer Workday, now relate the skills across a workforce.

In the report’s workforce strategies chapter, 85% of employers plan to upskill and 51% plan to move staff into growing roles. Organizations are looking to reinvest and reinvent.

Intentions aren’t programs, though, as Dan Maccarone argues in What the AI era owes you for UX Collective Editors. You own your career, not your company.

It’s up to you to figure out where the hockey puck is going, the advice Wayne Gretzky got from his father, Walter, and your task list shows which way it’s moving.

Try It in Claude

Run this on your strongest case study first. Then reuse it on the rest, and keep the list of adjacent jobs it produces.

Ask me for my strongest case study. Rewrite it around my decisions: the problem, the options I turned down, the tradeoff, how I used and corrected artificial intelligence tools (or that I didn’t), and the outcome. Ask for missing facts one at a time instead of inventing them. Then list four or five jobs whose tasks overlap most with mine, what I’d need to add for each, and which carry more exposure than mine, using the earlier test.

Conclusion

The tellers’ story has a second chapter, and the branch boom that saved their jobs didn’t last. The Bureau of Labor Statistics outlook for Tellers projects employment falling 13% from 2025 to 2035, as mobile deposits and online banking keep customers away from the window. The first wave of automation changed what tellers did, and the second is taking away where they did it.That’s why the task list is a recurring exercise. Models improve unevenly, and a task that failed the spec-and-check test last spring can pass it next spring. Redo the list every six months and move a few more hours toward the work a model can’t finish without you.

There will always need to be a human in the loop, the person who commits to what the system proposes, as my Human-in-the-Loop entry puts it. Beyond that, there has to be human agency: someone who decides rather than someone who clicks approve.

My mom won’t be able to explain my job, whatever the next title is. A model won’t need the title to find my exposed work, and it can point out where it is.

Run the first prompt next Monday, before the next reorganization or the next model release decides the mix for you and how you can explain it to your mom.

Action items

  • Draft your task list. Run the first prompt and correct the table it builds from your role, or log every task longer than 30 minutes for five days by hand, using the O*NET task list for your occupation to catch what you missed.
  • Score each task. Mark whether a finished version can be specified in two sentences and checked faster than it was made, and treat tasks that pass both as your exposure.
  • Trade one hour. Each week, move an hour from your most exposed task to a planning decision, a stakeholder conversation, or time with users.
  • Rewrite one case study. Rebuild your strongest portfolio piece around the decisions you made, including any evaluation criteria you wrote and what happened after launch, and note which adjacent job its tasks would also qualify you for.

title: I broke an Elementor site on purpose, then built a tool to find the bugs
description:
The night I broke my own site

I'm 53, I work in a factory, and in the evenings I build things in vanilla JavaScript.

Lately I've been looking at freelance WordPress jobs. Almost every one of them says the same thing: "Elementor site, layout is broken, fix it."

So I did something a bit crazy. I took an empty test site, installed Elementor, and asked an AI to break it for me — 5 hidden CSS bugs, packed into an encoded script so I couldn't just read the answer.

Then I tried to find them.

It was humbling. The page looked wrong, but the console said nothing. Of course: CSS doesn't throw errors. A bad rule is still a valid rule, so the browser applies it silently. That's exactly why clients say "everything moved and I don't know why."

I found the first bug the slow way — DevTools, Styles panel, unchecking rules one by one until I saw it:

.elementor-section, .e-con { margin-right: -60px !important; }

Twenty minutes for one line. I thought: there must be a faster way.

So I built one: CSS hunt

🐞 BeeLadybug is my zero-dependency debugging overlay. You paste one line in the console and it attaches to any page — WordPress dashboards, Elementor pages, mobile viewports. It already showed element size, classes, display type, FPS and memory.

Version 0.5 adds a new mode: CSS hunt (press F6).

When you hover an element, it tells you what's wrong with it:

  • !important rules that match the element, and where they come from (<style> inline or the stylesheet URL)
  • Overflow causes: which element actually leaves the viewport, plus negative margins
  • Invisible text: color: transparent, opacity: 0, or text the same color as its background
  • Click blockers: what sits on top of the element's center, including fixed ::before / ::after on html / body
  • Stretched images: natural ratio vs rendered ratio, when object-fit is fill

Press S to scan the whole page. Click a line and the element gets a red outline.

The hard part: telling the truth without noise

My first version was technically right and practically useless.

One card overflowing the screen produced ten red lines: the card, its article, its p, its h2… All "overflowing", because they inherited it. A fixed overlay blocking clicks? One warning per element underneath it.

A real developer doesn't want ten alarms. They want the culprit.

So the scan now:

  1. Reports the cause, not the containers. An ancestor is skipped if a descendant overflows by the same amount (±2px).
  2. Groups by cause. Instead of 12 lines you get: 
▾ body::after blocks clicks on 12 elements
    div.elementor-element-629ef32
    img#1301
    summary.elementor-element-3925463
    …
  1. Separates bugs from info. Red = bug. Grey = info, like unreadable sheet: fonts.googleapis.com (cross-origin stylesheets can't be read — that's a browser rule, not a problem on the page).
  2. Keeps the log calm. Hover and DOM-mutation lines are hidden unless you turn on verbose mode (F3). Each issue is logged once per element every 5 seconds. Press P to pin the panel on an element and read it in peace.

The real test

The demo page bugs are easy — I wrote them. The real test was the broken Elementor page, with Elementor V4 "atomic" widgets, Google Fonts, Altervista ad scripts and all the usual mess.

Result: CSS hunt found the click blocker, the negative margin overflow, the invisible button text and the stretched image on a live page I didn't build the bugs for.

Try it

Open any page, press F12, paste this in the console:

import('https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bee-ladybug@0.5.3/src/index.js')
  .then(({ BeeLadybugCore, WebDOMAdapter, CSSAdapter }) => {
    const bee = new BeeLadybugCore();
    new WebDOMAdapter(bee, { root: document.body }).attach();
    new CSSAdapter(bee).attach();
    window.bee = bee;
  });

Then press F6, hover, and press S.

No build step, no framework, no dependencies. Just vanilla JavaScript.

What I learned

  • CSS bugs are silent. The console won't help you. You need to look at computed styles and geometry.
  • The right answer is not enough. A debugging tool must point to the cause, or it's just another wall of text.
  • Breaking things on purpose is the best teacher. I recommend it to anyone who wants to do WordPress fixes for clients.

I'm still learning. If you try CSS hunt on a broken page and it misses something, tell me in the comments — that's how the next version gets better.

🐞 npm: bee-ladybug

title: Make your v0 or Cursor app stop looking AI-built in 10 minutes
description:
If you've built a landing page with v0, Cursor, Lovable or Bolt, you've probably had this moment: you put it next to someone else's and it's the same page. Purple-to-blue gradient, centred headline, one font, three feature cards with an icon in a circle, a pricing table, and a "Get started" button that does nothing you can see.

Nothing on that page is broken. It's the average of every landing page the model has seen, and that's what you get when you don't ask for anything specific. Visitors recognise it within seconds, though, and some of them decide the product behind it got the same amount of thought.

Here are the five tells I look for and a fix for each. Every fix is a couple of minutes in a Next.js App Router project with Tailwind CSS v4. I put the result in a free starter (MIT) so you can copy single pieces or start from the whole thing:

  • Repo: https://github.com/teodoravadani/qodesign-next-starter
  • Live demo: https://teodoravadani.github.io/qodesign-next-starter/

The five tells

  1. A gradient where a brand colour should be.
  2. One font at one weight for everything.
  3. Everything centred.
  4. An illustration where the product should be.
  5. Buttons that don't respond.

0. Get a page to work on (1 minute)

To try the fixes on a clean page:

npx create-next-app@latest my-app -e https://github.com/teodoravadani/qodesign-next-starter
cd my-app
npm run dev

Or open your own project. The steps assume Next.js 15 (App Router) and Tailwind v4, the setup where globals.css starts with @import "tailwindcss".

1. Swap the gradient for three colours (2 minutes)

Delete the bg-gradient-to-r from-purple-500 to-blue-500 (or whatever your hero has). In Tailwind v4 the palette lives in CSS, and every variable in @theme becomes a utility class:

/* app/globals.css */
@theme {
  --color-ink: #0a0a0d;
  --color-paper: #f3f1ea;
  --color-volt: #c6ff3d;
}

Now bg-ink, text-paper and bg-volt exist. Ink is the page, paper is the text (swap them for a light theme), and the accent goes on one or two things per screen: the main button, a status dot. Once the accent is on every element it does the gradient's job again.

2. Two fonts with some character (1 minute)

Pick a display face for headings and UI and a mono for numbers and small labels. The starter uses Space Grotesk and JetBrains Mono. The font @import has to be the first line of the file:

@import url("https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=JetBrains+Mono:wght@400;500;600;700&family=Space+Grotesk:wght@400;500;600;700&display=swap");
@import "tailwindcss";

@theme {
  --font-sans: "Space Grotesk", ui-sans-serif, system-ui, sans-serif;
  --font-mono: "JetBrains Mono", ui-monospace, monospace;
}

One trap I hit while testing this: a project set up with shadcn init (v0 projects use shadcn) already has an @theme inline block with --font-sans: var(--font-sans). That block wins, the variable points at itself, and the page falls back to Times New Roman. Edit the --font-sans and --font-mono lines inside that existing block instead of adding new ones. Also delete any font-family: Arial left on body by the default template, and put font-sans on <body>.

Then use contrast in size and weight: a bold 7xl headline with tracking-tight leading-[1.02], body text at text-lg and 60% opacity, mono at text-xs for the small stuff.

3. Move the hero off centre (1 minute)

Centred layouts are the default because they never look broken. A left-aligned hero with a width limit on the headline looks like someone placed it:

<section className="mx-auto max-w-6xl px-5 pt-28 pb-16">
  <h1 className="max-w-3xl text-5xl leading-[1.02] font-bold tracking-tight sm:text-7xl">
    Know your servers are down before your users do.
  </h1>
  <p className="mt-6 max-w-xl text-lg text-white/60">
    Uptime, latency and deploys on one screen. Set up in two minutes, no agent to install.
  </p>
</section>

Write the headline as one sentence about the visitor's problem. "Supercharge your workflow" is the copy version of the purple gradient.

4. Show the product (2 minutes)

Generated heroes get a blob or a 3D shape because the model has never seen your app. You have. Screenshot your best screen at 2x and put it in a plain browser frame:

import Image from 'next/image';
import shot from '@/assets/dashboard.webp';

<div className="mt-16 overflow-hidden rounded-2xl border border-white/10 bg-ink">
  <div className="flex items-center gap-1.5 border-b border-white/10 px-4 py-3">
    <span className="size-2.5 rounded-full bg-white/15" />
    <span className="size-2.5 rounded-full bg-white/15" />
    <span className="size-2.5 rounded-full bg-white/15" />
  </div>
  <Image src={shot} alt="The dashboard" priority sizes="(max-width: 1200px) 100vw, 1152px" />
</div>

The static import gives next/image the width and height, so nothing shifts when it loads, and it keeps working if you deploy under a sub-path. priority is there because it's the biggest thing above the fold.

No app to screenshot yet? The starter has a /dashboard route you can use as a placeholder. Swap in your real screen before you launch.

5. Make every button respond (3 minutes)

People feel this one without being able to name it. Click "Start free" on most generated pages and nothing visible happens. A loading state that turns into a confirmation tells the visitor their click did something.

I use the free Toast Stack component for this. It installs from a registry URL with the shadcn CLI, so the source lands in your project and you can edit it:

npx shadcn@latest add https://teodoravadani.github.io/qodesign-free/r/toast-stack.json

Mount the toaster once in app/layout.tsx:

import { Toaster } from '@/components/toast-stack/ToastStack';

// inside <body>
{children}
<Toaster />

Then wrap your signup call:

'use client';
import { toast } from '@/components/toast-stack/ToastStack';

const start = () => {
  toast.promise(createWorkspace(), {
    loading: { title: 'Creating your workspace…' },
    success: (name) => ({ title: 'Workspace ready', description: `${name} is live. The first check runs in 30 s.` }),
    error: () => ({ title: 'That didn’t work', description: 'Try again in a minute.' }),
  });
};

The spinner stays up for at least 600 ms so a fast request doesn't flash, then turns into a check. Hover the stack and the toasts fan out.

Pricing gets the same treatment. The Pricing Switch component replaces a static three-column table with a monthly/yearly switch whose prices roll like an odometer:

npx shadcn@latest add https://teodoravadani.github.io/qodesign-free/r/pricing-switch.json

<PricingSwitch
  plans={plans}
  header={<h2>Pay for monitors, not seats.</h2>}
  onSelect={(plan, yearly) => startCheckout(plan.id, yearly ? 'year' : 'month')}
/>

Its digits use Saira Condensed, so add &family=Saira+Condensed:wght@700;800 to the font import from step 2.

Bonus: motion that respects people (30 seconds)

If you add scroll-in animations, put them behind prefers-reduced-motion. In the starter the sections fade up with a CSS scroll timeline and no JavaScript:

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  .reveal {
    animation: reveal-up linear both;
    animation-timeline: view();
    animation-range: entry 0% cover 28%;
  }
}
@keyframes reveal-up {
  from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(28px); }
  to { opacity: 1; transform: none; }
}

Add className="reveal" to a section. The components in the starter check the same setting on their own.

If you'd rather hand it to Cursor

This prompt covers steps 1 to 4. I haven't compared how each tool handles it, so read the diff before you accept it:

Restyle the landing page in this Next.js App Router + Tailwind v4 project.
1. Remove every gradient background. In globals.css add --color-ink #0a0a0d, --color-paper #f3f1ea and --color-volt #c6ff3d to @theme. Use volt only on the primary button and one status dot.
2. Fonts: Space Grotesk for headings and UI, JetBrains Mono for numbers and small labels. Add a Google Fonts @import as the first line of globals.css. If an @theme inline block already defines --font-sans or --font-mono, change those lines instead of adding new ones. Put font-sans on <body>.
3. Left-align the hero: one-sentence headline (max-w-3xl, text-5xl sm:text-7xl, tracking-tight), one supporting line (max-w-xl).
4. Replace the hero illustration with next/image of src/assets/screenshot.webp (static import) inside a simple browser frame.
Don't change any other copy. Don't add dependencies.

What's in the starter

  • /: hero with a product shot, a log upload section with progress and retry (Upload Dropzone), pricing (Pricing Switch), toasts on every action (Toast Stack), and a light/dark switch (Day/Night Toggle).
  • /dashboard: Orbit, an observability dashboard with simulated live data.
  • Next.js 15.5, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind v4, Framer Motion 11. next build passes and every page is static, so it deploys anywhere. The README has a one-click Vercel button.

About me, and the links. I'm Teodor, and I make animated UI components at qodesign, so the components in this post are mine. Everything here is free and MIT: the starter and the free components and dashboards in qodesign-free. The paid components are $3 each or $29 for all of them, each with a React + Tailwind version and a PROMPT.md for AI coding tools, at qodesign.dev.

If you run the five fixes on your own app, I'd like to see the before and after.

I wrote this post with help from an AI assistant. The code is copied from the starter repo, and every command above was run in a fresh Next.js 15 app (one plain, one set up with shadcn init) with next build passing before publishing.

title: Top 5 Ways to Humanize ChatGPT Responses in Your App (2026): System Prompts, Post-Processing and Tools
description:
Updated October 2026.

If you've shipped an LLM feature, you've probably had this feedback: "It works, but it sounds like a robot." Users notice the bullet-point reflex, the "Great question!" opener and the closing "Let me know if you have any other questions!" These patterns make a support bot feel scripted and a writing assistant feel generic.

This is a practical list of fixes, from cheapest to most involved, for developers who want LLM responses that sound like their product rather than like a default assistant.

First, define "human" for your product

Nielsen Norman Group describes tone of voice along four dimensions: funny vs. serious, formal vs. casual, respectful vs. irreverent, and enthusiastic vs. matter-of-fact. Pick a point on each before you touch a prompt. "Casual, serious, respectful, matter-of-fact" is a spec. "Friendly" isn't.

1. Rewrite the system prompt with rules and examples

This fixes the most for the least effort. OpenAI's prompt engineering guide recommends specific instructions and examples of desired output, and that applies to voice as much as to format.

Voice: casual, serious, respectful, matter-of-fact.
- Answer in the first sentence. No greeting, no "Great question".
- Use bullets only for 3+ parallel items. Otherwise, prose.
- Max 3 short paragraphs unless the user asks for detail.
- Never end with an offer of further help.

Good example:
User: can I change my plan mid-month?
Assistant: Yes. You'll be charged the difference for the rest of the
month, and the new limits apply right away.

Honest note: the biggest single win, but long conversations drift; re-inject the rules.

2. Post-process with a deterministic filter

Some phrases survive any prompt. A small regex pass strips them before display:

const STRIP = [
  /^(great|good|excellent) question[!.]?\s*/i,
  /\s*(let me know|feel free to ask) if you have any (other|more) questions[.!]?$/i,
  /^certainly[!,.]?\s*/i,
];
export const tidy = (s) => STRIP.reduce((t, re) => t.replace(re, ""), s).trim();

Honest note: cheap and reliable for openers and sign-offs; don't use it to rewrite the middle of answers.

3. Run long-form output through a humanizer before publishing

For features that produce content (email drafts, product descriptions, blog sections) rather than chat replies, a dedicated humanizer is worth adding to the review step. UnAIMyText is a free AI humanizer that rewrites at the sentence level, varying rhythm and replacing stock phrasing while keeping meaning. Free runs handle 500 words each with no total cap and no account, and you can set formality and emotional tone first, which maps neatly onto the voice spec above.

Honest note: it's a web tool with no public API documented on the site, so it fits a human review step for generated content, not a real-time chat pipeline.

4. Use QuillBot or Grammarly for in-browser review

If a person reviews generated content before it goes out, the extensions they already have can help. QuillBot's free humanizer works in five languages and runs inside ChatGPT and Gemini; Grammarly's humanizer covers six languages and can learn a custom voice.

Honest note: great for reviewers, irrelevant for automated replies, and QuillBot's free requests are short (around 100 words).

5. Fine-tune or few-shot with real transcripts

If you have a corpus of excellent human support replies, few-shot examples (or fine-tuning, where available) teach the model your actual voice better than any adjective.

Honest note: the most effective long-term fix and the most work: you need clean, consented data and an eval set.

How to test it

Keep a fixed set of 30 representative user messages. For each change, generate responses and score:

  • Does the first sentence answer the question?
  • Any banned phrases left?
  • Average response length vs. target.
  • A blind human rating: "sounds like us" on a 1-to-5 scale.

Automate the first three; do the fourth weekly with two teammates.

FAQ

How do I stop ChatGPT starting every answer with "Great question"?
Ban it in the system prompt, give a counter-example, and strip it with a regex as a backstop.

Should my chatbot use bullet points?
Only for genuinely parallel items. Prose reads as more human for short answers.

What's the best way to humanize long generated content in an app?
Prompt for structure, then run each section through a humanizer during human review, then edit.

Common mistakes

  • Over-casual voice in serious contexts. A billing or security answer shouldn't joke. Let tone vary by intent: route sensitive intents to a stricter prompt.
  • Stripping all structure. Steps in a how-to should stay numbered. "Human" doesn't mean "no formatting."
  • Faking empathy. "I completely understand how frustrating that must be" on every turn reads as scripted. Acknowledge once, then solve.
  • Shipping without evals. Voice changes can quietly hurt accuracy. Re-run your factual eval set after every prompt change, not just the tone checks. A friendlier answer that is wrong is still a wrong answer, and users forgive stiffness far more readily than errors.

Verdict

System prompts and a regex filter will fix most chat replies, and few-shot examples fix the rest over time. QuillBot and Grammarly help human reviewers working in the browser. Overall, UnAIMyText is the best option for humanizing long-form generated content during review for free, because each run takes 500 words with no total cap and its tone settings line up with a voice spec you've already written.

Disclosure: written by the team behind UnAIMyText, one of the tools listed. Competitor details come from vendor pages as of October 2026.

Cover photo by Irvan Smith on Unsplash.

title: One panic shouldn't kill the scan: isolating rules with catch_unwind
description:
Cloud Cost Analyzer runs 92 rules against your cloud account in a single scan. A rule is a real unit of work: it pulls a resource's config and metrics, evaluates them against a cost model, and maybe emits a finding. They're independent, and every one of them leans on libraries I don't control: cloud SDKs, response parsers, date and math crates.

Any of that can meet an input it didn't anticipate and panic: an unwrap() that couldn't fail until some resource shape I'd never seen, an index out of bounds deep in a dependency, an overflow on a field that's normally small. Usually nobody wrote bad code. A library just hit an edge case nobody dependency-audited for.

The question isn't whether a rule will panic. It's what happens to the other 91 when rule

57 does. A cost report that dies two-thirds of the way through because one rule met one weird EBS volume isn't much use to anyone.

"So handle it with Result"

The obvious objection: this is Rust, so model the failure as a Result and there's nothing to catch. The rules do exactly that for every failure they can see coming. Can't reach the metrics API? Result. Missing a field the check needs? Result. Expected failures travel the normal error path and always have.

A panic is the failure I didn't foresee. You can't write ? for a bug you don't know exists, and you certainly can't for one buried three crates deep in a dependency that panics on input its author never tested. Result handles the errors you anticipated. catch_unwind covers the ones you couldn't, and it only exists in my code because Result can't reach into code I didn't write.

std::panic::catch_unwind runs a closure and hands you back a Result instead of letting the panic tear through your stack. Here's the real dispatch, one rule at a time:

let mut eval = std::panic::catch_unwind(std::panic::AssertUnwindSafe(|| {
    rule.evaluate(resource, metrics, costs)
}))
.unwrap_or_else(|_| {
    tracing::error!(
        rule_id = rule_id,
        resource_id = %resource.resource_id,
        "rule panicked during evaluate; skipping its finding"
    );
    None
})?;

A rule panics, we log which rule and which resource, return None for that one finding, and the loop moves on to the next rule. One panic costs one finding.

What AssertUnwindSafe actually promises

The compiler demands that wrapper, and it's worth understanding why before reaching for it.

catch_unwind only accepts a closure that's UnwindSafe. The idea: if a panic unwinds through the middle of your closure, any state it shared with the outside could be left half-updated, and UnwindSafe is the marker that says there's no such state to observe. My closure captures &rule, &resource, and friends by reference, so the compiler can't prove that on its own and refuses to compile.

AssertUnwindSafe is me telling the compiler I've checked, and that catching this panic won't let anyone observe a broken invariant. That holds here for a concrete reason: on panic I throw the result away. I return None and never read a partially-built finding. There's no torn state to see because I don't look. That's the bar for reaching for AssertUnwindSafe. You should be able to point at why the post-panic state is unobservable.

The setting that silently turns all of this off

catch_unwind only works if panics unwind, which is why it isn't a try/catch. Rust has two panic strategies, and you choose per build:

# Cargo.toml — a size-optimized profile
# Inherits all release settings, adds panic=abort to remove unwind tables
panic = "abort"

Under panic = "abort", a panic doesn't unwind the stack. It calls the abort handler and kills the process immediately, so catch_unwind never gets a chance to run. Every one of those careful per-rule guards becomes a no-op, and rule #57 takes the whole process down with it. That happens in the exact build you ship to production, because panic = "abort" is something you turn on to drop unwind tables and shrink the binary.

So panic isolation is a whole-binary decision rather than a library feature you add. If you want one bad rule to cost one finding, you have to keep the unwinding runtime, and eat the binary size, on purpose. No assert or catch_unwind call can buy that back for you. It's the trade you make once, in the profile, and it's invisible in the code that depends on it.

One more edge: poisoned locks

If a rule panics while holding a Mutex or RwLock, that lock is poisoned and the next rule to touch it inherits the panic. The isolation above holds partly because the shared data these rules read is immutable and lock-free, so there's no lock to poison. If yours mutates shared state under a lock, catching the panic isn't enough. You have to decide what a poisoned lock means.

Where it landed

Rules and the second-stage analyzers both run inside that catch_unwind, under an unwinding profile. When a rule, or a library it leans on, meets an input nobody anticipated, the cost is one missing finding and a log line naming the culprit. The isolation works because the binary is built to allow it, and I can say exactly why the post-panic state is safe to ignore: I never read it.

This is part of a series on building Cloud Cost Analyzer in Rust.
