title: useState vs useReducer: Stop Choosing Tools Before Understanding State
description:
Why React state management needs consistent decision criteria, not another library.

When should you use useState instead of useReducer?

The common answer is straightforward:

  • Use useState for simple state.
  • Use useReducer for complex state.

It's not necessarily wrong. But I think it's incomplete.

Because state management complexity isn't just about how many values we store. It's also about who owns the state, how it changes, which rules govern those changes, and how long that state needs to live.

That leads me to a more fundamental question:

Why do we start by choosing a state management tool before defining the criteria that should guide that choice?

1. The Problem with Tool-First Thinking

Imagine we're building a checkout flow in React.

We have a shipping address, payment method, discount code, and several validation rules.

We could use multiple useState hooks. Or we could combine the logic into a useReducer.

But having multiple state variables doesn't automatically justify a reducer.

What matters is how those values relate to each other.

For example, changing the shipping country might invalidate the selected shipping method.

Now we're no longer dealing with independent values. We're dealing with related state transitions governed by business rules.

And that's where the architectural decision becomes interesting.

2. Introducing a State Management Decision Authority

What if we separated the decision-making process from the tools themselves?

I like to think of this as a State Management Decision Authority.

It's not a new React API, an additional library, or an official design pattern.

It's a proposed architectural approach: define a consistent set of criteria that determines which state management strategy fits a particular problem.

Before choosing a tool, evaluate five dimensions.

State ownership

Who needs access to this state?

Is it owned by a single component, a feature, or multiple independent parts of the application?

Update complexity

Does updating the state involve assigning a new value, or applying several related business rules?

State relationships

Are state values independent, or must certain invariants remain true whenever one value changes?

State transitions

Are there explicit transitions between states, such as idle, processing, success, and error?

State lifecycle

Are we managing local UI state, shared client state, or server state that requires fetching, caching, and synchronization?

The answers should determine the tool, rather than the tool shaping how we define the problem.

3. When useState Is the Right Choice

Consider a simple toggle:

const [isOpen, setIsOpen] = useState(false);

The state is local, the update is straightforward, and there are no complex transition rules.

Introducing actions and a reducer here would add complexity without providing much value.

The same applies to many inputs, visibility flags, and independently updated UI values.

Importantly, the number of state variables alone is not a reliable decision criterion.

A component with five independent state variables might be better served by five useState hooks than by one reducer.

The goal isn't to minimize the number of hooks. It's to minimize unnecessary complexity.

4. When useReducer Becomes More Valuable

Now consider a payment workflow.

We have several possible states, and transitions between them must follow particular rules.

const initialState = {
  status: "idle",
  error: null
};

function paymentReducer(state, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case "PAYMENT_STARTED":
      if (state.status !== "idle") {
        return state;
      }

      return {
        status: "processing",
        error: null
      };

    case "PAYMENT_SUCCEEDED":
      if (state.status !== "processing") {
        return state;
      }

      return {
        status: "success",
        error: null
      };

    case "PAYMENT_FAILED":
      if (state.status !== "processing") {
        return state;
      }

      return {
        status: "error",
        error: action.error
      };

    default:
      return state;
  }
}

Inside the component:

const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(
  paymentReducer,
  initialState
);

Instead of allowing different parts of the component to independently decide how the state should change, we dispatch actions describing what happened.

The reducer calculates the next state.

This creates a useful separation:

What happened vs. how the state should respond.

But a reducer doesn't automatically guarantee correctness.

We still need to define valid transitions, protect state invariants, and keep side effects outside the reducer.

In this example, initiating an actual payment request is a side effect, not something the reducer should perform.

5. Decision Authority vs. Transition Authority

There's an important distinction here.

Decision Authority determines which state management approach we should use.

State Transition Authority determines how state changes are evaluated and applied.

A reducer can centralize transition logic within a particular state boundary.

But that doesn't mean every state variable needs a reducer, or that every reducer needs a full state machine.

The architectural objective isn't to centralize everything.

It's to make decisions consistently while preserving the simplest appropriate implementation.

6. Beyond React Hooks: Zustand, Redux Toolkit, and Server State

The same decision criteria can extend beyond useState and useReducer.

When multiple components need the same state, we can first consider lifting state up or using Context.

When multiple features need shared client state, tools such as Zustand or Redux Toolkit may become appropriate.

If the primary challenge involves remote data fetching, caching, invalidation, and synchronization, a dedicated server-state solution such as TanStack Query or RTK Query can be more suitable.

These tools aren't necessarily mutually exclusive.

An application might use:

  • useState for local UI interactions.
  • useReducer for a complex form workflow.
  • Zustand or Redux Toolkit for shared client state.
  • TanStack Query or RTK Query for server-state management.

The decision depends on the responsibility of each state boundary.

7. A Practical Decision Framework

Here's a lightweight framework I would use before making a state management decision.

Question Possible direction
Is the state local with simple, independent updates? Start with useState
Are transitions governed by related rules? Consider useReducer
Is state shared within a component subtree? Consider lifting state or Context
Do independent features require shared client state? Evaluate Zustand or Redux Toolkit
Does the state primarily represent remote server data? Evaluate TanStack Query or RTK Query

This isn't a rigid rules engine.

A shared state doesn't automatically require a global store, and a complex state doesn't automatically require useReducer.

It's a framework for asking better questions before committing to an implementation.

8. The Bigger Architectural Principle

State management discussions often become comparisons between libraries.

Which is faster?

Which has less boilerplate?

Which is easier to learn?

Those questions matter, but they're secondary to understanding the problem.

I believe we should first establish consistent criteria for choosing a state management strategy.

Then evaluate available tools against those criteria.

Unify the decision criteria, not necessarily the tools.

That's the architectural principle I'm exploring here.

The real skill isn't knowing every state management library.

It's understanding why, when, and where each one belongs.

Final Thoughts

useState and useReducer aren't competing solutions where one must win.

They're different approaches to managing state, each valuable in the right context.

And the same reasoning applies when we move toward Context, Zustand, Redux Toolkit, or server-state solutions.

Let the problem define the tool, not the tool define the solution.

I'd love to hear how other developers approach these decisions.

Do you follow explicit state management criteria in your projects, or do team preferences and existing architecture usually drive the choice?

Part 1 of the State Management Decision Authority series.

title: Flexbox or Grid? A simple rule for choosing
description:
"Should I use Flexbox or Grid?" is one of the most common CSS questions. Here is the rule I use.

Flexbox is for one direction. Grid is for two.

Use Flexbox for a row or column of items

Navigation bars, button groups, centering one thing:

.nav {
  display: flex;
  gap: 1rem;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: space-between;
}

The items decide how much space they take, and the container lines them up.

Use Grid for rows and columns together

Card layouts, page layouts, galleries:

.cards {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr));
  gap: 1.5rem;
}

This one rule gives you a responsive layout with no media queries. The number of columns changes as the screen gets narrower.

Combine them

A common pattern is Grid for the page and Flexbox inside each piece:

.card {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  justify-content: space-between;
}

That keeps the buttons at the bottom of every card, even when the text lengths differ.

Quick check

  • Laying things out along one line? Flexbox.
  • Need to control rows and columns? Grid.
  • Not sure? Start with Grid, and use Flexbox for the small parts.

Which one do you reach for first? Tell me in the comments.

title: 5 quick checks to make a website load faster
description:
A slow website loses visitors before they read a single word. Here are five checks I run on almost every site, in the order I do them. None need special tools.

1. Measure before you change anything

Open Chrome DevTools, go to the Lighthouse tab and run a mobile report. Note the scores for Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) and Total Blocking Time. Without a starting number you can't tell whether a change helped.

2. Compress and resize images

Images are usually the heaviest part of a page.

  • Convert photos to WebP or AVIF.
  • Resize them to the size they are actually shown at. A 4000px photo in a 600px box wastes bandwidth.
  • Add loading="lazy" to images below the fold: 
<img src="team.webp" width="600" height="400" alt="Our team" loading="lazy">

Setting width and height also stops the page from jumping around as it loads.

3. Cut unused CSS and JavaScript

Open DevTools → Coverage and reload. It shows how much of each file is never used on that page. Remove unused libraries and load scripts that aren't needed immediately with defer:

<script src="app.js" defer></script>

4. Turn on caching and compression

  • Enable gzip or Brotli on the server.
  • Send Cache-Control headers so returning visitors don't re-download files that haven't changed.

5. Check your fonts

Every font weight is a separate file. Use only the weights you need, and add font-display: swap so text shows straight away instead of staying blank:

@font-face {
  font-family: "Inter";
  src: url("inter.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-display: swap;
}

Recheck

Run Lighthouse again and compare it with your first result. Most sites improve a lot from just the image and script steps.

What is the biggest speed problem you've run into? Let me know in the comments.

title: Run a ByteChef workflow like a CLI command (no server, no database)
description:
Most automation platforms are built to stay up. ByteChef is no exception: the server stores your projects, fires triggers, listens for webhooks, and records every execution in PostgreSQL.

That's great until you look at where a lot of real work runs:

  • a nightly batch sitting in a Kubernetes CronJob next to twenty others, with alerting on failed pods
  • a CI step that should go red when something breaks
  • one task inside an Airflow DAG
  • a product with its own job runner that just wants to execute a workflow

In each of those, a standing server plus a database plus a message broker is overhead. You need the engine for the length of one run, and then you want it gone.

That's what the Runtime Job app does. You pass it a workflow name, inputs as JSON, and credentials as JSON. It boots the full Atlas engine in one JVM, runs the workflow to completion, and exits 0 or 1. Nothing to provision, nothing to clean up.

The Runtime Job app is part of ByteChef's Enterprise Edition. Source: server/ee/apps/runtime-job-app.

Same engine, different packaging

This isn't a lightweight interpreter. The coordinator, workers and task dispatchers are all there. What changes is everything around them:

ByteChef server Runtime Job app
Execution state PostgreSQL In memory, gone on exit
Message broker Redis, Kafka, SQS, RabbitMQ, JMS… In-process
Connections Encrypted store in the DB JSON passed at launch
Triggers Scheduler, polling, webhooks None. The run starts with the process
UI / API Yes No
Record of a run Execution history Exit code + log

The workflow JSON is identical in both, so the loop is: build and test in ByteChef, export, hand the file to the Runtime Job app.

A real example

A daily sales report: take a date, total the paid orders for that day from PostgreSQL, log a summary.

{
  "label": "Daily Sales Report",
  "inputs": [
    { "name": "reportDate", "label": "Report date", "type": "string", "required": true }
  ],
  "triggers": [
    { "label": "Manual", "name": "trigger_1", "type": "manual/v1/manual" }
  ],
  "tasks": [
    {
      "label": "Sum paid orders",
      "name": "postgresql_1",
      "type": "postgresql/v1/query",
      "parameters": {
        "query": "SELECT count(*) AS orders, coalesce(sum(total), 0) AS revenue FROM orders WHERE status = 'PAID' AND created_at = CAST(:reportDate AS date)",
        "parameters": { "reportDate": "${reportDate}" }
      }
    },
    {
      "label": "Log summary",
      "name": "logger_1",
      "type": "logger/v1/info",
      "parameters": {
        "text": "Sales for ${reportDate}: ${postgresql_1[0].orders} paid orders, revenue ${postgresql_1[0].revenue}"
      }
    }
  ]
}

Save it as ~/bytechef/data/workflows/daily-sales.json (the default lookup location). Note the task name postgresql_1 and component name postgresql; both matter for connections later.

Build and run:

./gradlew :server:ee:apps:runtime-job-app:bootJar

CONNECTIONS='{"postgresql": {"host": "localhost", "port": 5432, "database": "shop", "username": "etl", "password": "..."}}'

java -jar runtime-job-app.jar \
  --workflow=daily-sales.json \
  --parameters='{"reportDate": "2026-10-14"}' \
  --connections="$CONNECTIONS"

echo $?   # 0

On a laptop the whole thing took about 10 seconds, roughly one of which was the workflow itself. That's the trade: a few seconds of boot for zero standing infrastructure. Fine for a nightly batch; for a thousand calls a minute, use the server.

The flags

Flag Required What it does
--workflow=<file> yes File name, e.g. daily-sales.json. A lookup key, not a path.
--parameters=<json> no Workflow inputs as a JSON object.
--connections=<json> no Connection name → parameters. Repeatable; objects are merged.
--timeout=<duration> no 30s, 15m, 1h. Exit 1 if exceeded.
--outputs-file=<path> no Write the workflow's outputs as JSON on success.

Any Spring Boot property works too, e.g. --logging.level.com.bytechef=DEBUG.

Gotcha: --workflow is not a path

The app drops the directory, strips the extension, and Base64-encodes the rest into an id (daily-sales → ZGFpbHktc2FsZXM=). At startup it indexes every file in the enabled workflow repositories the same way, then looks the id up. So these are identical:

--workflow=daily-sales.json
--workflow=/anything/at/all/daily-sales.json

…and pointing at a file outside the repositories won't work. Repositories available: filesystem (default, ~/bytechef/data/workflows), classpath (workflows/ inside the JAR), and Git (off by default).

# read workflows from somewhere else
BYTECHEF_WORKFLOW_REPOSITORY_FILESYSTEM_LOCATION_PATTERN='/opt/workflows/*.json'

# or straight from Git, so a merge to main is a deploy
BYTECHEF_WORKFLOW_REPOSITORY_GIT_ENABLED=true
BYTECHEF_WORKFLOW_REPOSITORY_GIT_URL=https://github.com/acme/workflows.git
BYTECHEF_WORKFLOW_REPOSITORY_GIT_BRANCH=main

Tip: export workflows from the editor rather than hand-writing them. Component defaults are written into the JSON when you add a node, not at runtime, so a hand-written file can fail mid-run with Unknown value for : <property>.

Connections

No credential store means credentials arrive as JSON. Keys are connection names; values use the same property names as the component's connection form in the UI.

Before each task runs, its connection is resolved like this:

  1. By task name (postgresql_1) — applies to that task only.
  2. By component name (postgresql) — shared by every task of that component.
  3. No match — the task runs without one (fine for logger, fatal for a database).

Task-name keys let two tasks of the same component use different credentials, say a read replica and a primary. And you can split credentials across secrets by repeating the flag:

java -jar runtime-job-app.jar \
  --workflow=daily-sales.json \
  --connections="$OPENAI_CONNECTION" \
  --connections="$POSTGRES_CONNECTION"

Two caveats worth knowing up front:

  • Connection JSON is logged at INFO on startup. Treat the log as credential-bearing: restrict access and set retention.
  • Not every connector works this way yet. Database components (PostgreSQL, MySQL) and LLM providers that take an API key work. SaaS connectors whose auth is applied as an HTTP header by the platform (bearer, API key, OAuth2) don't get that header from --connections. Test before relying on them.

Exit codes are the API

Code Meaning
0 Job COMPLETED
1 Job FAILED or STOPPED, or --timeout hit
other non-zero Couldn't start: missing flag, bad JSON, unknown workflow
143 Killed by SIGTERM (eviction, drain, docker stop)

That's all a scheduler needs. A Kubernetes Job retries per backoffLimit, Airflow marks the task failed, CI goes red. Nobody parses logs.

Always set --timeout. Without it the app waits forever, and a stuck process is never retried because it never fails. This matters doubly for JavaScript/Python script tasks, which have no CPU or heap cap of their own.

Make writes idempotent. A 143 leaves no trace in the log, and a retry starts from scratch. Prefer upserts or check for an existing result.

Getting results out

Declare outputs in the workflow as usual:

"outputs": [
  { "name": "orders",  "value": "${postgresql_1[0].orders}" },
  { "name": "revenue", "value": "${postgresql_1[0].revenue}" }
]

They're logged as one JSON line on completion. For programs, use --outputs-file:

java -jar runtime-job-app.jar ... --outputs-file=/tmp/daily-sales.json
jq .revenue /tmp/daily-sales.json   # 1540.50

The file is only written for a completed job, so check the exit code first. Keep outputs small (counts, ids, a status); write anything big to where it's used and return a pointer.

Docker 

docker build -t registry.example.com/bytechef-runtime-job:2026-10-16 server/ee/apps/runtime-job-app/

docker run --rm \
  -v "$(pwd)/workflows:/workflows" \
  -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod \
  -e BYTECHEF_WORKFLOW_REPOSITORY_FILESYSTEM_LOCATION_PATTERN='/workflows/*.json' \
  registry.example.com/bytechef-runtime-job:2026-10-16 \
  --workflow=daily-sales.json \
  --parameters='{"reportDate": "2026-10-14"}' \
  --connections="$CONNECTIONS"

The image is about 2 GB (GraalVM base + a ~770 MB JAR with ~100 components and the polyglot runtime). Use immutable tags with imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent so each node pulls it once. Use the prod profile; local builds default to dev, which logs at DEBUG.

Kubernetes CronJob

This is where it fits best: a pod starts, runs one workflow, exits, and the exit code decides whether Kubernetes retries.

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: daily-sales
spec:
  schedule: "15 6 * * *"
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      backoffLimit: 2
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: Never
          containers:
            - name: runtime-job
              image: registry.example.com/bytechef-runtime-job:2026-10-16
              imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
              command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
              args:
                - >-
                  exec java -jar /opt/bytechef/runtime-job/runtime-job-app.jar
                  --workflow=daily-sales.json
                  --parameters="{\"reportDate\": \"$(date -d yesterday +%F)\"}"
                  --connections="$POSTGRES_CONNECTION"
                  --timeout=20m
              env:
                - name: SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE
                  value: prod
                - name: BYTECHEF_WORKFLOW_REPOSITORY_FILESYSTEM_LOCATION_PATTERN
                  value: /workflows/*.json
                - name: POSTGRES_CONNECTION
                  valueFrom:
                    secretKeyRef:
                      name: daily-sales-connections
                      key: postgresql.json
              resources:
                requests: { cpu: 500m, memory: 768Mi }
                limits:   { memory: 1Gi }
              volumeMounts:
                - name: workflows
                  mountPath: /workflows
          volumes:
            - name: workflows
              configMap:
                name: daily-sales-workflow

Why it looks like this:

  • restartPolicy: Never + backoffLimit — exit 1 fails the pod; each retry is a clean process.
  • --timeout — backoffLimit only retries failed pods, not stuck ones. (activeDeadlineSeconds works too, but it kills the pod with a silent 143.)
  • Memory — a small workflow used ~370 MiB. Measure a real run and size from that; OOMKilled exits 137.
  • sh -c + exec — computes yesterday's date, and exec keeps the JVM's exit code as the pod's.
  • Secret + ConfigMap — credentials stay out of the manifest; updating the workflow is a kubectl apply, not an image rebuild.

CI

Exit codes make it a normal CI step. GitHub Actions, generating release notes on every tag:

name: Release notes
on:
  push:
    tags: ['v*']

jobs:
  notes:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    container:
      image: registry.example.com/bytechef-runtime-job:2026-10-16
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Generate and publish release notes
        env:
          SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: prod
          BYTECHEF_WORKFLOW_REPOSITORY_FILESYSTEM_LOCATION_PATTERN: ${{ github.workspace }}/.bytechef/*.json
          OPENAI_CONNECTION: ${{ secrets.BYTECHEF_OPENAI_CONNECTION }}
        run: |
          java -jar /opt/bytechef/runtime-job/runtime-job-app.jar \
            --workflow=release-notes.json \
            --parameters="{\"tag\": \"${GITHUB_REF_NAME}\"}" \
            --connections="$OPENAI_CONNECTION" \
            --timeout=10m

The workflow lives in .bytechef/ in the repo it automates and gets code-reviewed like everything else. Same idea works in GitLab CI, Jenkins, or Airflow's KubernetesPodOperator.

What's in, what's out

In: ~100 components — HTTP client, script and Bash, helpers, CSV/JSON/XML/XLSX, PostgreSQL and MySQL, the major LLM providers, Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 basics, Slack, GitHub, Jira, HubSpot, Shopify — plus control flow (branch, condition, each, loop, map, parallel, fork-join, subflow, approval). Check the app's build.gradle.kts before depending on a specific one.

Out, on purpose: triggers, the UI and REST API, execution history (ship your logs somewhere), and scaling within a run (launch more processes instead).

Quick troubleshooting

Symptom Fix
Workflow with id: <base64> does not exist File isn't in a configured repository (or the volume isn't mounted). The directory in --workflow is ignored.
Unknown value for : <property> Re-export the workflow from the editor.
Auth error on a task Connection key doesn't match task/component name, or property names are wrong.
Process never exits Add --timeout.
Exit 143, nothing in log SIGTERM from outside. Check pod events.
Exit 137 / OOMKilled Raise the memory limit (and -Xmx).
No outputs file The job didn't complete. Check the exit code.

Server or Runtime Job?

Use the server when you need triggers, webhooks, a UI, run history, RBAC, a central credential store, or always-on/high-frequency processing.

Use the Runtime Job app for nightly batches, CI steps, and anything whose schedule already lives in Kubernetes, Airflow or GitHub Actions.

They're not competitors. A common setup: people build and test on a ByteChef server, and CronJobs run the exported, reviewed versions in production. Same JSON, unchanged.

Full reference: Runtime Job Runner docs. Originally published on the ByteChef blog.

title: We're fed up with Rust's borrow checker. It's time to break free.
description:
I like Rust. I also dread the moment the borrow checker says no and the compiler refuses to
explain what it assumed.

That is not a complaint about competence. Rust's borrow checker is one of the most valuable
things to happen to systems programming. It is a complaint about posture: the compiler stands
outside your program, announces a verdict, and the burden of proof lands on you. When the verdict
is wrong, there is often no receipt to inspect.

We built Loment around a different posture. It keeps the
checks; it moves the burden. This post is about what that means precisely, because "we removed the
borrow checker" would be a lie, and the interesting part is not the removal.

What Loment keeps

Loment is a systems language with a Rust-flavoured surface. It still checks the ownership
mistakes that matter most:

  • use after move (E006),
  • a mutable borrow alongside another borrow (E007),
  • a dangling reference (E012).

It also adds capability domains (capability disk[0..4] plus guard), compiles to a native
ELF/PE artifact with no runtime by default, and has two implementations — a Python reference and
a self-hosted one — that must emit byte-identical IR.

What it does not do is pretend to be Rust's borrow checker. The boundary is written down in
the repository: it proves three things and explicitly does not prove four others (no lifetimes, no
cross-function reasoning, no field-level moves, no branch-sensitive move sets). Keep that in mind
for the rest of this post.

From verdict to receipt

The change is a seventh choose dimension called LSPE — Loment Safety Police Espace. It does
not change any verdict. It changes what a verdict leaves behind.

With lspe_open_admin (the default), every allowance is recorded in the artifact's Potato v16
ledger: the site, the obligation, the evidence, and what is still unproved. With
lspe_close_admin, the recording is turned off; the LMS, runtime and capability decisions are
unchanged. The audit is not a second checker bolted on top — it is a ledger of the compiler's own
decisions, answerable offline.

The design document puts it more bluntly than I can:

Rust's borrow checker is a god. LSPE is a shop assistant.

A god stands outside the transaction and says "no". An assistant stands inside it, has to name the
price, and gives you a receipt. Concretely, LSPE has three outcomes instead of two:

  • PROVED — here is the evidence;
  • UNDECIDED — here is the site where my proof has a hole;
  • REFUTED — here is a counterexample, so this is a hard no.

"Undecided" is a first-class result. In strict mode it becomes E034; the ledger's own consistency
failures are E035–E037. The point is not that the compiler is always right. The point is that when
it is wrong, you can point at the site and the obligation instead of arguing with a verdict.

"Gentle" is a measurable claim

It is easy to say a checker is friendlier. We tried to make it falsifiable:

  1. Same verdicts. Compile the same corpus with the audit open and closed: the set of decisions is identical. The audit changes the ledger, not the language.
  2. No silent permit. Every allow has a source, or an explicitly recorded assumption. An allow with neither is an error in the ledger.
  3. No overclaiming. LSPE does not claim to prove more than Rust. What it adds is accountability, not completeness. The remaining cases are UNDECIDED and labeled.

That is the sense in which it is "gentler with nearly the same safety": not that it catches
everything Rust catches, but that the same checks no longer arrive as an unaccountable verdict.

Loment also has a memory-safety ladder, lms, with seven levels and four tiers
(lms_full, lms_forensic_admin, lms_daily_admin, lms_manage_only_admin). The default is
full; writing a lower tier is a downgrade and carries _admin. The literal-out-of-range check is
E028; use-after-free is E029.

What it looks like

The defaults, written out:

module demo
choose runtime
choose lms_full
choose lspe_open_admin

capability disk_slots : disk[0..4] revocable

fn write_slot(slot: u32) -> u32 {
    guard disk_slots(slot);
    return slot;
}

fn _start() {
    let xs: [u32; 3] = [1, 2, 3];
    let i: u32 = 5;
    if i < 3 {
        xs[i] = 7;          // a runtime index: you guard it, the language does not guess
    }
    syscall4(60, 0, 0, 0);
}

Two details matter here. guard bounds the index, not the subject — it is not authorization.
And the array write is still your responsibility: Loment refuses a literal out-of-range index
at compile time (E028), but a runtime index is not silently checked.

What this does not mean

I would rather say this before the comments do:

  • Loment is early. 0.1.5 is the release where LSPE lands; the packaged front end is still being finished. Do not rewrite your service in it this weekend.
  • It is not Rust. The borrow checking is a subset. No lifetimes, no cross-function reasoning, no field-level moves, no branch-sensitive move sets.
  • "No receipt" is not the same as "no bug". LSPE records the compiler's decisions; it does not make the compiler omniscient.
  • Defaults are not free. lms_full is the default and it changes the emitted artifact (inline bounds checks on alloc(<const>)-derived accesses). That exception is documented, not hidden.
  • The benchmark is a pilot. We measured an LLM agent writing Loment from the guide alone: three tasks, one attempt each, Rust and Python as controls. It is a direction, not a confidence interval.

The reason I care about the receipt is not abstract. Rust's own tracker has a soundness bug
(#164250) where an obligation was not rechecked after substitution, and it stayed invisible for
years — not because Rust's team is careless, but because a verdict-only compiler leaves nothing
to audit when the verdict is wrong. LSPE's answer to that shape is a record with a site id
(Q004 stale_wf), readable offline. That is the part I want other language designers to steal,
whether or not they like Loment.

Try it, then tell us where the receipt is wrong

  • Source: https://github.com/Loment-Lang/Loment

We are not asking you to believe the slogan. We are asking you to compile something, read the
ledger, and tell us which line is wrong. That is the whole point of moving the burden.

Disclosure: I'm one of Loment's authors. This draft was prepared with an AI assistant and
reviewed before publishing.

title: Build-as-Code, CI Integration, and Build Doctor
description:
• Why treat builds as code: eliminate drift and make builds a pure function
  • CI integration patterns for hermetic builds and remote cache clients
  • Designing and implementing a Build Doctor diagnostics tool
  • Rolling out at scale: onboarding, guardrails, and measuring impact
  • Practical checklists and runbooks for immediate action

Treat every build flag, toolchain pin, and cache policy as versioned code — not a local habit. Doing so converts the build from a mutable ritual into a repeatable, auditable function whose outputs are pure and sharable.

The pain is specific: slow pull requests because CI redoes work, “works on my machine” debugging, cache-poisoning incidents that invalidate hours of developer effort, and onboarding that takes days because local setups differ. Those symptoms trace back to one root cause: build affordances (flags, toolchains, cache policy, and CI integration) live as handwaves instead of code, so behavior diverges between machines and pipelines.

Why treat builds as code: eliminate drift and make builds a pure function

Treating the build as code — build-as-code — means storing every decision that influences outputs in version control: WORKSPACE pins, BUILD rules, toolchain stanzas, .bazelrc snippets, CI bazel flags, and the remote-cache client configuration. That discipline enforces hermeticity: the build result is independent of the host machine and therefore reproducible across developer laptops and CI servers.

What you get when you do this correctly:

  • Bit-identical artifacts for the same inputs, eliminating “it works on my machine” debugging.
  • A cacheable DAG: actions become pure functions of declared inputs, so results can be reused across machines.
  • Safe experimentation via branches: differing toolchain or flag sets are explicit commits, not env leaks.

Practical rails that make this discipline enforceable:

  • Keep a repo-level .bazelrc that defines the canonical flags used in CI and for canonical local runs (build --remote_cache=..., build --host_force_python=...).
  • Pin toolchains and third-party deps in WORKSPACE with exact commits or SHA256 checksums.
  • Treat ci and local modes as two configurations in the build-as-code model; only one (CI) should be allowed to write authoritative cache entries in the early rollout phase.

Important: Hermeticity is an engineering property you can test for; make those tests part of CI so the repository encodes the build’s contract rather than relying on implicit conventions.

CI integration patterns for hermetic builds and remote cache clients

The CI layer is the single most potent lever for accelerating team builds and protecting the cache. There are three practical patterns you will choose from depending on scale and trust.

  • CI-as-single-writer, developers-read-only: CI builds (full, canonical builds) write to the remote cache; developer machines read only. This prevents accidental cache poisoning and keeps the authoritative cache consistent.
  • Combined local + remote cache: Developers use a local disk cache plus a shared remote cache. The local cache improves cold-starts and avoids unnecessary network trips; the remote cache enables cross-machine reuse.
  • Remote execution (RBE) for speed at scale: CI and some dev flows offload heavy actions to RBE workers and take advantage of both remote execution and the shared CAS.

Bazel exposes standard knobs for these patterns; the remote cache stores action metadata and the content-addressable store of outputs, and a build consults the cache before running actions.

Example .bazelrc snippets (repo-level vs CI):

# .bazelrc (repo - canonical flags)
build --remote_cache=grpcs://cache.corp.example:9090
build --remote_download_outputs=minimal
build --host_jvm_args=-Xmx2g
build --show_progress_rate_limit=30

# .bazelrc.ci (CI-only overrides; kept on CI runner)
build --remote_cache=grpcs://cache.corp.example:9090
build --remote_executor=grpcs://rbe.corp.example:8989
build --remote_timeout=180s
build --bes_backend=grpcs://bep.corp.example   # send BEP to analysis UI

CI example (GitHub Actions, illustrating integration with existing cache steps): use the platform cache for language deps and let Bazel use the remote cache for build outputs. The actions/cache action is a common helper for pre-built dependency caches.

name: ci
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Restore tool caches
        uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: ~/.cache/bazel
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-bazel-${{ hashFiles('**/WORKSPACE') }}
      - name: Bazel build (CI canonical)
        run: bazel build --bazelrc=.bazelrc.ci //...

Contrast of caching approaches

Mode What it shares Latency impact Infra complexity
Local disk cache per-host artifacts small improvement, not shared low
Shared remote cache (HTTP/gRPC) CAS + action metadata network-limited, large benefit across team medium
Remote execution (RE) executes actions remotely minimizes dev wall-clock time high (workers, auth, scheduling)

Remote execution and remote caching are complementary; RBE focuses on compute scaling while the cache focuses on reuse. The protocol landscape and client/server implementations (e.g., the Bazel Remote Execution APIs) are standardized and supported by several OSS and commercial offerings.

Practical CI guardrails to enforce:

  • Make CI the canonical writer during pilot: developer configs set --remote_upload_local_results=false while CI sets it true.
  • Lock who can clear the cache and implement a cache-poison rollback plan.
  • Send BEP (Build Event Protocol) from CI builds to a centralized invocations UI for later troubleshooting and historical metrics. Tools like BuildBuddy ingest BEP and provide cache-hit breakdowns.

Designing and implementing a Build Doctor diagnostics tool

What a Build Doctor does

  • Acts like a deterministic, fast diagnostics agent that runs locally and in CI to surface misconfigurations and non-hermetic actions.
  • Collects structured evidence (Bazel info, BEP, aquery/cquery, profile traces) and returns actionable findings (missing --remote_cache, genrule calling curl, actions with nondeterministic outputs).
  • Produces machine-readable results (JSON), human-friendly reports, and CI annotations for PRs.

Data sources and commands to use

  • bazel info for environment and output base.
  • bazel aquery --output=jsonproto 'deps(//my:target)' to retrieve action commandlines and inputs programmatically. This output can be scanned for rogue network calls, writes outside the declared outputs, and suspicious commandline flags.
  • bazel build --profile=command.profile.gz //... followed by bazel analyze-profile command.profile.gz to get the critical path and per-action durations; the JSON trace profile can be loaded into tracing UIs for deeper analysis.
  • Build Event Protocol (BEP) / --bes_results_url to stream invocation metadata to a server for long-term analytics. BuildBuddy and similar platforms provide BEP ingestion and a UI for cache-hit debugging.

Minimal Build Doctor architecture (three components)

  1. Collector — shell or agent that runs the Bazel commands and writes structured files:
    • bazel info --show_make_env -> doctor/info.json
    • bazel aquery --output=jsonproto ... -> doctor/aquery.json
    • bazel build --profile=doctor.prof //... -> doctor/command.profile.gz
    • optional: fetch BEP or remote cache server logs
  2. Analyzer — Python/Go service that:
    • Parses aquery for suspicious mnemonics or commands (Genrule, ctx.execute) that contain network tools.
    • Runs bazel analyze-profile doctor.prof and correlates long actions with aquery outputs.
    • Verifies .bazelrc flags and remote cache client presence.
  3. Reporter — emits:
    • a concise human report
    • structured JSON for CI pass/fail gating
    • annotations for PRs (failed hermetic checks, top 5 critical-path actions)

Example: a tiny Build Doctor check in Python (skeleton)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import json, subprocess, sys, gzip

def run(cmd):
    print("+", " ".join(cmd))
    return subprocess.check_output(cmd).decode()

def check_remote_cache():
    info = run(["bazel", "info", "--show_make_env"])
    if "remote_cache" not in info:
        return {"ok": False, "msg": "No remote_cache configured in bazel info"}
    return {"ok": True}

def parse_aquery_json(path):
    with open(path,'rb') as f:
        return json.load(f)

def main():
    run(["bazel","aquery","--output=jsonproto","deps(//...)", "--include_commandline=false", "--noshow_progress"])
    # analyzer steps would follow...
    print(json.dumps({"checks":[check_remote_cache()]}))

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Diagnostic heuristics you should encode (examples)

  • Actions whose command lines contain curl, wget, scp, or ssh indicate network access and likely non-hermetic behavior.
  • Actions that write to $(WORKSPACE) or outside declared outputs indicate source-tree mutation.
  • Targets tagged no-cache or no-remote deserve review; frequent no-cache usage is a smell.
  • bazel build outputs that differ across repeated clean runs reveal nondeterminism (timestamps, randomness in build steps).

A Build Doctor should avoid hard fails on first rollout. Start with informational severities and escalate rules to warnings and hard-gate checks as confidence grows.

Rolling out at scale: onboarding, guardrails, and measuring impact

Rollout phases

  1. Pilot (2–4 teams): CI writes to cache, developers use read-only cache settings. Run Build Doctor in CI and as a local dev hook.
  2. Expand (6–8 weeks): Add more teams, tune heuristics, add tests that detect cache-poisoning patterns.
  3. Org-wide: Make CANONICAL .bazelrc and toolchain pins required, add PR checks, and open the cache for a broader set of write clients.

Key metrics to instrument and track

  • P95 build/test times for common developer flows (changes to a single package, full test runs).
  • Remote cache hit rate: percent of actions served from the remote cache vs executed. Track daily and by repository. Aim high; a >90% hit rate on incremental builds is a realistic, high-leverage target for mature setups.
  • Time to first successful build (new hire): measure from checkout to successful test run.
  • Number of hermeticity regressions: count CI-detected non-hermetic checks per week.

How to collect these metrics

  • Use CI BEP exports to compute cache-hit ratios. Bazel prints per-invocation process summaries that indicate remote cache hits; programmatic BEP ingestion gives more reliable metrics.
  • Push derived metrics to a telemetry system (Prometheus / Datadog) and create dashboards:
    • Histogram of build times (for P50/P95)
    • Time-series of remote cache hit rate
    • Weekly count of Build Doctor violations per team

Guardrails and change control

  • Use a cache-write role: only designated CI runners (and a small set of trusted service accounts) can write to the authoritative cache.
  • Add a cache clear and rollback playbook to respond to cache poisoning: snapshot the cache state and restore from a pre-poisoned snapshot if necessary.
  • Gate merges with Build Doctor findings: start with warnings and move to hard failure for core rules once false positives are low.

Developer onboarding

  • Ship a developer start.sh that sets up the repo-level .bazelrc and installs bazelisk to pin bazel versions.
  • Provide one-page runbook: git clone ... && ./start.sh && bazel build //:all --profile=./first.profile.gz so new hires produce a baseline profile that CI can compare to.
  • Add a lightweight VSCode/IDE recipe that reuses the same repo-level flags so the dev environment mirrors CI.

Practical checklists and runbooks for immediate action

Baseline measurement (week 0)

  1. Run a canonical CI build for the main branch for seven consecutive runs and collect:
    • bazel build --profile=ci.prof //...
    • BEP exports (--bes_results_url or --build_event_json_file)
  2. Compute baseline P95 build times and cache-hit rate from BEP/CI logs.

Setup remote cache and clients (week 1)

  1. Deploy a cache (e.g., bazel-remote, Buildbarn, or managed service).
  2. Put canonical flags into repo .bazelrc and a CI-only .bazelrc.ci.
  3. Configure CI to be the primary writer; developers set --remote_upload_local_results=false in their per-user bazelrc.

Ship the Build Doctor (week 2)

  1. Add collector hooks to CI to capture aquery, profile, and BEP.
  2. Run Analyzer on CI invocations; surface findings as PR comments and nightly reports.
  3. Begin triage for top findings (e.g., genrules with network calls, nonhermetic toolchains).

Pilot & expand (weeks 3–8)

  1. Pilot with three squads and run Build Doctor in PRs as info-only.
  2. Iterate on heuristics and reduce false positives.
  3. Convert high-confidence checks into gating rules.

Runbook snippet: respond to a cache-poison incident

  • Step 1: Identify corrupted outputs via BEP and Build Doctor reports.
  • Step 2: Quarantine suspect cache prefixes and flip CI to write to a fresh cache namespace.
  • Step 3: Roll back to last-known-good cache snapshot and re-run canonical CI builds to repopulate.

Quick rule: make CI the source of truth for cache writes during rollout and keep destructive cache administration actions auditable.

Sources

Hermeticity | Bazel - Definition of hermetic builds, benefits, and guidance on identifying non-hermetic behavior.

Remote Caching - Bazel Documentation - How Bazel stores action metadata and CAS blobs, flags like --remote_cache and --remote_download_outputs, and disk-cache options.

bazelbuild/remote-apis (GitHub) - The Remote Execution API specification and list of clients/servers implementing the protocol.

JSON Trace Profile | Bazel - --profile, bazel analyze-profile, and how to generate and inspect JSON trace profiles for critical-path analysis.

buildbuddy-io/buildbuddy (GitHub) - An example BEP and remote-cache ingestion solution that demonstrates how build event data and cache metrics can be surfaced to teams.

actions/cache (GitHub) - GitHub Actions cache action documentation and guidance for dependency caching in CI workflows.

The Bazel Query Reference / aquery - aquery/cquery usage and --output=jsonproto for machine-readable action graph inspection.

Treat the build as code, make CI the canonical actor for cache writes, and ship a Build Doctor that codifies the heuristics you already reach for in the hallway — those operational moves convert day-to-day build firefighting into measurable, automatable engineering work.

title: Crypto Market Data Is Useful Only When You Understand Its Context
description:
Crypto dashboards can show a lot of information in a small space: prices, daily changes, trading pairs, and lists of popular assets.

At first glance, more data seems like a good thing.

But I think the real challenge is helping people understand what the numbers mean without encouraging them to draw conclusions too quickly.

That's a useful way to think about market interfaces, including the one presented by AviorSwap.

A percentage change doesn't tell the whole story

Imagine seeing a token with a positive daily percentage change.

It's tempting to interpret that as a sign of strength. But the number alone doesn't explain the full market situation.

How liquid is the asset? How much trading activity supports the price? Is the movement part of a larger trend or a short-term fluctuation?

A daily percentage change provides a snapshot, not a complete analysis.

The same applies to assets showing negative performance. A single time window doesn't establish what will happen next.

Context makes a dashboard more useful

AviorSwap's public website presents market information alongside its exchange-related features.

I think this combination raises an interesting product-design question: how can a platform help visitors move from exploring market data to understanding a potential transaction?

A useful dashboard should make it easy to identify the asset, understand the time period behind a statistic, and distinguish market information from an executable quote.

That last distinction matters.

A displayed market price may not equal the price a user receives when swapping a particular amount. Liquidity, route selection, fees, and changing market conditions can all affect the result.

Less noise, more meaning

When designing a market dashboard, I'd prioritize three things.

Clear labels. Every percentage should have an understandable time period and reference point.

Relevant details. Users should be able to find liquidity, volume, and other useful context where those metrics are available.

Honest limitations. Market data can be delayed, incomplete, or different across sources. The interface should communicate relevant limitations instead of presenting every figure as universally definitive.

These details can make a dashboard more helpful without filling every available space with numbers.

Information should support decisions, not replace them

I don't think a market interface needs to tell users what to buy.

Its job is to present information in a way that supports independent judgment.

For example, a clear view of market movements can help someone decide what they want to research next. It shouldn't imply that an asset is a good investment simply because its price has risen recently.

That distinction is important in a market where prices can change quickly and losses are possible.

Final thoughts

Market data becomes more valuable when people understand its limitations.

Exploring the relationship between AviorSwap's market presentation and its exchange functionality highlights a broader principle for financial products: showing information is only the first step. Helping users interpret it responsibly is the harder part.

When you open a crypto dashboard, which information helps you most: price changes, trading volume, liquidity, or historical charts?

title: Dark Mode Design Best Practices: What Google, Apple, and the Research Say
description:
Dark mode is a table-stakes feature now, and most teams still build it the laziest way possible: take the light theme, flip the colors, ship it. The result is an app that looks like a photographic negative — gray text on black soup, brand colors that scream, cards you can barely tell apart from the background. Google and Apple both wrote detailed specs explaining why that approach is wrong. And the battery story that justifies half of it? For most users it's 3–9%, not the headline numbers.

The battery myth: 47% is real, and it almost never applies to you

The strongest battery claim comes from good science. Purdue researchers Pranab Dash and Y. Charlie Hu built a per-pixel OLED power profiler and tested four phones (Pixel 2, Moto Z3, Pixel 4, Pixel 5) across six Google apps. Switching from light to dark mode saved 39–47% of display power — at 100% brightness. That's the number everyone quotes.

Here's the part that doesn't fit in a headline: at 30–50% brightness, the saving was 3–9%. Most people use auto-brightness, which sits around 30–40% indoors. The researchers' verdict was blunt: the saving is so small at normal indoor brightness that most users wouldn't notice. On LCD screens — budget phones, most laptops, older iPads — it's essentially zero, because the backlight stays on regardless of pixel color.

Dark mode is a real battery feature outdoors at max brightness, where the 39–47% shows up. Everywhere else it's a comfort and aesthetics feature. Stop selling it as battery management and start designing it as what it is.

Don't invert — rebuild: what Google's spec actually says

Google's Material Design dark theme guidance reads like a direct answer to the invert-and-ship crowd. The baseline surface is #121212, not pure black. Text comes in two tiers: white at 87% opacity for high-emphasis text, 60% for medium. The big idea is elevation: since dark shadows are invisible on a dark background, depth is communicated by making higher surfaces brighter — thin white overlays on top of the base surface, getting stronger with elevation. In Google's codelab, a bottom app bar gets the base #121212 plus a 12% white overlay. Cards, dialogs, and sheets all follow the same logic.

Color gets a rule most teams skip: desaturate. Saturated brand colors vibrate against dark backgrounds, so Material tells you to pull them back and use them sparingly — "limited color accents," preferring the surface color over the primary color in most chrome. Even your error red needs a dark-mode version: the same fire-engine red that reads fine on white vibrates on black, so the guidance is a dustier, dimmer red. If your red is still shouting at the same volume in dark mode, nobody adjusted it.

Apple took a different path — and both agree on one rule

Apple's approach is semantic instead of numeric. iOS (since 2019's iOS 13) and macOS define colors as roles — label, secondaryLabel, systemBackground — that automatically adapt to the trait environment. Use UIColor.label and dark mode mostly handles itself; hardcode a hex for your text and you've broken dark mode before you tested it. Apple's actual values show the same discipline as Material's: label text is white at 85% opacity, elevated cards step up through dark grays (#1C1C1E, #2C2C2E) to signal depth, and community measurements put dark-mode systemBlue slightly brighter than its light-mode counterpart to hold its contrast.

One disagreement worth noting: Apple's base system background is pure black (#000000), where Material explicitly avoids it. The honest reading: Apple's black maximizes OLED savings and contrast for content; Material's dark gray is friendlier for long sessions and makes elevation layering visible. Both are defensible. What neither defends is a theme nobody designed.

Contrast doesn't retire when you go dark

A common assumption is that dark mode is automatically more accessible. The opposite can be true: light text on black at full strength causes halation — text that seems to bleed into the background — which is why the platforms cap text opacity at 85–87% instead of pure white. WCAG's 4.5:1 ratio for body text still applies; it just gets harder to eyeball on a dark canvas, especially for saturated accents.

Practical checks that catch the most failures: view the whole UI in grayscale to expose contrast problems instantly; re-check every accent color against its dark background (your light theme's accessible blue is often a failing blue in the dark); and never trust the simulator — test on a real OLED screen outdoors, where dark interfaces lose legibility fastest. For contrast science beyond the old 4.5:1 rule, the perceptual color work in my OKLCH and APCA guide applies here too.

Type, images, and the ten small things

The details that separate a designed dark theme from a flipped one: bump font weights slightly — thin type that was elegant in black-on-white turns spindly in white-on-black; small text may need a size bump too, since the readability gap between modes grows as type gets smaller. Images and logos need dark-mode variants or at least transparent backgrounds, or you'll ship white boxes around every logo. QR codes are a real gotcha: an inverted QR code won't scan. Interactive states (hover, pressed, disabled) must stay distinct without relying on brightness alone. And animate the theme switch with a subtle transition — a hard flash at midnight is the kind of detail users feel even if they never name it.

Respect the user: give them the switch, then listen to the data

Ship both modes, default to the system preference via prefers-color-scheme, and always offer a manual toggle that persists. A Nielsen Norman Group survey of 115 mobile users found opinion split exactly three ways: a third want dark, a third want light, a third switch. There is no default everyone loves.

And here's the finding every designer should sit with: in NNGroup's summary of the German readability research (Piepenbrock and colleagues, Institut für Experimentelle Psychologie Düsseldorf), light mode won on every measured dimension — visual acuity and proofreading, for young and old adults — and produced no difference in fatigue. Yet participants reported no difference in readability. As NNGroup puts it: don't listen to users. Measure the reading task.

The takeaway isn't "ship light mode only." It's that the mode that looks good in a screenshot and the mode that performs in a reading test are different problems, and a designed dark theme accounts for both.

What to do this week

Audit your dark theme with five checks: is your base surface dark gray rather than pure black (or pure black with a deliberate reason)? Does elevation make cards brighter instead of relying on shadows? Is your loudest accent color desaturated relative to light mode? Does body text clear 4.5:1 on the actual dark background? And can a user override the system default? If any answer is no, you don't have a dark theme yet — you have an inverted light one.

References

  • Nielsen Norman Group — "Dark Mode vs. Light Mode: Which Is Better?" — summary of Piepenbrock et al. readability studies; 115-user preference survey (1/3 dark, 1/3 light, 1/3 mixed)
  • ScienceDaily — "Dark mode may not save your phone's battery life as much as you think" — Purdue Dash Hu OLED profiler study (MobiSys '21): 3–9% savings at 30–50% brightness, 39–47% at 100%
  • Google Codelabs — "Design a dark theme with Material and Figma" — #121212 surface, 87%/60% text opacity, elevation overlays, limited color accents
  • Android Developers — Material Design 2 in Compose — elevation overlay behavior, primarySurface limited-accent guidance
  • Median.co — "Apple's Human Interface Guidelines: Dark Mode do's and don'ts" — semantic colors, vibrancy, base/elevated backgrounds
  • AppCherish — "Dark Mode Isn't Optional Anymore" — iOS semantic-color checklist, hardcoded-color pitfalls since iOS 13

title: Designing a Smarter Dog Breed Discovery Experience: UX, Data and AI
description:
Designing a Smarter Dog Breed Discovery Experience: UX, Data and AI

Choosing a dog breed is more complicated than it first appears.

People often start with appearance, popularity, or recommendations from friends. But finding a suitable dog requires considering several factors: lifestyle, available space, activity level, grooming requirements, and previous experience with dogs.

This creates an interesting challenge for anyone building a digital discovery platform.

1. Turning Complex Information Into Better Decisions

A dog breed directory can contain hundreds of pages, but more information does not automatically mean better decisions.

The challenge is organizing information so that visitors can compare breeds and understand which characteristics matter to their situation.

Useful design principles include:

  • Clear navigation and structured breed categories
  • Consistent presentation of breed characteristics
  • Mobile-first interfaces
  • Accessible descriptions and comparison tools
  • Transparent explanations of recommendations

2. The Potential of AI-Assisted Discovery

AI can help users explore large collections of information through more natural interactions.

For example, a breed discovery system could consider:

  • Daily activity and exercise preferences
  • Apartment or house living
  • Experience with dog ownership
  • Household composition
  • Time available for training and care

However, recommendations should never be presented as guarantees of compatibility. Individual dogs vary, and responsible decisions require more than a matching score.

3. Structured Data and Search Experience

From a web development perspective, structured content creates opportunities for better navigation and discovery.

A well-organized breed platform can benefit from semantic HTML, descriptive internal links, accessible components, and relevant structured data.

Performance matters too. Fast-loading pages and responsive layouts make complex information easier to explore across devices.

4. A Real-World Project:

One project exploring this space is Hunderacer.dk, a Danish website focused on dog breeds and helping people explore their options.

The project illustrates an interesting product-design challenge: combining breed information, intuitive navigation, and decision-support experiences in one accessible platform.

The broader lesson applies well beyond pet websites.

Whether building a product comparison engine, an educational platform, or a recommendation interface, the goal should be the same: help people make better-informed decisions without hiding complexity or overstating certainty.

5. What Would You Build Differently?

For developers and UX designers, several questions are worth exploring:

  • How should recommendation systems explain their results?
  • When should rule-based matching be preferred over machine learning?
  • How can structured content improve both usability and search discoverability?
  • How do we design interfaces that communicate uncertainty responsibly?

These questions are especially important when recommendations influence long-term decisions.

Final thought: Good discovery experiences do more than return results. They help users understand why those results matter.

Disclosure: I am associated with Hunderacer.dk. This article was prepared with AI writing assistance and should be reviewed before publication.

title: 2 Agent Skills Every Frontend Developer Should Try
description:
I love to try out new agent skills. Anything that can help me be more productive I'm all for. Today I found two new ones I want to share with you.

First one is Impeccable. Impeccable took a plain, AI-built website and gave it a design. It wasn't bad at all! Diagram Design took that same site and drew a diagram of how it works! Both install with one command, and both work with basically any coding harness. I used Kiro in my demos but you can use whatever you like.

I made a video walking through both if you'd rather watch:

Prerequisites

  • An agent that supports Agent Skills. I use Kiro, but Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex work too.
  • Node.js, so you can run npx.
  • A frontend project to try them on. Mine is a small website about cats.

Finding skills

I found both skills on Skill Leaderboard, which ranks skill repos by GitHub stars. You can filter by compatible agent, so I set it to Kiro. Skills are like recipes that work across most coding harnesses, so you'll usually be fine without the filter. Some repos are easier to install in one agent than another, though, and the filter saves you from finding that out the hard way.

Stars measure popularity. I cared more about what fits my own projects, so I picked the two that match what I build most, which is websites.

Before you install anything, read the SKILL.md and any scripts it pulls in. A skill is instructions and scripts that run with your agent's permissions, so check it the same way you'd check an npm package.

1. Impeccable

Impeccable is a design skill that started from Anthropic's frontend-design skill and builds on top of it. It has UX planning, a set of design commands like critique, polish, and audit, and it asks you a lot of questions.

To test it, I had Claude Opus 5.5 vibe code a site called the Great Cat Color Census. You spot a cat in the wild, click "Spotted one," and the counts and leaderboard update. Out of the box it came with a blocky card style and some hover animations. It looked okay. I don't think it looked bad, but it was pretty generic.


The default design Claude Opus 5.5 came up with.

Install it from your project root:

npx impeccable install

Then run init inside your agent:

/impeccable init

Init looks through the project, asks about anything it can't work out on its own, and writes a PRODUCT.md with what it learned. After that I asked it to make the site much nicer using its styles. It came back with five or six design directions. I picked the sticker one.


The sticker direction from Impeccable. Same features, new design.

It has basically the same features as before, and you can still summon a random cat. It looks a lot more polished, with extra animation and cats that look like peel-off stickers. The font gives it a Cat in the Hat feel. I don't have a very particular taste for frontend design, and I still like this version better. If you're a designer, tell me in the comments whether you agree.

A good way to use Impeccable is to have it build several of its directions on separate Git branches. Then you can run each one and compare them side by side before you commit to a look.

2. Diagram Design

Diagram Design draws diagrams as one self-contained HTML and SVG file. It supports 45 diagram types, from architecture diagrams and flow charts to radar charts and Venn diagrams. The screenshots in the repo don't do it much justice.

Install it with the skills CLI:

npx skills add cathrynlavery/diagram-design

I asked it for a diagram of the same cat site and didn't say what to diagram. There's no backend, so I wasn't expecting much. It picked the visitor flow. A visitor clicks, an action runs change() or reset(), the counts update, and the derived stats feed the left and right pages. It also shows the save and load path to localStorage, and it even carried over the pink styling from the site.


The diagram Diagram Design made from the cat site, open in Kiro.

It's a simple diagram, but I like the style, and I can see myself using it on my next project. It's also handy when you open a code base with little documentation. Ask it for a few diagrams before you start reading the code.

The rest of the list

I haven't spent much time with the other popular skills yet. These are my notes so far.

Ponytail gives your agent the personality of the laziest senior dev in the room. In its README, you show him fifty lines, and he says nothing and replaces them with one. The goal is less code and fewer tokens. In Kiro it loads as an always-on ruleset, so you don't get its slash commands.

Caveman makes the agent answer tersely to cut token usage. I haven't seen much savings myself. Someone in a Reddit thread on the top Kiro skill repos said it raised their token usage, even though the research the repo cites says otherwise.

Addy Osmani's agent skills add a spec, plan, build, and test workflow to your agent. Kiro has specs built in, but if your tool doesn't, this or Superpowers is how I'd add spec-driven development.

I haven't tried UI UX Pro Max or Graphify yet, even though they're near the top of the list.

If you build on AWS, look at the Agent Toolkit for AWS. It's our set of skills and MCP servers for working with AWS from your agent, and it's free on GitHub.

Wrap up

If you build websites, Impeccable is the one I'd install first. Diagram Design is right behind it, especially when you're new to a code base.

I'm thinking about testing whether Ponytail and Caveman save tokens in Kiro. Leave a comment if you want to see that, and tell me which skills you're using.

title: How I keep a living system map of Mầm Văn — every change, before & after
description:
Hi, I'm Vũ Xuân Toàn (Vu Xuan Toan), a software developer and indie maker from Bắc Ninh, Vietnam, and the founder of Vu Xuan Toan Tech. In my intro post I mentioned Mầm Văn — the literature-learning platform I'm building for Vietnamese middle-school students (React, TypeScript, Supabase, Gemini AI). Today I want to share the part of the project I'm most proud of, because it isn't a feature for users — it's how I keep the whole system understandable while it changes every week.

The problem: the system grows faster than memory

Mầm Văn has two big portals (teacher and student), an AI content studio, a question bank, XP and mastery engines, a knowledge tree, grading workflows, notifications, an admin area… After a few months of intense building, "how does this all connect?" stopped being a question I could answer from memory.

So I built a complete map of every flow in the system — 262 nodes covering every screen, every engine, and the relationships between them (for example: publishing a lesson → notifies students, or rejecting a gift request → refunds the student's total XP wallet). Every node also lists the exact code files and functions that implement it, verified automatically against the codebase.

The rule: the map is part of the code

The map only stays true if it can never drift. So I work under one strict rule:

  1. Before changing any flow, I open the map and identify which nodes and relationships the change touches.
  2. After the change, I update the map, regenerate it, and ship it in the same commit as the code.
  3. The map and a full change history are republished automatically to my website in the same round.

You can see both, live:

  • 🗺️ The system map (interactive, click a node to light up its cluster): https://vuxuantoan.me/so-do-mam-van.html
  • 📜 The change history — every work session: what changed, in which files, with lines added/removed: https://vuxuantoan.me/lich-su-mam-van.html

Before & after, for every flow change

The part I like most: whenever a change modifies a flow, the history page automatically gets two buttons — "flow BEFORE this change" and "flow AFTER this change". Every version of the map is archived immutably, so I can reopen exactly how the system looked before any change and compare. When I recently removed an AI status bar from the question bank, the before-map still shows its node in the tree; the after-map doesn't. That makes design review honest: nothing about the system's shape is ever lost or misremembered.

Why bother?

Because an indie maker's scarcest resource isn't code — it's clarity. The map has already caught wrong assumptions before I wrote a line of code, and it lets anyone (a collaborator, a teacher using the platform, future me) understand a fairly complex product in minutes.

If you build long-lived side projects, I'd genuinely recommend stealing this workflow: one living map, updated in the same commit as the code, with archived before/after versions.

—

I'm Vũ Xuân Toàn. My home on the web is vuxuantoan.me, my code lives at github.com/vut08905, and Mầm Văn itself is live at mamvan.vercel.app. Say hi!

title: I've tried a lot of dictation tools, and almost all of them ship your audio off to someone's cloud
description:
I've tried a lot of dictation tools, and almost all of them ship your audio off to someone's cloud. That always bugged me. So when I found Inaudio, a tiny desktop app that does all of it locally, I had to share it.
You press a keyboard shortcut and talk. It types. And it keeps a searchable history of everything you've dictated, so you can go back and grab that one sentence from yesterday.
It works the other way too. Paste text or copy something to your clipboard, and it reads it aloud with on-device speech synthesis. Great for proofreading your own writing (you hear the clunky sentences way faster than you see them).
Under the hood it's Electron, React and TypeScript, with sherpa-onnx doing the speech work. You download a model once, then everything runs on your CPU. One of the options is NVIDIA's Nemotron streaming ASR model for English, tuned for about 560 ms latency.
Is it perfect? No. This is a brand new project with only a handful of stars, so expect rough edges. And text insertion and permissions behave differently on Windows, macOS and Linux.
But if you want private dictation without a subscription, it's worth a try. And honestly, it's a great time to jump in and contribute while the project is still small.

shikki841 / inaudio

Offline dictation and read-aloud for the desktop.

Inaudio

Your voice, on your machine.

Offline dictation and read-aloud for the desktop.
Built with Electron, React, TypeScript, and sherpa-onnx

Downloads · Contribute · Report an issue

See it work

Watch the full recording with sound (about 4 minutes, recorded on Windows from a real run; History text is blurred).

Speak. Edit. Keep going.

  • Dictate with a keyboard shortcut and keep a searchable transcript history.
  • Transcribe what your computer plays, such as a meeting or a video, as it is heard. Grey provisional text keeps up with the speech, and a small floating window shows the transcript without opening Inaudio.
  • Pick the source: system audio, system audio with your microphone, or one audio device such as a virtual cable.
  • Clean up noise on the device: a voice detector skips stretches without speech, and an optional speech cleanup model filters background noise.
  • Read text or your clipboard aloud with on-device speech…
