title: How I Built a Suite of 100+ Dev Tools That Runs 100% in the Browser
description:
A few months ago, I was inspecting a JWT token using a popular online utility when I noticed network requests firing off every time I pasted a string into the input box.

That moment made me uncomfortable. Why do we send sensitive environment variables, API payloads, and tokens over the wire just to run standard string manipulation or formatting?

That inspired me to build WToolsKit — a pure frontend platform providing 100+ utilities that run entirely inside the client browser.

🏗️ The Architecture: Pure Client-Side Magic

To eliminate server dependencies, cloud bills, and privacy risks, I relied heavily on modern browser Web APIs:

  1. Client-Side Compression: Using HTML5 <canvas> and FileReader APIs to manipulate raw image data directly without sending files to an API endpoint.
  2. Zero Network Overhead: Formatting JSON or calculating text diffs happens in memory via Web Workers/pure JS functions, making execution instantaneous.
  3. Offline First Capability: Since there is no backend API, once the static assets load, tools function flawlessly even on slow or unreliable networks.

🚀 Key Tool Categories

  • Developer Tools: JSON Validator, RegEx Debugger, JWT Decoder, Base64/URL Encoding.
  • Design Helpers: Color Picker, CSS Shadow/Gradient Generators, SVG Cleaners.
  • Converters & Formatters: Text Diff, Markdown Preview, Image Format Converters.

🔗 Check It Out

You can explore the full collection of tools at https://www.wtoolskit.com/.

If you're a fellow builder, I'd love to hear your thoughts on pure browser-based web tools:

  • How do you handle sensitive data when debugging on web utilities?
  • What other browser-native APIs do you think are underutilized for dev tools?

Thanks for reading!

title: A liquid glass tab bar: the magnifying lens is a scaled copy of the bar
description:
Apple's liquid glass tab bars have a lens that sits on the selected tab and magnifies the icon under it. When you switch tabs it moves like a drop of water: it stretches on the way, then settles.

Most web versions of this effect use an SVG displacement filter inside backdrop-filter. That only renders in Chromium browsers; Safari and Firefox skip it. I built one for a music-app demo and wanted it to look the same in every browser, so the lens uses no filter at all. It's a small window onto a second copy of the bar, scaled up 1.42 times.

This post covers three pieces:

  1. The glass bar (plain backdrop-filter).
  2. The lens: a clipped, scaled copy, and the one line of math that keeps it lined up.
  3. The drop: a spring whose speed sets the lens width.

There's a single-file demo at the end you can paste into CodePen. If you build with Cursor or Claude Code, it also works as a reference file to hand to your agent: it's short, and every number in it is explained here.

1. The glass bar

The bar itself is ordinary frosted glass. Blur plus saturation does most of the work. The inset shadows draw a light top edge and a faint 1px rim so the bar reads as a solid object on any background.

This is the CSS from the shipped component (tabbar-liquid.css):

.glassbar {
  position: absolute;
  border-radius: 32px;
  background: var(--glass);
  -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(16px) saturate(1.9);
  backdrop-filter: blur(16px) saturate(1.9);
  box-shadow:
    inset 0 1px 0 rgba(255,255,255,.22),
    inset 0 0 0 1px var(--glass-line),
    0 18px 40px rgba(0,0,0,.45);
}

saturate(1.9) matters more than it looks. Blur alone washes colours out to grey. Saturation brings back the colour of whatever scrolls underneath, which is what makes it read as glass and not as a grey panel.

Keep the -webkit- prefix. Safari still wants it.

2. The lens is a copy, not a filter

Real magnification would need a displacement filter on whatever sits behind the lens. You can fake the part people actually notice, the icon under the lens getting bigger, with plain transforms:

  • Render the tabs a second time inside the lens element.
  • Give the lens overflow: hidden so you only see the part under it.
  • Scale the copy by M (1.42 here) around the lens centre.

The markup is a lens with an inner layer that holds the copy:

<div class="lens" aria-hidden="true">
  <div class="lensIn"><!-- the same tabs again, not focusable --></div>
</div>

The copy must stay out of the accessibility tree and out of the tab order, or a screen reader reads every tab twice. In the React component the copy is rendered with live={false}, which does exactly that:

const inert = live ? {} : { tabIndex: -1, 'aria-hidden': true as const };

The one line of math

.lensIn has transform-origin: 0 0 and fills the same box as the real bar. The lens has width w, height h, and centre (x, y) in bar coordinates, so its top-left corner is (lx, ly) = (x - w/2, y - h/2).

You want the point under the lens centre to stay where it is, with everything around it pushed outwards by M. Here's the render code from the shipped engine.ts:

const Ls = S.lens, lx = Ls.x - Ls.w / 2, ly = Ls.y - Ls.h / 2, M = 1.42;
lens.style.transform = `translate(${lx.toFixed(1)}px,${ly.toFixed(1)}px) scale(${Ls.sx.toFixed(4)},${Ls.sy.toFixed(4)})`;
lensIn.style.transform = `translate(${(-lx + Ls.x - M * Ls.x).toFixed(2)}px,${(-ly + Ls.y - M * Ls.y).toFixed(2)}px) scale(${M})`;

Why it works: a point p of the copy lands at M·p + t inside the lens, and the lens sits at lx. On screen that is lx + M·p + (-lx + x - M·x), which simplifies to x + M·(p - x). At p = x you get x, so the centre stays put and everything else spreads out from it by M. It's the textbook "scale around a point" transform, with the lens offset cancelled out.

Since the copy is real DOM, you can style it apart from the bar. Trimmed from the shipped CSS (the comments are mine):

.lens {
  position: absolute; left: 0; top: 0; overflow: hidden; pointer-events: none;
  background: rgba(255,255,255,.07);
  backdrop-filter: blur(3px) saturate(2) brightness(1.18);
  box-shadow:
    inset 0 2px 0 rgba(255,255,255,.75),     /* bright top rim */
    inset 0 -2px 0 rgba(198,244,50,.55),     /* lime bottom rim */
    inset 0 -12px 20px rgba(139,108,255,.4),
    inset 5px 0 9px rgba(255,90,170,.35),    /* pink left edge */
    inset -5px 0 9px rgba(90,220,255,.35),   /* cyan right edge */
    0 0 0 1.5px rgba(255,255,255,.4),
    0 12px 28px rgba(0,0,0,.5),
    0 0 34px rgba(198,244,50,.42);
}
.lensIn { position: absolute; left: 0; top: 0; transform-origin: 0 0; }
.lensIn .tab { color: var(--volt); }        /* the magnified icon turns lime */
.lensIn .tab i { opacity: 0 !important; }   /* hide the label inside the lens */
.lensIn .tab svg { translate: 0 8px; }      /* and drop the icon into the middle */
.lensIn .dockc {
  filter: drop-shadow(1.6px 0 0 rgba(255,70,150,.6))
          drop-shadow(-1.6px 0 0 rgba(70,210,255,.6));
}

Two details from that block:

  • The pink and cyan inset shadows on the left and right edges, plus two 1.6px drop-shadows on the copy, fake the colour fringing you see where real glass bends light. They're cheap and they sell the effect more than anything else in the file.
  • The label is hidden inside the lens and the icon moves down 8px. A magnified label gets cut off by the lens edge and looks like a bug. A centred icon looks deliberate.

The cost of this approach is that the content renders twice. For five icons that's nothing. The same component reuses the trick for a bigger orb that lifts out of the bar: the orb's copy holds the whole screen, scaled with the same formula.

3. The drop: speed sets the width

A lens that slides at a fixed width looks like a highlight pill. It reads as liquid once it stretches while it moves and goes back to round when it stops.

In the React version the lens x-position is a Framer Motion spring, and useVelocity reads how fast that spring is moving:

// live mode: the lens rides a spring, and its speed stretches the drop
const x = useSpring(tabX(0), { stiffness: 380, damping: 26 });
const stretch = useVelocity(x);

Every frame, the speed (px/s) maps to the lens size:

const v = Math.abs(stretch.get());
S.lens = {
  x: lx, y: g.cy,
  w: mix(66 + Math.min(92, v / 9), 56, c),
  h: mix(52 - Math.min(10, v / 90), 56, c),
  /* ... */
};

Leave out mix(..., c) for now. That's the compact state, when the bar shrinks on scroll. What's left:

  • At rest the lens is 66 × 52.
  • It gets 1px wider for every 9 px/s of speed, up to 92px more.
  • It gets thinner by up to 10px, so a fast move reads as a long, thin drop.
  • The clamps stop a very fast flick from stretching it across the whole bar.

The spring's overshoot does the rest. With stiffness 380 and damping 26 the spring is underdamped (damping ratio about 0.67), so it passes the target a little and comes back. The width follows the speed, so you get a wobble on landing without writing one keyframe.

Switching tabs is one line: x.set(tabX(i)).

Keyboard and screen readers

The real tabs are a tablist. Each tab gets role="tab" and aria-selected, and left/right arrows move between them:

if (e.key !== 'ArrowRight' && e.key !== 'ArrowLeft') return;
e.preventDefault(); i = (i + (e.key === 'ArrowRight' ? 1 : 4)) % 5;
screen.current?.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-dock] [data-tab]')[i]?.focus();

(+ 4 is - 1 modulo 5, so left arrow from the first tab wraps to the last.)

The lens, the copy and the rings are all aria-hidden. Only the real tabs are announced.

The single-file version

No Framer Motion here. The spring is about ten lines of Hooke's law with damping, using the same stiffness and damping as the React version. Paste it into CodePen's HTML panel or save it as a .html file and open it:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8">
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1">
<title>Liquid glass tab bar: magnifying lens demo</title>
<!-- MIT licence. Teaching version of the lens from qodesign's Liquid Glass Tab Bar (qodesign.dev). -->
<style>
  :root { --ink:#0A0A0D; --text:#F4F4F6; --muted:#8A8FA3; --lime:#C6FF3D; }
  * { box-sizing:border-box; margin:0 }
  body { min-height:100vh; display:grid; place-items:center; background:#050507; font-family:system-ui,sans-serif; color:var(--text) }
  .phone { position:relative; width:390px; height:700px; max-width:100vw; border-radius:44px; overflow:hidden; background:var(--ink) }
  .feed { position:absolute; inset:0; overflow-y:auto; padding:56px 18px 140px; display:grid; gap:14px }
  .card { height:150px; border-radius:22px; display:flex; align-items:flex-end; padding:16px; font-weight:600 }
  .card:nth-child(3n+1) { background:linear-gradient(135deg,#8B6CFF,#2a1d66) }
  .card:nth-child(3n+2) { background:linear-gradient(135deg,#ff6a3d,#5a1d0b) }
  .card:nth-child(3n)   { background:linear-gradient(135deg,#C6FF3D,#2d4a00); color:#0A0A0D }

  /* the glass bar */
  .dock { position:absolute; left:14px; right:14px; bottom:22px; height:76px }
  .bar { position:absolute; inset:0; border-radius:32px; background:rgba(28,30,40,.45);
    -webkit-backdrop-filter:blur(16px) saturate(1.9); backdrop-filter:blur(16px) saturate(1.9);
    box-shadow:inset 0 1px 0 rgba(255,255,255,.22), inset 0 0 0 1px rgba(255,255,255,.1), 0 18px 40px rgba(0,0,0,.45) }
  .tabs { position:absolute; inset:0; display:flex }
  .tab { flex:1; display:flex; flex-direction:column; align-items:center; justify-content:center; gap:3px;
    border:0; background:none; color:var(--muted); font:600 10.5px system-ui; border-radius:24px; cursor:pointer; touch-action:none }
  .tab svg { width:25px; height:25px; fill:none; stroke:currentColor; stroke-width:2; stroke-linecap:round; stroke-linejoin:round }
  .tab[aria-selected="true"] { color:var(--text) }
  .tab:focus-visible { outline:2px solid var(--lime); outline-offset:-4px }

  /* the lens: a window onto a scaled copy of the tabs */
  .lens { position:absolute; left:0; top:0; overflow:hidden; pointer-events:none; will-change:transform,width,height;
    background:rgba(255,255,255,.07);
    -webkit-backdrop-filter:blur(3px) saturate(2) brightness(1.18); backdrop-filter:blur(3px) saturate(2) brightness(1.18);
    box-shadow:inset 0 2px 0 rgba(255,255,255,.75), inset 0 -2px 0 rgba(198,255,61,.55), inset 0 -12px 20px rgba(139,108,255,.4),
      inset 5px 0 9px rgba(255,90,170,.35), inset -5px 0 9px rgba(90,220,255,.35), 0 0 0 1.5px rgba(255,255,255,.4), 0 0 34px rgba(198,255,61,.42) }
  .lens::after { content:""; position:absolute; left:14%; right:14%; top:5%; height:34%; border-radius:50%;
    background:linear-gradient(rgba(255,255,255,.5),rgba(255,255,255,0)) }
  .lensIn { position:absolute; left:0; top:0; transform-origin:0 0;
    filter:drop-shadow(1.6px 0 0 rgba(255,70,150,.6)) drop-shadow(-1.6px 0 0 rgba(70,210,255,.6)) }
  .lensIn .tab { color:var(--lime) }
  .lensIn .tab span { opacity:0 }
  .lensIn .tab svg { translate:0 8px }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<div class="phone">
  <div class="feed" aria-label="Feed">
    <div class="card">Daily mix</div><div class="card">Late night</div><div class="card">Focus</div>
    <div class="card">Running</div><div class="card">Vinyl finds</div><div class="card">Live sets</div>
  </div>
  <nav class="dock">
    <div class="bar"></div>
    <div class="tabs" role="tablist" aria-label="Sections" id="tabs"></div>
    <div class="lens" id="lens" aria-hidden="true"><div class="lensIn" id="lensIn"></div></div>
  </nav>
</div>
<script>
const TABS = [
  ['Home',    '<path d="M3 11l9-7 9 7v9a1 1 0 0 1-1 1h-5v-6H9v6H4a1 1 0 0 1-1-1z"/>'],
  ['Explore', '<circle cx="12" cy="12" r="9"/><path d="M15.5 8.5l-2 5-5 2 2-5z"/>'],
  ['Library', '<path d="M4 4v16M9 4v16M14 4l6 16"/>'],
  ['Inbox',   '<path d="M4 13l2-8h12l2 8v6H4z"/><path d="M4 13h5l1 2h4l1-2h5"/>'],
  ['Profile', '<circle cx="12" cy="8" r="4"/><path d="M4 21c1.5-4 4.5-6 8-6s6.5 2 8 6"/>'],
];
const tabHTML = (live) => TABS.map(([label, icon], i) =>
  `<button class="tab" type="button" ${live ? `role="tab" aria-selected="${i === 0}" tabindex="${i ? -1 : 0}"` : 'tabindex="-1"'}>
     <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-hidden="true">${icon}</svg><span>${label}</span></button>`).join('');

const $ = (id) => document.getElementById(id);
const dock = document.querySelector('.dock'), tabsEl = $('tabs'), lens = $('lens'), lensIn = $('lensIn');
tabsEl.innerHTML = tabHTML(true);
lensIn.innerHTML = `<div class="tabs">${tabHTML(false)}</div>`;   // the copy the lens magnifies
const tabs = [...tabsEl.children];
const M = 1.42;                                                     // magnification
const reduce = matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)');

// a tiny spring: same feel as Framer Motion's useSpring({ stiffness: 380, damping: 26 })
const spring = { x: 0, v: 0, target: 0, k: 380, c: 26 };
const centerOf = (i) => tabs[i].offsetLeft + tabs[i].offsetWidth / 2;
let active = 0;

function select(i, focus) {
  active = (i + tabs.length) % tabs.length;
  tabs.forEach((t, j) => { t.setAttribute('aria-selected', j === active); t.tabIndex = j === active ? 0 : -1; });
  if (focus) tabs[active].focus();
  spring.target = centerOf(active);
  if (reduce.matches) { spring.x = spring.target; spring.v = 0; }
}

function paint() {
  const W = dock.clientWidth, H = dock.clientHeight;
  lensIn.style.width = W + 'px'; lensIn.style.height = H + 'px';
  const speed = Math.abs(spring.v);                        // px per second
  const w = 66 + Math.min(92, speed / 9);                  // faster = longer drop
  const h = 52 - Math.min(10, speed / 90);                 // ...and a little thinner
  const x = Math.max(w / 2, Math.min(W - w / 2, spring.x));      // keep the drop inside the bar
  const y = H / 2, lx = x - w / 2, ly = y - h / 2;
  lens.style.width = w + 'px'; lens.style.height = h + 'px';
  lens.style.borderRadius = Math.min(w, h) / 2 + 'px';
  lens.style.transform = `translate(${lx}px, ${ly}px)`;
  // keep the point under the lens centre still, and scale everything around it
  lensIn.style.transform = `translate(${-lx + x - M * x}px, ${-ly + y - M * y}px) scale(${M})`;
}

let last = performance.now();
function frame(now) {
  const dt = Math.min(0.032, (now - last) / 1000); last = now;
  const a = -spring.k * (spring.x - spring.target) - spring.c * spring.v;   // Hooke + damping, mass 1
  spring.v += a * dt; spring.x += spring.v * dt;
  paint();
  requestAnimationFrame(frame);
}

// tap, drag across the bar, or use the arrow keys
const nearest = (clientX) => {
  const r = dock.getBoundingClientRect(), px = clientX - r.left;
  return tabs.reduce((best, t, i) => Math.abs(centerOf(i) - px) < Math.abs(centerOf(best) - px) ? i : best, 0);
};
tabsEl.addEventListener('pointerdown', (e) => { tabsEl.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId); select(nearest(e.clientX)); });
tabsEl.addEventListener('pointermove', (e) => { if (e.buttons) select(nearest(e.clientX)); });
tabsEl.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
  if (e.key === 'ArrowRight') { e.preventDefault(); select(active + 1, true); }
  if (e.key === 'ArrowLeft')  { e.preventDefault(); select(active - 1, true); }
});
addEventListener('resize', () => { spring.target = spring.x = centerOf(active); });

spring.x = spring.target = centerOf(0);
requestAnimationFrame(frame);
</script>
</body>
</html>

The parts worth reading in the demo:

// a tiny spring: same feel as Framer Motion's useSpring({ stiffness: 380, damping: 26 })
const a = -spring.k * (spring.x - spring.target) - spring.c * spring.v;
spring.v += a * dt; spring.x += spring.v * dt;

const speed = Math.abs(spring.v);              // px per second
const w = 66 + Math.min(92, speed / 9);        // faster = longer drop
const h = 52 - Math.min(10, speed / 90);       // ...and a little thinner
const x = Math.max(w / 2, Math.min(W - w / 2, spring.x));   // keep the drop inside the bar
lensIn.style.transform = `translate(${-lx + x - M * x}px, ${-ly + y - M * y}px) scale(${M})`;

The demo adds three things the shipped component doesn't have:

  • Drag along the bar and the lens follows your finger to the nearest tab, stretching over every tab it passes.
  • It clamps the drop inside the bar, because a 158px drop on the last tab hangs off the edge.
  • With prefers-reduced-motion: reduce it jumps straight to the new tab, with no stretch and no wobble. Do that in anything you ship. A drop that stretches across the screen is exactly the kind of motion that setting is for.

Easy ways to get it wrong

  • Scaling the copy around its own centre. The magnified icon drifts sideways as the lens moves. Use transform-origin: 0 0 and put the whole offset in the translate.
  • A CSS transition on the lens width. The width then lags behind the position. Set width, height and transform in the same frame, all read from the spring.
  • A focusable copy. Keyboard users tab through ten tabs instead of five. Mark the copy aria-hidden and give every button in it tabindex="-1".
  • Labels inside the lens. They get cut by the lens edge. Hide them in the copy.

About me, and the links. I'm Teodor, and I make animated UI components at qodesign. The tab bar in this post is one of them, so this is partly a post about my own product. The demo above is MIT: copy it, change it, ship it. The full component adds the orb that turns into a full-screen player, the compact bar on scroll, the badge pop, a React + TypeScript + Tailwind + Framer Motion version, and a PROMPT.md for AI coding tools. It's $3 on qodesign.dev. This week I'm also putting a few components on GitHub for free (MIT): two dashboards, a toast stack, a pricing switch and an upload dropzone. I'll add the link here when the repo is public.

If you build a lens with a real displacement map that works in Safari, I'd like to see it.

I wrote this post with help from an AI assistant. The code excerpts are copied from the shipped component, and the demo was run and checked in a browser before publishing.

title: Printing Urdu worksheets in Nastaliq from the browser: joined letter forms with ZWJ and print-to-PDF
description:
Urdu letters change shape when they join. ب on its own, at the start of a word, in the middle and at the end are four different shapes, and a child who only practises the first one cannot read بلی (cat). Most free Urdu worksheets online are the same few scanned PDFs mirrored on spam pages, and almost none show the joined forms.

I built Takhti, a free worksheet maker that prints them correctly, with the child's name on the sheet. Everything runs in the browser. Here are the three tricks that made it work without a server or a PDF library.

1. Ask the font for a joined form with ZWJ

You do not need a table of presentation-form code points. Put a ZERO WIDTH JOINER (U+200D) on the side where the letter should connect, and the shaping engine (HarfBuzz in Chrome, CoreText in Safari) picks the right glyph:

const ZWJ = "‍";
function forms(letter, joins) {
  if (joins === "both") return [letter, letter + ZWJ, ZWJ + letter + ZWJ, ZWJ + letter]; // alone, start, middle, end
  if (joins === "right") return [letter, ZWJ + letter];  // ا د ڈ ذ ر ڑ ز ژ و ے: two shapes only
  return [letter];                                       // ء never joins
}

The ten right-joining letters are the part teachers notice when a sheet gets them wrong: ر has no "start" or "middle" form, so a sheet that shows four shapes for it is teaching a mistake.

The same trick builds a "missing first letter" exercise. Remove the first letter of پتنگ and you get تنگ, which renders with ت in its initial form. Prefix the rest with ZWJ and ت shows its middle form, the way it looks inside the real word. If the removed letter is one of the right-joiners (ریل without ر), skip the ZWJ, because the next letter really does start fresh.

2. Nastaliq needs room, and a real font

Noto Nastaliq Urdu is SIL OFL, so it can be self-hosted. The variable TTF from google/fonts converts to a 260 KB WOFF2 with fontTools. Two things to know:

  • Nastaliq has tall ascenders and deep descenders. A line height under about 1.8 clips dots and the tails of ے and ی.
  • The glyphs are small for their em size compared with Latin text, so Urdu needs a bigger font size next to English to look balanced.

I also offer Noto Naskh Arabic as an option, since many teachers start small children on the simpler Naskh shapes.

3. Print to PDF is the PDF engine

Most client-side PDF libraries draw text glyph by glyph and do not run the shaping engine, so Nastaliq comes out as disconnected letters. The browser's own print path does shape it, and on Android and desktop Chrome "Save as PDF" is in the print dialog. So each sheet is a fixed-size element:

.sheet { width: 210mm; height: 297mm; padding: 11mm 12mm 9mm; box-sizing: border-box; overflow: hidden; }
.letter .sheet { width: 215.9mm; height: 279.4mm; }   /* US Letter for families abroad */
@media print {
  body > :not(#print-root) { display: none !important; }
  .sheet { break-after: page; }
}

On print, the script copies the sheets into #print-root, injects @page { size: A4; margin: 0 } (or letter), waits for document.fonts.ready, then calls window.print(). Headless Chrome's --print-to-pdf gives the same output, which made it easy to test every sheet type: the fonts embed as Type 3 glyphs with the joins intact.

For the on-screen preview on a 390 px phone, the same A4 element is scaled with CSS zoom set to the container width divided by 794 (A4 width in CSS pixels), so what you see is exactly what prints.

What it makes

Letter tracing in all joined forms, the whole alphabet, the child's own name (common names are converted from Roman spelling, and there is a tap keyboard for the rest), letter and picture matching, missing letter, joining letters into words, ginti 1 to 10, opposites, wahid jama and muzakkar muannas, and short graded stories with a Roman Urdu and an English line under each Urdu line for parents abroad who do not read the script.

Every sheet carries the site address in its footer, since worksheets get photocopied and passed around classes. It is free, with no signup: https://takhti.appin60.com

If you teach Urdu, or have children learning it, I would like to hear which sheet is missing: takhti@appin60.com.

title: Amazon WorkSpaces simplifies secure AI agent access to enterprise cloud desktops with less infrastructure to operate and manage
description:
WorkSpaces for AI agents now handles authentication and desktop connections as part of the managed Model Context Protocol (MCP) service, so you can connect agents to governed cloud desktops, removing the need to write custom code. This makes it easy to use WorkSpaces with any client that supports MCP.

Connecting an agent to a desktop previously required you to manage presession requirements; generate, invoke, and rotate streaming URLs manually, adding complexity every time a session expired. You can now create sessions with your existing AWS credentials through OAuth 2.0, and the service handles the connection lifecycle. You configure once which desktop stack to use, and your agents reach the right desktop without ever seeing or handling the underlying streaming connection. You can also query session state to see which desktop stack, fleet, and session an agent is connected to, and generate a link for real-time observability of your agent. This gives you visibility and auditability over active agent work to know what your agents are doing and where.

To help your agents work with multiple applications, they can now discover and launch applications through a catalog MCP Tool rather than navigating menus. Using these new tools, agents can list the available applications, launch one or several at runtime, and switch between them, replacing the start-menu and taskbar navigation with a programmatic, deterministic path that improves accuracy and reduces token cost. 

WorkSpaces for AI agents runs agent sessions inside the same network isolation and compliance boundaries that govern your human workforce, inheriting the VPC controls, data-loss prevention policies, and session-level security posture that enterprises have already configured. The service is also now available in four additional AWS Regions: South America (São Paulo), Europe (Milan), Europe (Spain), and Asia Pacific (Malaysia).

To get started operating AI agents on WorkSpaces, visit: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/appstream2/latest/developerguide/agent-access.html.

title: AWS announces TorchNeuron: Native PyTorch Support for AWS Trainium (Public Beta)
description:
Today, AWS launched the public beta of TorchNeuron, an open source native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium. Trainium is a portfolio of AI chips designed to deliver high performance and cost efficiency for deep learning AI training and inference workloads. TorchNeuron enables AI scientists and researchers to experiment and build models with PyTorch natively on Trainium.

With TorchNeuron, developers can enable their PyTorch code on Trainium simply by switching to .to('neuron') while maintaining full PyTorch compatibility with eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware.

TorchNeuron is available as open source through the TorchNeuron github repo for Amazon EC2 Trainium2 instances and Amazon EC2 Trainium3 instances.

To learn more about TorchNeuron and AWS Trainium accelerators, visit the AWS Neuron page.

description:
AWS Clean Rooms now supports Databricks as a data source, so collaboration members and their partners can securely analyze data managed in Databricks without moving or revealing the source data. Members query a Databricks table shared through Delta Sharing directly in a collaboration. Databricks joins AWS Glue, Snowflake, and Amazon Athena as supported data sources in AWS Clean Rooms.

Previously, members with data in Databricks had to export or replicate it into Amazon S3 to use it as a table in a collaboration, which added pipeline work and an extra copy of the data to govern. Now members can register a Databricks table directly by providing the workspace URL, schema, and table along with a Delta Sharing share, and make it available to a collaboration. For example, a retailer that manages its customer data in Databricks can collaborate with a media partner on campaign measurement in AWS Clean Rooms, running approved analyses against its Databricks data without first building and maintaining an export to S3.

AWS Clean Rooms helps companies and their partners easily analyze and collaborate on their collective datasets without revealing or copying one another’s underlying data. For more information about the AWS Regions where AWS Clean Rooms is available, see the AWS Regions table. To learn more about collaborating with AWS Clean Rooms, visit AWS Clean Rooms.

title: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails now supports Standard tier for contextual grounding checks
description:
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails now offers a Standard tier for contextual grounding checks, which detect and filter hallucinations by checking whether a model response is grounded in your reference source and relevant to the user's query. The Standard tier is more robust than the Classic tier. It supports responses that include reasoning or conversational content, scores differently worded responses with the same meaning more consistently, and provides more comprehensive language support, matching the Standard tier for content filters and denied topics. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails provides configurable safeguards for generative AI applications on any foundation model through the ApplyGuardrail API.

Until now, contextual grounding checks applied strict grounding suited to summarization, paraphrasing, and question answering. With the Standard tier, you can also apply contextual grounding checks to conversational applications and to responses that reason over the source. You choose the tier for each guardrail in the Amazon Bedrock console or API. Existing guardrails keep the Classic tier until you change them. Pricing is the same for both tiers. To use the Standard tier, your guardrail must use cross-Region inference with a guardrail profile.

The Standard tier for contextual grounding checks is available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (N. California), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (Milan), Europe (Paris), Europe (Spain), Europe (Stockholm), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock Guardrails documentation on contextual grounding checks and safeguard tiers, or visit the Amazon Bedrock Guardrails product page.

title: AWS Partner Central launches Program Navigator, Case Study Generator, and streamlined specialization review
description:
AWS Partner Central now features Program Navigator, a unified experience that lets partners discover, apply for, and track AWS Specialization program applications in one place. Partners can browse specialization designations, view requirements and benefits, and submit applications through a guided, step-by-step workflow.

The new Case Study Generator in AWS Partner Central gives partners a redesigned creation experience with three starting paths: build a case study directly with AI assistance, import from an existing customer success story URL, or auto-populate from an opportunity. Case studies created for go-to-market purposes now follow a streamlined review path, a lightweight policy validation that lets partners publish directly to AWS domains without a specialization review. The deeper specialization-level review applies only to case studies associated with Program Navigator applications.

Additionally, AWS has streamlined the specialization application review process through Program Navigator. Partners submitting applications can expect faster review times and more detailed, requirement-level feedback throughout the process. Partners applying for non-specialization programs continue to access those programs through the existing experience.

Program Navigator and Case Study Generator are available to all AWS Partners in AWS Partner Central. To get started, navigate to Program Navigator and Case Studies under the Go to Market section in the left navigation panel.

title: Amazon Bedrock Advanced Prompt Optimization now supports prompt shortening
description:
Amazon Bedrock Advanced Prompt Optimization now supports prompt shortening, an optional setting that reduces the length of your prompt while maintaining or improving your evaluation scores. Advanced Prompt Optimization optimizes prompts for any model on Amazon Bedrock against your own evaluation criteria. Until now, optimization focused on quality alone. Optimized prompts were often longer than the original. Longer prompts raise input token costs and can increase time to first token, which matters at scale and in latency-sensitive applications.

When you turn on prompt shortening for a prompt template in your input dataset, the optimizer reduces the prompt's length. The optimized prompt is returned only when it is shorter than your original prompt and scores at least as high on your evaluation. Otherwise your original prompt is returned, so the setting never leaves you with a longer or lower-scoring prompt. Results include a compression ratio and the original and optimized token counts, in the output file and on the console results page. For example, a compression ratio of 0.7 means the optimized prompt uses 30% fewer tokens. Prompt shortening works with any evaluation method, including steering criteria, LLM-as-a-judge rubrics, and custom Lambda evaluators.    

Prompt shortening is available in all AWS Regions where Advanced Prompt Optimization is available. To get started, enable prompt shortening for a prompt template in your input dataset and create an optimization job as usual. To learn more, see Shorten prompts in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide, the Amazon Bedrock pricing page, and the Amazon Bedrock product page.

title: AWS Transform for migrations expands support for existing landing zones
description:
AWS Transform now supports more types of existing AWS environments when building landing zones for your migration, including AWS Control Tower landing zones and landing zones built with AWS Organizations. AWS Transform runs a foundation gap analysis of your current environment against AWS best practices and expands your landing zone on top of what's already in your target accounts, so your team can start migrating sooner.

AWS Transform also now supports an Infrastructure as Code (IaC)-only mode for building landing zones for your migration. In this mode, AWS Transform analyzes your organization, generates recommendations, and produces IaC tailored to your migration plan in AWS CDK, Terraform, or Landing Zone Accelerator (LZA) format. IaC-only mode is designed for organizations that prefer not to grant AWS Transform direct access to their management account. AWS Transform can now connect through a delegated administrator (DA) account instead. It also benefits customers who manage their own deployment pipeline and don't need the agent to deploy automatically.

The AWS Transform for migrations landing zone agent automates landing zone design end to end, including foundation setup, organizational unit (OU) and account structure, service control policies (SCPs), and workload accounts aligned to your migration planning and waves. You can deploy directly or generate IaC for your own pipeline.

These new capabilities are available in all target AWS Regions supported by AWS Transform for migrations.

title: Amazon CloudWatch Alarms now supports tags in alarm actions payload
description:
Today, Amazon CloudWatch announces support for including alarm tags in action payloads and Amazon EventBridge events, enabling customers to route and filter alarm notifications by tag without additional lookups. When enabled on an alarm, CloudWatch adds the alarm tags to the messages it sends to Amazon SNS, AWS Lambda, and Amazon EventBridge each time the alarm changes state. This option is designed for customers who route many alarms through a shared notification pipeline and need to identify the owning team, environment, or service directly from the message.

With tags in actions payloads, customers can avoid the extra work of correlating tag metadata with alarm events after the fact. For example, a team that routes hundreds of alarms through a single SNS topic to a Lambda function previously had to call ListTagsForResource for each event to find the owning team before paging. With this feature, the tags arrive in the notification, so the function can route directly from the message. The setting is off by default and configurable per alarm, and customers can include all tags, only selected tag keys, or all tags except selected keys. It is supported for metric, composite, and log alarms.

Tags in actions and events for CloudWatch Alarms are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon CloudWatch is available except Middle East (UAE), and Middle East (Bahrain).

To get started, see  Alarm tags in action payloads  in the Amazon CloudWatch User Guide. To learn more about Amazon CloudWatch Alarms, visit the  Amazon CloudWatch  product page.

title: Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey now supports online migration with zero downtime
description:
Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey now supports online migration from self-managed Valkey and Redis OSS on Amazon EC2 with zero downtime. Zero downtime means zero Errors returned to the client during migration, measured the same way the ElastiCache SLA measures availability. Your application continues reading and writing through cutover, and you do not need third-party replication tools.

Online migration runs in three steps. You prepare the migration, start the data sync, and complete the cutover. ElastiCache gives you a migration endpoint your application can point to when you prepare the migration, and data replicates continuously from your source once you start the sync. You choose when writes move to the serverless cache, with a manual cutover or an automatic one once your data is in sync. ElastiCache records each step as an event on the cache’s Events tab, with the reason for any failed step.

Online migration connects to your source using encryption in transit (TLS) and authentication, and reads credentials from AWS Secrets Manager, so your existing security controls stay in place. Online migration supports self-managed caches in cluster mode on Amazon EC2 running Redis OSS 4.0 through 7.2 or Valkey 7.2 through 8.1, and you can migrate them straight to Valkey 9.0.

Migration usage is free for the first 180 days per AWS account, starting when the account first prepares a migration. After that, you pay per node-hour for the migration nodes that ElastiCache runs to replicate your data, for as long as a migration is active. The ElastiCache Serverless cache is billed separately at standard data storage and ECPU rates, including during the free period. For pricing details, see Amazon ElastiCache pricing. Online migration is available in all commercial AWS Regions, the China Regions, and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. 

To get started, create or select an empty ElastiCache Serverless cache to migrate into, then start the migration from the ElastiCache console or the AWS CLI. To learn more, see the documentation.

title: FOSSASIA PGDay 2027: Bangkok, 9 March – CFP Open
description:
We are happy to announce that FOSSASIA PGDay returns to Thailand on 9 March, 2027, bringing the PostgreSQL community together at True Digital Park, Bangkok. Visit the PGDay website for more details.

About Event

FOSSASIA PGDay is an annual gathering for PostgreSQL users, developers, and enthusiasts, bringing together the community from across Asia and beyond. Co-located with the FOSSASIA Summit, the event provides a focused forum for sharing knowledge, practical experiences, and insights into PostgreSQL and its growing ecosystem. Previous editions have taken place in Singapore, Vietnam, Thailand, and Indonesia, connecting local communities with contributors, users, and organizations from around the world.

FOSSASIA PGDay highlights PostgreSQL in real-world applications and its role as a scalable, secure, and cost-effective open-source data platform. It also creates opportunities to build connections within the PostgreSQL community and the wider open-source ecosystem.

Call for Proposals

The CFP is open until November 30, 2026. Slots are limited, so early submissions are encouraged. 👉 Submit your proposal here

Key Topics

FOSSASIA PGDay features a single-track program, giving all participants the opportunity to follow the same talks and discussions throughout the day. Following the technical program, a social event will provide an opportunity for community networking, informal discussions, and collaboration in Bangkok.

We welcome proposals on topics including:

  • PostgreSQL development and administration
  • Performance, scaling, and high availability
  • Security and reliability
  • Cloud, containers, and infrastructure
  • Data engineering and analytics
  • Extensions and ecosystem tools
  • Migration and modernization
  • Real-world deployments and case studies
  • PostgreSQL community and adoption

Call for Sponsors

PGDay is made possible through the support of sponsors. We invite you to share the prospectus with your company or contacts. For questions or to discuss sponsorship opportunities, please feel free to get in touch. 👉 View the Sponsorship Prospectus

title: RHEL 10.0 and 9.6 repositories are being retired
description:
The RHEL 10.0 and RHEL 9.6 repositories are being retired from the main PostgreSQL RPM repository, and are moved to the PostgreSQL YUM archive .

All PostgreSQL major versions that were built for these minor releases are available there, including PostgreSQL 18.

The rolling EL-10 and EL-9 repository RPMs are not affected.

If you are still on RHEL 10.0 or 9.6 (or on Rocky Linux / AlmaLinux 10.0 or 9.6), please either update to a newer minor release, or use the archive. The archived repositories section of the repository packages page generates the repository file and the install commands for each distribution version, architecture and PostgreSQL version:

https://yum.postgresql.org/repopackages/#archivedrepos

Please note that these repos will not receive further updates.

If you have any questions, please either email to pgsql-pkg-yum@lists.postgresql.org, or create a ticket at our issue tracker .
